Ukraine’s top artillery maker warns of production halt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:02:14 UTC
21:02:14 KST

- KZVV, maker of 70% of Ukraine's artillery, says it has had no state order for nine months and may halt production.
- The company confirmed a €750 million ($871 million) German contract for 200 Bohdana howitzers, deliveries scheduled for 2027.
Ukraine’s Kramatorsk Heavy Machine-Tool Building Plant, the maker of the Bohdana self-propelled howitzer, says it has not received a state order in nine months and may have to halt production and furlough workers if a new contract does not arrive soon, the company’s representative told Oboronka in an interview published September 3.
The plant, known by its Ukrainian acronym KZVV, said Bohdana systems now make up about 70% of Ukraine’s artillery, with more than 1,000 guns produced since the war began. Even if a new government contract arrives immediately, the company said it would still need to partially pause production for several months while it orders components, since preparing materials for a new batch takes roughly six months on its own.
KZVV representatives said the plant currently prices the self-propelled Bohdana at €2.5 million ($2.9 million) and the towed version at €1.6 million ($1.9 million). A new gun carriage in development, intended to replace Soviet-era Hyatsint carriages currently used on the towed version, will raise that price to roughly €1.8 million ($2.1 million) once it enters service, according to the company. KZVV said it plans to codify and unveil the new carriage in the coming months.
The company separately confirmed a German order for 200 Bohdana howitzers mounted on Mercedes truck chassis, a variant it calls Marta, worth €750 million ($871 million). KZVV said the Marta uses a shorter, 39-caliber barrel and is intended to replace shorter-barreled Western 155mm systems that Ukraine has found expensive to maintain, along with remaining Soviet-era 122mm and 152mm guns. Deliveries under the German contract are scheduled for 2027, the company said.
KZVV also confirmed it has localized production of the British 105mm L-119 howitzer in partnership with BAE Systems, a lightweight gun weighing 1.9 tons that the company said can be moved into forward positions using ground robotic platforms. The company said it is still waiting for Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense to decide whether it will order the weapon.
“We think it’s needed,” a KZVV representative said of the L-119.
The plant said it can manufacture gun barrels ranging from 25mm to 203mm and currently produces barrels in 25mm, 35mm, 40mm, 105mm, 122mm, 125mm and 155mm calibers, depending on government orders. KZVV has also supplied replacement barrels to BAE Systems for British-origin artillery systems used by Ukraine, including the M777, AS-90, L119, FH-70, Krab and Archer howitzers, as well as the Tridon air defense system.
On ammunition, KZVV said it now produces 155mm long-range, medium-range and short-range shells, but that Ukraine still lacks domestic production of gun propellant, forcing continued reliance on imported powder. The company estimated that building a facility capable of producing nitroglycerin, nitrocellulose and propellant for long-range shells, at a capacity of 8,000 tons annually, enough for just under 1 million long-range rounds a year, would cost about €800 million ($929 million).
KZVV said the plant currently operates across 20 sites, including in two countries outside Ukraine, employing about 7,000 people, 85% of whom relocated from eastern Ukraine. The company said it evacuated roughly 50,000 tons of equipment out of Kramatorsk during the war’s early months under Russian missile fire, a relocation effort that took 150 people 14 months to complete.

Why personal-guarantor recoveries are so tiny — and why Chandra’s was tinier still
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:01:43 UTC
21:01:43 KST

Subhash Chandra’s proposed repayment of a little over Rs 6 crore against more than Rs 22,000 crore of admitted claims worked out to less than 0.03%.That looks exceptionally small. And it was. But personal-guarantor insolvency cases have produced very low recoveries more generally.Data from the insolvency regulator shows that nearly 5,200 applications have been filed against personal guarantors since the process came into force in 2019-20. Only around 64 have so far ended in repayment plans approved by creditors and the tribunal. Across those cases, lenders recovered a little under Rs 235 crore — roughly 1% of their admitted claims.So the larger problem is not specific to Chandra — on September 1, a specially constituted five-member bench of the NCLT stayed the order approving it anyway — but that the amount a person guarantees can be very different from what is actually available by the time lenders try to collect.A personal guarantee creates a liability. It does not, by itself, preserve the wealth behind that liability.When lenders take a guarantee, they can look at the guarantor’s assets, liabilities, credit history and other guarantees already given. But unless specific property is separately pledged or mortgaged, those assets are not locked away for the lender.But years can pass between a loan being made and a guarantee being invoked.
In the meantime, assets can fall in value, be sold, be pledged elsewhere or be used to meet other liabilities.Chandra’s case shows how large that gap can become. Net-worth certificates submitted to banks in 2017 and 2018 put his worth at more than Rs 40,000 crore. During the insolvency proceedings, he said his assets were worth a little under Rs 32 crore, most of them already mortgaged, leaving around Rs 6.5 crore.(Chandra has disputed the earlier figure, saying it did not represent what he personally owned.)If the problem is that the wealth behind the guarantee can disappear or become unavailable, one way to make guarantees more useful is to make sure some of that wealth remains in place.Lenders can, for instance, require a guarantor to maintain a minimum net worth or a minimum amount of liquid assets while the loan is outstanding. Such covenants are used elsewhere. One US guarantee filed with the securities regulator required the guarantors to maintain at least $90 million in net worth and $8 million in liquid assets, and restricted transfers that would take them below those levels.Another option is to back the guarantee with a specific asset. A house, for instance, can be mortgaged against the guarantee. India already allows this, and such arrangements give lenders something more concrete than a general promise backed by whatever assets happen to remain later.
There is also the question of finding those assets once insolvency begins. Rules introduced in 2026 widened the disclosures that can be sought from personal guarantors to include assets held through nominees, trusts and companies, as well as assets they control or benefit from without formally owning them. Another rule allows certain undervalued transactions intended to put assets beyond creditors’ reach to be reversed.None of these measures can ensure full recovery. A guarantor can still genuinely lose wealth.But they can narrow the gap between what a guarantee appears to be worth when a loan is made and what lenders find when they finally try to enforce it.Get the full storyhere on TOI+Why did the government drag personal guarantors into insolvency at all? Not just to recover more — but to make corporate borrowing harder to shrug off
Does it work? A personal guarantor was once facing claims of over Rs 330 crore. She offered … Rs 1 lakh
How much can a personal guarantee really expose you to? In law, potentially the whole unpaid debt

====================================================================================================

The surprising reason our memories become blurred as we age, according to new neuroscience research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:52 UTC
21:00:52 KST

As people get older, their brains may shift how they process and store complex memories, moving from accurately recreating specific past events to blending them into broad, inaccurate categories. This change in brain function helps explain why older adults often experience memory errors in everyday life. The findings were published in the Cerebral Cortex.
The hippocampus is a small, seahorse-shaped structure located deep within the brain that is essential for learning and memory. It helps form episodic memories, which involve linking together the specific details of a past event. A 2016 study demonstrated that the hippocampus helps retrieve these memories by re-creating the precise neural activity patterns that were present when the event was first experienced.
These neural patterns are thought to be strengthened over time after learning, a process known as memory consolidation. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that sleep, compared to wakefulness, helps consolidate weakly formed associations, binding different elements of an event together. However, as people grow older, this memory-binding process often becomes less precise.
Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a brain-scanning technique that measures neural activity by tracking changes in blood flow, scientists have recently made strides in observing this hidden phase.
“Over the past decade, research in young adults has revealed consistent evidence that we can use fMRI to understand memory storage processes (called consolidation),” said study author Ian M. McDonough, an associate professor of psychology at Binghamton University. “This is exciting because the storage process has been well validated in animals, but previously unreachable in humans, making it more theoretical and inferred than actually measurable. Given that I do aging research, I thought that this new ability to test this consolidation stage might help us understand why memory declines in old age.”
Instead of failing to link information, older adults sometimes associate too many unrelated details. A 2024 review suggested that older adults tend to form excessive, unintended associations, leading to memory confusion.
“Memory for specific associations (e.g., faces and names) we have are not simply more likely to be forgotten as we get older, but instead we are more likely to confuse the associations with other associations,” McDonough explained. “These memory confusions start in middle-age and are partially due to changes in how our memory center of the brain (the hippocampus) works.”
The authors of the new study wanted to see how the brain’s replay of information shifts across the adult lifespan, tracking how memory patterns change from the moment something is learned to when it is recalled.
“A lot of studies investigating brain function focus on one stage of the memory process (learning, storage, or retrieval),” McDonough said. “More studies are needed like this one that take a holistic perspective and attempt to integrate brain measures across these stages because they are not independent.”
For the new study, McDonough and his co-author, Destaw B. Mekbib, recruited 61 adults separated into three age groups. The sample included 17 younger adults aged 18 to 30, 21 middle-aged adults aged 50 to 60, and 23 older adults aged 61 to 74. The participants underwent fMRI scanning to observe their brain activity during the experiment.
While in the scanner, participants completed a memory task that began with a learning phase. They viewed 64 visual pairings, each featuring a neutral human face presented alongside either an everyday object or a scene. Following this learning period, the participants rested quietly with their eyes closed for five minutes while the scanner recorded their baseline brain activity.
Finally, the participants completed a memory test. They were shown the previously studied faces and asked to select the correct associated object or scene from four different options. The researchers analyzed the data to see how closely the brain activity patterns in the hippocampus matched across the three phases: learning, resting, and remembering.
The results showed a decline in memory accuracy as age increased. Younger adults correctly identified the matching pairs 36 percent of the time, while middle-aged adults answered correctly 24 percent of the time, and older adults scored 20 percent. Forgetting rates, defined as failing to make any choice before the time ran out, did not differ significantly among the three age groups.
When looking at the brain scans, the researchers found that hippocampal activity patterns generally became less stable and less consistent with increasing age. In younger adults, a high degree of similarity in brain patterns between the learning phase and the memory test predicted better overall accuracy and less forgetting. This suggests that their brains were successfully reinstating the specific details of the initial experience.
For older adults, this relationship took a different form. High pattern similarity across the memory phases actually predicted an increase in a specific type of mistake. Older adults with closely matching brain patterns across the learning, resting, and testing phases were more prone to category-level errors, such as mistakenly selecting a scene when the correct answer was an object.
“We expected that as people age, they would simply show ‘less’ of the same brain patterns that young adults show,” McDonough said. “Instead, we found that the same ‘helpful’ brain patterns linked with accurate memory in young adults were associated with memory confusions in older age. That is, those ‘helpful’ brain patterns in young were now ‘harmful’ brain patterns in older adults rather than older adults simply showing fewer of the ‘helpful’ brain patterns.”
The data also highlighted the distinct neural profile of middle age. “One misinterpretation is that although episodic memory does start to decline in middle-age, the brain patterns we found were not the same in middle and old age,” McDonough noted. “Middle-age sits in between the two age bands, which means that when young adults show positive relationships between the hippocampal patterns and memory, older adults show negative relationships, then middle-age doesn’t always show much of a relationship. So this means the brain patterns in middle-aged adults don’t look like younger or older adults exactly.”
These findings suggest that as people age, the brain may shift from replaying precise, detailed memories to replaying broader, overlapping information. The researchers tested whether physical shrinkage of the hippocampus could explain these changes, but factoring in hippocampal volume did not alter the results. The memory errors were driven by how the brain functioned and organized information across the different memory phases, rather than just the physical size of the brain region.
While these functional brain changes help explain memory decline, they are only part of the puzzle. “Although we found strong declines in episodic memory with age (which replicated decades of studies in this area), the brain effects were modest,” McDonough told PsyPost. “We explained about 30% of that age decline in memory accuracy, leaving a lot left to figure out.”
The results align with a 2016 study covered by PsyPost, which indicated that older age is associated with a progressive loss of cohesive, coordinated brain activity during memory tasks. While that earlier research measured whole-brain network synchronization, the new study examined fine-grained representational stability within the hippocampus, assessing how consistently the brain reproduces the precise patterns of neural activity that code for a specific piece of information. The findings are also in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025 showing that aging degrades the precision of brain representations during learning.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study focused almost exclusively on the hippocampus, but memory relies on a broad network of interconnected brain regions. Future research will need to explore how other areas, such as the outer layers of the brain known as the cortex, contribute to these memory transformations.
Additionally, overlapping brain patterns do not exclusively indicate that a memory is being replayed. Similar brain activity could also reflect general similarities in how a person is paying attention or processing visual information during different parts of the experiment. The participant sample also lacked individuals between the ages of 31 and 49, meaning the researchers could not map a continuous, year-by-year trajectory of how these brain changes unfold across the entire adult lifespan.
These results also require broader confirmation. “One large caveat is that the brain patterns in middle-age and older adults need to be replicated in a separate group of people,” McDonough said.
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to explore ways to actively improve memory storage. These future approaches might include neurofeedback, which teaches people to voluntarily regulate their brain activity by showing them real-time readouts of their brainwaves, or neurostimulation, which applies mild electrical or magnetic pulses to stimulate targeted areas of the brain.
“Our long-term goals are to keep understanding how the brain prioritizes information during the memory storage phase and how we can leverage existing tools to change the brain during this phase to enhance memory,” McDonough said. “We are particularly interested in neurofeedback and neurostimulation techniques as a way to directly modify brain activity to enhance memory in old age.”
The study, “Aging shifts hippocampal reactivation from selective reinstatement to category-level misbinding during episodic memory,” was authored by Destaw B. Mekbib and Ian M. McDonough.

In 2016, Trump pledged to erase the federal debt. It just hit $40tn | Steven Greenhouse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:30 UTC
21:00:30 KST

Dear reader, I recognize that your eyes might glaze over at any mention of the nation’s $40tn federal debt. But your reaction to this mind-boggling number shouldn’t be ennui; it should be outrage and dismay.
Outrage is in order because the nation’s debt has climbed to more than $40tn under Donald Trump, even though back in 2016, when the debt was less than half what it is today, candidate Trump insisted that he’d totally eliminate the debt within eight years. That was yet another example of the Demagogue-in-Chief’s willingness to say anything, no matter how insincere or untrue, to woo voters.
Not only has Trump failed to reduce the debt, he has spectacularly increased it. Take Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” and the huge tax cuts it lavished upon the very rich and corporations. That legislation is expected to increase the nation’s debt by a whopping $3.4tn over the next decade. Worse, during Trump’s time as president, including his first term, the federal debt has climbed by a colossal $11.6tn.
Outrage is also in order because the trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis that is squeezing so many Americans. Those trillions could have gone to creating more affordable childcare for every family or increasing subsidies to hold down soaring healthcare premiums or expanding government aid to make college more affordable.
Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and the $40tn debt have worsened the affordability crisis in one important and painful way. They have helped push up long-term interest rates to their highest level in nearly two decades, and that has pushed up mortgage rates, too. The unhappy result: housing has become less affordable, when housing affordability has already been a big problem for young Americans. Higher mortgage rates often mean that homebuyers have to pay several hundred dollars more in interest each month.
Interest rates have climbed not only because investors are dismayed that the national debt has hit a record, but also because Trump’s tariffs and war against Iran have fueled inflation and because investors are unsettled by all the chaos Trump has created at home and abroad.
Outrage is also called for because of the way Trump and his Republican yes-men in Congress jumped to enact giant tax cuts when their super-wealthy donors and friends said jump. In a move that shows how rigged the system is, Trump and the GOP legislated these tax cuts for the rich and corporations even though the wealthy and corporations were already doing perfectly well and would continue doing just fine, with their mansions, yachts and private jets, even without those tax cuts. Of the $4.4tn in tax cuts in the “big, beautiful bill”, nearly half go to the richest 5% of Americans.
If any further evidence is needed to show that Republicans in Congress have sold their souls to billionaires, millionaires and corporations, the increased debt caused by the big, unbeautiful bill’s tax cuts will be a burden on our children and grandchildren for decades to come. By the mid-2030s, the nation will have to pay more than $2tn in interest payments each year to finance the federal debt. That’s double the $1tn a year we are paying now – $1tn is slightly less than what the government spends on Medicare, is higher than this year’s Pentagon budget and is more than five times what the federal government spends on education each year.
All this is maddening for another reason. In recent decades, Republicans held themselves out as the party of “fiscal responsibility”. But they’ve really become the party of fiscal irresponsibility. During George W Bush’s two terms, with his tax cuts tilted toward the wealthy and his expensive, ill-fated war against Iraq, the federal debt ballooned by 85% (by $4.9tn). In Trump’s first term, the debt soared by $7.8tn (a 39% increase), stemming from his initial big tax cuts for the rich as well as increased Pentagon spending – and then there was more than $2tn in emergency spending to stabilize the economy during the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic.
During Trump’s second term, the debt is likely to soar by nearly $8tn once again. Trump is pushing for a record $1.5tn annual defense budget, far higher than any previous year, even though it will send our country’s debt further into the stratosphere. Some of that money will go to redesigning aircraft carriers merely because Trump dislikes how the current ones look.
Bill Clinton was the last president to have an annual budget surplus, but Democratic presidents have also pushed up the federal debt. During Biden’s four years as president, the debt rose $8.4tn, partly because of the annual budget deficits he inherited from Trump and partly because of his $2tn-plus pandemic-era emergency spending package to stabilize families’ finances and ensure the US didn’t sink into a deep economic downturn.
The federal debt has grown even larger than the country’s overall gross domestic product. Indeed, the ratio of the debt to GDP will soon be higher than the record 106% where it stood when the second world war ended. Franklin D Roosevelt ran up huge debts for an urgent reason: to defeat Nazi Germany and its allies. In sharp contrast, under Trump, the US is running big deficits, of approximately $2tn a year, for the opposite of urgent reasons: to finance a disastrous war in Iran and to give big tax giveaways to two powerful groups that were already prospering, eg the ultra-wealthy and corporations.
It would be a very different thing if Trump were borrowing money to build a better future, as people do to build a new house or pay for college. But Trump is not jacking up the country’s debt to improve our future; he’s not spending to improve education, childcare or our country’s infrastructure or to fix the housing crisis.
I am not a fiscal conservative and nor are many Democrats, but it is a real concern that for the first time in US history, other countries and many investors seem truly worried about the record size of the federal debt. Those worries have spooked financial markets and pushed up interest rates.
As the midterm elections heat up, the Democrats should attack Trump and the Republicans over the huge, fast-growing federal debt. Democrats need to make clear that Republicans have become the party of fiscal irresponsibility.
We can agree that the $40tn debt isn’t a sexy issue, but the Democrats can and should turn it into a hard-hitting and winning campaign issue that they can use to hammer Trump and the Republicans, along with the affordability crisis and Trump’s calamitous war against Iran.
- 
  Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:29 UTC
21:00:29 KST

Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country.
In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family to Argentina.
There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire to wait out the apocalypse.
But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations.
Last week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.
“None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party.
Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive.
The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered.
One of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract.
Another, which failed, aimed to eliminate most of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina. A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services.
There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access.
In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests.
The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasingly pointed questions about whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered.
The land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversial Próspera development in Honduras – that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control.
“Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”.
Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”.
It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, who predicted in 2024 that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities.
Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera.
“But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.”
Thiel was approached for comment.

Are there any drinkable canned cocktails?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:29 UTC
21:00:29 KST

For somebody whose children recently learned how to crack open a tinnie, this week’s tasting was a perilous one. Cans covered in seductive, brightly coloured pictures of parasols, palm trees and their favourite fruits filled the kitchen, and both the seven- and the five-year-old tried to take a swig. Premix cocktails are disproportionately marketed to young drinkers – gateway booze, if you will, as the likes of Bacardi Breezer pineapple was for me – and often have a one-note, cloying taste. Absolut’s passionfruit martini and Malibu’s piña colada are cases in point: both have sugary, synthetic fruit flavours that mask, or even eliminate, the taste of the base spirits. Is it any wonder that, in 2024, Britain had the worst rate of child alcohol consumption in the world? These drinks make it easy to forget that you’re even drinking alcohol.
Perhaps more than any other theme, writing about premix cocktails has made me confront the very question of why we drink alcohol. Take me as an example. My Bacardi Breezer years were undoubtedly a question of booze for function; it loosened my teenage inhibitions and I had a laugh. The fact that this so-called “alcopop” was so saccharine chimed with my childish predilection for sweetness, and conveniently masked the flavour of the rum, which may at the time have offended my uninitiated palate. Twenty-five years on, and my palate is a different place, and I welcome the notes and nuances of a well-mixed drink. I now drink alcohol to savour it, and I like what I’m drinking to give me pause; it doesn’t need to be hard work, but I do like it to make me think.
That’s not to say there aren’t premix cocktails out there that can do this, and I tasted several that I found interesting. The Reina Mezcalita in today’s pick, for instance, is delicious – smoky mezcal meets zippy lime soda – and I’d happily sip it from the can in the park or, even better, from a glass rimmed with Tajìn at home.
Whitebox and Moth both produce good iterations of premix drinks (and in reassuringly small, potent formats) and are widely available in supermarkets; they feel a bit more grown up, too, both on the sugar front and because their ABVs skew higher, which you can taste (in the premix realm, quality seems to align with a higher ABV).
Marks & Spencer has the widest own-brand selection, some of them better than others, but, on the whole, its premium Served range has more character and acidity (a good thing) than you’ll find elsewhere – I enjoyed the mojito and the lychee martini especially.
Spritz cocktails, meanwhile, work particularly well in cans. M&S’s limoncello one is a crowdpleaser, while Aperol Spritz To Go is everything you want and need it to be: a failsafe, bittersweet symphony.
Five canned cocktails worth cracking open
Whitebox Cosmo £5 (100ml) Ocado, 16.8%. Vodka, cranberry, lime and triple sec: cosmopolitans are making a comeback, and this one has me here for it.
Reina Mezcalita £4.99 (200ml) Mex Grocer, 10%. A smoky, citrussy delight, and my favourite of the lot.
M&S Served Mojito £3.35 (250ml) Ocado, 8%. Unlike this store’s cheaper premixes, this one has some complexity. Rum, mint and lime.
Aperol Spritz To Go £3 (250ml) Waitrose, 5%. Inarguably good and utterly dependable. Literally does what it says on the tin.
Moth Mango Margarita £4.15 (125ml) Waitrose, 14.9%. Ripe mangoes meet Tequila Enemigo and triple sec: 100% toothsome.

Labor shuts down course linked to student visa misuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:00:11 KST

Labor shuts down course linked to student visa misuse
In short:
The federal government is preventing new enrolments in a graduate diploma it fears is being used by non-genuine international students to switch courses and prolong their stay in Australia.
The move is the first use of new course-cancellation powers designed to protect the integrity of the international education system.
What's next?
Existing students can finish the diploma, but providers will be prevented from recruiting or commencing new students.
A graduate diploma used as a vehicle for international students to remain in Australia will be effectively shut down under the federal government's first use of new cancellation powers.
Transfers into the Graduate Diploma of Management (Learning) have surged in recent years, with the government concerned students are using it to maintain their visa status rather than for genuine study.
The VET course crackdown is part of a broader effort to improve the quality of the international education sector and comes as the government is looking to slow migration arrivals.
Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill said Labor was acting to ensure Australia remained a "trusted global education destination" to protect students and "prevent misuse of the visa system".
"Australia continues to welcome genuine international students seeking a premium education and must maintain a ruthless focus on quality, integrity and a great student experience," he said.
Mr Hill accused the previous Coalition government of leaving a "shocking mess" with unsustainably high growth in the "least reputable" parts of the international education sector.
Earlier this year, Mr Hill imposed a 12-month freeze on private colleges and training organisations applying to offer new courses to international students, which he said would give the national regulator more time to investigate concerns about poor quality providers.
High transfer rate sparked concern about diploma
The cancellation of the management diploma was sparked by concerns around the large volume of international students who were already in Australia switching into the course.
Transfers jumped from 510 people in 2020 to 4,000 in 2025, with 77 per cent of the students switching to the diploma coming from elsewhere in higher education.
It meant students could switch into the course without necessarily needing a new student visa application.
Almost half of the people approved to enrol in the diploma did not commence in 2025, while completion rates were significantly below other VET courses.
There are 452 VET providers registered to deliver the course to international students with 41,033 active confirmed enrolments, including 15,772 students recorded as currently studying.
Students who have already started will be able to complete their studies; however, VET providers and education agents are prohibited from recruiting more international students.
Labor using visa regulation to slow migration intake
The government has been increasingly turning to regulatory and administrative levers to slow visas and new arrivals as it tries to bring net overseas migration (NOM) down.
NOM is running at about 300,000 a year, but Labor wants to get it back toward its forecast of 225,000 by 2028.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has changed visa processing priorities to favour skilled migrants already in Australia, effectively slowing applications from offshore workers.
Backpacker visas have also been slowed for applicants from 24 countries.
Mr Burke appeared to leave the door open to changing working holiday visa arrangements for British backpackers, before Prime Minister Anthony Albanese ruled them out.
Mr Albanese said the government would "continue to honour" the existing arrangements outlined in the Australia-UK free trade agreement.
The ABC has also previously reported the federal cabinet was considering stripping work rights from people whose protection claims had been rejected.
The number of people on bridging visas has risen from 130,450 in 2017 to 413,000 in 2026.
There was also a short-lived possibility Labor would cut Australia's humanitarian intake from 20,000 back toward the previous baseline of 13,750, but Mr Albanese has since guaranteed this would not occur.

Chinese military’s AI attack chain lags foreign models: researchers
PLA focuses largely on support functions while offensive combat uses are exploratory, says paper that drew heavily on US military analysis
China’s military AI models trail their foreign equivalents in performance, concentrating on support functions rather than combat, according to a study by Chinese researchers.
The findings appeared in a paper by researchers affiliated with the Armed Police Force Shandong Corps and the Engineering University of People’s Armed Police, published in the journal Defence Industry Conversion in China in July.
“The military’s AI applications are mainly used in auxiliary fields such as intelligent question-answering and content generation,” the authors wrote.
“They still lag considerably behind foreign large language models in performance, while offensive applications in actual combat remain at an exploratory stage, with relatively limited theoretical and empirical research.”
The paper comes as AI moves from an emerging military technology to a core component of the strategic competition between the United States and China, with both militaries exploring the use of artificial intelligence to sharpen command and control.

How 9/11 Shaped My Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

Twenty-five years later, Sept. 11 remains a watershed moment, one with both personal and global implications. To mark the anniversary, TIME spoke to people with very different connections to the day, to hear about what they experienced at the time as well as the ripple effects. For some, the legacy of the date is one of profound loss. Others know about the tragedy mostly from history class. One thing is clear: The attacks that changed the world also changed lives.
I was 4½ when my dad died. I have only brief memories of that day. I remember my mom taking my twin brother and me out of preschool. I remember watching the TV at home and then going over to one of her friends’, whose husband was also a firefighter, and watching it there. We were so young, we didn’t really grasp what was actually going on. But as you get older, you start to realize what you’ve missed out on. It’s not quite the same as being sad because you miss someone close to you. It’s more like you’re sad because you didn’t really get to be close to them.
My dad was a cop for 12 years and a firefighter for only 18 months, but joining the FDNY was always his plan. For as long as I can remember, I also wanted to be a firefighter. I did the entry exam when I was 18, even though they don’t take anyone until 21. I went to college, but I think I was just killing time. I dropped out after two years, as the process ramped up. My mom kept encouraging me to consider other things, but she knew I had put all my eggs in that basket. I loved the routine and discipline of the academy, and I really tried to earn my spot; I didn’t want to feel like I was getting special treatment.
A lot of things about the fire department don’t change, and I remember thinking my dad might have stood right where I was standing, worrying about getting yelled at by some drill instructor for having a button undone. I don’t have many shared memories with him, but that came close. He worked in Brooklyn, just on the other side of the tunnel from the World Trade Center. I wanted to go to a different firehouse, to let the guys make up their mind about me without having known his reputation, so I’m in the Bronx. The firefighters I meet that knew him, I feel like they're happy to see that I'm on the job.
On 9/11 I usually go to Mass at my firehouse and then drop by Ladder 101, where Dad worked. Last year for the first time I met someone who was actually riding that day, and he gave me the full rundown. They were staged at the mouth of the tunnel right under the towers, and as they sat there on the rigs, they watched the second plane come in. They could feel the impact and then they went straight in. From what I understand, his group went up a way, came back down, and were in the lobby when the building collapsed.
Dad was also a lifeguard at Overlook Beach in Long Island, and the lifeguards there put up a little memorial for him. My mom is not big on going to the firehouse or the ceremonies in the city on the anniversaries. I think it’s just too overwhelming. So we do a more casual gathering in the afternoon. It’s less somber, more a reason for everyone to just get together.
Sometimes the attention that comes with being a legacy firefighter is uncomfortable, but not for the reasons you might think. I don’t have trouble talking about it; it was something that happened when I was young, but I had a happy childhood and a very fortunate life. I’m not looking for sympathy—I feel lucky to have had that role model of selflessness and self-sacrifice. On the other hand, I do miss having had a real relationship with my dad.
Do I wish he was still alive? Of course. I sometimes wonder if I’d be different if I’d known my dad. But that event shaped my way of thinking and shaped me. I’m very proud of what he did, and I think it’s a very admirable and honorable way to die. And I wouldn’t want someone else to have been in his place because I don’t think that’s what he would have wanted. –As told to Belinda Luscombe
Kelsey Griffin
My journey of becoming a pilot started when I was 14, when I went to a youth summer camp sponsored by the Organization of Black Aerospace Professionals (OBAP). When I first told my parents that I wanted to be a pilot, of course they were a little bit concerned about the dangers that come with flight training at a young age, but they were also very supportive.
I took my first discovery flight with an instructor in 2022. At first I was definitely nervous, because there was so much going on in the plane at once. But once we were at around 2,000 feet, everything became incredibly peaceful. Looking down at the scenery gave me a sense of freedom that I never really experienced anywhere else. I knew at a young age that I never wanted to work a traditional nine-to-five job. I was also really big on traveling, and that discovery flight showed me that being a pilot was something I could do every day and enjoy. I took my first solo fight in 2024.
Flight training is expensive, but my parents made sacrifices to support me financially as I sought out scholarships and opportunities. I was drawn to the LeRoy W. Homer Jr. Foundation Scholarship, because of their mission to empower future aviators. He was an African American pilot, and a first officer for United Airlines on Flight 93. I wasn’t alive when 9/11 happened, so my understanding comes from learning about it through documentaries and conversations with my parents and grandparents and others.
The tragedies definitely impacted not only the lives of everyday people, but also caused major disruption in the aviation industry. When my mentor just started his career as a pilot, he got furloughed soon after 9/11 because the airline industry was completely devastated over Americans’ fear of flying. I have a family member that is still afraid to fly on aircrafts.
Before I went to college, I became a private pilot and a licensed drone pilot. I briefly stopped my training after one of my friends passed away, but getting the scholarship lifted my spirits and gave me an extra push to continue my goal. The scholarship exists because of somebody who lived with courage, professionalism, and commitment to serving others. Knowing that I’m representing his legacy motivates me to work harder and fly with integrity, and never take opportunities for granted.
At Middle Georgia State University, I'm enrolled in aviation courses to finish out my remaining ratings and license and also to, as we call it in the industry, time build. I have to get at least 1,000 flight hours before I can go to a regional airline. It will probably take me about six more years of training to become a major airline pilot. African American women make up less than 1% of professional pilots in the U.S. I have had the privilege of connecting with several of them through organizations such as Sisters of the Skies, OBAP, Aviation Career Enrichment, Pink STEM, and Youth in Aviation. Having this support gives me a sense of comfort and understanding that through hard work, I can also achieve it. –As told to Philip Wang
Alka Pradhan
I was infamous as an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins for choosing classes in the afternoon so I could sleep all morning. My more diligent roommate would try to wake me so she’d have someone to talk to. On 9/11, I thought that’s what she was doing. Maybe a minute or so after she got me to the TV, the second plane hit. It was terrifying.
Even at 19, I was on track to study the intersection of human-rights law and international humanitarian law. When it became clear in early October that we, the U.S., were going to strike Afghanistan in a way that seemed not entirely targeted and seemed to conflate the Taliban with al-Qaeda, that began my interest in all this. But to me, our actions didn't seem to comply with the law of war that I had been studying. I really did not anticipate that I would eventually use my specialization to litigate as hard as I possibly could against my own government. But that is what I have done for the past 13ish years in my work at Guantánamo.
I was already working with Guantánamo detainees when, in 2015, I got a call from a friend at the Department of Defense, who said the military commissions, which are prosecuting those actually alleged to have organized the attacks on 9/11, were hiring civilians. He asked if I’d be interested in representing Ammar al-Baluchi, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed’s nephew. I thought, well, there's nothing I can do that is deeper in the heart of this morass than the military commissions, because the CIA torture programs are at the heart of these cases. So I've been a defense attorney for Ammar al-Baluchi’s 9/11 case since 2015. It has been in pretrial hearings for 14 years.
For 9/11, the actual fact allegations against al-Baluchi are that he transferred money to people who ended up being the hijackers. We have never contested the fact that he transferred money. He was in Dubai, he was asked to transfer money, he transferred money. The $10,000 question is: What did he know at the time? And the government has no evidence that is not derived from torture that indicates he had any knowledge of what was happening on Sept. 11.
The 9/11 case really is all day, every day. It is the biggest criminal case in U.S. history. I hold a top-secret security clearance, and I still don’t have all the information I need about the torture at the black sites that impacted how Ammar is today and the statements he gave later. The trial has just been scheduled for June 2028, but I don’t know if it will ever happen, and I think that is a very hard truth, particularly for the victims’ family members. Witnesses have passed away, evidence has been destroyed by the government. The men themselves are deteriorating because the U.S. refuses to give them the medical care they need as undisputed torture victims. Millions and millions of dollars have been wasted on this exercise so far. It’s the Jarndyce v Jarndyce of the United States.
However I also think this is one of the most important things I will ever do because it shows fellow Americans that this is what dissent looks like, and I know it sounds trite, but this is also what patriotism looks like. I am both grateful for and have great contempt for what the Department of Defense has done over these 25 years. On 9/11 I will reach out to the victims’ family members who I am in touch with and convey my very deep sadness and anger over what happened. I will watch the commemorations. I will contemplate. Then I will start speaking again about everything that we are continuing to do wrong. –As told to B.L.
Jukay Hsu
I was student-body president at Stuyvesant High, three blocks from the World Trade Center. I had an early meeting that day with the principal about the plans for the year. So normally I’d be walking to school when the first plane hit. We evacuated, I think, just as the first tower fell, and I remember looking through these two-story plate-glass windows at this billowing black-gray kind of fog coming from one way as we went out the other way into a sunny sky.
I grew up in Queens. My mother was a social worker. I was lucky to get full financial aid to Harvard, and signed up for ROTC, then went to Iraq. I always thought service was public service. I was a second lieutenant leading a platoon of 40 men in Salahuddin province, kind of at the mid-end of the surge. Even with combat patrols, I ended up doing a lot around civil governance because counterinsurgency involves that. It was a very different kind of learning.
When I got out of the military, all my classmates were going into tech. I was like, If New York is going to become a tech sector, how can more people be included in that? All the soldiers I worked with never went to college. That's the difference between officer and soldier. Even though my platoon sergeant was 20 years older than me, I was in charge because I went to college. It really got you thinking: All these companies and jobs and wealth are being created, but two-thirds of Americans and two-thirds of New Yorkers don’t have a four-year college degree. In 2011, I ended up creating Pursuit. Our idea was to train working-class people in the skills tech companies tell us they need. The average student arrived making $16,000 and a year later has a job paying $94,000.
I left Pursuit to start a research organization called Bright Future to focus on AI alignment for the benefit of humanity. There’s this idea that AI is going to be so dominant, so superpowerful, not just tools, but creating a being—we’re trying to create like a god, essentially, right? It's kind of crazy. So what does that mean for humans? This year I also joined the New York City Economic Development Board, which oversees and shapes AI policy.
Perhaps the future is not college versus noncollege. Perhaps it’s going to be AI and non-AI. But hopefully, there’s a way to democratize that and enable cooperation. We're creating these new digital minds, so you have to consider their power and impact. Early on in high school, it was imprinted on me that what’s most important is what happens to all of us. And the ability to have agency in that. 9/11 helped cement that. Important critical junctures really can bring out the best in humanity, if we choose to respond.
Marc Rivera
I was born in Puerto Rico but have lived all but the first three months of my life on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. Next year, it will be 50 years that I'm pastoring down here. Primitive Church is within eyeshot of the towers. On 9/11, I saw the towers fall and then didn’t set foot outside lower Manhattan until March the following year.
I had just dropped my younger son at high school a block away from the Trade Center and I was going into the church office when I saw my secretary outside. She simply says, “Look.” Sure enough, there was a gaping hole in the north tower. I could see what I thought was debris falling. Later on, I discovered it may have been people. I turned around to get my son, but the police wouldn’t let me through, so I went back to the church, and all of a sudden, a sea of people filled with soot and stuff came walking down our street. We opened the church to them. We had four landlines that were somehow still working. Eventually my son walked in with a bunch of friends, all covered in soot. My older son also arrived from midtown. That was a rebirth moment for me. I was able to shift my attention to helping the helpers and healing the healers.
By day two after the collapse, I was doing what I've always done: galvanizing people and starting to help individuals, raising money to pay people's rent and medical bills and for funerals. We established the Ground Zero Clergy Task Force, which was simply clergy of different faiths, denominations, and traditions who gathered together to help at the site and to coordinate churches with FEMA and the New York City government. Every day, anywhere from 15 to 50 clergy would meet in the sanctuary, and then go down to the hole, to ground zero, to see what we could do. About a year afterward, I established a Northeast Clergy Group, which was broader and longer-standing. It tried to run the same program for people at the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania.
We closed those organizations eventually, but through them I saw the importance of not being so rigid or immovable in my theological training. Many religious people, regardless of faith tradition, tend to think that we have the patent on truth. This event broadened my perspective and really challenged me to make that change intellectually and also in my practice. When tragedy strikes, no one cares how much training you have, how many books you have written, how large your congregation is. Because the bottom line is love. I saw a fireman who looked so tired and I asked if I could pray for him. I didn’t ask what he believed first.
The most painful consequence for me personally was that my oldest son, Tim, was diagnosed with Stage IV colorectal cancer, one of the cancers that is covered by the 9/11 fund. He fought it courageously for three years, but this September will mark one year since his passing. He would have been 46. We believe he probably got it because we live down here.
One of my greatest concerns today is that there are still people in our congregation and in this community who may qualify for assistance through the 9/11 fund that the federal government set up, but some remain reluctant to apply. They’re more afraid of the system than they are of getting sick. So, more than two decades later, part of our ministry is still helping people understand that the consequences of Sept. 11 did not end on Sept. 11. We are still caring for people. We are still encouraging people to seek the help that is available to them. And we are still learning what that terrible day taught us from the very beginning: when people are hurting, our first responsibility is to love them.
Connie Stevanus
That day, I was working at a bank, and as I went from department to department, they were bringing this up on their computers. On my way home, it’s just a two-lane country road, and there was so much traffic. Cars were passing me in either direction. They were state police cars. When I finally got home, I see my husband picking things out of the yard, and I didn’t know what he was doing until I went to pull into our driveway. It was black, totally black, with small pieces of burnt debris. And it just hit me then what I was looking at. Flight 93 carried mail. We had mail in our trees, in our yard. The neighbor across the road from us had a piece of the United Airlines magazine in her yard.
We started volunteering at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pa., after my husband had retired from work, like five years after 9/11. People come from all over—Europe, Australia, different countries. They like to tell you where they were and their experiences of that day. And then they always ask, “Where were you when this happened?” We get a lot of school students, and they're very alert to what happened here, so they're usually very quiet and very respectful. My 21-year-old grandson wasn't born yet. And when he was in eighth grade, I think it was, his school came out.
I never get tired of talking about it. Probably 99% of them still feel the pain and show their emotions easily when we're talking. Sometimes it’s a little hard to be there, because I’m that person—I might not be able to say the right thing to you, but I can cry right alongside of you. At the Visitor Center, we have those three phone messages. You know that some of the passengers on Flight 93 had to leave messages because they didn’t get an answer? Those are very powerful.
Can I share one little story with you? This was just after they were done with the excavation and the road opened up. So it was about two weeks later. My husband and I stopped there after work one evening. And it was just like the day of 9/11. Sunny, bright blue sky, not a cloud in the sky. There was nobody around, just me and my husband. We looked down through the field, and you could just see where the crash site was, the fresh soil that covered that area. And we just stood there. And all you could hear were birds, the rustling of the high grass, and just silence. And there wasn't a flag. There was nothing where you would think something like this happened. You could see the little fence that they had around the debris field. But that is a moment that I'll never forget. –As told to Karl Vick
Shams Frough
I was going into fifth grade when 9/11 happened. I remember, because it was two days after a famous Northern Alliance commander was assassinated. Obviously, there was no TV in Kabul, but our ears were wide open and we did hear about it on the radio. (From a very young age, I was listening to BBC Persian.) Then came the bombings, and life in Kabul became a bit hard, so for a short period, I went back to my village, Kapisa, which is 100 km from Kabul, where I had shepherding duties. I remember very well the big difference when we returned to school; girls were going too, and we no longer had to wear black turbans. Everybody wanted the Taliban to go, but we didn’t know that eventually all these American soldiers would come and there would be a hot war again. We all thought the Northern Alliance would take over.
My mother died when I was young, and my father really worked to make sure his children did not have to work on the farm. I went to an elite Turkish-run high school; out of 6,000 applicants, only 100 were accepted—and some of those places were reserved for the children of government ministers. Most lessons were in English, but we also learned Turkish. I wanted to go to medical school, but I was young and male and I believed the hype, and in the last year of school I began working with the U.S. Army. I was sent to Kandahar as an interpreter. After I was nearly killed twice, I was transferred to the Department of Procurements in Kabul and ended up doing simultaneous translation for colonels and generals who were advising the Afghan military and police. I reported what looked like corruption in the Afghan procurement process, and then I knew I had to leave. It took three years, until 2014—a week or so after I resigned—for my Special Immigrant Visa to be processed.
My wife and I were initially assigned to Albuquerque, N.M., which was funny, because my Army friends always made fun of the mud huts in Afghanistan and there they were in America, only it was called adobe. When we moved to Chicago, I went to community college and so I took up driving taxis and Ubers. I’d study all week and then sleep in my taxi at the airport, because there was always a three-hour wait for a fare. Then in 2021, I started a business called Kapisa Rugs; it was rebranded as Rugistan in 2024, and we directly source hand-knotted rugs from Afghanistan. It’s not easy with Amazon and other competition, so to keep prices down, I’m here seven days a week. Right now we have two locations, but this is not the goal.
I love rugs. I'll always cherish them. But hopefully, in about a year, it will be profitable enough, and my wife will have taken over and I will be able to fire myself. Some of my high school friends who didn’t join the Army are already doctors here, so I sometimes feel like I haven’t lived up to my capacity in the way I could have in Afghanistan. I am currently completing my master’s of public health at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, and I hope to start medical school in 2028. I joke with my wife that I’ll probably graduate alongside our sons. –As told to B.L.
Sari Beth Rosenberg
My first day of student teaching was supposed to be 9/11. I was 26, in grad school, planning to observe a teacher teaching U.S. history at LaGuardia High School. My alarm-clock radio played Z Morning Zoo, a show known for its goofiness, but the hosts were talking about a plane crashing into the Twin Towers and I thought, “That’s not funny.” I turned on the TV, and that’s when I was like, “Oh my, no, this is actually real.” I got a phone call from one of my best friends who worked on Canal Street near the Twin Towers, and when I saw the first tower buckle, I yelled to her, “You have to run!”
The next semester, I was placed at Stuyvesant High School by what was once the Twin Towers. The air was constantly being tested in the cafeteria. And yet 9/11 never came up in the classroom. In the years that followed, I would have students interview a friend or family member about that day as a lesson in how history is remembered, showing them that they just collected primary sources.
Nowadays, students are more clued into current events on their devices and TikTok, so they’re asking really interesting questions about 9/11, like “Why did we attack Afghanistan?” Many students don’t understand the difference between why we went into Afghanistan in the early 2000s versus Iraq. Many adults don't know the difference if they don't really pay attention to the news or recent current events. How do you understand what’s going on in Iran now if you don’t understand the history of Iraq, Iran, the Middle East?
Kids don’t talk about the fear of terrorists coming from the Middle East. The thing that kids are more scared of today is what they see as domestic terror coming from ICE agents. I’ve had to explain that ICE was created in 2003 as part of the new Department of Homeland Security, which was established in response to 9/11, and now it’s being used to, in my opinion, terrorize communities.
I’m definitely going to bring up the 25th anniversary in class this year. They were born so long after 9/11, it’s history to them. We need to find ways to cover more recent history. In a U.S. history class—or any history class—there’s so much to cover, and we don’t get to the recent history, from 1980 to the present, because it’s not emphasized on tests and also you run out of time. –As told to Olivia B. Waxman
Allison Turkel
On Sept. 11, I was outside of Albuquerque, N.M. I worked for a not-for-profit then called the National Center for Prosecution of Child Abuse, and we were running a conference. And the receptionist where we were holding it said a plane just hit the World Trade Center, and you could go into our break room to watch it on TV. I went in just in time to see the second plane hit. Luckily I was able to reach my dad, who had a meeting downtown that day. I got him right before the phones went out in New York, and then we started driving back. We looked on our map. We tried to avoid missile silos because we thought that those might be under attack or shooting things. We had no idea. I drove crying. Not the whole time, but a lot. It’s a skill.
I lived in the D.C. area at the time, but I grew up in Manhattan, up in Washington Heights. I worked down in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which was actually in the zone. So all of it translates well into how and why I’ve been the Special Master of the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund for the last 3½ years.
We want as many people as possible to know, one, we’re still here. We are in business until 2090. We have as much funding as is necessary to pay every eligible claimant. And two, we serve people beyond first responders. We serve people that lived, worked, went to school in the New York exposure zone, who were at Shanksville and at the Pentagon. We really encourage people if they were there, to register with the VCF. In order to file a claim, folks need to get certified that they have a 9/11 illness from the World Trade Center Health Program, which is our sister program that runs out of HHS. We are receiving over 700 new claims a month.
Since 2011, when we reopened, we have received over 110,000 claims. We've paid out $18.5 billion compensation. [The original VCF closed in 2004 after paying out the $7 billion appropriated for those killed or physically injured on 9/11.] The CDC estimates that in New York alone, over 400,000 people may have been exposed to the toxins.
Remember “America Strong”? “Let everybody return”? “Let's begin to live, work, go to school, start over again”? People went back into the New York zone, and the consequence, of course, is they were exposed to these toxins that have made them ill. And people have died from it. On that day, 2,977 people perished at all three sites and on the planes. Since we reopened, we’ve had 6,100 of our claimants die from exposure to the toxins. And unfortunately, every year there are more people becoming ill. Today, 63% of our claimants have a cancer, and those cancers, because of the unique nature of what people were exposed to, may have long latency periods.
Every Sept. 11, the memorial and museum in New York City does the reading of the names of the victims, and there’s always six moments of silence, to mark the four moments of impact and two tower collapses. This year, they’re adding a seventh, to honor the people that have become ill from the toxins. I think that’ll help spread awareness that so many are still suffering and that the 9/11 VCF is here to help.
Christopher Ashley
I actually didn't behave that great that day. I almost got into a fistfight.
It was the first day of rehearsal for the play Wonder of the World, which I was directing. We canceled rehearsal for that day and the next, and I ended up walking back home to the West Village. Late that night, there was a very drunk man who put himself in front of me and asked if I was an Iraqi. He kept putting himself in front of me, and I kept trying to get away. Then he took a swing at me, and I punched him in the face.
It’s not automatic that people are their best selves in these moments. I think one of the things people do with traumatic situations is move on, so it was really meaningful to me to dig back into the feelings that that day created while directing Come From Away, a musical about 38 planes grounded in Gander, Newfoundland, and the people who took care of strangers at this moment of real terror. Telling that story around the world, onstage, on Apple TV helped me heal.
In 2011, the play’s authors, David Hein and Irene Sankoff, went to a 10th anniversary event reconvening a lot of the people who had been diverted there on 9/11. They expected to be there for a couple of days and ended up staying for weeks and weeks. Claude Elliott, the mayor of Gander, used to joke, "Wait, you guys are making a musical about making sandwiches?”
In the current world we're living in, it almost seems mythical that people would take this good care of each other because there are just so many things that pull us apart and make us suspicious of each other. We're all vulnerable. Nobody’s safely apart behind a wall. We're all going to have to figure out how to share the world and the space together. The world keeps changing, but the show remains about the responsibility we have to each other and the value of kindness and connection. Twenty-five years ago, if more people thought like the people in Gander—“these people are my problem, my responsibility, and I will take care of them, despite the fact that I didn't meet them until today”—I think we'd be in a better place. –As told to O.B.W.
Nancy Gibbs
Moments after 8:46 a.m., attention fixed on one incomprehensible event. As first responders scrambled and survivors fled, the rest of us skidded to a stop and watched.
At TIME, editor Jim Kelly launched a reporting army: correspondents around the world tracked the attacks and reactions in real time. White House correspondent Jay Carney was with President Bush in the press pool; writers and editors in the New York City headquarters headed downtown, or to city hospitals and command centers. My job was to curate and condense it all into a single story for a special issue of the magazine. “I just want you to tell the story of today,” Jim told me. “Think of it as a time capsule.”
In one sense we all saw something different. If you lived in New York City, not only did you see the smoke, you smelled it, tasted it. You heard the sirens, felt the fear. Elsewhere, the alerts jolted large towns and small. Local landmarks shivered and then shut down: Disney World and the Sears Tower, Congress and the Supreme Court, the Space Needle. Also, the entire airspace of the United States.
But at a deeper level, we all saw the same thing, a once unimaginable attack on what we soon started calling the Homeland, as though we were all residents of the same reality. No matter how different our individual experiences of that day, we lived through it together and emerged more united: By October, 60% of people said they trusted the government to do the right thing all or most of the time, a three-decade high.
It’s easier to put a jigsaw puzzle together when you can see the whole picture on the lid of the box. Yes, there were toxic rumors and conspiracies even without the yet-to-be-invented Facebook and X. But compared with what has transpired since then, the information landscape looks practically pristine. The demolition of the business model for traditional news sources corresponded with sinking institutional trust across the board. Journalism’s self-inflicted wounds and technological upheaval radically changed how people make sense of the world. Trust in government now sits around 17%. Trust in the media has hit an all-time low.
If you had told me 25 years ago, as we color-coded the threat level, cast a wide surveillance net, launched a Global War on Terror, that we would manage to avoid further terror attacks, I would have found it hard to believe. But I also couldn’t have imagined the maceration of the media as our news channels filled with content of all kinds streaming in from all corners. This year for the first time, more people globally rely on social and video platforms for news, rather than TV or news websites. As audiences migrate from broadcast and cable, print and radio, to creators on TikTok and YouTube, the very notion of a shared reality feels quaint. Eight in 10 of us say Democrats and Republicans can’t even agree on basic facts, which makes reasoned discussion of everything from security threats to education reform all but impossible.
Twenty-five years ago, like journalists everywhere, I focused on how to tell this story, in the belief that stories are stickier than bloodless fact. But what has happened since makes me wonder if I missed the actual war. Sept. 11 did not cause 21st century truth decay, but it coincided with it. Jolted out of the snug 1990s, people went searching for answers they could trust, tribes they could join, distraction as an antidote to alarm. We no longer hear the same stories and too many leaders are counting on that. We can each collect the puzzle pieces, but it's harder to see the full picture. Even when the country is broadly united around key values—reject political violence, protect the safety net, get money out of politics, regulate AI—the sense of division abides and people on both sides see mainly a caricature of their opponents.
Strong societies need good information; communities benefit from shared stories. On Sept. 11, many of those stories were of quiet, reflexive heroism, sacrifice, service. First responders and random strangers modeled courage under fire, and the rest of us were swept up in a wave of gratitude that helped drain the fear. Those are stories worth retrieving now. –Nancy Gibbs
Keira Unterzuber, Eric Johnson, and Freya Johnson
Keira: My first child was due on Sept. 3, and my doctor was going to induce me on the 13th. So the 11th was any other day, really. I was getting ready for work when my husband, who is a pilot and was home on family leave, said, “Keira, come here.” He explained that a plane had crashed in the World Trade Center, and I said, “But it's so sunny!” He's like, “Yeah, that's really weird.” And while we were watching the TV, the second plane hit. As the morning went on, I started to feel unwell. But then I don’t think anybody felt well that day.
Eric: We live near the Pentagon, and suddenly, it was like somebody pushed over a piano in the room next to us. It shook the whole house. The cats jumped off the bed and hid. I went outside and saw smoke. Sometime in there, Keira said, “I’m having the baby today.” I drove 80 to 90 miles an hour all the way  to the hospital. There was zero traffic. It was eerie, like driving somewhere in the middle of the night. 
Keira: Because of construction, we had to go through the emergency-room entrance and I remember all these emergency medical staff just waiting, and not for me. In the delivery room, Eric started to say he was ready to join the military and go fight the terrorists and because of the mood that he was in, he suggested several new names for the baby: Phoenix, America, Freedom, Liberty. I just said no, no, no. Eventually he picked Freya, who is goddess of war and love and a very strong woman. 
Freya: When I was young, I didn’t really understand the significance of the day. But around the 10th anniversary, I realized, “Oh, this is huge,” and then it became very depressing. On the morning announcements at school, they’d show a video tribute, and those videos were obviously very sad. In middle school, some kid told me that I was the reincarnation of Osama bin Laden. So I used to wish I was born on the 10th or the 12th. I actually didn’t celebrate my birthday from ages 10 to 13. It just felt inappropriate and weird to be so happy when everyone else was not. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve told people my birthday, and it becomes a whole conversation. When I need ID at a bar or when I have to pick up a prescription, and they ask me for my birthday, they’re like, “Really?” I’ve even had people ask me, “What was that like for you?” And I have to say, “Well, I was not even born yet so I was not aware of anything.” I’ve learned to just say my birthday is in September. However, as I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized that I like my birthday. It’s such a beautiful time of year. I’m at the point where I can acknowledge that it was sad, but I can also celebrate myself. All my friends tell me that when they think of 9/11, they think of me as their first thought. 
Keira: When something tragic happens, it’s a beautiful thing to be around a newborn baby. My brother’s wife lost her first husband on the 10th, and his funeral was on the 13th. She adores Freya because, in her world, she’s a bright light at a dark moment. We have a lot of friends who say that year after year: She was the shining light that day. –As told to B.L.

Malaysia's middle path between China and US faces new tests
