====================================================================================================

Gloria Steinem's Long and Revealing History With TIME
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:21:42 UTC
20:21:42 KST

Over the course of her long and influential life, Gloria Steinem went from being described in the pages of TIME as “one of the best dates to take to a New York party these days” and “smashing looking Gucci liberal” to being lauded as a “feminist icon.” If nothing else, the shift in the tone of her coverage in the magazine provides a window into the change in attitudes toward women that she helped engineer over the course of her 92-year life, which ended on Sept. 2.
Let’s add one more description to the list: durable dynamo. Steinem never outlived her ability to be relevant, inspiring several generations of women to organize and strive to be given the same opportunities as men. She never stopped blazing a trail for those who faced a particularly dense thicket and she never thought small. “I believe that things are a circle, not a hierarchy,” she said to TIME in 2011. “The kind of society we are striving toward is one in which things are linked not ranked. And one in which we understand that the women’s movement and the anti racist movement and the gay movement and the environmentalist movement, they’re all linked.”
Steinem was born on March 25, 1934, to a homemaker mother and a father with, she later said, only two points of pride: "He never wore a hat, and he never had a job. He was always going to make a movie, or cut a record, or start a new hotel, or come up with a new orange drink." She didn't spend a full year in school until she was 12, when her parents split and she ended up living with her mother, whose mental health was in a dire state, in East Toledo, Ohio. At 16, she was sent to live with an aunt in Washington. Before that, she says, "I'd never lived any place to invite anybody home to. I thought that people always ate out of refrigerators."
After graduating from Smith College in 1956, she spent two years in India on a fellowship (and also to get out of an engagement), then came home to work in Cambridge, Mass., for a group encouraging American students to attend Communist youth festivals abroad. It was later revealed to be CIA-funded, but Steinem was unfussed, saying she “was happy to use the Establishment's money against the Establishment."
In 1963, she famously published a first-person account of her glamour-free month undercover as a Playboy Bunny in Show magazine. It was her big break, and it also threatened to be her curse, since at first she almost exclusively got offered assignments along the same lines. This was the period when TIME thought it important to note an appearance in which she wore “a Luis Estevez creation that consisted of five widely spaced bands of chinchilla held together by transparent black net. In between was supposed to be little more than a bare bodkin.”
She later got hired at the fledgling New York magazine, where in 1968 her first story was about Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh’s stint as a New York City waiter and laundryman. As she steadily found her journalistic feet, she began to find her calling: to use her charm, wit and platform to promote equality. Steinem understood the fear that these ideas stirred up in people. “Women don't want to exchange places with men,” she wrote in an essay for TIME in 1970, shortly after the magazine identified her as “a trim, undeniably female, blonde-streaked brunette who has been described as 'the thinking man's Jean Shrimpton.' " She went on to add: “But we do want to change the economic system to one more based on merit. In Women's Lib Utopia, there will be free access to good jobs—and decent pay for the bad ones women have been performing all along, including housework.”
Inevitably, her activism moved beyond writing to organizing. In 1971, along with Shirley Chisholm, Bella Abzug, Betty Friedan and several others, she convened the National Women's Political Caucus to try to get more women into government offices. Shortly after that she co-founded Ms. magazine, which she described as “a how-to magazine; not how to make jelly but how to seize control of your life." TIME’s writers, by this time calling her “feminism’s superstar,” finally began to acknowledge her impact. A story about the 1972 Democratic convention—titled, alas, "Eve's Operatives"—opened with: “Gazing around the convention through her blue-tinted glasses, Gloria Steinem pronounced with satisfaction: ‘We've changed the population here. It almost looks like the country. What she meant was that women are 52% of the nation's population, and last week close to 40% of the convention delegates were women—a dramatic jump over their 13% representation at the 1968 Democratic Convention.”
There was a still way to go, however—both for women and for TIME. “Decorative as the women were in their bell-bottom trousers, miniskirts, jeans and hot pants,” the magazine went on to say, “they were not there to be on display but to seek power. Except for a couple of setbacks, they got enough to satisfy and even surprise them.” After the crushing loss of Democratic Presidential Candidate George McGovern to Richard Nixon, Steinem’s political campaigning took a backseat to her advocacy work. The 1977 women’s conference, which she has called "the most important event that nobody knows about," remained one of her proudest achievements, even as it sparked a conservative backlash and perhaps the founding of the religious right.
As the decades passed, Steinem’s activism grew to encompass more than women’s equality. She campaigned on behalf of native people, was arrested while protesting apartheid, publicly opposed the first Gulf War, advocated for disarmament in Korea, spoke against child abuse, female genital mutilation and pornography, and was an early supporter of LGB rights. (It took her a little longer to endorse the transgender movement.) Her advocacy was always couched in pragmatism and compassion. She pointed out that the pedestal women were put on was "as much a prison as any small, confined space" and called her 2019 memoir The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off! Writing, her first calling, remained one of her great loves—"the only thing that, when I do it, I don't feel I should be doing something else." She published books throughout her career, many of which, including her first memoir, 1983’s Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, were bestsellers; her latest, An Unexpected Life, is due out this fall. (She often joked that she wished her books didn’t get republished so much because it would mean they were no longer relevant.)
By the '90s, Steinem had scored a TIME cover, albeit one about a pushback against feminism, after her book about female self esteem—Revolution From Within—was a bestseller. “As she tours shopping malls, Steinem is being mobbed by crowds that, according to one bookstore owner, exceed those of Oliver North and Vanna White, the backlash icons of American manhood and womanhood,” Nancy Gibbs wrote. As well as writing her own books, Steinem contributed to countless others, appeared in more than 120 films, help produce several documentaries and inspired the 2019 Off Broadway play, Gloria: A Life. She cast her gaze domestically, locally, nationally and globally, founding Equality Now, which aimed to elevate and protect the rights of girls and women internationally.
Somewhere around the turn of the century, the times—and TIME— caught up with Steinem; her ideas became mainstream and her words and activities were covered with the kind of reverence reserved for icons. In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Half a century after writing her Women's Lib Utopia essay for TIME, she annotated it, warning that women had made many advances but that the "time of greatest danger comes after a victory, and that’s where we are now." (She also noted that she found out later that she had been paid less than the men who wrote for the same issue.)
Through it all she kept one of her less acknowledged gifts intact: her sense of humor. She did not come up with the classic feminist saying that women need men like a fish needs a bicycle, but she popularized it. She was always threatening to get a back tattoo for her 70th birthday. So frequently was she asked about her beauty secret that she came up with the perfect reply: "Revolution," she would say. "It keeps you young."
In 2011, TIME asked what she would do if she only had two years to live. “It seems to me one of the uses of age is to help you know what you want to do and keep from wasting time,” she said. “And I have this unfortunate notion that I’m immortal, which doesn’t cause you to plan very well. I think it would be mainly about writing and seeing friends, my chosen family. And writing what I believe. And maybe living with elephants. I do still want to live with elephants.”

Drone Wall Rises: Ukraine Bets on Its Best Corps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:21:18 UTC
20:21:18 KST

This is not a standard review but notes of developments spotted and noted quickly over the past two weeks, and some very limited comments. Expect this format next week, then return to standard after that.
Images are not particularly linked to any news item; they just seemed eye-catching to me when I spotted them, and so I’m passing them on.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
My guess is the most significant development of the past two weeks will play out to be:
1st and 3rd Corps have been assigned the mission of holding Slovyansk and Kramatorsk against the expected Russian offensive. Both commanders are self-made generals – Denys Prokopenko (1st Azov Corps) and Andriy Biletsky (3rd Army Corps) – who rose through Azov’s ranks; in other words, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) put its first team and best players into the Donetsk region.
These are two of the AFU’s hardest-fighting corps – although, to be fair, probably the 30th Marine and 7th and 8th Airborne Assault Corps are to that level. The presence of USF brass at the outset of the planning makes crystal clear the Ukrainian intent: when Russia launches its big offensive, probably after the fall wet season, the most effective Drone Wall buzz saw will be in place to meet it. Three months is a long time to let Ukrainians prepare…
This command move was the work of Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty and President Volodymyr Zelensky and although I know it’s not fashionable to observe positive leadership by Zelensky, this is an unchallengeable example. The man clearly is pushing for a younger, more modern, and more agile AFU leadership.
Russia to Close Goethe-Institut Branches in Retaliation Against Germany
On Aug. 26 the Ukrainians ran a typical-for-them complicated air strike with all manner of moving parts and preparatory operations; it appeared to have worked and at least one Russian army HQ was blown up.
The Play-by-Play (Note: None of the images are by me, all are pulled from open sources, order of images isn’t really tied to the text)
- Aug. 15 – The Chongar railroad bridge collapses of its own accord, ending heavy rail transport between Crimea and the rest of the world. Probably the Russians will build a bypass, but for trucks. Under present circumstances, laying down new track is probably impossible because of the drones.
- Aug. 15 – Flamingo missiles hit the Progress plant in Samara twice. This is the center of Russia’s national space effort. The missiles appear to have hit a pair of production buildings that manufacture Soyuz components in hyper-sterile conditions. In one building, manufacturing lines opened to the elements include electrical equipment, instruments and printed circuit boards. The second building is final assembly. Usually, Flamingos miss or get shot down, but not this time, it seems.
- Aug. 16 – Massive fires at two Wildberries warehouses outside Moscow, 600+ drones involved in strikes
- Aug. 16 – Drones take out a Bastion launcher for hypersonics in Crimea. This is another early indicator that the Ukrainians are actively hunting Russian ballistic/hypersonic launchers because the Ukrainians are out of Patriot interceptor missiles.
- Aug. 17 – Zelensky replaced the commander of the Logistics Forces of the Ukrainian Armed Forces: Yury Pogrebnoi was appointed instead of Volodymyr Karpenko. This is another step in the overhaul of the AFU senior command. Pogrebnoi is 41 years old and comes from the Sumy region. He has served primarily in military logistics and technical support, and his prior job was deputy chief of logistics of Joint Forces East.
- Aug. 17 – Ukraine tests its first “Uravnitel” guided aerial bomb, and it is already being procured for the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Roughly, Uravnitel in Ukrainian means “equalizer.” The bomb was developed by DG Industry. It features a 250-kilogram (550-pound) warhead and is capable of striking targets at a range of up to 130 kilometers (80 miles). Keep this in mind if you decide to read through to the Aug. 26 entry. The Ukrainians say it costs three times less than the American JDAM.
- Aug. 18 – Yet another massed strike at Moscow, 600+ drones, Wildberries warehouse burned
- Aug. 18 – Fines issued in southern Russia for complaining about gasoline shortages. A court in Volgograd fined a local woman for griping about fuel station queues and outages, charging her under the article prohibiting participation in mass gatherings.
- Aug. 18 – Russian Banderole jet-powered drones hit the village of Pechenihy, Kharkiv region, 10 dead, 17 injured. The strike appears to have targeted wholly civilian structures: cafe, post office, shop, private houses.
- Aug. 19-20 – Russia launches its long-awaited “big” strike, 45 missiles of which about 12-15 are ballistic missiles. The weapons came in two waves. Kyiv was the primary target and a border checkpoint in Odesa was the secondary target. One ballistic missile destroyed the top two stories of a five-story Kyiv apartment building. As of midday Thursday the casualty count was 16 dead and 45-50 injured. As per Ukraine air force policy, no stats were published on how many ballistic missiles were intercepted; based on air war networks, the figure for that probably is somewhere between “none” and “zero.”
- Aug. 20 – Drones hit six cargo ships off Tuapse, leaving one burning seriously, four more were hit on Aug. 24-25.
- Aug. 20 – Sevastopol – Authorities announced power shortages are so bad that the city is switching to a 2/6 electricity rationing, i.e., about two hours with power and up to six hours without power. Things have been much worse outside Crimea’s cities, with some outlying villages reporting no power – not making this up – for a month so far. Sevastopol, as the administrative and imperial heart of Russian occupation of Crimea, had managed to avoid serious blackouts. Not anymore.
- Aug. 21 – Russians hit a superstore in Kryvyi Rih with a double-tap strike, ballistic missiles, 16 killed, 130+ injured.
- Aug. 22 – Ukrainian forces hits Ozon warehouse, Samara, fires.
- Aug 22 – Substantial Russian strike, 200 drones, 10–20 missiles, Odesa and Kyiv targeted, seemingly railway and rail infrastructure primarily. Odesa was the primary target: 17 Banderol missiles, four Kh-59 and Kh-31 missiles, about 10 aerial bombs.

Two Russian army command HQs in Donetsk hit, heavy damage. 51 Army commander and staff reportedly killed in underground parking lot converted to command center; it appears six (!) SCALPs punctured the parking lot’s roof and blew up inside the command center.There was wide speculation that the second half of the strikes was carried out with US experimental JDAM-LR precision-guided bombs, which the US is only experimenting with and neither Washington nor Kyiv have mentioned as a possible sale to Ukraine. The key argument of the speculation was that the JDAM-LR can fly 150+ km and so might be launched safely outside the range of Russian air defenses, while the JDAM we know the Ukrainians have – JDAM-ER – only has a max range of 75 km or so and in practice the Ukrainian bombers can’t squeeze more than 45–50 km from the weapon, because they have to fly low to avoid Russian air defenses and glide bombs fly further if released at high altitude.If you’ve read this far you know the Ukrainians just tested their OWN JDAM-like glide bomb, and further, there was the SEAD strikes the Ukrainians had flown in SW Russia (next to Donetsk) in the past few days. So my sense is the Ukrainians either broke a hole in the Donetsk air defense coverage and sent a bomber into the gap, or, they waited for the Russian air defenses to go apesh*t from six incoming SCALP missiles and then timed the bomb drops for the point of maximum Russian air defense confusion. Or knowing the Ukrainians, they did both. But bottom line, this was a very sophisticated air strike that barely made news outside Ukraine.

- Aug 28 – SBU drones hit Engels airfield, Tu-95M bomber is hit and its wing blown in two. Rare destruction of irreplaceable strategic bomber.
- Aug 28 – Bloomberg reports Ukraine hit record number of Russia oil refineries 21 hit, it was 18 in July. Four of Russia’s 10 largest refineries hit during August. Very wide targeting including Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, Volga region, Yaroslavl and Moscow region. Russian crude processing is currently 3.8 million barrels/day for August; prewar August was 5.3–5.5 million b/d. Gasoline production down 20 percent on year, diesel production down 23 percent on year. Remember, the Allied bombing tactic that shut down the Wehrmacht was attacks against German fuel production. Damage is difficult to repair and it accumulates; meanwhile the military keeps drinking fuel.

Care workers and others fleeing UK modern slavery win visa reprieve
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:19:19 UTC
20:19:19 KST

Care workers, chefs and others in danger of losing their migration status under post-Brexit rules if they leave an exploitative employer will be helped by new visa changes, the Home Office says.
Officials said if an employee was found to be a victim of modern slavery they would be allowed to work for any employer for the remainder of their visa.
The migration status of people on skilled worker visas was tied to a sponsoring employer, under a scheme introduced to fill post-Brexit labour shortages by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government in 2021.
It meant workers on that route, who have no recourse to public funds, risked having to leave the UK if they lost their job and could not quickly find a new sponsoring employer.
Campaigners have been warning the rule was being exploited by rogue employers, who use workers’ precarious status in the UK to underpay them, force them to put in long hours, or to force them into zero-hour conditions.
From Thursday, the restriction tying an individual’s immigration status to a specific sponsor will be lifted if they receive a positive “conclusive grounds” decision formally recognising them as a victim of modern slavery through the national referral mechanism – the UK’s framework for identifying and supporting victims of modern slavery and human trafficking.
The Salvation Army’s deputy director of anti-trafficking and modern slavery, Maj Heather Grinsted, said: “Allowing survivors to work for another sponsor for the remainder of their visa is a crucial way to help them rebuild their lives safely and with dignity.”
However, Dr Dora-Olivia Vicol, CEO of the Work Rights Centre, cautioned that while the changes “could be a gamechanger”, the impact depended “on how accessible the modern slavery framework is”.
She added: “For almost three years we have warned the Home Office that the sponsorship system instituted after Brexit is a recipe for labour exploitation, and have urged officials to free people’s visas from their employers’ control.”
Last week the Guardian reported that the number of employers being stripped of their licence to sponsor workers for abuses had hit record levels.
More than 6,600 sponsors have been stripped of licences since Labour came to power. Of these, more than 4,400 were in the year to June 2026, a 140% rise on the year before.
Modern slavery can include abusive working and living conditions, withheld wages, deception, intimidation, threats, violence, controlled movement, or confiscated passports.
Ministers say the rule change will help care workers, chefs, hospitality staff and others who came to the UK in good faith, but faced abuse.
Where evidence of criminality is identified, sponsors will be referred to the police.
The minister for migration and citizenship, Jo White, said: “No victim of modern slavery should be trapped with an exploitative employer because of their immigration status. These changes will give victims the freedom to leave abusive workplaces and rebuild their lives.
“While we support them, we are also cracking down on those responsible. Rogue sponsors who exploit workers will face the full force of the law.”
The government says it is also making it easier, through the immigration white paper, for sponsored workers to change employer, strengthening protections against exploitation.
A lack of safeguards had led unions and some councils to introduce their own provisions, with Unison working with care workers and councils to produce a migrant care workers charter.
Last year 111,000 skilled worker visas were granted, 76% fewer than at the peak in the year ending December 2023. The fall came after new overseas applications for care worker visas were stopped after July 2025.

Sadiq Khan cleared of car tax conviction caused by ‘scam’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:19:07 UTC
20:19:07 KST

A car tax conviction against the mayor of London has been withdrawn after it transpired that he was targeted by a “scam” that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that was not his.
Sadiq Khan was found guilty last month under what has been described as a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each.
City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London.
The case was formally reopened at a magistrates court hearing at Hereford justice centre on Thursday and withdrawn by a panel of magistrates after a request from the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA).
Neither the mayor nor a representative from the DVLA were present at the court for the one-minute hearing.
A legal adviser told the panel of magistrates that they may be aware of the case since it was “widely publicised” on Wednesday, adding: “The DVLA have requested that the original matter, if you consider it to be reopened, be marked withdrawn.”
Chair of the bench, Mrs Digings JP, said: “We accept the reopening of the case as requested. Further to the request from the DVLA, we are going to mark the matter as withdrawn.”
The mayor has been the focus of protests in the past by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge.
After the conviction emerged on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Khan said the mayor had been the target of “a scam, which is a crime”.
“It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware,” they added.
Khan had been convicted in his absence by a magistrate – who was sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure – and was ordered to pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and to settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

The USS Abraham Lincoln crew received their first rest-and-recuperation day on Wednesday after 286 days at sea, deployed in the Middle East, with photos showing significant surface rust amid reports of mental health concerns, deteriorating onboard conditions, and a possible redeployment until 2027.

"Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our Sailors and Marines to rest and recharge," the commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, Rear Admiral Robert E. Loughran, said in a statement.
"What this strike group has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated by every member of this team during our operations."
Concerns of mental health amid reports of a new deployment
Shakeira Fairfax flew in from New Jersey and was waiting outside the Pattaya hotel to meet her 25-year-old daughter Jade, a crew member on the Lincoln.
She explained how there were moments during the long deployment after the start of the Iran war when morale was low, when contact was limited, and she feared for her daughter's safety.
"There was a period of silence," she said. "It was an uncertain time; it was a scary time. It was difficult, it was definitely difficult, but she has a support system," she told reporters.
"I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'Mom'; I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," she said.
Pentagon expected to extend deployment amid supply chain disruptions report
And while the crew is expected to rest while the ship undergoes maintenance, a report by The Wall Street Journal revealed that the Pentagon plans to extend deployment in the Middle East until at least 2027.
Sources said the military presence is intended to preserve President Donald Trump's ability to choose between continued economic pressure, limited military operations, and broader escalation.
Some aides have warned Trump that expanding the conflict beyond the recent exchanges of strikes could hurt Republican candidates in the November midterm elections, according to the report. Trump has maintained that electoral considerations are not guiding his military decisions.
The decision also comes amid reports by The New York Times about problems in the logistics chain to supply troops in the Middle East, with strikes on critical bases in the region forcing the US to use naval routes for resupply missions.
According to the report, the operations in the region require some 420,000 meals per week, which are brought to the soldiers using some 30 million liters of fuel.
The report noted that the strikes on a key logistical base in Bahrain forced the US to use the island of Diego Garcia (located some 3,500 kilometers from the conflict zone) and Singapore (6,000 kilometers away) as logistical points.
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

Iran war drives gasoline prices in Germany to record high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:16:18 UTC
20:16:18 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
The price of gasoline has reached a record high following the resurgence of the Iran war, Europe’s largest automobile association (ADAC) said Thursday.
The nationwide daily average price for a liter of E10 gasoline surged to €2.215 ($2.57) on Wednesday, surpassing the previous record of €2.203 set in March 2022, ADAC added.
Furthermore, low water levels on the Rhine river have also recently had an impact on prices, as they have increased transportation costs.
E10 is the cheapest common type of gasoline in Germany. It is generally 5 to 6 cents cheaper than Super E5, which is allowed to contain less biofuel.
High gas prices are often followed by calls to ease the burden on drivers. From early May through late June, a fuel rebate of 16.7 cents per liter was in effect, which cost the federal government approximately €1.6 billion, according to an estimate by the Finance Ministry.
The government has so far refused to renew the program. Germany’s public finances are already in the red due to the debt-financed investment package.
Nominal price records do not reflect, in any case, what percentage of their income citizens actually have to spend on energy, food, etc. This is because both prices and wages are rising. The statistical offices therefore always report the inflation rate on an adjusted basis.
In August, inflation had risen again to 2.9% overall due to the war in Iran.

Sobyanin also reported that from 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on July 19 to 5:00 a.m. Moscow time (2:00 a.m. GMT) on July 20, more than 400 enemy drones were flying toward the capital region; most of them were neutralized by air defenses at a distance, while 85 were destroyed as they approached the metropolis.
In addition, Sobyanin reported that from 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on July 27 to 6:30 a.m. Moscow time (3:30 a.m. GMT) on July 28, over 390 drones were flying toward the Moscow Region, and from 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on July 17 to the early morning of July 18, more than 370 drones, most of which were neutralized at a distance by air defense forces. The mayor also reported that from the evening of July 11 through the evening of July 12, over 300 enemy UAVs were destroyed, 45 of which were intercepted as they approached Moscow. On July 4, more than 200 drones were heading for the Russian capital.
The mayor reported the most extensive attempted attack on March 11, 2025. According to him, "74 drones were shot down as they approached Moscow, and hundreds of combat drones were shot down at various lines of defense."

The ministry responded to questions from reporters following its weekly press briefing at the Ozdemir Bayraktar National Technology Center in Istanbul.
The ministry said it was closely monitoring the dissolution process of SDF aimed at preserving Syria's territorial integrity and strengthening the principle of "one state, one army."
"In this context, claims that foreign elements affiliated with SDF will leave Syria and that some of them will come to Türkiye do not reflect the truth," it said.
“It is important that reports and comments on the matter other than our official statements not be given credence.”

Regarding the procurement of Eurofighter Typhoon aircraft from the UK to meet the operational requirements of the Turkish Air Force Command, the ministry said pilot training began in August.

Following eight months of flight training, our pilots will also undergo three months of instructor pilot training. Our pilots will continue to be sent for these training programs in batches," it said.
Mecca Defense Alliance secretariat to be based in Saudi Arabia, with Pakistani secretary-general to serve first 3-year term
Responding to questions about the scope and structure of the Mecca Defense Pact, the ministry said that the defense and foreign ministers and chiefs of general staff of Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia met in Istanbul on Aug. 31, 2026.
The steps to establish a more institutional structure for cooperation under the alliance were discussed, and it was decided to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia, headed by a secretary-general, to administer the alliance's secretariat.
"The post of secretary-general, which will rotate among the three countries, will initially be held for a three-year term by a secretary-general from the Islamic Republic of Pakistan,” said the ministry.
The aim is to enhance interoperability through joint planning, training, and exercises in the military field, while strengthening joint production, technology development, and the sharing of expertise in the defense industry, it added.
"These mechanisms are expected not only to strengthen the alliance's defense capacity and deterrence but also to contribute to regional peace and stability."

The Defense Forces struck the occupiers in Crimea — hitting a landing craft and more
Kyiv • UNN
The BK-16 landing craft was hit in Sevastopol, and the Krasukha-4 electronic warfare system was hit in the area of the city. The enemy's drone control centers and warehouses were also destroyed.
The Defense Forces struck a BK-16 landing craft in Sevastopol, an electronic warfare system and a drone command post in temporarily occupied Crimea, as well as enemy warehouses in the temporarily occupied territories. This was confirmed by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 3, UNN reports.
"On September 2 and during the night of September 3, 2026, units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine struck a number of enemy military targets," the statement said.
What was struck in Crimea
In Sevastopol, Crimea, a BK-16 landing craft was struck. The extent of the damage is being clarified
The BK-16, as indicated, is a high-speed Project 02510 transport and landing craft designed to transport and land troops, including on an unequipped coastline, as well as to perform patrol and counter-sabotage missions. The craft's full displacement is approximately 20.5 tonnes, and its length is approximately 16 meters. The crew consists of 2 people, and it can carry up to 19 troops. The craft may be equipped with machine-gun and grenade-launcher weapons.
In the area of temporarily occupied Sevastopol, a Krasukha-4 mobile electronic warfare station was struck.
"Krasukha-4" (1RL257), as noted, is a long-range mobile electronic warfare system designed to suppress the airborne radars of aircraft and helicopters, as well as the radar systems of unmanned aerial vehicles. The system is also capable of affecting communications equipment and other electronic systems.
"In the area of Mar'yine (the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea), an enemy UAV command post was struck," the General Staff stated.
What was hit in Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions
"In addition, in Donetsk region, an enemy unit's UAV warehouse was struck in Zhelanne, and an enemy ammunition warehouse was struck in the area of Ilovaisk. Among other targets, enemy facilities at the Vostochnyi training ground in Novopetrivka, Zaporizhzhia region, were struck," the General Staff said in its statement.
The extent of the damage caused is being clarified.

Government to discuss new defense minister candidates next week
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has ruled out Reform Party Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga as Estonia's next defense minister, saying the party will begin discussing candidates to replace Hanno Pevkur next week.
Although Reform Party Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga has been mentioned in the media as a possible candidate for defense minister, Prime Minister Kristen Michal ruled out the possibility, saying the two roles are incompatible.
Michal said Vaga would continue as Reform Party secretary general and suggested he take the speculation as a compliment.
Vaga also said he was not in line to become defense minister. He thanked journalists, businesspeople and friends who had asked about the possibility, calling the speculation "a great honor and a vote of confidence."
Vaga said he would remain focused on his work as Reform Party secretary general until the elections while helping the party find a strong new defense minister. He said the next minister should continue strengthening Estonia's defense capabilities, ensure transparency over defense spending of more than 5 percent of GDP and maintain Estonia's unwavering support for Ukraine.
According to Michal, Reform Party members will begin discussing potential candidates next week. The new minister will be able to take the oath of office when parliament reconvenes the following week.
Michal also praised outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur for taking political responsibility, while stressing that this did not mean Pevkur was personally responsible for any wrongdoing.
"If, in the course of helping Ukraine, someone in his area of government took risks that should not have been taken and for which he is assuming political responsibility, that does not mean he bears personal responsibility," Michal said.
Pevkur announced Wednesday on ETV news show "Aktuaalne kaamera" that he was resigning as defense minister. He had held the post since 2022.
Prosecutors opened criminal proceedings Tuesday to investigate circumstances within the Ministry of Defense's area of government that were addressed in National Audit Office audits this year and last year. No one has been named as a suspect.
It emerged Wednesday that Estonia had sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid €70 million in advance to Indian businesspeople who had reportedly never previously sold artillery shells.

Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:12:03 UTC
20:12:03 KST

Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
The industry has increasingly focused on the risks of what was previously a booming private credit industry
Hong Kong’s market regulator has reclassified some of the city’s authorised funds with exposure to private market assets above a certain amount as complex products, raising the threshold for selling these products to retail investors.
Funds with exposures to direct or indirect private market assets amounting to 50 per cent or more of their net asset value would be recategorised.
The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said that it observed some funds gaining indirect exposure to private market assets through layered structures and complex instruments, which might lack transparency.
This structure made it difficult for retail investors to fully understand the underlying risks, the SFC said in a circular released on Thursday.
Due to low liquidity, valuation challenges and higher credit risks, funds with exposure to private credit and private equity would need to enhance their transparency regarding underlying investments and associated risks, according to the SFC.
Funds classified as complex products are subject to the SFC’s selling requirements, which include ensuring product suitability, the regulator added.

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:09:58 UTC
20:09:58 KST

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
Indrajeet Rai / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Sep 03, 2026, 17:06 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
India-China ties have thawed since the border skirmish in 2020.
Former foreign secretary Vijay Gokhale argues that China waits for a strategic opening, acts pre-emptively and then builds a narrative of self-defence.His new book, “China’s Wars: The Politics and Diplomacy Behind its Military Coercion”, examines past conflicts and China’s recent grey-zone tactics.In an interview with Indrajeet Rai, Gokhale explains why the India-China relationship has entered an era of “armed coexistence”, why a full-scale war is not the most likely outcome but cannot be ruled out, and how political uncertainty after Xi Jinping could produce global economic shocks or military adventurism. Edited excerpts:You describe China as an opportunistic power. What does that mean, and when does Beijing decide to act pre-emptively?By opportunistic power, I did not intend to suggest that China is very different from other major powers. In the case studies in my book, China waited for the international situation to turn favourable, or for some advantage to accrue from its relations with other major powers, before carrying out conflict with a neighbour or another country. It used opportunity strategically to achieve its goals.The Chinese idea of preventive deterrence or preventive conflict differs from the Western concept. In the West, deterrence is a counteraction intended to stop the adversary from escalating. In the Chinese context, it is pre-emptive: China acts even before the adversary has had the chance to act first. The aim is to deliver a political and psychological shock so the adversary desists or fears retaliation.The 1962 conflict is one example. There was no indication that India intended to launch a military assault. But China used the words of then PM Jawaharlal Nehru and an international situation dominated by the Cuban missile crisis to act pre-emptively against India.
China often depicts its own aggressive action as defensive and blames the other side. How central is this narrative warfare to its strategy?The Chinese Communist Party utilised China’s difficult circumstances after the collapse of the empire and projected itself as the only organisation capable of pulling the country out of its problems. It placed the blame for China’s declining economy and global influence on external circumstances. It played the victim’s card: China was perennially the victim, and the party was the instrument that would restore it as a major power.
China’s grey-zone strategy seeks to steadily pressure and exhaust rivals while avoiding the escalation of tensions into full-scale war.
The blame, therefore, was always placed on somebody else: The colonial powers, the United States in the Korean War, India in the 1962 war and the Soviet Union in the 1969 conflict. There was never an acknowledgement that some responsibility also fell on China.This is not limited to foreign policy. The party does not take responsibility for major domestic failures either: The Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen incident. Blame falls on an external force or a few bad elements, never the party itself.You argue that China is pursuing sustained grey-zone coercion. How does this work against India?Since 1979, China has not fought a real conflict. The leadership made economic development the priority, and successive leaders after Mao Zedong focused on reform and opening up.But China was not willing to give up the use of force; it changed the manner in which force was used. Instead of hot wars or major conflict, it engaged and continues to engage in very low-intensity military conflict, popularly known as grey-zone warfare.Grey-zone warfare uses threats or actual force while staying below the threshold that might tempt the rival to launch a counteroffensive. It punishes or deters, but stops short of making the rival feel compelled to push back with force. We see it along the Line of Actual Control, in the South China Sea and in the East China Sea.I have characterised the situation on the LAC after 2020 as the end of peaceful coexistence and the beginning of armed coexistence. Armed coexistence does not mean conflict. It means China will continue to take grey-zone military action around the LAC to keep us tied down and to exhaust us not only financially - because keeping forces and equipment at those heights costs a lot - but also in terms of men and material.This fulfils a key Chinese objective: Keeping India confined to South Asia.
Apart from the United States, there are few potential rivals in this century, and India is one. If you look at India, it's geographical location, its population size, its territorial size, its talent, it's economic potential. All of it lends a credence to the belief that India can become a major power in this century. And clearly, China would like to delay that possibility.Does that mean a large-scale India-China war is unlikely in the foreseeable future?Nobody can predict this definitively. China and its decision-making processes are opaque, and there are no alternative channels of information such as free media or civil society.China is a mature state focused on becoming the strongest economy and power in the world. On a rational cost-benefit analysis, the price of a major war with India could exceed the benefits. Logically, China would be reluctant to engage in such a conflict.At the end of the day, however, it is impossible to predict. We have to be prepared for the worst, while logically understanding that a hot conflict with India may not be in China’s interest in the foreseeable future.China’s capabilities against Taiwan have grown, while the US is distracted by several conflicts. Could Xi Jinping move on Taiwan to secure his legacy?An American commander of the Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Philip Davidson, suggested that by 2027 China would have the military capability to launch an assault on Taiwan. Some interpreted that to mean China would attack by 2027, but he did not actually say this.China’s capabilities for an assault on an island have substantially increased: Landing craft, area-denial capabilities, communication systems and anti-ship missiles.It is one thing for a major power to bomb another country and destroy its infrastructure, and quite another to occupy or conquer it. That requires a very large commitment of forces and material, with no assured guarantee of victory.China’s demographic decline is already causing anxiety. An assault would mean mass casualties because boots on the ground would be required. After Galwan, India acknowledged within days that 20 soldiers had been martyred; China took much longer to admit fatalities. With Taiwan potentially producing casualties in the hundreds or thousands, Beijing will worry about the domestic impact.This is where democracy, for all its weaknesses, becomes a strength. A democratic government has electoral and constitutional legitimacy to act, including in war. In China, the party claims it has popular support but has never tested that proposition. The reaction to large-scale war casualties is unpredictable.Xi has removed the age and term limits that helped institutionalise succession. What happens after him and why should India worry?Deng Xiaoping introduced two reforms that stabilised succession: Those above 68 could not continue in top party positions, and the president was limited to two five-year terms. This helped ensure smooth transitions from Jiang Zemin to Hu Jintao and then to Xi Jinping.Xi has abolished the age and term limits. In an authoritarian system, no leader will voluntarily give up power because enemies may find it easier to target him, and he cannot be certain a successor will not misuse authority against him.China could enter a period of political uncertainty and potentially turmoil as Xi ages and factions emerge in a contest for power. It is unclear whether this happens before or after his death, or whether he intends to stand for a fourth term.Because China is the world’s second-largest economy, domestic turmoil would affect its economy, military and diplomacy and create huge ripple effects abroad. Beleaguered regimes also sometimes use an external threat to divert attention. India must consider whether turmoil could produce military adventurism and how to preserve its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.China has few formal allies and did little visibly to support Iran. Does it lack the partnerships needed to become a global leader?China lacks the United States’ large network of treaty allies. But we should not underestimate the goodwill it enjoys. The Belt and Road Initiative has been welcomed as an alternative route to development. Western assistance often came with harsh conditions; China offers fewer and less onerous strings. Nobody gives aid for free, but China has built substantial diplomatic influence.There was little need for China to do more in the Iran war. It could neither persuade the United States to stop nor force peace. It protected its oil interests and relations with Iran and the Gulf countries without entering the mediation game.
When the conflict ends, Iran will rebuild using its oil and gas wealth. It is unlikely to trust the West, while China can build infrastructure at a scale few others can match. China needs energy; Iran needs infrastructure and money. That creates an enormous downstream economic opportunity and a win-win situation. Why would China get significantly involved now when there seems to be no clear way out of the conflict?As US-China rivalry intensifies, which side of the emerging world order should India prefer?India should not look at the world order through an either-or lens. The United States and China will both remain major powers. The question is how, in a triangular or quadrangular relationship, including the European Union if it acts as a union, we create an international framework relevant to this century.
India has objective advantages: Its location, demographics and consumer base; tested political stability; an independent military capability and growing defence industry; and talent.I do not see how India can fail to become a major power in this century. The international order is disintegrating and all states are hedging their bets; India is doing so too. The task is not to choose a US-led or China-led order. It is to help build an order in which India is one of the leaders.
Indrajeet Rai is the editor for TOI Online. He holds a PhD in International Politics from JNU. He has experience in both research and the social sector. He enjoys the fast-paced world of “breaking news”—as well as the equally important work of breaking down news for readers.

Feminist Activist and Icon Gloria Steinem Dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:09:46 UTC
20:09:46 KST

Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist who inspired a generation of women and fought for gender equality, has died at age 92.
Her foundation announced the news in a social media post Thursday morning, sharing that Steinem had "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City the day before, surrounded by her loved ones.
"Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor," the statement read.
"Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle."
Steinem was a celebrated writer and magazine editor, who became the face of the women’s movement.
In the 1970s, Steinem co-founded a number of trailblazing initiatives, including the Women's Action Alliance, a feminist organization dedicated to fighting sexism, Ms. magazine, a publication focusing on women’s issues, and the National Women’s Political Caucus, a multi-partisan grassroots organization aimed at increasing women’s participation in the political process.
Steinem avidly campaigned for women's reproductive rights and later supported the legalization of same-sex marriage. Much of her work centered on pushing for equal rights and pay for women.
"Feminism has never been about getting a job for one woman. It’s about making life more fair for women everywhere. It’s not about a piece of the existing pie; there are too many of us for that. It’s about baking a new pie," she wrote in a 2008 op-ed for the Los Angeles Times.
Steinem’s early years
Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio, on March 25, 1934. The family moved a lot, somewhat due to her father’s profession as a traveling antiques dealer, and Steinem didn’t attend school full-time until she was around 12 years old. After her parents separated, Steinem lived with, and helped care for, her mother, who suffered from depression.
In her 2015 memoir, My Life On The Road, Steinem credited her mother for influencing her journey to activism.
“Depression is anger turned inward; thus women are twice as likely to be depressed,” she wrote. “My mother paid a high price for caring so much, yet being able to do so little about it. In this way, she led me toward an activist place where she herself could never go.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The latest denial came a day after Putin called reports of a possible mobilization following the elections “nonsense” and an “information attack.”
Putin has insisted that Russia has no need for a new mass call-up, claiming that Russians continue to join the military “voluntarily” by signing contracts with the Defense Ministry.
He also claimed Russia has “no problems” recruiting troops for the front, while alleging that Ukraine’s armed forces are shrinking by 8,000 to 12,000 personnel each month. He provided no evidence for the figure.
Despite Putin’s repeated denials, speculation about a new mobilization has intensified since the summer.

Ukraine says Russia is preparing for 600,000 more troops

Russia Puts TV Propaganda Chiefs Under Guard Amid Threat of Ukrainian Strikes
According to Ukrainian intelligence data cited by the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian authorities are planning to recruit 300,000 people this year and another 300,000 next year.
Ukraine says the plans are being driven by Russia’s loss of initiative on the battlefield, rising personnel losses and a significant slowdown in contract recruitment across Russian regions.
Russian forces suffered around 240,000 personnel losses between January and July 2026, according to Ukrainian figures, including at least 140,000 irrecoverable losses. During the same period, around 232,000 people were recruited under contract.
Ukraine’s military intelligence service also says Russia has expanded the categories of convicted prisoners eligible for military service, including people with outstanding or unexpunged convictions for serious crimes.
Western estimates indicate that Russia is now recruiting roughly 6,000 fewer troops each month than it loses on the battlefield. According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Russia’s total military losses, including killed and wounded, exceeded 40,000 in August for the second consecutive month.
A new mobilization may also not require a new presidential decree. The decree issued in 2022 that authorized the mobilization of 300,000 Russians remains in force, according to sources cited by The Economist.
The outlet’s Kremlin-linked sources said Putin could instead avoid a formal mobilization announcement and pressure Russian regions to recruit another 300,000 to 400,000 contract soldiers.
Russia has relied heavily on contract recruitment and large financial incentives to replenish its forces since Putin ordered a “partial mobilization” of 300,000 reservists in September 2022.
According to The Economist’s sources, Putin remains unwilling to end Russia’s war against Ukraine without achieving his stated goal of fully capturing the Donbas.

As Colombia slowly identifies conflict victims, families left waiting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:06:23 UTC
20:06:23 KST

As Colombia slowly identifies conflict victims, families left waiting
RIONEGRO, Colombia, Sept 3 - Roselly Gil watched as authorities carefully removed the blackened bones from the rotting wooden coffin, stored for decades in a cemetery in Rionegro, Colombia. They were, she hoped, the remains of her younger brother.
Now a willowy 59-year-old grandmother, Gil has been waiting more than two decades for information about what happened to her brother Jesus Arbey Gil, a Colombian soldier who disappeared in 2003.
She thought an answer was close in 2024, when a government agency set up to search for people disappeared during Colombia's conflict told her they believed Jesus Arbey had been buried in the cemetery in Antioquia province.
Gil traveled by overnight bus from her home in Segovia to attend the exhumation of the remains, which were delicately eased out of a ground-level concrete niche labeled "NN 18 MAS" or "No Name Male #18".
But two and a half years later, Gil's wait endures. The remains have still not been positively identified.
"How long must one wait, wondering where he is or what happened to him, whether he was buried or not?" she said via video call in late August.
Her case is a stark illustration of the suffering of families across Colombia, and the formidable challenge facing the Search Unit for People Reported as Disappeared (UBPD) as it seeks to find and identify the remains of some 137,000 people who went missing during Colombia's six decades of internal conflict.
As well as sheer numbers, they are often dealing with remains that are significantly decomposed or partial, stored in conditions that can worsen their deterioration. Some remains are mislabeled and the quality of records varies widely between cemeteries, while DNA testing even in presumptive cases like that of Jesus Arbey takes time.
"The main challenges continue to be the high volume of requests, the technical complexity of the cases, and the ongoing need to strengthen operational staffing capacity in order to respond more quickly to identification needs," said the Institute of Legal Medicine (IML), Colombia's national forensic service, which is responsible for conducting DNA testing on bodies found by the UBPD.
MANY BURIED IN CEMETERIES
For over 60 years, Colombia's left-wing rebel groups have battled the government and right-wing paramilitaries turned crime gangs in a civil war fueled by the cocaine trade. A 2016 peace deal between the government and the leading guerrilla group, the FARC, brought some respite, but crime gangs remain hugely powerful and smaller rebel groups persist.
Many of the disappeared — including activists targeted by paramilitaries, civilians killed extrajudicially by the military, soldiers killed in combat and rebel hostages — were abandoned, or interred in clandestine graves deep in the jungle or high in the Andes. But thousands of others are likely in cemeteries across the country, where they were buried as unidentified people.
The UBPD, which is helped by ex-rebels and former soldiers as part of their adherence to the peace deal, seeks to confirm identifications with DNA, dental records and other evidence.
Samples from mothers, or siblings who share the same mother and therefore identical mitochondrial DNA, are the best candidates for comparison, though other relatives, including children of the disappeared, can also give samples. Where bodies were autopsied but unclaimed, there may be historic samples from the body itself with which to compare.
In October 2025, some 19 months after Gil attended the exhumation, the IML forensic service informed the UBPD that the sample taken from the remains did not have enough genetic material for comparison, the UBPD told Reuters. The remains were then re-exhumed and handed over in their entirety to the IML, the UBPD said.
The IML told Reuters in June it was waiting on samples from the UBPD to compare with samples from the long-ago autopsy of Jesus Arbey. It was unclear why the IML would need UBPD samples if it is in possession of the remains.
FAMILIES IN THE DARK
Jesus Arbey, the seventh of 11 children, was 24 when he vanished while on leave, never making it to a girlfriend’s house to visit, nor back to the barracks. Records show the family's estranged father identified a body as his son in 2003, but Gil says he never told his other children where her brother was buried.
Gil, who remembered Jesus Arbey as a jokester and said that she wishes she could cook him a Sunday lunch, was not distressed at Rionegro's hilltop cemetery when the remains removed by forensic staff were found to be missing their skull and hands.
She had been told by the UBPD that the person they think is Jesus Arbey was buried without them.
“I came prepared to see remains,” Gil told Reuters at the cemetery, her daughter Consuelo standing beside her, after forensic staff delicately cleaned the bones with toothbrushes and cloths. “That surely he wouldn’t have a head, and that’s how it was, he didn’t have a head, nor hands, but he did have feet.”
The femurs belonging to the body were cleanly cut in half, evidence that a prior DNA sample was taken when the body was autopsied.
Jesus Arbey is not the only sibling who is missing from Gil's life — she said other brothers were killed by guerrillas or paramilitaries, or died by suicide. Another, Rodolfo, is also missing.
"It’s so sad to have brothers and at the same time not to have them,” Gil said at the cemetery. “There are many families in the dark with nothing.”
AGENCY USES TV COMMERCIALS
The UBPD sought out Gil when it found a presumed location for Jesus Arbey's remains. In late 2024 it launched a nationwide 'Reverse Search' program, which uses TV commercials and other methods to seek the families of unclaimed remains.
Overall, the UBPD, created in 2017, has recovered nearly 5,100 remains through May of this year and identified 587 through DNA, dental records and other forensic processes. The unit said it was working closely with the IML to speed identifications, including via six joint teams staffed by anthropologists, doctors, dentists, forensic assistants and case workers.
"Despite efforts to close the gap between recovered bodies and identified bodies, given the scale of disappearances in Colombia, a comprehensive strengthening is needed of the institutions responsible for search, identification, and dignified handover efforts," the UBPD said.
It said more resources and people were needed to carry out DNA testing, fingerprinting and comparisons with historic autopsies.
Colombia is facing deep fiscal problems and the UBPD competes against many other entities for funding. The unit said in late 2025 it had received operational funding some 27% below its proposal for this year.
The number of cases being submitted to the IML's regional laboratories in Colombia's northwest, which includes Jesus Arbey's, has increased "exponentially" in recent years, the IML said in a written response to questions from Reuters.
It said it received 1,025 cases for just that regional lab between 2016 and 2022, jumping to 1,372 between 2023 and 2025. As of June, the region had a backlog of 490 cases needing forensic analysis, the IML said. Turnaround times at its genetic lab average 90 days.
In the meantime, Roselly Gil waits. Late at night, she often turns on the radio or uses her phone to distract herself.
"For a while I hoped he would come back to me, that I would find him alive, that I'd get a phone call or something," she said. "But in the end you sort of lose hope, and you're back to the same thing again, just wanting some kind of answer about what happened." REUTERS

At the Eastern Economic Forum on Thursday, Putin said it was important that high borrowing costs not hamper business investment too much, but added that it remains critical for monetary policy to address inflation risks.
Annual inflation in Russia stood at 6.3% as of Aug. 31, according to the Economic Development Ministry.
Countering claims by businesses that credit has become off-limits for some, Putin said the government has developed multiple loan programs to support firms even in the high-rate environment.

Tusk vows no surrender to Russian intimidation after Leipzig bomb plot
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that Russia is intentionally escalating hybrid tensions across Central and Eastern Europe, declaring that the West "will not be intimidated" after Berlin blamed Moscow for a thwarted airport bomb plot.
Tusk's remarks came late on Tuesday evening after German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced that intelligence linked the Kremlin to an August 4 incident involving an explosives-laden drone targeted at a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport. In swift retaliation, Berlin ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and revoked the operational lease of the Russian House cultural centre in Berlin.
"Poland, the Baltic states, Romania, and now Germany. Russia is escalating tension across the whole region," Tusk wrote on X. The diplomatic backlash was echoed by Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who expressed "full solidarity" with Berlin.
"Poland stands foursquare behind every ally attacked by Russia's hybrid war," he wrote on X. "It is good that Germany is following Poland's example and closing the Russian consulate in Bonn in response to state terror," Sikorski added.
In Brussels, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte confirmed he had held urgent talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, saying that the alliance would aggressively reinforce its deterrence posture against malign state-sponsored actions. "Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail. Our support to Ukraine is unwavering, as is our ironclad commitment to NATO's collective defence," he wrote on X.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added that the EU stands in total alignment with Berlin and is actively preparing a fresh round of coordinated European sanctions against Moscow in direct response to the Leipzig plot.
German federal investigators established that the hostile drone deliberately struck the wing of a parked Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft. According to security findings, a catastrophic explosion at the major logistics hub was only averted because the device's detonator proved faulty. (PAP)

Kuwait's Iranians under pressure since start of US-Israeli war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:03:03 UTC
20:03:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Kuwait's Iranian community under pressure since start of US-Israeli war
A Persian restaurant in Kuwait has removed any mention of Iran from its name, a sign of the pressure the Iranian community in the Gulf country has faced since the US-Israeli war on Iran erupted more than six months ago.
Following weeks of calm, Iran resumed strikes on Kuwait as the Islamic republic and the United States returned to open conflict in a war that has rattled the region and the global economy.
Earlier this year, one Iranian restaurant in Kuwait City dropped the words "Iranian cuisine" from its title—a visible manifestation of the precarious line Iranians must now tread.
As Kuwaiti and foreign customers queued outside the restaurant for dinner in the middle of the week, an employee told AFP: "Management decided to remove the word Iran from the restaurant's name because of the sensitivity of the issue."
The restaurant's business, however, "has not been affected by the war", the employee told AFP during a reporting trip last month.
The war has thrust Kuwait's Iranian community into an increasingly delicate situation as Iran repeatedly strikes with missiles and drones.
"We are going through an extremely difficult time," Iranian resident Hussein told AFP, using a pseudonym to protect his identity over fears of a possible backlash for speaking about the issue.
"Of course we are sad," added the 35-year-old Shiraz native.
For more than six months, Kuwait has been hard hit by the war, with Iran and its allied armed groups striking its oil installations, civilian infrastructure and US military bases.
Kuwait was heavily targeted in July after Washington and Tehran's memorandum of understanding collapsed, with strikes pummelling the country on a near-daily basis.
This week, the country was hammered again with back-to-back barrages, including a drone attack that caused a fire in a residential complex in Kuwait City.
Around 52,000 Iranians live in Kuwait, where they mostly work as low-paid labourers employed on fishing boats, in vegetable markets and at bakeries. Others are prosperous merchants in the fabric and carpet trade.
Like many other Iranians, Hussein works in the historic Mubarakiyah market in the heart of the capital.
Hussein arrived in Kuwait 18 years ago and now runs a large fabric business with several branches across the oil-rich Gulf capital.
"We have been living here for many years and we don't want problems between the two countries," he said at his store in Mubarakiyah.
Iranian authorities suspended direct flights between the two near-neighbours on 28 February following the US and Israeli air raids that triggered all-out war.
Hussein said he has been unable to return to Iran, where his daughter lives.
Kuwaiti crackdown
Before the war, trade between Kuwait and Iran was robust, totalling roughly $300 million in 2024, according to Kuwaiti media citing the two countries' joint chamber of commerce.
Iranian exports to Kuwait consisted mostly of food and agricultural products, fish, carpets and construction materials.
Hussein says his business has yet to be affected.
"Our relationship with Kuwaiti customers is still good," he told AFP, as a Kuwaiti woman inquired about high-quality Iranian velvet.
Two other vendors agreed.
But the Iranian community remains under pressure. Kuwaiti authorities have cracked down on the slightest hint of subversion, arresting people suspected of links to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.
Kuwait's sole Iranian school was closed by authorities last month, a source at the education ministry told AFP on condition of anonymity, without disclosing further details.
'Caught in the middle'
"We just want to live and earn our daily bread," said Ali, an Iranian man in his 30s, who asked to use a pseudonym.
"We have not been harmed or harassed, but there is a general feeling of anxiety. That's natural during wartime," he told AFP at Kuwait City's gold market.
"Of course, we feel caught in the middle," he added, as he he watched a screen showing fluctuating gold prices across the globe.
At the Mubarakiyah market, Iranian vendors hawk sweets, including delicacies infused with saffron and tahini-based treats, drawing a steady stream of customers.
"Iranians are everywhere here," said a Kuwaiti woman in her 50s who declined to give her name because of the sensitivity of the issue. "They are part of Kuwait's history, and it is impossible to imagine going without them."

Israel faces hurdle for EU bond sales after Luxembourg decision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:03:01 UTC
20:03:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel faces fresh hurdle for EU bond sales after Luxembourg declines prospectus renewal
Luxembourg has declined to renew authorisation for a prospectus used by Israel to market government bonds in the European Union, creating a new obstacle for the country’s access to European capital markets as criticism of its genocidal war on Gaza continues to grow.
The approval, which expired at the end of August, had been granted by Luxembourg’s financial regulator, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF). It enabled Israel to use a Luxembourg-approved prospectus in offering bonds to investors elsewhere in the EU.
The decision does not stop Israel from issuing debt or block all European investors from purchasing Israeli bonds. But without an approved prospectus in an EU member state, Israel may have more difficulty promoting new issues across the bloc under the EU’s passporting system.
Israel will now need to identify another national regulator willing to approve the prospectus if it wants to continue reaching EU-based investors via the same route.
The development follows a similar dispute in Ireland, which previously oversaw the relevant prospectus arrangements but did not continue the role amid growing political opposition. Luxembourg subsequently became the approving jurisdiction, before allowing its authorisation to lapse this week.
Israel Bonds have become a focus for human rights advocates and pro-Palestine campaigners in their argument that European financial institutions should not facilitate borrowing by the Israeli state while its deadly military assault on Gaza – and the wider region – continues.
Israel’s government has relied heavily on borrowing to meet sharply increased expenditure since the start of the war in October 2023. While the proceeds from sovereign bonds enter general state finances rather than being formally allocated to military operations, campaigners say they nevertheless expand the government’s overall capacity to fund the war economy.
Amnesty International has called on European states to stop approving Israeli bond prospectuses, arguing that continued access to EU financial markets risks enabling grave violations in Palestine.
Limited financial blow, wider political consequences
Israel is unlikely to be shut out of international borrowing because of Luxembourg’s decision alone.
The country has a large domestic debt market and longstanding access to investors in the United States, where Israel Bonds have been sold for decades through the Development Corporation for Israel. Those channels are likely to remain far more important than the Luxembourg prospectus arrangement in immediate financing terms.
Nevertheless, the loss of an EU approval base could be significant. It forces Israel to find another regulator, exposes it to the possibility of further refusals and places European governments under pressure to explain whether they will continue facilitating Israeli debt issuance.
Luxembourg’s stance also raises questions about how EU prospectus rules are being interpreted. Its authorities have indicated that legal restrictions surrounding the transfer of prospectus approval were a factor in the decision.
However, the European Securities and Markets Authority has said national regulators can, in principle, accept the transfer of approval responsibilities in consecutive years, meaning that it leaves open the possibility that another EU state may agree to take on the role.
