Chirag vs Manjhi: SC ‘creamy layer’ debate puts Bihar NDA unity to test.
NEW DELHI: Could the open sparring over “quota within quota” between two prominent Dalit faces of Bihar last month open up a Pandora’s box for the BJP-led NDA government? Union ministers Jitan Ram Manjhi and Chirag Paswan engaged in an open war of words last week over a separate sub-category for the most deprived Dalit sections.Manjhi hails from the Musahar community and wants a sub-quota for the marginalised SC communities. Manjhi’s son Santosh Kumar Suman, who is the Bihar minor water resources minister, has demanded a review of the country’s reservation policy to assess which sections have benefited and which have remained deprived even after 79 years of independence. The father-son duo claims they are not against reservations but want either an increase in quota or separate arrangements for sections still deprived of its benefits after seven decades.Chirag Paswan, son of Late Ram Vilas Paswan, objected to calls to introduce the “creamy layer” provision in SC/ST reservations and insisted that those advocating such a move should first resign from their positions. He stressed that the reservation policy was not based on economic status but was designed to address centuries of social discrimination, exclusion and untouchability.
This is not the first time the two leaders have openly engaged in a war of words on issues.
There have been instances in the past when the two Dalit leaders have openly taken diametrically opposite stands. The latest point of friction was the Bharat Tiwari encounter case of Bhojpur district. While Chirag Paswan vowed to prevail upon Bihar's BJP-led government to ensure that punishment was meted out to all police officials involved in his encounter, Manjhi asserted that police were justified in having opened fire on the 28-year-old man with an "unlicensed" weapon. Tiwari, a self-styled social and political activist, was shot dead following a heated exchange on June 17 when officials of the local administration and police visited his place to interrogate him in connection with incendiary social media posts.Political observers feel the open friction between the two leaders is more of a political fight for Dalit leadership in the state. Analyst Naval Kishore Choudhary, who has observed Bihar politics for decades, says Manjhi and Paswan are engaged in a turf war."The two leaders represent two different constituencies within the SC community and are in race to establish themselves as a bigger leader within the NDA in Bihar. By taking contradictory stands, they are catering to their own constituencies within the community. There perhaps is a tussle between them to prove who is more important for NDA in Bihar," Choudhary said.However, the current issue of their discord, “quota within quota”, is not just contentious but also politically sensitive. The BJP has strategically avoided a debate on the issue of sub-quota within the Dalits, perhaps realising the uncertain fallout of any such debate.
Homogeneous group vs categorisation
A Supreme Court judgment in August 2024, in a 6:1 majority ruling, had allowed states to sub-categorise castes within the Scheduled Castes (SC) based on socio-economic backwardness and degree of under-representation in govt jobs to ensure that the larger pie of 15% SC quota goes to the backwards among them.It had also asked governments to devise suitable criteria to bar the ‘creamy layer’ among SCs and STs from availing reservation. In the process, the SC overruled an earlier judgment of a five-judge bench in EV Chinnaiah case, which had said the SCs were a homogeneous group and could not be sub-categorised.The Modi government had in 2017 constituted a four-member Commission headed by Justice (Retd.) G. Rohini in October 2017 to examine the extent of inequitable distribution of benefits of reservation among the OBCs and to work out the mechanism, criteria, norms and parameters in a scientific approach for sub-categorisation within them. The Commission submitted its report to President Droupadi Murmu on July 21, 2023. However, the report has not been made public yet.Clearly, the government perhaps wants to avoid opening a Pandora’s box. More so at a time when it faces a competing challenge from the upper caste communities also. There were protests against reservations in the national capital last month, and the government engaged with the protesters. On August 21, several people held a protest in the national capital following a call by Reservation Hatao Andolan (Scrap Reservation), an Instagram-based page. The protesters are demanding the scrapping of quotas, saying that economic criteria should be given precedence over caste in determining eligibility for government support and reservation.Later, the representatives of the group held a meeting with Union minister J P Nadda and engaged in a "cordial discussion". "Following the movement that took place at Jantar Mantar on 21 August, cordial discussions were held, as per the pre-determined schedule, with Harsh Dubey, Ran Bahadur Singh Chauhan, and Mrityunjay Pathak, members of the team. In this connection, we will meet again soon," Nadda said in a post on X after the meeting.Nadda's meeting with Reservation Hatao Andolan representatives drew questions from opponents. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke asked Nadda to explain the Modi government's stand on the anti-reservation movement and questioned what Prime Minister Narendra Modi has to say about the August 21 protest. AAP Delhi unit president Saurabh Bharadwaj also sought clarity from Nadda on the government's position, referring to the demand for reconsideration of reservations.
Two-fold challenge
These political attacks notwithstanding, the BJP has to keep in mind the upper-caste sentiments. The upper caste vote has largely been with the BJP barring some exceptions, but ahead of the crucial assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh there are reports of discontent in the community.For the BJP, the challenge is two-fold. On the one hand, it has to keep the anti-reservation protesters engaged without enraging the pro-reservation groups. On the other, it has to strike a balance between competing demands of allies on sub-categorisation within the SC community.The BJP already faces pressure from the marginalised groups after stay on University Grants Commission (UGC) rules calling out caste discrimination in universities. The saffron party is also battling opposition allegations that the 2027 caste census deliberately obscures caste data. The 40 questions which are part of the census ask for many personal details, which have not so far been required for any census. However, it does not have a drop-down box for caste, nor does it ask people to self-identify as OBC to allow for proper collation of caste data.Political analyst Uday Chandra says internal conflicts within the SC community is a reality. This is more so in Bihar where Dalit identity is not totally consolidated like in other states. “The “Jati” name takes precedence over the Dalit identity in Bihar and that explains why there is a competing interest between the two Dalit leaders in the state,” Uday Chandra says.“The BJP also faces the challenge of forming new social coalitions in the runup to 2029 Lok Sabha elections. The 2014 and 2019 social coalitions which helped the BJP electorally are starting to fray and may not be effective for electoral gains,” he adds.That perhaps explains why the BJP is treading cautiously and may not be averse to the idea of “quota within quota” like it exits within the OBCs. Nitish Kumar formed the group of EBCs in Bihar and they powered his politics for years.The BJP may also ponder at the prospect of making electoral gains by prioritising the deprived within the Dalits. No wonder, the opposition parties in Bihar are already accusing the BJP of using the two ministers to test people’s mood on the issue.
'BJP testing people's mood'
Bihar's leader of the opposition Tejashwi Yadav said: "The BJP is doing all this drama from behind. They are testing people's mood, putting pebbles in the water and seeing what happens." Referring to Majhi and Paswan, he said: "These people are merely characters. They only want posts. They are greedy for positions, chairs, bungalows and security, but have left society behind."Congress MP Pramod Tiwari said Union ministers making allegations against each other "goes against the Constitution". "Perhaps they do not realise that the principle of collective responsibility applies to the Council of Ministers. Whatever a minister says remains the government's position until it is contradicted," he said.But the BJP may not want to make any new experiment now as the very idea is fraught with huge political risks. Hence, to put the sparring Dalit leaders on the back foot, Bihar minister and senior BJP leader Lakhendra Paswan posed a pointed question to both the Union ministers.
Without directly endorsing either position, he asked how many people from their respective communities, beyond their immediate families, they had actually helped advance. He reiterated what he described as the BJP’s position on reservation, declaring, “If there is BJP, there is reservation.” BJP national spokesperson Dr Guru Prakash Paswan also reiterated that the government has a clear stand regarding the reservation issue. "Reservation will exist till discrimination exists in society, and our government has strengthened this system. Whatever one says on this can be their personal opinion, but for social justice, the BJP is committed to fulfilling the vows of B.R. Ambedkar," he said.So, while the BJP watches its two allies in Bihar fight, it would hope that the issue does not snowball into a controversy that goes out of hand.

Belgium logged nearly 3,000 excess deaths during successive heatwaves since June, health authorities said on Thursday, days after this summer was confirmed as the hottest on record in the northern European nation.
Some 365 excess deaths were observed between 28 July-16 August, when Belgium sweltered under its third heatwave of the season, which also saw the beginning of the country's worst wildfire in modern history.
That represented a "slight" uptick of 7% more deaths than normal, the Sciensano national public health institute said.
The figure added to a grim tally racked up during the previous two bouts of high temperatures, the institute said.
Belgium logged an excess mortality rate of 49% between 18 June-3 July, with 2,035 extra deaths.
Another 535 more people than usual died between July 4 and 17, bringing the total number of excess deaths over the summer to 2,935, according to a statement.
Earlier this week, the national weather agency said summer 2026 was the hottest on record, making Belgium the latest European nation to smash temperature records this year.
Temperatures in the official national reference station in Uccle, outside Brussels, averaged 20.3C, 2.4C above the mean of recent decades, according to the Royal Meteorological Institute (RMI).
Scientists warn that climate change is making extreme weather events more intense and resulting in heat records tumbling more often.
At the end of August, Germany registered a record of around 14,000 heat-related deaths this summer, official data showed.
While Spain's public health institute registered nearly 4,500 heat-related deaths since 1 June, figures showed, and French health authorities said they had seen more than 7,300 excess deaths over the same period.
Some 33 countries, spanning from western Europe to the Sahel and central America, recorded their hottest July since records began this year, according to analysis of data from the European Union's Copernicus climate observatory carried out by the AFP news agency.

Women are giving their partners the ‘Illiterate Boyfriend’ test: ‘Do your best to pronounce these words’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:00:51 UTC
20:00:51 KST

There are common non-negotiables we look for in a prospective partner. They should be kind, caring and thoughtful. Having a shared interest helps. So does remembering important dates and anniversaries. But how much does it matter if they know how to pronounce the word “gnocchi”?
Turns out that’s a potential dealbreaker, at least according to a (rather judgy) cohort on TikTok. See: the “Illiterate Boyfriend” trend, which is testing some couples on the app. Users have compiled a list of what are essentially SAT words for women to ask their male partners to read. Many of these men – this is an overwhelmingly heterosexual activity – fail to finish the list unscathed. They trip over entries such as “hyperbole”, “cynicism”, “diaphragmatic” and the oft-butchered French term, “hors d’oeuvres”.
“I want you to do your best to pronounce these words,” one woman asks her boyfriend in a clip viewed more than 8.8m times. He gamely nails his first attempt, reading off the herb “thyme”. But he’s less successful with “epitome”, “challah” and “fuchsia”. (“Foo-chia?” he guesses). “Conscientious” and “faux pas” also prove tricky. He ends up with a score of five out of 17, or 29% – very much a failing grade.
The couple laughed through the exercise, but viewers were not as charmed by an adult man struggling through what they considered basic vocabulary. “The fact that his vote matters just as much as mine is really pissing me off,” one woman wrote in the comments section. “I’m gonna be honest girl, this is worth breaking up with him over,” read another comment.
Two of the words the man correctly identified were “colonel” and “regime”, which, to one user, was evidence of a red flag: “he’s obviously a Republican”. (Maybe he just has an interest in military history, a time-honored hobby of boyfriends everywhere.) Regardless of political affiliation, it seemed fair game to dunk on Mr Foo-chia. One final quip from a viewer: “He’d be so upset if he could read these comments.”
The test made its way around TikTok, with more young couples joining in, to similarly bleak results. Even those men who did well got caught up in the pop-misandry circus. One man zipped through the list, ending with a perfect score and a self-satisfied grin. It was not the flex he might have hoped for. “This is the barest fckn minimumest [sic] of bare minimums,” one woman commented. “The men are being praised for literacy we’re in hell,” wrote another.
Distress over so-called “intelligence gaps” brings to mind a phenomenon that reverses decades of dating precedent: women are now more likely to marry less-educated men than men are to marry less-educated women. This is not necessarily by women’s choice; it is the new dating pool. According to a 2024 Pew Research report, in 1995, young men and women were equally likely to hold a bachelor’s degree. Now, 47% of women ages 25 to 34 have one, compared with 37% of their male counterparts.
“We do have in our mating market an oversupply of educated women and an undersupply of formally educated men – I’m talking academically, not necessarily in their skill set, emotional or social intelligence,” said Dr Wendy Walsh, a clinical psychologist and expert at DatingNews.com.
Dr Jess Carbino is a former sociologist for Tinder and Bumble who studies dating apps. When she polls people on what they look for in a partner, “intelligence” is rarely in the top three desired traits. “They say things like humor, kindness, attractiveness, typically,” she said. “Maybe people on the coasts – New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco – might say intelligence. But by and large, that’s not one of the top things being measured.” And there are so many different ways to consider intelligence, spelling being a way to formally test fourth-graders, not romantic partners.
One thing people do want is an equal. “It’s not necessarily that someone needs a specific degree or to know every word in the dictionary,” said Robin Hamilton, a couples therapist. “It’s more: are you able to communicate with me, are you able to meet me halfway with the subjects that I’m talking about?”
One of those subjects might be reading, an indicator of vocabulary range. Men’s rates of book reading have slipped over the past decade; nearly half of all women read just one novel or short story in 2022, but only one in four men did. According to data from Tinder, mentions of books in bios on the dating app jumped 40% this year among women, but only 23% among men. Women believe they see this disparity playing out on TikTok, even if it is through an ultimately meaningless list.
It is elitist – and naive – to draw any real conclusions about what makes a good partner based on a reading test. This “Illiterate Boyfriend” list contains words that may be more indicator of class than intelligence, conflating education with one trait women have prioritized for hundreds of years, mostly due to necessity: having money.
But the trend also reflects a wider disillusionment among straight women, who are significantly less likely to want to date than men are, partly because they say it’s hard to find someone who checks all their boxes. “He looks at the word ‘queue’ and pronounces it ‘qwi-wee’?” one woman said in a video responding to the test. “And you still have sex with him?”
“It’s rage bait for women who are frustrated and angry with the mating marketplace that is slanted unfairly” against women, Walsh said, adding: “It’s OK to date a guy who can’t say epitome or niçoise. I have a PhD, but I need spellcheck for hors d’oeuvres.”

The link between dark personality traits and online toxicity is more nuanced than expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:00:49 UTC
20:00:49 KST

A new study found that individuals with more pronounced dark personality traits tend to report more engagement in uncivil online interactions. However, analysis of their actual Reddit comments did not confirm this association—dark personality traits were not associated with any of the toxicity or linguistic features of their comments. The paper was published in Computers in Human Behavior.
Online social platforms have transformed how people communicate, exchange information, and build communities. However, they have also created new opportunities for harmful behavior. Toxic and hateful speech is particularly concerning because hostile online interactions can result in psychological harm, and, in some cases, offline violence. Research increasingly suggests that such behavior is shaped not only by the design of online platforms or specific situations, but also by individual personality differences.
Particular attention has been given to the so-called Dark Tetrad: Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy, and everyday sadism. These traits have been associated with behaviors such as trolling, cyberbullying, manipulation, hostility, and the production or endorsement of toxic content. For example, people with stronger sadistic tendencies may enjoy provoking or upsetting others, while psychopathic traits have been linked to more impulsive and hostile online interactions.
Because personality also influences how people communicate, researchers have become interested in whether psychological characteristics might be reflected in the language people use online. This has contributed to the development of computational approaches that attempt to infer personality traits from digital behavior and linguistic patterns.
Study author Aldo Cerulli and his colleagues explored the relationship between dark personality traits and the textual content people post online. More specifically, they wanted to see whether dark personality traits can be reliably inferred from textual materials on social media.
Study participants were 114 U.S. individuals recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, a crowdsourcing platform. After enrolling in the study, participants provided information the researchers needed to link them to their Reddit accounts. For this, the study authors developed a dedicated web application that interfaces directly with Reddit’s Application Programming Interface (API), allowing for the secure, automated collection of participant data.
The study authors used this link to collect participants’ Reddit comments. In total, this included 152,741 sentences that comprised 56,892 comments. The mean number of comments per participant was 499. By analyzing these texts, the study authors derived estimates of participants’ online toxicity, psycholinguistic characteristics, emotional expressions, contextual emotions, moral foundations, use of irony, and text-derived dark personality traits. Aside from this, study participants completed questionnaire assessments of dark personality traits (the Dark Side of Humanity Scale), cyberbullying and trolling (the Cyberbully/Troll Deviancy Scale), and six items regarding their social media use habits.
Results showed no significant associations between the self-reported dark personality traits and estimates of those traits derived computationally from participants’ text responses. Individuals whose self-reported trolling behaviors and dark personality traits, particularly Successful Psychopathy—a calculated, manipulative style combining psychopathy and Machiavellianism—were more pronounced tended to report using uncivil comments and content on social media more often. However, dark personality traits did not predict actual toxicity expressed in participants’ Reddit comments.
Unlike personality traits, participants’ own descriptions of their online behavior were associated with their actual Reddit behavior. More specifically, participants who said they often produced toxic content actually tended to have more toxic Reddit comments. Furthermore, people who reported being targets of toxicity also tended to produce more toxic comments, suggesting a form of perpetrator-victim reciprocity where exposure to hostility increases the likelihood of responding in kind.
“Our results underscore the importance of grounding computational approaches in validated psychological measures and point to the need for richer, context-aware representations to better understand the relationship between personality and online behavior,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to scientific knowledge about the associations between personality traits and online behavior. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a relatively small sample of participants and focused on Reddit comments only. Results of studies on larger samples, exploring wider sources of online behavior, and using different approaches to text analysis might differ. Additionally, the validity of estimates of psychological characteristics derived from features of text comments is unclear.
The paper, “Dark personality traits and online toxicity: Linking self-reports to Reddit activity,” was authored by Aldo Cerulli, Benedetta Tessa, Giuseppe La Selva, Oronzo Mazzeo, Lorenzo Cima, Lucia Monacis, and Stefano Cresci.

Construction of British deep space radar to begin in 2027
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:25 BST
20:00:25 KST

Construction of the British site for the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability will begin in April 2027 under a contract the United States Space Force signed with Northrop Grumman in August 2024, with planning permission sought in March this year and initial authority to operate already issued, according to a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what progress had been made on establishing the capability, referring to paragraph 81 of the Defence Investment Plan.
Mr Pollard said: “The Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) is a ground-based radar system that will provide 24/7, all-weather capabilities to detect, track, identify and characterise objects up to Geostationary Earth Orbit. DARC will require three permanent radar sites and a radar operations centre to provide 360-degree coverage: in Australia, the UK and the US. Construction of sites in Australia (Exmouth) and the US (IROC, Eglin) have been completed.”
He said: “The USSF signed a contract with Northrop Grumman on 23 August 2024 for construction of the UK site starting April 2027.”
On the regulatory position, he said the department has completed an environmental impact assessment including a landscape and visual impact assessment, to ensure the project has minimal impact on the local skyline, and that this formed part of a town planning application submitted to the local planning authority in March 2026.
He added: “The Defence Electromagnetic Authority, working with the Office of Communications, has issued an initial Authority to Operate. MOD and the Civil Aviation Authority is completing the necessary safety of flight procedures for local airspace.”
What DARC does
Most existing radars are optimised for low Earth orbit, where the majority of satellites and debris sit a few hundred kilometres up, and objects in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres have been tracked largely by optical telescopes, which depend on clear skies and darkness. A radar capable of reaching that altitude works regardless of weather or time of day, which is what the reference to 24/7 all-weather capability in the answer describes. The three sites, spread across Australia, Britain and the United States, provide continuous coverage of the geostationary belt as the Earth turns.
Geostationary orbit holds communications satellites, missile warning satellites and a substantial share of the space infrastructure military operations depend on, and both Russia and China have demonstrated satellites capable of manoeuvring close to others, which is a behaviour that cannot be characterised without being able to see it happening.
The United Kingdom site is at Cawdor Barracks in Pembrokeshire, west Wales, an existing defence site the Army had been due to vacate. The answer’s references to the local skyline and to safety of flight procedures for local airspace reflect the physical scale of the installation, which involves large parabolic dish antennas across a substantial footprint.
The programme is a trilateral effort under the AUKUS partnership, jointly funded by the three nations, with the American site at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and the Australian site at Exmouth in Western Australia, which the answer confirms are both complete.
Britain’s wider space programme sits under UK Space Command, established at RAF High Wycombe in 2021, which brings together military space operations alongside the existing space domain awareness assets including the Fylingdales radar in North Yorkshire, itself part of the American ballistic missile early warning system.

India targets weapons self-reliance with fully local assault rifle
India has been slowly trying to reduce its reliance on Russian-made weapons as Moscow prioritises its own needs for its ongoing war with Ukraine
The Sher, or Tiger, will replace the older, heavily criticised Indian National Small Arms System (INSAS) service rifles used by the Indian Army.
Complaints about the INSAS emerged just a year after it was adopted by the army. Indian soldiers fighting the high-altitude Kargil war in 1999 against Pakistan-backed forces in Ladakh, then a part of Kashmir, said the firearm tended to jam or its magazine would crack in the freezing temperatures.
After the Sher was successfully test-fired on August 23 at an ordnance factory in the northern town of Amethi, experts celebrated having cracked the Kalashnikov code without having to import any parts.
This is a significant victory as most of India’s military weapon systems – from Su-30MKI fighter jets to several warships and submarines – come from Russia.
India has been slowly trying to reduce its reliance on Russian-made weapons, as Moscow prioritises its own needs for its ongoing war with Ukraine, by buying equipment from France, Israel and the United States as well as boosting domestic manufacturing.

The Missing Pieces We Carry After 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

Early dawn. A slice of last night’s chocolate cake. Watching the rays of the sun spread over the city. Stealing a moment like this was a coveted morning ritual for some of the breakfast staff at Windows on the World, the restaurant that was on the 107th floor of the North Tower of the World Trade Center.
This was the meeting place where New Yorkers and out-of-towners went to celebrate birthdays and anniversaries; to revel with food and drink and to mark life milestones. And for many of the staff, it was a dream job.
“I would have worked there just for the insurance,” says Windows sommelier and waiter Paulo Villela, who immigrated from Brazil in order to get medical care for his son, who had a rare medical condition. “It was the best job.” He would tell his friends on staff, who hailed from dozens of countries—Bangladesh, Ivory Coast, Peru, China—“I’m never going to leave this place.”
On Sept. 11, 2001, so much changed. So much was lost. Most tragically, there are the 2,977 people who were killed, including 79 workers from Windows, and 91 of its guests. Those victims and their families are at the heart of this dark moment in history, which millions of us experienced from close or afar.
How one feels is at least partly determined by one’s proximity to the event. On that day, I was covering the Toronto Film Festival as a journalist. As a native New Yorker, I felt like I’d left my post. I was watching an 8:30 a.m. screening of Monsoon Wedding, a movie directed by Mira Nair, the mother of then 9-year-old Zohran Mamdani, who is now New York City’s mayor.
It’s a tenuous connection I mention because that’s what happened on 9/11; the attack cast in stark relief the myriad connections that are otherwise invisible in this city. Suddenly, we found out that our daughter’s fifth-grade teacher’s cousin worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, or a neighbor’s brother was a fireman who worked at Engine 54. On that day, the connections were rippled with panic. And then, for too many, grief. That manifested with the missing posters that filled the city for weeks; desperate pleas that became heartbreaking tributes.
Those posters were an early act of collective mourning. The city was still an open wound. You could smell the smoke almost everywhere for weeks. The randomness of the event—we were flooded with stories of those who died and those who didn’t by happenstance—draped over the city like an uncomfortable, existential veil.
One story was that of Michael Lomonaco, the chef at Windows on the World. He was in the basement of the World Trade Center, having decided at the last second to get his glasses fixed before he took the elevator to work. He felt the ground shake, saw debris raining from the sky, watched United Airlines Flight 175 crash into the South Tower, and observed people stranded above the 91st floor waving large sheets that were probably tablecloths from his restaurant.
“The memories are so vivid,” says Lomonaco, who helped start a fund for the families of his staff and who has gone on to run several successful restaurants in the city. “A generation has grown up since then, but it still seems like yesterday to me.”
A 25th anniversary marks a swath of time that can be illuminating because, to someone who is younger than 30, it feels like an eternity. Or a lifetime, which to someone who actually is 25, it is. But to someone who is over 50, as I am, it feels like a chapter. A long one, perhaps. But, still, a part of something else.
9/11 is a hinge of time that separates generations. It shouldn’t be surprising—but it always is—when I ask young folks about 9/11, and they just can’t get their hearts around it. It’s something that they learned about in class or saw on YouTube. They don’t feel it like I do. Like we do.
Those of us who are moved by this anniversary—no matter how close we were to the actual tragedy—should find some way to talk about it. “We have an obligation,” Lomonaco says. “When we talk about the people who died, we’re acknowledging the significance of their lives.”
But there’s a delicate balance. Many of us want to avoid the sadness: say “Never forget,” and move on.
Over 25 years, Lomonaco says he’s gone through the five stages of grief—denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance—and I would contend he has wisdom to share. “When we mourn with someone else, we’re actually mourning our own loss at the same time,” he says. “That creates a human bond.” He emphasizes the connections between us, which were so palpable in the days after 9/11, when lines of New Yorkers wanting to donate blood wrapped around the block.
For me, the interminable years that it took to clear Ground Zero and eventually build the new World Trade Center felt like a void. I won’t overstate it. It did not consume me. But it was there. And, at least partly to fill that hole, I wrote a book, in 2019, The Most Spectacular Restaurant in the World: The Twin Towers, Windows on the World, and the Rebirth of New York. It has been turned into a documentary created with TIME Studios, Top of the World, which CNN is airing on Sept. 7.
I wanted to tell the life of the restaurant and the people who went there and who worked there. It was a way of honoring the people and a part of New York City that was erased. And, as Lomonaco indicates, it was also my way of working through my own personal grief: I lost my father when I was 10 years old, in 1980, when he was killed in an automobile accident.
I recently read William Styron’s book Darkness Visible: A Memoir of Madness, which introduced me to the concept of “incomplete mourning,” which is pretty much what it sounds like. I can see myself wrestling with incompleteness in the way that my books—one is about the bygone video-store era, and another is about how author Kurt Vonnegut sought to reconcile his World War II experiences by writing his masterpiece, Slaughterhouse Five—share a theme of loss.
But is there even such a thing as complete mourning? I stumbled upon a 2023 eulogy by Park Avenue Synagogue’s Rabbi Elliot Cosgrove, in which he refers to The Missing Piece by children’s author Shel Silverstein. In the book, a circle goes looking for a wedge of itself that is missing. It rolls around and has adventures. And when it finally finds its missing piece, it is delighted—at first. But when it is complete, the circle rolls too fast and it is no longer able to talk to the bugs and other passersby and have the experiences it enjoyed during its journey. So, the circle decides to release the piece, preferring to live without it.
Cosgrove was commemorating the passing of another rabbi, Harold Kushner, who first made the connection between grief and The Missing Piece. In Kushner’s words, “We’re more complete if we’re incomplete.” I think that’s a beautiful way to approach grief.
We need to see the light in the darkness. “In the face of loss, we must see the preciousness of life,” Cosgrove says. Lomonaco agrees: “My appreciation of individual lives, of life, has grown,” he says.
It’s a bit of a trick to both grieve and grow, like keeping two contradictory thoughts in your head, except in your heart. I hope to be getting better at it. I’d contend that the city has managed pretty well with the 9/11 Memorial and its reflecting pools. They’re solemn and reverential and, at the same time, thriving with tourists. (A New Yorker’s sense of irony, and humor, helps with the grieving.)
And the Tribute in Light, those awesome spotlights that pierce the sky each Sept. 11, are a pitch-perfect way to memorialize the day.
“It’s like going into a church and lighting a candle,” Lomonaco says. “It’s an act of mourning. But a light also literally lights our path forward.”
Roston is an author of several books and a New York City high school teacher

Ugly AI Food Photos Are Only the Beginning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

I can’t stop staring at the AI-slop images of Mexican food I see during my morning walk to work. On the menu posted outside, the taco truck displays lunch options that appear uncanny and unappetizing, as if an alien who’s never eaten human food before drew a taco from memory. This food truck is not alone in putting AI-generated images on its menu. It’s everywhere.
AI menu slop is now going viral for being disgusting, and these posters seem to be an evolution of the “ChatGPT flyer pandemic.” Whether it’s a maggot-infested burrito or a plasticky pasta, consumers are expressing online how gross these fabricated images look. The aesthetic is distinctively off-putting, sometimes with random holes throughout a dish or otherworldly cuts of meat served as an entree.
The images are immediately noticeable but only scratch the surface of how generative AI tools have already overhauled restaurant menus. Sellers aren’t just generating AI images of burgers, they’re also relying on AI to decide what goes in between those two buns.
Digital Demands
The birth of the online menu set us on the path toward these monstrosities. More consumers started deciding what to eat based on online menus and by ordering delivery from their phones to their doorstep. Faced with growing pressure, restaurant owners digitized their menus and created additional visuals.
Stores wanted to capitalize on delivery sales and leaned into generative AI images, vying for a visibility boost on third-party apps like DoorDash without paying for a photoshoot. While the most powerful models currently on the market can output photorealistic images of food, many of these images appear to be generated by tools with worse capabilities, like the default setting of a free chatbot.
“I went to order pizza one night on Uber Eats,” says Brendan Sweeney, CEO and cofounder of Popmenu, a digital marketing software company for restaurants. “There were five different pizza places that were using the same AI-generated image.” He says if the food image appears “completely inauthentic” and “obviously AI,” then the restaurant is making a worse decision than foregoing photography altogether.
What was originally generated to satisfy digital demand is now creeping its way into the physical world. AI menu slop expanded from its online origins into posters in coffee shops and signs displayed as deli menus. Restaurant owners sometimes seem oblivious to how off-putting low-quality image generations look.
TasteGPT
Noticeably AI-generated images stand out on modern menus for all the wrong reasons. But AI tools are influencing what appears on your local coffee shop’s menu, beyond just images.
Tastewise, one of the largest data insights companies in the food and beverage industry, partners with companies like Nestlé, PepsiCo, and Kraft Heinz. It’s currently all-in on “agentic” automations for every step of the food creation process.
Tastewise’s library of automations is meant to help companies decide what foods to sell and how to sell them. There’s an agent to help you track how product launches are going, an agent to test new concepts (banana creatine smoothies, anyone?), and an agent to find opportunity gaps in current menus.
“I think the bigger question for them is how do they guide and train the AI on what should be in that burger and what should be on the menu,” says Michael Bortinger, Tastewise’s director of marketing and partnerships. “We have billions of data points understanding what consumers are doing with food, what’s actually happening on menus and in the retail landscape.”
The result is TasteGPT, a chatbot-style tool powered by food-specific insights. Companies can pay for access to the bot, though the website offers you a few free queries, so I tried it out.
Two of the suggested prompts were about what competitors are doing with protein-enhanced foods and the current trending flavors in plant-based snacks. When I picked the latter, TasteGPT flagged dates as a “standout rising star” and “cake-flavored plant-based snacks” as another relevant—though not as hot—trend. Looking at what’s already available, I’m not sure I’d ever buy some cake-drizzled mini-rice cakes.
Bortinger rattles off cold foam, hot honey, and strawberry matcha as flavors and menu additions that are high on the consumer interest list. “Ube is a trending flavor, but that also may be starting to be past its peak,” he says. When I asked about pickles, as a lover of the limited-time dill-flavored Grinch-themed fries from McDonald’s, he assured me that companies are still finding “new formats” for delivering the innovative, pickle-y goodness. The dill-pickle pizza slices I keep seeing on Instagram do look quite delicious.
Burger, Enhance
The tension between food marketing and reality existed before the generative AI boom. Food stylists for commercials have long used creative methods to present objects of consumption, like swapping ice cream for similarly textured mashed potatoes or painting the perfect grill marks onto a burger patty. While those changes often make the food seem more tantalizing than reality, most of the cheap menu slop I see day-to-day still looks puke-inducing.
Despite their many mistakes in deciding how to present food images, restaurant owners will keep turning to AI tools to automate aspects of their businesses and optimize their online offerings. Around 85 percent of restaurateurs currently "feel comfortable" using AI tools and plan to use them even more extensively in the future, according to a recent poll from Toast.
Rather than using fully AI-generated images, Sweeney wants restaurants to use software—like Popmenu—to enhance images of real food captured by the smartphones in their pocket. “AI can now very easily patch those up, plate them all the same, and make the lighting consistent,” he says. “I think that’s where the value is.” He sees these enhancements as a professional way to present the dish, based on what they are actually selling.
Not all food sellers want to put AI on their menu, though, and for good reason. These synthetic images of food are becoming a cultural touchstone in the broader, highly effective AI backlash. Popular local restaurants are going viral for their refusal to participate, posting handwritten notes about not using generative AI posters for promotion.
We are living under the uncanny reign of the AI slop menu. In a few years, even the cheapest AI image of food may look more tempting than these current iterations. That said, I don’t mind a slightly ugly, albeit real, photo of dishes on the menu when I dine out or order delivery. If anything, I prefer their more authentic rough edges.
When I walk home from work today, I think I’ll finally give that food truck a chance, keeping my fingers crossed that the tacos on my plate look better than the AI ones on the poster.

This tiny raccoon turned trash into toys—and taught her family how, too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:59:57 UTC
19:59:57 KST

It started when the pygmy raccoon dove into the wrong trash bin—not the bin known by her family for its tasty food scraps but the one with paper and plastic waste.
Last January Nessie O’Neil, a graduate student in biology at Miami University in Ohio, watched as a young pygmy raccoon plucked a receipt from the paper trash. The raccoon used her paws to repeatedly dunk the receipt into a bowl of water (a common exploratory behavior). After working the receipt into a ball and rolling it around in the sand, she began batting it across the ground, seeming to play with it.
At the time, O’Neil was observing families of these critically endangered raccoons, who live alongside tourists at a popular beach club and are only found on Mexico’s Cozumel Island. She was hoping to learn more about how human activity affects these animals’ health.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“In my mind, it wasn’t some big major discovery,” says O’Neil, who specializes in raccoon biology. “It was, ‘Look how cute! She’s making a ball!’”
But when she shared the “cute” video with her research advisor, O’Neil learned it likely was major. Her research, recently published in the journal Wild, may be the first documented evidence of any animal within the Procyonidaefamily—a group that includes raccoons, coatis and ringtails—displaying a form of “material culture”: behavior involving material surroundings that is passed along to others.
Such behavior has previously been seen in animals including chimpanzees, pigs, and dolphins, who have been observed teaching family members how to get food with different types of tools.
Study co-author Michelle Szydlowski, an anthrozoologist also at Miami University, was particularly fascinated to see the behavior transfer: The racoon’s family joined in after watching her create her own “toy.” Together, her mother and sister batted the ball and tried to make their own, with varying levels of success. “It became a social activity rather than just a tactile experience for one individual,” Szydlowski says.
Soon after, the pioneering pygmy raccoon died, likely from a combination of malnutrition and toxic exposure to human trash, according to the study. Even after she was gone, her sibling was observed making another ball from paper waste.
“We tend to assume that if we haven’t seen an animal do something, the animal’s not capable of doing that,” says psychologist Michael Kisley, whose research at the University of Colorado Colorado Springs focuses on human beliefs and behavior surrounding animals. Yet Kisley was not surprised by this observation despite its novelty; although raccoons are thought of as pests, they are “intelligent, special beings that deserve a little more protection than just being tossed tortilla chips” by tourists.
Kisley, who was not involved in the study, suggests that as we learn about these animals’ complex psychological processes, we’ll take their conservation more seriously. “It’s this type of careful, well-described observation that can open up new areas of study,” he says.

Ukraine takes Zelenskyy’s Russian airspace warning to UN aviation body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:58:49 UTC
19:58:49 KST

Ukraine formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) on 2 September that Russian airspace is unsafe for civilian flights because of increased military activity, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said. The letter behind the notification asks the organization to urge its member states to stop civil flights over Russia altogether, ZN reported.
ICAO, the UN aviation agency, cannot close Russian airspace or order carriers to reroute. European and US airlines already avoid Russia's airspace, while carriers from China, Türkiye, and the Gulf states have kept flying through it. Those remaining airlines must assess the safety of flying amid drone and air defense operations. Drone alerts during reported Ukrainian attacks have repeatedly shut Russian airports and delayed hundreds of flights.
The notification follows a 1 September warning by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who told airlines, insurers, and other aviation stakeholders that Russian skies were becoming unsafe as Ukrainian drones reached deeper into the country.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine's Foreign Ministry would pass information about the risks to international organizations. The letter to ICAO came from another office—Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine's minister for recovery, infrastructure, and transport, whose portfolio covers aviation.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Zelenskyy's statement amounted to "a bid for state terrorism" and that Moscow would find a way to respond if civilian "tragedies" followed.
Sybiha urged airlines to avoid Russian airspace and said the notice was meant to prevent unintended incidents, arguing that Moscow was failing to disclose the dangers its war had created. He invoked Ukraine’s inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, the provision that recognizes states’ right to defend themselves against an armed attack. The foreign minister further stated that the war was “returning home to Russia.”
In its separate statement, ICAO warned of rising threats to civil aviation worldwide. It did not mention Russia, endorse Ukraine’s assessment, or say Kyiv’s notification had prompted it.
The UN aviation body identified long-range weapons, drones, navigation-signal interference, and advanced air-defense systems as growing dangers to civilian aircraft. It reiterated that international aviation law prohibits the use of weapons against them.
ICAO urged member states to assess airspace under their control, share threat intelligence quickly, and improve military-civilian coordination.
Russian airports were already facing repeated closures
Russian airspace has not been legally or completely closed. The disruption has instead taken the form of temporary restrictions at individual airports.
From 5–7 May 2026, restrictions during reported Ukrainian attacks delayed more than 450 flights at Moscow airports, while limits at Vnukovo remained in place for nearly 18 hours.
On 6 July 2025, Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport canceled 171 flights, while airports in five other cities suspended operations. During an earlier wave on 22 May 2025, Domodedovo halted flights four times in one day and Sheremetyevo three times, while Vnukovo and Zhukovsky also restricted operations.
Airports in Kaluga, Nizhny Novgorod, Saratov, and Tambov were temporarily closed during a 27 May attack in which Moscow claimed 99 drones were intercepted. Two days later, another alert delayed 20 arrivals and 14 departures at Vnukovo, pro-Kremlin Telegram channels claimed.

Dutch authorities warn of emerging generation of young Western cybercriminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:55:57 UTC
19:55:57 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Dutch police and prosecutors warned Thursday about an emerging generation of young cybercriminals operating through loosely connected online networks in Western countries, local media reported.
The suspects are generally aged between 11 and 25 and are primarily motivated by money and status rather than political or ideological objectives, public broadcaster NOS reported, citing the Netherlands' annual Cybercrime Overview.
"These are individuals between the ages of 11 and 25," said Stan Duijf, the police official responsible for tackling cybercrime.
"They mainly come from Western countries, speak English, work in a sort of online network, and primarily commit data and crypto thefts," he added.
Duijf said law enforcement agencies had previously focused largely on cybercriminals based in countries such as Russia, where Western authorities have limited access.
"Now we see that there are genuinely Western criminals on the way who are collaborating online and committing serious forms of cybercrime," he said.
The report cited an attack earlier this year against Dutch telecommunications provider Odido, allegedly carried out by criminals operating under the name ShinyHunters.
The hackers demanded a ransom after stealing personal information belonging to 6 million customers. After Odido refused to pay, the data was offered for sale online.
Authorities warned that young people could be drawn into cybercrime through online games such as Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, initially engaging in minor misconduct before progressing to more serious offenses.
An estimated 2.5 million people in the Netherlands fell victim to cybercrime in 2025.
Police also warned that artificial intelligence was making cyberattacks easier to conduct while making scams, including phishing emails, increasingly difficult for the public to recognize.

Vanuatu moves against France at ICJ over 2 Pacific islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:55:52 UTC
19:55:52 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
The South Pacific nation of Vanuatu has mounted a legal challenge against France over sovereignty of disputed islands, according to an official statement.
“Vanuatu has instituted proceedings against France before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning sovereignty over Umaenupne (Matthew) and Umaeneg/Leka (Hunter) Islands and delimitation of a maritime boundary between Vanuatu and New Caledonia,” the Prime Minister’s Office of the island nation said in a statement Wednesday.
The Hague-based ICJ confirmed Vanuatu filed an application before it early this week on Monday relating to a dispute over islands, as well as “concerning the establishment of a single maritime boundary between the exclusive economic zones and continental shelf of Vanuatu and France (with respect to New Caledonia).”
New Caledonia became a French colony in 1853.
In its application to the ICJ, Vanuatu affirms that the islands “have always been part of Vanuatu long before colonization,” said the prime minister’s office.
The island nation’s Deputy Prime Minister Johnny Koanapo said: “After formal negotiations, and several decades of diplomatic engagement with no outcome, it is clear that judicial determination offers the clearest pathway to a lasting and internationally recognized resolution.”
Koanapo, also Vanuatu’s lead negotiator for maritime boundaries, sovereignty, and decolonization, said the islands “belong to the people of Vanuatu, and that the protection of Vanuatu’s territorial integrity is fundamental to Vanuatu’s nationhood.”
“The ICJ is the most lawful and constructive mechanism to resolve disputes between states. … (And) France is a global champion of international law, and the rules-based order. Agreeing to participate in ICJ proceedings will demonstrate their longstanding commitment to these principles,” he said.
According to the statement, bilateral negotiations with France “failed to resolve this dispute, despite sustained efforts from both sides.”
“Referring this issue to the ICJ is wholly consistent with the international rules-based order and principles Vanuatu and France support,” it added.
The ICJ said the application by Vanuatu has been transmitted to France.
“No action will be taken in the proceedings unless and until France consents to the Court’s (ICJ) jurisdiction in the case,” it said.

Brussels to open door to curbing Airbnb and second homes in bid to ease housing burden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:55:23 UTC
19:55:23 KST

As housing prices become increasingly unsustainable in Europe, the European Commission plans to clarify when and how national authorities can restrict short-term rentals in areas under pressure, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The European Commission will propose new housing rules that would give national and local authorities clearer rules for restricting short-term holiday rentals and the purchase of homes or land that are not used as someone's main home, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The prospect of a tougher crackdown comes as prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.
Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can't afford to buy or rent, but also aren't eligible for social housing.
Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move. EU data from 2024 reveals that nearly 10% of people living in EU cities spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing.
Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU's total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.
However, the Commission's upcoming restrictions would be allowed only in areas with clear evidence of serious housing pressure.
For Airbnb-style rentals, the EU is particularly concerned about commercial operators running several properties as holiday lets, rather than people occasionally renting out their own home. Under the proposal, cities would be able to target professional multi-property operators, but a person's ability to rent out their main residence would be protected.
"In order to limit the negative impact on the internal market of any measure restricting access to, or the provision of, short-term accommodation rental services or restricting acquisition and use of land and residential property, such measures should be limited to areas where the acute pressure on the availability and affordability of residential property justifies action to safeguard affordability and availability of residential property," reads the document.
However, the Commission acknowledges that short-term rental restrictions and limits on second homes can't solve Europe's structural housing shortage. Other challenges include high construction costs, expensive land, planning restrictions and lengthy permitting processes.
According to Housing Europe, the Brussels-based European Federation of Public, Cooperative and Social Housing, housing needs far exceed supply. Latest data show that France requires 518,000 homes annually (198,000 social), Germany 400,000 (140,000 social), the Netherlands nearly 1 million by 2031, and Sweden over 500,000 by 2033 – yet new provision consistently falls short of need, often by as much as 50%.
The Commission is working on a "Housing Simplification Package" aimed at cutting administrative barriers that slow down construction due in 2027.
Housing has also become an investment asset, making it increasingly difficult for younger people and middle-income households to buy.
EU lawmaker Leïla Chaibi (The Left/ France) told Housing Commissioner Dan Jørgensen on 2 September that financialisation and the widespread use of housing as an asset are among the main drivers of the lack of affordable housing in EU cities.
"It is time for the EU to act, and we know short-term rentals have an impact on the housing crisis, in our city centres, in our neighborhoods, as well as in the countryside everywhere in Europe now," Chaibi said.
The Commission is also considering encouraging national governments to step in when a particular area has house prices at least eight times higher than incomes, prices have risen over the previous decade, and the situation is not expected to improve within the next three years.
Housing is a national and local responsibility, leaving the Commission powerless to order member states or cities to build more of it. Instead, Brussels is trying to use EU funding, state-aid rules, investment and legislation to influence the market.
Commenting on a 2025 S&D study on short-term rentals, EU lawmaker Gaby Bischoff (S&D/Germany), vice-president for Sustainable Economy and Social Europe, warned that too many Europeans are facing evictions or are even at risk of homelessness. She attributed the crisis to growing socio-economic inequality and unsustainable housing systems that "prioritise profit over people".
An estimated 1.2 to 1.3 million people experience homelessness across the EU on any given night, driven heavily by the deepening housing crisis and rising living costs, according to the European Federation of National Associations on Homelessness (Feantsa).
The Commission is set to present its housing plan on 9 September.

Court orders release of euthanasia letter signatories
Unknown

Court orders release of euthanasia letter signatories
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A court in The Hague ruled on Thursday that the public prosecution service (OM) must hand over the names the 14 prominent doctors who signed a letter urging an investigation into the case of Milou, a 17-year-old died by euthanasia in 2023.
Her parents, who were subjected to death threats after the letter was leaked, sued to obtain the names of the medical professionals who penned the later.
The OM had refused to provide the names, six of which are already known, citing privacy concerns.
Judges in The Hague said that it was “unreasonable to refuse to provide the letter containing names to the parents” who have a “compelling interest” in the information.
The parents could choose to pursue disciplinary or civil legal action against the doctors.
Milou had suffered from mental health problems from the age of 11 following sexual abuse. She was again sexually abused in an institution by another patient.
After years of treatment and various suicide attempts, she chose euthanasia at the age of 17 on the grounds of unbearable mental suffering.
The psychiatrist who approved her decision acted in accordance with the guidelines, the regional euthanasia review committee RTE found.
The committee reviews all euthanasia procedures to make sure the correct procedures have been followed and reports back to the OM, which now has five days to hand over the names.

‘handmade utopia’ traces radical homes of northern california’s back-to-the-land movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:50:39 UTC
19:50:39 KST

documenting northern california’s back-to-the-land movement
Half a century after thousands of young Americans left urban life for rural communes, Handmade Utopia: Back-to-the-Land Architecture in Northern California returns to the homes that took shape during from one of the country’s largest urban-to-rural migrations. Created by David Jacob Kramer and photographer Michael Schmelling, the book travels along Northern California’shidden roads and through its redwood forests to document a generation that taught itself how to build, farm, and live differently. At a moment when questions around self-sufficiency, ecological building, and alternative forms of housing have returned with renewed urgency, these improvised structures offer a record of an earlier attempt to rethink what a home, and a way of life, could be.
Published by Edition Patrick Frey, the 496-page volume combines Schmelling’s contemporary photographs with Kramer’s oral histories from 38 people connected to the back-to-the-land movement. Archival material, historical texts, and locally produced publications from the period add another layer, positioning the houses within the broader social experiment that unfolded across Northern California after the Summer of Love.
Ed Stiles’ Treehouse Druid Heights, 2023 | all images by Michael Schmelling
architecture built outside the conventional system
The back-to-the-land movement saw thousands of young Americans leave cities for rural areas in the late 1960s and 1970s. Northern California became one of its centers, where people formed communes, learned to farm, and built their own homes as part of an attempt to live differently. Many had no formal training in architecture or construction, building through trial and error and using available materials. The homes were shaped by practical needs, personal ideas, and an interest in ecological materials and energy efficiency.
Without conventional professional training, many residents became their own builders, developing structures through experimentation and available materials. The homes built during that period range from practical shelters to highly personal constructions, shaped by imagination, ecological concerns, and the particular conditions of their sites.
One of the central questions of the book concerns what becomes of architecture when it is removed, at least intentionally, from the logic of resale and property speculation. According to the publication, many of these homes were never built with market value in mind. Their makers instead prioritized self-reliance, experimentation, and a direct relationship with materials and landscape, a position that feels particularly relevant today. Contemporary architecture increasingly confronts questions around affordability, housing speculation, environmental impact, and the limits of conventional development. The Northern California houses documented in Handmade Utopia do not necessarily offer ready-made solutions to these problems. Their circumstances were historically specific, and the countercultural movement was shaped by its own contradictions and privileges.
Mendocino County 2021
preserving a disappearing generation
Schmelling photographs the structures as they stand today, decades after they were built, while Kramer records the stories of the people who built and lived in them. Many of the original back-to-the-landers are now in their seventies and eighties, and some of these homes are rapidly disappearing. Together, the photographs and oral histories preserve a record of a generation and the experiment it set out to build.
The interest of the movement in ecological materials, energy efficiency, and self-building still resonates with contemporary conversations around architecture and housing. But Handmade Utopia also shows how personal these homes were. They were not designed as prototypes or built for resale. Often improvised and shaped over time, they reflect the particular people, landscapes, and circumstances behind them.
That makes the book as much about what remains as about what was originally imagined. Half a century later, the surviving houses offer a glimpse into a moment when thousands of people left urban life behind and tried to build something different. As the generation that created them grows older, Handmade Utopia documents both the buildings and the stories that might otherwise disappear with them.

Outrage grows in Malta after acquittal in journalist's murder case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:50:34 UTC
19:50:34 KST

Hundreds of people demonstrated in the Maltese capital Valletta after a wealthy businessman was found not guilty of masterminding the murder of an investigative journalist.
The verdict on Daphne Caruana Galizia's car-bomb killing in 2017 sparked outrage from Maltese civil society groups and international media freedom organisations.
The opposition Nationalist Party, which organised the demonstration late on Wednesday, has said lawmakers should be called back from their summer break for a special session of the legislature to discuss the case.
Hours earlier, tycoon Yorgen Fenech walked out of court after the verdict as a free man to shouts of "Assassin!" from some protesters.
Five people have been convicted so far in relation to the murder for supplying the explosives and carrying out the killing.
The Committee to Protect Journalists in a statement on Thursday said it would continue to "seek accountability for all those involved in her murder".
The European Centre for Press and Media Freedom said the verdict sent a "disturbing message", while Reporters Without Borders (RSF), another media watchdog, said it was "beyond outraged".
"The verdict means that almost nine years since the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese authorities have failed to identify and convict the mastermind," RSF said in a statement.
"Full justice must be served and Maltese authorities must implement the long overdue measures protecting journalists and media freedom."
The government on Wednesday said it "took note" of the verdict and appealed for "prudence in public comments" on the case.
'Institutional failures'
Dubbed a "one-woman WikiLeaks", Caruana Galizia exposed corruption at the highest level in the country, shining a spotlight on murky links between Malta's business and political elites.
Her slaying put Malta, the European Union's smallest member state, in the spotlight over its apparent rule-of-law failings.
The killing also led to a political crisis, and the resignation of then-premier Joseph Muscat in January 2020 after widespread anger and mass protests over his perceived efforts to protect friends and allies from the investigation.
A two-year public inquiry published in July 2021 concluded that the state should "shoulder responsibility" for the murder due to the "atmosphere of impunity" the government had created.
Fenech, a tycoon whose business interests spanned the energy and tourism sectors, was arrested on his yacht in 2019 as he tried to sail out of Malta after a middleman in the murder was offered a pardon to identify those involved.
Prosecutors had accused Fenech of ordering the journalist to be killed because she was on the brink of publishing a compromising article about his uncle.
Caruana Galizia was 53 when she died and left behind a husband and three sons.
In June 2025, Robert Agius and Jamie Vella were convicted of supplying the bomb that killed her and sentenced to life in prison.
The three men who carried out the murder — brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio together with Vince Muscat — are serving prison sentences after being found guilty of their role.
"Accountability is now overdue for all those who enabled, facilitated, or protected her murderers," her family said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Nine years after Daphne's brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed."

Urmas Paet: Russian frozen assets must be pressed into use to aid Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:49:00 UTC
19:49:00 KST

Urmas Paet: Russian frozen assets must be pressed into use to aid Ukraine
European Union countries must urgently return to the issue of utilizing Russian assets frozen following its invasion of Ukraine, writes MEP and European Parliament Committee for Foreign Affairs vice‑chair Urmas Paet (Reform).
Sweden, Poland, the Netherlands and Spain have renewed an initiative calling for discussions and a decision on using frozen Russian state assets to support Ukraine.
This is a very important new motion, as Russia's attacks on Ukraine are getting stronger and Europe must guarantee predictable and sustained financial support for Ukraine, something necessary to defend both the Ukrainian people and Europe as a whole. At the same time, the European Union must significantly boost pressure on Russia and hike the cost to it of its ongoing war of aggression. This needs further steps to ensure that Russia ultimately bears the financial cost of the destruction it has brought about.
The European Union's €90 billion loan to Ukraine for the years 2026–2027 is significant, but this support alone is not enough. Ukraine needs additional financial support in both the short and long terms, given the estimated cost of the destruction caused by Russia already exceeds €600 billion.
More than €200 billion‑worth of Russian state assets remain frozen within the European Union. It is highly embarrassing and regrettable that the European Council was unable to reach an agreement in December 2025 on utilizing these assets for Ukraine's benefit. Instead, the Council reaffirmed that, in accordance with EU law, Russian assets should remain frozen until Russia halts its war of aggression and compensates Ukraine for the damage it has caused.
The renewed initiative from Sweden, Poland, the Netherlands and Spain provides an important opportunity for EU countries to take the next step. It is consequently important that the Council of the EU quickly opens up a political discussion on how frozen Russian state assets could be used to support Ukraine.
The European Commission should present a new proposal to help overcome those obstacles which prevented EU countries from reaching an agreement last year, including a renewed option for a reparations loan backed by frozen Russian assets.
Any solution should ensure that potential risks get fairly shared across the European Union and that no member state will bear a disproportionate burden. To that end, Russia's frozen accounts should be transferred to a new EU instrument which would assume all legal obligations on the Russian central bank. This is a decision which can be taken under Article 122(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and it should be considered as a matter of urgency.
The principle should be clear: Russia must bear the financial costs of its war of aggression. Further use of frozen Russian state assets would not only provide Ukraine with the support it urgently needs, but also keep up the economic pressure on Russia.
The European Union has repeatedly stated its commitment to supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary. However, it must also ensure that this commitment gets backed by actual resources. Important decisions on this issue can be made during Ireland's current presidency of the Council of the European Union.

Poland moves to allow local communities to ban short-term rentals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:48:50 UTC
19:48:50 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals – the type of privately owned accommodation offered through services such as Airbnb and Booking.com.
Such services have boomed in Poland in recent years, like in other parts of the world. But that has prompted a backlash from many communities, which argue that short-term rentals can cause disruption, reduce the availability of housing, and drive up prices.
However, the proposed measures have already caused divisions within the ruling coalition and must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills.
❗ Rada Ministrów przyjęła autopoprawkę do projektu ustawy dotyczącego najmu krótkoterminowego.
Nowe rozwiązania dadzą mieszkańcom i samorządom konkretne narzędzia do reagowania tam, gdzie najem krótkoterminowy powoduje problemy z bezpieczeństwem i porządkiem publicznym.
➡️… pic.twitter.com/7KvW2O4AKW
— Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki (@SPORT_GOV_PL) September 2, 2026
Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that, following a “difficult process” of discussion, his coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, had agreed on the measures.
They would grant “greater rights for residents, communities, housing cooperatives and local authorities regarding the situation in the short-term rental market”, said Tusk. “Wherever order, safety and basic comfort of life are threatened, decisions can be made to exclude these types of businesses.”
The new rules would allow homeowner associations (wspólnoty mieszkaniowe) and housing cooperatives (spółdzielnie mieszkaniowe) to prohibit short-term rentals. If a majority of members voted to adopt such a ban, operators of short-term rental properties would have six months to end operations.
Municipal councils (rady gmin), at the request of the mayor, would also be given the power to designate specific areas within their territory in which short-term rentals would be banned or restricted (for example, to a certain number of days a year).
There would also be greater powers for residents and housing groups to initiate official inspections of properties if they believe there are violations of public safety and order rules. If a property violated such regulations three times within six months, it would be banned from operating for a year.
Tusk noted that, if the bill becomes law, it would not fully go into force until 2028, in order to give enough time for businesses and communities to adapt to the new rules.
If Poland does introduce the new measures, its cities could follow the example of many of their European counterparts, such as Barcelona, Paris and London, which have introduced various restrictions on short-term rentals. The European Union has also moved to more tightly regulate the sector.
EU to help tourism hotspots crack down on Airbnb-style holiday rentals https://t.co/0Y5nzfZZYF
— Financial Times (@FT) August 30, 2026
The measures have been subject to intense debate within the ruling coalition. When the legislation was first submitted to parliament in July, some parts that had previously been included, such as provisions allowing municipalities to ban short-term rentals in certain areas, were removed.
That prompted a backlash from two junior coalition partners in particular, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), prompting further discussions over the summer, resulting in the bill now being toughened again.
The Left celebrated the government’s decision to restore tougher elements of the bill, saying it would help avoid “situations where short-term rentals turn into a nightmare, stripping residents of their peace”.
The leader of Poland 2050, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, declared that they had “scored another goal against the lobbyists” by toughening the legislation. Previously, her party had accused the government of watering down the original bill due to industry lobbying.
Znowu wbiliśmy lobbystom gola. Właśnie spłynęła nowa wersja rządowej ustawy o Airbnb. Jest decyzyjność wspólnot, spółdzielni i samorządów.

It also appears that the bill could obtain support from the opposition.
In July, after the government initially removed parts of the legislation, the largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for them to be restored, saying that power should be put in the hands of local communities.
If the bill is approved by parliament, it also requires the signature of Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, before becoming law. He has vetoed a record number of government bills, but has signed an even larger number. It remains unclear what his position on short-term rentals is.
‼️ To mieszkańcy najlepiej wiedzą, co służy ich wspólnocie. Dlatego wspólnota powinna mieć prawo powiedzieć NIE, jeśli chodzi o najem krótkoterminowy.

Poland has seen a boom in tourism in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).
However, the growth in tourism has also prompted tensions. In 2024, Kraków, which is Poland’s second-largest city and its main tourist destination, appointed a new “night mayor”, who is responsible for reconciling the needs of the city’s residents, business owners and tourists.
Previously, in 2020, the city formed a partnership with Airbnb to promote responsible and sustainable tourism. The following year, it launched a “tourist patrol scheme” to inform visitors of the “rules and norms they should follow”.
In 2024, Kraków also appealed to the government to allow it to introduce a new tax on tourists. It warned that “overtourism has led to tensions and social discontent in many places in Europe…because residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.
