Lithuania opens Baltic region’s first cell therapy and personalised medicine centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

Lithuania on Thursday opened what officials and developers described as the Baltic region’s first centre dedicated to cell therapy and personalised medicine, a 61-million-euro investment aimed at developing next-generation medical treatments.
The 3,500-square-metre facility, developed by Northway Biotech, a subsidiary of the Northway biotechnology and pharmaceutical group, will develop and manufacture advanced cell therapies, personalised therapeutic vaccines and regenerative medicine products. It will also develop 3D human tissue printing technologies.
The centre is part of Northway’s Bio City life sciences ecosystem in Vilnius and is expected to create about 100 highly skilled jobs.
The investment is seen as supporting Lithuania’s goal of increasing the life sciences sector’s contribution to 5% of the country’s gross domestic product by 2030.
Bio City I already includes two biotechnology manufacturing facilities, while Bio City II is home to a gene therapy centre that opened in 2024. The broader ecosystem brings together expertise in biologic medicines, gene therapy and cell therapy.
Northway owner Vladas Algirdas Bumelis said Lithuania’s biotechnology sector had made significant progress over the past several decades.
“Fifteen years ago, we did not have the opportunity to build such centres and develop them, but what we had and still have is people” who helped turn the company’s ambitions into reality, Bumelis said at the opening.
Health Vice Minister Danielis Naumovas said the centre would develop products capable of saving lives, while Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said the investment would strengthen Lithuania’s competitiveness in life sciences and the wider regional economy.
ILTE, Lithuania’s development bank, has also supported the project. Its CEO, Dainius Vilčinskas, said the bank had invested about 100 million euros in the Vilnius Industrial Park where the centre is located.
President Gitanas Nausėda called the project an example for policymakers of how ambitious ideas can be successfully implemented.
“Such examples inspire us and encourage us to follow your example,” Nausėda said at the opening.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius described the centre as a major success for Lithuania, saying biotechnology was an area where the country had both expertise and human capital.
He said the life sciences sector currently accounts for about 3.4% to 3.7% of GDP, while the government aims to raise that share to at least 5%.
Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas said the centre demonstrated that Lithuania was not only adopting new technologies but developing them, including technologies that could improve medical diagnosis and treatment.
“Such centres as this one combine advanced cell therapies, personalised medicine and 3D biomanufacturing,” Olekas said. “They truly help people and raise Lithuania’s profile internationally.”

Are you dealing with subsidence or other issues caused by the hot weather?
During a dry spell, such as the successive heatwaves that affected some parts of the UK this year, houses built on clay-rich soil suffer as moisture is sucked away by trees and bushes. This causes the clay to shrink and foundations to drop, causing structural problems.

Putin announces transition to 10-year Far East development strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:47:05 UTC
19:47:05 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the transition to the next stage of the Far East's development – an updated development strategy for the next 10 years.
"We are moving to the next stage – implementing an updated development strategy for the Far East, the Far Eastern Federal District, designed for the next 10 years, through 2036. The key task is to maintain the strong pace of development achieved so far and launch new investment cycles in the region," Putin said at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
At the same time, the head of state stressed the need to radically increase investment in three key areas. "The first is industrial, infrastructure, tourism, creative and other projects geared toward domestic demand, increasing the capacity of Russia's national market, as well as meeting growing demand across the Asian region as a whole," Putin noted.
The second area, the president continued, involves attracting investment in innovative companies, developing infrastructure for the digital platform economy, and broadly deploying technologies, including artificial intelligence, biotechnology, new energy technologies and other promising fields, based on the country's most advanced regulatory framework.
"And the third – this is a fundamental priority – is new investment in education and healthcare, infrastructure, culture and sports, and the development of cities, towns and rural areas based on well-designed master plans, creating a comfortable, modern and well-developed environment for living, working and recreation," Putin said. He stressed that these were "not empty words." Developing these industries and innovative projects "requires people, and modern, well-educated people will not live in conditions that do not meet their expectations for a high standard of living." "Implementing all these plans requires bold, innovative solutions," the president concluded.
The Eastern Economic Forum is being held on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Russian government. TASS is the general information partner.

Kyrgyzstan hosts pivotal SCO summit amid global geopolitical shifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:45:16 UTC
19:45:16 KST

Kyrgyzstan hosts pivotal SCO summit amid global geopolitical shifts
Kyrgyzstan balances ties with global powers while leveraging geography to secure economic and political opportunities.
Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan – It was a round table of some of the most influential men in the world. Representing Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan – and when they extended to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Plus – Turkiye, as well as the United Nations Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres. Gathered here in Kyrgyzstan were countries at the centre of some of the world’s biggest geopolitical tensions.
What brings them together is not necessarily agreement on everything. It is the space to pursue their interests outside a Western-led framework. Moscow sees that space as evidence of a changing world.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3EU or Eurasia: Why Putin sparred with Armenia’s PM
- list 2 of 3China’s support for Iran shows its limits as US ramps up pressure on Tehran
- list 3 of 3SCO slams attacks, sanctions on Iran: Key takeaways from Bishkek summit
“Over the 25 years since its inception, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has evolved into one of the independent and influential centres of the emerging multipolar world,” Russian President Vladimir Putin told the summit.
The organisation, he said, had grown from six founding members in 2001 into what he described as the world’s largest regional association.
Kyrgyzstan is a small, mountainous, landlocked country with Russia to the north and China next door. The calculation is more immediate: how do you balance between giants?
As Europe and the United States are increasingly looking towards Central Asia, Kyrgyzstan needs to balance relations with all of them.
Shairbek Dzhuraev, president of the Crossroads Central Asia think tank, said the timing of the summit is particularly important.
“The members in the room are precisely heavyweights that are directly involved in key geopolitical conflicts of the day,” he said.
That balancing act is not new. Since independence in 1991, Central Asian states have largely operated through what is known as a multi-vector foreign policy.
Bishkek – like other Central Asian nations – operates by keeping Russia close and building ties with China, while keeping open doors to Europe and maintaining healthy relations with Washington.
For Kyrgyzstan, it is less about choosing sides than keeping options open, underscored by its geography. Being landlocked means dependence on transport corridors and being mountainous makes infrastructure more difficult. Dependence on imported energy and external markets leaves the economy exposed to shocks beyond its borders.
“The biggest weakness of Kyrgyzstan, geopolitically and geographically, is the dependence in terms of transport routes, in terms of energy, in terms of economic relationships”, Dzhuraev puts it bluntly.
So diversification becomes more than an economic ambition. Kyrgyzstan, being one of the smaller members, cannot dictate the SCO’s agenda. But it helped to shape the language.
For decades, Central Asia was viewed largely through the prism of the powers surrounding it. But the wars in the region and beyond have changed that – Russia is under sanctions, so is Iran, China is looking west, Europe is looking east. Suddenly the geography has acquired new value with highways, railways, pipelines, trade corridors, power networks and the periphery is becoming a strategically important passageway. Dzhuraev said: “Kyrgyzstan wanted the summit declaration to recognise that transformation, Central Asia’s movement into the centre stage of international politics”.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation is increasingly seen as a counterweight to US influence — a grouping through which China and Russia can advance a different vision of the global order. But the SCO is too diverse for a simple East-versus-West confrontation. That description comes with a qualification that the SCO is not a unified anti-American bloc.
Its members have competing interests, different relationships with Washington and, in some cases, deep disagreements with one another. The question is not whether the SCO rejects the West, it is whether it can resist being defined entirely in opposition to it.
Iran brings that to the centre stage – where geopolitical theory meets a much more immediate crisis. Tehran and Washington have returned to confrontation after more than a month of relative calm. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian used the SCO summit to put the diplomatic question directly on the table.
“I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action,” he said.
The Islamabad MoU signed in June collapsed, with Tehran and Washington blaming each other for violating its terms. Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, also called on Washington to return to what its president signed under the MoU. “In that case, everything can be put back on the right track,” he said.
For the SCO, however, Iran is not simply a diplomatic issue – it is an economic one. Washington has renewed sanctions on Tehran and expanded the threat of penalties for those doing business with Iran. For Central Asia, that matters, particularly for countries whose economies are deeply intertwined with Russia and increasingly connected to Chinese trade networks. Dzhuraev is sceptical whether countries such as Kyrgyzstan comply fully with sanctions, “The declaration will most likely not match the reality,” he said. “China and other countries have already rejected what they describe as unilateral sanctions.”
The reality is that sanctions can hurt, as they have hurt Iran and Russia. Not as intended for economic collapse, but they brought pain for the masses and put a spanner in their economies. But enforcement across a region built around cross-border trade is another matter. For Central Asian economies, complete compliance is difficult because the economic relationships are too dense, which is quite different from Western compliance. Both with Iran and Russia, transport and trade links have been growing steadily, so countries are unlikely to simply switch them off overnight.
That makes the SCO summit an important political moment.
Not necessarily because its members can defeat the sanctions regime, but because they can collectively signal where they stand on unilateral pressure.
When you speak to delegates from the global south, there is also a broader message: that the SCO is becoming a forum where countries that do not necessarily agree on everything can nevertheless agree on one principle: they want room to manoeuvre.
Putin calls that the emergence of a multipolar world, Pezeshkian is using the forum to keep diplomacy with Washington alive on Iran’s terms, China is defending its economic relationships, India is pursuing its own strategic interests, and Kyrgyzstan is trying to make sure none of these relationships closes the door to another.
But there is a second question confronting Kyrgyzstan — and it is not sitting around the summit table. How much of its rise belongs to Kyrgyzstan itself?
As transit trade has risen, the economy has been growing rapidly, wages have increased, construction has accelerated and exports have increased.
There is visible momentum in Bishkek, with new roads and buildings appearing to fill the empty spaces. Extraordinary circumstances have generated a lot, such as the war in Ukraine, which has altered regional trade and expanded Chinese investment. When trade routes shifted, money and demand moved across borders. The government is proud that much of the recent development has been undertaken without the external borrowing that characterised earlier periods. But buildings alone do not create a productive economy. External momentum can be a dangerous foundation for long-term growth, as Dzhuraev points out. “Productivity is growing. Exports are rising. More goods are being produced domestically. But much of the momentum remains connected to external factors — particularly the Russia-Ukraine war and Chinese investment. One of the biggest drivers of poverty reduction has been rising salaries.”
The harder question is what comes next? Where are the productive sectors that will sustain those incomes? Agriculture could be an obvious answer as Kyrgyzstan is an agricultural country. But glaciers are melting and climate change is having an impact. Plus, its long-term capacity to generate higher-value growth remains uncertain. That may ultimately be the more important story behind this summit. Not the speeches, the flags, nor the declaration.
Kyrgyzstan wants to convert geography into leverage and its vulnerabilities into options. But the wider questions remain, whether Central Asia can move from being the space between Russia, China, Iran and Europe to becoming a centre of its own? As well as whether today’s economic growth can survive when the external forces driving it inevitably change?
Kyrgyzstan finds itself at the centre of a changing region that brings opportunity but also pressure. Between the giants, keeping every door open may be the most important strategy of all.

‘The Blood of Dawnwalker’ Is a Bloody Balm for My Completionism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

I drink the blood of my fourth rat tonight. It’s only got so much life to give, so as soon as I drain it, I know I'll need to feed again. My hunger is not fulfilled. My health bar is only half full. I need more blood. Now.
I toss the rat away as my glowing eyes flicker to another, just across the street. I bare my sharp, bloody teeth, turn into a cloud of shadow and bats, and teleport to my unsuspecting prey. I bite down hard. It’s too late to realize my target has changed. As I swarmed, a human city guard happened to walk right in front of me. My teeth sink into his throat instead. I could let go, but I do not. I drink, drink, drink. Then he falls to the ground. Dead. I wipe my mouth as the last rat scurries away into the dark.
“Well, I guess I’m going to Hell anyway,” my character quips.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a vampire simulator and role-playing video game that launches today. It’s a dark adventure where you play as the titular Dawnwalker—human by day, monstrous vampire at night.
You can’t talk about The Blood of Dawnwalker without talking about The Witcher 3. They’re both third-person monster-slasher video games starring handsome protagonists with cool scars on their faces, both made by some of the same people.
Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, a former director at the Polish game studio and Witcher developer CD Projekt Red, was one of three directors of the very popular The Witcher 3. His new studio, Rebel Wolves, even feels like a cheeky nod to Geralt, the main character of The Witcher series who is often called the White Wolf. The gameplay and graphics feel very similar. Combat involves swinging your sword and blasting magic abilities, while cutscenes and dialog have familiar dialog trees and quick-time events. You have a special sense that makes important items glow so you can find footprints and track down monsters.
The music also sounds almost identical to The Witcher 3 soundtrack—think somber swelling violin strings plucking away while you wander a gloomy open world. I was almost ready to allege copyright infringement before realizing that Dawnwalker features the work of fellow Witcher composer Mikolai Stroinski.
Ah, so, “We have The Witcher at home,” is that it? Well, not exactly. The sameness might feel derivative at first, but give it a minute. Once you get through the prologue, the world opens up in a way that invites exploration of its very pretty, blood-soaked world. There’s no way to beat The Witcher 3 in depth, breadth, or sheer volume, but The Blood of Dawnwalker doesn’t try to replicate or surpass that scale. Instead, it gives you a simple goal and a limited time to pull it off. That sounds restrictive at first, but it plays out in a way that's more freeing than you’d expect.
Dawnwalker takes place in a fictional plague-era medieval world. You play as Coen (I call him Young Geralt), a poor peasant who lives with his family in a town controlled by evil vampires. After some inciting events, the Draculean boss vampire kidnaps Coen’s family and turns him into the Dawnwalker—a vampire hybrid that manifests as a human in the daytime and a bloodthirsty vampire at night. You’ve got 30 in-game days to save Coen’s family. You’re already running out of time.
Gameplay is split into day and night cycles, each with eight time segments. Completing a quest or doing anything of consequence will pass one or a few time segments. Otherwise, time does not pass idly. If you’re running around and exploring, you have all the time to fart around in the world that you need. The game warns you when something you're about to do will pass the time, so you can choose to keep going or leave and find something else to do.
I worried this system would feel constricting, like being forced on a set path in an open-world game. Turns out, it was exactly what I needed to stay motivated and keep exploring.
My problem with The Witcher 3 and open-world games like it is that there is so much of it. You’re tasked with some time-sensitive mission—rescue your daughter before the world ends, etc.—but then you while away hours and hours on side quests. Games like this can punish you if you rush the main storyline, cutting off quests, choices, and even characters that those smaller efforts would have unlocked. When I play, I feel obligated to do all the small stuff first, then build to the main quests. When a narrative and world gets that dense, it can start to feel like a chore.
Dawnwalker gives you many activities across the world. Some are clearly story quests; many are treasure hunts or things that feel much smaller-scale. Knowing I can’t do everything lets me prioritize what needs doing. A ticking clock always counting down on the screen usually would make me anxious in games, since failing to do the right things at the right time means you lose. Weirdly, Dawnwalker’s countdown feels less punishing and more like motivation to do the very best you can with the limited resources you have. If you know you can’t see everything in a single playthrough, it’s easier to let go of the things you miss.
It’s by no means a perfect game. The Blood of Dawnwalker is a clunky name. It really should be Blood of the Dawnwalker or just Blood of Dawnwalker. (Dawnwalker is your character’s title after all, not his name.) There is also undeniable jank throughout, like when you sheathe your sword, it floats directly behind the center of Coen’s butt. When you run with your heightened vampiric sense, the sword bounces around and spanks Coen’s behind as he runs. It is very funny, and I hope the devs don’t change it.
It is particularly unfortunate for Dawnwalker that the game is launching in the shadow of news that The Witcher 3 is getting a free remastered update later this month and a whole new expansion pack in 2027, 11 years after its original release.
Despite all the blood, gore, and sorrow, Dawnwalker has charm and a lightness to it. Combat is bloody, wet, and satisfying. At night, Coen’s vampiric abilities are a hoot, letting you teleport around across the rooftops, drink the blood of any crawly creature you like, and sprint across the map as a wolf. Most of the vampires, aside from smokeshow Coen, are the truly monstrous kinds, all claws and teeth and gory bloodsucking. But the world slowly reveals some real beauty. The other characters develop and become much more interesting than they first appeared. The voice acting that carries some pretty wrenching story beats and character moments is stellar.
Above all, it does something remarkable: It takes an established game formula and really infuses it with its own personality and quirks. It takes a bite out of the Witcher formula and makes it its own. And has a bloody good time doing it.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Air Force has completed mass production and deployed its Ching Tien I long-range supersonic cruise missile, while an upgraded version is reportedly being developed with a range exceeding 2,000 kilometers.
The ministry's proposed 2027 budget includes a program for the Air Force to contract the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology to provide follow-on support for the weapon system through 2031, per Liberty Times. The funding covers routine maintenance and periodic inspections, indicating the system has moved into operational service.
Ching Tien I, formerly known as the Yun Feng missile, uses a ramjet engine and can reach speeds of up to Mach 3. It has an estimated range of 1,200 to 1,500 kilometers, potentially allowing it to strike military targets in central and eastern China.
Because of its large size and earlier design, the first-generation missile is deployed primarily from fixed underground positions and mountain shelters, Liberty Times reported. The military is now pursuing an upgraded version designed to address the vulnerability of fixed-site deployment.
Ching Tien II is reportedly being developed as a road-mobile system, with plans to mount the missile on a European-made 12-by-12 heavy truck chassis. The military is also evaluating the possibility of using railway tracks for deployment and launch.
The upgraded missile is expected to feature improved propulsion technology, including a scramjet engine and solid-fuel rocket propulsion, according to Liberty Times. Its top speed is expected to exceed Mach 5, while its range could increase to more than 2,000 kilometers.
Such performance could put targets including Beijing and Wuhan within the missile's range. The system is expected to become a major component of the nation’s asymmetric deterrence capabilities.

Gloria Steinem, feminist icon, writer and pioneering journalist, dies aged 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:43:51 UTC
19:43:51 KST

Gloria Steinem, the feminist trailblazer, writer and activist who helped define the modern women’s movement in the US, has died at 92.
Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author, feminist activist and one of the most famous voices of the US’ women’s movement, has died aged 92.
She died on Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her and her foundation’s social media pages.
“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” read the statement. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor.”
The statement continued: “She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing. She has welcomed hundreds of guests into her living room for Talking Circles, a tradition she insisted will continue long after she is no longer with us. As Gloria wrote in her forthcoming book, 𝘈𝘯 𝘜𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘓𝘪𝘧𝘦, “I have now lived for more than fifty years in this brownstone, in rooms that have witnessed lives before mine, and will know others after I am gone.” This book, along with her commitment to her home becoming a center for social justice movements, are among the many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come. Gloria often quoted the adage: “The flap of a butterfly’s wing can change the weather hundreds of miles away.”"
It concluded: “In lieu of flowers, Gloria has asked that those wishing to honor her with a gift, may make a donation to Gloria’s Foundation.”
No cause of death was given, but Steinem battled breast cancer in the 1980s and was diagnosed with trigeminal neuralgia, a painful nerve condition, in the 1990s.
Born on 25 March 1934, in Toledo, Ohio, Steinem was one of the leading figures of "second-wave feminism" and one of the pioneers of the women's movement in the US in the 1960s.
She began her career as a freelance journalist in New York and got her breakthrough in 1963 when she went undercover as a Playboy Bunny for Show magazine. Her exposé revealed the working conditions faced by women in Hugh Hefner’s clubs.
In 1968, Steinem helped found New York magazine, where she worked as an editor and political writer. She published an article, "After Black Power, Women's Liberation" the following year, a piece which brought her national attention and positioned her as a feminist leader.
Steinem began to dedicate her life to causes such as reproductive freedom and domestic violence prevention, as well as workplace and political gender inequalities.
In 1971, she joined fellow activists Bella Abzug, Betty Friedan, Shirley Chisholm in establishing the National Women’s Political Caucus (NWPC), aiming to increase women’s participation in politics.
She delivered the famous speech "Address to the Women of America", one mostly remembered for the following quotation: "This is no simple reform. It really is a revolution. Sex and race because they are easy and visible differences have been the primary ways of organizing human beings into superior and inferior groups and into the cheap labor on which this system still depends. We are talking about a society in which there will be no roles other than those chosen or those earned. We are really talking about humanism."
A year later, she co-founded Ms. magazine, which became one of the defining publications of the feminist movement, bringing topics like domestic violence, sexual harassment and abortion into the mainstream. Steinem herself had an abortion in 1957 when the procedure was still illegal - something she only publicly revealed in 1969.
Steinem went on to found other organizations including the Ms. Foundation for Women and the Women’s Media Center.
Steinem was also a prolific author, with books like “Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions” (1983), “Revolution From Within: A Book of Self-Esteem” (1992), “Moving Beyond Words” (1993), “The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off!” (2015) and her celebrated memoir “My Life on the Road” (2016).
In 1998, she faced controversy for an opinion piece for the New York Times, in which she supported then-President Bill Clinton in the face of sexual harassment allegations. “He is not guilty of sexual harassment,” she wrote, only “a gross, dumb, and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life”.
In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest US civilian honour.
Steinem remained an outspoken advocate for equality into her 90s and continued speaking and writing about women’s rights, including supporting female reproductive rights, LGBTQ rights, and the Times Up movement.
In September 2020, while Donald Trump was president, Steinem told The New York Times: "The most painful criticism or attacks come from people who share your values, not people who don’t share your values. If Trump spoke well of me, I would shoot myself.”
After years of dismissing marriage as an institution that ruined relationships, Steinem married environmental activist David Bale in 2000. She remained close with her stepson, the actor Christian Bale, after his father’s death in 2003.
When asked why she changed her mind about marriage, she told National Geographic: “If I had married when I was supposed to get married, I would have lost my name, my legal residence, my credit rating, many of my civil rights." She added: “That’s not true anymore. It’s possible to make an equal marriage.”
She told The New York Times in 2020: “Even if I live to 100, which I have every intention of doing, it’s not that long left. I just hope that I don’t die saying, ‘But! Wait!’."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Memory chipmaker Nanya Technology Corp. reported its record monthly revenue in August, as tight supplies of older-generation products boosted sales.
The company posted consolidated revenue of NT$44.7 billion (US$1.4 billion) for the month, up 560.85% year-on-year. Its revenue for the first eight months totaled NT$220.2 billion, an increase of 638.19% from the same period last year, according to CTEE.
The development of AI chips and customized processors is driving demand for high-bandwidth memory and DDR5, prompting major international manufacturers to shift more production capacity toward these higher-end products. This has tightened the supply of DDR4, creating favorable conditions for Nanya Technology.
The company has strengthened its position in the DDR4 market as availability becomes more limited, with analysts forecasting prices to rise by more than 20% in the second half of the year. Meanwhile, AI-driven demand for high-end dynamic random access memory (DRAM) is also expected to support Nanya Technology's growth.
DRAM is a type of memory that temporarily stores data while processors are operating. Since it is produced on a large scale, prices are particularly sensitive to changes in supply and demand. DRAM prices are forecast to see quarterly increases in the latter half of the year, according to Sinotrade.
Nanya Technology is accelerating capacity expansion to prepare for future growth. Its board in August approved an increase of up to 34% in this year's capital expenditure budget, raising the ceiling from NT$52 billion to NT$69.7 billion.
The company plans to invest up to NT$346.6 billion from this year through 2029 to build a new plant, with trial production scheduled to begin in the second half of 2027. The facility is expected to provide additional capacity for advanced DRAM products.

Supreme Court corruption scandal rocks Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:42:58 UTC
19:42:58 KST

Supreme Court corruption scandal rocks Brazil
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, September 3: There's outrage in Malta after a tycoon was found not guilty of masterminding the murder of high-profile investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. In Brazil, a Supreme Court justice who was pivotal in sentencing former President Jair Bolsonaro to prison is implicated in a corruption scandal of his own. Plus conservationists marvel after a mating frenzy of the endangered kakapo – a flightless, nocturnal parrot native to New Zealand.
We start with a court verdict from Malta: the acquittal of a man accused of orchestrating the killing of prominent journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. She was known for her investigation of the Panama Papers and had made a name for herself reporting on government corruption, nepotism and money laundering. This made her a target – she was killed in a shocking car bombing in 2017. The man accused of ordering her killing is Yorgen Fenech, who is one of Malta's richest men. A court verdict found him not guilty of involvement in her murder. The decision, as the Guardian says, came as a blow, not just to Caruana Galizia's family but to those who saw the trial as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom in Europe.
Caruana Galizia's death triggered one of the biggest political scandals in Malta's postwar history. It also contributed to the resignation of Joseph Muscat, the then prime minister. "Yorgen Fenech NOT GUILTY" reads the headline from the Malta Independent, although it's hard to gauge how the paper really feels about the verdict. The front-page article is fairly neutral, reporting on the Caruana Galizia family's anger, but it chooses to go with a photo of Fenech coming out of the courthouse rather than Caruana Galizia herself. There are also little to no editorials and scant opinion pieces about what this verdict represents for Malta's stance on prosecuting crimes against journalists. The Times of Malta has, for its part, gathered reactions from activist groups and opposition political parties. Republikka, a civil society in Malta fighting for good governance and democracy, says that despite the verdict, the trial forces Malta to "confront uncomfortable truths" about political corruption. The Green Party says the verdict is an "indictment of the state of Malta", adding: "Daphne has been murdered a second time."
Meanwhile, Brazil's press is headlining on a Supreme Court justice who was pivotal in bringing down former president Jair Bolsonaro. He is now implicated in a corruption scandal of his own. The Washington Times reminds us that Alexandre de Moraes was the Brazilian Supreme Court justice who sentenced Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years in prison for a coup attempt. He's now come under scrutiny after newly released federal police documents show very close ties between Moraes and disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro. The latter is the owner of Banco Master and was behind what some call the largest bank fraud in the history of Brazil.
Brazilian daily O Globo's editors offer details of Moraes' alleged corruption: airplanes, helicopters, credit cards provided by Vorcaro to Moraes and his family. Vorcaro also sent him dozens of messages in the lead-up to his own arrest. This included attempts to obtain information about the investigation into Banco Master and asking Moraes for advice on whether he should leave the country. Folha de Sao Paulo headlines on President Lula's attempts to distance himself from de Moraes and the scandal, just one month before general elections in Brazil.
Finally, there's some good news for the endangered populations of the world's heaviest parrot, the kakapo! The cute, hefty flightless parrots native to New Zealand are nocturnal, with owl-like faces. They are also critically endangered. The birds were once widespread across New Zealand, but their numbers plummeted due to hunting, habitat loss and predators, with the kakapo nearly going extinct in the mid-1900s. Now, thanks to conservation efforts and a bumper crop of the fruit of rimu tree this year, which is key to the reproductive capacities of the birds, the kakapos were thrust into a mating frenzy. Some 90 chicks were born in recent months and their population is now up to 324 – a milestone not seen for 75 years!

Autistic Turkish ultra-marathon swimmer Tuna Tunca crossed the Catalina Channel to complete the fourth leg of the Ocean’s Seven challenge despite unusually high waves and strong tides.
The 22-year-old athlete departed from Doctor’s Cave on Santa Catalina Island in California, swimming the 35-kilometer route to Smuggler’s Cove in Los Angeles. He finished the grueling open-water course in 11 hours, 3 minutes and 20 seconds.
During the route, the swimmer navigated severe tides and thick kelp forests reaching 50 meters in length, which created significant difficulties. His coach Mert Onaran, Emre Deliveli and his mother Gül Nur Tunca supported him from an escort boat throughout the crossing.
Tunca previously conquered the English Channel, the Strait of Gibraltar and the North Channel. He achieved a historic milestone by swimming the 40-kilometer North Channel in about 16 hours.
The young swimmer, who hails from the western province of İzmir, began his aquatic journey at 3.5 years old when he jumped into a pool without a flotation device. Recognizing his profound connection to the water, his mother supported him in starting swimming lessons.
Before his Ocean’s Seven campaign, Tunca completed a 36-kilometer swim from Capri Island to Naples alongside his coach, crossed the Bosphorus and Çanakkale straits and became the first autistic individual to swim from the Greek island of Chios to the coastal town of Çeşme.
The Ocean’s Seven is widely considered one of the most formidable open-water swimming challenges in the world, consisting of seven treacherous maritime channels. Bengisu Avcı currently stands as the only swimmer from Türkiye to complete the entire marathon swimming series.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul did not respond to a question on whether Russia was behind the arson attack on the defense company in Munich.
“I can’t say much about this publicly. After all, the security of Germany and the security of our allies take priority,” he said. “But we are always in a position to investigate these matters. The incident in Leipzig demonstrated this, and we are also always in a position to provide a response. This will continue to be the case in the future.”

External support sustaining Sudan war, war crimes: UN probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:34:00 UTC
19:34:00 KST

External supports, including weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks, are prolonging Sudan's civil war conflict and enabling the warring sides to carry out drone strikes against civilians in remote areas, a U.N. fact-finding mission revealed Thursday.
Sudan's war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
In a report, the U.N. mission said more than 1,000 people were killed in drone strikes in the first five months of 2026, accusing both sides of serious violations of international humanitarian and human rights law in drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes.
The RSF and Sudan's military did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters. In the past, both have denied abuses.
The mission said investigators found grounds to believe a network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
It said up to 2,000 Colombian contractors had helped operate and maintain drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF. Some were present during operations around the city of el-Fasher in Darfur, which was captured by the RSF in October 2025 and where the U.N. mission has previously said mass killings bore hallmarks pointing to genocide.
The UAE's diplomatic mission in Geneva rejected allegations of involvement in the war, saying it had not provided arms or other military-related materiel, and "remains committed to open and constructive dialogue with the Fact Finding Mission."
Somalia's government said it took the report's allegations seriously. It did not permit its territory, airspace or ports to be used by parties to the conflict for military purposes, but there had been "gaps" in information-sharing between the federal government and regions.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Chad and Libya did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan's military was at an early stage but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions – which can hover over an area before striking a target – had expanded the army's long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
Expanded drone range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan's military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites, the report said.
Between May and July 2026, repeated RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of el Obeid, which was under army control as RSF pressure intensified in June this year.
Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were army strikes that investigators said killed at least 70 people at Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of an arms embargo on the Darfur region and urged the U.N. Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan.

Spain's premier says no solid evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta migration crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:32:54 UTC
19:32:54 KST

Alyssa McMurtry
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Thursday said there is no solid evidence that Morocco orchestrated the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta, as politicians across the political spectrum challenged the government's account of the crisis.
Sanchez told parliament that Spanish intelligence services rule out Moroccan involvement in the mass crossings "for now," while vowing to act firmly if evidence emerges.
His comments came a day after Spanish media reported on a police intelligence report alleging that Moroccan security forces helped guide the arrival of around 72,000 migrants in Ceuta on July 30-31 in an operation whose purpose went beyond migration.
Sanchez also revealed Thursday that Spain had summoned Moroccan Ambassador Karima Benyaich on Aug. 21 to protest comments by Moroccan ministers concerning Ceuta and Melilla.
Morocco's justice minister had described the Spanish enclaves as a "historic and geographical right" of Morocco and called for a "definitive solution" that would return them to the country.
News of the summons prompted opposition politicians to question why it had not been disclosed, with opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo calling Sanchez a "coward" for handling it "covertly."
Feijoo also accused the government of knowing about and concealing Morocco's alleged role in the migration crisis and called on Sanchez to resign "for incompetence or complicity."
"The operation came from Morocco, was consented to by Morocco and there are indications that Morocco coordinated it," Feijoo said.
Criticism also came from the government's left-wing allies. Enrique Santiago of Sumar accused Morocco of organizing the influx, while fellow Sumar lawmaker Aina Vidal said the government's “appeasement policy with Morocco has failed.”
Gabriel Rufian, parliamentary spokesman for the Catalan separatist ERC party, accused Morocco of deliberately sending tens of thousands of people toward the border to destabilize the Spanish government in collaboration with Washington, Tel Aviv and elements of Spain's political right.
He also accused the government of sacrificing Spain's "dignity" in its dealings with Rabat, questioning whether Sanchez was withholding information about the alleged Moroccan role to avoid a confrontation with Morocco that Spain would struggle to win.
Sanchez acknowledged shortcomings in the government's response, saying: "We have had our successes, also our mistakes, like everyone."
He also announced plans to seek a permanent presence of the EU border agency Frontex in Ceuta and said King Felipe VI should visit Ceuta and Melilla "in the coming weeks."
Government estimates suggest around 5,000 migrants who arrived during the mass crossings remain in Ceuta, a small Spanish enclave with a population of about 80,000.

Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has criticised Israel over its military offensives in the region, accusing it of violating the territorial integrity of Syria and Lebanon and undermining regional and global stability.
Speaking at the ministry’s weekly press briefing at the Ozdemir Bayraktar National Technology Centre, Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk said Israel was continuing to encourage what he described as “illegal settler terrorism” in Palestine and carrying out provocative actions that violate the historical and legal status of Muslim holy sites in occupied East Jerusalem.
According to Akturk, Israel’s policies were damaging not only regional peace and security but also global stability, while further weakening confidence in international law among populations across the region.
Türkiye would continue its efforts to promote peace and stability, Akturk said, while calling on the international community to take concrete and effective measures against what he described as Israel’s “expansionist and genocidal” approach.
Ankara rejects claims over foreign SDF members
The ministry also rejected reports that foreign members of the terror group YPG-led SDF would leave Syria and that some of them would subsequently travel to Türkiye.
In a statement issued following the briefing, the ministry said it was closely monitoring developments related to the process aimed at preserving Syria’s territorial integrity and strengthening the principle of “one state, one army”.
“Claims that foreign SDF members will leave Syria and that some of them will come to Türkiye do not reflect the truth,” the ministry said.
It urged the media and public to disregard reports and commentary on the issue that fall outside the ministry’s official statements.
Türkiye and Syria complete second floating bridge
Akturk said Türkiye and Syria were continuing their efforts to contribute to stability and the normalisation of daily life in Syria.
A second floating bridge over the Euphrates River, jointly constructed by the Turkish and Syrian armed forces, was completed on 30 August, he said.
The bridge replaces a crossing that was previously destroyed by flooding and is expected to facilitate transport between the two banks of the Euphrates.
Akturk described the project as a tangible demonstration of cooperation and solidarity between the armed forces of Türkiye and Syria.
Eurofighter pilot training to begin on 7 September
Akturk said procurement activities for Eurofighter Typhoon jets were continuing with the United Kingdom to meet the operational requirements of the Turkish Air Force.
The ministry said Turkish pilots had begun training in August as part of the procurement programme.
Pilots who have completed their terminology training are scheduled to begin flight training on 7 September 2026. The flight training will last eight months, followed by three months of instructor pilot training.
Turkish pilots will continue to be sent to the UK for training in successive groups, according to the ministry.
Somali authorities rescue hijacked vessel
The ministry also provided an update on a vessel seized by pirates in Somali territorial waters.
It said Türkiye had provided the necessary support to Somali authorities in coordination with the Turkish Foreign Ministry and within the framework of agreements between the two countries.
Following an operation conducted by Somali authorities, the pirates left the vessel and the ship was successfully recovered, the ministry said.
Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia deepen defence cooperation
The ministry also outlined the structure of the Mecca Defence Alliance involving Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Defence and foreign ministers, together with chiefs of general staff from the three countries, met in Istanbul on 31 August to discuss steps towards giving cooperation under the alliance a more institutional structure.
The three countries agreed to establish a secretariat in Saudi Arabia headed by a secretary-general. The position will rotate among the three countries, with Pakistan providing the first secretary-general for a three-year term.
The alliance is expected to focus on joint military planning, training and exercises, as well as improving interoperability among the three armed forces.
Defence industry cooperation will include joint production, technology development and the exchange of expertise.
The ministry said the mechanisms would strengthen the alliance’s defence capabilities and deterrence while contributing to regional peace and stability.

For reference: The General Staff reports that the BK-16 is a high-speed Project 02510 transport and landing craft designed to carry and land troops, including on undeveloped shorelines, as well as to perform patrol and counter-sabotage missions. The craft has a full displacement of about 20.5 tonnes and is approximately 16 metres long. Its crew consists of two people, while it can carry up to 19 troops. The craft can be equipped with machine guns and grenade launchers.
The Krasukha-4 (1RL257) is a mobile long-range electronic warfare system designed to suppress the airborne radars of aircraft and helicopters, as well as radar systems on unmanned aerial vehicles. The system can also interfere with communications equipment and other electronic systems.

Russia’s Second-Largest Oil Refinery Halts Crude Processing After Ukrainian Drone Strike
Russia’s Kirishi oil refinery in the Leningrad region, the country’s second-largest by processing capacity, has completely halted crude processing following a Ukrainian drone attack on August 30, The Moscow Times reported on September 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Kirishinefteorgsintez refinery, also known as KINEF, has an annual processing capacity of around 20 million tonnes, second only to Russia’s Omsk refinery, which can process approximately 22 million tonnes per year.
According to Reuters’ sources, the August 30 attack damaged two primary crude-processing units at the facility. The AVT-6 unit, capable of processing 22,860 tonnes per day, accounts for around 40% of the refinery’s total capacity, while the AT-1 unit, with a capacity of 4,860 tonnes per day, represents another 8%.
The refinery has two additional primary processing units, AT-6 and AVT-2, which together account for the remaining 52% of its capacity. However, both were already offline when the latest attack occurred, the sources said, leaving the refinery unable to process crude.
The Kirishi refinery is operated by Russian oil company Surgutneftegas and is one of the country’s largest oil-processing facilities.
Situated in the city of Kirishi, more than 900 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border, the facility is the only major oil refinery in northwestern Russia.
Ukrainian defense technology company Fire Point confirmed the August 30 strike, saying Ukrainian drones had targeted the facility, which accounts for approximately 6.6% of Russia’s total oil refining capacity.
The Kirishi strike was part of a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s energy and military infrastructure throughout August. During the month, Ukrainian Defense Forces targeted 12 major Russian oil refineries, along with gas-processing and petrochemical plants, fuel terminals, oil depots, defense industry facilities, military airfields, and other logistics infrastructure.

Feminist activist Gloria Steinem dies at age 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

19:31:11 KST

Gloria Steinem, who made feminism a force, dies at 92
- Gloria Steinem co-founded Ms. Magazine and championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women.
- In 1963, she worked as a Playboy bunny for 11 days for a story exposing the poor pay and sexist treatment Playboy bunnies – originally waitstaff – endured.
- Steinem was often critical of the limitations of marriage, but she wed environmentalist David Bale when she turned 66.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Gloria Steinem, the American writer, lecturer, activist and organiser who fought for gender equality and women’s civil and reproductive rights for more than five decades, has died. She was 92.
The co-founder and consulting editor of Ms. Magazine, Steinem championed the feminist movement from the late 1960s onwards and inspired generations of women.
She died on Sept 2, her foundation said in an Instagram post.
“From reluctant spokesperson to a beacon of positive change, hers is a singular journey – an American leader who can speak to us all”, film and theater director Julie Taymor said of Steinem in a 2017 New York Times interview.
Taymor directed the 2020 film The Glorias, depicting Steinem’s life across the years and based on her 2015 best-selling autobiography My Life On The Road.
She was also the subject of a 2018 play, Gloria: A Life, and a 2011 HBO documentary Gloria: In Her Own Words.
Steinem said she considered herself “an entrepreneur of social change”.
“I want to do justice to the women I meet, to tell their stories,” she told the New Yorker magazine in 2015. “It’s making connections, and using myself to listen, because we can’t empower women without listening to their stories.”
Steinem founded the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 with former US lawmakers Bella Abzug and Shirley Chisholm and writer Betty Friedan, whose 1963 book, The Feminine Mystique, ushered in the second wave of feminism.
Among other groups, she also created the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Women’s Media Center, Voters for Choice, and the Ms Foundation for Women.
In 2013, then President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest US civilian honour.
With her signature long, blonde-streaked, centre-parted hair and aviator glasses, Steinem was the glamorous, hip symbol of the feminist movement, which she emphasised should embrace women of every race.
“If you’ve suffered discrimination, you’re sensitive to it on every level. I learned feminism largely from Black women. Women of colour basically invented feminism,” she told the New Yorker.
‘A Bunny’s Tale’
Steinem was born on March 25, 1934, in Toledo, Ohio, the younger of two daughters.
Her father was a travelling antique dealer. Because the family moved frequently, she did not attend school regularly until about seventh grade.
Her parents separated when she was 11, following which Steinem lived with and took care of her mother, who had a mental breakdown and suffered from depression.
The experience impacted Steinem’s views on social injustice and marriage, which she believed robbed women of choices and many of their civil rights.
“I’d already been the very small parent of a very big child, my mother. I didn’t want to end up taking care of someone else,” she was quoted as saying.
After graduating from Smith College, Steinem began freelancing as a journalist.
In 1963, she worked as a Playboy bunny for 11 days for a story for Show magazine. Her two-part groundbreaking expose, A Bunny’s Tale, detailed the poor pay and sexist treatment Playboy bunnies – originally waitstaff – endured. The story was made into a 1985 TV movie starring Kirstie Alley.
In 1968, Steinem helped found New York magazine, where her essay titled “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation” established her as a feminist leader at a time of roiling social change.
But it was not until she attended an abortion speak-out in a New York church the following year that Steinem – who had had a then-illegal abortion in London when she was 22 – said her life as a feminist activist really began.
Ms. Magazine, which she co-founded in 1971, tackled abortion and other issues such as sexism, equal pay and domestic violence, a far cry from the diet of beauty, cookery and supporting-your-husband topics that were the staple of magazines aimed at women.
An early issue included the names of 52 women, including Steinem, who had had abortions, and called for the procedure to be legalised ahead of the landmark 1973 Roe v Wade ruling that recognised women’s constitutional right to abortion in the US for nearly half a century.
‘Quintessence of female revolution’
Steinem was often critical of the limitations of marriage.
“Women are not going to be equal outside the home until men are equal in it,” she said.
She had no children of her own, and it was not until she turned 66 that she decided to wed – to South African businessman and environmentalist David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale.
“I hope this proves what feminists have always said – that feminism is about the ability to choose what’s right at each time of our lives,” she said in a statement about the marriage.
David Bale died of brain cancer in 2003.
Steinem continued working into her 80s. She wrote numerous books, including 1986‘s Marilyn: Norma Jean about Marilyn Monroe, Revolution From Within: A Book Of Self-Esteem, about personal development, and books of essays.
She narrated and conceived the idea for an Emmy Award-winning documentary about child abuse, Multiple Personalities: The Search For Deadly Memories, for HBO in 1993 and produced the Lifetime film Better Off Dead.
She also hosted Woman, a documentary series about violence against women, for the Viceland TV channel.
Author Carolyn Heilbrun – who penned 1995 biography Education Of A Woman: The Life Of Gloria Steinem – described her as “the epitome of female beauty and the quintessence of female revolution”. REUTERS

The Best Air Quality Monitor for Outdoors and Indoors in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:31:00 UTC
19:31:00 KST

Having An air quality monitor for your home is more important than you may think. As climate change speeds up and wildfires increasingly engulf large swaths of land, leaving behind smoke that makes air potentially hazardous to breathe, it's more important than ever to ensure you're breathing clean air. An at-home air quality monitor is a simple way to ensure that, whether it be car exhaust, wildfire smoke, pollutants from seasonal changes, or simply fumes from your gas stove, the air around you is safe to breathe.
These air quality monitors test the air quality both indoors and outdoors, and on top of measuring PM2.5 (particulate matter) in the air and AQI (air quality index), they can also give insights into the air you're breathing, including measuring temperature, humidity, CO2, VOCs, and more.
Our top pick, IQAir's Air Visual Pro ($330), measures for several factors and has an easy-to-read display, while our more basic budget pick, Temptop S1 PM2.5 Air Quality Monitor & Indoor Thermometer ($28), has been solid throughout prolonged testing.
For more ways to keep your air quality in check for a healthier environment, take a look at our guides to the Best Outdoor Air Quality Monitors, Best Air Purifiers, and Best Multiuse Air Purifiers. Plus, check out how we test them and how to pick the right air purifier for your home.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Indoor Air Quality Monitor
The AirVisual air quality monitor has an easy-read 5-inch LCD display screen and a graphic of a boy’s face along with the AQI color scale that lets me know my indoor air quality from across the room. As the air quality gets poorer, the little boy will stop smiling with a green background and become solemn with a yellow background; finally, if the air is truly dangerous, he’ll put on a gas mask and the color turns dark purple. I like that I don’t have to log on to the internet or open an app to know if I have clean air. Plus, the AirVisual has the added feature of giving both indoor and outdoor air quality data. This saves me the extra step of checking the outdoor air quality on my phone. And it cycles through various displays—it has the time, then it will show both indoor and outdoor readings, along with congratulating me for achieving excellent indoor air quality or it will recommend that I open a window. The AirVisual air quality monitor measures PM2.5 and CO2 and displays the temperature and humidity. It has an easy-to-read dashboard on the app and keeps data for a year, but its biggest strength is its display, especially when I burn a pizza and the boy gets sad and dons a gas mask. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Best Dual Indoor-Outdoor Air Quality Monitor
The Zen air quality monitor uses the EPA AQI color scale: green for good air, yellow for moderate, orange for unhealthy for sensitive groups, red for unhealthy, purple for very unhealthy, and deep violet/maroon for hazardous. The colored glow’s intensity can be controlled by the number of taps of your finger and can be mounted onto a pole or wall or can be placed on its circular stand. Each Zen air quality monitor can be linked to the crowdsourced PurpleAir’s Real-Time Air Quality Map. Linking the Zen is optional, but to see the actual Air Quality Index number that the Zen is reading, I had to link my specific monitor with its unique ID code to the PurpleAir website. There’s an option to have the monitor be public or private; by clicking public, you get to contribute as a citizen scientist to the Real-Time Air Quality Map. I was surprised to see just how many PurpleAir monitors there are in New York City, not to mention Brooklyn. It gave an accurate close-up of my block and my neighborhood. In this current climate of extreme weather, the PurpleAir Real Time Map is especially useful. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Best Cheap Air Quality Monitor
I've been testing air purifiers, measuring each unit’s efficacy by using a sealed tent and smoke pellets to see how quickly each air purifier clears the pellet smoke and returns the air to healthy quality when on auto mode. I time both visually when the air turns clear again and also measure with this little guy above for each test—comparing my results to the built-in AQI monitor numbers on the machines or their connected app to ensure that the measured levels (especially for PM2.5 and air quality) are correct. I'll be honest, this cheap monitor doesn't do everything that the more expensive models do, but it has worked for the simple tests I run.
This compact device measures and displays PM2.5, AQI, temperature, and humidity levels. It only measures PM2.5 particles and uses US EPA Standards to calculate the AQI. It doesn't measure for any other pollutants, so if you want a more comprehensive assessment with pollutants like CO2 or VOCs, you'd need another model. It has eco mode, which takes samples of the air every 30 minutes and lasts up to 60 days on a single charge; A mode, which samples air every three minutes and lasts about 20 days; and real-time mode, which samples air every 1.5 seconds for the most up-to-date and accurate current air quality readings—though it needs to be plugged (with a USB charger) in to work in this mode. This cheap device isn't perfect—it would get stuck in certain readings and not update, and I'd be forced to restart or plug in for accurate measurement. However, it's suitable for measuring indoor and outdoor environments and can operate within a range of -14 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit. If you just want a simple air quality monitor to gauge both indoor and outdoor pollutants, this model will do.
Best Indoor Air Quality Monitor With a Radon Sensor
Airthings' solid, unassuming minimalist design has an easy-to-read display screen, and it’s the first indoor air quality monitor I’ve tested that has a dedicated radon sensor. It also measures PM2.5, CO2, VOCs, temperature, humidity, and air pressure. And while the Airthings View Plus has an easy-to-use app, the monitor will not work without internet/Wi-Fi. It also needs time to calibrate. I saw radon, PM2.5, and humidity almost immediately, but the app told me I needed to wait days before the monitor calibrated the CO2 and VOC sensors. You'll also need to wave your hand in front of the device for an air quality check. The movement from my hand triggers the sensor to show any value above the recommended levels, along with the indicator light, which shows green for good, yellow for fair, and red for poor. The more I test air quality monitors, the more I appreciate those with color-coded indicator lights that I can see from across the room. I recommend Airthings because of its ability to measure everything from radon to PM2.5, and it also has backup batteries in case of a power outage. —Lisa Wood Shapiro
Compare Our Picks
How I Tested
In the past, I've relied on my phone's weather app to measure the air quality around me, and the government’s free AirNow website, where you can plug in your zip code and see its easy-to-read air quality meter. Now, as I test air purifiers, I always make sure to corroborate the purifiers' built-in PM2.5 or AQI measurements with an independent outside source—a separate air quality monitor—to test both the accuracy of the machine and the purifier's efficacy in filtering pollutants and getting the air quality back to a healthy level.
These air quality monitors were tested in various locations around my house, when cooking on my unventilated gas stove, under my living room window that draws in a lot of building and exhaust fumes, and outside my cat's litter box. Plus, I did additional testing outdoors, where I measured the monitors’ readings against local weather apps. And when field testing air purifiers with a sealed tent and smoke pellets as mentioned above, I always use an air quality monitor to check pollutant levels and the purifiers' efficacy when timed to get back to healthy levels.
Why Do I Need an Air Quality Monitor?
Like I mentioned above, I think it's especially important to have an air quality monitor to test whether your air both inside and outside the home is healthy if you don't have an air purifier. But it's also important to have one to measure the efficacy of the air purifier(s) in your home to ensure they are doing their job as efficiently as claimed. Especially since after prolonged use (and time), the built-in sensors can clog and give inaccurate readings.
When placing or installing an air quality monitor, try to measure at the breathing zone height, around 3 to 6 feet off the floor. An air quality monitor is especially helpful against some of the more harmful effects of things like wildfire smog, which can't always be smelled or seen. But an air quality monitor can sense that there is too much bad air, and then you can adjust the air purifier fan(s) accordingly.
It can also help to instill healthy habits, as WIRED Reviews contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro notes, using air quality monitors taught her to turn on the kitchen exhaust fan and crank up an air purifier before she turns on her gas stove. In the past, she didn’t think much of a little smoke from cooking. Now she takes proactive steps to avoid inhaling harmful pollutants.
Once you start noticing bad air and take steps to correct it, you'll notice fewer allergy symptoms and, often, fewer upper respiratory sicknesses and improved sleep. Even innocuous household things like lit candles, cooking on a stovetop without an exhaust fan (guilty), or aerosol air fresheners can negatively impact indoor air in real time. Get yourself an air quality monitor and see for yourself.
What to Consider Before Buying
Even though many current air purifier models have built-in air quality sensors, having a designated air quality monitor is a great way to independently corroborate or monitor air quality and pollutants. Plus, these handheld monitors are also portable and able to more accurately test air quality outdoors.
Before you purchase your own indoor air quality monitor, here are some things to know: Sensors on the WIRED-tested AirVisual Pro and PurpleAir all performed well in an independent study. Low-cost consumer air quality monitors are much cheaper (in the $200 or less range) than what's used by the professionals, but are also less accurate and not as easily calibrated. When testing multiple air quality monitors, they will not usually give the exact same AQI, but they are usually very close.
Consumer air quality monitors use sensors to detect tiny invisible particles in the air and other contaminants, with some sensors using light scattering to detect fine particulate matter known as PM10, like the dust visible in light, and invisible health hazards like PM2.5, which can reach the deepest parts of the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

Jaishankar is on a three-day visit to Ukraine and Poland from September 3 to 5
External affairs minister S Jaishankar speaking in Kyiv said that India is ready to contribute to efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war “in any manner” possible.“If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there,” Jaishankar said, as quoted by news agency Reuters.Jaishankar is on a three-day visit to Ukraine and Poland from September 3 to 5, his first visit to Kyiv since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. During the visit, he is holding bilateral consultations with Sybiha as well as Polish Deputy Prime Minister Radoslaw Sikorski.Jaishankar’s remarks come days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi renewed his call for an end to the conflict during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek.“Every day spent in the war pushes humanity back. And every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We will have to move from an endless war to an end of war, which is very important for humanity's well-being,” PM Modi said.
He added: “That all issues are resolved peacefully as soon as possible is the call of humanity. This is the message of India. This is the message of the land of Gandhi and the land of Buddha - the path to peace.”
PM Modi has repeatedly called for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the conflict. In 2022, he told Putin that “this is not the era of war”, while during his 2024 visit to Moscow, he said that no solution could be found on the battlefield.Jaishankar’s Kyiv visit comes amid heightened hostilities and concerns in New Delhi after an Indian was killed in the Ukrainian capital this week following a Russian strike. India has also raised concerns over attacks on merchant vessels in the Black Sea.

DOGE Affiliate Asked for College Credits for Participating in Takeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Christopher Sweet, an affiliate of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, requested college credit for his time in government, according to new documents obtained by a Freedom of Information Act request filed by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit legal organization.
Sweet was stationed at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), and in emails between Sweet and Scott Langmack, another DOGE affiliate at HUD, it appears that Sweet was looking to frame his work at HUD as an independent study worth three college credits. Sweet joined HUD in the spring of 2025 as an undergraduate college student at the University of Chicago to work on building an AI tool that would crawl through the agency’s rules and regulations and flag them for rescission, or the cancellation of contracts. The tool, called SweetRex, was intended to be rolled out across the federal government.
In an August 26, 2025 email titled “which of these should go to U Chicago,” Langmack wrote to Sweet saying, “I need to send them something that has specific framework of the different courses/credits we want them to give you.”
Documents attached to the email show that Sweet’s work was divided into four potential courses, “Advanced AI Prompt Engineering for Legal Reasoning,” “Applied Data Science for Federal Regulatory Analysis,” “Computer Programming for Scalable Al-Legal Systems,” and “Legislative & Regulatory Authority in AI-Driven Reform.” It appears these were meant to lead to a final proposed thesis focused on “the design, implementation, and impact of integrated AI, data science, software engineering, and legal authority analysis to rationalize outdated federal regulations.” The documents make clear that Sweet’s work was not an internship but, “graduate-level, multi-disciplinary research producing real-world outputs that are already influencing federal regulatory reform."
It appears that the final outline that was created to send to the University of Chicago for approval was created by AI. In an August 27, 2025 email, Langmack tells Sweet “I did the outline on ChatGPT.”
HUD and the University of Chicago did not reply to requests for comment. WIRED confirmed that Sweet did, in fact, graduate from the University of Chicago this June with a degree in economics, though it is unclear if credits from his time with DOGE contributed to the school’s requirements.
Langmack came to HUD from the property technology company Kukun—whose website describes it as being on “a long-term mission to aggregate the hardest to find data”—with zero experience in the federal government. He is now the executive director of deregulation AI at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), according to his LinkedIn. Langmack did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“These documents raise serious concerns about how one of DOGE’s unqualified employees has been entrusted to handle legal work, rewriting rules and regulations that affect millions of Americans, while attempting to count this work towards an undergraduate degree,” says Daniel McGrath, special counsel for oversight at Democracy Forward, describing the case as part of the “Trump-Vance administration’s relentless pursuit to cripple the important work of the federal government.”
