Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on September 3, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
18:29:28 CST
19:29:28 KST

At the invitation of Member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Minister of Foreign Affairs Wang Yi, Secretary of Foreign Affairs of Mexico Roberto Velasco Álvarez will visit China from September 6 to 7.
CCTV: Yesterday, President Xi Jinping successfully concluded his state visit to Egypt. Can you share more information about this visit?
Guo Jiakun: This is President Xi Jinping’s first state visit to Egypt in 10 years. As this year marks the 70th anniversary of the establishment of China-Egypt diplomatic relations, the visit carries great significance in building on the past achievements and charting the future of our bilateral ties. During the visit, President Xi Jinping held talks with President El-Sisi and had an in-depth exchange of views on China-Egypt relations, bilateral cooperation across the board, and international and regional issues of mutual interest.
President Xi pointed out that in recent years, the China-Egypt comprehensive strategic partnership has realized leapfrog development. Faced with the changing and turbulent international and regional situation, the two countries should support each other, deepen cooperation, and continue to build a China-Egypt community with a shared future. He emphasized that the two sides should firmly support each other, maintain the momentum of high-level exchanges, intensify exchanges and cooperation across different areas and levels, and strengthen the exchange and mutual learning of governance experience; the two sides should advance mutually beneficial cooperation, enhance synergy between development strategies, unleash cooperation potential in traditional areas, and foster new cooperation highlights in areas such as green energy; the two sides should promote people-to-people exchanges by expanding exchanges and cooperation across the board in areas such as culture and education, and increasing the flow of personnel, in order to boost connectivity between the two peoples; the two sides should strengthen security cooperation by jointly combating transnational crime, deepening international cooperation against corruption, and firmly supporting each other’s counter-terrorism efforts, so as to safeguard the two countries’ common security; and the two sides should enhance international and multilateral collaboration by coordinating and cooperating more closely at multilateral platforms such as the United Nations and BRICS, and jointly advancing the building of the China-Arab States Cooperation Forum and the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, to oppose unilateralism and bullying acts together, and promote a more just and equitable global governance system.
President Xi made a four-point proposal on improving the common security of the Middle East. First, unleashing the internal momentum of regional common security. The people in the Middle East should be the masters of their own affairs. Regional countries should be supported in strengthening dialogue on peace and security. Second, advancing the comprehensive governance of regional common security. The many highly interrelated hotspot issues in the Middle East require comprehensive solutions. Third, cementing the development foundation of regional common security. Lasting stability and security in the Middle East relies fundamentally on development. Fourth, enhancing international coordination on regional common security. The UN Charter and international law serve as the basic guidelines for handling Middle East affairs. The UN should be supported in playing a tangible role in regional affairs.
After the talks, the two presidents jointly witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents in areas including Belt and Road cooperation, artificial intelligence, economy and trade, and industrial and supply chain cooperation. The two sides issued the Joint Statement on Deepening the China-Egypt Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. During the visit, the two sides also signed more than 20 cooperation documents in areas such as digital economy, science and technology, education, and transport.
Pheonix TV: Yesterday, you said that China was preparing the third batch of relief supplies for Nepal. Could you share with us the latest progress? What cooperation has been carried out between China and Nepal on meteorological monitoring and disaster early-warning?
Guo Jiakun: The third batch of emergency relief supplies from China to Nepal has been sent this morning, including tents, blankets, mortuary refrigerators, medical protective suit and satellite communication equipment. China also sent a second group of DNA forensic experts to assist Nepal. The Xizang Autonomous Region has sent two Bailey bridges to Nepal. The Red Cross Society of China and China Foundation for Rural Development donated emergency relief supplies to Nepal. Associations of overseas Chinese and Chinese companies in Nepal have also offered support and donations. China will continue to provide emergency assistance and conduct international search and rescue cooperation in light of Nepal’s needs.
In the wake of the disaster, China’s meteorological, water resources and other authorities have conducted close cooperation with relevant Nepali authorities in sharing monitoring information and disaster response. The China Meteorological Administration (CMA) established immediate contact with the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology of Nepal. The two sides have held weather consultations via video link and shared information in real time. The CMA urgently developed a customized cloud edition of MAZU system and delivered it to Nepal for trial use to provide meteorological support for Nepal’s rescue and relief efforts. China’s Ministry of Water Resources has continuously shared with Nepal information on hydrological monitoring, early-warnings and forecasts. Nepal expressed deep appreciation to China for standing side by side with it in responding to the disaster and providing vital support for its relief efforts, and stated that this reflects the great friendship between the two neighbors. China will continue to enhance cooperation with Nepal in related areas and strongly support Nepal in its emergency rescue and relief efforts.
Xinhua News Agency: You just announced the upcoming visit by Mexican Secretary of Foreign Affairs Roberto Velasco Álvarez. How does China view the current bilateral ties with Mexico? What does China expect from the visit?
Guo Jiakun: Mexico is a major country in Latin America and an important emerging market. China and Mexico are comprehensive strategic partners. Over the past five decades since the establishment of diplomatic ties, China-Mexico relations have continued to develop in depth, with fruitful exchanges and cooperation across the board and close coordination and collaboration in international and regional affairs.
The upcoming visit will mark Mr. Velasco’s first visit to China since he took office in April. Through the visit, China hopes that the two sides will have an in-depth exchange of views on bilateral relations and international and regional issues of common interest, further enhance political mutual trust, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation, promote the steady growth of China-Mexico relations, and deliver more benefits to both peoples.
Reuters: Among the 21 dead already found on the Chinese side of the disaster so far, have their identifies been verified and are there foreign nationals among the deceased?
Guo Jiakun: The authorities of the Xizang Autonomous Region shared relevant information at their press briefings. We will continue communicating and coordinating with relevant parties to properly verify their identities and handle follow-up matters.
Global Times: The 2026 defense white paper recently issued by Japan’s Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed that Japan will further seek “enemy base strike capability.” The MoD also requested a record 8.89 trillion yen for fiscal year 2027. Comments say that Japan is stepping up effort to break free from postwar pacifism, abandon the “exclusively defense-oriented” policy and seek offensive capability. But some say that Japan has the right to become a “normal country” and develop military strength. Today marks the 81st anniversary of the victory of the Chinese People’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Do you think Japan is challenging the outcomes of WWII victory? How will China respond?
Guo Jiakun: The designation of the Victory Day of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression is to remember the profound suffering that Japanese militarist aggression imposed on the people of China and the rest of the world, to remind the public not to forget history, and to uphold the outcomes of WWII victory and postwar international order.
Over the years, Japanese right-wing forces have tried to turn the verdict on the history of aggression, and break free from the postwar international arrangements and their international obligations. It needs to be stressed that a series of international instruments including the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and Japan’s Instrument of Surrender have affirmed in legal terms Japan’s status as a defeated state, and explicitly stipulated the obligations of defeated states, including eradicating militarism, abolishing military industries, dismantling war capability, and not rearming for war. These postwar international arrangements help uphold historical truth and international justice, set up an institutional line of defense against the resurrection of militarism, and embody the outcomes of the victory of the World Anti-Fascist War.
Our solemn message to Japanese right-wing forces: the right way forward for Japan is to fulfill its international obligations, fully remove the pernicious influence of militarism, and keep to peaceful development. China will stand together with peace-loving countries in the world to firmly hold back the malevolent emergence of Japanese neo-militarism under the pretext of making Japan a “normal country,” and prevent it from wreaking havoc to the region and beyond.
Bloomberg: Some in Nepal are demanding climate compensation from the world’s biggest emitters of greenhouse gases. This would be the U.S., India and China. This comes after the deadly flood that killed many people. Would the foreign ministry like to comment?
Guo Jiakun: Climate change is a global challenge that requires the collective efforts of all parties. China has been a steadfast actor and major contributor in promoting global green development. We are making active and sound efforts towards the carbon peak and neutrality goals and expected to make the world’s biggest cut in carbon emission intensity. As the largest developing country, China firmly upholds the legitimate and lawful rights and interests of the developing world, strives for a fair and equitable global climate governance system for win-win cooperation, and provides assistance to other developing countries to the best of its capability via South-South cooperation.
China and Nepal are a community with a shared future linked by mountains and rivers. And China is also severely affected by this cross-border disaster. We are ready to strengthen cooperation with Nepal and the rest of the international community to jointly prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change.
NHK: The Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union is reportedly considering sending a delegation to China this month, which consists of young lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties. How does the Chinese side view this initiative and what’s your expectation？
Guo Jiakun: Some visionary people in Japan are deeply concerned over the current state of China-Japan relations and wish to make an effort to improve bilateral ties. We are ready to engage with them in the hope of enhancing mutual understanding and trust as long as they abide by the four political documents, support a friendly China policy, and cherish China-Japan relations. We call on those running the government of Japan to listen to and value the voice of reason at home and create the conditions necessary for normal exchanges between China and Japan with concrete actions.
Reuters: The president of Palau and current chair of the regional Pacific Islands Forum said today he was hoping to gain consensus from member nations to condemn a Chinese missile test recently held in the region. What is the foreign ministry’s comment?
Guo Jiakun: China has more than once made clear its position on the test launch. Palau has repeatedly raised this issue in an ill-intentioned attempt to hijack the position of other member states of the Pacific Islands Forum. It will not have its way.
China is committed to peaceful development and a national defense policy that is defensive in nature. We never engage in military expansion. China stands ready to work with South Pacific countries to contribute to peace, stability, development and prosperity of the South Pacific region.
Bloomberg: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said that China won’t have any debt claims to the revenue from new oil production in Venezuela. If this happens, can you provide more details of how China might protect its interests in Venezuela? Does China feel like it can rely on international law to protect its interests in this case? Finally, are you worried at all that the U.S. attitude on oil and Venezuela might set a precedent and encourage Washington to seize Chinese assets in Latin America or elsewhere?
Guo Jiakun: China-Venezuela cooperation is protected by international law and laws of both countries. The cooperation does not concern any third party and should not be subjected to interference by any third party. China’s lawful rights and interests in Venezuela must be protected.
Shenzhen TV: Viet Nam’s foreign ministry spokesperson reportedly said in a recent statement that Viet Nam has sovereignty over the Paracels and reiterated that “all foreign activities in the Paracel Islands, including at Ba Ba Island and at Hai Sam Reef, conducted without Viet Nam’s permission are completely illegal, null and void.” The country has made serious representations and demands an immediate end to such activities and that they not be repeated, she added. What’s China’s comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: Xisha Qundao is China’s territory without any dispute. It is within China’s sovereign rights to conduct necessary construction on its own territory. There is no room for unwarranted accusations from Viet Nam.
AFP: The coast guard of Taiwan said today that it deployed vessels to monitor two Chinese ships operating in waters to its east, saying it firmly rejects China’s campaign of “law enforcement in name, jurisdictional expansion in practice.” Does the Chinese foreign ministry have a reaction to this?
Guo Jiakun: This is not a question about foreign affairs.

Moscow airports cancel flights after Zelensky's 'closed skies' warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:29:11 UTC
19:29:11 KST

Flights in and out of Moscow's Vnukovo and Sheremetyevo airports were restricted for the second night in a row on Sept. 2, after Ukraine warned of a new campaign to "close" Russian skies.
"Temporary restrictions on the arrival and departure of aircraft have been introduced," Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsia) said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 1 warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drones.
Zelensky gave few details about what the new campaign would entail, other than making clear it would involve lots of drones.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said, as he warned "every airline that uses Russian airspace" against flying over the country.
Most Western airlines stopped flying to Russia after the launch of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. One exception is Turkey's Pegasus Airlines, which on Sept. 2 announced that "flights to Russia scheduled overnight from 1 to 2 September were canceled due to technical and operational reasons."
It added that flights from "Sept. 2 onwards are operating as scheduled."
But FlightRadar24 live tracking of arrivals at Sheremetyevo Airport showed almost every flight scheduled for the afternoon of Sept. 3 either delayed or canceled. A similar situation was reported at Vnukovo Airport.
FlightRadar24 also reported that overnight on Sept. 2, 21 flights were canceled and 235 delayed at Sheremetyevo, while 22 flights were canceled and 94 delayed at Vnukovo.
Zelensky's announcement comes at a time when, in the absence of meaningful changes on the front lines, both Ukraine and Russia are looking for other ways to increase pressure on each other.
For Russia, this has meant a drastic escalation in drone and missile strikes, particularly on Kyiv.
For Ukraine, lacking the long-range missile firepower of Russia, it means becoming more creative with long-range drones.
Forcing the closure of Russian airspace using drones is not a new idea, and Ukraine has been employing the tactic for nearly a year and a half.
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) began Operation Carpet in the spring of last year, with the aim of disrupting Russian airport operations by deliberately flying drones over them, people familiar with the matter, who did not want to be named for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.

Gloria Steinem, feminist activist and journalist, dies at 92

Gloria Steinem, feminist activist and journalist, dies at 92
September 3, 2026
Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem has died, her foundation announced Thursday.
She was 92.
Steinem "passed away peacefully at her home in New York City" on Wednesday, her foundation said.
"Gloria's near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end," it added. "Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor."
Who was Gloria Steinem, feminist trailblazer and journalist?
Steinem became one of the most visible symbols of the US women's movement, helping lead the country's second wave of feminism. She was a fierce advocate for feminist causes throughout her life.
She spent much of her life on the road, speaking at college campuses, community centers, rallies and marches.
"She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing," her foundation said.
From caretaking daughter to Playboy bunny
Born on March 25, 1935, in Toledo, Ohio, as the younger of two daughters, Steinem did not attend school regularly until around seventh grade due to her father's work as a traveling antique dealer and the subsequent frequent movement of her family.
Her parents separated when she was 11, pushing her to take care of her mother, who suffered from depression and had a mental breakdown. It was her earliest lesson in social injustice and the constraints she believed marriage placed on women, shaping her belief that the institution robbed women of choices and many of their civil rights.
"I'd already been the very small parent of a very big child, my mother. I didn't want to end up taking care of someone else," she was quoted as saying.
She began freelancing as a journalist following her graduation from Smith College.
In 1963, she had a brief stint with Playboy as a bunny. She used her experience to produce her groundbreaking expose "A Bunny's Tale" for Show magazine, where she shed light on the poor pay and sexist treatment Playboy bunnies endured.
She then helped found New York Magazine in 1968. Her essay "After Black Power, Women's Liberation" is credited with kickstarting her status as a feminist leader.
For Steinem, her activism work gained momentum a year later, when she attended an abortion speak-out in a New York church. She had to get a then-illegal abortion in London at 22, making the topic of the speak-out very personal.
Steinem's feminist career and focus on race
In 1971, Steinem co-founded Ms. Magazine, where issues such as abortion, sexism, equal pay and domestic violence were tackled, in sharp contrast to the topics covered by women's magazines of the time.
She also founded the National Women's Political Caucus in the same year.
Other groups she created or helped create include the Coalition of Labor Union Women, the Women's Media Center, Voters for Choice and the Ms. Foundation for Women.
With her signature long, blonde-streaked, center-parted hair and aviator glasses, Steinem became the glamorous symbol of the feminist movement.
She believed the movement should represent women of every race.
"If you've suffered discrimination, you're sensitive to it on every level. I learned feminism largely from Black women. Women of color basically invented feminism," she told the New Yorker.
In 2013, then-President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest US civilian honor.
Steinem never had children and only married at 66 to South African businessman and environmentalist David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale. He died of brain cancer in 2003.
"I hope this proves what feminists have always said - that feminism is about the ability to choose what’s right at each time of our lives," she said in a statement about the marriage.

&quot;The war will not be resolved through the purchase or non-purchase of oil&quot; — India&apos;s Foreign Minister

"The war will not be resolved through the purchase or non-purchase of oil" — India's Foreign Minister
Kyiv • UNN
Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said in Kyiv that India respects Ukraine's position on this issue. At the same time, he emphasized the difficulty of supplying India's population with energy.
India's Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said that the war would not be resolved through buying or refusing to buy oil and other costly resources. He said this in Kyiv at a press conference with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, emphasizing the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and negotiations, reports UNN.
Details
Subrahmanyam Jaishankar emphasized the complexity of supplying India's population with energy and of the global energy situation in general.
I believe it is important that you all understand the complexity of supplying one and four billion people with energy at a time when the global energy situation is very, very difficult
He also added that Ukraine has its own position on this issue, which India respects, just as it expects its own position to be respected.
I would say that this is an issue on which the Ukrainian side has its position, which we respect, and we have ours, which I would expect others to respect as well. But let me add this. This conflict, which has now been ongoing for the fifth year, will not be resolved because someone buys or does not buy oil, alumina, minerals, metals or fertilizers. This conflict will be resolved through dialogue, diplomacy and negotiations, and that is precisely what we will support
We remind you
Indian oil refineries are reducing purchases of Russian oil from elevated levels, amid the impact of damage on supplies from the country's leading supplier.

Dartmoor firing times
Information on Dartmoor Training Area's firing times.
Documents
Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.

Guidance: Dartmoor firing times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:26:57 BST
19:26:57 KST

Dartmoor firing times
Information on Dartmoor Training Area's firing times.
Documents
Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.

South Korea seeks indictment of K-Pop mogul behind BTS over alleged investor fraud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:26:43 UTC
19:26:43 KST

South Korean police are pushing for an indictment of music tycoon Bang Si-hyuk, the chairperson of the agency behind K-pop supergroup BTS, over alleged investor fraud.
The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency referred Bang to the Seoul Southern District Prosecutors’ Office on Thursday, asking him to be indicted on a charge of violating the capital markets act, according to the police agency and the prosecutor’s office.
Police have been investigating Bang, the billionaire founder and chairperson of Hybe, over allegations that he misled investors in 2019 by indicating that Hybe had no immediate plans to go public, prompting them to sell their shares to a private equity fund shortly before the company proceeded with an initial public offering.
Police earlier said that the fund may have paid Bang somewhere around 200 billion won ($147 million) in a side deal that promised him 30 percent of post-IPO stock sale profits.
South Korean media reported that police referred four other people, including Hybe executives and private equity fund officials, to prosecutors on Thursday as well, asking for their indictment.
Hybe officials have said Bang denies any wrongdoing.
“We have consistently responded to the allegations with objective evidence and facts," Bang's legal team said in a statement on Thursday. "We expect the allegations to be fully and transparently resolved through the legal process.”
Police earlier sought Bang’s arrest twice in April and May. But prosecutors rejected those requests, saying police failed to provide sufficient grounds for his arrest and failed to comply with prosecutors' demand for further investigation of Bang.
Observers say prosecutors could again ask for further police investigation, rather than indicting Bang immediately.
News of Bang’s legal troubles flared after BTS returned and launched a much-awaited world tour earlier this year after a nearly four-year musical hiatus due to the band members’ mandatory military service in South Korea.

Putin's 'global battle' against US & NATO: Russia 'testing' NATO since 2022 Ukraine invasion began
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:26:42 UTC
19:26:42 KST

Putin's 'global battle' against US, NATO: Russia 'testing' NATO since 2022 Ukraine invasion began
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Anna Borshchevskaya, Senior Fellow at The Washington Institute. She interprets Russia’s reported missile support for Iran not as an isolated arms transaction, but as part of a broader geopolitical strategy in which Moscow treats Ukraine, Iran, NATO, and the United States as interconnected fronts. In her analysis, Vladimir Putin’s objective is less about pursuing direct military confrontation with Washington than about altering the strategic environment around it: strengthening actors hostile to the United States, increasing the costs of American and Israeli military action, and repeatedly probing Western thresholds for retaliation.
Putin relentlessly tests where Western “red lines” actually lie rather than where Western governments say they lie: Russian drones entering NATO territory, cyberattacks, disinformation, support for Iran, and the continuing war in Ukraine become different expressions of the same strategic logic. Her “bigger chessboard” metaphor captures this interpretation particularly well. It presents Putin as connecting geographically distinct conflicts through a common calculus of pressure, escalation, and opportunity.
There is also an important political dimension to her argument. Borshchevskaya suggests that Moscow has a strong interest in the survival of the existing Iranian regime, because the emergence of a pro-Western government in Tehran would represent a major strategic setback for Russia. On this reading, Russian military assistance does more than improve Iranian capabilities: it helps preserve a regional order advantageous to Moscow. Her broader warning is that insufficiently enforced Western red lines can themselves become strategically consequential, encouraging further attempts to determine just how far Russia could go.

Son of Iran's former vice president received over $2 million in Canadian gov't contracts - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:25:36 UTC
19:25:36 KST

The son of Iran's former vice president received over $2 million in contracts from the Canadian government as he worked to further the regime's missile program and help it evade sanctions, Global News reported on Wednesday, citing obtained documents.
According to the report, 45-year-old Mohammad Reza Ghafouri Fard, son of Iranian politician and former vice president Hassan Ghafouri Fard, operated under the pseudonym Sal Ghafouri while living in Edmonton.
He received the government contracts while participating in an official Canadian trade mission to Latin America, Global News reported, with the intention of the funds being to help Fard “propose legislation” to Canada's government.
Fard is already the subject of a long-running investigation by the Canadian government into his suspected ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the report added.
Global News cited a recently declassified Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) report, which said Fard was “involved in the research and development of Iranian military technologies.”
Specifically, he assisted the regime in its attempts to "confront American aircraft" through the development of an anti-aircraft missile system and jamming system, having participated in a “covert procurement structure” designed to procure components for such projects.
Canada: Fard admitted to participating in activities beneficial to regime
The CSIS report cited by Global News further claimed that Fard “admitted to active participation in procurement activities that benefited the Iranian military, including the IRGC.”
CSIS noted in its report that Fard had traveled to Iran in 2015 to meet with members of Iran's Intelligence and Security Ministry on two separate occasions, during which he "provided details of his employment in Canada."
“During the second meeting, he was given detailed instructions and warnings, as they related to police or intelligence services approaching him while living in Canada,” CSIS was cited as saying.

SCO summit injects vitality into regional development: Chinese FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
18:25:26 CST
19:25:26 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Through the collective efforts of all parties concerned, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit in Bishkek has injected vitality into regional development, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has said.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks while briefing reporters on the conclusion of Chinese President Xi Jinping's attendance at the SCO Bishkek Summit and state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt.
The SCO summit also fostered synergy for global multipolarity, and provided fresh impetus for improving global governance, which once again demonstrated the vitality and capacity for action of the organization, said Wang.
At the Bishkek Summit, Xi said the SCO's most significant achievement has been its gradual transformation into a new type of regional cooperation organization that spans the largest geographical area, represents the largest population, and possesses enormous development potential in the world.
He said the SCO's most valuable spiritual asset is the pioneering proposal of and steadfast adherence to the "Shanghai Spirit" of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations and pursuit of common development.
The SCO's most important experience for cooperation is that it has found the right way of coexistence featuring non-alliances, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, while bringing countries in the region together to build a common home, he added.
Xi put forward a four-point proposal at the summit: stay committed to putting development first, and open up the prospects for shared prosperity; stay committed to taking security as a key goal, and foster an environment of common security; stay committed to a people-centered approach, and cement the foundation for everlasting friendship; and stay committed to dialogue and consultation, and strive for more equitable and orderly governance.
Wang recalled last year's SCO Tianjin Summit, where Xi and leaders of other SCO member states charted a blueprint for the organization's development over the next decade, ushering in a new stage of high-quality development for the SCO. The outcomes of the summit are being implemented at an accelerated pace, he noted.
At this year's SCO summit, Wang said, the strategic blueprint drawn up in Tianjin is gradually becoming a reality, with the organization's structure becoming more optimized, its operations more efficient, and its cooperation more effective. ■

Interview: Egypt-China ties set example of community with shared future -- Egyptian official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
18:25:19 CST
19:25:19 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, Egypt and China are joining hands to build a better future based on a long-term vision and make their relationship a model for building a community with a shared future for humanity, a senior Egyptian official has said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has concluded his state visit to Egypt on Wednesday. Osama El-Gohary, assistant to the Prime Minister of Egypt and chairman of the Information and Decision Support Center, said Xi's visit carries significance beyond bilateral relations.
"Head-of-state diplomacy provides strategic vision and political guidance for the development of Egypt-China relations," he said in a written interview with Xinhua, perceiving close communication between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Xi as an important driving force behind the growth of bilateral relations in recent years.
Since the establishment of diplomatic ties 70 years ago, the two sides have upheld mutual respect and equality, respected each other's development paths, and pursued mutual benefit and win-win cooperation, said the official.
"The political mutual trust accumulated over 70 years has not only provided a strong basis for building a better future, but also laid a solid foundation for a dynamic partnership capable of meeting challenges," he said.
Looking back on the development of bilateral relations, El-Gohary said Egypt-China cooperation has shown strong adaptability and creativity, with its scope continuing to expand. Despite frequent geopolitical conflicts and growing economic uncertainty around the world, the two countries have remained firmly committed to maintaining and developing their bilateral relations amid an ever-evolving global landscape, he said.
"With this valuable strategic resolve, both sides have strengthened consultations and coordination, and continuously expanded the scope of cooperation, which is particularly valuable in an era of uncertainty," the official said.
El-Gohary said the strategic guidance of head-of-state diplomacy is helping the two sides turn political consensus into more practical joint projects and expand areas of cooperation.
Egypt was the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China. El-Gohary said the two countries have maintained coordination on international and regional issues and are playing an increasingly important role in Arab-China, Africa-China and South-South cooperation.
He described Egypt as a potential bridge linking China with the Arab world and Africa, while viewing China as an important partner in Egypt's drive for development and modernization.
"Deepening the partnership between the two countries can generate positive effects beyond the bilateral framework and contribute to regional development, stability and cooperation," El-Gohary said. ■

Xi's Kyrgyzstan visit promotes permanent good-neighborliness, friendship: Chinese FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
18:25:19 CST
19:25:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Kyrgyzstan has strengthened the bonds of permanent good-neighborliness and friendship between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has said.
It has also opened up new prospects for shared prosperity, deepened commitment to a shared future and demonstrated China's principle of amity, sincerity, mutual benefit and inclusiveness in its neighborhood diplomacy, he noted.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks while briefing reporters on the conclusion of Xi's attendance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit in Bishkek and state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt from Aug. 30 to Sept. 3.
The visit to the Central Asian nation came as China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation has ushered in a "golden period" of rapid development, as noted by Xi in a written speech delivered upon his arrival, with the two countries working to translate their longstanding friendship and strong political mutual trust into broader cooperation and greater benefits for their people.
During the Kyrgyz leg of the trip, the two sides signed more than 30 cooperation documents covering trade, transportation, science and technology, education, cultural and people-to-people exchanges, among other areas.
The most significant political outcome was the signing by the two heads of state of a treaty on permanent good-neighborliness, friendship and cooperation, which legally cemented their commitment to everlasting friendship, Wang said.
The treaty marks a new level of political mutual trust, mutual support and strategic coordination, while opening broader avenues for future relations, he noted.
The two heads of state also agreed to elevate practical cooperation, with high-quality Belt and Road cooperation as the main focus, consolidating trade and investment, connectivity and green minerals cooperation while expanding into emerging fields such as the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence, Wang added.
Xi, during his talks with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, said the two sides should ensure the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, calling it a major transportation artery that carries the development aspirations of the people across the region.
Japarov, for his part, said Kyrgyzstan stands ready to actively advance the construction of the railway project, so as to turn it into a "steel Silk Road" for the new era and a new bond of friendship between the two countries. ■

Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:25:06 UTC
19:25:06 KST

Feminist activist and journalist Gloria Steinem died on Wednesday at age 92, a post on her official Instagram page stated.
She "passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her," the post read.
Steinem was a symbol and perhaps the most recognizable icon of second-wave feminism, when feminism grew from women's suffrage into a broader campaign for equality in all spheres.
She also worked to include all women in the feminist movement, regardless of race.
"If you've suffered discrimination, you're sensitive to it on every level. I learned feminism largely from Black women. Women of color basically invented feminism," she told the New Yorker.
Steinem gains attention from Playboy expose
She first gained notice as a journalist when she went undercover as a Playboy bunny in 1963 to write an expose on the working conditions within Hugh Hefner's Playboy clubs.
Steinem later stated that she worried the article damaged her career, causing editors to see her as a Playboy bunny first and a writer second. She had already been described as "this year's pretty girl," who "pretends to be a writer" by renowned writers Gay Talese and Saul Bellow.
But after covering a group of women who had begun to discuss the indignity and physical danger they encountered while seeking abortions, feminism became a larger part of Steinem's life, ultimately causing her to decide the article had been worth it.
Steinem founded Ms. magazine in 1971, a groundbreaking magazine written for women by women which tackled abortion and other issues such as sexism, equal pay, and domestic violence - a far cry from the diet of beauty, cookery, and supporting-your-husband topics that were the staple of magazines aimed at women.
One of its early features listed prominent women who publicly declared that they had received abortions, including Steinem herself.
Steinem's work founding information center, political groups
Steinem also helped to found the Women's Action Alliance, a national information center that specialized in nonsexist, multiracial children's education; the National Women's Political Caucus, a group that works to advance numbers of pro-equality women in elected and appointed office at the national and state level; and the Women's Media Center.
She was president and co-founder of Voters for Choice, a pro-choice political action comittee, and co-founder and board member of Choice USA, a national organization that supports young pro-choice leadership and works to preserve comprehensive sex-education in schools.
She was also the founding president of the Ms. Foundation for Women, a national multi-racial, multi-issue fund supporting grassroots projects to empower women and girls. She was a member of the Beyond Racism Initiative, a three-year effort in which activists and experts from South Africa, Brazil, and the US compared the racial patterns of those three countries and learned cross-nationally.
Steinem received multiple awards for her activism, writing, and production of documentaries on violence against women and children.
She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Barack Obama in 2019.

Historic Hong Kong pawn shop gets new lease on life as vibrant community space
One Bite Social and Lion Rock Heritage Foundation transform Chun On Pawn Shop into pop-up community and exhibition space
Inside a pre-war building in the heart of Hong Kong’s busy Wan Chai district, coffee, curios and Cantopop are now the fresh attractions breathing new energy into a historic pawn shop that closed its doors two years ago.
As the nostalgic tunes of late Cantopop legend Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing spin on vinyl and fill the air, curious passers-by step inside to see the shop – located in the venerable tong lau or tenement building – that’s been granted a new lease on life.
Built in 1924, the four-storey structure became home to Chun On Pawn Shop more than eight decades ago. After ceasing operations in 2024, the shop reopened in mid-August as a pop-up community and exhibition space. The venue now features old pawnbroking artefacts, historical photographs and workshops and community activities.
At 11am on Thursday, roughly a dozen residents dropped by to explore the building, whose ground floor was traditionally covered by a large screen to protect the transactions and privacy of clients.
Paula Chan, a retiree who has lived in Wan Chai for 50 years, said she was drawn by the nostalgic charm of the pawn shop while on her way to purchase groceries in the nearby wet market.

‘Even I can’t mess this up’: Behind the lens in Iceland with the ‘really bad photographer'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:21:11 UTC
19:21:11 KST

What happens when Iceland’s most beautiful landscapes meet the ‘world’s worst photographer’? Icelandair set Blanche Mortemard on a 10-day adventure, and here’s what her itinerary looked like.
As the old adage goes, a picture is worth a thousand words. Light, shadows, depth of field and colour can all be used to capture a sense of place and tell a destination’s story. Icelandair, however, decided to turn that theory on its head.
And typically, when an airline launches a search for a new photographer, you’d expect a pristine portfolio to be part of the application. That was not the case with Blanche Mortemard, who had something rather different: a “camera roll of bad photos”, as described to Euronews Travel.
Out of 127,642 people who came forward to share their, well, lack of photographic talent in the hopes of being crowned the “world’s worst photographer”, it was Mortemard’s collection of snaps that stood out.
The carrier set out to prove that even someone with zero photography skills can take great photos of the Nordic island as part of its "Really Bad Photographer" campaign.
“This is part four of our 'Real Unreal' umbrella,” Gísli S. Brynólfsson, Icelandair's director of global marketing, told Euronews Travel, adding that since 2025, the carrier has been emphasising the country’s authenticity and realness as a destination of choice against the rise of AI-generated images and spread of misleading travel information.
“When it comes to representing Iceland in images, there simply is no need for AI.”
Real Unreal started when Icelandair shared photographs on its social media platforms of eruptions in the volcanic Reykjanes Peninsula as well as scenes from the Northern Lights.
“This sparked conversation about whether the photos were real or not, and we realised people had just stopped trusting images on the internet related to Iceland,” Brynólfsson said.
So, when it came to their latest campaign, the idea was simple: the real Iceland doesn’t need filters to impress, nor a skilled photographer either.
“We believe that Iceland is that real and that beautiful that even the worst photographer is able to take a beautiful photo in Iceland,” he added.
What made Mortemard’s portfolio stand out? Well, as you might imagine, choosing one bad photographer out of a mountain of applications was no easy task.
In Mortemard’s case, however, her “lack of talent isn’t something you can imitate”, Brynólfsson said.
Ten days in Iceland
Over the course of 10 days, Mortemard, a Paris native who until recently had never visited Iceland, took as many as 7,000 photos of the island.
“I knew what the country looked like, thanks to there being so many photos of Iceland online,” she told Euronews Travel.
“Before ever visiting, I had seen the landscapes, the glaciers, mountains and waterfalls, but I never would have believed there would be so many different landscapes all around me that I would see during such a short period of time.”
Her excursion began fresh off the plane, in Reykjanes, around 50 kilometres away from the capital, Reykjavik, as she launched her unconventional career as a bad photographer.
With her trusty camera in hand, she saw the peninsula’s lava fields, the geothermal water of the Blue Lagoon, met locals and even challenged a fellow tourist to a worst photographer battle to see who could snap a terrible picture.
After working up an appetite, she was treated to freshly baked rye bread, which reminded her of French “pain de campagne” – a rustic sourdough loaf.
The rest of her photography expedition took her to Icelandic attractions such as the picturesque Seljalandsfoss waterfall, Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon and the Hverfjall volcano.
Along the way, she also had a bingo card of challenges, which included taking an “iconic selfie”, witnessing a geyser erupt, taking a photo with a funny road sign, and seeing 20 waterfalls.
Exploring the country’s remarkable landscapes, however, didn’t shake her bad photographer crown, even an inch.
“There were lots of times where I would see the mountains and waterfalls and think, ‘even I can’t mess this up', but I’m still credible as a bad photographer,” she said.
Perusing through a sneak preview of her recent portfolio, this travel journalist did spot her finger occasionally making an appearance in the frame.
“As time went on, I did improve,” she said. “I started thinking more about what I wanted to capture and where my fingers are – in fact, most of my photos had my fingers in them,” she said, adding that there ought to be at least one award-winning snap in the bunch.
While a coveted photography award may not be in the bag just yet, what’s for certain is she is leaving the experience with her own personal favourite snaps.
“I feel the best photo of the trip was at Kerlingarfjöll,” she said, adding that the colours of the mountain range, plus her newly found composition skills, showed up so well on her camera.
“The second would be at Vestrahorn – here I think was a turning point for me,” she said.
“I managed to capture the atmosphere: the mountain had a crown of clouds and the sand was gliding across the ground. This was one of the first times I didn’t just press ‘click’, I decided the angle and what I wanted to share with everyone through my picture.”
Not only does she leave the experience with new-found photography skills, Mortemard said she’s now a different traveller, too.
After her road trip through Iceland, where she got to see and experience different things in one trip, she sees herself doing that in the future: “I’ll think more about road tripping, rather than just staying in one place for too long.”
If, like this travel journalist, you’re eager to see the final product of Mortemard’s unique style of photography and meet her in person, her photos will be gracing the walls of London’s White Rabbit Studios from 11-12 September. There are also future plans to showcase her talents across other cities in Europe and North America.
Exploring Iceland with the ‘really bad photographer’
Where Blanche Mortemard went
- Reykjanes Peninsula, southwest Iceland
- Gígjagjá cave (otherwise known as the “Yoda Cave”), in Hjörleifshöfði. Mortemard was especially fascinated by the black sands
- Stuðlagil canyon, in Jokuldalur Valley
- Hverfjall, in Mývatn where Mortemard went hiking
- Önundarfjörður Pier in the Westfjords A full map of where her Icelandic travels took her can be found here.
New foods she liked (and perhaps didn’t like so much)
- Rúgbrauð: Icelandic rye bread
- Kjötsúpa: Icelandic hearty lamb stew and Mortemard’s personal favourite from the trip
- Hákarl: A fermented shark dish, which, according to Mortemard, is “nice to try… but only once”.
- Plokkfiskur: Fish stew made with a béchamel sauce and potatoes
- Pönnukaka: Thin pancakes

El Niño is surging. Months of extreme heat could follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:21:04 UTC
19:21:04 KST

El Niño is surging. Months of extreme heat could follow
Fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters, the El Niño climate pattern is intensifying and has yet to peak. Forecasters are almost certain it will persist through February 2027 – with unusually warm conditions expected across much of the world in the coming months.
El Niño is strengthening rapidly in the Pacific Ocean, raising the prospect of months of extreme heat, floods, drought, and disruptive weather around the globe.
The phenomenon, already firmly established, is expected to become “very strong” and peak around the end of the year, according to new forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
The likelihood that El Niño will persist through February 2027 is now close to 100 per cent. Never before has the UN weather agency issued such an unequivocal forecast for El Niño or its cooler counterpart, La Niña.
A supersize problem
And beneath the surface of the tropical Pacific lies another cause for concern. An enormous reservoir of unusually warm water that could continue feeding El Niño in the months ahead.
In some parts of the Pacific, subsurface temperatures in July and early August were more than eight degrees Celsius (around 14 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal.
The combination points toward an unusually powerful climate event unfolding on a planet already significantly warmer because of greenhouse gas emissions.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a press release on Thursday. “The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern that typically develops every two to seven years, when waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific become unusually warm. That warming can alter atmospheric circulation thousands of miles away, shifting rainfall and temperature patterns everywhere.
But this El Niño is developing against an unusual backdrop. The oceans are already exceptionally warm, providing a hotter baseline on which the natural climate cycle is playing out.
Scientists have not established that man-made climate change is increasing or intensifying El Niño. But a warmer atmosphere and ocean can amplify some of its consequences, increasing the heat and moisture available to fuel extreme weather.
The latest measurements show how quickly the current event is developing.
The Niño 3.4 index, a closely watched measure of ocean temperatures in the central tropical Pacific, averaged 1.5°C above normal from May through July. By July, it had reached 2°C, and weekly readings from late July through mid-August climbed as high as 2.6 degrees.
The heat extends well below the surface – a sign that the warming is not fleeting and that El Niño has considerable fuel left.
A global pattern, uneven consequences
A very strong El Niño does not mean that every region will experience disasters of the same magnitude.
From September through November, however, forecasters expect above-normal temperatures across nearly the entire Earth’s surface.
Rainfall patterns are also taking on the characteristic signature of El Niño, with greater chances of heavy rain and flooding in some places and drought in others.
Other forces could complicate that picture. A positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole – another large-scale shift in ocean temperatures – is expected to develop, while the tropical Atlantic is forecast to remain unusually warm.
Those overlapping patterns make it impossible to translate the strength of El Niño into a precise forecast for any individual country. But collectively, the signals point toward a period of heightened risk.
“El Niño means ‘little boy’ in Spanish, but it has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies around the world,” Celeste Saulo, head of WMO, said. “We are already seeing the disruption and devastation caused by droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to worsen as El Niño intensifies.”
Historic mobilisation
The forecast has prompted an unusual response. It’s the first time ever WHO has launched a mobilisation of this scale with national weather agencies, seeking to strengthen forecasts and early-warning systems as the risks mount.
The effort is intended to help governments and humanitarian organizations prepare for the effects on particularly vulnerable sectors, including agriculture, public health, energy and water supplies.
“This exceptional El Niño demands exceptional preparedness and response,” Ms. Saulo said.
That underscores how much of this El Niño still lies ahead. The phenomenon is already exceptionally strong, and it has yet to peak.
The question is no longer whether El Niño will strengthen, but how much heat – and disruption – it will leave behind.

Nepal floods leave 22,000 children without safe water: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:20:46 UTC
19:20:46 KST

Nepal floods leave 22,000 children without safe water: UNICEF
More than a week after flash floods struck the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river basin in Nepal, at least 22,000 children urgently need safe drinking water, sanitation and hygiene support, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Thursday.
Water systems have been damaged across affected districts, while toilets and other sanitation facilities have been damaged or destroyed, raising the risk of waterborne and infectious diseases.
“Every parent in these districts is now making the same calculation several times a day,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative in Nepal. “Where can I get water, and is it safe to give to my child?”
Crowded living conditions
Affected families are now living with host communities or in holding centres— crowded spaces that make it difficult to maintain safe hygiene practices.
This week, the World Health Organization (WHO) highlighted how flooding, displacement, overcrowding and stagnant water can increase the risk of communicable diseases such as dengue and scrub typhus.
“The risk of waterborne disease increases rapidly in these conditions, but it is preventable,” Ms. Akunga insisted.
Supplies reach communities
UNICEF has dispatched water, sanitation and hygiene supplies for around 19,000 people in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, among the hardest hit areas.
These items include more than 3,800 hygiene kits, 3,300 collapsible 10-litre jerrycans, 3,500 buckets, 3,500 one-litre mugs, 4,000 bottles of water treatment solution and more than 1,000 tarpaulin sheets.
Staff are also working with government counterparts and partners on disease surveillance, hygiene promotion and outbreak prevention.
Critical infrastructure destroyed
The flooding was triggered by a glacier collapse on the Nepal-China border on 27 August. The death toll has surpassed 1,100, according to international media reports.
Infrastructure such as roads, bridges, telecommunications networks as well as water systems were damaged, complicating access to communities and delivery of aid.
UNICEF estimates that at least 19 schools have been damaged, including eight that were completely and eight partially destroyed, while more than 10,000 school-age children need immediate psychosocial support and access to safe learning spaces.
Young lives upended
“Before all this, I used to spend most of my time in school and hang out with friends when I was free,” Swostik Paudel, a 14-year-old from Nuwakot, recently told the agency. “Mostly we would play football.”
Swostik is now living in a shelter with his parents and sister where he tries to remain connected to his former life.
“Some children have brought a football here,” he said. “Even though it’s punctured, we’ve been passing it around. Some friends have also been playing matches.”
Building back better
As access improves, UNICEF will scale up emergency water supply, household water treatment, water-quality monitoring, temporary sanitation and handwashing facilities, and essential hygiene and menstrual hygiene supplies in communities and holding centres.
Ms. Akunga said restoring safe water and sanitation “is not a one-week job”. She stressed that damaged water systems, pipelines, pumps, toilets and other sanitation infrastructure need to be repaired and rebuilt to withstand future floods.
“We need to make communities safer and more resilient,” she said. “Otherwise, we will be having the same conversation again after the next disaster, and it will be children paying the price yet again.”

A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choose in the glare of the world’s attention.
The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “dilapidated” off-grid home in Italy last year.
It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles.
They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children.
In September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities.
In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling.
Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling.
On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “gradual reunification process”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility.
“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a gradual reunification process, allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend overnight stays with their family,” their lawyer, Simone Pillon, said.
In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”.
They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they chose Italy for reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds.
The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”.
“We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote.
“How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents?
“How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?”
Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. She expressed “alarm” over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping.
But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education.
After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen.
The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote.
“We are deeply saddened by this.
“We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.”
The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification.

One in five children in 21 nations faced tech-facilitated sexual abuse: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:20:15 UTC
19:20:15 KST

One in five children in 21 nations faced tech-facilitated sexual abuse: UNICEF
About 20 million children aged 12 to 17 – one in five across 21 countries – were sexually exploited by perpetrators using technology such as social media, according to a UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) report released on Thursday.
Key points
- Nearly 60 per cent of cases occurred on social media
- Many children do not report abuse
- UNICEF calls for safer platforms and stronger laws
More than 15 million children in this age group were exposed to unwanted sexual content, nine million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will and four million had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.
UNICEF said the total figures are likely much higher.
“The report reveals a painful reality,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said. “More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play and connect with friends.”
Exploited on social media
Nearly 60 per cent of all recorded instances of exploitation in the report occurred on social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and WhatsApp, and 14 per cent happened on online games, with the platforms’ features often used to exploit trust.
Some 38 per cent of children first encountered the perpetrators online, and evidence shows abuse is often facilitated through intentional features that allow perpetrators to hide their identities.
In Montenegro, more than 80 per cent of reported cases involved social media.
Across the 21 countries, 57 per cent of exploitation cases involved perpetrators the children knew, including peers, friends and family.
Exploitation raises risks of self-harm
In interviews with researchers, children who endured sexual exploitation described impacts on their emotional wellbeing, sense of safety and trust in others, including fear, shame, confusion and isolation.
“I didn’t know how to react…I felt a little in shock,” said a young woman from the Dominican Republic after private images were circulated without her consent at age 14.
Children who experienced technology-aided sexual exploitation were four times more likely to report suicidal thoughts or behaviours and self-harm and reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, according to the analysis.
In Pakistan, the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher for children who had been exploited.
Unsure where to turn for help
More than 40 per cent of cases of tech-facilitated abuse were never shared with anyone, while fewer than one per cent were reported to authorities.
The most common reason was children not knowing who to tell.
“These experiences cause profound emotional and mental distress,” UNICEF chief Ms. Russell said. “Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away.”
Stakeholders must act
“All of us, including governments and technology companies, must do more to protect children online,” Ms. Russell said.
The researchers issued calls for help to prevent abuse:
- Tech companies should include stronger protections for children and improve their reporting systems
- Governments should strengthen accountability and enforcement mechanisms
- Societies should address harmful gender norms that normalise the sexualisation of girls and stigmatise survivors of sexual violence

G7: A new approach to development Development assistance G7 News Published on : April 30th 2026 Updated on : May 07th 2026 At a time when development policies are undergoing major changes, the members of the G7 are reflecting on how to build a renewed approach to development assistance based on mutually beneficial partnerships. This new approach to development is based on four main principles: resilience, sovereignty, effectiveness and coherence. The priorities are: Reaffirming solidarity with the most vulnerable countries to strengthen their resilience and help them anticipate food and public health crises and natural disasters to prevent them from developing; Strengthening the capacities of partner countries to finance essential sectors for sustainable development such as childhood, education, health, food security and nutrition; Improving the effectiveness of development assistance and promoting a new approach to development; Developing and updating the framework for international partnerships, to better take into account all of the flows contributing to development and include new partners. THREE QUESTIONS FOR ÉLÉONORE CAROIT, MINISTER DELEGATE FOR FRANCOPHONIE, INTERNATIONAL PARTNERSHIPS AND FRENCH NATIONALS ABROAD 1. How can the effects of the war in the Middle East on the most vulnerable countries be mitigated? The supply crisis caused by the closing of the Strait of Hormuz and the substantial, lasting damage to oil and gas infrastructure are posing major risks for the most vulnerable countries. These include the risk of an oil crisis, a food and humanitarian crisis, and worsening financial difficulties for partner countries. Along with our partners, we are working to identify solutions to help the most vulnerable countries faced with these crises, in particular food crises. We will also discuss the reconstruction of infrastructures in countries affected by conflict, as we wish to promote new methods of financing cooperation. 2. How can we reaffirm the need for solidarity with the most vulnerable countries? International solidarity must prioritize early childhood development, education, food security, nutrition, health and the fight against extreme poverty. France wants to support partner countries faced with the risk of health crises by proposing a new approach to health funding. This new approach aims to support domestic resource mobilization, the activities of national development banks and the coordination of health funding with the strategies established between partners countries and the World Bank. France also wants to strengthen the support of the G7 and its partners for the Global School Meals Coalition, an initiative launched by France and Finland in 2021 to ensure that every child worldwide has access to meals at school to allow them to properly learn and grow. France also wants to help increase the resilience of the most vulnerable countries to natural disasters by strengthening early warning systems. With this aim, France will announce a commitment of €3 million and will seek to mobilize its partners through the CREWS initiative. For more than a decade, the CREWS initiative has contributed to strengthening the resilience of 77 countries, including 80% of the least developed countries and small island developing States. Today, it has the capacity to support all of these countries with basic early warning systems. 3. How can the fall in development budgets be addressed? We wish to strengthen our partners’ funding capacities, key to their independence and sovereignty. We are working to support domestic resource mobilization as well as private capital and blended finance, and innovative mechanisms such as remittances and diaspora investments. We are supporting this approach in essential sectors advancing the sustainable development, sovereignty and resilience of partner countries, such as health, education and rural development. We are also stepping up dialogue with public development banks, which will come together on 29 April at an event convened by the Finance in Common (FiCS) network, as well as with the main foundations. The French G7 Presidency is the first to support the creation of a dedicated engagement group, the F7. World Press Freedom Day Freedom of expression Statement On : May 03rd 2026 On World Press Freedom Day, France condemns the attacks and acts of violence against journalists and media professionals. It pays tribute to those, too many again this year, who have been killed while carrying out their work around the world, in Palestine, Ukraine, Sudan and elsewhere. We honour the memory of Antoni Lallican, a French photojournalist, who was killed on 3 October 2025 in a Russian drone strike. Russia has made press freedom a target. During the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2025, France, alongside 21 other countries, demanded the protection of journalists and media professionals in Gaza, in accordance with international humanitarian law. France called on the Israeli authorities to allow independent foreign media access to Gaza. In southern Lebanon, four journalists have died since March in strikes carried out by the Israeli army. The deliberate targeting of journalists, where established, constitutes a war crime. France supports the Lebanese authorities in their efforts to fully investigate these tragedies and ensure that justice is served. France is mobilizing the international community in support of an honest, free and regulated information space. The Partnership for Information and Democracy, launched with Reporters Without Borders, is supported by 57 countries. In October 2025, at the Paris Peace Forum, 34 States committed to multilateral action to safeguard information integrity and media independence. France has renewed its support for the International Fund for Public Interest Media (IFPIM). It supports the international rollout of the Journalism Trust Initiative (JTI), a certification framework promoting media outlets that meet standards of ethics and independence. In the face of restrictions on freedom of expression and press freedom in many countries around the world, and the spread of disinformation and increasing manipulation of information, France reaffirms that the freedom to inform and to be informed is essential to democracy. The release of arbitrarily detained journalists and media professionals is imperative. France continues to engage with the Algerian authorities to secure the release of Christophe Gleizes and his return to France.

G7 Trade Ministers - Boosting the resilience and fairness of global trade Foreign trade G7 News Published on : May 04th 2026 Updated on : July 22nd 2026 As global balances are reshaped, the members of the G7 wish to reaffirm their commitment to open, fair and rules-based global trade. Ahead of the Leaders’ Summit in Évian (from 15 to 17 June), the Trade Ministers of the G7 countries – Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States – will meet in Paris on 5 and 6 May. The aim is to identify common focuses to address the transformations of global trade and enhance cooperation between partners. THREE QUESTIONS TO NICOLAS FORISSIER, Minister Delegate for Foreign Trade and Economic Attractiveness, attached to the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs 1. What is the context surrounding this G7 Trade Ministers’ Meeting? This meeting comes amid major uncertainty for global trade. Supply chains are under strain, market volatility is rising and structural imbalances persist in the global economy. Geopolitical crises, particularly in the Middle East, are also stifling trade and energy flows, with a direct impact on supply conditions and prices. In this context, the G7 is an essential setting to engage in dialogue, coordinate analysis and identify common solutions in order to guarantee a more stable and predictable trade environment. 2. What can we say about global trade? Several trends are setting in. Firstly, certain non-market practices are continuing to create distortions that feed into industrial overcapacities, unfair competition and unnecessary trade pressures. Moreover, the vulnerabilities of value chains, including in strategic sectors such as critical minerals, are thrown into sharper relief, with excessive dependencies and risks of breakdowns in supply. Finally, the swift rise of e-commerce has brought new challenges as regards regulation, security and fairness. For example, we want to bring an end to the imbalances caused to our markets by massive shipping of small, low-value packages. 3. How will this meeting address these challenges? This meeting should bring tangible and coordinated progress. We are going to enhance our collective analytical capacity, improve transparency and sharing of information, and draw on tools to better address market distortion. We will also speed up work on the resilience of supply chains, including as regards critical minerals, by identifying vulnerabilities, diversifying supply sources and developing cooperation with trusted partners. Finally, we will foster initiatives to modernize the global trade framework, including WTO reform and better regulation of e-commerce. Our aim is clear: to build effective common responses to today’s challenges. Read here the G7 Trade ministers' Communiqué Photo: Archives/MEAE

More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:19:03 BST
19:19:03 KST

More than 80 migrants feared dead after boat rescued off Canary Islands
- Published
More than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died in a boat which was adrift in the Atlantic Ocean for 27 days.
Spanish Maritime Rescue teams located the vessel some 65 nautical miles southwest of Gran Canaria's coastal town of Arguineguín on Wednesday and found 44 survivors, with five dead bodies also on board.
The boat is believed to have departed The Gambia in West Africa in early August with 127 occupants on board. Human rights activist Helena Maleno Garzón, founder of Spanish charity Caminando Fronteras, said 83 people had lost their lives.
Rescuers were forced to leave the five bodies they found due to the rough sea conditions, Maritime Rescue said.
The organisation was unable to verify how many people were originally on board.
The 44 survivors are men from sub-Saharan Africa, Maritime Rescue said in a statement.
"Once the rescue was complete, adverse weather conditions in the area - featuring 20-knot winds and 2.5m waves - made it impossible to recover the five bodies found on board the vessel," it added.
Three of the survivors were airlifted to hospital in critical condition.
The rest were transported by sea to Gran Canaria, where they disembarked in the early hours of Thursday morning.
Fernando Clavijo, head of the Canary Islands government, posted on X: "It is intolerable that lives continue to be lost. The Canaries cannot get used to or accept as normal the fact that the Atlantic continues to be a death trap."
The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings.
Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey each year seeking to reach Spanish territory despite the risks posed by rough seas, strong currents and long distances.
