Consul General of India in Los Angeles Ambassador Dr. K. J. Srinivasa and Ambassador of India to Azerbaijan Abhay Kumar undertook a series of high-level engagements in Karnataka
NEW DELHI: Consul general of India in Los Angeles Ambassador Dr K J Srinivasa and ambassador of India to Azerbaijan Abhay Kumar held a series of high-level meetings in Karnataka as part of a diplomatic visit aimed at strengthening the state's global outreach and exploring partnerships in technology, investment, innovation and industry.The two ambassadors called on Karnataka governor Thaawarchand Gehlot and CM D K Shivakumar, with discussions focusing on the state's growing international profile and its strengths in technology, innovation, industry and skilled human resources.They also met senior members of the Karnataka government, including Electronics, information technology and Biotechnology minister Priyank Kharge, Large and medium industries and Infrastructure development minister M B Patil, energy and tourism minister K J George, and transport minister Byrathi Suresh.
Focus on technology, investment and innovation
The discussions centred on expanding Karnataka's global footprint, facilitating investment and technology partnerships, promoting its startup and innovation ecosystem, and strengthening links with international technology and business centres.The meetings also explored opportunities to showcase Karnataka's tourism potential and skilled workforce while developing stronger technology, education, innovation and investment linkages with global partners.
As part of the visit, Srinivasa and Kumar visited Sarvam AI in Bengaluru, where they interacted with the company's leadership and were briefed on India's evolving artificial intelligence ecosystem, including indigenous foundational models and multilingual AI.The interaction also explored opportunities to strengthen international technology partnerships and connect India's innovation ecosystem with technology hubs abroad.
Aerospace, defence and advanced manufacturing
The ambassadors also visited the Karnataka Aerospace Park and Centum Electronics, where they reviewed the state's capabilities in aerospace, defence electronics, advanced manufacturing and high-technology innovation.The engagements highlighted opportunities for international investment and technology collaboration, as well as stronger links between Karnataka-based companies and global manufacturing and innovation networks.The visit covered sectors including artificial intelligence, frontier technologies, aerospace and defence, advanced manufacturing, clean energy, tourism, startups and entrepreneurship.For the consulate general of India in Los Angeles, the visit also provided an opportunity to identify areas for closer cooperation between Karnataka and the US West Coast, particularly Southern California, in AI and emerging technologies, aerospace, higher education, startups, clean energy, investment and innovation.
The consulate said it would continue working to facilitate institutional and business linkages between India and stakeholders in its jurisdiction and support efforts to promote trade, investment, technology, education and people-to-people partnerships.

Gold’s surge in August marks fastest monthly gain in over half-year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:49:48 UTC
18:49:48 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Gold rose 10% last month, its fastest monthly gain in seven months, amid the US Treasury’s expanded long-term bond buyback operation, weakening expectations that the Fed would hike rates and a relative easing of geopolitical risks.
During this period, demand for the US dollar increased as its safe-haven feature came to the fore amid uncertainties, leading to selling pressure in commodities, especially precious metals.
Gold gained 12.4% in January and 8.5% in February but began to decline with the outbreak of the US-Israel-Iran war at the end of February.
Gold fell 11.3% in March, 1% in April, 1.8% in May and 11.7% in June before gaining 0.9% in July.
The US Treasury expanded its long-term bond buybacks, US inflation slowed, employment in the country weakened Fed rate hike expectations and geopolitical risks relatively eased in August, driving gold up 10% at the end of the month to $4,449 per ounce.
Silver saw a similar trend, as the precious metal rose 15.4% in August to $66.5 per ounce due to easing rate hike expectations, also marking its fastest rise in seven months.
Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodity markets expert, told Anadolu that the US Treasury’s announcement drove up gold prices, as did central bank gold purchases.
Ergezen stated that there have been very large-scale gold purchases resembling those of a major institutional investor or a central bank.
He mentioned that the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) purchased 19 metric tons of gold last month and that these central bank purchases could continue in September.
He added that the US dollar, bond yields or oil prices did not significantly decline last month, noting that the rise in gold prices last month could have been a result of reactive buying.

You go to bed Kuwaiti, you wake up stateless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:45:03 UTC
18:45:03 KST

Breadcrumb
You go to bed Kuwaiti, you wake up stateless
Since the decrees withdrawing Kuwaiti nationality began to pour down, Sunday, the day on which the official gazette Kuwait al-Youm appears, has become a day of anxiety. Kuwaitis feverishly await its appearance, snap it up immediately to see if their name is in it, or if they are to remain Kuwaiti for another week.
Since 2024, with the accession of Sheikh Meshaal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah to the ruler’s throne, the campaign of re-examining and withdrawing nationality has acquired new dimensions. Indeed, the new Emir announced that he meant to put an end to the cases of fraudulent nationality acquisition - the use of forged documents, false declarations, etc. – and to track down cases of dual nationality, forbidden by the law of the land.
The net turned out to be cast wide, since several categories of citizens naturalised quite legitimately were caught in it: people whose residence In Kuwait since 1965 or before had been one of the criteria for naturalisation on the basis of the 1965 census; people who had been granted citizenship in recognition for “eminent services” rendered to the nation”; women having acquired it through marriage to a Kuwaiti; as well as certain children of a Kuwaiti mother and foreign father who did not acquire citizenship automatically through their mother but could be naturalised. These citizens had started families. Their children and grandchildren were born and had grown up under these perfectly legal regulations.
Now those who cannot point to a “nationality of origin” risk becoming stateless, and swelling the ranks of the hundreds of thousands of biduns, the “withouts”, the approximately 10% of the population who are stateless. Mostly from the bedouin tribes, these residents did not acquire Kuwaiti nationality when the country became independent in 1961. They are now deprived of most of the rights of citizens, mainly the right to vote, and to access various other privileges such as property ownership and state support.
This radical change in the notion of citizenship has far-reaching consequences since it affects by extension the children and grandchildren of the excluded, who may became excluded themselves. It is still too recent for its effects to be to fully measured (some will be specified by decree) and to understand its deeper reasons. However, the consequent stiffening of nationality policy appears to be the fulfilment of the promise “to give Kuwait back to its original inhabitants, cleansed and rid of its impurities” made by the new sovereign when he ascended the throne.
A broad aim
Kuwait’s nationality law makes a sharp distinction between citizens “of origin” and citizens “by naturalisation”. That distinction is reaffirmed by the 2026 reform: Kuwaitis of origin are defined in particular on the basis of their establishment in the country before its creation in 1920 and the resulting affiliation, along with continuity of residence, while people having acquired the nationality through naturalisation – as well as their descendants in certain cases – remain legally bound by this status. The rules for withdrawal or revocation are not identical in these different categories and in certain cases specified by law, may have consequences for the descendants. According to the new dispositions, naturalised citizens no longer have voting rights, and are no longer able to stand in elections or be appointed to any representative body.
Among those affected by the withdrawal of nationality are prominent figures in Kuwaiti public life: doctors, professors, historians, athletes and former diplomats. Some have represented Kuwait or contributed for decades to its institutions and cultural and scientific life. Such is the case with Bader al-Awadhi, former Kuwaiti ambassador to the United Kingdom, deprived of his Kuwaiti citizenship by filiation in January, a repercussion of the posthumous withdrawal of his father’s nationality. Since May, this high-ranking civil servant has been a citizen of neighbouring Bahrain.
These revocations have also hit people known for their political stances.
How to live?
An official decision can take just a few lines. Its consequences may begin the very next day. Losing Kuwaiti nationality isn’t just a matter of losing one’s passport. Citizenship is linked to a vast array of rights, services and accesses: voting, education and scholarships, certain public sector and military offices, housing, health care, pensions, subsidised welfare benefits, certain banking services, inland travel, stability of one’s judicial status. The question which the excluded person asks is not “What have I lost?” but “How can I live?”
After their citizenship has been withdrawn, the person concerned can only travel for a short time on their Kuwaiti passport. When that has expired, someone who hasn’t been able to get a passport corresponding to their original nationality or some other travel document, may find themselves unable to leave the country.
According to several witnesses, the regularisation procedure involves great pressure to hand over their nationality documents, to have their fingerprints taken and sign documents connected with their change of status. They explain that the non-fulfilment of these procedures can have consequences for their family’s access to certain benefits, especially in the areas of education and health. So for many families what is involved is not merely an administrative formality but an unavoidable step if they want to leave their children’s daily lives undisturbed.
The latter are in some cases the first collateral victims if one of their parents should lose their Kuwaiti nationality: it’s called “revocation by dependence”. Their number is unknown but some estimates put the total at 200,000.
Consequences for employment, housing, property
The change of status also directly affects work. Public service jobs reserved for Kuwaiti citizens are no longer open to these people. In the military and security sectors, where only citizens can be engaged, certain employees may be transferred to civilian functions, in the best of cases. Access to certain management or supervisory positions may also be restricted. When the person concerned is also the family’s main breadwinner, these modifications have a direct effect on the economy of the whole family.
The change of status may also entail major financial burdens, in particular for people who have benefitted from a public real estate loan. Several people questioned about this explain that they were informed by the Kuwait Credit Bank that they could be obliged to pay back all the remaining capital due in a relatively short time, which might amount to more than $100,000.
Housing is also a major source of worry according to many witnesses. Several people deprived of citizenship explain that they no longer benefit from the same property rights or public facilities as a Kuwaiti citizen. In the event that the accommodation had been obtained via some state agency, some families say they have had to look for a trustworthy Kuwaiti citizen in whose name to register their property.
The wall of regularisations and appeals
For many, regularising their situation does not simply mean filling out some administrative forms: it means having to reconstruct, in just a few months, a judicial status and daily security which up till then had been taken for granted.
In practical terms, the “deprived” have to establish a “nationality of origin”, then regularise their legal situation within a limited amount of time. But how do you find a “nationality of origin” when you were born in Kuwait, when your father and grandfather were also born there and when your family lived there under the British protectorate? How can you demonstrate your connection with another state in which no one in your family has ever lived and from which your family may not possess a single document?
Today several thousand people, including those with nationality revoked by dependence, are simply unable to claim a “nationality of origin”. Their official status is that of “non-Kuwaiti”. This does not yet mean that they are legally stateless, but this status shows that no other nationality has been established.
In Kuwait, nationality issues count as “acts of sovereignty”
The shock of the announcement is compounded for many by not knowing the reasons. In many cases, no precise or personalised justification is provided, which in itself makes any attempt to lodge an appeal useless. An online portal for complaints was opened by the authorities in May 2025, but it has been deactivated since the beginning of 2026. So in practice anyone who has been deprived of their nationality in 2026 has no access to that means of recourse, any more than those who lodged an earlier appeal.
In Kuwait, nationality issues are treated as “acts of sovereignty”, which drastically limits the criteria for submissions to the courts in the event of an appeal. The possibilities for review are slight indeed, despite appeals from human rights organisations and UN experts in favour of legal oversight and more effective channels for appeal.
Becoming an “illegal resident”
The fear of statelessness is very real in a country which officialised this status shortly after independence, considering as “irregular residents” the tens of thousands of (mostly) bedouins who were not registered with the nationality committees set up under the Nationality Act of 1959, shortly before independence in 1961.
People stripped of their nationality without recourse talk of “civil death”, witnessing as they do the disappearance of the rights that structured their place in society, while remaining physically present there. “What am I after losing my nationality?” What seemed to constitute one’s life in the city has suddenly taken the form of a stack of files to be updated: ID papers, education, employment, travel, accommodation, income, as well as the children’s rights.
I am still attached to my country, though the way I’m defined has been changed on paper. I look at the country where I was born and grew up and for the very first time, I ask myself a question I would have thought impossible: If I am no longer Kuwaiti, what am I?

Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:42:18 UTC
18:42:18 KST

Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More students in the Netherlands are staying in their parents’ home or giving up the search for a place of their own, as the shortage of student housing remains high despite thousands of new rooms being built each year.
The country is short of more than 20,200 student rooms, barely down from 21,000 a year earlier, according to the annual student housing monitor from knowledge centre Kences, published this week.
Social housing providers have built nearly 5,000 units a year since 2022, meeting the targets they were set.
Kences had expected the shortage to climb, because private landlords have been selling up in response to new rent rules and higher taxes. Some 32,300 fewer students have rented from private landlords since 2024.
That did not translate into a sharp rise, largely because student numbers have also dropped, including among international students. The share of students living away from home has fallen from 50% to 43% over eight years.
Fewer rooms, riskier ads
 The rooms still on the private market are increasingly hard to rent safely. Many are advertised above the legal limit.
Scammers, meanwhile, have flooded TikTok with fake listings that pocket deposits for rooms that do not exist.
Internationals are especially exposed to housing fraud, as they rarely have a family home to fall back on and often do not know their rights.
Kences wants the profit tax paid by housing associations scrapped, which it says would fund 15,000 to 25,000 more student homes over ten years. “Every euro we hand to the tax office, we would rather put into housing,” director Reijnder Jan Spits told broadcaster NOS.
Even if every current building plan goes ahead, the centre warned, the shortage could still stand at between 10,000 and 35,000 rooms in eight years.

Putin's autocratic regime not enough to freeze assets of Russia-linked companies, EU's court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:41:42 UTC
18:41:42 KST

Autocratic rule alone is not enough to freeze the assets of Russia-linked firms, the EU's top court has said in an influential ruling on Thursday. National authorities need solid, objective proof of actual control.
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled on Thursday that Russia's autocratic regime is not, on its own, enough to justify freezing the assets of a company indirectly linked to someone under EU sanctions, as any such measure must be backed by objective and solid evidence.
Brussels has currently blacklisted around 3,000 entities and individuals considered to be part of the Russian industrial-military complex that is participating in the invasion of Ukraine, pending extension on 15 September.
The judgment sets clear limits on how far national authorities can go when freezing the assets of entities not directly listed under EU sanctions, but alleged to be linked to a sanctioned individual.
The case concerns Inter Rao Lietuva, a Lithuanian electricity company that Lithuanian authorities placed on the national asset-freeze list despite it not being directly targeted by EU sanctions against Russia.
Lithuanian authorities argued that the company's ownership structure made it sufficiently connected to sanctioned individuals to justify the freeze: 51% of its shares are owned by Rao Nordic, a Finland-registered company wholly owned by PJSC Inter RAO, a major Russian state-controlled energy firm.
Since the company was ultimately controlled by the Russian state, the authorities concluded it was under the indirect control of President Vladimir Putin, who is himself subject to EU sanctions.
The CJEU rejected that reasoning, ruling that restrictive measures must rest on proven control over the entity concerned, supported by objective and sufficiently solid evidence.
As a result, the judgment concludes that the mere fact that Russia's political system is autocratic and oligarchic — giving Putin virtually unlimited power — does not by itself amount to sufficient evidence of his control over the company.
At the same time, the national authorities might take into account all relevant information to assess the effectiveness of the control, even of an informal nature, by another person or entity subject to EU sanctions.

Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:41:30 BST
18:41:30 KST

Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race
- Published
The Italian Grand Prix has been declared a heat-hazard race as high temperatures continue in the country following the summer heatwave.
A heat hazard is an official designation for an event where it is forecasted that temperatures will be more than 31C at some point during the race on Sunday.
The ambient temperatures around Monza, north-east of Milan, are expected to be in the mid-30C region all weekend.
They peaked at 36C on Wednesday afternoon near Milan's Linate airport.
The ruling means drivers can use a system that flows cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls.
The cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure they do not have a competitive advantage.
- How to follow Italian Grand Prix on the BBC 
  - Published2 hours ago
Italy is the second race this year to be declared a heat hazard. The first was Austria early in the summer heatwave.
Some drivers prefer not to use the cooling kit because of discomfort, and because there have been issues with the coolant running out before a grand prix is finished.
In that case, the liquid ends up at car temperature, which is considerably higher than ambient.
Temperatures in the cockpit of an F1 car can be more than 40C, and drivers are wearing several layers of fireproof clothing in addition to a balaclava and helmet, so overheating is a serious concern.

IN BRIEF: Russian Foreign Minister on Ukraine conflict, Europe’s military buildup

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov spoke about the West’s position on the Ukraine settlement, NATO and European Union policies, and Germany’s militarization during a lecture organized by the Znanie Society at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
He also addressed the status of the Russian language and the Ukrainian Orthodox Church in Ukraine, and the situation in the Asia-Pacific region.
TASS has compiled the foreign minister’s key statements.
West’s position on Ukraine
The West’s position on Ukraine is disgraceful, as it disregards key provisions of the UN Charter: "The UN Charter states in its first article that everyone must respect human rights regardless of race, sex, language or religion. Moreover, Ukraine’s constitution still states that the state guarantees the rights of Russians and other national minorities. Nobody cares about that. They passed laws that contradict the UN Charter and the constitution, and everyone says these are supposedly European values. I consider the West’s position absolutely disgraceful."
EU and NATO policies
The North Atlantic Alliance is unlikely to survive much longer, as its attempts to find new reasons to extend its existence cannot continue indefinitely: "I don’t think the North Atlantic Alliance will last much longer. Its attempts to find new reasons to extend its existence, including by expanding its dominance into Southeast and Northeast Asia under the slogan of ‘containing China,’ cannot continue indefinitely. The Taiwan issue continues to gain momentum, and this effort will eventually run out of steam. Once again, voters will ask: What are we doing there?"
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is a "fuhrer" pulling Europe back toward Nazism: "We call European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen "Fuhrer Ursula." She is trying to pull powers and responsibilities into the European Commission that, under decisions by the European Union as a whole, were never transferred to Brussels and remain with national governments. This tendency is becoming increasingly pronounced."
The European Union’s "open-door" policy has triggered a migration crisis for the bloc itself: "The dominance of newcomers is becoming a problem for domestic development. It is causing discontent among the native population, which is forced to pay taxes to support people who have arrived. Ukrainian citizens also fall into this category. EU countries have provided them with subsidies and benefits since the beginning of the special military operation, when they fled their country, and in some cases, these benefits significantly exceed the unemployment benefits available to those countries’ own citizens."

Britain wants laser armed ground vehicle drones
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:39:27 BST
18:39:27 KST

Britain is seeking counter-drone technology that could lead to autonomous laser weapons mounted on Army vehicles and, later, uncrewed ground vehicles, with £5 million available immediately through a new Ministry of Defence competition, the department has said.
Project PANOPTES, launched by UK Defence Innovation on behalf of the MOD, is intended to develop an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System force-protection capability able to deal with massed and low-cost aerial threats without rapidly exhausting conventional ammunition stocks.
The MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
Although the competition is open to a range of technologies, laser directed-energy weapons are specifically identified as an area of interest. The MOD said: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The intended configuration would place the counter-drone capability on a military ground platform. According to the procurement documents: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
The system is intended to protect deployed forces against complex and saturation attacks involving small uncrewed aircraft, including simultaneous threats designed to overwhelm local air defences or force troops to expend comparatively expensive missiles and ammunition.
The MOD stated: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus covers representative Class 1 UAS and other small aerial targets. These could include individual drones as well as repeated, sequential or simultaneous attacks used for surveillance, targeting, disruption or attempts to exhaust defensive systems.
A later objective would move the capability onto an unmanned ground platform. The MOD stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
UK Defence Innovation has confirmed that Project PANOPTES is open to UK-based innovators and that a share of £5 million is available immediately. Stage 1 will act as an initial screening process, with applicants outlining their proposed technology before successful teams are invited to develop more detailed proposals.
The first phase is not intended to produce a complete operational counter-drone system. The MOD said: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
Successful technologies could then be matured through later phases into demonstrable Minimum Viable Products before selected systems are developed into Minimum Deployable Capabilities for an initial operational user group.
The notice states: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record.”
The wider procurement has an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, rising to £150 million including VAT. That figure is not an approved programme budget. The MOD stated: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.”
Stage 1 submissions are due by midday on 23 September. A launch webinar will be held on 9 September to provide potential suppliers with further information on the operational requirement before the competition moves into its subsequent stages.

'Supersized' El Nino could be strongest on record, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:39:00 UTC
18:39:00 KST

'Supersized' El Nino to persist into 2027, UN says
September 3, 2026
The El Nino weather phenomenon is set to intensify and will almost certainly last until February next year, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in an update Thursday.
The UN weather agency warned El Nino would develop into a "very strong" event in the coming months, heightening the risks of extreme heat, drought and flooding while threatening livelihoods and economies.
"El Nino is being supersized before our eyes," UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said in a statement. "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up."
WMO head Celeste Saulo told a press conference in Geneva that, on the current trajectory, the El Nino, "may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began, so literally off the charts we have used for the past four decades."
What is El Nino?
El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that happens every two to seven years and is not caused by climate change. But scientists say it can worsen the impacts of global heating caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels.
The WMO classifies El Nino events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, with the current El Nino set to reach the highest intensity level on that scale.
The phenomenon begins with the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, triggering changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns around the world.
For example, it often brings dry conditions and drought to Australia, Indonesia and parts of the Amazon, while East Africa and the southern US may experience heavy rainfall.
El Ninos typically begin between March and June, peaking toward the end of the year and lasting around nine to 12 months.
Ocean temperatures already 'exceptionally' high
WMO head Saulo said there was "an exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100% that El Nino will persist through to February 2027," adding that it was the first time the organization had "expressed such a degree of certainty. "
Sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific region , which drive El Nino and reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometers away, are already well above average and continuing to rise, according to the UN agency.
"Subsurface ocean temps are also exceptionally high and in some areas more than 8 degrees Celsius above normal during July and early August," Saulo said.
While El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of the year, its knock-on effects will likely last well into 2027, she added.
Global average temperatures are often particularly high the year after an El Nino. For example, the 2023-2024 El Nino contributed to 2024 being the warmest year on record.
"We should not be surprised if this record is broken," Saulo said.
'We have no time to lose'
Saulo said droughts, floods and extreme heat were already causing disruption and devastation, and warned these impacts would "multiply and cascade as El Nino intensifies."
Saulo stressed that the weather phenomenon would "deliver a major blow to communities, economies and supply chains across the globe" and called for preparations to safeguard climate-sensitive sectors.
"We have no time to lose," she said.

More than 1,270 people have been killed, and more than 4,700 are still missing, authorities said on Thursday.

“We still hope there are some survivors inside,” Sanjay Kc, an officer from the Nepalese army engineering department, said, in front of bulldozers trying to remove huge piles of mud blocking the entrance of a tunnel in the Rasuwa district, one of the worst affected areas in Nepal. “Because it’s a big power house inside, so it’s a big room, and we feel that the whole power house is not flooded,” he told Al Jazeera.

Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the NDRRMA, told the Reuters news agency that about 20,000 houses would have to be rebuilt, including 7,500 that have been destroyed.
“There is no point in rebuilding the houses in the same locations, as that would expose people to the same risks,” Upreti told the news agency, adding that authorities were trying to identify safer areas to relocate the communities and build up new settlements. As of Monday, the UN said more than 3,400 displaced people were living in 27 displacement sites in Nuwakot and Rasuwa, mostly in schools.
Nepali authorities have pointed to the role of major greenhouse gas emitters that have a “historical responsibility to compensate vulnerable nations like Nepal”, said Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal. He added that the government has officially filed a “formal climate compensation claim letter” to international partners.

Vigils held in US for Haitian student Pierre Damas Bel who died by apparent suicide after forced to wear ankle monitor, stripped of TPS status

The 20-year-old resident of Springfield, Ohio was one of more than 300,000 Haitians who had recently lost their TPS designation under the direction of US President Donald Trump, who has made anti-immigrant policy one of main platforms.
"Pierre is dead because a policy stripped away his protection and threw his life into crisis,” said Khalid Turaani, executive director of CAIR-Ohio, in Columbus, where a vigil was held Wednesday evening to honour the life of Bel.
“This wasn’t an accident of fate, it was the direct, expected result of an immigration system that has grown crueler by design, and a political climate that has made it acceptable to humiliate people like Pierre,” he said in a public statement.
It is believed this is the first suicide by a Haitian in the US following the reversal of TPS for Haitians. Hours before his death on Monday, Bel had called his parents and said he felt humiliated for having to wear an ankle monitor, which he said his school mates had bullied him over.
He drove on the interstate highway and parked his car on the right shoulder and then walked into oncoming traffic. He succumbed to his injuries at the scene. His death saw strong responses that crossed party lines.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, described Bel’s death as a “horrible tragedy.”
“Fran and I, since we learned about this, are thinking of this young man, Pierre, Pierre’s mom, and dad, and family. This is a horrible, horrible tragedy,” DeWine said, according to local news reports.
“He had graduated from high school here. He was well-liked; he was in a junior ROTC. And I’m told by those who knew him, he had great dreams about what he could do in this country and what he could contribute to this country,” the governor continued.
Bel was an honours student at Wright State University, where he played soccer and was a member of the ROTC (Reserve Officers’ Training Corps). He had dreamed of becoming a doctor. He previously attended high school in Springfield, Ohio.
In 2024, Springfield became known for unsubstantiated rumours that local Haitians were eating domestic cats and dogs. Trump brought up the accusation during a presidential debate in an attempt to paint his opponent, Kamala Harris, as soft on immigration. Since then, racist rhetoric against Haitians, particularly in the Springfield area, has surged.
TPS is a humanitarian programme that started in 1990 with the purpose of giving legal protection to people from countries where returning would be too dangerous (due to extreme cases, such as war or natural disaster). There are currently 1.3 million people from 17 countries holding Temporary Protected Status (TPS). Most are facing the likely loss of their protected status.

US company Apogee Enterprises will acquire Latvian high-tech glass coating manufacturer Groglass for 62.5 million euros. Groglass develops and manufactures innovative anti-reflective glass coatings, the company said.
The transaction is expected to be completed by November 2026.
Apogee Enterprises is a manufacturer of innovative coated materials and a provider of architectural and construction products and services. The company is headquartered in the United States and is publicly traded.
The total value of the transaction is 62.5 million euros, of which 10 million euros will be paid separately if Groglass achieves certain financial targets within three years.
Riga-based Groglass manufactures anti-reflective and UV-protective glass coatings. Its products are widely used in museums, electronics, architecture and other industries around the world. The company employs 190 people.
“Groglass joining the company will strengthen our position in global target markets by adding unique glass coating technologies and strong research expertise to Apogee Enterprises’ capabilities. This will enable us to expand into new markets,” said Don Nolan, CEO and Chairman of Apogee Enterprises.
The transaction also provides for continued investment in innovation, people and manufacturing in Riga. Groglass is expected to remain an important research and development and manufacturing centre within the Apogee Enterprises group.
Groglass CEO Sergejs Kostjučenko noted that joining Apogee Enterprises gives Groglass the opportunity to become part of a financially strong, publicly traded company with extensive experience in investment and innovation. As part of Apogee Enterprises, Groglass will gain access to additional resources, expertise and global opportunities that will accelerate the company’s growth.
The company explained that by combining the knowledge, experience and technological expertise of both companies, new solutions will be developed for the protection and preservation of artworks and cultural heritage, as well as other specialised glass surface products for customers worldwide in the architecture and electronics sectors.
The sellers were advised by leading financial adviser Oaklins, which also approached potential buyers and led the negotiations. Law firm Cobalt provided legal support.

Starting January 1, 2027, the region will introduce a special legal regime for drones, and Putin said the Far East will test low-altitude drone delivery of civilian cargo.
Putin said a unified preferential regime for businesses will also take effect at the start of the new year across the Far East and the Arctic, while existing special business regimes — including those in the port of Vladivostok and on Russky Island — will remain in place.
Discussing efforts to protect the region’s wildlife, including programs to preserve the Amur tiger and the Far Eastern leopard, Putin also recounted an encounter with a tiger:
We were driving through the forest by car. A tiger comes out, walks right in front of the car, wagging its tail, not going anywhere: the master of the taiga. It was very interesting to see all the richness of these places.

EU foreign ministers fail to break deadlock over Israel and Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:34:09 UTC
18:34:09 KST

EU foreign ministers fail to break deadlock over Israel and Ukraine
EU foreign ministers met in Ireland but failed to agree on imposing trade sanctions on Israel or military support for Ukraine.
Wicklow, Ireland – “We have reached an impasse,” said Ireland’s Foreign Minister Helen McEntee at a gathering of European Union officials on Tuesday, summing up the bloc’s increasingly fractured position on trade sanctions on Israel.
Ireland, which currently holds the European Council’s presidency, and Spain pushed for EU-wide trade curbs on goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank at the September 1-2 meeting in Wicklow amid escalating settler violence against Palestinians.
France pressed for a stronger European response to Israeli rhetoric against Palestinians. “Condemnations from Israeli officials have been a good start, but they are not enough,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told reporters, referring to Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s call for mass displacement in the Gaza Strip.
But several EU nations, including Germany and Hungary, opposed the move during the two-day informal gathering.
The Gymnich meeting, as the gathering is called, opened on Tuesday with renewed efforts by Dublin to revive discussions on sanctions against Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank – a proposal that has largely stalled in recent months because of divisions among member states.
The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade standing at more than $50bn.
Deadlock over Israel
Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, acknowledged that the absence of unanimity had once again prevented the bloc from moving forward on measures against Israel, despite growing pressure from several governments for a stronger European response to illegal settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Ireland has argued that the EU’s credibility depends on applying international law consistently, regardless of the conflict under discussion. Dublin has also pointed to what it sees as a disparity between the bloc’s willingness to impose sanctions and other measures in response to Russia’s actions in Ukraine and its reluctance to take comparable action against Israel despite its ongoing genocide in Gaza and alarming rate of violence in the occupied Palestinian territory.
The disagreement is not simply over how member states view the Israel-Palestinian conflict, but over what practical steps the EU should take. Ireland and several other governments have pushed for stronger measures, including action against individuals involved in settler violence and restrictions on trade linked to illegal Israeli settlements, while other member states have been reluctant to support such proposals.
Divisions over Ukraine
Ukraine dominated much of the first day’s talks, with Kyiv continuing to call for greater European military support.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has entered its fifth year, with Moscow escalating drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Kyiv again urged European governments to provide additional air defence systems after months of sustained Russian drone attacks.
Yet ministers again failed to bridge their differences.
Greece and Spain maintained their opposition to using common EU funds to finance further purchases of air defence systems, leaving Ukraine without the additional missiles and interceptors it had hoped for from the meeting.
On the sidelines of the talks, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha appealed directly to European media, warning that delays in military support would come at a growing cost as Russia has intensified its aerial campaign. It did not seem to move the needle much.
The Ukraine debate also exposed another longstanding fault line within the bloc.
While Poland, Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands renewed calls to use frozen Russian sovereign assets to finance Ukraine’s military effort, Belgium, which holds the largest share of those assets, again resisted the proposal, citing unresolved legal and financial concerns.
Broader security challenges
Meanwhile, ministers also turned their attention to the wider Middle East.
The US-Israel war on Iran, now in its seventh month, has left European governments with limited diplomatic leverage despite the conflict directly affecting the continent, including concerns over energy security for the upcoming winter months.
The future of Lebanon, which continued to be attacked by Israel, was also discussed, with ministers considering a possible EU mission to train the Lebanese army as the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) ends this year.
Elsewhere, on August 30, EU forces operating in the Mediterranean boarded a tanker suspected of being linked to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, as part of broader European efforts to enforce sanctions against Moscow and disrupt attempts to evade them.
Internal strains persist
And if the external crises were not enough, the ministers also had some internal fires to deal with.
Just a day before the meeting, Italy renewed enhanced air and land checks on travellers arriving from Spain following a dispute linked to migration and border controls. Madrid responded by extending reciprocal measures.
The dispute followed an influx of migrants in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta, after which Italy introduced additional checks on some travellers from Spain.
Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares urged other member states to support Madrid’s position on the border measures while criticising governments that, he said, had failed to support Spain during the Ceuta crisis.
At the end of the two-day meeting on Wednesday, ministers left having said more or less what they had said before.
“We are a dog that barks but doesn’t bite,” Luxembourg’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Xavier Bettel said at the meeting, expressing his frustration at the lack of support to sanction Israel.
After the meeting, the bloc is more or less where it started – plenty of shared concern, but very little shared action. The unanimity rule remains the EU’s Achilles heel – everyone has to agree, which means, in practice, almost nothing gets done.

Police arrested a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian citizens, at a gas station. Their connection to the incident is part of an ongoing investigation.
No information was immediately available on a possible motive or the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Emergency responders found another incendiary device at the scene that had not detonated. Special forces from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office rendered it harmless, and the area was cordoned off during the operation.
In 2021, unidentified perpetrators set fire to a power line near the Rohde & Schwarz facility that had been left exposed in an excavation pit. A letter posted online claimed responsibility and described the act as an attack on the "defense contractor."
The 2021 incident remains unsolved. The sabotage caused a power outage affecting 20,000 households in eastern Munich, although the company said it was not affected.

China Focus: Typhoon Saudel makes third landfall along east China coast
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:33:30 CST
18:33:30 KST

Police officers set up cordons and traffic cones to guide traffic on a road in Zhangzhou City, southeast China's Fujian Province, Sept. 3, 2026. Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of 2026, made its third landfall in Fujian Province on Thursday, with maximum sustained winds of 23 meters per second near its center, according to the provincial meteorological observatory. Local authorities have quickly carried out rescue and flood drainage operations as persistent heavy rain battered parts of the province. (Photo by Zhan Zhaoyu/Xinhua)
FUZHOU, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of 2026, made its third landfall in east China on Thursday morning, prompting tens of thousands of people to be evacuated amid warnings of strong winds and heavy downpours.
Saudel made the latest landfall in Zhangpu County under the city of Zhangzhou, Fujian Province, at around 6:30 a.m. with maximum sustained winds of 23 meters per second near its center, according to the provincial meteorological observatory.
Previously, Saudel had made landfall twice along the coast of Zhejiang Province, also in east China, on Aug. 28, prompting the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people across the east of the country.
Authorities in Fujian had evacuated more than 83,000 people by 7 a.m. on Thursday as persistent heavy rain battered parts of the province.
Heavy rain prompted the suspension of work, business activities and school attendance in parts of the city of Zhangzhou. Schools were also closed in other cities in Fujian including Fuzhou, Quanzhou and Ningde, provincial authorities said.
As of 7 a.m., eight sections of major roads had been closed, 657 transport services suspended, work halted at 152 construction sites, and over 150 major tourist attractions shut across Fujian.
The province raised its flood-control emergency response on Wednesday while maintaining a response for the typhoon.
China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) issued a blue alert for the typhoon on Thursday morning.
Saudel is forecast to move westward at 15 to 20 kilometers per hour and gradually weaken, the NMC said.
From Thursday afternoon to Friday afternoon, heavy to torrential rain is forecast across most of Fujian, eastern and northern Guangdong Province, southern Jiangxi Province, southern Hunan Province and much of Taiwan.
Two to three more typhoons are expected to make landfall in or significantly affect China in September, mainly along the country's eastern and southern coasts, said Gao Rong, deputy director of the National Climate Center.
Gao added that there is a risk that some relatively strong typhoons could move northward and affect northern China.
Monitoring data showed that 24 typhoons had formed over the northwestern Pacific and the South China Sea as of Sept. 1 this year, 10.4 more than the historical average for the same period. Seven made landfall in China, 2.1 more than average.
Typhoon activity was particularly high from June to August this year, with prolonged and widespread strong winds and heavy rain.
The period also saw above-average rainfall across China and frequent extreme precipitation. The country was hit by 15 widespread rainstorm events, with daily rainfall at 44 national meteorological stations breaking historical records, according to the data.
Gao urged relevant regions to closely follow short-term typhoon forecasts and updated risk warnings, and guard against mountain torrents, urban waterlogging, heavy rain, strong winds and storm surges. ■

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Norway's seizure of the Russian research vessel Professor Molchanov is real piracy, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in an interview with TASS on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"Seized is a better word than detained. Detained is about something legal. Now we see the big picture of what's happening. Earlier, perhaps even 10-15 years ago, one could have harbored illusions that this was some kind of legal procedure, that there were some legitimate claims that could somehow be fought off in court or arbitration. You see what's happening now. The West has legalized, or rather, I would say, simply lifted the veil on piracy, uncovering a seemingly relic, not even of the Cold War – there was nothing like this during the Cold War – a relic of the period <...> from the Middle Ages to the Great Geographical Discoveries, literally making Jack Sparrow its own symbol of modernity," Zakharova said, answering a related question.
"This is precisely one element of this new interpretation of maritime affairs, or the maritime agenda, in the West. Previously, in recent decades, the post-war period, and even the pre-war period, maritime affairs were dominated by maritime law. It was developed, it was elaborated at the national level, at the regional level, at the international level. It was precisely this law that was relied upon in dealing with civil matters. The militaries and navies of various countries had their own laws, both for their conduct in peacetime and for the conduct of military operations. Today, everything is jumbled, everything is thrown off, everything is mixed up. They have simply resorted to real piracy. This is monstrous, this is degradation, this is throwing them and the entire world back. But this is also reality," Zakharova stated. "What you are talking about, is one of the manifestations."
Earlier, the official website of the Governor of Svalbard published a statement that Norwegian authorities had seized the Russian research vessel Professor Molchanov following a complaint from the Ukrainian company Naftogaz.

In his speech, Shi Yuanqiang, charge d'affaires of the Chinese Embassy in Pakistan, said that livestock farming is a traditional competitive sector and a pillar of Pakistan's rural economy, building a solid foundation and enormous development potential.
The leaders of both China and Pakistan attach great importance to agricultural cooperation, making agriculture one of the priority areas of bilateral cooperation, he said, adding that China's experience, models, and achievements in livestock development can provide valuable lessons for Pakistan.
It is hoped that this donation of veterinary vaccines will serve as an opportunity to further strengthen cooperation between China and Pakistan in the livestock sector, continuously deepen practical agricultural cooperation, and constantly benefit the people of both countries, he said. ■

Feature: Ancient Chinese dragon boat racing thrives in inland Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:32:47 CST
18:32:47 KST

by sportswriter Sun Zhe
URUMQI, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- In a county on the edge of the Taklamakan Desert, the world's second-largest shifting sand desert, where annual rainfall averages just 47.7 millimeters, water is a precious resource.
But every summer, the sound of drums and splashing paddles fills a small pond in Yutian County, as dozens of villagers climb into dragon boats and race across the water.
Dragon boat racing, an ancient sport born on the rivers and lakes of southern China, has found an unexpected home in the arid landscapes of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.
Crews race long boats decorated like dragons, rowing in unison to a drummer's beat, with teamwork and coordination key to reaching the finish line.
For participants like Adiljan Abduegni, the sport opened a window to a world they had rarely seen.
"Most of us used to play football or basketball," the 25-year-old said. "Before we tried dragon boats, we didn't know how to row. Some people couldn't even swim."
Yutian is a typical desert county, far from China's major rivers and coasts. For generations, residents dreamed of water sports but had few opportunities. That began to change in 2022, when the county launched its first annual summer dragon boat race.
Yusupjan Erkin, an official with the local sports department, said nearly 20 townships soon formed teams to take part. Participants were not professional athletes but ordinary people from different walks of life, including taxi drivers, construction workers and, most commonly, farmers.
"At the beginning, people made the boats themselves," Yusupjan recalled. "It was a funny scene because the dragon boats were of different lengths and the paddles came in all kinds of shapes."
The competition was held on a small local fishpond, one of the few available venues. Limited space did not dampen enthusiasm as crowds gathered around the water, eager to watch the novel spectacle.
Races were far from professional. Many crews lacked rowing technique, some boats lost direction and others capsized, but laughter, not frustration, filled the pond.
"The purpose of holding the race was to bring happiness to villagers and let them experience the unique charm of the sport," Yusupjan said.
As interest grew, local authorities purchased standard dragon boats and paddles, and the sport gradually became more organized.
Last year, the county selected more than a dozen paddlers to compete in China's national Dragon Boat Super League in Miluo, a city in central China's Hunan Province, widely recognized as the birthplace of dragon boat culture and the place associated with ancient Chinese poet Qu Yuan.
After a month of hard training, Adiljan and his teammates arrived in Hunan but quickly felt the gap with more experienced competitors.
"Adapting to the environment was one challenge, but the biggest issue was the equipment and experience," Yusupjan said. "Our team still used wooden paddles, while other teams used carbon fiber ones. They lent some to us."
Despite the challenges, dragon boat racing has continued to spread across Xinjiang.
In places without suitable waterways, organizers have introduced land-based races, where teams carry a simulated boat along roads. In northern Xinjiang, even frozen lakes have become places for winter dragon boat competitions.
At Sayram Lake, boats were fitted with blades underneath and brakes at the rear so teams could race safely on ice.
"We installed ice skates under the boats and added brakes at the back," said referee Huang Jin. "After crossing the finish line, teams can use the brakes to slow down."
The sport reached a new milestone in August, when dragon boat racing made its debut at the Xinjiang Ethnic Traditional Sports Games in Kashgar. Twelve teams from across the region took part, including Adiljan's squad.
"We came here aiming for the championship," he said. "But we finished only fourth in the 200-meter race on the first day. There are many strong dragon boat teams in Xinjiang."
For Adiljan, however, victory is not the only measure of success.
"The result is not the most important thing. What matters is feeling the charm of the sport," he said. "One person may paddle fast, but cannot go far alone. Only when everyone works together can we move faster and farther." ■

====================================================================================================

Smart Toilets Are Already Using AI to Analyze Your Poop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

It was only a matter of time before wellness trackers—already out there trying to optimize our heart rate, sleep, stress, steps, blood sugar, and menstruation—came for perhaps the most private biosignal of all: our poop.
The global gut health market is expected to reach nearly $106 billion by 2029, and a handful of companies are betting they can use stool data to provide in-depth health insights, nudge people to change their diets or lifestyles, and advise them to see a doctor if their bathroom habits seem amiss. But gastroenterologists are skeptical that products that rely on AI to analyze images of what’s going on in your toilet bowl are worth the price just yet, and data-privacy advocates warn that people can get locked into long-term subscriptions just to access their own health data.
Among the companies touting smart toilets are Kohler Health—an offshoot of the eponymous plumbing giant that sells its device for $449 plus $130 for an annual family membership—and Throne, a startup that raised $10 million in July. Its product is $399 plus $70 for an annual membership.
Both companies’ stool trackers are sleek white devices that clip to the toilet and have cameras facing down into the bowl. (They are adamant that the cameras cannot turn skyward.) When you sit down, the device uses a light sensor to record a video of your deposits, then feeds them into an algorithm that analyzes your urine and stool consistency and color, as well as other metrics. A few minutes later, you get your bathroom-break report card care of an AI-powered app that tracks gut health and hydration scores.
The companies say they are taking a completely different approach from at-home gut microbiome test kits. Those kits, which claim they can use stool samples to identify food sensitivities, provide dietary guidance, and more, come with thin to nonexistent evidence of their efficacy. The new stool trackers aim to identify what's normal for an individual rather than issuing a binary healthy-or-not verdict.
“This is all deeply personal and very individual—digestive patterns are very different,” says Nora Tophof, Kohler Health’s managing director.
Even so, for healthy people with regular bowel movements, stool trackers may not offer much in the way of new insights, says Daniel Freedberg, a gastroenterologist in New York and a spokesperson for the American Gastroenterological Association.
“It kind of seems like overkill,” he says. “If you want to look at your stool, you can just look at it yourself. I don't know that the AI is bringing a lot of new science to this.”
Tophof says that for healthy people, the real value comes from long-term tracking to identify patterns they can act on—for example, if they realize they’re always dehydrated over the weekend or that a particular food or medication tends to upset their stomach.
Scott Hickle, Throne’s cofounder and chief executive officer, says people with inflammatory bowel disease or other digestive conditions can benefit from regular, automated stool monitoring. “Their physicians ask them to track, or keep stool logs … and compliance for that is basically zero,” he says. “No one wants to journal about their poop.”
Throne plans to offer more than helping users track their gut health. Rates of colorectal cancer have risen among younger adults over the past decade, and it is now the leading cause of cancer death among those under 50. Doctors don’t quite know why, but exposure to ultra-processed foods, microplastics, and antibiotics are prime suspects. Screening for colon cancer typically involves a colonoscopy—or a stool-based test that looks for hidden blood in feces.
Hickle says the next generation of Throne’s device will be capable of detecting blood in fecal matter using multispectral imaging that is much more sensitive than the naked eye. Early tests with a prototype are promising, he says, and the updated device could launch within two years. The company has yet to determine a price, but Hickle says Throne's goal is “to make it as accessible as possible so that this can benefit as many people as possible.” He hopes that blood-based data will eventually help detect colorectal cancer, though it’s not clear whether this approach would be as good as testing in medical labs.
“We don't want to be in the business of making diagnoses,” Hickle says. “Looking for those patterns of bleeding over the course of weeks and months should be enough to get someone to at least escalate the conversation they have with their physician.”
Kohler Health says its tracker already alerts users when it detects blood in the toilet. While often harmless—common examples include menstrual blood and hemorrhoids—it can also be a sign of serious health conditions.
“We really want to help people and ultimately save lives,” Tophof says.
Even if the trackers’ blood-detection technology bears out as a clinically meaningful signal, they are still too expensive to be widely used as screening tools for cancer or other health risks, says Gianluca Ianiro, an assistant professor of gastroenterology at the Catholic University of Rome.
“A screening test should be non-invasive but also cheap—and this is not cheap,” Ianiro says.
Would-be buyers should also consider how much personal data they’re willing to give up for what they get out of using the device—especially because “you’re having to pay time and time again in order to access and analyze your own information,” says Lauren Hendry Parsons, a digital rights advocate at the Mozilla Foundation. If customers keep re-upping their subscriptions, “it may feel harder to detach yourself if you've got years and years of data and information about yourself inside that particular service,” she adds.
In addition to the contents of your toilet bowl—and any details you tell the app about your health, such as diet or medication—Throne and Kohler Health both collect the usual litany of personal data, including name and demographics. Kohler Health also tracks your precise location, while Throne does not.
Both companies say they don’t share user health information for targeted advertising purposes, but they can still share this data with law enforcement, another company in a merger or sale, and third-party service providers for things like IT, customer service, and engagement, according to their privacy policies.
Tophof says Kohler Health doesn’t plan to sell users’ health data. Throne also says it will never do so without express permission. Eventually, Hickle wants to share user health data with universities doing gut health research—but people will have to opt in, and refusing will not affect their ability to use the app or device, he says.
Hendry Parsons has advice for privacy-minded buyers: “Be informed. Know what the trade-offs are, know what you're sharing, know what your data is being used for, and weigh that up against the benefit that you are deriving from the product.”
That calculus might be different for someone “suffering from Crohn’s disease, and this is something which will materially improve your day-to-day life,” she says, compared with a “health optimizer who's casually thinking it might be fun to understand the impact of your homemade kombucha.”

Swiss economy posts strong growth in second quarter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

Swiss economy posts strong growth in second quarter
The Swiss economy grew by 1.5% in the second quarter of the year, compared with the previous quarter, according to the second estimate published on Thursday by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO).
This figure, adjusted for sporting events, confirms the estimates released in mid-August, which point to a marked acceleration following a rise of just 0.55 in the first quarter.
According to federal economists, this represents “the strongest GDP growth since the third quarter of 2021”.
“The strongest impetus came from the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, but value added also rose in many other sectors,” said SECO.
Exports, excluding transit trade, posted a significant rebound of 9.7% during the period under review, following a 1.2% decline between January and March. Investment in capital goods also picked up, accelerating by 0.8% following a decline of 1.2%.
More
Truth or tale: Is it true that forced labour exists in Swiss supply chains?
Private consumption, one of the driving forces behind the Swiss economy, remained sluggish, however, showing only a modest increase of 0.3%, following a rise of 0.1% in the first quarter.
By sector, the chemicals and pharmaceuticals sector (+10.5%) performed exceptionally well, despite uncertainties surrounding United States tariffs. Manufacturing (+4.5%) also grew, as did financial services (+1.9%) and transport (+1.9%). Growth in the services sector (+0.7%), meanwhile, remained moderate.

It has become possible to get a divorce online through &quot;Diia&quot; - how to do it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:29:47 EEST
18:29:47 KST

It has become possible to get a divorce online through "Diia" - how to do it
Kyiv • UNN
Spouses without joint minor children can get a divorce through «Diia» after a video conference. The electronic record will appear within 24 hours.
Divorce in Ukraine became available online in the "Diia" app starting September 3. UNN reports this, citing the Ministry of Justice and "Diia".
We are launching online divorce in the "Diia" app. The service is available to couples who have jointly decided to end their marriage
Who can use the service
According to the Ministry of Justice, couples can use the service in the "Diia" app if both spouses are Ukrainian citizens, are at least 18 years old, and meet the following requirements:
-  mutual consent of both spouses to the divorce; 
-  no minor children in common; 
-  each spouse has a verified taxpayer registration number (RNOKPP) and "Diia.Signature"; 
-  possession of an ID card or biometric international passport; 
-  a marriage record in the State Register of Civil Status Acts (DRATS). 
"It is important that without the consent of both parties, it will not be possible to submit an application for divorce," "Diia" stated.
How it works
Previously, the mutually agreed divorce procedure generally involved personal visits to a DRATS office: to submit a joint application and, after the one-month waiting period had expired, to register the divorce with the state.
From now on, the main stages can be completed online in the "Diia" app:
-  Application creation: one of the partners submits an application through the "Diia" app and chooses a convenient date and time for a video conference with the registrar (no earlier than one month and two days from the date of submission). 
-  Confirmation and signing: the other spouse receives a notification and, within 12 hours, confirms the necessary information  and signs the application using the "Diia.Signature." 
-  Application verification: information about both partners is checked against state registers. 
-  Video conference: at the specified date and time, the spouses join a video conference with an employee of the DRATS office, during which the partners confirm their intention and certify it with their "Diia.Signatures." 
-  Receiving the result: an electronic display of the divorce record is generated in "Diia" for each spouse within 24 hours after the video conference. Paper divorce certificates are sent by JSC Ukrposhta to each spouse at the address specified in the application. 
"The marriage will be dissolved in a month. If you change your mind during this time, you can withdraw the application — no later than four hours before the video conference," "Diia" stated.
If the spouses have children
If the spouses have minor children in common, the divorce, as before, takes place through the court. Those who do not use "Diia" can still submit an application in person at a DRATS office.
"Marriage Online" extended for another two years10.08.26, 11:57 • 5672 views

For India, Bangladesh’s talk of joining ‘Islamic Nato’ raises red flags
Joining the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani security alliance offers Dhaka leverage, but could also threaten its non-aligned stance
Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament on August 27 that Bangladesh was considering joining the Mecca pact, a security framework signed last month. Earlier reports citing unnamed sources said the invitation originated from Riyadh.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir also told reporters: “If there is a security arrangement among Islamic nations in the Middle East, it is not unusual for us to consider participating. It is being viewed positively.”
Under the agreement signed on August 7 in Mecca, an armed attack against any signatory is treated as an attack against all members – earning the arrangement the informal moniker “Islamic Nato.”
Shafi Md. Mostofa, an associate professor at the University of Dhaka, said that joining the pact would compel India to be “much more cautious and respectful while dealing with [Dhaka].”

UNRWA closes Palestinian refugee school in Lebanon's Tripoli
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:24:52 UTC
18:24:52 KST

Breadcrumb
UNRWA closes school for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon's Tripoli
The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) has announced the closure of Rafah School in the northern Lebanese city of Tripoli and the redistribution of its students among other schools.
The agency is also moving towards closing Al-Bireh School in the Burj al-Barajneh camp in Beirut, while there have been reports of plans to reduce some programmes at the Siblin Vocational and Technical Training Centre.
These reductions come amid difficult conditions faced by Palestinian refugees, raising serious questions about their educational and social impact on students and their families, as well as teaching staff.
Closing a school and transferring its students to other schools is not simply a change in the location of their studies. It also results in the dispersal of students, increased classroom overcrowding in receiving schools, and additional burdens on families in terms of transport and time.
"There are several educational and social repercussions that must be taken into consideration regarding the decision to close Rafah School. About 40 of its students live in the Nahr al-Bared and Beddawi camps, and closing the school will force them to return to the schools in the camps. This will result in a change to the educational environment they have become accustomed to," Ahmed Ghanoumi, head of the Palestinian Popular Committees in northern Lebanon, told The New Arab.
"The rest of the school's students live in the Mina area and are expected to move to Lydda School in the Zahriyeh area. This move will place additional financial burdens on families and will also increase the time students need to travel to and from school," he further said.
"Lydda School has about 140 students from the Nahr al-Bared and Beddawi camps, and they will also be asked to return to the schools in the two camps. This could lead to a change in their educational level because of differences in teaching methods and educational conditions. Rafah School classrooms are characterised by their small size, with between 16 and 20 students in each class. In the camp schools, however, there are up to 40 students in each class," Ghanoumi added. "Therefore, transferring the students will negatively affect their ability to absorb and concentrate as a result of overcrowding and differences in the educational environment."
"Lydda School currently has about 300 students. If Rafah School students move there, the number will rise to about 450," he continued. "This would lead to significant classroom overcrowding, negatively affecting the quality of education and the ability of teachers and administrators to provide an appropriate educational environment for students. Rafah School also has about 30 administrative and teaching staff members. They are not expected to lose their jobs but will instead be distributed among schools where vacancies are available."
"However, this measure will have a direct impact on the employment opportunities available to people who sat recruitment examinations and passed them," Ghanoumi concluded.
On 27 August, the Education Programme for the Palestinian Refugee Community in northern Lebanon stated preparations for the 2026-2027 academic year at UNRWA schools in Lebanon.
It said the agency was continuing efforts to improve the learning environment and facilities available to students in preparation for the new academic year.
The statement said Jenin and Jordan River schools in the Beddawi camp had been refurbished, providing students with more comfortable learning spaces.
It also said the building of Batouf Primary School for Girls in the same camp had been expanded by adding 15 classrooms, a rooftop playground and a lift to improve access for students with disabilities.
This would allow the school to accommodate more students and reduce classroom overcrowding.
The statement added: "For students enrolled at Rafah School, new arrangements will be adopted. Most students live in Beddawi camp and will be accommodated in schools in the camp, allowing them to continue learning close to their homes and avoid travelling to Tripoli. The same applies to students from Nahr al-Bared camp, while Rafah School students living in Tripoli, numbering about 140 boys and girls, will be accommodated at the nearby Lydda School. UNRWA will ensure that all students affected by these arrangements have places in schools, and no teacher or employee will lose their job as a result of these arrangements. UNRWA considers education a priority and remains committed to ensuring that no Palestinian refugee child is left without education and that every child has access to a safe learning environment."
The Palestinian Popular Committees in northern Lebanon, for their part, issued a statement rejecting the closure of Rafah School and the dispersal of its students.
They warned UNRWA of the consequences of failing to reverse its decision because of the direct harm it would cause to the educational process, students and their families.
The factions said the closure of Rafah School could not be treated as an ordinary administrative measure and came as part of an ongoing policy of merging schools, reducing services and closing centres.
This negatively affects the situation of Palestinian refugees and increases the living, social and educational burdens they face.
The Palestinian Popular Committees stressed that they would not stand idly by in the face of any step affecting the rights of refugees and their basic services, foremost among them their children's right to education.
They said they would pursue the issue with all relevant parties and take appropriate steps to defend the school, its students and their rights.

No evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta border surge: Spain's PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:24:01 UTC
18:24:01 KST

Spain has found no evidence to conclude that July's deadly border rush from Morocco into its enclave of Ceuta was orchestrated or carried out by Moroccan authorities, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told lawmakers on Thursday.
Sanchez's comments in the lower house of parliament followed a police report that emerged this week saying that the mass entry into Ceuta was not a spontaneous migration event but a planned and phased operation designed to overwhelm border controls.
"I can assure you that no institution — not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body — has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever," Sanchez said.
However, he said Morocco's Gendarmerie police did allow crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on July 30, when migrant arrivals peaked. Spanish authorities had yet to determine whether this was due to inaction or inability to contain the influx, Sanchez added.
The police report, seen by Reuters, alleged that Moroccan security forces were initially deployed in smaller numbers than usual near the Tarajal breakwater separating the enclave from the North African country and did not make a serious attempt to disperse the crowds.
Some uniformed Moroccan officers gave directions towards the crossing point, while other unidentified people appeared to guide or monitor the flow of people, the report said, but it did not identify individual officers or provide independently verified evidence of orders from Moroccan authorities.
Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
On the other hand, Spanish politicians and commentators have accused Israel of helping inflame the migration crisis in Ceuta amid deteriorating relations over Spain’s stance on Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The claims intensified after Israeli UN Ambassador Danny Danon attacked Madrid over its immigration policy and questioned Spain’s control of Ceuta and Melilla.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente responded that the events were becoming “quite clear,” without elaborating further. Lawmaker Gabriel Rufian also echoed claims that the crisis was serving Israeli interests.

Families hold symbolic funerals as flood death toll hits 1,273 with nearly 4,800 missing
