Families in flood-hit areas of Nepal are holding symbolic funerals for missing loved ones as the death toll from last week's flash floods rose to 1,252, with more than 4,200 people missing, official data showed on Thursday.
In neighbouring China, 21 people were killed and 541 remained missing, including 261 foreigners, according to local authorities.
The combined death toll from both countries stood at 1,273, while 4,757 people remained missing, including 844 foreign nationals.
In Rasuwa, one of Nepal's hardest-hit districts, families created funeral effigies using kaas-kush, or sacred grass, and performed final rites to "liberate the souls" of missing relatives after losing hope of finding their bodies, the Kathmandu Post reported.
On Wednesday, dozens of such effigies were cremated in a mass funeral at Pashupati Aryaghat temple in Kathmandu on the banks of the Bagmati River.
In Chitwan, another badly affected district, authorities buried unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples because the number of remains made individual identification and storage difficult.
Many flood victims have been left without places to observe mourning rituals after floodwaters swept away both family members and homes in several districts.
Those who lost everything and travelled to Kathmandu seeking shelter have also been unable to find space at public facilities for the rituals.
Military personnel, police and others continued search and rescue operations in flood-hit areas on Thursday.
Rescuers, however, faced difficulties as roads, power supplies and communications remained disrupted across wide areas.
They were also working to deliver relief supplies and maintain hygiene in shelters to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 metres, triggering an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley, while also burying the Gyirong border crossing in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.

Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
Nigeria has confirmed that around 200 US troops deployed to support its fight against armed groups will begin leaving the West African country, with most expected to withdraw by late September.
A smaller advisory and intelligence team will remain, while cooperation in training and information sharing will continue, Nigerian military spokesperson Major General Samaila Uba said on Tuesday. “The deployment of United States personnel was tied to specific operational and counterterrorism objectives,” Uba said, according to AP.
The troops arrived in February to provide intelligence, targeting, and training support. Washington subsequently deployed MQ-9 Reaper surveillance drones to Bauchi Airfield in northeastern Nigeria. The mission came after US President Donald Trump accused the Nigerian authorities of failing to protect Christians and threatened military action.
Nigeria rejected claims that Christians were being systematically targeted, saying jihadist violence, banditry, and communal conflicts affect citizens of different faiths.
The two countries conducted coordinated airstrikes against alleged Islamic State fighters in Sokoto State in December 2025. In May, Nigeria’s Defense Headquarters and US Africa Command said a joint operation in the Lake Chad Basin killed senior Islamic State figure Abu-Bilal al-Minuki. Trump described him as the group’s second-highest-ranking leader globally.
US Africa Command chief General Dagvin Anderson announced in July that most of the American troops had been withdrawn, saying the campaign had successfully degraded Islamic State’s leadership and disrupted its wider network. Samuel Memeh, chairman of Nigeria’s Democratic Leadership Alliance, disputed that assessment. Memeh told RT that the deployment had produced no significant improvement in security and argued that foreign forces alone could not defeat the country’s armed groups.
Nigeria continues to face overlapping threats from Boko Haram and its Islamic State-affiliated offshoot in the northeast, armed bandits operating across the northwest and central regions, and intercommunal violence. More than 40,000 people have been killed since the insurgency began in 2009, UN News reported in January.
Major attacks continued during the US deployment. On August 21, gunmen attacked several communities in Niger State, reportedly killing 30 people and abducting hundreds of worshippers from a mosque. Residents put the number of captives as high as 600, although the authorities said the figure had not been verified. At least 2,000 people reportedly fled into neighboring Benin.
Lagos-based security consultancy SBM Intelligence said in a report last month that at least 7,825 people were abducted across Africa’s most populous nation between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase from the previous 12-month period.

China lambasts France’s ‘discriminatory’ fast-fashion law
China on Thursday called on France to abandon a new law on ultra-fast fashion that would impose fees of up to almost €20 per garment, calling it "clearly discriminatory". The law, which targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein and Temu, aims to curb the industry's environmental and local economic impacts.
China urged France on Thursday to abandon its recently implemented law on ultra-fast fashion, lambasting the new measure targeting major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein and Temu as "clearly discriminatory".
The law, which came into effect on Tuesday, imposes fees on certain items that will eventually reach almost €20 per garment, part of a push to curb the industry's environmental and local economic impacts.
Read moreFrance targets Shein and Temu with new fast fashion levy
"China urges France to immediately halt the implementation of the anti-ultra-fast fashion law," commerce ministry spokeswoman Huang Ling said when asked about the law at a news conference.
Huang said that China is in "firm opposition to France's insistence on pushing forward this trade-restrictive measure, which is clearly discriminatory".
"Should France persist in this course of action, China will take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises," she warned.
"France will bear full responsibility for all consequences arising from this."
Under the French legislation, ultra-fast fashion is determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
Shein, known for its ultra-low prices and rapidly produced clothes, made a tepid Hong Kong Stock Exchange debut on Tuesday, after previous plans for initial public offerings in New York and London were derailed.
The online retailer moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, which analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.

‘I would rather die than return to France’: the brutal reality of the UK’s one in, one out scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:21:14 UTC
18:21:14 KST

At the end of last year, two men fled Iran. Aso and Baran* were strangers at the time. The way their stories would cross, then diverge, reveals the cruel arbitrariness of the UK asylum system in general, and the government’s controversial one in, one out scheme in particular.
Before he left Iran, Aso, 28, had converted from Islam to Christianity, putting his life in imminent danger. “I had to keep my conversion to Christianity a secret,” he says. “I knew if I was caught, I risked being executed by the Iranian regime … one of my relatives, who I trusted, paid smugglers to get me out last November.”
A few weeks later, at the end of December, Baran fled too. The 33-year-old had been politically active against the Iranian government, he says, and “feared being punished by the ministry of intelligence. I had previously been targeted by the Iranian authorities, shot at with rubber bullets and hit on the back of my head. My house was raided by intelligence officers one day when I wasn’t at home. They confiscated my ID. Relatives contacted me and warned me not to return home. They took me to another village and, from there – with the help of these relatives, who paid smugglers – I was taken out of Iran and crossed the border to Turkey.” A rubber bullet remains lodged in his genitals.
The men made their way separately to northern France. There, their paths converged – but they were still yet to meet.
In January this year, Aso and Baran boarded the same small boat, bound for the UK. Aso says the crossing was “terrifying”. His legs had been hit with a pipe by the smugglers the night before, and he spent eight excruciating hours in the dinghy on his knees. “There was no room to sit, and the waves were crashing into us. It is the most frightening thing in the world.”
On arrival, they were taken to a detention centre, where they finally met. Aso says he could immediately see that Baran “was a good and kind person, despite the difficult conditions in the detention centre – being locked in our cells for up to 12 hours a day, not knowing what was going to happen to us and feeling terrified of being returned to France. Despite all the stress, Baran was very calm and I always felt comfortable with him.”
Their fears about being sent back to France were well founded. The UK government’s one in, one out scheme was announced last July by then prime minister Sir Keir Starmer and France’s president, Emmanuel Macron. It is being piloted until 1 October, and aims to deter people like Aso and Baran from crossing the Channel in small boats to seek sanctuary in the UK. Since it began, more than a thousand asylum seekers have been selected by the Home Office, apparently at random, to be returned to France.
The idea is that one person who arrives here in a small boat is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another who is brought legally to the UK from France. Those who are brought to the UK are distinguished by the fact they have not previously tried to cross the Channel in a small boat. The aim of the scheme is to make the UK so unappealing that refugees choose somewhere else – anywhere else – to seek safety. In effect, people like Aso and Baran, who want to settle in the UK, are used as reluctant human shields to protect our border from others in the same predicament as them.
Today, Baran is living on the outskirts of Lille, sleeping under a tree in the park. I meet him in the centre of the city, and he appears to have no belongings beyond the frayed jeans, battered trainers and ancient fleece he is wearing, and a package wrapped in black plastic, holding his Home Office documents. His curly hair is prematurely streaked with grey, and the smell of wood smoke hangs around him, from his time spent huddled over an open fire.
In January, when Baran first realised he was at risk of being returned to France, he begged the Home Office not to deport him. His Home Office detention notes, shared with the Guardian, refer to his “food and fluid refusal” – a hunger strike – and it is recorded that he told officials: “I would rather die than return to France.”
They ignored him. He was returned to Paris in the middle of February.
“When I was returned to France, I was in so much pain from the bullet lodged in my genitals that I travelled to the local hospital to see if they could treat me,” he says. The smugglers knew the location of the shelter where he was being housed and found him there. “Because I was sent back to France, rather than staying in the UK, my family did not pay the smugglers, so they came after me to catch me and punish me, because they didn’t get their money.
“After they caught me, they took me to the Jungle in Dunkirk [an informal refugee encampment, known for its poor conditions], beat me with sticks and with their hands, and threatened me with guns. I was a slave for the smugglers. They forced me to wash dishes and clothes for eight to 10 hours every day, without breaks … even to go to the toilet. When I did not follow their instructions, they hit me in the mouth and used a log to hit me in the leg.”
Many of those who have been returned to France, after failing to access immigration lawyers who could successfully fight their case, have boarded the flight from Stansted to Paris’s Charles de Gaulle airport in a quietly hopeless state. But there have also been protests against these forced removals inside detention centres, and multiple suicide attempts.
In March, a month after Baran was sent back to France, Aso was sent back there too.
He says he was accompanied by Home Office guards on the flight out of the UK, which he found frightening. “It really is a terrible feeling. Two officers hold you and sit right next to you on the plane, treating you as if you’ve committed a major crime, as if you had killed someone or you are a dangerous person. My mental health was completely shattered.”
On arrival, Aso was placed in an immigration camp in Paris, “that was incredibly cold, with inhumane conditions and inadequate food”.
He sent me a message: “Please help me. I don’t know what to do here. We cannot have a shower because the water is ice cold. We are completely lost and confused. I am so scared. Please let me be safe. I don’t want to die. I want to live. I am deeply heartbroken. It has been four months since I last had any news of my mother and my country is now torn by war. If I am sent back to Iran, I will be executed, because I converted to Christianity.”
He was later evicted from the shelter – returnees are generally only accommodated there for a few days – and left homeless. “I found no support in Paris, and went back to the Jungle in Dunkirk, living in the forest there with a couple of other people I knew.” On 28 March, Aso sent me a WhatsApp message from the Jungle: “l am terrified here. These smugglers are heartless. They will hurt me wherever they find me.”
While Aso was searching for a safe place to stay in France, Baran was already back in the UK. At the beginning of March, he travelled back to Britain. A lorry brought him to Dover, and he was found hiding in it before being arrested and returned to a UK detention centre for the second time.
Baran is far from the only refugee who has been deported under the one in, one out scheme, then risked their life to return.
The Guardian has tracked more than 30 people who have been forcibly returned to France after arriving in the UK on a small boat. All say they have received minimal support in France and, at times, outright hostility. Some have crossed borders to Italy, Germany, Sweden, Spain and the Netherlands. While critics and Home Office officials call this “asylum shopping”, the asylum seekers see it very differently. They say all they are looking for is a place they can live safely without being thrown out, detained or forcibly returned either to their home country or another country they passed through on their journey.
Many, like Baran, have returned to the UK after being deported, finding conditions in France too difficult, particularly due to threats from the people smugglers who transported them across the Channel the first time.
Asylum seekers themselves estimate that approximately 200 of those who have been deported have returned to the UK – some, like Baran, by lorry, a route that smugglers have been using increasingly since the start of the scheme.
Previously, all asylum seekers crossing the Channel declared themselves to the Home Office on arrival in the UK, hopeful that they might be granted asylum and the chance to build a new and legal life. But now some are living under the radar, a development that critics claim actually reduces control of UK borders. The Home Office accepts that about 50 returnees have been detained a second time after returning to the UK. The Guardian has been given names, ages and nationalities of more than 30 returnees from 10 different countries, including Somalia, Georgia, Afghanistan and Syria, some of whom are living under the radar.
Every time I called Baran at the detention centre he was anxiously awaiting news about his case. “Many other asylum seekers have been released into the UK community or sent to France by plane,” he said. “But I am being locked up for many months here with no update about my case. Do you know what will happen to me?”
Aso was still struggling in France. On 3 May, I received another message from him. “Even though I am only 28, I feel like a 60-year-old man because of all the stress, grief and depression I’ve experienced. I am constantly living in fear of falling back into the hands of the smugglers or being deported to Iran by France.
“Unfortunately, the Home Office didn’t listen to us when we said France wasn’t safe. I’m aware that many asylum seekers in France burn off their fingerprints to avoid being sent back to countries like Bulgaria. A question: if you burn your fingerprints, will your fingerprints disappear?”
By 16 May, he was even more frantic. “I don’t want to hide it from you,” he wrote. “I can’t stay in France any more. Either I will return to Iran and let them execute me or I will go back to the UK. I have no choice. My life is ruined here. I have no money, no clothes and there is absolutely no one to help me. Living here is like dying every single day. It has been 50 days since I returned. I’m losing my mind. Of course I am under threat in the Jungle. I am so stressed, I don’t know what to do. I’m dying here every single day.”
In the middle of June, Aso returned to the UK in a lorry, just as his friend Baran had three months before. He was immediately detained too. “If France were safe and my life were not in danger, I would never have risked returning to the UK,” he told me. “I do not feel safe anywhere else. The United Kingdom is the only place where I am protected from the Iranian regime and criminal smuggler networks.”
Baran ended up being detained for more than four months on his return to the UK, longer than the usual timeframe for people detained under the one in, one out scheme. While in detention, he was told he needed surgery to remove the rubber bullet from his genitals. The Home Office declined to arrange it and said the surgery could be performed in France.
In July, France finally accepted the readmission request that had initially been made for him in March. Although Baran’s ability to speak and write English is very limited, he drafted a note to the Home Office in clear script just before his second removal to France, stating: “I can’t go back to France because over there is not safe for me. Don’t let them to send me back.” Since being returned there, he has been unable to access any health, housing or welfare services.
Aso’s life took a different path. While in detention in the UK, not knowing whether he would be returned to France for a second time, he became increasingly distressed. But a friend in Swansea offered to support and accommodate him, and he was overjoyed to be granted bail. For the first time since I got to know him, his messages became more positive.
“I feel like I’m getting better. I’m feeling safe,” he said in a message on 12 August. “It’s very hot here. I’ve decided to hit the beach for a dip to cool off.”
But Aso is desperately concerned about his friend. “I really don’t know why they sent Baran back to France for the second time but have allowed me to stay in the UK. It is honestly such a sad situation for Baran.” The two men have been in contact on WhatsApp, but Baran sometimes struggles to charge his phone, so many of Aso’s calls go unanswered.
The images of people in orange lifejackets arriving in the UK on overcrowded dinghies have been used by Reform UK and other right-wing political parties and commentators to claim the country is being overrun. In fact, the UK takes only a tenth or less of asylum seekers arriving in Europe and ranks 15th in Europe per head of population for asylum claims.
One in, one out was supposed to act as a deterrent, but it is not clear whether it has succeeded. The number of asylum seekers who have crossed the Channel so far in 2026 is down 40% on the same period last year, but that is in the context of asylum seeker arrivals to Europe being down significantly overall. Windy weather has also made crossings more difficult, and some people are travelling to the UK from France in lorries, uncounted in the immigration statistics. The Home Office has been reticent about what, if anything, will replace one in, one out when the pilot scheme finishes.
In Lille, Baran remains downcast. I offer to take him to the supermarket so he can choose a few essentials. He is too dejected to even look at the shelves. His chin sinks towards his chest and he says food no longer interests him. Under pressure from me to choose something, he puts a single apple, two bananas, a packet of nuts and a box of Ritz crackers in the shopping basket.
“I don’t have any friends in France or any plan,” he says. “A few guys who live near the park I’m sleeping in help me with food and sometimes let me have a shower at their place. The smugglers caught me before and I am frightened all the time that they will catch me again. My only hope is to find a way to return to the UK. But I don’t know how.”
Baran last made contact with the Guardian just before midnight on 24 August. His current whereabouts and condition are unknown.

South Korean police seek tycoon behind K-pop supergroup BTS to be indicted
Bang Si-hyuk is being investigated for alleged investor fraud over the initial public offering of the agency Hybe
The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency referred Bang to the Seoul Southern District Prosecutors’ Office on Thursday, asking him to be indicted on a charge of violating the Capital Markets Act, according to the police agency and the prosecutor’s office.

Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Elmar Vaher took responsibility for the fact that the National Audit Office did not receive the contract for a €70 million artillery shell deal despite repeatedly requesting it.
The National Audit Office has previously criticized the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), which is responsible for procurement, for failing to provide it with the contract for a €70 million artillery shell deal despite repeated requests. RKIK maintained that the contract had been sent on June 5. The National Audit Office maintained that it had not received the contract.
Anastassia Kovalenko-Kõlvart (Center), chair of the Riigikogu Anti-Corruption Select Committee, asked for an explanation of the situation at Thursday's meeting.
RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher said he was responsible for the error. He explained that at 3:26 p.m. on June 5, RKIK's head of audit sent four contracts to the National Audit Office. "We were convinced that the contract had been sent, but it turned out it hadn't been," Vaher said.
He added that he had also spoken with National Audit Office Director Janar Holm, who asked why RKIK had not sent the contracts. "I asked my staff and they said we had sent them and that was where the matter ended," Vaher said.
In his view, RKIK was at fault for failing to make sure the email had reached the National Audit Office. "We didn't put them in the cloud," Vaher said. He noted that the files consisted of four PDF documents that should have gone through by email. "I don't understand why they didn't," he said.
Kovalenko-Kõlvart then asked whether, given that the contracts were confidential, RKIK should have obtained confirmation from the National Audit Office that the email had arrived. "I wouldn't be inclined to regulate everything," Vaher replied. He added, however, that RKIK could do a better job of sending documents in the future.
The Anti-Corruption Select Committee held an extraordinary public meeting Thursday to discuss problems with the use of funds and corruption risks in the defense sector in light of a National Audit Office audit.

El Niño to be 'very strong' and last until February, UN climate agency warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:19:41 UTC
18:19:41 KST

El Niño tends to peak late in the year but heat in the oceans releases more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the following year.
El Niño is set to become "very strong" in the months ahead, with the weather phenomenon near certain to persist through to February, the United Nations' climate agency warned on Thursday.
The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said El Niño would peak towards the end of this year, though its knock-on impacts for the climate will continue well into 2027.
"El Niño is firmly established and will intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, with big impacts on rainfall and temperature patterns and associated risks of floods, drought and extreme heat," the WMO said.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.
But scientists expect it will exacerbate the heat of a planet already warming from burning fossil fuels, while amping up weather extremes.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes," said UN chief António Guterres.
"The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather," he said.
"The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race."
'Massive blow' to economies
El Niño tends to peak late in the year but heat in the oceans releases more slowly into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures the following year.
The hottest year on record is 2024, following the last El Niño.
"This exceptional El Niño...has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world", said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies."
She put disaster management authorities and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water on notice, saying there was "no time to lose" in getting ready.
El Niño warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Niño and its opposite La Niña, with neutral conditions in between.
"Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, El Niño is expected to strengthen further during the coming months to a very strong intensity," the WMO said.
The UN agency classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong, meaning it is set to reach the highest level out of four.
The WMO said there was an "exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 percent" that El Niño will continue through to February.
Pacific Ocean heating up
El Niño can reshape weather and climate patterns thousands of kilometres away from the tropical Pacific.
Every El Niño is different, but major events often follow familiar patterns. This includes drought across parts of the Amazon, Indonesia and Australia, disrupted monsoons in India, and shifting rainfall throughout the tropics.
For September-November, WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures "across almost all land areas", alongside rainfall patterns showing a "pronounced and classic atmospheric response to the strong Pacific El Niño", the UN's weather and climate agency said.
The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central eastern equatorial Pacific has strengthened from an average 1.5C above normal between May and July.
Weekly values between late July and mid-August ranged from around 2.2C to 2.6C above average, indicating continued El Niño intensification.
In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8C above average during July and early August.

West Nile virus: 290 cases and 24 deaths in Greece — Cyprus calls for calm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:18:56 UTC
18:18:56 KST

Pressure on Greek hospitals remains high. In Cyprus, figures still stand at four confirmed West Nile virus cases, with two more under investigation.
West Nile virus circulation in Greece is particularly intense this year, with Attica accounting for the largest share of cases. The burden is also increasing in Thessaly and Central Macedonia as the Hellenic National Public Health Organisation (EODY) expects new cases in the coming weeks.
According to the EODY's latest weekly report, with data up to 2 September, 290 domestically acquired West Nile virus infections have been diagnosed and reported since the start of the current transmission season. In the past week alone, 58 new cases were added, indicating that transmission remains at high levels.
Of the 290 cases, 199 had neurological symptoms affecting the central nervous system (CNS), including encephalitis, meningitis or acute flaccid paralysis. The remaining 91 patients had milder symptoms or no CNS involvement. The median age of patients who developed central nervous system manifestations is 74 years.
As of 2 September,24 deaths had been recorded, all in people over the age of 65. The median age of those who died was 83.
Pressure on hospitals remains significant. A total of 63 patients were in hospital, 32 in intensive care units and 31 in ordinary wards, while 182 patients had already been discharged.
Where most cases are being reported
Attica is clearly at the epicentre of this year's surge. Adding up the municipality-level data published by EODY shows that around 166 of the 290 cases are in Attica — more than half of all cases nationwide. Thessaly and Central Macedonia follow, with 52 cases each.
Three cases have been recorded in Crete, two in Central Greece and one in the Peloponnese, while the place of exposure for another 14 cases is still under investigation.
The EODY describes this year's circulation of the virus in the Region of Attica as "particularly intense", noting an increase in cases compared with previous years. In total, cases have been detected in 69 municipalities, 20 regional units and six regions: Attica, Thessaly, Central Macedonia, Peloponnese, Central Greece and Crete.
At the municipal level, Larissa has the highest total number of reported cases, with 27. It is followed by Spata–Artemida with 19 cases, Markopoulo Mesogaias and Agia Paraskevi with 14 each, the Municipality of Pella with 13, and Vari–Voula–Vouliagmeni and Halandri with 12 cases each.
Particular caution is required in Eastern Attica. Spata–Artemida has recorded 17 patients with CNS involvement, Markopoulo Mesogaias 11 and Vari–Voula–Vouliagmeni 11, while significant numbers are also reported in Pallini, Marathon and Acharnes. In the Northern Sector of Athens, Agia Paraskevi and Halandri each have 10 severe cases with CNS manifestations.
At the same time, EODY has designated additional municipalities as "high risk", even though no human cases had been recorded there up to 2 September. These include municipalities in Attica such as Iraklio, Nea Smyrni, Palaio Faliro, Nea Filadelfia–Nea Chalkidona, Dafni–Ymittos and Ilion, as well as areas in Trikala, Serres, Thessaloniki, Pieria, Kilkis, Corinthia, Heraklion in Crete, Thasos and Tinos. The designation is based on a combination of epidemiological, geomorphological and other risk data.
EODY points out that further cases are expected to be diagnosed both in already affected areas and possibly in new ones, stressing that the geographical spread of the virus cannot be predicted with certainty. For this reason, it recommends individual protection measures against mosquitoes throughout the country for the entire period of their activity.
Cyprus: Four confirmed cases – Health Services call for calm and vigilance
In Cyprus, the Health Services are urging calm and vigilance, stressing that, based on the data so far, there is no particular cause for concern over West Nile virus.
The Deputy Head of the Health Services, Herodotos Herodotou, speaking on the "Protoselido" programme on SIGMA, said that there is no need for anxiety, while underlining the need for caution and vigilance so that the competent services are in a position to deal with any developments.
As he explained, the virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito, and he noted that the Health Services have been implementing measures to control mosquitoes and address related risks for decades. He also clarified that this particular mosquito species is not imported into Cyprus but has existed on the island for many years.
Four confirmed cases – two under investigation
The situation in Cyprus remains at four confirmed cases of West Nile virus, while a further two cases are under investigation.
According to Herodotou, the Health Services continue to apply prescribed measures around the areas where cases are detected. Among other actions, immediate spraying is carried out around patients' homes, along with on-site inspections and door-to-door tracing.
Removal of standing water and self-protection measures
Particular emphasis is being placed on prevention, with the main recommendation being the removal of standing water from plant pots, fountains, gutters and other places where water may accumulate, as such spots can become breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
For individual protection, the public are also urged to use window screens, especially in places where elderly people live, as well as fans, which can help limit mosquitoes.

Ukrainian ground robot survives five FPV strikes, finishes mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:16:47 UTC
18:16:47 KST

- A Ukrainian Droid TW-12.7 ground robot survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its mission before a sixth strike disabled it.
- The system, built by DevDroid and armed with a 12.7 mm M2 Browning machine gun, has previously held a frontline position for 45 days.
A Ukrainian armed ground robot survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth strike finally disabled it, according to DevDroid, the Ukrainian company that builds the system.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion remotely operated the Droid TW-12.7 during an operation to clear an area where enemy personnel had gathered, DevDroid said. As the unmanned ground vehicle approached enemy positions, two FPV drones struck it almost simultaneously. One hit damaged its aiming module, but the machine stayed mobile and continued toward its objective, according to the company.
Operators kept firing on the target using the weapon’s barrel direction to aim after the aiming module was damaged, DevDroid said. Two more FPV strikes hit the UGV during the engagement, and it remained operational and completed the mission. A fifth strike hit the system on its way back, and it kept moving. A sixth FPV drone finally disabled the Droid TW-12.7, according to the company.
DevDroid said the enemy troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces took losses. The operation was carried out remotely, without exposing Ukrainian soldiers to direct contact with enemy forces, the company said.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission,” said Yurii Poritskyi, CEO of DevDroid. “For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile, it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result.”
The Droid TW-12.7 is a tracked ground robot built around a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning machine gun. According to specifications published by its distributor, the system can engage targets out to 1 km, reaches a top speed of 7 km/h (4.3 mph) and has an operational range up to 25 km (15.5 miles), with a tactical deployment radius of 5 km (3.1 miles) from its control station. It combines manual control with AI-assisted automatic targeting and communicates over radio, with mesh, LTE or satellite links available as options. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has codified the system, clearing it for supply to Ukrainian forces.
The platform has seen extended combat use before this engagement. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps said in November that a Droid TW-12.7 operated by the corps’ NC-13 Strike Company held a frontline position for 45 straight days, standing in for an infantry unit at a contested crossroads while taking no Ukrainian casualties. The unit said the robot left its position briefly every two days for maintenance and to reload ammunition, handled by a crew stationed roughly 2.4 miles behind the front line.
DevDroid said the Droid TW-12.7 combines remote control, an integrated ballistic computer and AI algorithms to detect, track and engage targets while reducing risk to personnel. Beyond engaging infantry fighting vehicles, armored personnel carriers and other armored targets, the company said the system can strike unarmored vehicles and equipment and suppress enemy positions, including platoon strongpoints and firing points. It also carries cameras and data links that let operators maintain situational awareness from a distance, according to DevDroid.

Gulf insecurity fuels US energy dominance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:16:20 UTC
18:16:20 KST

Gulf insecurity fuels US energy dominance
The no-war, no-peace status quo with Iran increasingly benefits the US, its energy sector and its ally Israel.
The global energy order is changing.
US President Donald Trump celebrated on Truth Social what he called the “biggest oil deal in history” – a 100-year concession on 17 oil fields in Venezuela that would secure 65 billion barrels of oil.
Around the same time, QatarEnergy informed Edison, one of its biggest European customers, that force majeure on its liquefied natural gas (LNG) deliveries would continue until early November. Five more cargoes were cancelled, taking the total to 29, or about 3.8 billion cubic metres of gas.
The contract has run since 2009 and normally covers roughly a tenth of Italy’s annual consumption. Edison has kept supplying its customers by finding replacement cargoes elsewhere, including in the US.
For decades, the bargain between Washington and the Gulf was clear. The US protected the region and kept its sea lanes open; Gulf producers supplied the energy on which the global economy depended and settled their sales in dollars to benefit the US economy.
That bargain has been turned on its head. America no longer simply protects Gulf energy. It competes with it, and increasingly profits when the Gulf cannot deliver due to insecurity.
Six months of war have reportedly impacted Qatar’s LNG exports significantly. Other Gulf countries like Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have seen a substantial drop in oil exports as well. Meanwhile, US oil and gas have moved into the space left behind, with US energy giants raking in record-high profits.
It is important here to distinguish between the US as a government and the dense network of private interests that operates around it. Washington wants strategic leverage over Iran and continued influence over the Gulf states. Energy companies want access to reserves, favourable regulation, profitable prices and new customers. Trump brings the two together under the banner of energy dominance. State power opens the door; private capital walks through it.
Israel adds another layer. Chevron operates its two main offshore gas fields, owning almost 40 percent of the Leviathan gasfield and 25 percent of the Tamar gasfield. Leviathan is expanding after a $35bn agreement was signed last year to increase exports to Egypt.
Israel is therefore not an independent energy rival to the US in the way Qatar is. Its growing role as an Eastern Mediterranean gas hub is tied to a US operator and fits comfortably within a US-backed regional system linking Israel, Egypt and Jordan.
Chevron is the thread running through much of this story. It has major interests in US production, controls Israel’s most important gas assets and is positioned to expand in Venezuela. This does not mean Chevron determines foreign policy. It does show how easily the exercise of American power can translate into commercial opportunity for American companies.
Israel is also determined not to let the confrontation with Iran end on terms it considers not to be in its interest. The US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June fell well short of Israeli war aims. Israel said it was not bound by all its provisions, insisted on freedom of action in Lebanon and briefly resumed attacks while the US was trying to sustain negotiations.
For Israel, ceasefires have tended to be pauses, not settlements: opportunities to regroup while preserving the option of striking again. The reasons are chiefly strategic. Israel wants to prevent Iran from rebuilding its nuclear, missile and regional capabilities, while Israeli leaders fear accepting a deal and looking weak ahead of elections.
The consequences of Israel pushing for continuous conflict align with US energy interests. Continued pressure on Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz insecure, Gulf exports vulnerable and risk premiums for energy transport high. Israel and US energy companies do not need to be following a common plan for their interests to reinforce one another.
Price is where the argument becomes clearest. Trump talks constantly about cheap oil, but US producers cannot prosper if it becomes too cheap. A Dallas Federal Reserve survey found that US companies needed an average price of about $43 a barrel to operate existing wells and $66 to drill new ones profitably. The two main Permian basins sit at roughly $61 to $62.
Trump therefore needs a narrow band: oil cheap enough to contain inflation, but expensive enough to keep shale, fracking and export investment alive. Gulf insecurity helps maintain it. The disruption need not be catastrophic. It only has to keep prices at a point where the next American well makes economic sense.
This may help explain the attraction of a no-war, no-peace outcome. A full regional war could close Hormuz, send prices soaring and threaten Chevron’s Israeli operations. A durable settlement would remove the risk premium, restore confidence in Gulf supply and limit Israel’s freedom of action.
Managed insecurity sits conveniently between the two: enough restraint to protect US-linked production, but not enough diplomacy to make Gulf energy entirely dependable again.
Israel keeps Iran under pressure. Washington retains leverage over its allies. US producers gain customers and commercially supportive prices. The danger lies in the convergence: Several powerful actors now have something to gain from preventing the crisis from reaching a final resolution.
The Gulf still holds vast reserves and enjoys production costs US companies cannot match. But reserves alone no longer decide market power. Reliability does. Only an estimated 3.5 to 5.5 million barrels a day can bypass Hormuz through Saudi and Emirati pipelines. The rest remains exposed to a single point of failure, despite decades of arms purchases, foreign bases and security guarantees.
The greatest threat to the Gulf’s energy future is not depletion. It is that customers learn to live without it. Every delayed tanker strengthens the case for an Atlantic alternative. Every Qatari cargo replaced by US LNG creates a relationship that may endure long after the war.
US power once rested partly on protecting the flow of Gulf energy. It now rests increasingly on replacing it.

Why Finland is staging Europe's biggest civil defence drill since WWII
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:16:15 UTC
18:16:15 KST

Finland is carrying out one of Europe's largest civil defence exercises since World War II, with more than 2,000 people in the central city of Kuopio rehearsing how to respond to missile strikes, cyberattacks and disruptions to critical infrastructure amid heightened security concerns over Russia.
The two-day exercise, known as Shelter 2026, is taking place from September 2 to 3 at an underground sports and events centre in Kuopio that can be converted into a civil defence shelter for about 7,000 people, AP reported. Authorities, students, volunteers, businesses and other organisations are taking part.
The scenario involves a deteriorating security situation in which critical infrastructure has been disrupted and the threat of military force has increased. Participants are practicing how to move large numbers of people into shelters and how authorities and other organisations would coordinate if normal services were disrupted.
Inside the shelter, Finnish conscripts are practicing radiation monitoring and other emergency procedures. Hundreds of participants are also sleeping overnight in the facility to test how it could function during a prolonged emergency.
The exercise is not being held in response to an immediate threat. Finnish authorities describe it as a planned preparedness exercise aimed at testing decision-making, communications, situational awareness and cooperation during a crisis.
But the scale of the exercise reflects the way Finland has changed its security planning since the Russia-Ukraine war.
Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 1,300 kilometres from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle. In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following the Russia-Ukraine war.
Russian aircraft have entered Finnish airspace
Finland's concern about Russia is not purely theoretical.
Drones have entered its airspace this year, although at least one was identified as Ukrainian, while Finnish authorities linked the incidents to the war in Ukraine.
Russia has also tested Finland's airspace.
On August 20, Finland said it suspected a Russian military aircraft had entered Finnish airspace over the Gulf of Finland. The Finnish Border Guard later identified the aircraft as an IL-20 reconnaissance plane and said it had remained inside Finnish airspace for about three minutes.
Finland had reported another suspected violation by a Russian military aircraft in May.
Sweden is also increasing its military presence in Finland, with jets and a naval vessel due to support surveillance and protection of Finnish territory through the end of 2026 as regional security concerns grow.
Sweden will deploy its Gripen jets and a corvette warship to Finland to support the surveillance and protection of Finnish territory through the end of 2026, according to Finland's defence forces.
Swedish Defence Minister Pal Jonson stated that Sweden might assist Finland in repelling any territorial violations.
Finland fought several wars with the Soviet Union
In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11 percent of its territory, and more than 400,000 people, around 12 percent of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.
At Kuopio's veterans’ museum, Risto Moonkkoonen, 95, showed AP a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.
“I cannot forget it,” he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father’s friends.
Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.
Aili Toivanen, 92, told AP she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.

China demands France scrap fast fashion law targeting Shein and Temu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:15:19 UTC
18:15:19 KST

Beijing has threatened with unspecified measures in response to France’s new environmental penalties on ultra-fast-fashion retailers.
China has urged France to halt its recently implemented law targeting ultra-fast fashion, describing the measure as discriminatory.
The underlying law, which took effect on Tuesday, raises the contribution paid by producers of qualifying clothing, footwear and household linen sold through ultra-fast-fashion business models by between €0.25 and €12 per item in 2026, with the maximum rising to €20 from 2030.
The legislation affects major e-commerce platforms including Shein, Temu and AliExpress.
“China urges France to immediately halt the implementation of the anti-ultra-fast-fashion law,” commerce ministry spokeswoman Huang Ling told a news conference on Thursday.
She said China was “strongly dissatisfied” with France’s decision to proceed with what Beijing considered a discriminatory trade restriction.
China believes the legislation uses environmental and sustainability standards to apply double standards and may breach World Trade Organization rules on non-discrimination, Huang said.
“If France insists on proceeding, China will take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” she added.
“France will bear all consequences arising from this.”
What does the law say?
The law defines ultra-fast fashion using two criteria: how many new products a company introduces and whether customers are encouraged to repair rather than replace them.
The legislation is intended to reduce the fashion industry’s environmental impact and protect France’s domestic clothing sector from an influx of low-cost products.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
The charge is levied on producers rather than directly on consumers, although companies could pass on some or all of the cost through higher prices.
Shein, known for its low prices and rapidly changing product range, made a subdued debut on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Tuesday after earlier plans to list in New York and London stalled amid scrutiny of its Chinese supply chains.
The online retailer moved its headquarters from China to Singapore in 2022, a step widely viewed as an attempt to distance the company from growing international scrutiny of Chinese businesses.

A new Channel 13 News poll published Wednesday shows far-right parties led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and hard-line former general Ofer Winter both passing the electoral threshold, boosting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc and weakening his rivals as he works to consolidate parties to his right.
The poll projects both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs would have 53 seats each, a five-seat reduction from the previous survey for Netanyahu's top rival, while Arab parties receive 14.
As in a series of recent polls, the survey shows a majority of 67 seats for parties opposed to Netanyahu's government. However, some parties in the Eisenkot bloc oppose joining with Arab parties, leaving the bloc without a majority in the Knesset.

The Arab-led Joint List receives nine seats, down one. Yisrael Beiteinu and United Torah Judaism each receive eight seats, with the latter gaining one. Shas and Otzma Yehudit each receive seven seats, unchanged from last week.
Smotrich's far-right Religious Zionism party, which on Tuesday merged its list with fringe far-right libertarian Moshe Feiglin's Zehut party, receives six seats. United Arab List receives five, while Winter's Amcha Yisrael party receives four.
Three parties fail to cross the electoral threshold: Chili Tropper and Yoaz Hendel's Bayit Tzioni, with 2 percent; Benny Gantz's Blue and White, with 1.2 percent; and Gilad Erdan's Ha'Ahdut, with 0.6 percent.
The poll was conducted by Hamadad, led by Shmuel Rosner and Noah Salpakov, in cooperation with Stat-Net, led by Yosef Makladeh; Project Hamigdam, led by Dr. Ariel Ayalon; and Askaria, led by Dudi Dror. Additional data was provided by Hive, with statistical consulting by Prof. David Steinberg.
The survey included 940 respondents and has a sampling error of 3.4 percent.

Strong El Nino expected to raise extreme weather risks into 2027: UN weather agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:13:23 UTC
18:13:23 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
El Nino is firmly established and expected to strengthen further in the coming months, increasing risks of floods, drought and extreme heat, the UN weather agency said Thursday.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) forecast indicates an "exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100%" that El Nino will persist through February 2027, according to its latest update.
Driven by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific, El Nino is expected to reach very strong intensity and peak toward the end of 2026, with climate impacts continuing into 2027.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said droughts and floods were already causing disruption and damage and that impacts were expected to increase as El Nino intensifies.
"This exceptional El Nino demands exceptional preparation and response," she said, adding that the WMO is working with national meteorological and hydrological services to strengthen preparedness and early-warning efforts.
Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region associated with El Nino, are already well above average and continue to rise, according to the WMO.
The Nino 3.4 index, which measures sea surface temperature anomalies in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, averaged 1.5C (2.7F) above normal from May to July 2026 and reached 2C above normal in July.
Weekly values then rose further between late July and mid-August, ranging from approximately 2.2C to 2.6C above average, the organization said.
For September-November 2026, the WMO forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of above-normal temperatures across almost all land areas, while rainfall patterns are expected to show a response associated with the strong Pacific El Nino.
However, the strength of an El Nino event alone does not determine the severity of its impacts in individual countries or regions.
The WMO said effects vary by location and season and can be influenced by other climate drivers, including conditions in the Indian and Atlantic oceans.
The organization said a positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole is also expected to develop, while the equatorial Atlantic is forecast to remain generally warm.
These conditions may reinforce, weaken or alter typical El Nino impacts in different regions.
El Nino and La Nina are opposite phases of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation, a naturally occurring climate pattern. El Nino is characterized by warming sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
The WMO said El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon and is not caused by climate change.

Intelligence, drones and air defence: Germany steps up military support for Ukraine after Russian attack in Leipzig
The German government plans to increase military support for Ukraine after Berlin concluded that Russia was responsible for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. In particular, Berlin aims to strengthen cooperation between German and Ukrainian intelligence services.
Source: Der Spiegel, citing sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to the outlet's sources, Germany also plans to supply Ukraine with thousands of attack drones and missiles for IRIS-T air defence systems in September.
Der Spiegel reports that the government is considering providing further assistance to Ukraine in obtaining target coordinates for counterattacks against Russia.
More broadly, Germany's intelligence services are expected to be granted greater powers. The Bundestag is due to pass legislation on the intelligence services this autumn that would allow them to take "active measures" to counter attacks.
This would allow agents of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service (BND) to infiltrate attackers' computers and servers and delete stolen data. They would also be authorised to interfere with supply chains, including by replacing components in shipments destined for hostile states. In cases of particularly serious threats, BND agents could even hack IT systems at facilities such as drone manufacturing plants or chemical weapons laboratories to sabotage production.
Meanwhile, the German government intends to increase pressure on Russia. In addition to measures already announced – the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin – Germany aims to push for tougher sanctions at the EU level. These would include increasing pressure on Russia's shadow fleet, introducing new restrictive measures and tightening controls on the entry of Russian citizens into the EU.
Background:
- During an informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Wicklow on 2 September, ministers resumed discussions on banning former Russian combatants from entering the European Union, with the proposal receiving broad support.
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on the European Union to impose new sanctions on Russia after Berlin accused Moscow of carrying out a hybrid drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Scale
- Between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on September 2 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on September 3, air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 416 Ukrainian aircraft·type unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry said.

Fayyad Alnoman, assistant undersecretary at Yemen’s Information Ministry for television affairs, said in a post on US social media company X that a local authority source in Taiz reported the ballistic missile attack on the bridge.
The bridge is located along a road network connecting the coastal city of Mocha with Taiz city through western parts of the province.
The attack came amid intensified fighting in western Taiz, with clashes reported in areas including Maqbanah, Al-Kadha and Mawza.
Alnoman also said his correspondent reported that four bodies of Houthi fighters were found at a position in Maqbanah after the group withdrew from the site.
No information was immediately available on casualties or damage from the ballistic missile attack.
Separately, Yemen’s government-aligned National Resistance Forces said Thursday that they destroyed an explosive-laden boat that attempted to target the strategic Mocha port near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The forces’ military media said in a brief statement that the boat was destroyed before reaching the port, without providing further details. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
The development came hours after the Yemeni army said the Houthis had targeted areas in Taiz and the western province of Al Hudaydah with 14 ballistic missiles Thursday.
*On Wednesday, the army reported material damage after Houthi shelling targeted homes and residential neighborhoods in Taiz and the southwestern province of Al-Dhale, according to the military-run September Net website.
Fighting between government forces and the Houthis has intensified since early July across several provinces, including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhale and Taiz.
Yemen had experienced a period of relative calm since April 2022 in a conflict that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital Sanaa and several other areas since September 2014.

Zack Polanski will seek to stand as a candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, he has announced.
The leader of the Green party in England and Wales told the Camden New Journal on Thursday he would “stand up for people struggling to pay their bills” if he was elected as the representative for the area, which became vacant when Keir Starmer announced he was standing down as an MP.
In an effort to stave off accusations he was parachuting himself into the seat, Polanski said he had lived and worked in “this community” over many years. “I know it well and I love it. It represents so many of the things that make London so special. I am so excited by the prospect of representing this place in parliament,” he said.
Local Green party members will have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands that they are supportive of Polanski running, and that there is no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him.
The Green leader, who has led the party to record election results in Camden – the local authority that covers the constituency – and across the country, already represents the area as a city-wide member of the London Assembly. “Holborn and St Pancras has everything that’s the best of our country and so much potential – but for too long now it’s been held back by governments who have failed to make the changes to improve people’s lives.”
Polanski said he was confident that the Greens could win the seat. Holborn and St Pancras has traditionally been viewed as a Labour stronghold, but the Greens have gained ground there over the last year.
“We know that the Greens can win here, and by electing me, voters will have someone who will always fight their corner – never scared of big donors or the party whip,” said Polanski. “Too often Labour has stood up for corporations and big money. I will stand up for people struggling to pay their bills.”
Adding that the byelection was a chance for the community to “make history” by electing London’s first Green MP, Polanski emphasised that the contest would be a two-dog fight between Labour and the Greens.
“We know that people are struggling – that the things we used to afford are increasingly out of reach – and this is a chance to send a very clear message that we won’t sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top,” he said.
The Greens are likely to pose the greatest threat in the byelection to Labour, which has held the central London constituency continuously since the seat was created in 1983, winning at least 40% of the vote at every election.
Only two Labour MPs have ever represented Holborn and St Pancras: the former health secretary Frank Dobson, from 1983 to 2015, then Starmer.
At the most recent general election in 2024, Starmer held the seat with 48.9% of the vote, ahead of the independent candidate Andrew Feinstein in second place on 18.9% and the Greens in third on 10.4%.
The Conservatives came fourth on 7.2%, Reform finished fifth on 6.1% and the Liberal Democrats were sixth on 5.8%.
The popularity of the independent and Green candidates at the 2024 contest, finishing second and third respectively, may have been partly owing to former Labour voters protesting against Starmer’s refusal to take a stronger position on Israel’s actions in Gaza in its war with Hamas.

Desperate to save Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Ukrainian forces counterattack and reinforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:08:34 UTC
18:08:34 KST

- The pace of the Russian advance across Ukraine slightly increased in August
- The Russians' main objective is unchanged: to get forces in place for a siege of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk no later than next year
- Ukrainian counterattacks and reinforcements could slow the Russian plan
In August, Russian gains ticked upward in key sectors along the 1,200-km front line of Russia's 55-month wider war on Ukraine.
The coming winter could slow Russian advances as the trees lose their leaves and infantry infiltrators have nothing to conceal them from overhead drones. But for the next month or two, the trees will still have their leaves, and the infiltrators will still have their cover.
And that means, as fall wears into winter, Ukraine may lose yet more ground in the north and especially in Donbas region in the east, where Russia enjoys a substantial manpower and firepower advantage. "Russian forces still hold the operational initiative and are slowly capturing ... Donetsk Oblast as well as border zones in Sumy and Kharkiv Oblasts," mapper Thorkill warned.
The Russian gains belie a greater truth, however. In the middle of the fifth year of wider war, the situation on the ground only changes along the margins even as thousands die.
According to Thorkill's tally, the Russians occupied just under 220 square km of Ukrainian soil in August. That's 25% more territory than they captured in July. "The situation has deteriorated sharply in the Donbas in August," mapper Clément Molin explained.
To be fair, the Russians are advancing much more slowly than they did a year ago. "Compared to August 2025, Russian gains are down by nearly half," Molin noted. That's cold comfort to Ukrainian civilians and defenders in the areas where the Russians are still gaining ground, however. And the sheer proximity of the most aggressive Russian formations to the most vulnerable Ukrainian settlements means it might not take much more effort on the part of the Russians to turn these settlements into battlegrounds.
The Russians' main effort is still directed at the last big free cities in Donetsk. Inching forward at great cost from several directions, Russian forces are slowly closing a pincer around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk and the tens of thousands of civilians who still live in the adjacent cities.
Thorkill's map places the forwardmost Russian forces in Mykolaivka, just 4 km east of Sloviansk. This is the middle joint of the Russian pincer. The pincer's southern claw is a zone of disputed control stretching along the road between the ruins of the city of Kostiantynivka and the battleground town of Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka.
If the Russians can march through Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka, they can lay siege to the town of Druzhkivka, a few kilometers to the northwest. If they can capture Druzhkivka, they can turn north and assault Kramatorsk, a mere 6 km away.
Ukrainian counterattacks
The most fragile part of the claw is to the north. Bucking the overall trend of Russian gains in August, Ukrainian forces counterattacked in several sectors the same month. Most dramatically, a clutch of Ukrainian mechanized and air assault brigades extended a slow advance through the town of Nove, mostly cutting across a 100-square-km salient of Russian forces around 25 km northeast of Sloviansk.
The Nove counterattacks offer some hope that targeted Ukrainian action may slow the Russian march on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk from the north. Meanwhile, a reshuffling of Ukrainian units south of Kramatorsk could improve Ukrainian defenses against an assault on the twin cities from the south.
As new Ukrainian commander-in-chief Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi gradually addresses some of the imbalances in the Ukrainian ground forces, certain key units are getting help. Most notably, the 425th Assault Regiment is now subordinate to the 1st Azov Corps, which is responsible for the defense of Kramatorsk.
Trending Now
Keenly aware that the Russians intend to slowly infiltrate front-line settlements with small teams of infantry rather than rushing them with masses of easily-droned armored vehicles, the 1st Azov Corps has assigned the aggressive 425th Assault Regiment "to clear enemy infiltrators from the brigades’ areas of defense," the corps stated.
Infiltrators aren't the only problem, however. The Russians' favorite tactic combines small teams of infantry with massive aerial firepower in the form of precision-guided KAB glide bombs flung by supersonic Sukhoi Su-34 fighter bombers.
"Glide bombs hurt," Ukraine's 4th National Guard Brigade reported. "It's about 200 kg of explosives flying your way. And you can't really shoot them down like you can shoot down drones. They can collapse fortified buildings, bunkers, and entire urban blocks much more effectively than artillery."
After the dust settles from the glide bomb impacts, Russian infantry "infiltrate through the damaged areas, using the ruins for cover and concealment," the national guard brigade explained.
The same lack of long-range air defenses that exposes Ukrainian cities to relentless Russian bombardment also deprives front-line forces of protection from the Su-34s and their glide bombs. And so the Russians can keep bombing and keep infiltrating as long as the trees offer some concealment for the infantry.
The clock is ticking. The Russians will aim to position their forces for more direct assaults on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk no later than next year. The Ukrainians will aim to slow down the Russians, trading a little space for more time. Time Drapatyi may use to institute further reforms in the Ukrainian ground forces.
Zooming out and taking the long view, no one should expect major changes on the map of Russia's wider war as the fifth year of fighting grinds toward the sixth. Yes, the last two big free cities in the Donbas are in trouble. But "the overall situation remains unchanged since October 2023," Thorkill wrote.
The Russians slowly advance. The Ukrainians slowly fall back. And losses deepen on both sides.

Maduro, wife seek dismissal of drug trafficking indictment on immunity grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Maduro, wife seek dismissal of drug trafficking indictment on immunity grounds
New York — Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife asked a judge on Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
In papers filed in Manhattan federal court, lawyers for Maduro said a judge was required by law to reject the indictment because it cannot be brought against a foreign leader.
"No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought," the lawyers wrote. "That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own."
Maduro and his wife are scheduled to go on trial on drug trafficking charges next June 1. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein has set oral arguments for Nov. 17 on motions to dismiss the indictment.
Maduro, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, 69, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York.
In separate papers filed Wednesday, lawyers for Flores said she too has immunity from U.S. prosecution on sovereign immunity grounds.
"It is an attribute of Venezuela's sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it," her lawyers wrote.
Maduro's lawyers said that even if Maduro were not entitled to sovereign immunity as the head of state, the case against him must be dismissed because he is also entitled to conduct-based sovereign immunity.
Meanwhile, the lawyers argued, Maduro "vehemently denies the allegations against him."
"If this case were to proceed to trial, it would be apparent that he has been falsely accused," they said.
Both have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against numerous alleged co-conspirators. They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
Federal prosecutors are scheduled to file a response to the arguments later this month.
President Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
U.S. prosecutors say Maduro carried out a conspiracy to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the U.S. by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins.
Maduro has remained defiant. On Sunday, he posted pictures of himself from prison on social media, saying he was "standing firm."
"I send these photos as a small gift to all my grandsons and granddaughters, to the boys and girls, and to all the noble people who love us," he wrote.
"I want you to know that we stand firm, with our hearts full of your love, that love that reaches us transformed into prayer, into constant action, into solidarity and true support. Infinite thanks for every word, for every gesture, for every blessing," he went on to say.
On the Telegram messaging service, he added, "We will remain strong, calm and confident: God is with us. God will provide. Venezuela will rise again," French news agency AFP reported.

El Niño likely to intensify, may become strongest ever recorded, WMO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:06:11 UTC
18:06:11 KST

'Supersized' El Niño may become strongest ever recorded, UN says
GENEVA, Sept 3 - The El Niño weather phenomenon is set to intensify further into 2027 and could be the strongest ever, raising risks of extreme weather into next year, the World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday.
The U.N. weather agency said its forecasts showed a near 100% likelihood that El Niño would persist through February 2027, fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific Ocean temperatures. This is the first time it has expressed such a degree of certainty, the WMO said.
"If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began. So literally off the charts," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told a Geneva press conference.
El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. It occurs every two to seven years and tends to last up to 12 months, causing intense rains and droughts across Latin America.
A very strong El Niño can significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, and fuel extreme weather, such as droughts and typhoons.
WARMING OCEAN
While it is a naturally occurring phenomenon and not directly linked to fossil fuel-driven climate change, it can be intensified by warmer ocean temperatures, which are.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," said U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Sample Pacific Ocean temperatures in this year's El Niño - one of just four categorised in the top "very strong" bracket in records dating back to 1950 - are already more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, the WMO said.
The event has already had an impact on soft commodities in tropical areas, causing a severe food crisis across Central America's Dry Corridor.
'PULSE' IN GLOBAL TEMPERATURES
It is set to peak towards the end of this year, the WMO said in a statement. But its effects will continue into 2027 and are set to leave higher global temperatures next year in its wake, WMO officials said.
"Normally after an El Niño event we tend to see a pulse in the global temperatures - a temporary one," Wilfran Moufouma Okia, the WMO's chief of climate prediction services, told reporters, referring to 2024, which was the hottest year so far. "2027 has the potential to be the warmest on record."
The WMO said it was stepping up preparedness and early warning efforts in preparation to allow states to take early action, such as switching to drought-resistant crops in some places.
"WMO is committed to working closely with partners across the United Nations and humanitarian system to provide the climate intelligence and insights needed to support disaster management and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water resources," Saulo said. REUTERS
