US locks on drone imports with up to 100pc tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:26:50 UTC
17:26:50 KST

New US tariffs of up to 100 percent took effect on Thursday on drones and certain components, as Washington pushes to lower its import reliance in an industry that China dominates.
US President Donald Trump signed an order setting out the duties in August, as the White House flagged "the national security threat posed by imports of drones and their components."
The order also aims to boost domestic supply chains.
Drones with a takeoff weight exceeding 25 kilogrammes, as well as those with thermal imaging capabilities and docking stations, face a 100 percent tariff.
Smaller drones face a 25 percent duty.
Some components of drones that are "not particularly sensitive" will also face duties, but those only come into effect on February 9.
China expressed opposition to the planned tariffs shortly after they were unveiled by Trump, with Beijing urging Washington to withdraw the duties.
A Commerce Ministry spokesman said the tariffs would "disrupt the global drone supply chain and further undermine a fair and competitive market environment."
He said China firmly opposed the move.
DJI, China's leading drone maker, which was founded in 2006, has captured more than two thirds of the global market in recent years, according to several studies.
Since 2022, however, DJI has been put on a list of companies determined to pose unacceptable risks to US national security.
DJI has fought its inclusion on the list. (AFP)

designboom’s guide to paris design week 2026: highlights in and out of maison&objet

designboom guide to Paris Design Week 2026
Paris Design Week returns from September 10th to 19th, 2026, bringing exhibitions, installations, showrooms, galleries, and events to venues across the French capital. Taking place alongside Maison&Objet Pulse, the 2026 edition once again spreads across four districts, with designers and brands presenting new work in museums, historic buildings, galleries, boutiques, and public spaces.
With hundreds of events spread across the city, knowing where to begin can be a challenge. designboom’s guide to Paris Design Week 2026 highlights the exhibitions, installations, launches, and unexpected encounters worth seeking out, while designboom itself joins the program with paris.designboom, its temporary home at 72 rue des Archives, hosting podcast sessions, workshops, and the paris.designboom apéro, bringing together the wider design community for drinks and conversation.
illustration by Haus of Grace
MAISON&OBJET pulse 2026
Maison&Objet’s September edition returns as Maison&Objet Pulse, running from September 10th to 14th, 2026, at Paris Nord Villepinte. The new identity marks a shift for the fair, which positions its September edition around design in motion, emerging talent, craftsmanship, and new approaches to interior architecture, retail, and hospitality.
The theme for this edition, Pulse in Motion, focuses on movement, collective energy, and the role of design in bringing people together. Across seven sectors, the fair presents immersive spaces, new products, craftsmanship, materials, and emerging designers, alongside programs including Design District, Future On Stage, the Rising Talent Awards South Africa, and (im)Pulse.
For 2026, Valencia-based studio Masquespacio serves as ambassador for both Maison&Objet Pulse and Paris Design Week. The duo has developed installations for the fair and the city, as well as the visual identity for the September edition, bringing their colorful and expressive approach to the theme of movement.
where: Paris Nord Villepinte, ZAC Paris Nord 2, 93420 Villepinte, France
when: September 10th – 14th, 2026
visual by Studio Masquespacio
Paris Design Week Factory 2026
For its 2026 edition, Paris Design Week Factory brings together a new generation of designers across four venues in the Marais. Curated by Jean-Baptiste Durand and Simon Geringer, the program takes an intentionally open approach to emerging design, bringing together practices across design, art, and craftsmanship.
At Espace Commines, around 40 proposals are presented within a scenography conceived like a photographic studio, with each work isolated and framed to give it a sculptural presence. The exhibition continues at 116 rue de Turenne, where the works are arranged as a more experimental environment, allowing different objects and practices to overlap and enter into dialogue.
The Factory also expands beyond emerging French design. At 10 rue de Turenne, the China Creative Pavilion presents BON GOÛT! GOODTASTE!, bringing together designers, artists, and creators working across design, materials, and gastronomy. At 16 rue des Minimes, established designers and publishers present work spanning contemporary design, materials, and craftsmanship.
where: Espace Commines, 17 rue Commines; Galerie Joseph, 116 rue de Turenne and 16 rue des Minimes; China Creative Pavilion, 10 rue de Turenne, Paris
when: September 10th – 14th, 2026
Fringe Friends by Maori Kimura Design Studio (Commines)
paris.DESIGNBOOM apéro
During Paris Design Week, designboom opens the doors of paris.designboom, its temporary home in the French capital, for an informal evening bringing together the wider design community. Friends, partners, creatives, and collaborators are invited for drinks and conversation, with no formal program or agenda.
The gathering takes place within a space that serves as designboom’s base throughout the week. Alongside the evening event, paris.designboom hosts 11 podcast sessions with INDX|Global and a Topology x Clarks workshop, turning the temporary venue into a meeting point for conversations and activities around design. RSVP here

installations and exhibitions
Joseph Walsh – Arcanum Formae
Irish designer Joseph Walsh presents Arcanum Formae at the Hôtel de Sully. The site-specific installation brings two monumental outdoor sculptures to the historic 17th-century hôtel particulier, placing Walsh’s work between the Orangerie and its surrounding grounds. The exhibition remains on view through Paris Fashion Week and Art Basel Paris, allowing the sculptures to be experienced in relation to the architecture, gardens, changing light, and history of the site.
where: Hôtel de Sully, 5 Place des Vosges, 75004 Paris, France
when: September 10th – October 25th, 2026
scale model of the Magnus Monumental Sculptures in the courtyard and garden of the Hotel de Sully | image courtesy of Joseph Walsh
Hanjimania – Hôtel de la Marine
At the Hôtel de la Marine, Hanjimania brings French and Korean designers together around hanji, the traditional Korean paper made through a centuries-old craft tradition. Curated by Catherine Lurault and An KangEun, the exhibition pairs six French designers, Studio KO, Pierre Yovanovitch, Constance Guisset, Aline Asmar d’Amman, Harry Nuriev, and Jérémy Pradier-Jeauneau, with Korean artists and master artisans working with hanji.
A second parcours through the intendants’ apartments brings works by Korean artists into the monument, while perfumer Domitille Michalon has created a fragrance inspired by hanji to extend the material exploration beyond the visual. The exhibition is co-organized with the Province of Gyeongbuk as part of the 140th anniversary of diplomatic relations between France and Korea in 2026.
where: Hôtel de la Marine, 2 Place de la Concorde, 75008 Paris, France 
 when: September 9th – 27th, 2026
image by ChangKi CHUNG
Maison Lacmé — Astre Mobile
Maison Lacmé presents Astre Mobile at the Hôtel de la Marine, a transparent car reimagined as a mobile cabinet of curiosities. Artistically directed by Antoine Tauvel, ten French craftspeople collaborate for this project, reinterpreting familiar automotive components through materials including onyx, porcelain, wood, leather, lacquer, feathers, and shells.
Astre Mobile approaches the car as a collection of individual objects. A speedometer becomes a feather marquetry piece, the gearshift is made of porcelain, the steering wheel uses driftwood, and white onyx hubcaps can be detached and used as lamps. Other details, including the car’s logo, are transformed into jewelry, turning the automobile into a display of craftsmanship as much as a functional object.
where: Hôtel de la Marine, Cour de l’Intendant, 2 Place de la Concorde, 75008 Paris, France
when: September 9th – 27th, 2026
Frederik Molenschot — Legenda
Carpenters Workshop Gallery’s Legenda is an exhibition of three new sculptures by Dutch artist Frederik Molenschot. The works, CL Sable, CL Mer, and CL Paradis, are part of his City Light series and draw on the dune landscapes and beaches of the Dutch coast, where Molenschot lives and regularly walks.
Form, volume, and balance are central to the artist’s process, with color introduced afterward and drawn from the landscape. In this series, the palette acts as a kind of key to the coastal environments that inform each sculpture, translating the changing character of sand, sea, and terrain into abstract form.
where: Carpenters Workshop Gallery, 54 rue de la Verrerie, 75004 Paris, France
when: September 17th – December 19th, 2026
image courtesy of Carpenters Workshop Gallery
WU BIN (W.DESIGN) — THE PAVILION OF TIME
Chinese designer and interior architect Wu Bin of W.DESIGN presents The Pavilion of Time in the Palais-Royal Garden for Paris Design Week. The installation uses mirror-polished stainless steel and a translucent membrane inspired by the texture of traditional Xuan paper to explore the relationship between architecture, light, reflection, and the passing of time.
The pavilion’s reflective surfaces capture the surrounding trees, sky, and visitors, allowing the structure to visually shift with its environment. Its circular plan is divided into three 120-degree sectors, creating a route through the installation rather than a single fixed viewpoint. As sunlight passes through the translucent membrane, changing conditions of light alter the interior throughout the day. The pavilion therefore uses the movement of the sun as part of its spatial experience, turning light and reflection into elements that continuously reshape the architecture.
where: Palais-Royal Garden, Paris, France
when: September 9th – 20th, 2026
image courtesy of W.DESIGN
de gournay x antoine billore
For Paris Design Week, de Gournay invites antiques dealer and scenographer Antoine Billore to take over its Rue des Saints-Pères premises. The presentation brings together de Gournay’s hand-painted wallpapers and porcelain with pieces designed by Billore, alongside newly installed wallpapers and fabrics.
Known for his eclectic selection of historic and unsigned objects, Billore approaches interiors through combinations of pieces with distinct characters and histories. His contribution introduces this sensibility to de Gournay’s artisanal environment, creating a setting where the company’s painted surfaces and porcelain meet antique and upcycled furniture.
where: de Gournay, 15 rue des Saint-Pères, 75006 Paris, France
when: September 10th – 13th, 2026
image courtesy of de Gournay
Pli Office — Tout est Chaos
Following Pour que tu m’aimes encore at the Pavillon de l’Arsenal in 2024 and Design Disco Club at Lafayette Anticipations in 2025, Pli Office returns to Paris Design Week with Tout est Chaos, an exhibition at La Gaîté Lyrique. Curated by Christopher Dessus and staged by PAF atelier, the exhibition brings together 10 designers around the theme of wonder.
The project looks at a world increasingly filled with objects that are designed to solve problems, questioning what happens when function, efficiency, and mass production leave little room for surprise. The invited designers are asked to create installations, objects, or specific situations that make space for gesture, storytelling, experience, and doubt.
Alongside the main exhibition, Pli Office is launching an open call for designers with less than five years of experience, inviting a younger generation to present work that finds its capacity to surprise through materials, form, use, history, or production methods.
where: La Gaîté Lyrique, Paris, France
when: September 10th – 14th, 2026
ROCHER FATALE | image courtesy of Pli Office
Yves de la Tour d’Auvergne — Plier la matière
Pulp Galerie presents Plier la matière, a retrospective of French designer and sculptor Yves de la Tour d’Auvergne (1927–2023), bringing together works from the 1980s and 1990s and focusing on the artist’s exploration of folding, a gesture he translated from paper into furniture and sculpture.
Initially trained as a painter, de la Tour d’Auvergne began experimenting with paper sculptures through an interest in light, using folding, tearing, and cutting to shape the material. He later developed a process combining resin and marble powder, allowing him to reproduce the whiteness and texture of paper while giving the works greater structural and sculptural qualities.
The exhibition includes the Alpha armchair (1982), Demi-Lune stool-table (1984), Olta chairs (1984), Albatros lamps (1988), Marmora chairs (1989), and Ellipse Pise table (1994). Across these pieces, the fold functions less as decoration than as a way of constructing form, organizing space, and catching light.
where: Pulp Galerie, 30 rue de Seine, 75006 Paris, France
when: September 10th – October 31st, 2026
image courtesy of Pulp Galerie
Visteria Foundation — The Matter of Earth
Visteria Foundation’s debut in France, The Matter of Earth: A New Generation of Polish Collectible Design on view at the Institut Polonais de Paris, brings together 11 Polish artists and designers whose work explores the relationship between material, landscape, memory, and place.
Curated by Eleonora Bojanowska and Bartosz Brylewski, the exhibition continues From the Same Earth, a project first presented in Warsaw in 2024, expanding it with new artists and commissions. Across sculpture, craft, and collectible design, the participating makers work with processes including forming, firing, carving, casting, joining, and transforming raw materials. Film and photography shown alongside the objects document these processes and the artists’ relationships with their materials and landscapes.
Presented in collaboration with the Polish Institute in Paris, The Matter of Earth marks and places contemporary Polish design within a broader conversation around craftsmanship, cultural memory, and material experimentation.
where: Institut Polonais de Paris, 31 rue Jean Goujon, 75008 Paris, France
when: September 10th – October 4th, 2026 closed September 26th – 27th, 2026
image by Tomo Yarmush
Anthony Guerrée — Contrepoint at Musée Bourdelle
French designer Anthony Guerrée installs Contrepoint across the permanent collections of Musée Bourdelle, creating a dialogue between contemporary design and the sculptural language of Antoine Bourdelle. Guerrée extracts lines, curves, tensions, and counterforms from the sculptor’s work and translates them into furniture, stained glass, textiles, and terracotta.
The installation unfolds across three areas of the museum. In the plaster hall, four stained-glass and ash-wood screens introduce colored light around Bourdelle’s monumental sculptures. In the sculpture studio and adjoining garden, mixed-clay surfaces, modules, objects, molds, and matrices foreground the processes behind the finished works. The painting studio presents the Orbe chaise longue by La Chance in a specially developed jacquard, alongside small pieces of furniture.
The project also connects with the museum’s existing design history through its collection of furniture and archives associated with Michel Dufet, Bourdelle’s son-in-law and an important figure in French Art Deco.
where: Musée Bourdelle, 18 rue Antoine-Bourdelle, 75015 Paris
when: September 8th – 27th, 2026
image courtesy of Anthony Guerrée
UCHRONIA AT GRAND PALAIS
Paris-based multidisciplinary collective Uchronia takes over the Grand Palais during Paris Design Week with a series of installations and design objects that extend across the historic monument. From September 11th to 20th, 2026, the collective founded by Julien Sebban presents Le Grand Bouquet, a monumental floral installation inside the Rotonde du Palais d’Antin, alongside an outdoor installation and a selection of objects at the museum’s Design & Craft boutique.
At the center of the presentation, Le Grand Bouquet transforms the Rotonde with a monumental flower inspired by the Grand Palais’ own decorative details. Drawing from the floral motif of the building’s mosaic floor and the vegetal mouldings along its arcades, the installation introduces illuminated petals that appear to emerge from the ground and follow the circular movement of the space. Circular seating at its base invites visitors to gather around the work.
The presentation begins outdoors at Square Jean Perrin with Équilibres Éphémères, an installation of colorful inflatable sculptures with rounded forms. Inside the Grand Palais’ Design & Craft boutique, Uchronia’s world continues through a selection of ceramics, lighting, cushions, furniture, and design accessories.
Among them is DAYDREAM, Uchronia’s furniture collaboration with French design studio Tiptoe. The collection reworks selected Tiptoe pieces through Uchronia’s approach to color and form, introducing wavelike solid-wood tabletops and altered silhouettes. Its four colors, Magma Orange, Chocolate Brown, Ice Cream Beige, and Astral Purple, are conceived as distinct emotional states.
where: Grand Palais, Paris, as part of Le Grand Bouquet; also Design & Craft boutique
when: September 11th – 20th, 2026
Uchronia at Grand Palais – LE GRAND BOUQUET
1000 VASES
Returning to Paris for Paris Design Week, 1000 VASES brings together unique works by hundreds of independent designers from more than 60 countries, all exploring the same deceptively simple object. The exhibition turns the vase into a framework for comparing radically different approaches to form, material, and craft, from minimal and geometric pieces to sculptural, irregular, playful, and highly ornate works.

SCULPTURE / LANDSCAPE New Figures of the French Formal Garden
Artist Johanna de Clisson brings Sculpture / Landscape to the garden of the National Archives, placing around ten white stoneware planter-sculptures along the courtyard’s formal axes. Set against the site’s columns, conical boxwoods, and classical architecture, the installation reworks the geometry and symmetry of the French formal garden through a more contemporary and unconventional language.
The pieces sit between planter, vessel, sculpture, and human-scale form, drawing on both the traditions of the formal garden and modernist precedents including the work of Rita Lawrence and Willy Guhl. Their simple, architectural volumes accommodate plants with Mediterranean hues, turning the landscape into part of the sculptural composition.

UK mortgage borrowers brace for rate jump amid global bond sell-off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:25:18 UTC
17:25:18 KST

Homeowners in the UK are braced for a jump in mortgage rates, driven by higher inflation and interest rate increase expectations amid turmoil in the global bond markets.
UK swap rates, which lenders use to price mortgages, have risen to a three-year high, as this week’s global bond market sell-off ripples through the economy.
The five-year swaps rate rose above 4.52% on Wednesday, the highest level since October 2023. This is expected to result in higher interest rates on fixed-term mortgages.
A jump in oil prices, as the US and Iran have exchanged fire this week for the first time in a month, has led to fears of higher inflation, leading investors to sell bonds, which pushes up their yield, or interest rate. The moves in gilts, as UK government bonds are known as, have been bigger than those in other countries.
Although the turmoil in the bond markets eased on Thursday, the consequences of the jump in bond yields could be serious for borrowers.
That is because UK swap rates – the interest rates that banks charge when they borrow from each other – have been pushed up by the rise in gilt yields.
Russ Mould, the investment director at the trading platform AJ Bell, said: “Credit card, mortgage and auto loan interest rates will rise if bond yields rise, as the lenders seek to preserve loan book margins and manage their risk.”
If the cost of government borrowing continues to remain high, it could undermine Andy Burnham’s efforts to ease cost of living pressures.
The new prime minister attempted to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday, using his first appearance at prime minister’s questions to promise decisions for the autumn budget would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.
He spoke as the yield on UK 10-year government debt hit its highest level since 2008 for a second day, before retreating thanks to a drop in the oil price. On Thursday, Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dipped 0.6% to $95 a barrel.
Oil has been one of the key factors driving the bond market sell-off, as inflationary pressures from high prices could force central banks to raise interest rates, along with worries over high government spending. Government bonds are also competing with a flurry of corporate debt issuance by technology companies keen to fund their spending on AI infrastructure.
Tom Simpson, the managing director of homes at Yorkshire Building Society, said swap rates were now 0.7% above where they were a year ago, but there was “much more volatility” in March, at the start of the Iran war.
“All things being equal, you would expect a modest increase in mortgage rates based on what we’ve seen so far,” he told the BBC, advising people who were worried about this to speak to an independent mortgage adviser.
“When there is a movement in the market, that can pull forward demand. People will try to lock those rates in.” However, he added that the 0.1 percentage point increase over the past week was below the 0.5 percentage point increase in the 10 days after the US and Israel first launched airstrikes on Tehran.
Fixed-year mortgage rates were unchanged on Thursday, according to the latest figures from Moneyfacts. The average two-year fix is 5.59%, while a typical five-year fixed deal costs 5.63%.

US Senate pushes UBS for new details on Nazi-linked accounts

US Senate pushes UBS for new details on Nazi-linked accounts
UBS is coming under renewed United States pressure over Credit Suisse’s handling of Nazi-linked accounts.
The Senate Judiciary Committee is demanding new responses from the Swiss lender’s management to dozens of questions as part of its investigation.
UBS’s previous responses “did not fully address this Committee’s questions,” Senator Charles Grassley said in a July 17 letter to the bank. UBS declined to comment on Senator Grassley’s letter, which hasn’t previously been disclosed. The bank is currently working on a response, according to a person familiar with its planning.
+Read more about the Holocaust assets controversy
The back-and-forth is the latest flashpoint in a tense year between the bank and the committee, which has called on UBS to ensure a complete and transparent investigation of the handling of Nazi-linked accounts by Credit Suisse. UBS bought its troubled rival out of near collapse in 2023, acquiring all its legal liabilities in the process.
Senators criticised UBS at a hearing in February, but the bank has pushed to end a six-year-old probe at the end of this year and limit its scope, criticising the independent ombudsman overseeing it as biased.
The bank has argued that a settlement reached with Jewish groups in the 1990s under which it paid $1.25 billion to Holocaust victims covers all potential exposure from its ties to its handling of Nazi-related accounts, saying the current probe is purely aimed at completing the historical record.
More
US court rules UBS cannot limit liability over Nazi-linked accounts
But those groups, backed by the Senate panel, have argued that the investigation is revealing new information potentially not covered by the 1990s settlement. The latest probe began after records emerged showing Credit Suisse serviced accounts for Nazis and related entities, including the so-called Rat Lines through which they escaped to Argentina after World War II.
Grassley who chairs the committee, remains committed to ensuring a thorough investigation of Nazi-linked accounts at Credit Suisse and continues to call on UBS to fully cooperate and produce the records requested by the ombudsman, according to a committee official.
The Republican senator from Iowa plans to hold another hearing on the issues, although he hasn’t set a date, and wants to create a historical repository of Credit Suisse records linked to the Nazi accounts. He included a list of 62 questions for the bank to answer in his July letter.
In May, Neil Barofsky, the ombudsman overseeing the investigation, wrote to the committee, accusing UBS of making “false and misleading statements” related to “previously unreported examples of Credit Suisse executing forced transfers of Jewish clients’ assets into the accounts of Nazi-affiliated banks” and withholding records from the probe.
UBS fired back with a public statement saying it rejects Barofsky’s narrative as lacking objectivity. The bank turned down his appeal for more time, saying he should complete his report by the end of the year.
More
Historian claims Swiss banks may hold further Second World War secrets
The Senate Committee and Barofsky last month gained an ally in Helen Junz, an economist and respected former member of the Volcker and Bergier Commissions, which led the the original 1990s-era investigation into the Swiss banks’ Nazi past.
In a five-page letter to the committee chairmen on August 6, she criticised UBS’s response for taking an overly broad view of the terms of that 1998 settlement, which the bank argues covers any potential future exposure.
The suggestion that any actively concealed Nazi-linked assets would be covered in the settlement is “inconsistent with, and violative of, the principles of good-faith that are the bargained-for core” of that settlement, she wrote.
“The bank’s response — in fact non-response — is part and parcel of a long-established pattern of Credit Suisse’s stonewalling any and all investigations into these matters.”
“This pattern appears now to have been embraced by UBS after the merger with Credit Suisse with regard to the legitimate demands for access to records that reveal the Swiss banks’ links to Nazi entities,” she wrote.
UBS says it has spent more than $100 million financing Barofsky’s team of investigators and shared more than 19 million documents with them. The bank is willing to cooperate with inquiries it views as legitimate, but will not continue to let the investigation drag on indefinitely.

UK seeks vehicle-mounted laser defence against drone swarms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:23:35 BST
17:23:35 KST

The Ministry of Defence has opened a competition for new counter-drone technologies intended to protect deployed troops from mass and low-cost aerial threats, with particular interest in laser directed-energy weapons and a requirement for an eventual system capable of autonomous operation from an Army vehicle, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The tender notice published on 2 September begins an iterative procurement process through the Commercial X Dynamic Market. The wider procurement carries an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, or £150 million including VAT, although the MOD makes clear that this funding has not yet been approved and later stages will depend on future funding decisions.
Setting out the operational requirement, the MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
On existing counter-UAS approaches, the notice states: “Current approaches are constrained by limited magazine depth, high cost-per-engagement, limited manoeuvrability, workforce intensity and the difficulty of adapting capabilities at pace as UAS threats evolve.” The MOD added: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The first phase will focus on technologies which already exist and could be accelerated towards a deployable system rather than procuring a finished counter-UAS capability immediately. The MOD stated: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
For later phases, the department said: “Over later Phases, the Authority’s intent, aligned with their Integrated Procurement Model, is to identify and rapidly mature promising technologies as demonstrable Minimum Viable Products (MVPs). The Authority may then, at its discretion (and the criteria detailed below) select projects to be iteratively developed, integrated and proven as Minimum Deployable Capabilities (MDCs) for an initial operational user group.”
The notice continues: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record. Suppliers will be notified of the criteria, selection processes, and competition format as these Phases arise.”
The intended configuration is also set out in the requirement. The MOD stated: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
On the attacks the system is expected to counter, the department said: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus is on representative Class 1 uncrewed aerial systems and related small aerial threats, covering single attacks as well as repeated, sequential and simultaneous profiles. The notice states that this includes threats intended to disrupt operations, conduct surveillance, target fixed or mobile assets, overwhelm local defences or force the disproportionate use of high-cost munitions.
The MOD also plans for the system to move beyond a crewed Army vehicle. It stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
Stage 1 will assess whether industry proposals can meet the problem statements, with suppliers required to submit an evidence-based high-level programme plan supported by demonstrations, modelling, analysis and testing where appropriate. The MOD states: “No contract shall be awarded at this stage, but success is required to continue to Stage 2. All suppliers who demonstrate achievement of the threshold criteria shall be invited to Stage 2.”
Stage 2 will require successful suppliers to develop their initial proposals into fully costed and contractable projects running for around six months. Contracts at this point will be awarded according to evaluation scores and available funding within a £5 million limit, with technical factors expected to account for between 60% and 80% of the assessment and commercial factors between 20% and 40%.
Stage 3 could involve either a further competition or negotiation of a single direct award depending on how many suppliers remain. The MOD says contracts at that stage will cover scaling and production alongside testing, assurance, safety and security, with break points where aspects of the system cannot be demonstrated within the required timescales.
The department states: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.” It adds: “The intention is to begin Stage 1 with immediate effect, but future stages will not proceed until funding has been allocated and approved.”
The MOD also warns suppliers that later funding is not guaranteed, stating: “There is no guarantee that future funding will be allocated or approved and the Authority may cancel the procurement process at any time. Bidders proceed knowing and accepting this risk that no effort shall be compensated.”

1 in 5 children in 21 countries face tech-facilitated sexual abuse, UNICEF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:23:12 UTC
17:23:12 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
An estimated 20 million children aged 12 to 17, or nearly 1 in 5, experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse in a single year across 21 countries, UNICEF said.
The findings are included in a new report titled Through Children’s Eyes: How Digital Technologies Enable Child Sexual Abuse, which combines survey data with testimonies from children who experienced abuse.
“The report reveals a painful reality. More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play, and connect with friends,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said.
“Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away,” she added.
The report estimates that more than 15 million children were exposed to unwanted sexual content, while 9 million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will.
Around 4 million had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.
Most cases occurred on social media platforms
Nearly 60% of cases occurred on social media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and WhatsApp, while 14% took place in online games, according to the report.
The report found that 57% of cases involved someone the child already knew, including peers, romantic partners, friends and family members. At the same time, 38% of children first encountered the perpetrator online, with abuse facilitated through tools such as fake accounts and private messaging.
The experiences had a significant impact on children’s emotional well-being, sense of safety and trust in others, with research participants describing feelings of fear, shame, confusion and isolation, according to the report.
Children who experienced technology-facilitated exploitation were four times more likely to report suicidal thoughts or behaviors and self-harm, and also reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, the analysis found.
In Mexico and North Macedonia, the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviors was more than eight times higher among children who experienced abuse, while in Pakistan the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher, according to the report.
Children suffer in silence
More than 40% of cases were never shared with anyone, while fewer than 1% were reported to authorities, including police, social workers or helplines.
The most common reason children remained silent across the countries surveyed was not knowing where to go or whom to tell, UNICEF said.
The report calls on governments, technology companies and other stakeholders to strengthen protections for children online, including stronger privacy safeguards, restrictions on unsolicited contact from adults, safer recommender systems and improved detection and reporting of abuse.
It also calls for stronger laws and enforcement measures, improved reporting and support systems, and greater support for families, schools and communities.
“All of us, including governments and technology companies, must do more to protect children online,” Russell said.
The report draws on nationally representative surveys of approximately 21,000 internet-using children aged 12 to 17 across 21 countries, alongside in-depth interviews with 100 young people who experienced abuse in childhood.
UNICEF said the survey findings are representative of internet-using children rather than all children, particularly in countries with lower internet connectivity.

Spain's PM Sanchez says no evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta border surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:21:15 UTC
17:21:15 KST

Spain's PM Sanchez says no evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta border surge
MADRID, Sept 3 - Spain has found no evidence to conclude that July's deadly border rush from Morocco into its enclave of Ceuta was orchestrated by Moroccan authorities, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Thursday, countering allegations in a Spanish police report.
Speaking in parliament, Sanchez responded to claims in the report that emerged this week suggesting the entry of over 70,000 people into Ceuta was not a spontaneous migration but a planned effort to overwhelm border controls.
"I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever," Sanchez said.
However, Moroccan police did allow crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on July 30, when migrant arrivals peaked, he said. Spanish authorities had yet to determine whether this was due to inaction or inability to contain the influx, Sanchez added.
Sanchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat's cooperation in returning the majority of the migrants in the days following the surge.
But on Thursday he said Spain summoned Morocco's ambassador on August 21 because of "unacceptable statements" made by two Moroccan ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, Spain's other North African enclave. Morocco's Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi last month publicly reiterated Rabat's sovereignty claims over the cities.
FEWER MOROCCAN POLICE THAN USUAL AT BORDER
The police report, commissioned by a High Court judge last month and seen by Reuters, alleged that Moroccan security forces were initially deployed in smaller numbers than usual near the border breakwater and did not make a serious attempt to disperse the crowds.
Some uniformed Moroccan officers gave directions towards the crossing point, while other unidentified people appeared to guide or monitor the flow of people, the report said. It did not identify individual officers or provide independently verified evidence of orders from Moroccan authorities.
It cited some migrants as saying in interviews they had received guidance from Moroccan security forces to make the crossing.
"The police response in Morocco to the mobilisation and mass influx of migrants into Ceuta has been, to say the least, one of total permissiveness, with no serious attempt recorded to reduce, disperse or remove the crowd from the border perimeter," the report said.
Moroccan authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment but previously denied any permissiveness, blaming the crossing on traffickers, the misinterpretation of a Spanish court ruling that appeared to open a legal loophole for arrivals by sea and the use of social media to disseminate information about a mass crossing.
Justice Minister Ouahbi told Al Arabiya TV on August 22 that Moroccan authorities did not attempt to stop people marching toward Ceuta in order to avoid bloodshed, but they handled the crisis "wisely and with sang-froid".
The police report said trafficking groups in Morocco could mobilise a maximum of about 300 migrants a day, lacking the capacity to orchestrate an event of those dimensions. REUTERS

‘Military production cannot be the answer’: Critics slam Volkswagen’s defense plan with Israel’s Rafael
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:21:11 UTC
17:21:11 KST

- 'We reject the false claim that the only alternatives are unemployment or arms production,' Left Party's Thorben Peters says
- ‘Production for an Israeli arms company amounts to de facto support for the wars Israel is waging against the Palestinians, Lebanon, Iran,’ peace activist Marie Dominique Guyard says
Volkswagen's revived plan to produce military equipment at its Osnabruck factory with Israel's Rafael has drawn fresh opposition after reports that the state of Lower Saxony could step in to help overcome objections that had stalled the project.
The proposal comes as Volkswagen undergoes a sweeping restructuring amid falling profits, weaker demand in China and growing competition from lower-priced Chinese brands in Europe, with vehicle production at the Osnabruck plant set to end after 2027.
Thorben Peters, co-chair of the Left Party in Lower Saxony, said thousands of jobs at the factory, along with its industrial expertise and know-how, must be preserved without a shift to arms production.
"Replacing civilian production with military production cannot be the answer to the automotive industry's current crisis," Peters told Anadolu.
"The state of Lower Saxony, in particular, should not use public funds to participate in an arms-related joint venture. We reject the false claim that the only alternatives are unemployment or arms production."
Volkswagen confirmed in March that it was in talks with several defense contractors about the Osnabruck plant.
A blocked plan and a new workaround
The proposal has faced opposition from peace groups, labor movements and opposition parties for months, particularly over potential cooperation with Israel's state-owned defense firm Rafael.
In July, Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, Volkswagen's third-largest shareholder, blocked the plan.
Now, management has revived the idea with a structure that could overcome that obstacle.
According to recent German media reports, Volkswagen would transfer parts of the Osnabruck site to the state of Lower Saxony, which could then form a joint venture with Rafael to manufacture military equipment. 
The project could manufacture key components for Israel's Iron Dome air defense system, including launchers, transport vehicles and power generators.
The Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung reported that Lower Saxony could invest at least €200 million ($232 million) in the project.
The Left Party argues that if the state is prepared to spend public money to preserve production and jobs at the site, it should instead invest in civilian alternatives.
Peters said those could include special-purpose and environmentally friendly vehicles for public transport.
Volkswagen's supervisory board is due to meet on Sept. 4.
Peters said his party opposes converting civilian industrial capacity to military production as a matter of principle, regardless of the nationality of the company involved.
In the case of Israeli defense company Rafael, however, he said the war in Gaza raises additional concerns.
"Given the massive human rights violations and serious allegations regarding breaches of international law in connection with the war in Gaza, there must be particularly rigorous scrutiny,” he said.
"The guiding principle for public investment must be that human rights and international law are non-negotiable."
'City of Peace' pushes back
The debate has particular resonance in Osnabruck, a city that has long promoted itself as a "City of Peace" because of its role in the negotiations that led to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War.
The prospect of military production at the Volkswagen plant has sparked repeated protests in recent months, bringing peace activists, anti-war groups and local initiatives onto the streets.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative argues that Lower Saxony should use any public money earmarked for the plant to support a socially responsible and environmentally sustainable transition rather than subsidize weapons production.
"Production for an Israeli arms company amounts to de facto support for the wars the state of Israel is waging against the Palestinians, Lebanon and Iran," Marie Dominique Guyard, spokesperson for the initiative, told Anadolu.
"Defense equipment for the Iron Dome plays a role in Israel's aggressive, offensive military activities, as it provides the protective shield enabling Israel to act aggressively toward its neighbors."
Speaking on behalf of the Osnabruck Peace Initiative, Guyard said the group's position is also informed by international legal proceedings concerning Israel's conduct.
She pointed to a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory unlawful and said states must not provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by that presence.
She cited International Criminal Court arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant on war crimes and findings by a UN commission of inquiry and Amnesty International accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
But she also pointed to Osnabruck's own history to explain the depth of local opposition.
The city was repeatedly bombed during World War II, when it was home to arms-related industry. About 65% of Osnabruck was destroyed, including 95% of its historic old town.
For Guyard, the prospect of military production returning to the city some eight decades later makes the debate about more than the future of one Volkswagen factory.
"When arms factories are once again established in the city some 80 years after the last war, one can only despair at the decision-makers' disregard for history," she said.
“We do not wish to support such a disastrous development and will continue to build opposition to ensure that work in the city serves peace rather than war.”

Spy planes swarm Russia’s borders in rare surge
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:17:33 BST
17:17:33 KST

Two RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft, at least two P-8A Poseidons and American tanker support are operating across the High North in a concentration of intelligence-gathering flights rare in both scale and composition, according to open-source tracking.
The account DefenceGeek, run by one of our team members Jon, logged the aircraft operating from the United Kingdom and Iceland, watching across the border into Russia. Among them were the Royal Air Force Rivet Joint ZZ666 using the callsign ASCOT 7202, an American RC-135W as JAKE 17, and a KC-135R tanker as RAKE 67 providing refuelling.
A United States Air Force Rivet Joint is operating within the European Command area for the first time in a while, flying near Russia’s naval base complex at Murmansk. It is likely to be operating with fighter escort given an active tanker bridge in the area. A second Rivet Joint, this one British, was tracked along the border between Russia and Finland, with a Poseidon monitoring the Baltic at low altitude. American Rivet Joint aircraft have concentrated elsewhere in recent years, which is what makes an appearance over the Barents notable.
NATO Eyes on Russia Continues
Two RC-135 “Rivet Joint” SIGINT platforms and at least 2 P-8A “Poseidon” aircraft are operating out of the UK & Iceland today in the high north, watching across the border into Russia, supported by US tankers:
🇬🇧 RC-135W “ASCOT7202” ZZ666 #43C39D… pic.twitter.com/dqKU3KIQuv
— DefenceGeek 🇬🇧 (@DefenceGeek) September 2, 2026
What they are looking at
Murmansk and the wider Kola Peninsula hold the Russian Northern Fleet, including the ballistic missile submarines that carry the sea-based portion of the Russian deterrent, along with the attack boats that transit south into the Atlantic. It is the single most concentrated collection of Russian naval power anywhere, and the point from which any submarine deployment towards the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap begins.
The RC-135W does not take photographs, no, it is an electronic surveillance aircraft, and its crews survey the electromagnetic spectrum to collect communications, radar emissions and other signals, building a picture of what is switched on, where it is, and how it behaves. Flying a track along a border allows the aircraft to map air defence radars and communications networks without entering the airspace they cover.
The P-8A Poseidon does a different job, of course. It hunts submarines, using sonobuoys dropped into the water and its own radar and acoustic processing, and the Royal Air Force operates nine of them from RAF Lossiemouth in Moray. A Poseidon working the Baltic at low altitude is looking at what is on and under the surface.
Britain operates three Rivet Joints from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, converted from KC-135 airframes under a co-operative programme with the United States Air Force, which flies a larger fleet of the type from Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska.
The flights come at the end of a fortnight of unusually heavy allied air activity along the Russian frontier. Around 25 aircraft from several nations operated over the Baltic region on 18 August in a package overseen by the United States, including an EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft and an ARTEMIS II intelligence platform, with further flights on the two days following. NATO E-3A Sentry aircraft and Multinational MRTT Fleet tankers have been operating over Lithuania and Poland since.
Germany formally attributed the attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russian intelligence on Tuesday, announcing the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn along with new sanctions and entry restrictions, in a step Estonia’s prime minister described as Russia taking its hybrid attacks in Europe to a new and dangerous level.
Surveillance flights of this kind are deliberately visible, as readers will know. Aircraft on these missions generally transmit, and their tracks appear on civilian monitoring platforms, which is a choice rather than an oversight.
The Russian Navy has meanwhile had no presence in the Mediterranean since June, with a NATO official telling us last week that allied warships outnumber Russian vessels in European waters by roughly three to one.
Neither the Ministry of Defence nor United States Air Forces in Europe comments on individual intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sorties.

AEVEX, Divergent team up on new autonomous aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:17:12 UTC
17:17:12 KST

- AEVEX Corp. and Divergent Technologies announced a collaboration to build a new autonomous aircraft using Divergent's 3D-printing manufacturing platform.
- Neither company disclosed a contract value, funding source, or timeline for a prototype.
EVEX Corp. and Divergent Technologies said Tuesday they will jointly develop a new autonomous aircraft platform, combining AEVEX’s unmanned systems work with Divergent’s 3D-printing based manufacturing process.
The companies did not disclose a contract value or say which government customer, if any, the resulting aircraft is intended for. AEVEX, based in Solana Beach, California, builds unmanned aerial systems and unmanned surface vessels and trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker AVEX. Divergent, headquartered in Torrance, California, manufactures parts and structures using a platform it calls the Divergent Adaptive Production System, or DAPS, which combines 3D-printed metal components with AI-assisted design and robotic assembly.
“Working with Divergent allows us to evaluate next-generation manufacturing concepts that could improve responsiveness and bring new flexibility to how future unmanned systems are developed and delivered,” said Manan Patel, Chief Technology Officer at AEVEX.
“We’re proud to collaborate with AEVEX to deliver mass at the pace of need,” said Lukas Czinger, Co-Founder and CEO at Divergent. “Divergent is a force multiplier for our customers’ programs, and we’re excited to integrate DAPS with AEVEX’s field-proven expertise to set a new standard for delivering capability at speed and scale.”
The two companies said early work will focus on adaptable airframe designs, faster integration processes and production methods intended to cut part counts and shorten development timelines.
This is not Divergent’s first partnership built around DAPS with a larger aerospace player. As The Defence Blog reported in June, Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works division used the platform with Divergent to build a 2.7-meter (9-foot) wingspan drone called Replicator, taking it from concept to a first physical article in under a year. Lockheed Martin made a $25 million strategic investment in Divergent in 2024 to explore applications across advanced munitions and unmanned aircraft. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth viewed the Replicator during a stop at Divergent’s facility as part of his “Arsenal of Freedom” tour of American defense manufacturers.
Divergent also holds a spot on the US Air Force’s Eglin Wide Agile Acquisition Contract, a multiple-award vehicle with a ceiling of $46 billion for developing and fielding weapon systems. The company is building a 430,000-square-foot (40,000-square-meter) factory in Long Beach, California, meant to house 64 of its Monolith One metal printers and eventually produce tens of thousands of missile airframes and warhead casings a year. Divergent raised $290 million in a Series E funding round earlier this year at a $2.3 billion valuation, led by Rochefort Asset Management.
AEVEX has delivered unmanned systems to national security customers, including intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance aircraft, electronic warfare equipment and unmanned surface vessels. The company completed an initial public offering in April, raising roughly $312 million and listing on the NYSE. AEVEX had operated as a portfolio company of Madison Dearborn Partners before the offering. It employs about 650 people across manufacturing sites in the United States.

 Families in flood-hit areas of Nepal are holding symbolic funerals for missing loved ones as the death toll from last week's flash floods rose to 1,252, with more than 4,200 people missing, official data showed Thursday.
In neighboring China, 21 people were killed and 541 remained missing, including 261 foreigners, according to local authorities.
The combined death toll from both countries stood at 1,273, while 4,757 people remained missing, including 844 foreign nationals.
In Rasuwa, one of Nepal's hardest-hit districts, families created funeral effigies using kaas-kush, or sacred grass, and performed final rites to "liberate the souls" of missing relatives after losing hope of finding their bodies, the Kathmandu Post reported.
On Wednesday, dozens of such effigies were cremated in a mass funeral at Pashupati Aryaghat temple in Kathmandu on the banks of the Bagmati River.
In Chitwan, another badly affected district, authorities buried unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples because the number of remains made individual identification and storage difficult.
Many flood victims have been left without places to observe mourning rituals after floodwaters swept away both family members and homes in several districts.
Those who lost everything and traveled to Kathmandu seeking shelter have also been unable to find space at public facilities for the rituals.
Military personnel, police and others continued search and rescue operations in flood-hit areas on Thursday.
Rescuers, however, faced difficulties as roads, power supplies and communications remained disrupted across wide areas.
They were also working to deliver relief supplies and maintain hygiene in shelters to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
The disaster struck on Aug. 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet), triggering an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley, while also burying the Gyirong border crossing in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.

Leasing or royalties: The Finance Ministry may resolve the issue over which the BEB is pursuing airlines
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:14:47 EEST
17:14:47 KST

Leasing or royalties: The Finance Ministry may resolve the issue over which the BEB is pursuing airlines
Kyiv • UNN
The Finance Ministry plans to unify the taxation of airlines’ lease payments to non-residents. The UTP will not change the law, but may affect unresolved BEB disputes.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine may use a general tax consultation to establish a unified approach to applying legal provisions that state bodies interpret ambiguously. This is the mechanism planned for resolving the issue of taxation of Ukrainian airlines’ leasing payments in favor of nonresidents. UNN examined the legal force of a general tax clarification, whether regulatory authorities must take it into account, and whether it can affect the existing claims of the Economic Security Bureau against representatives of the aviation business.
Why is the Finance Ministry’s clarification needed on the issue of aviation leasing?
The issue of taxing aircraft leasing became the subject of a dispute between the aviation business and state authorities. It arose after the Economic Security Bureau decided to interpret aviation leasing not as the rental of vehicles, but as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers should have paid royalties for leasing aircraft and helicopters.
The ESB is investigating criminal proceedings against at least 5 air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Urga," H3Operations, and "Skyline Express." The cases were opened despite the fact that almost all air carriers had successfully passed tax audits, and the tax authorities’ comments concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of legal provisions and requires the establishment of a unified state approach. They call the Bureau’s approach to interpreting aviation leasing, without amending tax legislation, pressure that could destroy an entire sector of passenger and freight transportation. After all, according to the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
That is why the issue of aviation leasing was submitted for consideration by the tax committee of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the establishment of a working group under the Finance Ministry, which is to develop a draft general tax consultation regarding the taxation of leasing payments in favor of nonresidents.
In response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and international treaties of Ukraine. It is worth noting that tax legislation in this area has not changed for several decades and, until 2024, had raised no questions either among tax authorities or law enforcement agencies.
The aviation industry hopes that the general tax clarification will settle all questions regarding the taxation of aviation leasing. But is that really the case?
What is a general tax consultation?
As lawyer Yuliia Panasiuk of Prykhodko & Partners Law Firm explained to UNN, a general tax consultation is an officially published position of the Ministry of Finance regarding the practical application of certain provisions of tax and other legislation, compliance with which is monitored by regulatory authorities.
"It is formulated on the basis of a generalization of individual tax consultations provided to taxpayers, or in cases where the Finance Ministry identifies ambiguity in the application of certain legal provisions," Panasiuk explained.
According to her, such a clarification is approved by an order of the Ministry of Finance.
Tax policy expert Danylo Monin noted that the Finance Ministry usually generalizes the practice of applying legislation with regard to a specific problem or topic.
"As the body that formulates state financial policy, the Finance Ministry has the right to generalize the practice of applying legislation concerning disputed issues and, on this basis, issue a general tax consultation. Usually, this is done regarding a specific problem or a particular topic," Monin explained.
Thus, the situation involving differing interpretations of the taxation of leasing payments is precisely the kind of case in which the mechanism of a generalized tax clarification can be used to establish a unified approach.
Can the Ministry of Finance establish new rules for airlines?
As experts explain, a generalized tax consultation does not amend legislation. Through this mechanism, the Ministry of Finance cannot create a new tax, change its rate, or impose on airlines an additional tax obligation that is not provided for in the Tax Code.
"Such a consultation does not create new tax rules and cannot amend the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine. Its task is to provide an official position on how an already effective provision should be applied in practice," Panasiuk emphasized.
In the context of aviation leasing, this means that the task of the generalized tax clarification will not be to establish a new taxation regime, but to clarify how the current provisions should be applied to payments for the leasing of aircraft from non-residents.
At the same time, according to the lawyer, if an individual tax consultation contradicts a generalized one, the provisions developed by the Ministry of Finance apply, pursuant to paragraph 53.1 of the Tax Code.
Should state authorities take the Ministry of Finance's position into account?
Controlling authorities must take into account the position formulated by the Ministry of Finance in a generalized tax consultation when applying the relevant legislative provisions.
At the same time, for a taxpayer, the clarification does not become a new provision of law. Businesses must primarily follow the Tax Code, while conduct that complies with a generalized consultation provides the taxpayer with the legal guarantees stipulated by law.
This may be of fundamental importance for airlines if the position formed by the Ministry of Finance differs from the approach previously applied by controlling or law enforcement authorities to leasing payments.
"If the Ministry of Finance has published a GTC that interprets the relevant provision differently from the way a controlling authority previously did, the taxpayer may refer to such a consultation both during a tax audit and at the stage of administrative or judicial appeal," Panasiuk noted.
Going forward, a taxpayer's compliance with the provisions of tax consultations may constitute grounds for exemption from financial liability. The legislation also provides for cases in which no penalty interest is accrued or already accrued penalty interest is subject to cancellation.
What will happen to aviation leasing cases?
One of the key questions in this situation is whether the Ministry of Finance's clarification will be able to affect disputes and proceedings that arose before its adoption.
According to Panasiuk, a new generalized tax consultation does not in itself automatically change the tax consequences of transactions carried out previously. In other words, the appearance of the consultation will not mean the automatic termination or review of all disputes related to the taxation of leasing payments.
However, for cases that have not yet been finally resolved when the document appears, its significance may be substantial.
"If a tax dispute has not yet been concluded, the taxpayer may refer to the new GTC as the Ministry of Finance's official position on the interpretation of the relevant legislative provision," the lawyer explained.
According to her, in such a case the court will assess the consultation together with the provisions of the Tax Code, the circumstances of the specific case, and current judicial practice.
Under the provisions of the Tax Code, generalized tax consultations must be published on the Ministry of Finance's official website within five calendar days of their issuance.
"The Tax Code does not establish a separate period after the expiration of which controlling authorities may begin taking a GTC into account. Therefore, in practice, primary attention should be paid to the date on which the Ministry of Finance's order approving the relevant GTC enters into force," the lawyer warned.
If the Ministry of Finance develops an unambiguous position on the application of the relevant provisions of the Tax Code and international treaties, it could serve as a guideline for the further practice of the supervisory authorities and as a strong argument for airlines in cases handled by the Economic Security Bureau, where aircraft leasing is interpreted as royalties. That is why the development of a UPT may become one of the key stages in resolving the situation.

Embattled Spanish PM Sánchez insists no prior warnings before Ceuta crisis
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:14:17 BST
17:14:17 KST

Embattled Spanish PM insists no prior warnings before Ceuta crisis
- Published
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said no-one foresaw the influx of 72,000 migrants in the exclave of Ceuta, as pressure mounts over his handling of the crisis.
"It's absurd to think that the government knew and did nothing," Sánchez told Spain's parliament on Thursday, hours after tens of thousands of people joined protests across the country backed by opposition parties.
Sánchez also maintained there was no evidence Morocco was behind the mass crossing and there had been "close co-ordination" between the two countries.
A Spanish police report has highlighted the "total permissiveness" of Moroccan security forces, although senior officials insist it does not point the finger at Rabat.
Although most of the migrants have been sent back to Morocco, some 5,000 remain on the streets and beaches of Ceuta, on the North African coast, including as many as 1,400 children.
There have been several reports that Spanish officials had been warned of a rise in sea arrivals over the border at Ceuta, following a Spanish court ruling that many migrants misunderstood to mean they would not be pushed back if they swam across.
Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo accused the government of lying and a cover-up, and said the prime minister should resign.
Spain's handling of the migrant influx angered some of its European partners, and Italy responded by imposing border restrictions on arrivals from Spain.
The large turnout for the demonstrations in Madrid and other cities on Wednesday underlined the pressure Sánchez is under domestically too.
The protests were ostensibly held to express support for the people of Ceuta, but as frequent anti-government chants have shown, they also reflected public anger at the ongoing crisis.
As Thursday's fierce debate in Congress showed, the situation in Ceuta has developed from a humanitarian and logistical crisis into a major political challenge for the Socialist leader.
One of the issues Sánchez is having to explain is his government's bilateral relationship with Morocco.
He has tried to walk a delicate line between defending his refusal to blame Morocco while reprimanding it for the sovereignty claims it has been making in recent weeks on both Ceuta and its fellow Spanish exclave of Melilla.
Sánchez has been careful until now not to criticise Rabat and he said he would stick to "proven, verified facts", although he did complain of "unacceptable" statements by two Moroccan ministers about Ceuta and its sister city Melilla.
Moroccan Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi has spoken of his country's "historical and geographical right" to the cities and proposed talks with Spain on the issue.
The two cities have the EU's only land borders in North Africa and Sánchez told parliament: "Ceuta is not the border of Spain, it is Spain on the border [of Europe]."
- Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say 
  - Published1 day ago
- Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues 
  - Published5 days ago
Politicians to both his left and right point to what they say is Morocco's track record of using the border with Spain as leverage when it has a grievance.
Many have interpreted the police report pointing to the role of Moroccan security forces in the July crossing as reinforcing this theory, although Sánchez maintained there was no solid evidence of government involvement.
The report, commissioned by a High Court judge, said security forces had "made no serious attempt" to stop the influx and quoted some migrants saying Moroccan gendarmes had even provided guidance.
Responding to the revelations, as well as media reports before the influx, Feijóo told MPs that the crisis had "originated in Morocco, was consented to by Morocco and there are indications that Morocco co-ordinated it and the government knew because it had been warned about it".
Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.
Sánchez said King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta and Melilla in the coming weeks to convey Spain's commitment to the two cities, although officials say no date has been set.
He praised the response of Ceuta police who had chosen to "defend human life" when the influx took place, rather than defend the border. He also highlighted close co-operation with Moroccan authorities over the return of more than 90% of the migrants in the following 72 hours.
He addressed the "difficult times" faced by the residents of Ceuta, as he explained the "complexity" of what had happened on 30 and 31 July.
He spoke of an "episode in which numerous actors and interests converge", doubling down on his assertion that hoaxes and rumours spread by social media had sparked the crisis.
He has already blamed trafficking gangs and angered Russia and Israel for highlighting social media linked to both countries along with "an international far-right movement". He told MPs that there was no evidence of state actors being involved but doubled down on his allegations of accounts linked to the two countries.
Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", he added.

Foreign support, drones fuel Sudan war and possible war crimes, UN probe says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:14:11 UTC
17:14:11 KST

Foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike deep into civilian areas, a United Nations fact-finding mission said in a report published on Thursday, warning that some attacks may amount to war crimes.
Sudan's war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Sudan's military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) ahead of a planned transition to civilian rule. The conflict has devastated the country, displaced more than 14 million people and created what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The UN mission said investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
The UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia, the RSF and Sudan's military did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
UAE, Chad deny allegations
The UAE rejected allegations that it had provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF, and Chad said it remained neutral in the war and denied knowledge of weapons transfers through its territory, according to the report.
The UN mission also said it obtained evidence that Colombian contractors played a significant role in operating and maintaining drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF. It estimated the total number of Colombian contractors involved could approach 2,000 and said some were present during operations around al-Fashir in Darfur.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Mass killings of non‑Arab communities when the RSF captured al‑Fashir bore hallmarks that point to genocide, the UN mission said in a previous report in February.
In the past, the RSF has denied such abuses, saying the accounts have been manufactured by its enemies and making counter-accusations against them.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan's military was at an early stage but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions, which can hover over an area before striking a target, had expanded the army's long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
Drone warfare violated international human rights law, UN says
The report found both sides committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in their drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes. Both sides have previously denied allegations of human rights abuses.
Expanded range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan's military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.
More than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes between January and May 2026, according to figures cited by the report.
Between May and July 2026, repeated RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of El Obeid, which was under SAF control as RSF pressure intensified in June this year. Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege, the mission said.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were SAF strikes on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur that investigators said killed at least 70 people and left the facility non-functional.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and urged the UN Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan.
