Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah terrorists, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.
Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources, and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
Hezbollah has said in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.
The IDF has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the US had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the US Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.
IRGC forces holed up, officials say
Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.
The third source, a foreign official with direct knowledge of the message, said it was delivered around mid-August and that as a result of US pressure, Israel had put off storming Ali al-Taher.
Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message but said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.
"Iran considers any Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June US-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.
Iran fired missiles towards Israel in early June in retaliation for attacks on Hezbollah on the Lebanese capital's outskirts.
Israel seeks to besiege Hezbollah fighters
Despite a ceasefire announced in June, the Israeli military has said Hezbollah is still operating around the ridge and twice over the last week launched explosive drones towards Israeli troops near the ridge.
In July, it said it had launched an air strike on a Hezbollah fighter near an access shaft to the underground site at Ali al-Taher and vowed not to allow Hezbollah to operate in the area or pose a threat to Israeli soldiers.
An Israeli military official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters in June that Hezbollah fighters were stuck underground without food or water. Israeli newspaper Maariv, citing a military source, said on Thursday that the Israeli military assessed there were no IRGC forces in Ali al-Taher and that some Hezbollah fighters had died without food and water.
The third official said Israel's military was trying to smoke out Hezbollah and IRGC personnel by besieging them, shooting down attempted drone deliveries of food and water to the ridge.
"What we have seen over the past month is Israeli pressure to besiege Ali al-Taher in order to impose a reality within this facility that renders it uninhabitable. This approach, and the absence of a large-scale attack, means that it is possible a message was conveyed through several countries -- this is a natural conclusion," Hezbollah's media office told Reuters.
Hezbollah threatens retaliation
A Lebanese source briefed by Hezbollah said the group's fighters can still access their positions through the ridge's northern side.
Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher, which Israel's military has included in a self-declared security zone occupied by its troops and off-limits to Lebanese.
Despite Iran's warning, the Lebanese source and a senior Lebanese security official said an Israeli military operation to capture the ridge was still possible in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah said any large-scale attack on Ali al-Taher would mean a return to full-blown war, and could see missiles landing on northern Israeli communities.

India, Sri Lanka, and Israel’s overlooked Indian Ocean opportunity  - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:13:43 UTC
17:13:43 KST

While Sri Lanka is not an obvious priority in Israel’s Asian policy, with India, Japan, and Singapore receiving far more strategic attention, it has considerable potential because of its location, its development needs and the direction its relationship with India is heading.
During my recent visit, this became particularly clear. The island sits close to major sea lanes and within India’s immediate maritime security environment. For New Delhi, Sri Lanka is not simply another neighbor. Access to its ports and maritime infrastructure carries significance beyond bilateral relations.
Indian concerns about China’s research and survey vessels illustrate this sensitivity. The issue is not simply Chinese commercial investment. New Delhi is also attentive to the possibility that external actors could gain access to ports, infrastructure, or oceanographic information with potential dual-use applications close to India’s coastline.
Sri Lanka should not be reduced to another arena of India-China competition. Colombo has strong reasons to maintain relations with multiple partners, including China. Any Israeli strategy framed primarily around containing Beijing would misunderstand Sri Lanka’s interests and risk narrowing the space for cooperation.
India’s own approach has become broader. During Sri Lanka’s economic crisis in 2022, New Delhi provided some $4 billion in assistance. Since then, the relationship has moved beyond emergency support toward longer-term cooperation in energy, infrastructure, digital connectivity, trade, and security.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s April 2025 visit marked an important step. The two countries signed agreements on electricity interconnection, digital transformation and development, and, for the first time, a formal memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Defence Cooperation.
India, Sri Lanka and the United Arab Emirates also agreed to cooperate on developing Trincomalee as an energy hub.
The defense agreement did not create bilateral security cooperation: India and Sri Lanka already had substantial ties in training, naval visits, exercises, and capacity-building. Yet the MoU gave this relationship a more formal framework. Cooperation includes joint exercises, maritime surveillance, hydrography, capacity-building, and the provision of defense platforms and assets.
SLINEX is a regular bilateral naval exercise, and in April 2026 the two navies conducted their fourth bilateral diving exercise in Colombo, including complex underwater operations. Sri Lankan personnel have also participated in India’s wider IOS Sagar initiative.
Taken together, these developments suggest that India is progressively embedding Sri Lanka within a wider Indian-led maritime security architecture. This does not mean that Colombo is surrendering its strategic autonomy or that India is constructing a formal alliance system. India continues to prefer flexible partnerships. But New Delhi increasingly sees regional security as something built through training, maritime domain awareness, interoperability, capacity-building, and institutional cooperation.
For Israel, this creates an opportunity that deserves attention.
For years, Israel-India relations have been viewed primarily through defense cooperation, technology, and an expanding strategic convergence. Those ties remain important. But as India’s regional role grows, Israel should consider whether that partnership can also provide a basis for selective cooperation with third countries.
Sri Lanka offers a useful test case; there is evidence of Sri Lankan interest in expanding relations with Israel. In August 2026, Sri Lanka’s new ambassador to Israel identified agricultural technology, defense, and trade as areas in which Colombo would like to deepen cooperation.
Agriculture is an obvious starting point. India and Israel have spent years developing Centers of Excellence that combine Israeli agricultural technology with Indian institutions, local adaptation, and training. A similar trilateral initiative could bring together Israeli technology, Indian implementation experience, and Sri Lankan development priorities.
The potential goes further.
Maritime security is one area where Israeli capabilities could complement rather than compete with India’s regional role. Israel has relevant experience in sensors, electro-optics, unmanned systems, and maritime infrastructure protection. Cybersecurity and artificial intelligence are also important as ports, energy facilities, and digital systems become connected and vulnerable.
Israel’s comparative advantage lies not in establishing a military presence in Sri Lanka but in providing niche capabilities, technology, and practical solutions. India brings geographical proximity, political weight,and military-to-military engagement. Israel can contribute specialized expertise in maritime surveillance, cyber defense, AI, and critical-infrastructure protection.
This does not require a formal India-Israel-Sri Lanka strategic triangle. A more realistic model would be functional trilateralism: concrete projects addressing Sri Lankan needs. The India-UAE-Sri Lanka cooperation around Trincomalee provides a useful precedent, illustrating that third-country participation can complement Indian interests rather than challenge them.
Israel must also recognize Sri Lanka’s political sensitivities. Colombo has historically supported the Palestinian cause and continues to support a two-state solution. Treating Sri Lanka merely as another market for defense technology would therefore be politically shortsighted. A broader relationship combining agriculture, water, technology, trade, and carefully calibrated security cooperation would be more sustainable.
The larger lesson extends beyond Sri Lanka. As India becomes more influential across the Indian Ocean, Israel should think about India not only as a bilateral strategic partner but also as a platform for regional cooperation.
For decades, the focus has been on what India and Israel can do together. The next question is what their accumulated experience and complementary capabilities might allow them to do together elsewhere.
Sri Lanka may be one of the best places to begin.

Taiwan drones yet to see steady foreign demand

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – There has been no long-term foreign demand for drones despite export spikes in recent years, a DSET report published on Wednesday said.
Author Cathy Fang said exports grew from 3,472 units in 2024 to 122,726 in 2025 and 191,373 in the first half of 2026. She added that the main export markets are Poland, the Czech Republic, and the US, with a NT$1.5 billion (US$47.18 million) shipment to Saudi Arabia in June.
Fang said that European demand is tied to the war in Ukraine, which is unsustainable. She added that government contracts outside the US are also limited.
On cooperation, Fang said that instead of signing agreements with allies on one-time exchanges, Taiwan should seek joint development and licensing to gain ownership of software and hardware. She noted future purchases and collaborations should stem from operational experience.
Fang also mentioned technological gaps in flight controls, communications, and positioning, as core components and flight software are sourced overseas. Although the economics ministry has approved NT$326 million (US$10 million) for domestic development, firms could take up to two to three years for testing before mass production.
On materials, Fang said most batteries and rare minerals used to make components are imported from China, despite government efforts to establish a non-China supply chain. She urged working with allies to mine or develop alternative sources.
On testing, Fang suggested more flight tests with signal cutoffs, electronic interference, and long-distance patrols. She said ministries should coordinate on flight zones, test sites, and safety.
DSET is a government-funded research institute. Its full name is Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology.

The ceremony began at 10 a.m. with the sound of drums and bells. A band then played the national anthem.
Lai served as chief officiant of the ceremony. He was accompanied by Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰), Examination Yuan President Chou Hung-hsien (周弘憲), Presidential Office Secretary-General Pan Men-an (潘孟安), and National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮).
Lai presented flowers at the memorial tablets of martyrs. After the memorial address was read, he led officials and other participants in three bows in tribute to those being commemorated. The ceremony concluded with Lai greeting and shaking hands with representatives of the families of the deceased.
The annual fall ceremony is held on Sept. 3, Taiwan's Armed Forces Day, while a corresponding spring memorial is held March 29. The ceremonies are part of a tradition of honoring people who died in military or other national service, per a Presidential Office press release.
Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) was notably absent from Thursday's ceremony, marking his second consecutive absence from the central government's memorial ceremonies at the shrine. His office said he had other engagements and therefore could not attend Thursday's event, per CNA.
Han's absence is notable because the legislative speaker traditionally participates alongside the president and other senior government officials. Acting Judicial Yuan President Hsieh Ming-yang (謝銘洋) was also absent Thursday. He was reported to be overseas on official business.

Norway Seizes Russian Ship to Enforce $4.2Bln Claim by Ukraine’s Naftogaz

Norway has seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.2 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets following the 2014 annexation of Crimea, officials said late on Wednesday.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a 24-hour standoff with the Norwegian Coast Guard, according to Covington, the U.S. law firm representing Naftogaz.
Russian state news agency TASS quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesperson as saying the seizure of the ship amounts to an act of "piracy."
Naftogaz has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea.
A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.2 billion plus interest and legal costs.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said.
Covington, the law firm, said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a Russian-owned vessel that is used for commercial cruises, for months.
Anticipating the ship's arrival in Svalbard en route to Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement, Naftogaz's lawyers applied to a Norwegian court for the vessel to be arrested there and subject to a compulsory sale.
The application was approved by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court on Monday. In its ruling, it required the governor of Svalbard to enforce the order, supervise the vessel and ensure that it is not moved.
The governor's office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held on Svalbard.
Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement measures across multiple jurisdictions, including the United States, France, the United Kingdom and Finland, where Russian assets have been frozen. Russia is appealing the process, saying no notice was given.
"We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid," the Ukrainian company said.

Germany blamed Russia for a sabotage attempt discovered in early August, when a drone rigged with explosives was found near a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport. On September 1, Germany responded with retaliatory measures, closing Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the “Russian House” in Berlin and tightening entry controls for Russian nationals.

Police raid northern Israeli Hasidic community over suspected child marriages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:12:00 UTC
17:12:00 KST

Police raided several locations in Yavne’el on Thursday morning and detained 16 suspects for questioning — minors and adults — on suspicion that they had recently married or had begun making concrete preparations for an illegal wedding ceremony involving underage brides.
Among the suspects is a prominent activist in the fight against child marriage in the town, who is suspected of having organized a wedding for her daughter when she was 16
“The Northern District Police is conducting an ongoing campaign against the phenomenon of child marriages allegedly taking place illegally within a small and closed community whose main activity is centered in the town of Yavne’el in the Lower Galilee. After more than 20 suspects were detained for questioning several weeks ago on suspicion of involvement in child marriages in the community, dozens of Northern District officers again raided several locations in Yavne’el this morning and have so far detained 16 minors and adults for questioning,” the Israel Police said in a statement.
This is the second wave of detentions, after more than 20 suspects were questioned in June over alleged involvement in child marriages in the community.
According to police, the weddings are usually held in the morning with only a small number of people present, and the location is not disclosed until the ceremony begins. They are held without photographs or cellphones, out of concern that the wedding will be documented.
“After the religious ceremony, in many cases another event is held for the wider public under the guise of an ‘engagement party,’ to which all relatives of the bride and groom are invited,” police said.
In light of these efforts to conceal the ceremonies, police are unsure whether the activist campaigning against the phenomenon ultimately married off her daughter, or whether the wedding did not go ahead. However, police say they have evidence that allegedly points to preparations for such a wedding.
In recent months, the child marriage affair in the town has drawn public attention, in part following ynet reports about underage girls from the local Hasidic community who arrived to give birth at nearby hospitals.
Police explained that enforcement is complicated because the wedding ceremonies are generally held in secret. Even when police discover a festive gathering, participants do not issue invitations using the word “wedding,” do not sign a ketubah, or Jewish marriage contract, and do not hold a chuppah ceremony in front of guests, so that there will be no evidence that a wedding took place.
“Kudos to the Northern District fraud unit, which is conducting this complicated investigation. We will not relent until all the offenders who abuse underage girls and boys are behind bars, ”Knesset lawmaker Meirav Cohen of Beyachad-Yesh Atid, chair of the Knesset Committee on the Status of Women and Gender Equality, said.
Cohen visited the community Wednesday after, according to her, a school principal married off her daughter while she was still a minor to a young man from the community. During the visit, Cohen entered a local council meeting, where her personal aide said he was shoved and nearly assaulted by one of the employees there.

Swiss inflation rate jumps to highest level in two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:11:12 UTC
17:11:12 KST

Swiss inflation rate jumps to highest level in two years
Swiss inflation accelerated far more than analysts anticipated to the fastest pace since September 2024, suggesting a weaker franc is feeding through to the economy.
Consumer prices rose 0.8% in August from a year earlier, up from 0.4% in July, the Federal Statistical Office said on Thursday. The result was higher than every single forecast of 16 economists in a Bloomberg survey.
The reading is the last that Swiss National Bank (SNB) officials will see before their interest-rate decision later this month. While the result notably exceeded expectations, it remains consistent with the average for the current quarter predicted by the central bank.
More
How the war in Iran is affecting Swiss consumers
The pick-up in inflation will be welcomed by policymakers in a country where consumer price growth has often been feeble and even turned briefly negative last year. The outcome still underscores how benign the Middle East energy shock has been for Switzerland at a time when its neighbors are seeing costs surge.
In the euro area that surrounds the country, consumer prices rose 3.3% in August, the highest in almost three years. Following the harmonised European methodology, that compares to a Swiss rate of 0.9%.
Clothing prices down
SNB has predicted a mild, temporary acceleration of consumer-price growth that may now be assisted by the weaker franc, which this week reached a one-year low against the euro.
+ Rising rents are heavy burden on many Swiss households
The franc extended gains after the data to rise 0.4% to CHF0.9385 per euro, after Wednesday’s CHF0.9435 low.
With rates at zero, the central bank expects the quarterly average to peak at 0.8% by early next year, comfortably within its targeted range of 0-2%.
Last month, higher costs for petroleum products were partly offset by lower ones for clothing and footwear, the statistics office said. So-called core inflation, which excludes volatile elements such as energy, picked up to 0.4% from 0.3% – that’s the first acceleration this year.
More
Switzerland faces a steep energy bill due to the Middle East conflict
The reading coincides with a potential upswing of the Swiss economy. Output adjusted for major sports events expanded by 1.5% in the second quarter, five times more than had been expected.
That growth was driven by exports, particularly in pharma and chemicals, according to a detailed breakdown of drivers published Thursday.
Manufacturing contributed more than services, which is unusual for Switzerland. Government spending continued to outpace private consumption for a third quarter.
Rate hike possible
While economists question if that the reading might be an outlier rather than a sustainable acceleration, a key leading indicator of growth has reached the highest level in almost five years. Also, wages appear to keep rising, outpacing inflation, and manufacturing in August exceeded expectations.
Helping the outlook for export-focused Switzerland is a trade deal with China that will remove almost all tariffs on goods bound for Asia’s biggest economy. The agreement, which has yet to be ratified, envisions Swiss signature goods including watches, pharmaceuticals and precision instruments being imported fully duty-free.
While the Iran war prompted a surge in the franc earlier this year that alarmed the SNB enough to spark interventions to stem the gains, the currency has dropped against the euro since then. Officials have still kept up the threat of cutting borrowing costs below zero if necessary.
In July, Bloomberg reporting indicated that inside the SNB the rate is expected to stay at zero through next year before it then probably rises. That view is still in line with what most economists predict.
“Price risks have shifted to the upside in Switzerland as well,” Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank in Vaduz, said in reaction to the inflation data. “A rate hike in December cannot be completely ruled out.”

German startup TYTAN debuts new rocket-boosted interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:11:10 UTC
17:11:10 KST

- TYTAN Technologies said it showed German Cabinet officials a new rocket-boosted interceptor drone during the government's August retreat in Brandenburg.
- The company has not disclosed the new system's speed, range, or a timeline for testing or production.
Munich-based counter-drone company TYTAN Technologies said it demonstrated a new rocket-boosted interceptor drone to the German Federal Cabinet last month, presenting what the company described as a new category of system built for greater range and speed against aerial threats.
TYTAN said the demonstration took place during the Cabinet’s annual retreat at Schloss Neuhardenberg in Brandenburg. The two-day retreat, held August 25 and 26, brought together Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and other Cabinet members to discuss economic growth, competitiveness and technology policy, according to the German government. TYTAN said Merz, Klingbeil and Pistorius were the first officials to see the new interceptor.
The company said the system uses rocket boosters to extend its range and speed compared with TYTAN’s existing interceptor line, and that it was developed in response to changing drone threats observed in Ukraine. TYTAN has not disclosed the new interceptor’s speed, range, altitude ceiling, or a timeline for testing or delivery.
TYTAN’s existing product line includes the EOS, a short-range multicopter interceptor built for NATO Class I drones weighing up to 150 kg (330 pounds), and the METIS, a long-range fixed-wing interceptor for Class II drones between 150 and 600 kg (330 and 1,320 pounds). The company has said METIS can reach speeds of 350 km/h (217 mph), fly out to 25 km (15.5 miles) and operate at altitudes up to 5,000 meters (16,400 feet). TYTAN’s smaller interceptor drones use computer vision to track and ram hostile drones rather than carrying an explosive warhead, with a reported top speed above 250 km/h (155 mph), a range beyond 15 km (9.3 miles) and a weight around 5 kg (11 pounds).
TYTAN raised €30 million ($34.8 million) in a Series A round in February 2026, co-led by Armira and the NATO Innovation Fund. In January, the company signed a cooperation agreement with German sensor maker HENSOLDT to integrate TYTAN’s interceptors with HENSOLDT’s Elysion Mission Core command-and-control software.
The company said it was founded by two international engineering students two and a half years ago and has grown to around 200 employees. TYTAN opened a serial production line in Bavaria this year with capacity for 3,000 interceptor drones per month, with production activity scheduled to begin in August, CEO Balázs Nagy told Defense News in June.
TYTAN said its interceptors are already deployed in Ukraine, along with Germany and Baltic states listed among its customers. The company said frontline feedback from Ukrainian operators is incorporated into its systems through software updates rather than hardware redesigns, which it said lets it shorten the gap between identifying a capability gap and fielding a fix.
Nagy has said the company’s pricing model is built around cost, telling Defense News in June that TYTAN aims to protect the same airspace “200 times cheaper than with legacy systems.”

UK Green leader to seek parliament seat vacated by Starmer
LONDON, Sept 3 - The leader of Britain's left-wing Green Party intends to stand in an election for a seat in parliament vacated by former Labour prime minister Keir Starmer, a local newspaper reported on Thursday.
Zack Polanski told the Camden New Journal he would be the Green candidate for Holborn and St Pancras, a left-leaning constituency which Starmer held comfortably in 2024 though with a much-reduced vote share.
"Labour stands up for corporations and big money," Polanski posted on X. "I'll stand up for people and our communities."
In an election two years ago, an independent candidate who campaigned primarily on opposition to Israel's war in Gaza took nearly 19% of the vote while the Green candidate received over 10%, giving the party hope of taking the seat this time.
Since Polanski became Green leader a year ago the party has had success in taking support from Labour's left, winning a surprise by-election victory in Greater Manchester – where current Prime Minister Andy Burnham was a long-serving mayor – and nationally polling as high as 20%.
But Polanski's personal popularity took a hit after he criticised police officers for the way they arrested a man who allegedly stabbed two Jewish people in north London in April, according to pollsters YouGov.
A national YouGov poll on Wednesday put Labour tied with the right-wing populist Reform UK party of anti-Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage on 23% with the opposition Conservatives on 20% and the Greens on 13%. REUTERS

Manipur violence: 306 killed, 49 missing since May 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

17:08:37 KST

At least 306 people have been killed and 49 remain missing in the ethnic violence that broke out in Manipur in May 2023, state home minister Govindas Konthoujam told the Assembly on Thursday.Responding to a query by BJP MLA Sapam Ranjan Singh on the second day of the ongoing Assembly session, Konthoujam said the figures were recorded as of August 31, 2026.“Since the violence started on May 3, 2023, 306 people have died, and 49 people are still missing as of August 31, 2026,” he said.
The ethnic clashes between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities began on May 3, 2023, after a ‘Tribal Solidarity March’ was organised in the hill districts to protest the Meitei community’s demand for Scheduled Tribe status.Meiteis account for around 53 per cent of Manipur’s population and live mainly in the Imphal Valley, while tribals, including Nagas and Kukis, constitute around 40 per cent and reside predominantly in the hill districts.The prolonged violence resulted in widespread displacement and triggered significant political developments in the state.
President’s Rule revoked earlier this year
President’s Rule was imposed in Manipur on February 13, 2025, after then chief minister N Biren Singh resigned amid the prolonged ethnic conflict. The 60-member Assembly was subsequently placed under suspended animation.President’s Rule was revoked on February 4, 2026, paving the way for the formation of a new government under BJP leader Yumnam Khemchand Singh as chief minister.

India wants tariff edge before signing US trade deal, says commerce minister
India will announce the final details of its proposed Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) with the US only after Washington agrees to offer preferential tariff terms over India's competitors, Indian commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday.
"As soon as the US is able to give us the preferential rate in comparison to our competition, we will finalize the BTA and announce the final details," Indian news agencies quoted Goyal as saying.
US President Donald Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi first announced negotiations for the US-India Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) in February 2025.
But strained ties and global conflicts have delayed negotiations, with the talks only restoring momentum this year.
In February, Washington and New Delhi released the framework for an interim trade agreement.
Under the deal, India will "eliminate or reduce tariffs" on all US industrial products and a wide range of US food and agricultural goods.
The US agreed to reduce Trump's tariffs from 25% to 18% and rescind the punitive extra 25% tariff imposed on India for its purchase of Russian oil.
But negotiations on the final deal were deferred after the US Supreme Court struck down the Trump administration's sweeping tariffs.
In June, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer visited New Delhi, where he met Goyal and reviewed core elements of the BTA.
Goyal is now set to travel to the US later this month for the G20 Trade Ministerial in Milwaukee and engage in bilateral talks with Greer.
India ready to help end Ukraine war, Jaishankar says during Kyiv visit
India is ready to help end the war in Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said as he arrived in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Thursday.
"If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said as he addressed the media alongside Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Sybiha welcomed Jaishankar for what he described as the "first-ever dedicated bilateral visit" of an Indian foreign minister to Ukraine.
"India is a global power and we welcome Prime Minister Modi's call to move from an endless war towards an end to the war. Ukraine stands ready for diplomacy," Sybiha wrote on X, referring to comments the Indian leader made during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan earlier in the week.
Jaishankar's trip to Ukraine comes more than a week after he attended the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation in Moscow with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
The Indian foreign minister also met Putin during the Russia visit.
Since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine, New Delhi has been under pressure from Kyiv's Western partners over its cooperation with Moscow, India's decades-long ally.
"This historic moment takes place amid escalating Russian attacks against our cities, port infrastructure, and civil shipping. Our capital is constantly under attack and I appreciate my colleague's brave visit," Sybiha said as he talked about Jaishankar's Kyiv visit.
The Ukrainian minister added that he and Jaishankar discussed the need to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, global food security, and bilateral cooperation.
"From infrastructure and pharmaceutical sector to technological innovation and digitalisation, we are ready to realise our full potential," Sybiha said.
Air Force veteran to be Ram Temple's first CEO
A trust that runs India's grand Ram Temple in Ayodhya has roped in an Indian Air Force veteran to be the Hindu shrine's first chief executive officer (CEO) in a leadership shake-up following a donation embezzlement row, Indian media reported.
Air Marshal Jeetendra Mishra, who retired from the Air Force in April 2026, was appointed CEO of the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust on Wednesday.
According to news agency ANI, more than 5,000 applicants were vying for the post.
The temple in Uttar Pradesh was inaugurated in 2024 by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, fulfilling a key Hindu nationalist pledge.
The temple site has been a controversial flashpoint because it was built on grounds where the 16th-century Babri Masjid, or Mosque of Babur, once stood. The mosque was demolished by Hindu mobs in 1992, triggering bloody riots that left nearly 2,000 people dead.
Mishra's appointment comes after the Ram Temple became embroiled in controversy in recent months following allegations of theft involving donations and offerings worth millions of rupees.
Mishra served as chief of the Indian Air Force's Western Command during the 2025 Indian military strikes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, which New Delhi said targeted "terrorist infrastructure" in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
"I also consider this the blessings of Lord Ram that after 43 years of service to the nation in the Air Force, He has given me the opportunity to serve Shri Ram Mandir (temple) and Shri Ram bhakt (devotees)," Mishra told news agency ANI.
Opposition slams move
The appointment has also drawn political criticism, particularly in the wake of the donation-related allegations surrounding the temple trust.
The opposition Congress party has questioned Mishra's appointment.
"Will appointing a new CEO or bringing in new people in the Trust bring back the donations by devotees? Has action been taken against the thieves?" Uttar Pradesh Congress chief Ajay Rai said in an interview with ANI.
"Will the retired Air Marshal take action against these thieves and send them to jail? When will the action be taken and the stolen money be brought back?" he added.
Congress leader Imran Masood told news agency PTI that the job was for "saints and seers."
"Now, instead of saints and seers working inside the Ram Temple, a retired Air Marshal will be doing the work," he said.
US Secretary of State Rubio reacts to Modi- Pezeshkian meeting
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said he does not believe India and Iran are discussing a trade deal, two days after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modiheld a bilateral meeting with Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO in Bishkek.
The Monday meeting between Modi and Pezeshkian was their first since the start of the Iran war.
Rubio reacted to the leaders' meeting during an interview on "The Brian Kilmeade Show" on Fox News Radio on Wednesday.
When asked by the host whether New Delhi and Tehran were pursuing some form of trade deal, Rubio said: "Well, I don't think there's a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are - countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime."
Later in the interview, the secretary of state issued a sanctions warning and reiterated US President Donald Trump's stance that no nation should help Iran evade sanctions.
"No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we're going to have to sanction them too," Rubio said.
Foreign Minister S Jaishankar arrives in Poland, next stop Ukraine
India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has reached the Polish capital of Warsaw as he kickstarts an official visit to Poland and Ukraine on Thursday.

Jaishankar's trip to Poland comes amid speculation about a visit by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to India.
Earlier in August, Poland's top envoy to India said that Tusk's visit, which would be his third to New Delhi, would send a strong signal for cooperation.
There is yet to be formal confirmation of Tusk's India tour.
The visit also reflects broader efforts by New Delhi to deepen engagement with Central and Eastern European partners.
Following the Poland leg of his tour, Jaishankar will head to Ukraine.
Jaishankar's Ukraine visit comes after key Modi-Putin meeting
The Ukraine leg of Jaishankar's tour comes days after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday. During the meeting, Modi urged an end to the war in Ukraine.
Ahead of Jaishankar's arrival in Kyiv, Ukraine's First Deputy Head of the Office of the President, Sergiy Kyslytsya, said on Tuesday that he had met India's Ambassador to Ukraine, Anjani Kumar, to discuss Kyiv-New Delhi ties and India's role in efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Kyslytsya said he discussed with Kumar Modi's message to Putin in Bishkek, in which the Indian prime minister urged a "move from endless war to end of war" in Ukraine.
"We look forward to continued dialogue with India and to translating this shared interest in peace into concrete steps," Kyslytsya added.

BERLIN, September 3. /TASS/. The German government intends to intensify cooperation with Kiev through its intelligence services and is considering assisting Ukraine in obtaining the coordinates of potential targets in Russia, Der Spiegel reports, citing its own sources.
The magazine recalled that, following the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport, Berlin decided to step up military support for Kiev. "Thousands of attack drones are to be delivered, along with IRIS-T air defense missiles as early as September," Der Spiegel reported. According to government sources cited by the magazine, Berlin also plans to "intensify cooperation between the intelligence services" of Germany and Ukraine.
Der Spiegel noted that such cooperation "could have serious consequences," as the German government is considering helping Ukraine collect target coordinates in the future.
On September 1, the German government officially blamed Russia for the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. Berlin also announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, the termination of the Russian House’s activities in Berlin, and other measures.
The Russian embassy in Berlin described the incident as a hastily concocted provocation, saying it "serves exclusively the goals of Kiev and the militaristic wing of the European political class." Russia’s ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev categorically rejected Berlin’s accusations against Moscow, calling them unsubstantiated and absurd.

Estonia's second quarter average monthly wage up to €2,243

Estonia's second quarter average monthly wage up to €2,243
Estonia's average monthly gross wage rose 5.5 percent on year to €2,243 in the second quarter of 2026, Statistics Estonia said Thursday.
Average wages increased in every county last quarter, though growth varied significantly by region, said Krista Vaikmets, a leading analyst at the agency.
"The increase in average gross wages was the biggest in Ida-Viru County at 8% and Hiiu County at 7 percent, and somewhat more modest in Põlva, Jõgeva and Valga counties, where the rise in wages was around 4 percent," said Vaikmets.
Harju County had the highest average monthly wage at €2,488, followed by Tartu County at €2,285. Wages rose 5 percent in both counties.
In Tallinn, the average gross wage reached €2,611, up 5.3 percent on year from €2,479.
Information and communication still highest-paying sector
Information and communication remained the highest-paying economic activity in the second quarter, with average gross wages of €3,837. However, wage growth in the sector slowed to 3.6 percent.
Wages in electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply, meanwhile, jumped 19.6 percent to €3,783. Vaikmets said the sharp increase partly reflected a low reference base, as wages in the sector grew just 0.8 percent a year earlier, as well as restructuring in the energy sector.
The lowest average wages were again recorded in accommodation and food services, at €1,389, followed by other service activities at €1,430. Wages in both sectors grew about 4 percent on year.
Among other major sectors, average wages rose 6 percent in manufacturing, 5.7 percent in trade and 5.1 percent in construction.
Median wage up to €1,840
According to Statistics Estonia figures, there were 588,710 registered employees nationwide in the second quarter of 2026, down 5,183 from the same quarter last year.
Manufacturing accounted for the largest share with 101,085 workers, or 17 percent of all employees, followed by wholesale and retail trade (including automotive repair), education, and human health and social work.
Compared with the first quarter, employee numbers were up by 8,611. Vaikmets attributed part of the increase to seasonal hiring.
Estonia's second quarter median gross wage rose 6.1 percent on year to €1,840.
"The trends for median wages are similar to the trends for average gross wages both by county and by economic activity," Vaikmets added.

Denmark’s looming leadership void
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:05:16 UTC
17:05:16 KST

On November 10, 1982, Soviet state television interrupted its programming to play Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake. Viewers had learned to recognize the cue: somewhere in the Kremlin, another old man had died.
It was Leonid Brezhnev, General Secretary for eighteen years, dead at 75. His successor lasted fifteen months before he too was gone. The man after him made it barely a year. Three state funerals, three general secretaries, in under three years. By 1981, the average age of the men running the Soviet Union was 69 – thirteen years older than Ronald Reagan’s own cabinet. It took that string of deaths, and the arrival of a 54-year-old outsider named Mikhail Gorbachev, before the pattern finally broke.
It’s tempting to file that away as a curiosity of late-Soviet dysfunction. It’s less comfortable to notice that a quieter, more mundane version of the same pattern is now playing out in one of the world’s most functional economies: Denmark.
In 2024, more than one in three Danish managers – approximately 35.8% – were aged 55 or above.1 A decade earlier, in 2014, that figure was 26.7%. That’s a 9.1 percentage-point rise in ten years, and with roughly 125,000 managers in Denmark, it works out to about 44,800 people approaching retirement in a single leadership generation. With Denmark’s retirement age at 67, most of these 44,800 managers will leave the workforce within the next decade – not gradually, but as a single, unusually large cohort retiring at roughly the same time.
The natural question is whether this is just what happens to any aging population – a Nordic story, not a Danish one. So I turned to Eurostat’s harmonized labor force data, which lets managers across ten Northern European countries be compared using the same occupational classification, the same age band (55–64), and the same methodology.
The results say otherwise: Denmark’s trend still holds even under this stricter, internationally comparable measure – the sharpest rise of the ten countries screened.2 Norway and Germany also rose, but by less. Sweden, Ireland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Estonia, and Finland all rose only modestly. And Iceland – a much smaller Nordic welfare state, but one facing the same demographic and economic pressures – went the other way entirely: its share of managers aged 55–64 fell, from 28.2% to 22.8%.
It would be easy to explain this away with a simple story: Danes are just retiring later, so of course more managers are staying on past 55. And there’s something to that – Denmark’s early-retirement age has climbed from 60 to 64 since 2014, and the state pension age from 65 to 67, part of a reform that ties retirement age to life expectancy, automatically rising as Danes live longer. Iceland’s retirement age, by contrast, has stayed flat at 67 for years, with no such escalator built in – so if rising retirement ages were the whole story, Denmark and Iceland should never have been comparable to begin with. But when I looked closer, the story didn’t hold up as neatly. That same rise in effective retirement age has been roughly three times steeper for less-educated workers than for university-educated professionals – and managers overwhelmingly fall into the latter group.3 If anything, managers are the workers least affected by the reform, yet they’re the group whose numbers shifted the most. Something else is doing the real work here.
While the full answer is subject to further inquiry, the best place to start looking is a handful of sectors.1 In the metal industry, the share of managers 55 and older rose from 28.6% to 48.2% in ten years – among the steepest increases anywhere in the Danish economy. Textiles, electrical equipment, and food and beverage manufacturing all rose nearly as sharply. Education is the one clear exception: its share of older managers actually fell over the same period, the only sector in the Danish data to get younger. Whatever is driving the leadership void, it is concentrated in specific corners of the economy.
Denmark built its prosperity on being able to renew itself – a small country punching above its weight through the quality of its institutions and the people running them. If more than a third of its managers are now over 55, and its closest Nordic peer is trending the opposite way, that gap deserves more attention than it’s gotten so far. Perhaps it’s time to take a closer look at our Nordic neighbor, and ask what it is doing differently.
Ebba Hansen is a Copenhagen-based Advisor at Voluntas, where she advises on leadership strategy and executive succession, and former Head of Office at Voluntas India in Mumbai. She is currently writing a book on the global leadership succession crisis.
- Analysis based on data from Statistics Denmark, table KAS301, including the industry-level breakdown by age.
- Analysis based on Eurostat’s EU Labour Force Survey (lfsa_egais), harmonised across countries by occupation, age band, and year.
- Denmark’s retirement-age reforms stem from a 2011 law tied to the 2006 “velfærdsaftale,” which indexes retirement age to life expectancy. The finding on the uneven effect by education level is based on analysis by Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd (AE), a Danish economic think tank.
The author: Ebba Hansen is a Copenhagen-based Advisor at Voluntas, where she advises on leadership strategy and executive succession, and previously spent three years as Head of Office at Voluntas India in Mumbai. She holds an MPhil from the University of Oxford and an MA from the University of Aberdeen. This piece draws on research for a book she is currently writing on the global leadership succession crisis.

Badenoch condemns Reform UK's 'authoritarian' press bans, saying Farage shouldn't be MP if he can't handle scrutiny
Q: [From Emilio Casalicchio from Politico] Reform UK have banned seven reporters from their conference, including the one who revealed Nigel Farage got a £5m donation he did not declare. What do you think of that in terms of free speech? And would you do something like that?
Badenoch replied:
Absolutely not … Conservatives believe in free speech, where people are welcome to criticise us as much as they like.
If you look at Nigel Farage’s attacks on the press, some of them very personal … you look at the things that Zia Yusuf says about journalists constantly, you know what kind of government they would be – authoritarian and using state power to pursue opponents. [That is] what they’ve effectively been threatening.
We do not do that. It’s absolutely not something that we believe in. We believe in free speech. We believe in a free press. And yes, of course, that might be painful for us as politicians, but public scrutiny is part of the gig.
If Nigel Farage can’t handle difficult questions about his dodgy £5m, then he shouldn’t be a politician.
But that comes with, working as an MP and standing to be leader of the country.
Badenoch has not always been comfortable with press scrutiny herself. As a minister in the last government, she was criticised for her aggressive response to journalists reporting on her. But as Conservative leader she has been more tolerant of criticism, and while the Tories don’t exactly welcome negative press coverage, they are more pro-media than Reform UK.

Care workers, chefs and others in danger of losing their migration status under post-Brexit rules if they leave an exploitative employer will be helped by new visa changes, the Home Office says. Chris Osuh has the story.

Badenoch claims Tories don't give peerages to people based on donations
Q: Nigel Farage said in a BBC interview yesterday that he would not give peerages to people donating to Reform UK. Is that a policy that you will follow?
Badenoch replied:
We don’t give people peerages based on donations, or government contracts. I am someone who believes in meritocracy.
We give people peerages because we think they’re going to do a good job.
You look at the peerages that I have given: Gen Sir Patrick Sanders, the former head of the British Army, he has joined our benches. We have people that are serious and that are credible joining conservative benches.
Who did Keir Starmer put in? That Matthew Doyle guy and another person whose credentials turned out to be out to be completely fake.
So I’m not worried about the people who I’m putting in the House of Lords.
As Badenoch delivered this answer, some journalists reacted with astonishment. While Badenoch has tended to favour her ideological allies when nominating people for the Lords, there is a very long history of major donors to the Conservative party getting peerages. Badenoch says UK must prepare for war if it wants to ensure peace

Q: [From Jonathan Walker from the Express] Are you ready to lead the country into war if necessary?
Badenoch replied:
If you want a peace, you have to prepare for war. And I believe that strong countries don’t get attacked. It’s countries that look weak that get attacked.

Kemi Badenoch is about to give her speech on defence spending. These are from Peter Walker, who is at the venue.
I’m in the magnificent if slightly bonkers Scotland House London to hear Kemi Badenoch set out how she would pay for more defence spending - with a lot of the money coming from cuts to housing benefit. You’d think that might bring some knock-on cost repercussions, but let’s see what she says.
One plan would be to cut Local Housing Allowance rates, used to calculate housing benefit for private tenants. These have already been frozen since 2024 and don’t cover the rent for the vast majority of homes.
Last month the Tories announced a Reform-style plan to remove all non-UK nationals from social housing, something that you’d think would also add to emergency accommodation costs - not to mention risking a Windrush part two.
As with all Badenoch’s events in central London it’s filled with well-heeled Westminster Tories. My guess is very few people here are struggling financially. And they will be cheering a plan to fund defence in part by cuts to the very poorest in society. It’s all a bit unsettling.
Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, is introducing Badenoch now.
This is from the Labour MP Emily Thornberry, who represents Islington South and Finsbury, on Zack Polanski standing in Holborn and St Pancras, which is next to her constituency.
Polanski was a Lib Dem activist before he left and joined the Green party in 2017. His departure came after he failed to be selected as the Lib Dem candidate for the Richmond Park byelection. But he says he left the party over policy, and not because of the selection decision.

Middle East’s biggest shipping hub at risk amid Hormuz blockade — FT

LONDON, September 3. /TASS/. Jebel Ali, the largest shipping hub in the Middle East, has come under its most serious strain in decades amid the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times (FT) reported.
According to the British newspaper, in the early weeks of the conflict around Iran, shipping through the port that has driven Dubai’s transformation into one of the world’s great commercial hubs declined more than 90%. Volumes plunged as 17 vessels a day on the average transited in the week to August 28, compared to 135 a day before the United States launched the war on Iran, the FT wrote.
The port and free-trade zone alone is responsible for more than a fifth of the emirate’s GDP. Last year, Jebel Ali accounted for 30% of the revenues of state-owned DP World, the newspaper added.
The UAE is looking for alternatives beyond the Hormuz Strait. DP World is planning to build two port terminals in Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman coast. However, experts doubt those could replicate the system built around Jebel Ali as its advantage includes not only port capacity but also the network of businesses and transport links, the newspaper argued. "Dubai as we know it would not exist without Jebel Ali," the FT quoted Jim Krane, a fellow at Rice University in Texas, as saying.

U.S. Army taps AZAK’s wheel-centric robot for fielding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:01:01 UTC
17:01:01 KST

- AZAK signed an Other Transaction Agreement with the Army's G-TEAD directorate after soldiers tested its wheel-centric unmanned ground vehicle.
- The company has demonstrated a 227 kg robot towing a 24,040 kg Army truck, more than 100 times its own weight.
Denver-based robotics company AZAK has signed an Other Transaction Agreement with the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, the company said in a statement. AZAK said it is one of the first companies selected for the program directly by soldiers who tested the system in the field.
G-TEAD, established in late 2025, is an Army directorate built to move new technology from demonstration to fielded units in as little as 180 days, using Other Transaction Agreements and soldier-led evaluations instead of the service’s traditional acquisition process. The directorate has already fielded counter-drone systems including the Merops interceptor, built by Perennial Autonomy, and the FD One quadcopter, according to prior reporting.
AZAK builds unmanned ground vehicles around a wheel-centric, chassis-free design. Each wheel functions as a self-contained power unit, housing the motor, motor controller, gearbox, control electronics, battery management system and battery. AZAK CEO Ben Meager has said the design keeps those components below the wheel’s center point, giving the vehicle a low center of gravity and allowing it to climb obstacles rather than route around them.
The Army evaluated AZAK’s platform through 2025 at events including the xTechOverwatch competition and a rotation at the National Training Center. Army and special operations units have looked at the system for resupply runs, casualty evacuation, counter-drone payloads and drone-launch platforms, the company has said.
In a demonstration released in July, AZAK showed a 227 kg (500 pound) robot towing a 24,040 kg (53,000 pound) Palletized Load System truck, plus an additional 454 kg (1,000 pounds) of ammunition, a combined load more than 100 times the robot’s own weight.
AZAK said the new OTA will let the mobility systems it has been testing move into the field on G-TEAD’s timeline. The company did not disclose the contract’s value, the number of systems involved, or a delivery schedule.
G-TEAD Director Col. Christopher Hill has said the directorate is built to compress that kind of transition. In one case involving a counter-drone system in Europe, Hill has said the Army went from identifying the operational need to a signed contract with industry in about 148 days.
AZAK’s demonstrations have centered on the S26 wheel, first shown publicly at DSEI 2025. Meager has said each wheel carries all the components needed to operate independently, letting the company scale a vehicle’s torque by adding wheels rather than redesigning a drivetrain. The company has said this allows the same wheel system to be configured into different vehicle types without a full redesign.

Global South must ensure AI sovereignty – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:59:23 UTC
16:59:23 KST

Global South must ensure AI sovereignty – expert
The Global South cannot merely remain consumers of artificial intelligence but should also author the norms governing the technology, to avoid it being used against their sovereignty and security, an Indian cyber and AI law expert has said.
China, India, and Russia will become integral to this norm-making process, Pavan Duggal told RT on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
The Global South can no longer be a mere spectator, but must be “an actual author of the norms for AI before they get crystallized,” Duggal told the gathering on Wednesday. He added that China, India, and Russia represent the collective thought leadership and vision of the Global South and will play a major role in creating the governance framework for AI.
Duggal said that a country’s sovereignty now extends beyond its traditional territorial boundaries and encompasses cyberspace and emerging technologies such as AI. Countries need to create stricter laws for providers of AI services anywhere in the world, as long as the services are delivered within their respective territories.
Nations of the Global South also have to ensure that their data does not fall into other countries’ hands, so it is not used to “prejudicially impact their sovereignty, security, and integrity.”
“We don’t want to be just consumers of AI services provided by someone else and governed by their respective norms,” he told RT.
Duggal’s arguments come at a time when emerging economies are taking a harder look at how to protect their security and economic interests in a turbulent world. A meeting of the national security advisers of the BRICS group in July took a wider view of the security challenges they face, including cybersecurity and emerging technologies that could be exploited by extremist organizations.
Security cooperation is also expected to remain on top of the agenda for the BRICS summit later this month in India.
It is a strategic requirement of sovereign countries that AI must ultimately be accountable, Duggal said. However, he said existing legal frameworks are not adequate to deal with these emerging technologies, because they were drafted keeping in mind the acts of a human versus another human.
Current AI regulations across countries focus on the risks of the technology but don’t deal with making it accountable, he added.
Duggal said countries like India are beginning to see a new trend of “cognitive colonialism,” where people are ready to become “cognitive slaves” of big tech companies so long as their day-to-day work is done by AI.

The numbers behind China's pharma rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:58:35 UTC
16:58:35 KST

The numbers behind China’s pharma rise
For decades, China was known for producing cheap copycat drugs and ingredients for large pharmaceutical firms. But it now has its own cutting-edge drug industry, creating opportunities and competition for big pharma players like Swiss firms Roche and Novartis.
China’s biopharmaceutical industry has long been characterised by its fast-follower nature and large-scale manufacturing base – that is, replicating proven therapies, producing generic medicines at scale, and supplying lower-margin inputs into global pharmaceutical supply chains.
Innovation was predominantly driven by US and European firms. But this has changed in the last decade. Drugs discovered by Chinese companies, such as cancer therapy ivonescimab are beatingExternal link Western-developed blockbusters in head-to-head trials. Others like blood cancer treatment zanubrutinib (Brukinsa) developed by BeOne Medicines are achieving annual sales in the single-digit billions.
More
China’s pharma companies turn to Europe for growth
“In just three years, China’s biopharmaceutical industry rose from near irrelevance to dominance,” a US congressional commission reportExternal link on the future of US-China biotechnology competition noted last year.
How did China evolve into a global pharmaceutical player and where is the world’s second-largest economy making its mark on the industry? We looked at the data.
$1.03 trillion – Gross Domestic Expenditure on R&D
That’s how much China spent on research and development in 2024 when adjusted for purchasing power parity – edging out the US for the first time, which spent $1.01 trillion (CHF820 billion), accordingExternal link to the OECD. China’s spending was 12.3% more than the previous year.
Massive investment in research and development over the last decade has paid off in both quantity and quality of scientific output. China publishes more papers in the world’s most prestigious scientific journals than other countries, according to the Nature IndexExternal link.
It also has a steady supply of science and technology graduates from top-tier domestic universities and has lured back many foreign-trained Chinese scientists with the help of financial incentives.
Biotech has been a major beneficiary of this scientific boost. The Chinese government has called out biotech as a priority sector for investment to slash import dependence and compete globally.
It has poured billions into drug manufacturing and innovation parks and clusters to. It has also used state-guided venture funds to pull in private and local government investment.
“The government put in place policies 15-20 years ago to reshape the environment for biotechs,” said Celia Deng, president of consulting firm SAI-med in Beijing. “They realised that producing cheap generics isn’t a long-term strategy and that they need to do real innovation.”
Starting in 2015, the country ushered in major regulatory reforms to align with international quality standards, speed up clinical trials and drug approvals, and encourage biotech start-ups.
31% – China’s share of drug pipeline
China’s share of the global drug development pipeline has risen from 18% in 2021 to 31% at the start of 2026, according to consulting firm CitelineExternal link.
China’s growing importance in the pipeline of new drugs is most pronounced in early-stage trials (up to phase 2). In 2015, only 8% of early-stage drug development programmes originated in China compared to 48% in the US, according to a studyExternal link led by researchers at Georgetown University. By 2024, China’s share soared to 32% and the US share fell to 37%. In the third quarter of 2025, China even surpassed the US.
Although many of these trials are run by Chinese companies, “more Western biotechs are considering doing trials in China because they can get early-stage data for much less money”, said Dusan Kladar, co-founder of advisory firm Vision Lifesciences.
In cancer, China is remaking the treatment landscape. According to GlobalData’s Clinical Trials IntelligenceExternal link, China was responsible for 25% of global oncology trials with a start date in 2016, rising to 31% by 2018. By 2025, this share surged to 55%. The US, which represented 27% of global oncology trials in 2016 and 26% in 2018, declined to 14% by 2025.
One key reason for China’s emergence is its ability to launch trials faster and cheaper than anywhere else. This is thanks to expedited regulatory processes along with many trial sites and a large patient population to draw from for trials.
Consulting firm McKinseyExternal link estimates patient enrolment for clinical trials in China is two to five times faster, depending on the therapy type.
More
Six charts show challenges facing Swiss pharmaceutical industry
19% – China’s share of global biopharma companies
Some 19% of all research-based biopharma firms are now headquartered China, compared with 13% in 2023, according to CitelineExternal link. The share of companies from European countries, including Switzerland, had fallen to 17% in January 2026, compared with 25% three years ago.
More Chinese companies rival Western companies when it comes to research and development. Hengrui Pharmaceuticals has at least 178 drugs in development, giving it the 12th-largest pipeline of any pharma company, according to Citeline. Swiss pharma giant Roche had the largest pipeline of any company with 262 drugs under development.
In 2026, two Chinese drug companies – Hengrui, and BeOne Medicines (formerly BeiGene) – also ranked among the top 30 pharmaceutical companies for innovation in the UK-based boutique consultancy IDEA pharma’s Innovation and Invention IndexExternal link. BeOne, which was founded in Beijing and now has its global headquarters in Basel, has three US FDA-approved products on the market.
The surge in Chinese pharma firms in the last few years is in part due to an influx of financing. Between 2019 and 2024, Chinese biopharmaExternal link firms attracted $26 billion in private equity and venture capital. More than 80 went public (predominantly Hong Kong and Shanghai’s STAR Market), according to McKinsey.
This was thanks to a rule change in 2018 that allowed pre-revenue biotechs to list on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Over 265 biotech and healthcare companies are now listedExternal link on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange with a combined market cap currently exceeding HK$5 trillion (CHF520 billion).
$137 billion – the value of out-licensing deals
In 2025, Chinese firms struck out-licensing deals with global pharma firms worth potentially $137 billion, according to data provider PharmCube and ReutersExternal link. That’s more than double the amount ($52 billion) in 2024 and nearly a tenfold increase on 2021’s total of $13.9 billion. The total number of deals also soared from ten in 2016 to 186 in 2025.
Prior to 2020, most Chinese pharma licensing deals, which grant a company rights to produce or sell a drug for a fee, were of global pharma firms looking for a local partner to sell their drugs in the Chinese market.
But the tide has turned. Now Western firms are in-licensing innovation from China to refill pipelines as a record number of drugs go off patent in the next decade and Chinese companies seek commercial opportunities abroad.
In 2024, major pharmaceutical companies in-licensed 31% of their innovative pipeline assets from China, according to a report by investment bankExternal link Stifel. By deal countExternal link, roughly half of all large pharma licence deals in the first half of 2026 were sourced from China.
“Fifteen years ago, Chinese biotechs were copying successful projects from the West,” said Kladar. “But now you can see more innovation coming out of China that you can’t find anywhere else.”
Individual deal size has also been on the rise. This year, UK-based AstraZeneca signed a deal with CSPC Pharmaceutical Group in Hebei province for several obesity drug candidates. The deal is worth up to $18.5 billion, one of the largest this year.
28.7% – the share of drugs launched in China before the rest of the world
The share of drugs launched first in China grew from 3.3% in 2004 to 28.7% in 2024, according to a studyExternal link by the US-based National Health Council. Over that same period the share of first launches in the US fell from 45.9% to 37.8% and in Europe from 26.2% to 8.5%.
Chinese companies are a growing source of global first launches. In 2024, 31% of first launches were developed by US-headquartered companies, 20.7% by European companies, and 26.2% by Chinese companies. This is in stark contrast to 2004 when only 1.7% of drugs that had a first launch were traced back to Chinese firms.
China’s growing attractiveness for first launches is due to streamlined approval and reimbursement processes as the government seeks to bring more innovative drugs to Chinese patients
In June, China approvedExternal link the world’s first solid tumour CAR-T therapy, which was developed by Shanghai-based CARsgen Therapeutics. Up to now the technology, which engineers a patient’s own T cells to fight cancer, has been used only for blood cancers.
China has expanded commercial health insurance coverage for innovative drugs while extracting steep price concessions from drug companies to get included on the list. The total numberExternal link of Western and Chinese patented medicines on the list has grown from 1,535 in 2000 to 3,253 in 2025.

In Brief
- The Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion was due to report on 14 December.
- It will now report on 18 December, following concerns from the Jewish community.
The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has had its deadline extended by four days so that it does not clash with the anniversary of the Bondi Massacre.
The months-long royal commission was slated to hand down its final report on 14 December, the first anniversary of the mass shooting that left 15 people dead. The commission will now report on 18 December.
In a statement, commissioner Virginia Bell AC SC said she requested the extension from the federal government so that her final report did "not overshadow the first anniversary of the Bondi Chanukah attack".
"The 14th of December will be a solemn occasion marked by memorials," the statement said.
"I am aware of concern within the Jewish community that delivery of the report on the anniversary would be a distraction. I welcome this short extension."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Established on 9 January, the royal commission heard evidence from 348 witnesses over 62 days of hearings in Sydney and Melbourne.
Bell is currently preparing her final report, which will examine this evidence alongside more than 20,000 public submissions.
On 26 August, the final day of public hearings, Bell told the commission her focus had been on the lives of ordinary Jewish Australians.
"The Bondi Chanukah attack came after more than two years of a marked increase in antisemitism throughout Australia," she said.
"Laying out the picture of the lived experience of antisemitism is a critical part of any steps to combat that phenomenon."
She also flagged that she would seek the four-day extension.
An interim report was released on 30 April and made 14 recommendations to strengthen counterterrorism responses.

Taylor's claim teachers push 'political agenda' prompts backlash
Unknown

2026-09-03
07:55:06 UTC

Teachers hit back at Nationals claim about 'anti-boy' ideology in schools
In short:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says teachers are pushing political agendas to students, while his counterpart rallied against anti-boy ideology in the classroom.
A teachers' union has labelled the remarks "ignorant".
What's next?
It remains unclear how the government intends to give Australians more control over their content amid pressure to back an algorithm opt-in model.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says teachers are pushing agendas in the classroom, while his Nationals counterpart believes the school curriculum is teaching "anti-boy" ideology.
The comments have sparked a backlash from teachers, who labelled the views "fundamentally incorrect".
Nationals leader Matt Canavan rallied against the "lecturing" of young men in schools, alleging that a state-funded Respectful Relationships curriculum could be turning them to harmful online content.
He said the program provided opportunity for "young boys to reflect on their male privilege and power", and while well-intentioned, could be having an adverse effect.
"I think this anti-boy ideology has no place in our schools," he told reporters on Thursday.
"They have counter-productive results and then drive young boys to toxic voices online because they're looking for someone to provide them with respect and support."
The Respectful Relationships national framework, established to teach both primary and secondary students about respectful relationships, gender equality and consent, does not mention male privilege.
Its inclusivity outcome instructs teachers to help students, without specifying gender, "to consider how their identities and experiences — including those related to power and inequality — affect their relationships and lives, in ways that suit their age and development".
It also sets out to help "boys and young men to explore concepts of masculinity in healthy ways".
The debate was initially stirred up on Wednesday, when Senator Canavan blamed the "feminisation" of the curriculum for driving young men towards "manosphere" content online.
He said programs like Respectful Relationships were "essentially a recruitment ground for Andrew Tate", a self-proclaimed misogynist with a large online following.
Teacher fury over 'agenda push' remarks
Asked about Senator Canavan's comments on Thursday, Liberal leader Angus Taylor pushed back against the "politicisation" of the curriculum by teachers.
"The idea that we have a balanced curriculum being run at the moment, that there are not agendas being run by some teachers, I think is wrong," he told the ABC.
"We do see those agendas being run."
Mr Taylor insisted teaching consent was important, while calling for a "degree of balance".
The Australian Education Union has fired back at the criticisms, labelling them a "fundamentally incorrect portrayal" of the education system.
"These comments are either a malevolent mischaracterisation of Australia's education system for political gain, or a display of complete ignorance of how the teaching profession operates," the union said in a statement.
The teachers' union said the remarks by Senator Canavan, Mr Taylor and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who claims schools are "brainwashing students", further fueled the "aggression and disrespect" towards teachers, which was already on the rise.
Last week, a national survey of 2,600 teachers, conducted by Monash University, found that 78 per cent had observed or experienced sexism or misogyny in school.
One in three teachers said that the presence of gendered violence made them "occasionally" consider leaving the profession.
The report's author, Stephanie Wescott, said for many teachers, schools had become "unbearably hostile places to work, with levels of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment that have made their jobs untenable".
A separate government-funded study into misogyny and youth radicalisation found one in three teenage boys express "misogynistic attitudes, mistrust of women and a belief in traditional gender roles".
Almost a quarter of generation Z males believed feminism "should be resisted with violence if necessary".
Call for more male teachers
While Senator Canavan did not offer any alternatives for respectful relationship and consent education on Thursday, he doubled down on a call for more male teachers.
"Maybe we should look at getting more male teachers in. That used to be an agenda, I don't know what's happened to that. But maybe we should have more male role models in schools," he told Nine.
"I just know young boys often feel that they don't get any kind of instruction, leadership. They're not cherished there."
Currently, only one in four teachers are male.
While Education Minister Jason Clare agreed that students would benefit from more male teachers, he said ultimately, it was a discussion about respect.
"Teaching boys to respect girls isn't woke, it's common decency," he told reporters.
Mr Clare said the focus should not be on teachers, who he labelled "heroes".
“The bad guys here are the big tech companies, they're the ones poisoning our kids with algorithms that are shovelling shit into their heads."
On Wednesday, sexual consent advocate Chanel Contos called on the government to mandate an opt-in model for social media algorithms, to allow teenagers to avoid harmful messaging including manosphere content.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has flagged support for giving Australians more control over their online content but has stopped short of backing the algorithm opt-in model proposed by Ms Contos.

At the heart of the project is a deeply symbolic musical transformation: popular songs originally written in a minor key will be performed in a major key. The “Hits with a 1% Change” campaign will continue with two more musical surprises, which will be unveiled in the coming weeks.
