LeVanta Tech shows off its unusual HALIA drone at sea test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:53:51 UTC
16:53:51 KST

- LeVanta Tech demonstrated its unusually shaped HALIA float-and-fly drone with partner STR at ANTX Coastal Trident.
- HALIA can land on the open ocean, float for weeks, then relaunch at speeds LeVanta Tech has reported above 100 knots.
LeVanta Tech said it demonstrated its HALIA unmanned system at ANTX Coastal Trident last month, showing how the platform can link air, surface, subsea and seabed assets over long distances.
Photos of HALIA show an unusual design. The drone sits low in the water with a dark, angular hull riding hull-down, mostly submerged. Two cylindrical engine pods sit side by side on top of the fuselage, feeding what appear to be ducted fans, while swept white wings and twin tail fins jut out near the back, just clear of the waterline. A small sensor mast pokes up from one wing root. Little about the shape resembles a conventional aircraft or boat.
HALIA is a “float-and-fly” drone: it flies to a location, lands directly on the open ocean, and can sit there for weeks in a low-power floating mode before relaunching to reposition or leave the area, according to LeVanta Tech, which profiled the company in September 2025. The company said HALIA does not require a dedicated ship or fixed infrastructure to operate, since it can move between the air and water on its own.
At Coastal Trident, LeVanta Tech worked with STR, a defense technology firm with undersea systems and sensor work based near Boston, to demonstrate a communications architecture connecting air, surface, subsea and seabed systems. STR provided what the companies called a “rapidly repositionable” command-and-control air-water gateway, using what the companies described as high technology readiness level components to deliver over-the-horizon, real-time command-and-control links to subsea and seabed systems.
ANTX Coastal Trident is an annual exercise run by the Naval Surface Warfare Center Port Hueneme Division at the Port of Hueneme, California, bringing together Navy, other government agencies, academia and industry to test maritime and port security technology in an operational setting.
LeVanta Tech, founded in 2023, started out building real-time maritime monitoring tools for the offshore wind industry before shifting to a defense-first focus. The company’s leadership includes CEO Kelly Echols, an engineer and patent attorney by background; Chief Aviation Officer Jon Smith, a former P-3C Orion instructor pilot and Navy unmanned aircraft test project manager; and CTO Johnny Doo, who has more than 40 years in aircraft and hovercraft development, according to Defense Tech Signals.
The company was one of six finalists selected from 260 applicants for the 2024 Gulf Blue Navigator accelerator. A demonstration that year drew interest from the Air Force, which led to a $1.8 million Direct-to-Phase II Small Business Innovation Research award. The Air Force Research Laboratory followed with a Phase II SBIR contract worth $1.76 million running through December 2026, covering a project titled “Floating and Loitering Ocean Advanced Technology Sensing,” according to federal contract records cited by Defense Tech Signals. LeVanta Tech has also raised more than $1.1 million in early funding, including an $800,000 credit investment from Leonid Capital Partners in April 2025.
LeVanta Tech is developing HALIA in two configurations: a battery-electric version for tactical missions and a hybrid-electric version built for longer range. Both are designed to scale into larger platforms, the company has said. HALIA uses variable buoyancy combined with a hovercraft-assisted launch and recovery system, intended to let it take off and land in rough seas. Its top speed has been reported at more than 100 knots (185 km/h), with loiter times of weeks in its powered-down floating mode.
The platform carries a modular payload bay that LeVanta Tech says can support intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sensors, electronic warfare packages, kinetic payloads and communications equipment, feeding into wider command-and-control networks. The distinctive hull shape and twin engine pods are part of what LeVanta Tech describes as a design built specifically for surviving repeated transitions between air and water, rather than adapted from an existing aircraft or boat.

Germany Identifies Russian-Backed Suspects in Leipzig Drone Sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:52:11 UTC
16:52:11 KST

- Category
- World
Germany Identifies Russian-Backed Suspects in Leipzig Drone Sabotage
German law enforcement agencies have identified two suspects involved in an attempted FPV drone sabotage operation at Leipzig Airport, according to Bild.
The incident took place on August 5, when explosive-laden drones were discovered near four Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators determined that the planned attack was carried out by a native of Russia holding a Latvian passport and a Belarusian citizen who also holds Russian citizenship. Authorities are currently searching for at least four individuals whose movements and phone numbers were tracked using cell tower location data.
German Federal Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt stated that Russia directly organized the attack, with the perpetrators acting on instructions from Russian intelligence services.
The Federal Criminal Police Office suspects that more unmanned aerial vehicles may have been deployed than initially thought, as remnants of three devices have been recovered so far.
The first suspect, a Russian native, acted as a logistical coordinator and instructor while maintaining direct ties to Russian intelligence. He arrived in Germany at the end of July via Berlin Brandenburg Airport, traveled toward Leipzig in a rental vehicle, and departed the country by plane two days before the attack was executed. The second suspect, a citizen of Belarus, was identified through DNA evidence left at the scene.
Traces of his genetic material were recovered directly from one of the drones, from the inner side of a tin can containing explosives, and from a signal amplifier antenna mounted on a tree near the airfield. Matching these genetic traces against European databases revealed prior records in Lithuania and Finland, where the individual had previously been prosecuted for other offenses.
He entered the Schengen zone using an Italian tourist visa issued in Minsk in late April. The sabotage attempt unfolded on the night of August 5, when a shuttle bus driver spotted the first explosive drone at 00:42 near four Ukrainian An-124 heavy transport aircraft.
Following the discovery of a second device, air traffic over the airport was completely suspended. During the airspace closure at 01:03, a inbound DHL cargo plane was forced to abort its landing approach and collided with another flying object, likely a second drone, at an altitude of 400 meters. A third drone was discovered on August 14 in a field in the municipality of Kabelsketal, bordering the western side of the airport.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the drone incident at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport as an attack carried out by Russian intelligence operatives using military-grade materials on European Union territory.
Speaking in Brussels ahead of a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, von der Leyen stated that the EU would not tolerate such actions and expressed full solidarity with Germany. She noted that if Russia had intended the incident to make European countries reconsider their support for Ukraine, it had instead strengthened their determination to continue backing Kyiv.
Von der Leyen characterized the sabotage operation as a new escalation on EU territory directly linked to Moscow, forming part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous hybrid activities. Consequently, she pledged that the EU would maintain and intensify pressure on Russia until it ended its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, emphasizing that the bloc remained prepared to introduce additional sanctions and close existing loopholes.

With an eye on Russia, Finland runs Europe's largest civil defence exercise since WWII
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:51:51 UTC
16:51:51 KST

Western officials say Russia is carrying out a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe that has involved fires, attacking power stations and sending drones into EU airspace.
In a civil defence shelter cut into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation levels as they take part in an exercise to turn a cave into a place of safety for thousands of people.
Inside, in what is normally a sports hall, hundreds of people are sleeping overnight on camp beds.
More than 2,000 people including volunteers and students are taking part in the biggest civil defence exercise in Europe since the end of World War II.
In the scenario, critical infrastructure in the central Finnish city of Kuopio, including power and water, has been disrupted by cyberattacks and there’s the threat of missile strikes from Finland’s neighbour, Russia.
The goal is for local authorities and ordinary people to rehearse what they would do if they came under attack for real.
But while underground bunkers and shelters may offer some protection from missiles, they are no defence against the campaign of sabotage and disruption that Western officials say Russia is carrying out across Europe.
That has involved starting fires, attacking water facilities and power stations and sending drones on sabotage operations into European Union airspace.
Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 1,300 kilometres from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle.
In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Until then, Finns were prepared to defend themselves against Russia largely alone.
Lessons from Ukraine
Finland’s defence, said retired Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, relies not only on the military but on the “mindset” of ordinary Finns who are ready to take responsibility for their country’s security.
Muhonen, who organised the exercise in Kuopio, said that comes partly from the system of conscription which continued in Finland, even after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Not everyone is happy about doing national service but “it’s our duty to serve and protect this country like people have before us. That’s why we have our independence,” said Jyry Pietikainen, 23, a conscript who was taught how to run the Kuopio shelter overnight.
Finland also needs to learn lessons from Ukraine, Muhonen said.
While the biggest shelter in Kuopio can accommodate 7,000 people, Ukrainians sometimes only have a few minutes to run to a subway station or underground parking lot.
That means people need a shelter they can reach easily that offers some form of protection and not necessarily one that can withstand a nuclear attack, he said.
Dmytro Untila, 20, a Ukrainian student at the university in Kuopio, was at home in Odesa when Russian missiles struck his city on 24 February 2022, the first day of the war. He sheltered in the entrance hall of his building because he didn’t have anywhere else to go, he said.
Training for such a situation would have definitely helped in Ukraine, he said, “because nobody knew this could happen.”
The biggest threat to energy infrastructure in the Kuopio region is heavy snowfall, storms and bad weather, said Juha Räsänen, CEO at the Savon Voima electricity company.
But since the invasion of Ukraine and the company’s decision to stop buying Russian biofuel, the number of cyberattacks against the network has significantly increased, Räsänen said.
Last year, engineers also found at least 10 stickers placed on particularly vulnerable parts of the energy network infrastructure. Other energy companies in Finland have also found them and don’t know where they came from, he said.
“If there was an explosion at that point, it could destroy a whole dam,” Räsänen said. Drones have also been spotted over power lines but those responsible have not been identified, he said.
It is not possible to guard against all threats, Räsänen said, which is why it’s important people are prepared to look after themselves without help for at least 72 hours, if the power supply goes out, or if water becomes undrinkable.
The Finnish Security and Intelligence Service said it investigated “a wide range of observations” and found nothing of concern.
Since 2022, people have been more vigilant because of the security situation and therefore have reported things like reflective stickers related to land survey works, it said in a statement. Drone sightings, it said, have “largely been explained by everyday occurrences.”
“Small things are happening all the time,” including Russian jamming of GPS signals, said Vuokko Lahtinen, 32, who was visiting a sauna in Kuopio.
For that reason, “the best defence of Finland is to make it not worth attacking,” she said.
That relies on the country’s military and defence forces but also Finnish people who feel like “we have something we want to fight for,” she said.
In Finland, she said, there is a “general feeling of responsibility,” which has grown out of local community groups and even initiatives such as recycling.
“On a very simple daily level, if you do things that matter, then it has a butterfly-wing effect,” Lahtinen said.
Finland vs the Soviet Union
In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11% of its territory and more than 400,000 people, around 12% of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.
At Kuopio's veterans’ museum, Risto Mönkkönen, 95, showed a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.
“I cannot forget it,” he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father’s friends.
Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.
Aili Toivanen, 92, said she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.
The first time, she looked back and saw her home burning, set on fire by Finnish soldiers who did not want to leave anything behind, she said.
The second time, she explained, the Soviet air force bombed the family’s departing train and they jumped out, hiding in ditches before they took refuge in Kuopio.
When Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, she said, with tears in her eyes, that she worried she would have to leave her home for a third time.
A country worth fighting for
At the shelter in Kuopio, thousands of people filed in, including schoolchildren and university students.
“Kids would need to know this, because they might have to do something alone. The adults can’t always help,” said Amanda Hill, 11, whose school studied in the shelter for the day.
Sitting on the floor of the shelter with his fellow conscripts, Pietikainen explained why it’s not crazy to practice what happens in a crisis.
“We’re Finns, so we’re kind of pessimistic about life in a way,” but history shows what can happen with Russia, he said.
When it comes to the threats from Moscow, Muhonen said, “don’t believe what they say but observe what they do.”

The Prime Minister has told the Commons that he has already committed to a pathway to spending three per cent of gross domestic product on defence, in response to a question pressing him to do so urgently rather than waiting for a future fiscal event.
Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the Defence Committee, put the question at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday.
He said: “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority. That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later. Indeed, defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just will not be enough.
“Rather than kicking the can down the road, waiting for a fiscal event in a future year, will the Prime Minister urgently commit to charting a pathway to reaching 3% of GDP being spent on defence by 2030? As his Chancellor rightly noted, that is critical to keeping our country safe.”
Andy Burnham replied: “I have made that commitment, I have made it very clearly, and I have done so for a considerable time. I was in Ukraine last week for a very specific reason: to repeat it on the world stage. My hon. Friend can be absolutely sure of that.”
He went on: “Alongside our commitment to defence, we also have to build the resilience of Britain. We need to ensure that the maximum amount of the funding committed to the defence investment plan goes back into the reindustrialisation of our communities. We should do more to maintain sovereign manufacturing and production capability here, and that will be a theme of my Government. We will make sure that British taxpayers’ money goes to supporting industry in our own country, to make us more resilient going into the future.”
The exchange turns on a distinction between committing to a figure and setting out how it will be reached. Dhesi’s question asked for a pathway, and specifically for one that does not wait on a future fiscal event, which is the point on which the government has previously declined to be drawn.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, has argued that announcing a spending figure without setting out how it will be funded invites a loss of market confidence and rising borrowing costs. He has said he has every confidence the Defence Investment Plan will be fully funded, and has not ruled out tax rises as part of the answer.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has previously put the cost of reaching three per cent at an additional £17.3 billion in 2029-30. Behind the domestic argument sits NATO’s push towards 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035, agreed at the alliance summit in The Hague.
The second half of Burnham’s answer picks up a theme the government, current and former, has been developing through the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to defence over four years.
The department has pointed to figures published last month showing that spending with industry supported 274,000 jobs across the United Kingdom in 2024/25, with £31.9 billion spent, including 12,200 direct jobs in Scotland where shipbuilding and submarines account for 7,900 of them. Jobs supported by spending on weapons and ammunition manufacturing rose 51 per cent across the country over the same period, an increase the department attributes to the drive to rebuild what it calls an always on pipeline of munitions supply.

Rabbit farms face prosecution over abuse footage
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Sixteen Dutch rabbit farms could face criminal prosecution after undercover footage showed bunnies being lifted by the ears and thrown into crates, and sick animals beaten to death, junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has said.
The images, filmed by campaign group Animal Rights, were shot at 16 companies that export live rabbits to slaughterhouses in Belgium. They show the animals being picked up by the ears, fur, legs or head and thrown in large numbers into transport crates and shopping trolleys, where they can be crushed.
“What can be seen in the footage is terrible,” Erkens said in answer to parliamentary questions from D66 and the animal rights party PvdD, calling the treatment unacceptable. Some people, he added, appeared to feel free to handle animals this way when no inspector was nearby.
The food safety board NVWA has received a large amount of recent footage and is checking it for authenticity. If abuse is found companies are prosecuted. In 2024 a slaughterhouse was fined for cruelty after activists released undercover video.
Footage seen so far points to structural and serious failings in how the animals are handled, Erkens said. He has also set up new checks on how rabbits are caught and loaded – a stage of animal transport that inspections had largely overlooked, and will update parliament by the end of the year.

US army is grappling with profound crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:50:01 UTC
16:50:01 KST

There were also disagreements between the White House and military commanders during Donald Trump's first term, but according to the Washington Post, the level of changes and tensions in the command structure during the current Trump administration is unmatched. The removal of more than 20 senior officers and the blocking of dozens of commanders' promotions have raised concerns about the stability of the US military's command structure.
This is especially significant when the US military is also engaged in a long and costly war in the Middle East. The resignation of US Army Secretary "Dan Driscoll" is the latest sign of this tension. Driscoll left his post after growing differences with US War Secretary Pete Hegseth. The differences between the two officials were not just personal or administrative, but also related in part to the way the military command is managed and to widespread changes at the top levels of the military.
The departure of a few commanders or a political official may not seem so important, but in a military structure, the stability of command is part of combat power. The army is not just a collection of planes, missiles, ships and tanks. The experience of commanders, coordination between forces and trust between the political and military structure are part of the same power that must be demonstrated during the war.
From this perspective, the Iran war has put additional pressure on the US military. Of course, we cannot yet speak of the "collapse" or "impotence" of the US military. The United States still has the most powerful military in the world in terms of technology, air and naval power, intelligence, space power, and logistical capacity. But the problem is that even the most powerful military in the world does not have unlimited resources. One of the most important limitations is weapons stocks.
The White House has put the direct cost of the war at about $37.5 billion, but that figure is only a fraction of the true cost of the war. The cost of replacing spent ammunition, repairing equipment, long-term deployment of troops, and rebuilding military capabilities is not fully reflected in this figure.
The United States has used up a significant portion of its precision munitions and interceptor systems during the war. Reports of dwindling stocks of Patriot missiles and other air defense equipment have raised concerns among military officials and US allies. The importance of this issue becomes clearer when we realize that the United States is not just stockpiling weapons for the Middle East. Washington must also have military capabilities for Europe, the Pacific, and other regions of the world. So every interceptor missile fired in the Middle East is not just spent ammunition; it is part of a stockpile that could be used in another crisis.
This is where the Iran war directly ties into America’s competition with China and Russia. If the war in the Middle East is prolonged and the US is forced to keep significant amounts of troops, aircraft, ships, ammunition, and defense systems in the region for months, the US military’s flexibility to respond to other crises will be reduced.
This concern is particularly important for America’s Asian allies. Washington’s East Asian allies are not just looking at America’s political promises; they are also looking at how many planes, ships, missiles, and munitions the United States has at its disposal in a real crisis, and how quickly it can get them to the region. So the depletion of military reserves can become a political issue.
The longer the war drags on, the more resources the US will have to devote to rebuilding its stockpiles. This means more pressure on the defense budget, increased arms orders, and years to restore some stockpiles to pre-war levels.
But the cost of war is not just equipment; manpower is also depleted. The US military structure needs experienced commanders and a stable chain of command to maintain readiness in several regions of the world. Extensive changes at the top of the military, while American forces are still engaged in military operations, can have a cost that is very difficult to measure in financial statistics. That is why the Iran war has become a strategic test for the United States.
A war that was supposed to showcase American military might has now become a debate about the limits of American power. Washington is forced to simultaneously consider the cost of war, the depletion of weapons stockpiles, the attrition of forces, the stability of command, and the ability to counter threats from China and Russia.
This does not mean that America no longer has the military power it once had. In fact, the opposite is true; America still has enormous power, but the Iran war has shown that even that power has limited costs and capacity. Military power is not just the ability to start a war; it is the ability to continue it, to replace ammunition, to maintain the readiness of forces, and at the same time to be ready for the next war.
If the United States is forced to reduce its capabilities on other fronts to win on one front, then a regional war becomes a global issue. For this reason, the true cost of the Iran war to the United States may not be apparent today but in a few years, when Washington will have to rebuild its weapons stockpiles, train new commanders, and prove to its allies that it can still manage multiple crises simultaneously.
The Iran war has perhaps questioned the concept of "unlimited American power" more than it has challenged American power in a specific operation. And for Washington, this is perhaps one of the most important strategic consequences of this war.

Meta is imposing its new AI agent on employees
Kyiv • UNN
Meta has canceled employee evaluations based on the frequency of AI use. At the same time, employees are actively testing the Hatch agent, increasing token consumption.
Meta no longer plans to evaluate employee performance based on how frequently they use artificial intelligence tools, but employees are still being encouraged to test the company’s new AI agent called Hatch. Wired reports this, according to UNN.
Details
In an internal announcement this week, the social media giant told employees that evaluations of their performance would no longer depend on how often they used artificial intelligence tools, three employees who received the announcement told WIRED. But as Meta employees are simultaneously beginning to test a new agentic artificial intelligence tool known as Hatch, they say their token consumption continues to grow
Previously, Meta linked employee evaluations to how much they used AI to improve their daily work. Employees even received labels such as "AI Native," "AI First," or "AI Enabled."
Now, in new performance evaluation guidelines, the company said it would assess employees primarily based on their contributions, rather than how they achieved them.
The new performance evaluation guidelines presented this week replace references to evaluating employees based on criteria such as "AI usage" and their designation as "AI Native" with looser wording suggesting that "these results may be supported by AI or other means." This shifts Meta’s focus back to evaluating employees based on their impact, with less emphasis on how that impact is achieved. Some Meta employees told WIRED that the changes are minor but welcome, freeing them from feeling pressured to use AI in situations where it does not make sense
Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton said that this merely emphasizes the approach the company had used previously.
According to the publication, despite the relaxed requirements, Meta employees are actively using the new agentic AI tool Hatch. As a result, employees say, token consumption continues to grow.
For months, according to some Meta employees, their colleagues repeatedly—or, as they saw it, frivolously—suggested that artificial intelligence tools maximize internal usage metrics, such as the number of tokens or AI units consumed. The Tokenmaxxing era peaked when one Meta employee created an internal leaderboard to track how many employees were using AI, giving them titles such as "Token Legend." After details of the dashboard leaked online, the employee deleted it in April. A few months later, Meta began rationing employees’ use of artificial intelligence
Recall
Meta reported that its AI model unintentionally gained access to data from another system. This is the third such case in recent weeks, following incidents involving Anthropic and OpenAI.

More teachers, better access, fewer pupils: India’s government school paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:49:04 UTC
16:49:04 KST

Schools are back in focus. In larger policy discussions and political debates. The Opposition, emboldened by its NEET protest victory, is looking to up the ante by exposing ramshackle school infrastructure in different states, starting with Rajasthan. TOI ground reports, too, have found gross inadequacies in government schools across different parts of the state. Particularly jarring is the fact that in Kota, widely called the coaching capital of India, many government schools are in a dilapidated state.A wider ground report by TOI reporters across the country found that Rajasthan was hardly an outlier. In Bihar, nearly 200 children from four classes were sharing a single room at one school while cattle occupied two others. In Uttarakhand, leaking roofs meant buckets and umbrellas had become classroom fixtures. In Madhya Pradesh, TOI found schools struggling with teacher shortages and unsafe buildings. Keralam was a prominent exception to this broader picture.However, the fact remains that in a country of 1.4 billion people, structural gaps are perhaps expected, if certainly not desired. A good metric of how much the school system has improved over the years is to look at the data furnished by the central government and its allied agencies.
The pan-India numbers make for interesting reading. Rajasthan had 7,200 single-teacher schools in 2025-26, while only 36.4% of schools reported ramps with handrails and 26.3% had toilets tailored for Children with Special Needs (CwSN).The country has nearly a lakh fewer government schools than it did a decade ago, and those schools are losing pupils. It also has more teachers, far fewer children in single-teacher schools, more teenagers reaching higher secondary and internet access in about two-thirds of schools. Fewer than half of schools, however, report a toilet designed for children with special needs. Yet despite improvements in many metrics, government-school enrolment is falling.
From buffaloes and buckets to what the national numbers say
Most of what is known about India's schools comes from UDISE+, the Unified District Information System for Education Plus. It is an annual, census-like administrative database covering schools across management types. Schools report on their pupils, teachers and infrastructure, from enrolment and staffing to toilets, electricity, ramps, computers and internet access, and they are incorporated into the Union education ministry's national school statistics.The system grew out of UDISE, created in 2012-13 by merging separate elementary and secondary databases. UDISE+ became its online successor from 2018-19. The government uses it to locate infrastructure gaps, and states draw on it when seeking support for classrooms, toilets, drinking water, electricity, libraries and digital facilities under schemes such as Samagra Shiksha.A school can figure in the database as open and equipped with a particular facility, but reality can be very different. TOI's visits across states repeatedly brought out that distinction.
Nearly 1 lakh fewer govt schools, but access improves on paper
India had 11,04,796 government schools in 2015-16. Ten years later, UDISE+ records 10,05,245, a difference of 99,551 schools or 9%. The rider is that a school leaving the UDISE count can reflect closure, merger, rationalisation, reclassification or other administrative change.The decline is stark in some states. Madhya Pradesh had 1,21,976 government schools in 2015-16; by 2025-26 the count was 91,199, a reduction of 30,777. Uttar Pradesh fell from 1,62,645 to 1,37,103, a reduction of 25,542. Together, the two states account for about 56.6% of the national net decline over the decade.
Nearly 1 lakh less government school in 10 years
There have also been changes in school mapping and verification, with UDISE+ replacing the older UDISE system from 2018-19. Questioned in Parliament, the Centre has said that decisions on opening, closing and rationalising schools lie largely with states and Union territories, while the Right to Education framework requires elementary schools to remain accessible within prescribed neighbourhood limits.Between 2018-19 and 2024-25, the Gross Access Ratio rose from 88.24% to 95.35% at the secondary level and from 65.05% to 94.97% at higher secondary. GAR measures the proportion of habitations or villages with a school available within the prescribed distance; it is not an enrolment ratio. So although there are fewer schools, the measured access ratio has improved. This is also part of the government's defence.
Govt schools are losing pupils even as the system improves
Government-school enrolment fell from 12.75 crore in 2023-24 to 11.89 crore in 2025-26, nearly 85.9 lakh fewer pupils in just two years, a decline of 6.7%. Over the same period, enrolment in private unaided schools rose from 9.00 crore to 9.89 crore, an increase of about 88.3 lakh, or 9.8%. The thinning out is also visible over a decade with average enrolment per government school falling from about 132 pupils in 2014-15 to 120 in 2024-25, a decline of roughly 9%; the latest UDISE+ figures put it at about 118 in 2025-26.One figure from the government's own parliamentary reply captures the scale of it. In 2024-25, government institutions accounted for 68.9% of all schools in India but 49.2% of all enrolment.
The changing mix
A movement this large might be expected to have triggered a substantial investigation. On July 29, 2026, the government was asked why government-school enrolment had fallen from about 12.8 crore to 11.9 crore while private enrolment rose from around 9 crore to 9.9 crore.The ministry confirmed the numbers but did not cite or summarise such an assessment in its reply. Instead, it listed the interventions being made to strengthen government education.NITI Aayog's 2026 UDISE+-based review says the broader decline in enrolment through 2024-25 is partly attributable to demographic shifts, particularly falling fertility and a smaller school-age population, alongside school consolidation and challenges in retaining pupils at higher levels.Ranabir Bhattacharyya, teacher-in-charge of the English-medium primary section of Chetla Boys' High School in Kolkata, points to some of the practical issues with UDISE+ and also offers context for the dwindling numbers. He says the data had many issues at one point, but the pipeline has increasingly been made more robust as the government seeks to bring all students onto the platform to roll out various developmental schemes aimed at schoolchildren.He alleges that there was earlier an incentive in certain quarters to inflate pupil numbers, but says tighter vigilance has reduced that tendency and the numbers now being reflected are closer to reality. Ranabir, however, flags other problems like the website can be difficult to use and often suffers technical glitches, while the absence of additional staff increases the workload of those responsible for keeping the data updated. As a result, underreporting can happen too, according to him.
More teachers nationally, TOI finds the gaps locally
India had 96.96 lakh teachers in 2020-21 and 102.73 lakh in 2025-26, nearly 5.77 lakh additional teachers in five years. Single-teacher schools fell from 1,10,971 in 2023-24 to 1,00,843 in 2025-26, and the number of children enrolled in them dropped more steeply still, from 39.94 lakh to 29.12 lakh. Nearly 11 lakh fewer children are now in such schools.But the national improvement hides striking state differences. Andhra Pradesh alone has 16,357 single-teacher schools; Jharkhand has 9,827, Maharashtra 9,269, Karnataka 8,042 and Uttar Pradesh 7,874. Those five states together account for just over half of India's 1,00,843 single-teacher schools.And this is one area where the statistical picture intersects sharply with what TOI reporters saw. In Madhya Pradesh, TOI found 70 children and one teacher operating from a single dilapidated room at a school in Bhopal's Kolar, while students in Classes XI and XII at a PM SHRI school in Mandla had gone without teachers for newly introduced streams for a year.
Single teacher school decreasing
Uttarakhand has 2,655 single-teacher schools, about 11.8% of its entire school network, alongside its unusually high proportion of very small schools. The Centre acknowledges the problem. It has told Parliament that recruitment and postings are primarily state responsibilities; and that it repeatedly presses states on faster recruitment and redeployment while supporting them under Samagra Shiksha.Ranabir highlights another issue involving children of migrant labourers. He says that when a student shifts from one school to another, the subsequent UDISE+ entry does not always move smoothly as it requires manual intervention. West Bengal School Education Minister Dipak Barman, speaking to TOI, says many private schools in the state have not uploaded their student lists. Barman says the state is working to get the figures updated. It is hard to know whether similar anomalies exist elsewhere, but if they do, they could significantly undermine the purpose of what the central government is trying to achieve with the UDISE+ platform.
More children stay on, but Class X remains a fault line
The encouraging part is that reported dropout rates are falling. In many states, girl students are incentivised to continue school education. At the same time, higher-secondary Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) rose from 56.2% in 2023-24 to 61.7% in 2025-26, and the secondary dropout rate fell from 14.1% to 9.5% over the same period. Here too, the national number hides enormous variation. Keralam, for instance, reported secondary retention of 99.1% in 2025-26.
Drop-outs decreasing
For many from financially weaker sections, there is a significant opportunity cost to staying in school after Class X. The government has therefore deployed a range of measures to keep more students in the system. Parliamentary replies point to PM POSHAN, residential schools and hostels, KGBVs, transport assistance, free textbooks and uniforms, enrolment campaigns and vocational education, and more recently to Vidya Samiksha Kendras and APAAR IDs as tools for tracking students who drop out or move between schools.
Digital access surges, but TOI finds a different classroom reality
In step with the government's Digital India push, digital infrastructure has expanded rapidly. In 2020-21, 24.5% of schools reported internet access; by 2025-26, 67.4% did. Computer availability rose from 41.3% to 69.9%. The approved budget for ICT labs, smart classrooms and other digital initiatives rose from ₹381.1 crore in 2018-19 to ₹3,221.1 crore in 2025-26.NITI Aayog's 2026 UDISE+-based analysis of functional smart classrooms shows coverage rising from 14.9% of schools in 2021-22 to 30.6% in 2024-25. In other words, even after rapid expansion, nearly seven in ten schools still lacked one.The interstate divide is striking. Punjab reported functional smart classrooms in 80.1% of schools and Delhi in 75.7%; the corresponding figures were only 4.3% in Meghalaya, 5.7% in West Bengal, 14.9% in Bihar and 19.8% in Uttar Pradesh. Tamil Nadu offers the opposite story: its reported coverage went from virtually zero in 2021-22 to 60.8% in 2024-25.TOI's ground visits underline why infrastructure numbers need context. In Uttar Pradesh, schools visited by reporters had toilets and drinking water, but digital resources were missing; in Himachal Pradesh, strong coverage of basic facilities coexisted with substantially weaker smart-classroom and disability-access indicators.Regarding West Bengal's poor showing, Barman says many of the state's UDISE+ figures have not been properly updated and that the government is working to correct them, and is looking to start 2000 smart classrooms in the next one year. He says Bengal expects to be among the top 10 when the next calculation is made.
Toilets on paper, TOI finds the functionality gap on the ground
India is now close to universal provision of toilet facilities in schools, at least on paper. UDISE+ reports girls'-toilet availability in 98.5% of girls' and co-educational schools in 2025-26. But availability and functionality are not the same.TOI's ground reporting provides a simple illustration of that distinction. Schools visited in Uttar Pradesh had separate toilets for boys and girls, but reporters found many of them unclean, with teachers blaming the absence of sanitation workers. This issue of not having adequate sanitation staff is something Ranabir also flagged repeatedly.The same NITI Aayog analysis, using 2024-25 data, puts national functional girls'-toilet coverage at 94%, up from 85.17% a decade earlier. Yet the state map remains uneven.In 2024-25, Bihar and Odisha were both at 98.1% functional girls'-toilet coverage and West Bengal at 99.6%, while Rajasthan stood at 87.3%. Meghalaya was at 68.7%, Arunachal Pradesh 73.7% and Manipur 74.5%.
The basic-access gap remains
In 2020-21, 24.5% of schools reported internet access and 41.3% computers. About 48.3% reported ramps with handrails and 25.3% toilets for children with special needs. By 2025-26, internet availability had reached 67.4% and computers 69.9%. Ramps with handrails were at 58.2%, while CwSN-friendly toilets stood at only 40.1%.The state contrasts are revealing. Himachal Pradesh reports functional electricity in 99.1% of schools and computers in 87.2%, but internet reaches only 66.2% and CwSN-friendly toilets 34%. At the same time, 18.3% of its schools are single-teacher schools and almost half have 30 pupils or fewer.
Basic access gap remains
Keralam, the prominent exception in TOI's ground reporting, also stands apart on several UDISE measures. Computer availability is 99.5%, internet access 92.6%, and only 67 schools, about 0.4% of its network, are single-teacher schools. Secondary retention is 99.1%. The state is not without gaps, only around 51.7% of schools report CwSN-friendly toilets but the overall contrast with many other states is striking.The Accessibility Code was notified in 2024, and Samagra Shiksha and PM SHRI provide funds for facility upliftment. Ranabir says funds often come in a trickle or are regularly delayed. As a result, he says, many of these metrics do not improve as smoothly as desired. He also highlights that many rural schools have irregular electricity supply, and hence while internet and other digital facilities are present on paper, reality can be different.Taken together, most of these service and outcome indicators have moved positively. Yet government-school enrolment is falling. That may partly reflect an aspirational society where some parents are looking to private schools for stronger English-language exposure, soft skills, peer networks and perceived advantages in college and beyond. Anecdotally, one can also see the mushrooming of English-medium schools in suburbs and mofussils.
But the national data do not by themselves establish why families make these choices. Some of the decline may also reflect cleaner data and ironically even lack of proper uploading of data as pointed out by the Bengal education minister.There is no one-size-fits-all solution for such a large country. The data show substantial progress on several fronts, yet the lived reality may be different in some places. For now, the government will need to tick the boxes on what should be absolutely non-negotiable in terms of core deliverables, including the lacunae exposed in those reports. Winning the larger battle for aspiration may be a challenge for another day, or another decade.

'Humble but ambitious' - the return of fallen giants Schalke
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:48:46 BST
16:48:46 KST

'Humble but ambitious' - the return of fallen giants Schalke
- Published
On matchday, even for friendlies, Gelsenkirchen pauses as locals turn their attention to Schalke's Veltins-Arena.
Everywhere you look, swathes of fans in blue and white are arriving by tram, on foot or by car.
In the team's first game back in the Bundesliga for three years, 6,000 away fans stayed after the final whistle to support the players despite a 3-0 defeat at Augsburg.
"It's a kind of religious feeling that people have towards Schalke," said Professor Frank Eckardt, who grew up in the Schalke-Nord area.
"It feels like people think, 'OK, we don't have anything else, but we have Schalke. It's our club.'
"If you go to graveyards, for example, you will find that people have Schalke on their graves in one way or the other. So it is really something deep.
"You can take everything from us, but you will never take Schalke from us. That's what they really believe."
When Schalke fell to Bundesliga 2 for the first time in 21 years and insolvency looked a genuine possibility - because of massive debts brought on by rash spending, failure to qualify for Europe and Covid-19 - the only guarantee was the fans would remain.
Despite the threat against the club's existence, Schalke bounced back to the top flight straight away in 2022.
But that was a false dawn.
A year later they were in the second tier again, and that is where they would stay for the next three seasons, with the first two campaigns showing little hope for the future.
A 10th-placed finish was followed by an even more dismal 14th - only two places above a relegation play-off spot.
German football expert Mark Lovell said: "They suffered with the burden of expectation. They were expected to basically walk the league every season despite having huge financial problems.
"There's sympathy for Schalke, but they've been their own worst enemies by chasing success and extending themselves too far.
"They've been living beyond their means for many seasons. When you do suffer relegation something has to give, and they haven't been able to buy their way out.
"They had to live more to their needs and get rid of their best players, and then sort of start again with a real skeleton type operation."
After finishing 14th, new figures were brought in - including former Plymouth Argyle manager Miron Muslic - who helped build Schalke's promotion to the Bundesliga last year.
Robin Haack, who covers Schalke for local newspaper WAV, said: "He is the face of the Schalke promotion.
"He is the hero because his way of coaching is so powerful. He gave the people the belief back.
"Nobody knew him before. Some Austrian who was relegated to the third league in England - he must be bad.
"But he proved all the haters wrong in an incredible way. Fans love him like I've never experienced a coach has been loved before."
Muslic operates with a high-press style and has created a team that represent Gelsenkirchen's working-class nature with committment and effort.
"Muslic was the perfect match," said Haack.
If Muslic was the cover star, working behind the scenes was former director of football at Werder Bremen and Germany international Frank Baumann, who joined Schalke in June 2025.
Andreas Ernst, who also reports for WAV, said: "He had the whole club, but it lay on the ground.
"They said do whatever you want to do. But with no money. We have a bad team. But come here - a very great club.
"Frank Baumann did everything out of nothing."
Lovell said: "At Schalke right now there's some very intelligent football people behind the scenes.
"Frank Baumann's a real top football man, and just a decent person, which Schalke didn't have."
Baumann's most eye-catching signing was former Manchester City forward Edin Dzeko, who joined in January after a torrid spell in Italy with Fiorentina.
He has scored eight goals in 13 games, including two this season in Schalke's DFB Pokal cup win.
Muslic told BBC's Euro Leagues podcast: "I grew up in Austria, but I'm from Bosnia. And Edin Dzeko for us is Gary Lineker. He's our Johan Cruyff. He's our Franz Beckenbauer. He's just an idol.
"He's 40 years old, and he's still able to perform. That means he was super professional the last 25 years.
"That's why he's a role model and that's why he will also have his impact and he will leave also his fingerprints in this upcoming Bundesliga season."
With his experience at top-flight clubs across Europe, Dzeko's will also offer something invaluable to Muslic's team.
Schalke defender Christian Fuchs told BBC's More Than The Score podcast: "Where it's a player like this... there's so much respect towards him from his team-mates.
"It's so important to build a club culture, to hold players accountable, to keep them all in check.
"Even if it's a small piece in the bigger puzzle, there is so much value that you need to give to that.
"Dzeko plays an important part in growing stability in the club."
Dzeko had been established with every club he has played for, but for others they have had to rebuild their careers with Schalke.
Former Liverpool goalkeeper Loris Karius has questioned multiple times whether to end his career, but has managed to regain a starting spot and become a key figure in Muslic's team.
Muslic said: "He is the face of this new Schalke, the face of this new resilience, this new mindset.
"After tough years behind him, he found a new home. He found new trust - like so many other players from Schalke who had some rough moments in their careers.
"They found a safe heaven. And then it was just about, let's do this together and let's start from scratch and let's do it in our way."
Schalke will need to showcase this new mentality against champions Bayern Munich in their first home game of the season on Saturday, after the Augsburg defeat.
This match will not define Schalke's season. Neither will the fierce rivalry with Borussia Dortmund. Instead, it will be shaped by every game at the Veltins-Arena, which will be packed with 62,000 passionate fans.
Fuchs said: "I know Dortmund. They don't admit it, but I'm sure they miss Schalke.
"Schalke is just a club that in my eyes belong into the Bundesliga and I hope... we'll see them there for a very long time."
Many Schalke fans do not have high expectations this season, with some saying they simply need to avoid relegation.
Muslic said: "We know the glory of the past. But we know also the present and the future.
"We are very humble but ambitious. Right now it's all about playing another year in the Bundesliga."

How Israel kidnapped a senior Hamas security official in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:48:18 UTC
16:48:18 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israeli forces kidnapped a senior Hamas security official from Gaza City
Israeli forces kidnapped a senior Hamas security official from his home in western Gaza City on Tuesday during an armed operation that killed his wife and wounded his son, according to Palestinian and Israeli sources.
Moen al-Arabid, head of Hamas' internal security apparatus in the Gaza Strip, was kidnapped after an Israeli special forces unit entered the area near the Katiba in western Gaza City, according to a Hamas source who spoke to The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The source said the Israeli force, dressed in civilian clothes and travelling in two vehicles, including a white bus, entered the densely populated area before being discovered and engaging in an exchange of fire with Palestinian fighters.
Israeli drones subsequently carried out several strikes around the area, the source said, adding that the airstrikes provided cover for the Israeli forces during the operation.
According to the source, al-Arabid and his wife, Samah al-Khalidi-al-Arabid, confronted the Israeli soldiers inside their home.
Samah was killed during the confrontation, while their son, Obaida, was wounded, the source said, who added Obaida had been scheduled to celebrate his engagement on Wednesday.
The Israeli forces later arrested al-Arabid and removed him from the area while he was wounded, according to the source.
The source described the operation as a kidnapping rather than an attempt to kill al-Arabid, saying the Israeli forces had entered the area specifically to capture him alive.
One video appeared to show al-Arabid crawling along the ground while attempting to find cover. An Israeli bus then approached, and several projectiles were thrown in his direction.
The Hamas source said the projectiles were sound grenades rather than offensive grenades and were intended to distract the wounded man and prevent him from taking cover, facilitating his capture.
Israeli media later published a photograph purportedly showing al-Arabid after his arrest, depicting a handcuffed man who appeared to be injured.
Meanwhile, Palestinian sources also said that a vehicle attempting to leave the area toward eastern Gaza City came under attack about 200 meters from the site of the operation, causing additional casualties, including children.
Videos and photographs circulated on social media showed damage around al-Arabid's home, including a white bus with damaged windows and what appeared to be bullet marks.
Israel confirms arrest
Israeli officials confirmed that al-Arabid had been abducted during an operation in Gaza City.
Israeli Defence Minister Yisrael Katz said in a televised statement that Israeli forces were continuing their operations in Gaza City and had recently arrested a senior Hamas official.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that al-Arabid was one of the "most prominent Hamas leaders in Gaza."
Netanyahu accused al-Arabid of helping hide and transport Israeli captives, attempting to rebuild Hamas' capabilities, participating in efforts to restore Hamas' rule over the Gaza Strip and spreading what Israel claimed was misinformation concerning the disarmament of Gaza.
"My directives are clear," Netanyahu claimed, saying that Israel would continue pursuing Hamas leaders and those involved in the 7 October 2023 attack.
Israeli Channel 12 reported that al-Arabid was wounded during the operation and transferred to Israel for medical treatment.
The Israeli Broadcasting Corporation, Kan, also quoted a security official as saying, "The target was wounded during the operation in the Gaza Strip and transferred to Israel for medical treatment."
According to Israel's Channel 11, the operation was planned and approved in recent days by Netanyahu and Katz. Kan reported that the Shin Bet security agency managed the operation.
Israeli sources cited by the channel said the operation was intended not only to obtain intelligence but also to send a message to senior Hamas leaders that they remained subject to Israeli pursuit despite the ceasefire.
Casualties in residential area
The operation caused casualties and damage in the surrounding neighbourhood in Gaza, which includes shelters for displaced Palestinians and is located near an American field hospital and a kindergarten.
Zaher al-Wahidi, director of the Information Centre at Gaza's Health Ministry, told TNA that ambulance and civil defence crews recovered four bodies and treated eight wounded people following the Israeli operation.
He said two children and two women were among those killed, including Samah al-Arabid, al-Arabid's wife.
The dead and wounded were transferred to al-Shifa Medical Complex, he added.
For residents living near the site, however, the operation was experienced not only through its casualties but through the sudden fear it caused among families, particularly those with children nearby.
Marwa Ezzat, a resident of the area, said her children were inside a nearby kindergarten when the clashes began.
She told TNA that the sudden gunfire and airstrikes sent residents into panic as families rushed to reach their children and move away from the area.
"We were terrified because our children were inside the kindergarten and we could hear the gunfire and explosions around us," Marwa said. "Everyone was trying to find a way to reach their children and get them to safety."
"After the operation subsided, displaced families gradually returned to their shelters and homes," she added. "Some found their tents and belongings damaged by shrapnel, while many children remained frightened by the possibility of renewed gunfire or airstrikes."
Intelligence and security objectives
Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that the operation appeared to have several objectives, including demonstrating Israel's ability to reach senior Hamas figures inside Gaza.
"Israel could have targeted al-Arabid from the air if its objective had been to kill him but instead chose to send a ground force to capture him alive," he said.
He added that the decision could indicate that Israeli security agencies wanted to obtain information from al-Arabid while he was alive, given his senior position within Hamas' security apparatus.
"The operation sends a message that the ceasefire does not prevent Israel from carrying out security operations inside Gaza," Ibrahim noted.
He explained that the arrest of a senior security official could give Israel access to sensitive information and create additional security risks for Hamas.
Hamas condemned the operation as a "serious crime" and accused Israel of deliberately endangering civilian lives.
The movement called on mediators and the U.S. administration to pressure Israel to stop what it described as violations of the ceasefire agreement.
In a press statement, Hamas said it had contacted mediators and Nikolay Mladenov, the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, requesting "maximum pressure" on the Israeli government to halt its operations and implement the ceasefire agreement.
The operation came amid continuing tensions over the implementation of the ceasefire, with Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violations.
According to Gaza's Health Ministry, 1,326 Palestinians have been killed and 4,398 wounded in the Gaza Strip since an alleged ceasefire agreement took effect on 10 October 2025.
The ministry said the cumulative Palestinian death toll since the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war in October 2023 had reached 73,462, with 174,509 people wounded.
The kidnapping of al-Arabid adds another point of tension to the fragile ceasefire, as Israel says it will continue pursuing Hamas figures while the Palestinian movement and mediators seek to preserve the agreement and advance its implementation.

The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:48:14 UTC
16:48:14 KST

The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
- Date:
- September 3, 2026
- Source:
- Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters
- Summary:
- Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.
- Share:
The universe is producing fewer stellar "babies." Over the past 4.5 billion years, the rate at which new stars form has fallen to less than half its previous level. Yet the supply of one of the most important types of "fuel" for star formation has changed surprisingly little.
That finding comes from an international research team led by scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), working with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) project. Using China's Five hundred meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), the researchers made precise measurements of cosmic neutral atomic hydrogen across the past 4.5 billion years.
Their results show a striking mismatch. Star formation has declined sharply, while the amount of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), an important reservoir of gas within galaxies, has decreased only modestly.
The findings were published online in Nature Astronomy on Sept. 1.
Why Is the Universe Making Fewer Stars?
Understanding why star formation has become less active as the universe ages is a major question in research on galaxy formation and evolution. One seemingly straightforward explanation is that galaxies have gradually consumed the cold gas needed to produce stars.
If dwindling supplies of cold gas were primarily responsible, however, astronomers would expect the dramatic fall in star formation to be accompanied by a similarly large decline in the available gas. So far, observations have not shown such a sharp depletion.
HI plays a central role in this puzzle. It is an important cold gas reservoir inside galaxies, connecting the broader cosmic supply of gas with the processes that eventually produce new stars. Astronomers primarily detect HI through its extremely faint 21-centimeter radio emission line.
Detecting that signal from distant galaxies is difficult because it is often overwhelmed by background noise.
FAST and DESI Survey Millions of Galaxies
For years, astronomers faced a major observational challenge. Very deep surveys could achieve the necessary sensitivity but could not examine large regions of the sky. Surveys covering much larger areas, meanwhile, generally lacked the sensitivity needed to detect such faint radio signals.
As a result, scientists have struggled to directly and reliably determine how the universe's total HI mass has changed across the low- to intermediate-redshift universe.
The new research tackled this problem by combining the exceptional radio sensitivity of FAST with the enormous optical spectroscopy data set provided by DESI. The team studied about 2.5 million galaxies spread across nearly one-third of the sky.
The researchers used an HI spectral stacking method to combine radio signals that would have been too faint to detect individually. Using precise measurements of each galaxy's redshift, they aligned the weak signals and stacked them together. This process allowed the average HI signal to emerge from the background noise.
The approach enabled the scientists to track changes in cosmic neutral hydrogen using a sample of unprecedented size and with exceptionally high statistical precision.
Star Formation Fell Much Faster Than Hydrogen
The results exposed a major difference between the evolution of star formation and the supply of neutral hydrogen.
About 4.5 billion years ago, the cosmic star formation rate was approximately 2.5 times higher than it is today. Over the same period, however, neutral atomic hydrogen density was only about 1.4 times higher than its present level.
In other words, star formation dropped dramatically without a comparable disappearance of the universe's HI reservoir. The findings indicate that rapidly exhausting neutral hydrogen cannot by itself explain why star formation has declined so strongly.
The Cosmic Mystery Shifts
According to the researchers, the results change the central question from "whether the gas is depleting" to "why it is increasingly difficult to form stars despite abundant neutral hydrogen reserves."
Stars do not form directly from most neutral atomic hydrogen. They are mainly born inside much denser clouds of molecular gas. Neutral atomic hydrogen occupies an important intermediate position between the universe's larger gas supply and the molecular hydrogen that can ultimately fuel star formation.
The researchers suggest that the most important changes in the more recent universe may involve how gas moves through the baryon cycle rather than how much HI exists overall.
As the flow of gas from the cosmic web becomes weaker and gas densities decrease, galaxies may become less efficient at converting HI into molecular hydrogen. Under this scenario, the overall HI reservoir can remain relatively stable while supplies of the molecular gas directly responsible for creating stars gradually decline.
Why the Universe's Star Factories Are Fading
The implications therefore extend beyond simply determining how much hydrogen exists in the universe. The findings offer an important new clue to why the universe's enormous star-forming engines have been gradually slowing down.
According to the researchers, combining observations from FAST and DESI provides a new observational benchmark for studying the cosmic gas cycle during the universe's later evolution, the long-term decline in star formation, and the broader processes shaping galaxies.
The research was led by scientists from the National Astronomical Observatories of China, the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory of CAS, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, together with researchers participating in DESI.
Contributors came from research institutions across Asia, North America, and Europe. The collaboration demonstrates the scientific potential of combining highly sensitive radio observations with enormous optical spectroscopy surveys.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chuan-Peng Zhang, Hong Guo, Yizhou Gu, Amélie Saintonge, Xiaohu Yang, Dirk Scholte, Ming Zhu, Peng Jiang, Hu Zou, Manasvee Saraf, Wenlin Ma, Yirong Wang, Y. P. Jing, Zheng Zheng, Zhejie Ding, J. Aguilar, S. Ahlen, D. Bianchi, D. Brooks, T. Claybaugh, A. de la Macorra, P. Doel, E. Gaztañaga, G. Gutierrez, M. Ishak, R. Joyce, S. Juneau, R. Kehoe, D. Kirkby, A. Kremin, O. Lahav, C. Lamman, M. Landriau, L. Le Guillou, M. Manera, A. Meisner, R. Miquel, J. Moustakas, S. Nadathur, W. J. Percival, F. Prada, I. Pérez-Ràfols, G. Rossi, E. Sanchez, D. Schlegel, M. Schubnell, H. Seo, J. Silber, D. It's still an October 6 election - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:46:55 UTC
16:46:55 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- It's still an October 6 election - analysis
It's still an October 6 election - analysis
Oct. 6, in a metaphorical sense, as a stand-in for the months before the massacres, when Israel's politics were dominated by a social-cultural fight over universities, the media, the judicial system
For the last 48 hours, Israel's election campaign has been dominated by an argument over who did what on the morning of October 7. As with so much in Israeli politics, the fight presents itself as one over October 7. At a deeper level, it's actually about October 6.
October 6, of course, in a metaphorical sense, as a stand-in for the months before the massacres, when Israel's politics were dominated by a social-cultural fight between political camps over universities, the media, the judicial system, and the civil service. The right argued that, as a rising majority, it should have the power to change institutions where a privileged left-wing elite still held sway decades after it lost public support.
On the left, protesters claimed that a majoritarian sweep would bring corruption, erode good governance, and eat away at civil and human rights.
That fight hit its crescendo in the spring and summer of 2023, with riling weekly protests and stormy arguments at meetups on Friday mornings and around Shabbat dinner tables on Friday nights. On October 7, it was said, all was pushed aside. The country needed to unite
A war that would take in seven fronts would not tolerate sharp division.
Except that the division never went away. It just put on a disguise. So the camps argued about what kind of commission should investigate October 7, one appointed by or through politicians or one dominated by retired judges. On the surface, an argument about October 7. In reality, an argument about October 6.
And so, for two days, Israelis have digested the comments of both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his wife Sara that political opponent Yair Golan had advance notice of the October 7 attacks while the military failed even to wake up the prime minister in the immediate run-up to 6:29 a.m.
The claim about Golan is widely seen as a conspiracy theory with no evidence supporting it. The claim about the military's relationship with Netanyahu is consistent with Netanyahu's long-running claim that the military has primary responsibility for October 7, and not he.
The facts are crucially important for Israel's historical record and for learning lessons for Israel's national security policy. But for Israel's politics—and for understanding the October 27 election—what's important is the nature of the argument.
For this, too, is October 6 in disguise. The true argument, the underlying one, is whether an entrenched left is again arrogantly sidelining (or worse) an elected prime minister. Or whether a power-hungry demagogic right is aiming to do away with democracy's safeguards and guardrails.
And so after all of the angst, all of the heartache, all of the tragedy, all of the anger, and all of the nerves of the past three years, we have an Israeli society in many ways both scarred and changed. We also have a politics where the fight between political camps is so deep, so long-running, and so resilient that, despite all, it just won't go away. And it is still with us, to dominate these elections, too.

FUZHOU, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of 2026, made its third landfall in east China's Fujian Province on Thursday, with maximum sustained winds of 23 meters per second near its center, according to the provincial meteorological observatory.
Before landing along the coast of Fujian's Zhangpu County at around 6:30 a.m., Saudel made landfall twice along the coast of east China's Zhejiang Province on Aug. 28.
Authorities in Fujian had evacuated more than 83,000 people by 7 a.m. on Thursday as persistent heavy rain battered parts of the province.
Heavy rain prompted the suspension of work, businesses and schools in parts of Zhangzhou City. Schools were also closed in other cities including Fuzhou, Quanzhou and Ningde, the provincial authorities said.
As of 7 a.m., eight sections of major roads had been closed, 657 transport services suspended, work halted at 152 construction sites, and over 150 major tourist attractions shut across Fujian.
The province raised its flood-control emergency response on Wednesday while maintaining a response for the typhoon.
China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) issued a blue alert for the typhoon on Thursday morning.
Saudel is forecast to move westward at 15 to 20 kilometers per hour and gradually weaken, the NMC said.
From Thursday afternoon to Friday afternoon, heavy to torrential rain is forecast across most of Fujian, eastern and northern Guangdong, southern Jiangxi and southern Hunan. ■

Study shows men and women follow different aging timelines
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:45:00 CST
16:45:00 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- A new study from China has found that men and women age in strikingly different ways -- and the clues lie hidden in the results of everyday blood tests and health checkups.
The study, recently published in the journal Nature Aging, was jointly conducted by researchers from the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB), under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), the Institute of Zoology of CAS, Xuanwu Hospital of Capital Medical University and other institutes.
Researchers looked at health data from more than 104,000 adults across China, aged 18 to 98. They focused on 172 common measurements, like weight, cholesterol, and blood sugar. From this, they built special "aging clocks" to show when human bodies go through the biggest changes over time.
They found that for men, the most important turning point came between ages 35 and 45. During this decade, their metabolism shifted noticeably -- body mass index went up, along with triglycerides and cholesterol. For women, the big change happened later, between 55 and 65, around the time of menopause. At that stage, women experienced strong hormonal changes, along with rising fat and cholesterol levels. Yet despite these distinct aging trajectories, the physical differences between men and women tended to diminish as they grew older.
The study also showed that certain substances in our blood -- including glucose, lipids, uric acid, and two tumor-related markers called CEA and HE4 -- build up as we age and are linked to faster biological aging. To test this, the scientists exposed human blood vessel cells to higher levels of these substances in the lab. The cells began to show clear signs of senescence, suggesting that these factors are not just markers of aging but may actually help cause it.
But there is some encouraging news. The researchers found that some aging effects might be reversible. For example, a common diabetes drug called metformin helped protect cells from the aging damage caused by high glucose levels. In another experiment, mice that were switched from a high-fat diet back to a normal diet showed clear improvements in liver aging.
"This suggests that lowering metabolic stress -- by improving diet or controlling blood glucose -- could be a potential strategy to slow down aging," said Xiong Muzhao, a researcher from CNCB.
The findings suggest that reducing age-related metabolic burden may be a promising strategy for promoting healthy aging. They also highlight the importance of sex-specific assessment and intervention throughout the lifespan, said Li Jiaming, a researcher from CNCB. ■

SYDNEY, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- An international study involving researchers in Australia has identified more than 1,200 genetic variants associated with personality traits.
The findings showed that genetic variants linked to personality were also associated with a broad range of outcomes, including mental and physical health, educational attainment, career trajectories, longevity and social relationships, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute.
Published in Nature, the study examined the "Big Five" personality traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, the statement said.
By examining how personality and genetics interact with other health traits, researchers can better understand the underlying causes of disorders and identify the most appropriate treatments and interventions for individuals, it said.
The study found no evidence of a single "personality gene," with personality differences arising from the combined influence of many genetic variants, each having a very small effect.
QIMR Berghofer researchers contributed family-based genetic analyses to help separate genetic influences from the influence of shared family environments. By comparing relatives within families, the team was able to show that many of the observed genetic associations could not be explained simply by growing up in the same household.
The findings provide a new understanding of how biology and environment work together to shape personality, said the study's co-author, Associate Professor Michelle Lupton of QIMR Berghofer.
Common genetic variation could explain up to 16 percent of the variation in personality, with the remainder attributable to environmental factors including life circumstances and experiences, Lupton said.
The study also found links between personality-related genetic variants and a range of behaviors and lifestyle factors, including daytime activity levels and night-owl tendencies. ■
