Feature: "I left a part of my heart in China," says retired U.S. teacher
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:44:44 CST
16:44:44 KST

Ronald Sakolsky arrives at Washington Dulles International Airport after his trip to China, near Washington, D.C., the United States, on Sept. 1, 2026. "I came back home today, but I left a part of my heart in China." Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky told a small group of reporters after landing at Washington Dulles International Airport late Tuesday, reflecting emotionally on his 10-day trip to China. (Photo by Li Yuanqing/Xinhua)
WASHINGTON, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- "I came back home today, but I left a part of my heart in China."
Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky told a small group of reporters after landing at Washington Dulles International Airport late Tuesday, reflecting emotionally on his 10-day trip to China.
Returning to China for the first time in 26 years, he reunited with Yin Yuzhen, a farmer and a pioneer in combating desertification.
Their friendship began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province -- more than 11,000 km from his home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
One ordinary evening, a television program caught his eye. On the screen was Yin, planting trees to help hold back the advancing sands of the Maowusu sandy land.
Stretching across parts of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Ningxia, the Maowusu has been one of the front lines in China's fight against desertification in the north -- an effort launched in 1978 and slated to continue through 2050.
"I was so touched that I started to cry," Sakolsky recalled, thinking back to that evening. "I honestly cannot tell you why. Something just happened to me. I just felt like I needed to help."
Moved by her endeavor, he raised 5,000 dollars to help Yin and her husband plant trees and combat desertification. Today, the saplings purchased with the donation have grown into more than 50,000 trees.
In May this year, Yin took to social media to find the American teacher who had once helped her plant the trees. In late August, Sakolsky was invited to return to Inner Mongolia, where he reunited with Yin.
Sakolsky said he had never imagined that trees could be grown in the desert. But Yin's dedication and perseverance turned sand into soil and "made it alive." Sakolsky recalled touching the trees and hearing the soil. "They are my children. Ms. Yin said to me that my children were waving because it was windy and the trees were moving."
After 26 years, Sakolsky and Yin did not need many words when they met again. There were tears, embraces and a sense of familiarity that seemed to bridge the years between them.
Throughout his 10-day trip to China, Sakolsky said, there were many moments when the two understood each other without speaking. "Because we spoke from the heart," he said.
"If a lady that lived in the desert in China, with no telephone, no roads, no television, no electricity, can meet a simple American history teacher, and we can create together a forest ... If one and one can do it, 10 and 10 can do it, 100 and 100 can do it, a million and a million can do it," he said.
For Sakolsky, their story was also a reminder that meaningful change can begin with just two people.
He believes ordinary Americans and Chinese alike want a better relationship between their two countries. Yet fear can grow out of a lack of understanding, he said, while ignorance and prejudice often take root in a lack of education.
That is why he hopes more Americans will learn about China -- by visiting the country, reading about it and opening themselves up to its culture. He likewise encouraged Chinese people to learn about and embrace American culture.
"It is up to the regular common people," he said. "Stop listening to everybody else. Do what you know is the right thing to do."
During his 10-day trip to China, Sakolsky visited Ordos and Hohhot in Inner Mongolia, Luoyang in Henan Province, and Beijing, where he also reunited with some of his former students.
The reunion was among the most memorable moments of his visit. But even as he boarded his flight home, Sakolsky was already thinking about what might come next.
"I would not be here if it was not for a teacher exchange program," he said, adding that to improve relations between the two countries, "start with the children and the students." ■

Lithuanian agriculture minister says regulating food prices is impossible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:44:00 UTC
16:44:00 KST

Regulating food prices is an impossible task, Lithuanian Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika said Thursday, arguing that the experience of a government-appointed food council showed the difficulty of achieving such a goal.
“The goal of regulating food prices is probably impossible, as we can see from reality,” Mažeika told the Žinių Radijas radio station.
Mažeika recently abolished the Food Council, established by the government of then-Prime Minister Gintautas Paluckas in 2025 with the task of monitoring food prices. He said the council had failed to produce any results and that some of its own members had become frustrated with its work.
“Several dozen people would meet and discuss things for several hours, but no decisions were made,” Mažeika said. “From the statements of some council members, it was clear that they were disappointed.”
The Food Council was abolished in late August. It was replaced, along with the Agriculture Science Council, by a new ministry body known as the College.
According to Mažeika, the College will analyse trends in agricultural supply chains and food and raw material prices and will bring together experts to provide advice, discuss possible measures and seek solutions.
“The restructuring is probably emotionally important for the other council members who will continue their work,” Mažeika said. “It’s not that completely different people will participate in the College. Experts will be brought together for consultations, discussions and the search for solutions.”
The Food Council began work in February 2025. At the time, then-Agriculture Minister Ignas Hofmanas said its initial task would be to analyse the food supply chain and develop proposals for reducing food prices.
By February this year, the council had yet to identify measures to lower prices. Then-Prime Minister Inga Ruginienė said it should meet more frequently and work more actively.
The 27-member council included representatives of government ministries, farmers, food processors and retailers, as well as universities and the State Consumer Rights Protection Authority.

Iran Red Crescent urges ICC probe into deadly US strike on wedding party
Outrage grows over US strike that killed four people and wounded 67 at a wedding party in Kuhestak.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate a missile attack by the United States that hit a wedding party in the southern town of Kuhestak, killing at least four people and wounding dozens.
In a letter to the court on Wednesday, the humanitarian group said the attack warrants “an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation” given the “civilian character of the location”.

The strike, which took place at 9:30pm local time (18:00 GMT) on Tuesday, killed at least four people and wounded 67, the group said, warning that the number of deaths may increase “given the critical condition of some of the injured”.
Those killed were two women and two children, aged four and 16. An Iranian official said most of the wounded were also women and children.
The Red Crescent said the attack could amount to a “war crime”, noting that international law prohibits directing attacks against civilians or civilian objects, or launching a strike while knowing it could cause disproportionate civilian harm.
‘Horrifying’ attack
The US Central Command said it was aware of the reports about the attack in Iranian media, but said it does not target civilians.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected the claim, with spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei citing past US strikes on civilians in Iraq and Afghanistan. He noted on X that such attacks have also been portrayed in US television shows.
“The reality is so horrifying that even American propaganda has never dared make the claim [the CENTCOM] is making today,” he wrote. “Sirik is not a story. The civilians are real. The victims are real.”
Neither the US nor Iran are party to the ICC’s Rome Statute, meaning the court does not have automatic jurisdiction over either nation.
But Dawn, a human rights group, has previously said Iran could still accept the court’s ad hoc jurisdiction over crimes committed on its territory from a specific date. “By filing such a declaration, set to the beginning of the war, Iran would grant the ICC jurisdiction over every strike on Iranian soil,” the group said.
The strike in Kuhestak came as the US launched a wave of attacks on Iranian coastal areas near the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, accusing Tehran of attempting to launch strikes against US troops and commercial shipping in the waterway.
Iran’s Ministry of Health said at least 18 people were killed in Tuesday’s strikes, while 142 were wounded.
UN urged to condemn attack
Iran’s envoy to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, called on the UN Security Council to denounce the Kuhestak attack.
“The Islamic Republic strongly condemns this horrific and appalling crime,” he wrote, adding that “the deliberate targeting and killing of civilians, including children, constitutes a grave violation of the fundamental rules of international humanitarian law and amounts to a war crime.”
Iranian authorities say at least 3,468 people were killed in the initial phase of the US and Israel’s war, which began on February 28 and ended with a ceasefire on April 8. A second round of hostilities, from July 27 to August 24, killed a further 59 people and wounded 666.
The deadliest single attack of the war, in terms of civilian casualties, destroyed an elementary school in Minab on the war’s first day. At least 156 people, including 120 children, were killed. A separate strike that day hit a sports hall in Lamerd, killing 21 people, including four children.
Over more than six months of war, the US and Israel have also struck oil and gas facilities, fuel depots, steel and petrochemical factories, airports, ports, bridges, power installations, medical centres and water facilities across Iran.

San Diego USV maker says Quickfish has entered production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:41:01 UTC
16:41:01 KST

- Seasats said its Quickfish interceptor USV has entered production, offering 40-plus knot speeds and weeks-long endurance at sea.
- The company deployed Quickfish and four other USVs during the Navy's Silent Swarm 2026 electromagnetic warfare exercise in Alpena, Michigan.
San Diego-based unmanned surface vessel maker Seasats said its Quickfish interceptor-class USV has entered production and is now available at scale.
The company said Quickfish is built on Seasats’ existing technology stack and can sprint at more than 40 knots (74 km/h) while remaining at sea for weeks at a time. It has a large modular payload bay designed to carry a range of mission systems, including unmanned aircraft, according to Seasats. The company said the hull is self-righting and built to survive Sea State 10 conditions, the roughest classification on the World Meteorological Organization’s sea state scale.
Seasats took part in Silent Swarm 2026, a two-week Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations experimentation event run by the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division. The exercise took place July 13 to 24 at the Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center in Michigan, part of the National All-Domain Warfighting Center, and drew participants including the Michigan National Guard, NOAA, the Army’s C5ISR Center and the Air Force Test Center.
Seasats said it deployed a fleet of five autonomous surface vessels during the exercise, including its Lightfish and Quickfish platforms, to demonstrate coordinated multi-platform operations with a small number of operators. The company said the event also involved integrating maritime sensing and electromagnetic spectrum equipment across the fleet.
A production-run Quickfish completed the full two-week exercise while carrying multiple payloads, Seasats said. The company described Quickfish as built on the Lightfish hull and electronics stack, adding high sea state performance, long range and a payload bay sized for aerial vehicles. Seasats also said the boat includes an on-station patrol mode that allows it to stay deployed for weeks without refueling.
Seasats credited the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division for the opportunity to test the technology.
The company said Quickfish’s payload bay is watertight and can hold several unmanned aircraft of different types and sizes. That allows a single vessel to be reconfigured for different missions, such as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications relay or strike, without modifying the boat itself, according to Seasats. Because the aircraft ride inside the enclosed bay, the company said a Quickfish on patrol gives no outward sign of what it is carrying.
Seasats linked that capability to the Defense Innovation Unit’s Suitable Warfighting Adaptive Payloads program, known as SWAP-USV, which is seeking mature, affordable unmanned surface vessels that can integrate with unmanned aircraft to counter asymmetric threats at sea. The company said Quickfish is in production now and can be delivered on DIU’s timeline.

MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. Current conditions of combat operations with the use of drones make it impractical for Ukraine to use IRIS-T missiles, which cost about €400,000, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
Earlier, the N-tv channel, citing sources in the German government, reported that the German government plans to provide Kiev with additional missiles for the IRIS-T air defense systems in September.
"One such missile costs about €400,000. This is significantly less than the cost of Patriot missiles, but they are nonetheless quite expensive. Given the tactics of combining various types of drones, including decoy drones, their consumption would be unjustified from the standpoint of military economics," Stepanov said.
In addition, he noted the cost of the IRIS-T systems themselves. "A battery of six launchers costs nearly €1 billion. De facto, this battery can protect a fairly limited area and will most likely be prioritized for defending the Kiev Region," the expert noted.
"It turns out that such an expensive system will not be the solution capable of protecting the entire airspace of the territories controlled by the Kiev regime," he concluded.
IRIS-T missiles are manufactured by Diehl BGT Defence for the armed forces of Germany, Greece, Italy, Spain, Norway, and Sweden. They can be deployed either as ground-based anti-aircraft guided missiles or as air-launched missiles for European Eurofighter Typhoon fighters, American F-16s, and Swedish JAS 39 Gripen fighters.

Report: Iran warns US of major retaliation if Israel storms Hezbollah-held ridge in Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:39:27 UTC
16:39:27 KST

Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on the mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon known as the Ali al-Taher ridge, where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah fighters, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.
Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources, and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
Hezbollah has said in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.
The Israeli military has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the U.S. had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.
IRGC forces holed up there, officials say
Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.
The third source, a foreign official with direct knowledge of the message, said it was delivered around mid-August and that as a result of U.S. pressure Israel had put off storming Ali al-Taher.
Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message but said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.
"Iran considers any Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.
Iran fired missiles towards Israel in early June in retaliation for attacks on Hezbollah on the Lebanese capital's outskirts.
Israel seeks to besiege Hezbollah fighters
Despite a ceasefire announced in June, the Israeli military has said Hezbollah is still operating around the ridge and twice over the last week launched explosive drones towards Israeli troops near the ridge.
In July, it said it had launched an air strike on a Hezbollah fighter near an access shaft to the underground site at Ali al-Taher and vowed not to allow Hezbollah to operate in the area or pose a threat to Israeli soldiers.
An Israeli military official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters in June that Hezbollah fighters were stuck underground without food or water. Israeli newspaper Maariv, citing a military source, said on Thursday that the Israeli military assessed there were no IRGC forces in Ali al-Taher and that some Hezbollah fighters had died without food and water.
The third official said Israel's military was trying to smoke out Hezbollah and IRGC personnel by besieging them, shooting down attempted drone deliveries of food and water to the ridge.
"What we have seen over the past month is Israeli pressure to besiege Ali al-Taher in order to impose a reality within this facility that renders it uninhabitable. This approach, and the absence of a large-scale attack, means that it is possible a message was conveyed through several countries -- this is a natural conclusion," Hezbollah's media office told Reuters.
Hezbollah threatens retaliation
A Lebanese source briefed by Hezbollah said the group's fighters can still access their positions through the ridge's northern side.
Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher, which Israel's military has included in a self-declared security zone occupied by its troops and off-limits to Lebanese.
Despite Iran's warning, the Lebanese source and a senior Lebanese security official said an Israeli military operation to capture the ridge was still possible in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah said any large-scale attack on Ali al-Taher would mean a return to full-blown war, and could see missiles landing on northern Israeli communities.

Diesel prices in Estonia top €2 per liter amid global oil surge
Diesel prices at Estonian filling stations rose above the €2 per liter mark again on Wednesday at a time of soaring oil prices worldwide.
The conflict between the Donald Trump administration in the U.S. and the Iranian regime, which started in late February, has plunged global oil markets into a deep crisis, pushing crude oil prices to their highest levels in recent years.
By midday Wednesday, diesel prices in Estonia had risen above €2 per liter at a number of filling stations nationwide. The Circle K station (pictured) adjacent to the Methodist Church in central Tallinn posted a diesel price of €2.029.
Diesel prices last exceeded €2 a liter on March 20, when fuel prices were at their highest level since spring 2022 in the immediate aftermath of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Gasoline prices at the pump have risen too – the same filling station was quoting a price of €1.999 for a liter of 95‑octane. In late April, the price had fallen to below €1.600 a liter.
Market participants' biggest concern has become the threat to the strategically critical Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil consumption passes. U.S.‑Iran tensions and recent strikes have disrupted Persian Gulf supplies, with crude oil prices rising sharply — Brent crude futures rose 1.1 percent to over US$95 a barrel on Wednesday, following a four‑dollar jump on Tuesday, as hopes of a quick easing of Middle East tensions faded.
Trump remained confident this was only a temporary state of affairs, back in April. "The gas will go down as soon as the war is over. It will drop like a rock. There's so much of it. It's all over the place, sitting all over the oceans of the world, and it'll go down," he said at the time.

UK summons Russian charge d'affaires over attempted drone attack in Germany
he UK on Thursday summoned the Russian charge d'affaires to condemn an attempted drone attack at Germany's Leipzig/Halle airport last month.
Earlier this week, the German government held Russia responsible, and European Union foreign ministers this week have signalled they will be working on a new package of sanctions targeting Russian individuals and entities.
"The UK stands in full solidarity with Germany following Russia's egregious and reckless attack on Leipzig Airport," a UK Foreign Office spokesperson said.
This incident was "the latest in a clear pattern of attempts by the Russian state to undermine our collective security," the spokesperson added.
Russia has rejected the allegations, which German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has said were a part of a "well-established patter of Russian hybrid operations in Europe."
The UK has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and enforces its own heavy sanctions, while supplying arms.
Earlier this week, when asked if Russia would launch strikes on military facilities inside the UK in retaliation for British weapons being used on Russian soil, President Vladimir Putin said with sarcasm, "that's a secret, a military secret." 
Fuel prices in Germany crack all time high
Gasoline prices in Germany have reached a new record high, the ADAC automobile association said on Thursday.
On Wednesday, drivers paid an average of €2.215 per liter for E10, the lowest-cost gasoline grade, the ADAC reported. That corresponds to about $9.73 per US gallon.
The previous record was set in March 2022, after Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions disrupted energy supplies.
This time, high prices are being driven by the ongoing war in Iran, which has driven up oil prices. Germany had applied a temporary fuel tax discount on gasoline to alleviate pressure on consumers, but that expired at the end of June
The ADAC considers the current price of gasoline to be too high, "because the price of oil is well below the highs reached in the spring."
German economic institutes raise growth forecasts
Germany's RWI and Ifo economic institutes have lifted growth forecasts for the German economy, citing stronger fiscal spending and exports.
In its latest assessment, the RWI said Germany's economy will grow by 1.3% in 2026, a sharp upward revision from the 0.8% growth predicted in June. The Ifo said German gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow by 1.4% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027, both up from previous estimates of 0.8%.
According to the Ifo's assessment, the German federal government's debt-financed investment package and increased demand from abroad are contributing to this positive trend.
The Munich-based institute said that government spending on infrastructure, climate neutrality and defence provided fiscal stimulus worth €40 billion ($46.36 billion), or 0.8% of GDP, in 2026.
Both institutes assessed that fiscal spending and exports have been able to outweigh the drag from higher energy prices.
However, RWI cautioned that this export momentum would likely fade later this year because the recent gains were a temporary effect of the rebound from disruptions related to US tariffs last year.
Additionally, the RWI said high energy prices, bureaucracy and weak competitiveness continue to weigh on investment.
This comes along with severe weaknesses in Germany's critical automotive industry, which is hemorrhaging jobs and closing factories.
Russia closes Germany's 'Goethe Institut' cultural centers
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Thursday that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centers would be closed in Russia.
"Of course they will be closed after our cultural center was expelled from there [from Berlin]," Lavrov said, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
"They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS.
The comes after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany's response to that incident included closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn.
Goethe operates in around 100 countries worldwide, promoting the study of the German language and providing information about German culture and society.
Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The Goethe-Institut is one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia.
Police say Munich arson attack may have targeted defense company
Following an arson attack on a construction site in Munich, the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office (LKA) said Thursday it suspects the fire was an attempted attack on a company involved in the defense industry.
Investigators are looking into a possible political motive, an LKA spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not immediately identify the company involved.
However, the Bild newspaper reported that the fire was set at a construction site near the headquarters of Rohde & Schwarz, a technology company that produces communication systems for the Bundeswehr, among other things.
A spokesperson for the company confirmed the police and fire department response, emphasizing, however, "our company premises themselves are not affected," local public broadcaster BR reported.
Police said multiple incendiary devices were thrown from a vehicle at the construction site in Munich's Berg am Laim neighborhood early Thursday morning around midnight.
According to the LKA, various defense contractors are based in the nearby building complex.
At least one of the incendiary devices sparked a fire that police officers extinguished. Despite the fire, no major damage was caused, a Munich police spokesperson said. However, another incendiary device had to be defused by special forces.
Following a short manhunt, a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, which the LKA said are both Bulgarian citizens, were arrested at a nearby gas station, and were being questioned Thursday.

Türkiye’s annual inflation eases to 31.51 pct in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:33:55 UTC
16:33:55 KST

Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation eased to 31.51 percent in August from 31.75 percent in July, official data showed on Sept. 3.
Consumer prices rose 1.84 percent month-on-month, slightly faster than the 1.78 percent increase recorded in July, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).
Both readings were just below forecasts in an AA Finance survey, which had put monthly inflation at 1.86 percent and the annual rate at 31.52 percent.
Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said inflation continued to decline despite seasonal increases in education costs and war-related pressure on fuel prices.
Annual core goods inflation fell to 15.9 percent, its lowest level since November 2020, while annual rent inflation dropped to its lowest level in 46 months, he said.
“We are taking steps to limit the inflationary impact of global price shocks while continuing our structural policies in line with our goal of lasting price stability,” Şimşek said.
Consumer prices rose 22.07 percent from the end of 2025, while the 12-month average increase stood at 31.79 percent.
Among the three groups with the largest weight in the index, housing costs rose 39.77 percent annually, followed by transport at 35.08 percent and food and non-alcoholic beverages at 33.79 percent. Food made the largest contribution to annual inflation, at 8.12 percentage points.
On a monthly basis, transport prices increased 4.82 percent, housing costs 2.26 percent and food prices 0.22 percent.
Prices rose in 134 of the 174 subclasses tracked by TÜİK, declined in 35 and remained unchanged in five.
The B index, which excludes unprocessed food, energy, alcoholic beverages, tobacco and gold, increased 1.84 percent monthly and 30.68 percent annually.
Domestic producer prices rose 2.57 percent from July and 27.95 percent year-on-year. Among the main industrial groups, energy recorded the largest monthly increase at 6.99 percent, while manufacturing prices rose 2.35 percent.

A Vietnamese court in Ho Chi Minh City sentenced 11 people to death on Thursday for drug trafficking in a major case involving 227 defendants, local media reported.
The Ho Chi Minh City People’s Court handed down the sentences after a two-week trial in the case known as VN10, according to the VnExpress media outlet.
The court identified Ha Danh Nam, 52, as a key figure in the drug trafficking network, saying he was involved in several branches of the operation.
Two other defendants, Hoang Sy Thang and Bui Van Anh, were sentenced to life imprisonment for illegally transporting drugs.
The case came to light in March 2023 when customs officers at Tan Son Nhat International Airport in Ho Chi Minh City detected drugs in luggage carried by four flight attendants arriving from France.
Authorities found more than 8 kilograms (18 pounds) of ecstasy and more than 3 kilograms (7 pounds) of ketamine and cocaine in the luggage.
The four flight attendants were initially detained but were later not prosecuted after investigators found insufficient grounds to establish their involvement in the trafficking.
The investigation expanded to more than 2,700 suspects in 477 cases, while transactions linked to the network totaled nearly 29 trillion Vietnamese dong ($1.1 billion).
The court is continuing to announce sentences for the remaining defendants.
The VN10 case involves charges including drug trafficking, illegal transportation of drugs, drug possession and organizing illegal drug use.

U.S. Army awards AV $464.8 million laser weapon deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:31:46 UTC
16:31:46 KST

- The US Army awarded AV a $464.8 million contract for 26 LOCUST X3 laser weapons under its first formal directed energy program of record.
- The Other Transaction Agreement runs five years and follows a June demonstration where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth watched the system shoot down drones.
The US Army has awarded defense contractor AV a $464.8 million contract to produce high-energy laser weapons under the Enduring High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program, the Army’s first formal directed energy program of record, according to Laser Wars.
Under the Other Transaction Agreement, AV will deliver 26 of its 30 kilowatt LOCUST X3 laser weapons to the Army over the next five years. The systems are meant to counter low-cost weaponized drones.
The X3 was formally unveiled in March and built specifically for the E-HEL program. It is the latest version of AV’s LOCUST Laser Weapon System, which American troops have already used for counter-drone missions from the Middle East to the US-Mexico border.
The Army’s fiscal year 2027 budget request called for the procurement of two E-HEL systems at $17.4 million apiece, with plans to field up to 24 additional units over the following five and a half years, according to a draft request for proposals from the service’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires published in January.
“This award marks a defining moment not only for AV, but for the future of modern defense,” said AV Chairman and CEO Wahid Nawabi.
“The transition of directed energy from experimentation to an enduring, fielded capability reflects years of collaboration, innovation, and operational success alongside the US Army. We are proud to deliver these production systems and support the Army’s mission with scalable, modular, and cost-effective defense solutions.”
The Army first announced E-HEL in a July 2024 special notice, describing it as a modular system built on lessons from two earlier LOCUST-based programs. One is the 20 kilowatt Palletized-High Energy Laser, which conducted live-fire testing from the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) in October 2025. The other is the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, a vehicle-mounted system tested over the past year from the back of the service’s Infantry Squad Vehicle and Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
The Department of War has gradually expanded its use of laser weapons overseas to protect troops from drones. The Army sent several Palletized-High Energy Laser systems to an undisclosed location, likely within the US Central Command area of operations, starting in 2022. Four Stryker-mounted, 50 kilowatt Directed Energy Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense systems followed in 2024 for in-theater testing before that program was later canceled. In July, the US Air Force disclosed it had deployed several Boeing Compact Laser Weapon System units across Europe as part of a layered air defense network.
The Army’s requirements for E-HEL call for three distinct engagement profiles: 30 one-second shots per minute against high-density target sets, six nine-second shots per minute against low-density sets, and three 17-second shots per minute against hardened targets. The system must also sustain full power for a full minute, with a recharge cycle capped at four minutes.
The draft RFP also required that an E-HEL system arrive with production capacity already in place. AV said it met that requirement with a $30 million manufacturing expansion in New Mexico announced in March.
The contract follows a June demonstration at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth personally observed AV’s LOCUST shoot down drones, according to Laser Wars, which first reported the event. That demonstration also featured nLight’s “P5 version” of the DE M-SHORAD system and Lockheed Martin’s 300 kilowatt Indirect Fire Protection Capability-High Energy Laser prototype, known as Valkyrie. Weeks later, the Pentagon awarded nLight and Lockheed Martin contracts for the 300-500 kilowatt Joint Laser Weapons System, part of the “Golden Dome for America” missile defense effort.
Earlier Army laser efforts struggled to reach production. The Mobile Test Unit, the first vehicle-mounted laser weapon, was judged “neither scalable nor robust enough for Army standards,” while the Government Accountability Office found the DE M-SHORAD system “not mature enough” for full production.
Separately, the US Air Force’s Recovery of Airbase Denied by Ordnance system, a 3 kilowatt Zeus III laser mounted on a Cougar 4×4 MRAP vehicle, is already in sustained production, with contractor Parsons under contract for 29 units.

Belgium reports about 3,000 excess deaths over summer due to heat
Unknown

Belgium reports about 3,000 excess deaths over summer due to heat
BRUSSELS – Heatwaves from June 18 through Aug 16 caused 2,935 excess deaths in Belgium, or 22.6 per cent excess mortality, public health body Sciensano said in a report on Sept 3.
From June 18 through July 3, Belgium recorded its highest excess mortality, with 2,035 additional deaths, or 48.8 per cent above expected levels, Sciensano said.
Starting on June 18, maximum temperatures of around 30 deg C were recorded for 10 consecutive days, including three days of temperatures around 35 deg C, with nights during that period also exceptionally warm.
Sciensano said mortality from June 18 through July 3 was the highest recorded during a heatwave since the start of its analyses in the year 2000.
The two other heatwave periods, from July 4 to 17 and July 28 to Aug 16, saw lower excess mortality, with 535 excess deaths (14.8 per cent) and 365 excess deaths (7 per cent), respectively.
While people aged 65 and older account for most heatwave-related deaths, Sciensano said excess mortality also occurs among younger people.
Europe experienced several heatwaves during the summer, with the UN weather agency in August saying periods of extreme heat are becoming more frequent, intense and longer-lasting as climate change warms the planet. REUTERS

Russia to shut Goethe-Institut branches in response to Germany closing Russian House
Moscow will close all branches of Germany's Goethe-Institut in Russia in response to Berlin's decision to shut down the Russian House of Culture following a drone incident, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Sept. 3.
Drones were discovered at Leipzig Airport on Aug. 4, one of which struck a cargo plane. Another reportedly carried explosives that were intended to strike a Ukrainian Airlines Antonov cargo plane stationed.
Media reports, U.S. intelligence, and then the German government on Sept. 1, all identified Russia as responsible for the hybrid attack.
In addition to closing the Russian House of Culture, Berlin plans to shut Russia's consulate in Bonn and push for tougher sanctions on Moscow, stricter entry controls for Russian citizens and increased pressure on Russia's so-called shadow fleet.
"They consciously took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
The Goethe-Institut is a German non-governmental organization that promotes the German language and international cultural cooperation. It has three branches in Russia, in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk.
Lavrov said Russia plans to close all three. He dismissed accusations that Russia was behind the drone attack at Leipzig Airport.
Western officials have been raising alarm over increasingly frequent cases of suspected sabotage, arson, and cyberattacks, many of which were linked to Russian intelligence.

Dutch swimming water is still polluted

Dutch swimming water increasingly polluted, researchers find
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Swimming water in the Netherlands is still often polluted with chemicals and bacteria, according to new research by an environmental group and The Netherlands Institute for Ecology.
The researchers investigated the water quality from 205 official swimming locations and 57 other popular urban swimming spots
They were looking for 122 pollutants and found excess quantities of 35 substances in ponds, rivers and lakes around the country.
According the report, the number of locations with pollution rising. In particular incidents of blue-green algae have gone up in the past five years.
Water quality testing in the Netherlands focuses primarily on contaminants that cause acute health risks like blue-green algae and E. coli, and doesn’t include industrial substances and pesticides.
The group is calling for for stricter licensing of waste water disposal and increased monitoring of bathing waters.

Nalsar row: SC strikes down BCI orders, says it has 'no statutory power to regulate conduct of students'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:26:11 UTC
16:26:11 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday held that the Bar Council of India has "no statutory authority to regulate the conduct of law students". The court set aside two BCI notifications issued against students of Hyderabad's Nalsar University of Law.A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the order.
The orders were linked to the students' protest over Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's proposed participation in the university's convocation.The court's observation came after the BCI initially directed state Bar Councils not to enrol Nalsar's 2026 law graduates as advocates following a student campaign opposing CJI Surya Kant's proposed participation as chief guest at the university's convocation.Also read - BCI action, U-turn and SC rebuke: How NALSAR students' protest against CJI kicked up a rowThe BCI later withdrew the directive and allowed the graduates to be enrolled while an inquiry was pending.
How the NALSAR row began
The controversy began after several Nalsar students submitted representations asking the university to reconsider its invitation to CJI Surya Kant. The students referred to remarks attributed to the CJI during a hearing concerning alleged police excesses against protesters during a July 20 march to Parliament.
At least six representations were submitted by students from different batches, with the first being sent on July 23. The students argued that inviting the CJI was inconsistent with the university's stated commitment to constitutional rights, access to justice and reasoned engagement with grievances.One representation cited the CJI's response to an offer to show videos of the alleged police action: "We are not interested in videos; we don’t have time to watch." It also quoted him as telling counsel: "Don’t waste our time, and don’t waste your time".The students maintained that their objection was rooted in constitutional values and not disrespect towards the judicial office."We respect the CJI’s position. But we have been taught the Constitution and constitutional values, and we don’t want to support something that goes against those values," a student who was also part of the Student bar council had told TOI.The dispute escalated when BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra directed state Bar Councils not to enrol Nalsar's 2026 law graduates as advocates until further orders.The BCI sought a report from Nalsar identifying students who had allegedly initiated, organised or mobilised the campaign against CJI Surya Kant's participation in the convocation.The council's initial communication stated, “Till further orders, no student of Nalsar University of Law, who has obtained law degree in the year 2026, shall be enrolled by any state bar council as an advocate.”It also said, “A student of Law, having no regard or respect for the highest judicial office of the country, is not expected to be a responsible or sensible advocate, teacher or a judge. Such persons shall always be a liability on the profession. Such conduct reflects adversely upon the person’s suitability for entry into or association with the legal profession and is inconsistent with the dignity, discipline and ethical standards of the legal profession.”The BCI further alleged that some members of Nalsar's academic staff had been involved in "misleading, instigating and misguiding" students.“As per some reliable sources, there exists groupism and dirty politics among some of the academic staff and they have played a very active role in misleading, instigating and misguiding the students. This is a very serious matter. The teachers, instead of involving themselves in their teaching job, are doing nasty politics in the campus. BCI, being the regulator of Legal Education cannot be a mute spectator of such a serious situation.”The directive drew criticism from sections of the legal fraternity, with Supreme Court bar association president Vikas Singh describing the move as arbitrary, illegal and disproportionate, while maintaining that he did not support the students' opposition to the CJI's invitation.
The BCI withdrew its original directive within hours amid the criticism. In its revised communication, Mishra said the council had “thoroughly discussed and deliberated” on the earlier letter and modified its direction.He said the “vast majority” of Nalsar's 2026 graduating students were innocent and “were not inclined to take part in the move of disrespect”. However, he added, “It has been further reported by some reliable sources that a handful of teachers and outsiders were instrumental in instigating innocent students.”The revised decision permitted the 2026 graduates to be enrolled while the BCI awaited an inquiry report from Nalsar.

Pakistan’s Punjab allows ‘secret’ terrorism trials: Why it’s controversial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:25:51 UTC
16:25:51 KST

Pakistan’s Punjab allows ‘secret’ terrorism trials: Why it’s controversial
A single unnamed official can order anonymous judges, prosecutors and witnesses in terrorism cases, with no time limit.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Politicians in Punjab, Pakistan’s most populous province, have passed a law allowing terrorism trials to be held in near-total secrecy, with the judge, prosecutor and witnesses permitted to remain anonymous.
Under the law, a person facing the country’s most serious criminal charge could be convicted without learning who heard the case against them, who prosecuted it or who testified.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What are Pakistan’s controversial constitutional amendments about?
- list 2 of 4Pakistan passes amendment empowering parliament to pick top judge
- list 3 of 4How would Pakistan’s 27th Amendment reshape its military and courts?
- list 4 of 4Pakistan’s Punjab police kill 900 people in eight months: What’s going on?
The trial record can be sealed, and an appeal could be heard by judges never told who presided over the original trial.
The Anti-Terrorism (Punjab Amendment) Bill 2026 passed the Punjab Assembly on August 31, after opposition politicians staged a walkout in protest.
Four days earlier, the government had appeared to relent, agreeing to have the bill reviewed by the law department or a parliamentary committee.
When it returned to the floor, it was unchanged and passed without amendment on Monday.
The law has drawn criticism from opposition politicians, lawyers, rights groups and analysts, who say it concentrates enormous power in a single, unnamed official and could be used against government critics.
What does the new law do?
The law lets the government appoint a senior bureaucrat as a “designated authority” tasked with deciding what cases are to be heard under the special provisions earmarked in the legislation.
The official’s identity is kept confidential, known only to the chief justice of the Lahore High Court.
The official can declare any terrorism case, or even a whole category of them, a “special security case” if they conclude that the people involved need special “protection”.
The law does not clearly define the parameters that need to be met, and the accused cannot contest being placed under this category. Once the official requests it, the chief justice assigns the case to a sitting anti-terrorism court judge. A panel of five public prosecutors is drawn up, and the official picks one.
From there, the identities of the judge, prosecutor, police officers, witnesses and defence lawyers cannot be disclosed under any circumstances. Official titles are used instead of names, and court orders are signed without revealing who signed them.
Witnesses are identified only by codes. Hearings can be held over videolink, including from inside a prison, with voice-altering technology used to disguise participants.
The case file is sealed and held jointly by the chief justice and the official.
The law includes no expiry date, and a final clause allows the government to adopt “such other measures as it may deem appropriate”, leaving room to add further powers without further legislation.
Why is the government doing this, and why now?
The government’s official justification, laid out in the bill itself, points to increased cases of attacks by armed groups, and rising threats faced by judges, prosecutors, investigators and witnesses. It argues that the existing law does not adequately protect them.
Speaker Malik Muhammad Ahmad Khan, on the floor of the assembly, invoked Pakistan’s toll from terrorism over the past two decades to argue that the assembly was the right forum to strengthen prosecutions.
Khalid Mahmood Ranjha, the legislator who tabled the bill, told Al Jazeera that the chief justice, not the designated authority, nominates the trial judge.
“There is no interference of the executive,” he said.
He dismissed fears that the law could be used against political opponents.
“It is just an apprehension,” the politician said, calling the criticism “propaganda to politicise and make the law controversial”.
“This law [is] only for hardened terrorists.”
But no single attack or case has been publicly named as the trigger.
Punjab also records only a small share of Pakistan’s terrorism-related deaths each year.
The vast majority occur in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, which together account for more than 90 percent of the country’s terrorism deaths.
Al Jazeera contacted Azma Bokhari, Punjab’s provincial minister for information, Marriyum Aurangzeb, senior minister in the Punjab government, and Rana Muhammad Iqbal, Punjab’s law minister, but did not receive a response.
What are critics saying?
Rida Hosain, a Lahore-based constitutional lawyer, said the threats facing judges, prosecutors and witnesses in Pakistan are real.
“There is no denying that Pakistan’s people and land have paid a devastating price for terrorism,” she told Al Jazeera. But she said no one who has actually read the amendment “can reasonably claim that it is consistent with due process”.
Opposition politicians argued the law violates the constitutional right to a fair trial and hands judicial-style powers to an unelected official with no oversight.
Ahmer Rasheed Bhatti, the independent legislator affiliated with jailed opposition leader Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaaf (PTI) party, led objections on the floor.
“It creates a parallel procedure in which the executive, not the court, decides what a fair trial will look like,” he told Al Jazeera.
The designated authority must consult the chief justice, he said, but does not need their agreement.
Hosain said the secrecy itself removes a basic safeguard.
“By introducing faceless courts, an accused is deprived of the ability to challenge judicial bias and safeguard judicial impartiality,” she told Al Jazeera. “While this law remains in force, the right to a fair trial and due process is effectively suspended in Punjab.”
The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) also raised the alarm.
“The bill does not adequately define the circumstances in which these extraordinary powers may be invoked,” the commission’s spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
That, HRCP said, creates scope for abuse against ordinary citizens, political opponents or protesters in the name of security.
Mian Dawood, a Lahore-based constitutional lawyer, said existing law already lets courts protect witnesses and hold closed hearings under a judge’s control.
The new law, he said, moves that control to the executive rather than filling a gap. He said someone wrongly caught up in the system would have little recourse. Remedies such as a malicious-prosecution claim exist on paper but are “impracticable” in Pakistan’s courts, he said.
“A citizen has to suffer the misuse of powers by the state authorities,” the constitutional expert said.
Majid Nizami, a Lahore-based analyst, told Al Jazeera that Punjab province’s original antiterrorism law — enacted in 1997 and now amended with the controversial new provisions — was also misused.
“It looked very good on paper too,” Nizami said. “But what happened, eventually, was that it was used for political point-scoring and political manoeuvring.”
He said the law has, since 1997, been applied against nearly every major political party in Pakistan.
Nizami said he could not identify a Punjab case in the past decade where witness intimidation had derailed a prosecution — the ostensible justification for shielding the privacy of prosecutors and judges under the new amendments.
But there are older precedents. One case that stands out involved rebel commander Malik Ishaq. Ishaq co-founded Lashkar-e-Jhangvi, a sectarian group blamed for killing hundreds of people, most of them Shia Muslims.
Named in more than 200 criminal cases, he repeatedly walked free after witnesses and even judges grew too frightened to move against him, until he was killed in a 2015 shootout after armed men freed him from police custody.
Has Pakistan tried this before?
Punjab itself passed a law last year giving authorities the power to detain terrorism suspects for up to three months without charge, part of a wider wave in which Balochistan and the federal government passed near-identical detention powers in 2025.
Balochistan passed a similar law in September 2025, letting a senior official anonymously flag cases for the same kind of concealed proceedings. It has been in force for about a year, without any publicly known case of its use.
Ranjha told Al Jazeera that Balochistan and Sindh had “already passed this law,” and that Punjab needed to follow.
While Sindh has amended its own antiterrorism law, it is only to let the provincial government resize or abolish antiterrorism courts based on caseload. It introduces no comparable anonymity or secrecy provisions. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has not amended its law along either track.
Salman Ghani, a political analyst, said Punjab’s situation differs from Balochistan’s for a simpler reason. “Punjab is still governable, and we don’t see terrorism incidents here every other day,” he told Al Jazeera.
Bhatti argued that gap was telling.
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which, alongside Balochistan, faces the overwhelming majority of the country’s terrorism violence, has not adopted secret trials; Punjab, which faces almost none of it, has.
“The federal government looks instrumental,” Bhatti told Al Jazeera. “Provinces appear to have been asked to enact similar amendments.”
He does not believe Punjab’s government developed that appetite on its own. “You are not looking at a local caseload,” he said. “You are looking at a request.”
What happens next?
A legal challenge looks likely.
Opposition politicians have argued that the law conflicts with the constitution’s fair-trial guarantees and oversteps what a provincial assembly can legislate, since antiterrorism law falls under federal jurisdiction.
With no sunset clause built in, the law does not expire on its own; whether it survives will most likely be decided in court rather than by the assembly that passed it.
Bhatti drew a comparison with the last time Pakistan departed this far from ordinary courts: military trials for civilians, introduced only through a constitutional amendment after the 2014 Peshawar Army Public School massacre, and built with a two-year limit unless parliament renewed it.
“You do not need a faceless provincial trial in the safer province,” he told Al Jazeera, “Unless the facelessness is the point.”

Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations against companies in Denmark's defense industry, public broadcaster DR reported Wednesday, citing the Danish intelligence service.
"We see that Danish companies are also targets for concrete Russian sabotage planning, and that Russian intelligence services are actively preparing sabotage operations aimed at the defense industry in Denmark," said Emil Graesholm, head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET).
Graesholm also told Danish newspaper Berlingske that authorities had uncovered specific Russian plans for sabotage operations against companies in Denmark.
"Therefore, this is not just a warning that it might come to Denmark one day. We are already seeing the planning now. Very concretely," he said.
The companies that could be targeted include firms in the defense industry linked to military aid to Ukraine, according to PET.
The intelligence service said it has identified "concrete examples" of Russia attempting to recruit ordinary Danes through social media and other online platforms.
Such individuals could be asked to perform tasks including photographing companies or installations for use in planning sabotage operations, PET said.
"It is extremely serious if ordinary Danes help Russian intelligence services – either intentionally or unknowingly," Graesholm said.
PET said it works closely with Denmark's Defense Intelligence Service and the Danish Agency for Social Security and Preparedness, and regularly updates police districts on the threat assessment.
"We have continuously briefed selected companies and industry organizations on the threat picture, and together with other authorities we have advised on specific security measures," Graesholm said.
He added that the defense industry broadly needed to take the “necessary security measures" to protect itself.
Graesholm said PET considered the threat sufficiently concrete to publicly warn about it.
"It is such a concrete identification and preparation that we find it necessary to go out with the message that it is a threat that must be taken seriously," he said.
The Confederation of Danish Industry said it was taking PET's assessment seriously and was in close contact with relevant authorities.
"The changed threat picture calls for increased attention from companies, but also for calm and proportionality," said Rasmus Anderskouv, head of security and preparedness at the organization.
Anderskouv said companies should assess their specific exposure and ensure their security and emergency preparedness measures were functioning properly.
Flemming Splidsboel, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, described PET's announcement as serious and said the threat was "new," "concrete" and "advanced."
Former Defense Intelligence Service chief analyst Jakob Kaarsbo said PET's decision to speak publicly could be intended to signal to Russia that Danish authorities were aware of its activities.

Russia preparing new AK-12+ rifle for serial production

- Kalashnikov unveiled a mock-up of its new 5.45mm AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, saying serial production is being prepared.
- The rifle, built for special forces, has a thicker barrel, modified sights and removed sling, bayonet and grenade launcher fittings compared to the standard AK-12.
Kalashnikov Concern unveiled a mock-up of its new AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, presenting a 5.45mm weapon built for improved shooting precision.
The rifle is on display in the Voin Center pavilion at the Far East Street exhibition, part of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, running September 1-4 on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University.
Kalashnikov, part of the state defense conglomerate Rostec, said the weapon is now being prepared for serial production. The company described the AK-12+ as a high-precision small-arms system built on the existing AK-12 platform, intended primarily for special forces units.
The system was developed under the supervision of Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Presidential Plenipotentiary Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev, the company said.
The AK-12+ carries a thicker barrel than the standard AK-12, with a threaded muzzle designed to accept a flash suppressor or a muzzle brake. Kalashnikov modified the rifle’s mechanical sights and widened the contour of the gas cylinder to match the new barrel profile. Fittings previously used to attach a sling swivel, an underbarrel grenade launcher and a bayonet have been removed. The mock-up shown in Vladivostok featured an extended stock.
The rifle will also carry electro-optical sights. Kalashnikov said the sights are meant to improve accuracy at medium range in both daytime and nighttime conditions.
At the forum, Kalashnikov and the Voin Center signed a cooperation agreement. Under the deal, the two organizations will jointly develop engineering skills among the center’s cadets and expand the material and technical resources at its regional branches.
The Voin Center, formally the Center for Military-Sports Training and Patriotic Education of Youth, was created on presidential order in 2023. It trains teenagers aged 14 to 18 and reservists aged 18 to 35, and now operates branches in more than 20 Russian regions.
Kalashnikov already produces several variants of the AK-12 platform. The baseline AK-12 is chambered in 5.45x39mm, weighs about 3.6 kg (7.9 pounds) unloaded, has a 415 mm (16.3 inch) barrel and fires at a cyclic rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. The family also includes the AK-15, chambered in 7.62x39mm, and the export-oriented AK-19, chambered in 5.56x45mm NATO.

Chalmers can't avoid questions on house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Unknown

2026-09-03

analysis
Chalmers questioned about house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Jim Chalmers sits alone in a darkened press conference room, selfie camera on, chatting to his social media followers about the latest economic data.
But of course he wasn't asked any questions in his pre-filmed video. It was more an avenue for him to declare the economy was "robust" despite challenges from the Middle East war, point out more people are switching to EVs and that housing construction is up before he had to face reporters half an hour later.
He fronted up to the press conference for a tense back and forth where almost every single question was house prices.
When the government made the U-turn on its promise not to wind back negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, it did so armed with Treasury forecasts. Growth, the budget papers said, would slow by 2 per cent over a number of years.
Property data firm Cotality this week flagged drops in every capital city in August, and predictions from the Commonwealth Bank that prices could drop as much as 13 per cent have some mortgage holders understandably worried.
Chalmers has largely brushed off movements in price as not unusual and backed in his department's forecast. "Buying a house is a long-term proposition," he said.
The major factor at play here is recent interest rate rises, he argued, not the government's tax changes.
That argument wasn't made easier for him either, after fellow frontbencher Matt Thistlethwaite declared on News24 (formerly Sky News Australia) there was "no doubt" the tax changes contributed to house prices falling.
"I think that's one of a number of reasons," Chalmers told ABC's Sally Sara when asked again this morning.
Opting out of algorithms?
Thistlethwaite may have made the sell a little bit harder for Chalmers, but the treasurer named the "disturbing rubbish" pushed by social media algorithms as the thing making his job more difficult.
"Our society, our social cohesion, the way that we come at big problems including in my part of the shop in the economy is hampered, not helped, by the way algorithms are dominating people's day," Chalmers said.
It's a similar argument that's been put before by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who has said algorithms are fuelling polarisation. Albanese is supportive of the idea that Australians should have more control over what they are shown online.
But that doesn't go as far as what consent advocate Chanel Contos has put forward: an opt-in algorithm for social media accounts. If adopted, it would be a world where we'd return to chronological feeds where our friends' content is shown instead of strangers. It's an idea backed by some of the crossbench and the Greens amid concerns social media is exposing young people to misogynistic content.
There seems to be no disagreement among the leaders of the major political parties that some of the content fed to people is toxic. But for some it's a bit of a chicken and egg argument.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan, for example, this week argued it is the "feminisation" of the school curriculum and a lack of male teachers that pushes boys towards such content. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor also accused teachers of running agendas in the classroom.
Contos argued the algorithm is the missing piece here — young boys are being shown this content whether they seek it out or not.
Coalition focuses on tobacco
Meanwhile, the Coalition finally released its plan to slash the tobacco excise. The plan also included a proposal to legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches.
An estimated 80 per cent of the cigarettes and other nicotine products consumed in Australia last year were illegal, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Last month, One Nation revealed its own plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent. The opposition went one further, revealing a proposal to cut the excise by 80 per cent. It argues it would be enough to tip the scales and redirect customers towards legal tobacco.
The Parliamentary Budget Office costed the policy but the Coalition has not released the costings or the assumptions underpinning them.
It says its plan, paired with a further $200 million spend on law enforcement to support more raids, arrests and closure of illegal tobacco shops, would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over the first four years — double the current forecasts.
That hinges on the idea that cutting the price would encourage Australians to ditch the black market and that illegal distributers wouldn't also drop prices to compete — something Taylor disagrees with.
Back in the Pacific
While this was all going down at home, Albanese returned to palm tree-lined beaches and crystal clear blue water of Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF).
It's not the first time the prime minister has visited — he made the trip to the small Pacific nation last year for a pre-wedding holiday with now wife Jodie Haydon.
The early stages of the meeting were overshadowed by tensions between China and Taiwan about Taipei's increased presence at the gathering (Palau has diplomatic ties with Taiwan) and the number of leaders who decided to skip the annual forum.
Albanese said he wasn't distracted by all that as he pressed on with discussions about climate change and tackling the issue of drug trafficking in the Pacific, where Australia and New Zealand's appetite for illegal drugs has caused real issues.
Leaders were also due to discuss the matter of China's test-fire of a nuclear-capable missile carrying a dummy warhead in the Pacific — with host nation Palau indicating it would like to issue a united statement about the test.
Despite escaping PIF without another T-shirt faux pas, it wasn't all smooth sailing for Albanese, who had a tense press conference of his own at the forum about United Nations climate event being held in Fiji and Tuvalu next month.
The pre-COP events are organised by Australia and are part of the compromise Australia struck with Türkiye last year after we bowed out of hosting the climate conference in Adelaide.
But so far just five leaders from outside of the Pacific have confirmed they're making the trip, which was designed to highlight the impact of climate change on Pacific nations. It's not typical that leaders usually attend a pre-COP event.
Asked about this, Albanese said the focus on the non-Pacific leaders was "disrespectful".
Loading
Treaty yourself
And finally, have you been looking for the perfect gift for the Kiwi in your family? Or perhaps you have a long-distance American pen pal you need a stocking stuffer for?
Don't worry, Defence Minister Richard Marles has you covered for inspiration. He presented a framed copy of the full text of the ANZUS Treaty on vellum, and signed by Albanese, to a member of the Trump administration.
Vellum is a thin, translucent material made of calfskin and commonly used by artists.
Why are we presenting Albanese autographed military treaties to our allies? To mark the 75th anniversary. You can't get that at the shops.

The head of the powerful Badr militia, Hadi al-Amiri, appears to have admitted that his group was behind the killing of thousands of protesters in Iraq in October 2019. For years, it was known that Iranian-backed militias were likely unleashed by the government to suppress the protests. However, there was a lack of confirmation and evidence for the role of the militias. Now, the head of the powerful Badr militia. In Iraq, social media is focused on this story.
In 2019, Iraq was in a transition period. Adil Abdul-Mahdi was prime minister. He was relatively weak and ineffectual. Powerful Iranian-backed militias that had been empowered by the war on ISIS were increasing their control across Iraq. Instead of Iraq receiving a kind of “peace dividend” when the war on ISIS largely ended in 2018, Iraq transitioned to new rounds of violence and economic stagnation. Militias also began targeting US-led Coalition forces.
Tishreen movement
This led to protests in October 2019. The protests have often been called the Tishreen movement. Amnesty International noted in 2025 that “Iraqi authorities continue to persecute activists and protestors while failing to deliver meaningful justice and accountability for the killings of hundreds and the maiming of thousands of protesters by security forces and militias or to reveal the fate and whereabouts of those disappeared, Amnesty International said today.”
Amiri uses the word “fitna,” which has a number of meanings but essentially accuses the protesters of sedition and heresy. It accuses the protesters of undermining the state and trying to create civil strife. Amiri was basically admitting that the Iranian-backed militias, such as Badr, massacred hundreds or thousands of people. He was accusing the protesters of being traitors who were then put down.
Amiri’s speech comes as Iraq is seeking to disarm and rein in the militias. Several of the most powerful militias have said they will not disarm or have presented new conditions to placing their arms under state control. These include Harakat Hezbollah al Nujaba, Kataib Hezbollah and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada. Badr is not usually seen as one of the most extreme militias. However, Amiri has long played a role as a power behind the throne in Iraq, with Badr as an enforcer of Iran’s agenda.
Lawyer submits report to Prosecutor General
Amiri’s comments have now led to controversy in Iraq. Some social media have been circulating images from the October 2019 protests showing the protesters being oppressed. A report on September 2 said that a lawyer has now submitted a report to the Prosecutor General of Wasit Province, demanding an investigation and lawsuit into Badr and the comments by Amiri. Al-Sharqiya TV in Iraq described the lawyer as seeking to sue Amiri after his statements.
There is debate in Arabic media in the region now about what Amiri said.
Has he revealed the “true face” of the “resistance” by appearing to admit the mass killings? “Was it a slip of the tongue by Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization and one of the most prominent leaders of the Coordinating Framework that runs the sectarian power structure in Iraq?” another report asks. One question is whether his statement is actually a threat today that the militias could use force again against protesters or against a government that seeks to disarm them.
Asharq al Awsat in Arabic notes that “the wave of anger and popular criticism against the head of the Badr Organization, Hadi al-Amiri, continues, following statements in which he admitted the involvement of what he called the ‘resistance’ in the events that accompanied the ‘October Movement’ of 2019, which lasted for about two years and during which more than 600 demonstrators were killed and more than 20,000 others were injured.” Families of victims now say they will file lawsuits. There are calls to prosecute Amiri.
This is important because unlike some of the other militia leaders, Amiri has always been able to avoid sanctions and controversy. Badr has been the one major Iranian-backed militia in Iraq that is not sanctioned by the US. Most of the others are seen as Foreign Terrorist Organizations or Specially Designated Terrorist Groups. As such, Badr has a unique role. It continues to play a major role in the Interior Ministry and other parts of Iraq.
The role of the militias in the massacres is very similar to the IRGC’s role in Iran in massacring protesters. In January 2026, Iran was accused of massacring tens of thousands of people. It has done this before, and it has exported this model to Iraq and other countries. The militias have also kidnapped journalists and assassinated people. They have also attacked Americans and targeted the Kurdistan Region.
