“Shielded his comrades with his body”: How Russian propaganda turned a pedophile fugitive into a war hero
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
06:03:21 UTC
15:03:21 KST

On Sept. 2, schools across Russia’s Komi Republic held lessons in courage dedicated to Alexander Vlasenkov, a corporal who was killed fighting in Ukraine. By decree of Vladimir Putin, Vlasenkov was posthumously awarded the title of Hero of Russia. A monument and several memorial plaques have been erected in his home region, and a museum dedicated to him has opened at his former school. On the day of the lessons, schoolchildren watched a film about Vlasenkov and learned about his life. The campaign to glorify the fallen corporal’s “feat” was spearheaded by Alexander Matovnikov, a former member of Putin’s security detail who also happened to advise Vlasenkov to volunteer for the war. However, as The Insider has found, Vlasenkov had been placed on a special Interior Ministry register for pedophilia and went to the front to evade police supervision and escape massive debts.
Expelled from the Interior Ministry university after trying to rape a teenager
Alexander Vlasenkov, a world and Russian junior champion in hand-to-hand combat, took out 500,000 rubles in loans in his own name between 2019 and 2021, and nearly another 400,000 rubles using his grandmother’s passport. By then, he had spent a year evading both debt collectors from RVS LLC and court bailiffs. He even skipped a promotional event in Kaliningrad, fearing he would be detained at the airport during a police check.
Police officers also made regular visits to Vlasenkov due to the fact that he was on a special Interior Ministry register for pedophilia, a legacy of his days as a cadet at the St. Petersburg University of the Interior Ministry, where he tried to rape a 13-year-old boy before being scared off by passersby.
The university authorities quickly swept the scandal under the rug, but Vlasenkov, who was in his second year, was immediately expelled. Mandatory military service in the air defense forces, however, spared him from prison.
After being demobilized in 2019, Vlasenkov found work as a coach in Irkutsk before police officers came to the school and warned its management about their new trainer's sexual proclivities. Vlasenkov was eventually forced to return home to the village of Chim in Russia’s Komi Republic and live with his grandmother, Zoya Ivanovna, who had raised him. That grandmother, incidentally, is well known throughout the area and is fondly called “our craftswoman” for her decades of work making unique dolls.
It wasn't Vlasenkov's first homecoming. In 2015, when he won the Russian junior hand-to-hand combat championship, the entire village turned out to welcome him, and a red carpet was rolled out in front of his school. The second return home was far less triumphant — Vlasenkov took a job as an electrician, and occasionally, at the request of his first coach, Khodzhar Isaev, he gave hand-to-hand combat seminars. He was deeply afraid that the local police officer supervising him might reveal something about his past.
The village of Chim has a population of just 297. It boasts a community center located in a barracks and an orphanage where Vlasenkov’s grandmother worked all her life. Most of the houses are in a dilapidated state, and there is virtually no work.
In early 2022, desperate to climb out of debt, Vlasenkov turned to his brother Igor and his coach Isaev for financial help. But his brother, who lived in Syktyvkar, was heavily in debt himself, while Isaev said he was ill and spending large amounts of money on expensive treatment. He died in 2023.
Vlasenkov then traveled to Moscow to seek help from the International Hand-to-Hand Combat Federation (IHCF). He was well known there: in 2009, he won the national Children of Beslan Memorial Tournament, took first place in the "My Republic Is a Sporting Republic" competition, and in 2015 became the Russian junior hand-to-hand combat champion.
In Moscow, Vlasenkov was received by Alexander Matovnikov, chairman of the IHCF supervisory board and a former member of Putin’s security detail. A colonel general, Matovnikov has served as deputy commander-in-chief of Russia’s Ground Forces since January 22, 2020. Pro-Kremlin media have described him as a “true Russian officer.”
However, the general told Vlasenkov that the federation had no spare money and advised him to volunteer for the “special military operation,” which Vlasenkov did. The State Duma only banned people suspected of pedophilia from signing contracts to serve in the “special military operation” in 2024.
Vlasenkov served as a reconnaissance sniper with the 200th Coastal Defense Brigade, attached to the Northern Fleet (military unit 08275). He was killed on Sept. 2, 2022, during fighting near the village of Udy in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region.
The awards office
Vlasenkov’s story might have gone unnoticed, like the deaths of hundreds of thousands of other Russians who signed a contract with the Ministry of Defense. But General Matovnikov, the man who had advised him to volunteer for the front, changed all that.
After the disastrous start to the “special military operation,” Kremlin propaganda needed heroes, and Vlasenkov was an ideal fit: a young man from the provinces, practically an orphan, an athlete and a champion. That was when the campaign to build up his fresh image began.
Propaganda needed heroes, and Vlasenkov was an ideal fit: a young man from the provinces, practically an orphan, an athlete and a champion
Matovnikov himself began his career at the KGB’s Alpha Special Operations Center, eventually rising to become the unit’s first deputy commander. He took part in the storming of the hospital in Budyonnovsk in 1995 after it was seized by Shamil Basayev’s gang and was one of the commanders of the counterterrorism operations to free hostages at the Dubrovka theater in Moscow in 2002 (known as the Nord-Ost siege) and at the school in Beslan in 2004 (where hundreds of people were killed).
Matovnikov was later assigned to the security detail of Chechen head Akhmad Kadyrov as the FSB’s representative and acquired the nickname “Chekist.” On May 9, 2004, Kadyrov was killed in a bombing at Dynamo Stadium in Grozny. Matovnikov was in Moscow at the time, celebrating Victory Day.
Matovnikov’s immediate superior is Alexei Dyumin, who has been touted as a possible successor to Putin. After Dyumin moved to the Defense Ministry, Matovnikov took over his post as head of the Special Operations Service, serving as a deputy head of the GRU. In that capacity, Matovnikov repeatedly traveled to Syria on inspection missions. He did not take part in combat, but Putin awarded him the Hero of Russia title in 2017.
This past June, the Navalny LIVE YouTube channel published an investigation into how Matovnikov built his career under Putin, turning the war into a source of multibillion-ruble enrichment.
By the time of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Matovnikov was serving as deputy commander-in-chief of Russia’s Ground Forces. Through the Defense Ministry’s press service, pro-Kremlin media, and Z-bloggers, he set the propaganda machine in motion to promote Vlasenkov's memory.
On Oct. 22, 2022, a month and a half after Vlasenkov’s death, Putin issued a decree posthumously awarding him the title of Hero of Russia. His grandmother, however, was not invited to the Kremlin — the award was presented to her at the Komi Republic's regional administration building in Syktyvkar.
A source for The Insider in the Presidential Administration explained how such awards are processed:
“In short, Vladimir Vladimirovich doesn’t deal with routine matters — he has plenty of other things to worry about. State orders, medals, and certificates of honor are handled by Vladimir Osipov, head of the Presidential Directorate for State Awards. He is also a former KGB officer, and the president trusts him completely. Or they are handled by his deputy, Ivan Kalashnikov, who came to the Presidential Administration from the Ministry of Construction.
Before the start of the special military operation, there was stricter oversight: candidates were checked for criminal records and anything questionable in their backgrounds. But now all those checks have become pointless — the guys are overwhelmed. The Defense Ministry submits nominations for awards in huge batches, and half of those killed have criminal records.
Initial checks are carried out by the department responsible for preparing documents for state awards, headed by Irina Valyaeva, whose husband is a military pilot.
Heroes of Russia are a separate matter. If the candidates come from the FSB or intelligence services, their cases are handled by the department responsible for classified documents within the awards directorate. Irina Mitetele is responsible for processing the paperwork in those cases.
Sometimes a nomination may have a note attached saying, ‘Request from Slutsky, LDPR,’ or ‘From Zhdanov, SVR,’ or ‘Vavilov, Almaz-Antey,’ or simply ‘from Rotenberg.’
The documents then go to the presidential administration office. Its computers already contain completed, numbered forms bearing seals and Vladimir Vladimirovich’s facsimile signature — all you have to do is enter the surname. Award ceremonies at the Kremlin are timed to coincide with various dates. For the most part, the documents are sent to military enlistment offices in the deceased recipient’s place of residence. That’s the whole process.”
"He asked us to call him Shurik"
State propaganda went into full gear to glorify Vlasenkov. A monument was erected in his hometown, and at the school he attended, a museum was opened with funding from Transneft-Sever JSC. Among the exhibits is the desk used by the slain mercenary.
A postage stamp was issued soon afterward, and a photo of Vlasenkov was posted on the website of the All-Russian Federation of Applied Hand-to-Hand Combat (AFPRB). He appears alongside Matovnikov, Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov, and Alexei Katerinichev, a former FSB officer who was killed near Kherson in September 2022 in a Ukrainian missile strike.
In December 2022, the Komi Republican Television Channel (YURGAN) released a documentary titled Alexander Vlasenkov’s Last Height, produced in the style of a Soviet propaganda film.
The film makes no mention of the fact that Vlasenkov had effectively fled to the front to evade police supervision and court bailiffs. Instead, it dwells on the purported details of his final battle near the village of Udy:
“When Vlasenkov saw that the nationalists had decided to surrender, he believed: here it is, another victory! So he stepped forward toward the raised white flag. Perhaps Vlasenkov wanted to save the lives of those who had realized that there was no point in resisting. But the enemy proved treacherous and, instead of surrendering, met our soldiers with bullets. The hero shielded his comrades with his body.”
“He asked us to call him Shurik. I still keep his poems,” his first teacher, Nina Torlopova, says in the film.
“One of Alexander’s favorite subjects was history. The Order of the Patriotic War made an indelible impression on him,” the narrator says.
“He was never afraid to take responsibility and always tried to help. And patriotism was not just a word to him,” says Abdusator Niyazov, the military commissar for Udorsky District, reading from a teleprompter.
The propaganda piece ends on an equally bombastic note: “He always strove for the heights, and he conquered this height too, although it turned out to be his last.”

“Islamic NATO”: how will the new alliance between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia affect the region?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

In August 2026, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca. It will operate, in a sense, on the principle of NATO: an attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all. The idea of an “Arab” or “Islamic NATO” has been discussed for years, but previous initiatives never developed into full-fledged defense alliances. The current group emerged against the backdrop of the confrontation between the United States and Iran, but its goal is not war with Tehran, says Middle East expert Marianna Belenkaya. The alliance is intended not for military action but to deter other regional players, including Israel — a prospect that is certainly cause for concern in Jerusalem.
The Mecca agreement
On Aug. 7, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the “Joint Defense Agreement,” better known as the “Mecca Agreement” as a result of the location of the meeting. In a joint statement, the three leaders made clear that “an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be considered an attack on all participants in the agreement.”
Under the alliance, a ministerial committee modeled on NATO will be established, along with a secretariat headquartered in Saudi Arabia. The countries also plan to hold joint military exercises, develop weapons, and introduce various technologies. At the same time, the parties do not seek to replace any existing alliances, and their trilateral partnership does not obligate them to withdraw from other blocs or agreements.
The document itself has still not been made public. Its details are known only from statements by the participating countries. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, for example, compared the agreement with Article 5 of the 1949 North Atlantic Treaty, which provided the legal foundation for NATO.
He also said that the new alliance is not directed against Iran or any other country, but serves as a joint commitment to ensure the security of the three allies. No country will be considered a threat unless an attack is carried out against one of the member states. In that event, the country under attack will have to request assistance and determine what kind of help is needed.
According to Fidan, support could range from intelligence and logistical assistance to the supply of ammunition and, at a later stage, the deployment of military units, depending on the scale of the threat.
Support could range from intelligence and logistical assistance to the supply of ammunition
Notably, even after the signing of the “Mecca Agreement,” new attacks on Saudi Arabia by pro-Iranian forces led neither Pakistan nor Turkey to announce any direct military intervention.
Storm clouds over Saudi Arabia
On July 13, the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia after forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by Riyadh, struck Sana’a airport in order to prevent a plane from Tehran from landing there.
Reuters later reported, citing four sources, that the plane was carrying commanders and advisers from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as well as components for missiles and drones (even if Iran and the Houthis denied this). According to Reuters, Tehran asked the Houthis to be prepared to block the oil route through the Red Sea in the event of further U.S. strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure.
On July 20, the Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, followed by attacks on Saudi oil facilities toward the end of the month. All this threatened Saudi Arabia’s alternative energy export corridor through the Red Sea at a time when instability in the Strait of Hormuz had already disrupted the traditional shipping routes used by the Gulf states.
The Houthis are believed to have acted in coordination with Iraqi pro-Iranian groups under the supervision of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and some of the attacks against Saudi Arabia did indeed come from Iraqi territory. The attacks continued into August, but there was no announcement that the collective defense mechanism had been invoked or that Pakistan or Turkey would respond militarily — not even after three Pakistani nationals were killed in a Houthi attack on a vessel in the Red Sea. In response to that incident, Islamabad merely issued a strong condemnation of the strike.
Saudi Arabia has been busy on the coalition-building front. On July 30, the kingdom announced the creation of the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition (MMDC) to protect the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden. Representatives of 43 countries and the European Union attended its first meeting, while 14 states endorsed the joint statement. By Aug. 14, the number of signatories had risen to 15.
The coalition’s full list of participants has not been published, but media reports have named Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Pakistan, Turkey, Egypt, Jordan, Yemen, Bangladesh, Sudan, Djibouti, Somalia, the Comoros, and Nigeria. It is also known that the coalition will be commanded by a Saudi representative, with a Pakistani nominee serving as his deputy, at least initially.
The coalition is envisioned as a defensive structure operating within the framework of the UN Charter and international maritime law. Its stated goal is to ensure freedom of navigation, rather than to attack any particular state or organization.
Operationally, it envisages coordinated naval patrols, surveillance, intelligence sharing, joint operational planning, and initiatives to strengthen military capabilities in the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden. Participation in military operations remains a sovereign decision for each member state.
As with the trilateral pact, the emphasis appears to be on deterrence. It is no coincidence that NATO, of which Turkey has been a member since 1952, is cited as the model.
According to Turkish Foreign Minister Fidan, NATO’s main deterrent capability is defensive in nature and is based on the message: “When attacking us, bear in mind that we are a military power, a large community. Do not test our strength.”
Not the first attempt at an “Islamic NATO”
There have been repeated attempts to create an “Islamic (and/or narrower Arab) NATO.” For example, the Arab League considered establishing joint armed forces, but all such plans foundered either on rivalries among member states or on changing political realities.
The Baghdad Pact of 1955, an anti-Soviet military and political alliance between Iraq, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, and the United Kingdom created at London’s initiative, was more symbolic than a genuine military bloc, and it did not last long. Iraq withdrew in 1959 in the aftermath of its revolution the previous year, after which the pact was renamed the Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) before collapsing completely as a result of the 1979 Islamic Revolution in Iran.
After the 1990–91 Gulf War, the Arab monarchies, Egypt, and Syria adopted the Damascus Declaration and sought to establish a more robust regional security system, but the project did not survive disputes over funding and mutual distrust. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) likewise failed to develop into a fully fledged joint defense alliance, even if it still has joint military structures, including the Peninsula Shield Force, established in the 1980s.
Efforts to create a common defense system were repeatedly hampered by differing perceptions of threats among the Gulf states, particularly over Iran, as well as rivalry among the monarchies themselves. The 2017 crisis was a particularly clear example: three GCC members — Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain — severed ties with the fourth, Qatar.
A more practical example was the Saudi-led Arab coalition in Yemen, established in March 2015 to support the government of Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi against the Houthis. Unlike many “Arab NATO” projects, it actually conducted a years-long joint military campaign. But it, too, had its limitations: Pakistan refused to send the troops requested by Riyadh, Qatar was expelled from the coalition after the 2017 crisis, and the interests of Saudi Arabia and the UAE also diverged.
Attempts to establish a regional system were made from outside the region as well, primarily by the United States. Under the administration of Barack Obama, Washington discussed two competing proposals with regional states — the Saudi-backed “Islamic Forces” and the Egyptian “Arab Forces” — while also seeking to expand the Arab League’s capacity for peacekeeping, stabilization, and humanitarian operations.
Experts noted that the United States was interested in reducing its burden of providing security in the Middle East, but disagreements among the Arab states emerged at the outset: who would lead whom and who would answer to whom?
Disagreements among the Arab countries emerged from the outset: who would lead whom and who would answer to whom
During Donald Trump’s first term saw the proposal to create a Middle East Strategic Alliance (MESA) made up of the six GCC states, plus Egypt and Jordan. Containing Iran’s influence was one of its main objectives, but the project never developed into a fully fledged structure. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Bahrain took the toughest stance toward Tehran, while Qatar, Kuwait and Oman preferred to keep channels of communication open, and Egypt and Jordan did not want the alliance to become a mechanism for military confrontation with Iran. These differences were compounded by the Qatar crisis, a struggle over leadership, and disputes regarding the new organization's general operations.
The fact that the new "Mecca Agreement" consists of just three countries makes the alliance more flexible and, consequently, more sustainable. Still, the partnership between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia is hardly enough to justify calling it an “Arab NATO” — at least for now.
3+?
According to Hakan Fidan, the preferred model would see Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan retain their status as founding members — responsible for developing the alliance’s principles, standards, and long-term structure — while allowing other countries to join with the approval of the core of original members.
One of the first candidates is Egypt, which in March joined Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan in a new consultation format at the foreign minister level, known as R4. The ministers have met four times in the months since then — an unusually high level of activity.
Against this backdrop, the signing of the agreement in Mecca last month led regional media to raise the question: why did Egypt not join the alliance? Fidan maintains that the delay is merely technical.
Meanwhile, The Middle East Eye (MEE) published a report claiming that Saudi Arabia had opposed Egypt joining the group, “at least for now.” The outlet’s sources attributed this to Riyadh’s growing dissatisfaction with the policies of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. Saudi Arabia, which provided around $25 billion in support for the Egyptian economy after Sisi came to power, believes Cairo has given little in return. Its grievances reportedly include Egypt’s limited role in the fight against the Houthis and its position during the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Egypt’s absence from the alliance is reportedly linked to Riyadh’s growing dissatisfaction with the policies of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi
Another source of irritation is Egypt’s relationship with the UAE. During the Iranian attacks, Cairo sent air defense systems and fighter jets to the Emirates, while Sisi met repeatedly with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed. No comparable steps were taken toward Saudi Arabia, and according to MEE sources, this deepened Riyadh’s suspicions regarding Cairo’s alignment with Abu Dhabi. This comes on top of the difficult relationship between the UAE and Saudi Arabia themselves, which came close to armed confrontation late last year.
At the same time, Egyptian sources claim that Cairo itself declined to join the “Saudi political bloc,” fearing that doing so would limit its autonomy on security and diplomatic matters. Egypt is developing its cooperation with Greece and Cyprus, which have disputes with Turkey, as well as with India, Pakistan’s main regional rival. And that is without even considering the need to balance relations between Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
Who are they banding together against?
Cairo, like many other regional players, naturally wants an answer to the question: who are we banding together against? The reply that the new alliance has no specific adversary does little to resolve the issue. The Soviet Union was likewise not named as an enemy in the 1949 North Atlantic Treaty, but the historical context of NATO’s creation left little doubt that the alliance was formed primarily as a mechanism for deterring Soviet expansion in Europe.
There is no such clarity yet in the case of the Mecca Agreement. Saudi Arabia is primarily focused on Iran and proxy forces aligned with Tehran. For Pakistan, India remains its main traditional rival. Turkey is increasingly speaking about threats stemming from Israel’s growing strength. Potential members and observers are therefore trying to understand not only which adversaries the agreement is formally not directed against, but also which threats the three countries actually regard as common.
“One of the conditions for the success of any alliance is identifying a common enemy. So who is the enemy for the countries in this alliance?” — asks Emirati political scientist Abdulkhaleq Abdallah.
Voices from Abu Dhabi are particularly important. Throughout the latest war with Iran, the UAE consistently called on the Gulf monarchies to coordinate more closely on security. “We have no alternative but to unite our ranks,” UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash stressed in July.
Yet Abu Dhabi has so far found itself on the sidelines of the new structures that have emerged around Riyadh this summer: the UAE was not even among the 14 states that signed the declaration establishing the Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition on July 30.
Against the backdrop of tensions between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, this is hardly surprising. More broadly, the “Mecca Agreement” is beginning to look like a counterweight to the Abraham Accords — the series of Trump-brokered agreements between Muslim (initially only Arab) countries and Israel to normalize relations.
In 2020, the UAE and Bahrain were the first countries to join the Abraham Accords, followed by Morocco and Sudan. The accords were not a defense treaty and were primarily aimed at normalizing diplomatic and economic relations. However, security cooperation was an important component from the outset.
The Trump administration viewed the process as part of a broader restructuring of the region’s security architecture, including against the backdrop of its confrontation with Iran. In this context, Washington placed particular emphasis on normalizing relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
In the fall of 2023, Israel and Saudi Arabia were close to reaching an agreement. But Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israeli territory, followed by the war in the Gaza Strip and later in Lebanon, dramatically altered the regional balance of power. Riyadh abandoned its rapprochement with Israel, making its willingness to resolve the conflict with the Palestinians and accept the establishment of a Palestinian state a condition for further negotiations. The shift was predictable, and Hamas had counted on such an outcome — after all, one of the objectives of the October 7 attack was to derail the Saudi-Israeli normalization process.
It is therefore hardly surprising that Israel is wary of Riyadh’s rapprochement with Ankara and Islamabad, both of which have tense relations with Jerusalem.
Riyadh’s rapprochement with Ankara and Islamabad, both of which have strained relations with Jerusalem to varying degrees, is raising concerns in Israel
“From Israel’s perspective, this is a very worrying development,” says Gallia Lindenstrauss, a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS). “It adds a military component to a political front that demonstrates a staunchly anti-Israeli position. It is also concerning because both Saudi Arabia and Turkey are potentially exploring the nuclear option and could gain a great deal from close defense cooperation with Pakistan.”
At the same time, she believes the door to normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia has not closed, even if the chances of such a deal have diminished.
According to Yoel Guzansky, a former National Security Council official and head of the Gulf Program at the INSS, the trilateral alliance is “not a military alliance against Israel, but it is anti-Israeli in its orientation,” adding that “both Erdoğan and the Pakistanis are very anti-Israeli. Saudi Arabia joining such an alliance could lead it to distance itself from Israel and, under pressure from these countries, adopt a more confrontational policy toward Israel."
It is important to note here that the three countries began working on a joint defense agreement in December 2023, just two months after the Hamas attack on Israel and the outbreak of the war. Even then though, the Iranian factor was already present, as Tehran was being widely accused of encouraging Hamas and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah. Still, there had not yet been an open military confrontation between Israel and Iran, let alone between the United States and Iran; Bashar al-Assad was still in power in Syria, and the region looked very different.
By the time the agreement was signed, after two years and eight months of negotiations, the war in the region had already affected dozens of countries (whether directly or merely economically). During that time, the balance of power shifted repeatedly, but the fundamental question remained: who will shape the future of the Middle East?
Against this backdrop, the Emirati newspaper Al Khaleej notes that the new alliance can be understood as an attempt by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan to prevent Iran or Israel from unilaterally reshaping the regional order. All three countries share, to varying degrees, concerns that Israel could emerge from the latest conflicts as the region’s dominant military power.
At the same time, Tehran has reacted to the new regional alliance in broadly positive terms — or, at least, it has sought to give that impression. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said that “there is no reason to worry that the pact is directed against Iran.” On the contrary, he said, it is a sign that the three countries “have concluded that they cannot rely on U.S. security commitments.”
“Iran is working to convince the monarchies around the Persian Gulf and other Arab countries that the American presence in this region does not strengthen their security and defense. They cannot protect their bases, they cannot protect you, and, in fact, their presence provokes the very war you hope to avoid,” Vali Nasr, a professor at Johns Hopkins University and an Iran specialist, explained in an interview with the Financial Times.
In his view, Tehran welcomes the “Mecca Agreement” because it means the United States has to compete with other security structures in the Gulf in order to remain relevant. Nasr believes that even if the new alliance cannot yet be considered a full-fledged military pact, its emergence itself demonstrates the degree to which doubts about the reliability of the United States as a security guarantor have become a serious concern.
Not instead of the U.S.
As a result of the war with Iran, which saw the United States effectively leave the Gulf monarchies exposed to attacks by Tehran and its proxies, the Middle East no longer regards Washington as an unquestioned security guarantor. Still, similar disillusionment had emerged earlier — for example when the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in 2019 drew only a muted response from Washington.
In recent years, regional players have increasingly come to believe that they need backup options. Even before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, this included exploring partnerships with Moscow and joining or moving closer to organizations such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and BRICS (where Beijing also plays a significant role). Another form of insurance is the search for transregional alliances, such as the partnership between Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia. On the other side are Israel, India, and the UAE, but all six of them are tied together by their partnerships with the United States, which they ultimately have no intention of abandoning.
Notably, Washington itself welcomed the new alliance. “This shows how the Middle East is coming together and how countries will finally be able to defend themselves more effectively. Congratulations to the great leadership of the three countries mentioned. This is a big, bold, and important first step,” President Trump wrote on Truth Social. In effect, this is in line with U.S. hopes of shifting part of the burden of regional security onto the shoulders of its partners where possible.
In any case, Washington will neither be able nor willing to withdraw from the Middle East completely. It is no coincidence that Trump has posted images depicting the Strait of Hormuz as U.S. territory.
In any event, the process is far from over. The order that took decades to build — who is allied with whom and who is at war with whom — has collapsed. A new one has yet to be built.

Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
06:00:45 UTC
15:00:45 KST

The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden.
Charles, who does not want to be fully identified, and his Swedish wife, Lily, were summoned to the police station at 10am on Tuesday, where he was told he would be held at a detention centre and deported within the next two weeks.
Lily, who is a lawyer, was told to go home and get his passport despite her protests that there was a court process under way appealing the deportation order.
“I feel shame,” said Lily, who asked that their family’s surname not be published.
“To me, Britain represents freedom for human beings, and then to see this British man in detention just because he wants to be with his wife and live in his house, this is not right.
“What kind of country are we living in? Is this civilisation? They don’t care about human rights. This is a European country, but it looks like Sweden is like somewhere like Afghanistan,” she said.
Lily met her husband in the UK after starting a law degree in London in 2010.
She now works for the local authority in Stockholm and returned to Sweden in 2015, with her soon-to-be husband joining her in 2017, three years before Brexit.
A former business consultant, now retired, Charles made an application to remain in the country before the deadline for applications after Brexit.
His application was rejected two years later in 2022 and the family have been fighting deportation ever since with “six or seven” appeals, said Lily. “The Migration Agency has hunted us for five years.”
During the summer the couple received a text asking them to show up at their local police station on 1 September.
“They told us they needed to talk and we should show up at 10am. They didn’t say anything about deportation or to bring passports.
“When we arrived they told us that they needed to talk to Charles privately, and after three hours they told me they were taking him to the detention centre and that they would deport him.
“I told them that they can’t do this because his case is in court and they have to wait for the outcome, but they told me they were going ahead,” said Lily.
She has pleaded with Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, to intervene.
“Why can’t Andy Burnham talk to the Swedish government? How many British families have to suffer in Sweden before Andy Burnham gets involved? How many families have to leave their homes, be forced into selling their houses?
“This is not humanity. This is not right. They should threaten the trade agreement,” she added.
Charles’s case comes amid growing controversy over Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement, which is supposed to have protected EU citizens in the UK and British citizens settled in the bloc before Brexit.
Among those threatened with removal in the past month are 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old man in dementia care who has been in the country for 24 years.
A 34-year-old man revealed this week he was deported from Sweden in January despite having been in the country since he was 10 and being married to a Swedish woman in Gothenburg.
Two years ago another British woman, Kathleen Poole, was threatened with deportation because she had not provided financial statements to the Migration Agency while in full-time dementia care.
The Swedish migration minister defended the country’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement, saying the Migration Agency was following the rules and had granted a number of residency permits for Britons who had “reasonable grounds” for late applications.
However, concerns have been raised formally by the UK government through the EU-UK specialised committee, the official platform to raise issues over the working out of the Brexit deal, over the high number of late applications for post Brexit residency being rejected.
Sweden, along with 12 other EU member states, opted for a constitutive system requiring citizens to formally apply to extend their residency rights post Brexit. Others, like Spain, opted for a declaratory system requiring Britons to simply register their presence initially.
Lily says she and her husband phoned the authorities and used the correct form for residency and have been fighting ever since.
The latest statistics from the 2024 European Commission annual report show that 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency have been decided in Sweden.
According to analysis by the UK government, 27.5% (3,918) of applications have been refused, “a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3 and 4%”.
Sources added that this “constitutes 12% of all refusals across the EU member states, even though UK nationals in Sweden makes up only 1.55% of the total population of WA beneficiaries in EU member states”.
Denmark faced a similar controversy two years ago, but legislation was introduced to give British nationals a second chance to make the residency application.

The 2026 El Niño Is Being ‘Supersized’ as Impacts Worsen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

The world’s leading weather organization is sounding the alarm about this year’s super El Niño, issuing its most certain forecast in the history of the organization.
In an update issued early Thursday, the World Meteorological Organization predicted a “nearly 100% likelihood” that the El Niño will last through February. The strong language from the World Meteorological Organization—the United Nations’ weather and climate agency—underlies just how historic this El Niño is shaping up to be.
“This is the first time that a WMO El Niño/La Niña Update has been so unequivocal,” the agency says, noting that certainty reflects “the strong agreement within WMO’s extensive network.”
El Niño is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon defined by warmer-than-normal ocean temperatures in the eastern tropical Pacific, a pattern that disrupts weather patterns around the world. Scientists have been warning since the start of the year that a particularly strong El Niño was set to develop. The latest forecasts indicate it will be the strongest on record by a wide margin, and impacts are already being felt throughout the world—and they’re likely to intensify in the coming months.
“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement. “The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather.”
In addition to affecting regional weather, El Niño also tends to bump up the global average temperature by roughly 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius (0.2 to 0.4 degrees Fahrenheit) by releasing heat into the atmosphere. But this year’s iteration could provide an even bigger boost. The intensity of this El Niño means this year is likely to be the hottest on record; because it takes a while for the added heat to work through the climate system, 2027 is forecast to be even hotter.
This extra warming is a red alert when compounded on top of the warming caused by manmade climate change. The UN warned in a separate report issued this week that the world will likely cross 1.5 degrees C of warming over the next few years.
Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says this El Niño will be so big, “with consequences that are so large, I’m not sure we fully understand them.” The intensity of the El Niño, Swain says, means that it may cause unexpected and extreme weather, and he cautions against making certain predictions about what, exactly, is going to happen over the next year. But the impacts, he says, will almost certainly be massive.
“This is probably one of the larger, if not the largest, climate events—aside from long-term warming, which really isn't a singular event—that anybody alive is potentially ever experiencing,” he says. “That's a very big deal. And I think there’s certainly going to be dramatic outcomes from this.”
While the El Niño won’t reach its full strength for another few months, the world has already seen some impacts: The US just lived through the hottest summer on record, and the heat was almost certainly juiced up by El Niño. Regions that are typically dry during El Niño have also seen drought emerge. In Sudan, low water levels in the Nile are exacerbating a yearslong hunger crisis, while Puerto Rico has turned to water rationing due to dry conditions and infrastructure failures. Fisheries in the eastern Pacific have also been thrown into disarray by the hotter-than-normal waters there.
“The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people,” Guterres said in the release. “We must win that race.”

The drone plot at Leipzig airport has given European countries that have long pushed for tighter restrictions on Russian travellers a new argument.
German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported on Wednesday that one of the two suspects identified by German authorities was a Belarusian man travelling on a Russian passport. Investigators believe he entered the Schengen area using a tourist visa issued by Italy. The second suspect was identified as a Russian-born man with a Latvian passport.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Later in the day, Kaja Kallas, the EU foreign policy chief, said after an informal meeting of foreign affairs ministers that capitals had shown “broad support” for an EU-wide visa ban on current and former Russian combatants, alongside tougher rules for Russian tourists.
“Many member states have flagged… that actually these kinds of tourist visas are used for sabotage acts,” Kallas said.
The measures were included in the EU’s latest sanctions package against Russia but watered down after resistance from France, Italy and Greece. France and Italy were also among the EU countries that issued the most visas to Russian tourists in 2025, Euractiv first reported.
The Leipzig case has put Italy in an uncomfortable spot. The reported use of an Italian visa by one suspect could intensify pressure on Rome and other reluctant capitals to tighten their rules as Russia steps up sabotage and other forms of hybrid warfare across Europe.
Foreign Airlines Begin Suspending Flights to Russia Following Kyiv’s Warning That Its Airspace Is Unsafe
On the margins of the meeting, Antonio Tajani, Italy’s foreign minister, told Eddy in a huddle with journalists that Italian authorities would investigate the report “to verify the facts.” He was responding to a question about whether the case could prompt Rome to rethink its position on Russian visas.
The scrutiny comes after Italy’s former ambassador to Uzbekistan and an embassy aide were detained in May over an alleged scheme to issue long-term Schengen tourist visas to Russian citizens who did not meet the eligibility requirements.
For Estonia and its allies, which have long viewed Russian travel as a potential channel for espionage and sabotage, Leipzig strengthens the case for closing what they see as a dangerous gap in the EU’s Russian tourist visa rules.
“The lesson should be obvious,” Margus Tsahkna, Estonia’s foreign minister, said on X. “This must stop.”
Kallas fights back
Kaja Kallas resisted calls to fold her European External Action Service into the Commission, after foreign ministers chewed over a German-led proposal in Ireland on Wednesday.
“There was broad support for the current institutional set-up,” Kallas said after the meeting. Germany’s ideas got a rather frosty reception, according to two other people briefed on the discussions.
The proposal, backed somewhat less enthusiastically by the French, caught many foreign ministers by surprise.
A technical fix would be more apt, Kallas suggested. “The problem is not the treaties, not the institutional setup. The problem is the implementation of that setup,” she said, pointing not-so-subtly at the Commission for “duplicating” her service’s tasks. Smaller EU states wouldn’t be happy to lose the co-ordination provided by her double-hatted role.
Then she changed gear. Kallas said she could get on board with the proposal on one condition: that she was genuinely empowered to oversee all foreign policy areas in the Commission, from migration and development to trade. That was unlikely, she suggested, while there was “somebody above me that is actually deciding” – in other words, Ursula von der Leyen.
Kallas may already have lost control of the reform process she launched. Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister, seems to have seized the initiative, inviting ministers to a conference in Berlin on 2 December. The future of the EEAS is likely to come up, alongside his rather doomed proposal to move away from unanimity in foreign and security policy.
Frankly speaking about the budget
Thomas Byrne, Ireland’s Europe minister, told Rapporteur that negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget were entering a new phase as he hosted ministers for a two-day meeting at Dublin Castle.
“I think we’ve gone beyond the scoping phase and we are in the phase now of seeking a landing zone,” he told Eddy. Despite holding strong national positions, capitals understand that a compromise has to be found, he added.
By the end of this week, Byrne will have sat down one-to-one with more than half of his counterparts as he seeks a deal before the end of the year. The tone has been “frank,” he said. António Costa, meanwhile, is two-thirds of the way through his tour of the European capitals to build consensus on the budget.
Meanwhile, Sigitas Mitkus, who could inherit the negotiations when Lithuania assumes the rotating Council presidency in January, told our budget reporter Victoria Becker that every country wanted to meet Costa’s year-end deadline. But Lithuania was “prepared to finalise the deal” if necessary. Read the full interview.
Did Poles tip Iceland’s vote?
European integration drew Poles to Iceland in search of work and a different future. Many stayed, raised families and formed the country’s largest immigrant community.
Long-established Polish residents who spoke to my colleague Magnus Lund Nielsen argued that the roughly 3,000 Poles eligible to vote in the referendum to restart accession talks had leaned against Iceland’s potential membership.
The EU may have transformed Poland, but it offered Iceland less, they said. Benefiting from European integration does not necessarily make someone an integrationist. Read Magnus’ final dispatch from Reykjavík.

Oil prices fell amid uncertainty surrounding U.S. and Iranian strikes
Kyiv • UNN
Brent fell to $95.04, while WTI fell to $90.63 per barrel. Investors are assessing the risks of supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices edged lower on September 3. This came as investors assessed the uncertainty surrounding the resumption of strikes between the United States and Iran, which could disrupt supplies from the Middle East, UNN writes, citing Reuters.
How prices changed
Brent crude oil futures fell 59 cents, or 0.62%, to $95.04 per barrel at 05:09 GMT (08:09 Kyiv time).
West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures fell 38 cents, or 0.42%, to $90.63.
During the previous trading session, Brent and WTI prices fluctuated between a $2-per-barrel gain and a $1-per-barrel decline. Session highs for both benchmarks reached their highest levels since July 24.
What are the reasons
Oil prices fell amid earlier signs of a de-escalation in the latest flare-up, as there had been no confirmed exchanges of fire since midday Wednesday Sydney time, IG analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note.
The latest strikes marked the largest exchange of fire between the United States and Iran since July, and the war has now entered its seventh month.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on September 2 that the renewed U.S. campaign against Iran would not last "too long" and that American forces had struck Iranian radar and missile systems.
"We destroyed all the new equipment they were trying to install along the Strait of Hormuz – some defensive, some offensive… It was a very powerful attack last night, and we are ready to conduct another one anytime we want," Trump said.
The new U.S. campaign against Iran will not last too long - Trump03.09.26, 02:02 • 26221 view
What analysts say
"If this easing persists, and that is a big question, oil shipment volumes through the Strait of Hormuz via so-called \"shadow vessels\" and ship-to-ship transfers will soon return to the levels we saw at the end of last week," Sycamore said.
According to preliminary data from Kpler published on Wednesday, four commercial vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz, below the 10-day average of about 13.
What actions has Iran taken
Iran has also added several more vessels to the list of those it considers, non-compliant and that could face fines, confiscation or detention if they attempt to pass through the strait.
Iraq increased its oil exports in August to approximately 2.34 million barrels per day from around 1.35 million barrels per day in July, two Iraqi energy ministry officials said on Wednesday. Exports are also expected to rise in September, as significant discounts and Iran's approval for Iraqi tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz encouraged buyers.
How much oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz
On Tuesday, the United States said that 17 million barrels of oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, calling it the largest volume of oil to pass through the waterway since the start of the American-Israeli war against Iran.

Has Iran modified its rocket systems to fire mines into the Strait of Hormuz?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
05:57:20 UTC
14:57:20 KST

Has Iran modified its rocket systems to fire mines into the Strait of Hormuz?
Fighting escalated in the Middle East over the weekend after US airstrikes on Sunday targeted Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak. The exchange of fire was instigated by the US in retaliation against Iran’s new capabilities for firing mines from rockets into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s use of rocket launchers to deploy sea mines into the strategic waterway would be unprecedented, but not implausible. Even so, some analysts remain sceptical.
The motive behind the US strikes on Sunday, which hit Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, appears to have been the prevention of a new threat to shipping in the vital waterway.
Officially, the US military decided to resume its strikes after a month-long hiatus because Iranian forces from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) were preparing to “launch rockets loaded with sea mines into the strait.”
Read moreIran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade squeezes Iran oil exports
Rocket launchers as mine launchers
Some maritime security experts say they were taken by surprise by the US’s claim.
“This alleged new capability by the Iranians to deploy mines into the strait is puzzling,” said a specialist in maritime conflicts who preferred to remain anonymous.
Since the conflict with the United States and Israel began, Iranians have typically transported sea mines in small, fast boats and then scattered them across the Strait of Hormuz. This has made the strait extremely dangerous as vessels have had to navigate it not knowing the exact location of the underwater explosives.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Sea mines have also been delivered typically by small submarines or dropped by aircraft flying at very low altitudes.
They can be positioned on the seabed or moored above it – or left just beneath the surface of the water where they detect passing ships before exploding on contact with a vessel.
A not so new novel method?
According to Dirk Siebels, a maritime security specialist at Risk Intelligence, using land-based rocket launchers to shoot sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz “would, as far as I know, be a novel method”.
Harlan Ullman, a former US Naval officer, agreed. In an interview with Al Jazeera, he said it was “unlikely” rocket launchers would be used to fire mines because they would be “highly likely to be damaged upon impact with the water,” he said.
However, reports have been circulating for several months about Iran’s capacity to use missiles to lay sea mines.
Iranian state television broadcast a report on the Fajr-5 Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS) as early as January 2025, referring to it as the newest weapon for mining in the Strait of Hormuz.
Read moreHow ships are risking ‘safe’ passage through the Strait of Hormuz
“Iran has been conducting tests with Fajr-5 multiple rocket launchers for this purpose for some time now,” said Sidharth Kaushal, an expert on the impact of new technologies on naval warfare at the Royal United Services Institute for Defense and Security Studies (RUSI), one of Britain’s leading strategic think tanks.
A quicker way to deploy sea mines
In principle, weapons can be used to deploy mines.
“Missiles carry the explosives and drop them over the target area,” said Mark Hilborne, an expert in aviation and space security at King’s College London.
“The impact can be minimised by equipping the mines with small parachutes, for example.”
If Iran has indeed begun launching mines into the strait using Fajr-5 systems, it would greatly undermine the rhetoric from US President Donald Trump and the Pentagon, who have boasted of having “completely destroyed the Iranian navy”.
For Iranians, “this would be a way to demonstrate their ingenuity and their ability to overcome the destruction of their fleet by the Americans,” explained Shahin Modarres, an Iran specialist at the International Team for the Study of Security (ITSS) in Verona.
And it would give the Iranian regime yet another advantage. “It’s also faster. Using a boat requires loading the mines, assembling the crew, travelling to the site, and dropping the mines. With a rocket launcher, all you have to do is load and fire,” Kaushal said.
Time saved can make all the difference.
“It limits the opportunities the Americans have to detect and prevent a threat,” the RUSI analyst added.
Despite its strategic merits, the rocket system is not a panacea. There are practical reasons why using boats is preferable. First, it’s possible to carry more mines on a boat.
“A naval mine is a fairly large and heavy warhead because it must be powerful enough to damage a ship’s hull. It’s difficult to fit many of them into a single rocket launch, because to travel a long distance, the warhead must be lightweight,” Kaushal explained.
Second, rocket-launched mines are not particularly precise compared to other methods. The rocket system tends to scatter mines once they have been fired, making it difficult even for the Iranians themselves to ascertain their location.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Propaganda or a veritable escalation?
Siebels considers the military tactic “rather reckless”, suggesting that Iran would be shooting itself in the foot because “Iranian cargo ships also need to know exactly where the mines are in order to avoid them.”
Without knowing the whereabouts of these mines, it is impossible to guarantee ships safe passage through the strait, even if they have paid the transit fee Tehran is demanding.
Siebels said he is doubtful that rocket launchers are being used. Despite the drawbacks of naval missions – particularly the risk to crews – these more traditional methods would align more with Iran’s overall strategy in the Strait of Hormuz.
Others share his scepticism.
“It’s war propaganda,” argues Christian Bueger, a specialist in maritime security issues at the University of Copenhagen.
He said he believes that the United States needed to find a new threat to maritime traffic to “justify the strikes” and to reassure shipping companies.
“The United States is seeking to demonstrate that the mine threat is under control,” Bueger said.
Regardless, it cannot be ruled out that laying mines is part of the psychological warfare being waged by these military rivals. With their January 2025 video touting the new capabilities of the Fajr-5, the Iranians sought to demonstrate that they could still wreak havoc in the Strait of Hormuz – whether it is true or not.
“The advantage of mines is that the mere risk of their existence may be enough to discourage ships from passing through the Strait of Hormuz,” Bueger said, adding that the official response by the US to the bombings on Larak Island would be justified because of Tehran’s actions in the strait.
Modarres is less convinced.
“The use of rocket launchers is typical of how Iran employs unconventional methods to thwart enemy plans.”
Confronted by Washington’s declaration of an all-out economic war, he said Iran may want to demonstrate that it is still capable of imposing its military might over the Strait of Hormuz, blindsiding the Americans by wielding a new weapon to disrupt the vital maritime route.
Whatever the reality – whether bluff and psychological warfare or a veritable threat to the strait – this latest development in the intransigent conflict between Iran and the US reveals that, in an era where drones and AI-enhanced warfare dominate, the threat of mines remains highly effective.

Ben-Gvir revives failed Gaza emigration plan in campaign push that could complicate Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
05:56:18 UTC
14:56:18 KST

Governance out, voluntary emigration in: National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir will present one of the central components of his election campaign to the public Thursday: “Disengagement 710,” a national plan to encourage voluntary emigration from Gaza. The initiative — which comes after Ben-Gvir instructed his campaign staff to play down his plan for crocodiles outside prisons — will also be a key demand by Otzma Yehudit in any negotiations to join the next government.
It must be said at the outset that beyond the fact that the initiative is likely to spark an uproar in the political system and draw harsh international criticism, no country has so far been found that is willing to accept migrants from Gaza. In addition, Ben-Gvir’s migration plan is the equivalent of the governance plan he promised in the previous campaign and largely failed to deliver, given the surge in murders in Arab society.
Trump’s initiative
Since October 7, the idea of voluntary emigration from Gaza has come up repeatedly: first by U.S. President Donald Trump in February 2025, after a meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and later in diplomatic discussions and Cabinet meetings. While Netanyahu expressed reservations behind closed doors about a broad move of this kind, Ben-Gvir was an enthusiastic supporter.
At certain stages, Netanyahu even advanced the plan in an effort to persuade Ben-Gvir to remain in the government. Netanyahu also held several dedicated discussions on the issue and briefed members of the narrow Cabinet on contacts underway with several African countries, including Ethiopia, Congo and Somaliland, in an attempt to persuade them to accept Palestinians who would leave Gaza.
But the plan never really got off the ground. The Americans backed away from Trump’s idea, and the U.S. president’s 20-point plan explicitly stated that Gaza residents would remain in the Strip and that voluntary migration would not be encouraged.
A senior Israeli official said Wednesday in this context: “Do you know a country willing to take in Gazans in significant numbers? If so, give me one. For emigration, you need people who want to migrate and a country willing to take them in. The second part exists even less than the first. If people wanted to leave and there were a country willing to accept them, it would happen — no one could prevent it. And there have been departures. There still are today. On a more limited scale — medical treatment, studies. At the beginning of the war, there was somewhat greater movement into Egypt.”
The Emigration Ministry
But Ben-Gvir is not giving up and intends to market the migration plan as a central part of his election campaign. He says he has been working for months on a comprehensive plan, which he will unveil to the public Thursday.
The plan, called “Disengagement 710,” sets an ambitious target: the voluntary departure of 250,000 Gaza residents in the first year, 1.11 million within three years and about 1.86 million within seven years.
Under the plan, every individual or family choosing to leave Gaza would receive a personalized pathway that includes an approved destination country, legal status, documents and visas, travel funding, initial housing, vocational training, employment assistance and support for up to 24 months. Among the countries being considered as possible destinations, according to Ben-Gvir, are Turkey, Ethiopia, Congo and a number of Arab states.
The plan is based on 12 principles: voluntary departure only; no departure without a destination country and regulated legal status; an individual file for every person and family; preservation of family unity; creation of a broad range of destination countries; employment, study, medical, family and community sponsorship tracks; an absorption and rehabilitation package; payments to countries and absorption agencies based on performance; individual security screening; international partnership; annual implementation targets; and transparency through monthly reporting on the number of applications, approvals, departures, costs and absorption in destination countries.
The cost of the plan is astronomical: an initial Israeli investment of 10 billion shekels to establish and launch it, alongside an Israeli matching framework of up to 50 billion shekels, subject to international participation and agreements with receiving countries.
Otzma Yehudit will make the plan a condition for joining the next government. As part of coalition negotiations, Ben-Gvir will demand the establishment of a dedicated government ministry for voluntary emigration, including a minister, director general, budget, authorities, an international negotiating team and an independent implementation apparatus.
Ben-Gvir has previously demanded the establishment of a national authority to encourage the emigration of Israeli Arabs deemed “disloyal” to Israel, as well as Palestinians — plans that were never advanced because they had no realistic chance of implementation.
For Ben-Gvir, this is also an ideological closing of the circle. In the 1990s, it was Rehavam Ze’evi and the Moledet party who caused an uproar by introducing the idea of transfer into public discourse. Ben-Gvir is seeking to present a different model: not forced expulsion, but the creation of economic incentives and a legal, regulated pathway for voluntary emigration.
Ben-Gvir presents the plan as a direct lesson from October 7 and the 2005 disengagement: “On October 7, the conception that it was possible to withdraw, retreat behind a fence and buy quiet through money and concessions collapsed. ‘Disengagement 710’ is not a repeat of the disengagement — it is its correction.”
Ben-Gvir, incidentally, is planning a broad billboard campaign to promote the initiative. He is also planning a similar billboard campaign in several African countries.
Will it remain a gimmick?
The question is whether Ben-Gvir’s plan will remain merely an election gimmick or be incorporated into the next government’s basic policy guidelines. That depends first and foremost on who forms the next government and whether there is a right-wing government.
With this plan, Ben-Gvir is seeking to outflank Netanyahu from the right and lock him into the idea of voluntary transfer. The person who brought the voluntary emigration plan back to the forefront is Ofer Winter, who included it in his election platform.
It is important to stress: There is considerable doubt that the Trump administration would support the idea, and the plan would certainly face fierce opposition from the international community. There is also serious doubt that any countries would openly agree to accept significant numbers of Gazan migrants. Israel has already held talks with several countries in the past and ran into a wall.

Details: Lavrov said that following Germany's decision to terminate the agreement governing the operation of the Russian House in Berlin, Russia would respond by closing all three branches of the Goethe-Institut in the country – in Moscow, St Petersburg and Novosibirsk.
"Of course, they will be closed after our cultural centre was expelled from there. Otherwise, we would have no self-respect," the Russian foreign minister said.
He added that by deciding to close the Russian House in Berlin, Germany had "deliberately taken a step that unequivocally meant ending its cultural presence in the Russian Federation, which had been maintained despite all the Ukrainian-related twists and turns in our relations with the West".
Background:
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of carrying out a hybrid attack at Leipzig Airport in early August and announced measures in response, including the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul summoned the Russian ambassador in connection with this, as did many other European capitals.
- The Russian Foreign Ministry threatened Berlin with a "fitting response" and summoned Germany's chargé d'affaires in Moscow.

More than 800 students and teachers in Indonesia suffer food poisoning after eating government free meals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
05:54:15 UTC
14:54:15 KST

More than 800 Indonesian students and teachers have fallen ill in separate incidents of food poisoning linked to President Prabowo Subianto’s free-meals program this week, with dozens hospitalised after they with struck with nausea, vomiting and stomach aches.
The president’s flagship free-meals program was launched last year to tackle malnutrition, with meals distributed to more than 62 million students and pregnant women across the country.
But the multi-billion policy has been plagued by controversy, including recurrent cases of food poisonings, alleged corruption, leadership changes, and complaints it is a major lag on the budget.
This week 566 students fell ill after eating the government’s free meals in Sidoarjo, East Java, with 88 of them hospitalised. In Nganjuk, also in East Java, 49 students fell ill on Wednesday after eating a free meal of fried rice, chicken and tofu.
Another 237 students and teachers in Agam, West Sumatra, also fell ill after their meals on Wednesday, according to local media reports. Eggs were suspected to be the cause.
The regional government in Agam has reportedly suspended distributing the meals, pending an evaluation. The kitchen linked to the Sidoarjo case was also suspended on Wednesday.
In the past year many Indonesians have complained about the program, writing on social media about maggots in tempeh, shards of glass in rice, and food trays washed in dirty water.
Overall, 37,600 people are believed to have suffered food poisoning linked to the free meals as of 8 Aug., according to Network for Education Watch, a non-governmental watchdog.
Charles Honoris, a lawmaker and member of the sole political party outside the governing coalition, described the situation as a “failure of the system”.
The National Nutrition Agency has blamed previous cases of food poisoning on improper food storage and late delivery of cooked meals.
Prabowo has also played down the scale of the problem, saying that of more than a billion meals served, poisoning cases represented just “0.0017% – quite a proud achievement”. He also said the policy had improved school attendance and achievement.
In July, a survey by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed only a third of people were satisfied with the scheme, with the reported cases of poisoning cited as a major reason.
Despite the mounting criticism, Prabowo told parliament last month the program would be continued, and promised that improvements would be made.
“We start with the most fundamental aspect: nutrition. Our children must not study while hungry. No child can learn effectively if they are hungry,” he said.
“We cannot accept a situation where one in four Indonesian children suffers from stunting,” he continued, “We cannot accept that.”

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:52:33 EEST
14:52:33 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has launched four unscheduled inspections of banks in connection with the bail case for former Energy Minister Herman Haluschenko, Deputy Chairman of the regulator Dmytro Oliynyk announced during a meeting of the Verkhovna Rada’s Temporary Investigative Commission (TIC) on Economic Security.
He noted that the entire collateral amount was not processed through Sense Bank. An analysis of the movement of funds in four consecutive links from the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) account has not yet revealed the use of cash.
"We have discovered in these four links that there are other banks that have no fewer questions than Sense, and some even more," the NBU Deputy Governor stated. According to him, the Central Bank will evaluate the actions of all four banks through which the funds were transferred – Sense Bank, Idea Bank, OTP Bank, and FUIB.
Oliynyk also suggested that the cash may not have been deposited into the banking system at all, but may have been sold to companies with excess liquidity. The funds could then have passed through 80-100 legal entities, been concentrated in one company that had been inactive for about two years, and from there, distributed among the four banks for transfer to the HACC account.
At the same time, the National Bank has not yet established the use of a separate technical or technological mechanism at Sense Bank to circumvent financial monitoring procedures and cannot confirm the intentional disabling of established restrictions or control mechanisms. Inspections of the banking systems and internal investigations are ongoing.
As reported, on August 19, Yaroslav Zhelezniak, head of the Committee, citing a petition filed by a NABU detective, released information on the movement of UAH 150 million in bail for Haluschenko through Sense Bank, FUIB, OTP Bank, and Idea Bank.
According to the information he released, UAH 46 million from Giran Construct LLC and UAH 4 million from Pelet Service LLC were transferred to the HACC account through Sense Bank. Another UAH 41 million in bail was deposited through FUIB, UAH 54 million through OTP Bank, and UAH 5 million through Idea Bank.
On August 21, the NBU demanded that Sense Bank dismiss Liudmyla Snihur, director of the financial monitoring department, and announced the continuation of proceedings regarding possible interference with the bank’s operating systems. On August 25, Sense Bank suspended Snihur from her duties and blocked her access to the bank’s corporate network and systems.

Russia attacked with 163 drones, up to half of them jet-powered: how air defense performed and the situation across the regions
Kyiv • UNN
As a result of Russia’s nighttime attack, Odesa, the Kyiv region, and the Khmelnytskyi region were among those affected. The number of injured is approaching two dozen, including three children.
Russia launched 163 drones at Ukraine overnight, 135 of which were shot down or suppressed. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 3, UNN writes.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of September 3 (from 18:00 on September 2), the enemy attacked with:
-  163 Shahed-type attack UAVs (about half of them jet-powered), S8000 "Bandероль", Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones; 
-  from the following directions: Millerovo, Orel, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. 
How the air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defense had shot down/suppressed 135 targets:
-  135 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. 
"Hits by enemy air-attack weapons were recorded at 15 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at 4 locations. The attack is ongoing; enemy UAVs are in the airspace," the statement said.
Which regions came under attack
-  Odesa. According to the State Emergency Service, 17 people, including 3 children, were injured as a result of the Russian strike on Odesa overnight. The shelling damaged apartments from the 10th to the 17th floors of a 21-story residential building; 
-  Kyiv region. As reported by Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, a man sustained shrapnel wounds as a result of the enemy attack in Boryspil district. He was hospitalized. The enemy damaged warehouse facilities, an administrative building, a store, and kiosks. The Russian attack continued in the morning — the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported jet-powered UAVs in the Kyiv region, heading toward Brovary/Boryspil and over Kyiv; according to local public channels, explosions were heard in the region; 
-  Khmelnytskyi region. As reported by the State Emergency Service, Russia attacked the Khmelnytskyi region twice overnight with attack drones. In Khmelnytskyi, UAV debris fell on the premises of an enterprise, setting a truck on fire and damaging a warehouse. The vehicle’s driver was injured; the man sustained shrapnel wounds and was hospitalized. During the repeated attack, a fire broke out on the premises of another enterprise in the region. The fires were extinguished; 
-  Ternopil region. As noted by Taras Pastukh, head of the Ternopil Regional Military Administration, jet-powered UAVs attacked the Ternopil region again overnight. No casualties or destruction were recorded. There was a report of a fire in grassy areas, but its origin is being clarified. Two more jet-powered UAVs were detected south of Ternopil in the morning; according to the head of the Regional Military Administration, both aerial targets were destroyed; 
-  Kyiv. Explosions were heard in Kyiv, according to data from the Center for Strategic Communications. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko had already reported in the evening that air defense was operating in the city and that new enemy UAVs were heading toward the capital; 
-  Dnipropetrovsk region. As reported by Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration, the enemy attacked 3 districts more than 20 times with drones, artillery, and an aerial bomb. A fire broke out in Pavlohrad, in particular. An enterprise was damaged in Synelnykove district. In total, air defense forces shot down 10 enemy UAVs overnight in various districts of the Dnipropetrovsk region; 
-  Kharkiv region. A hospital building in Zolochiv was damaged by strikes from Russian Molniya-type drones overnight on September 3, Zolochiv Military Administration head Viktor Kovalenko told journalists. A 59-year-old man was injured in Zolochiv as a result of the Russian drone attack, the regional police reported.
