Iran war escalation raises concern over civilian death toll
CAIRO/WASHINGTON – The sudden recent escalation of the Iran war has cast renewed attention on its civilian toll after Iran reported 18 dead in the last US assault, including four killed and dozens wounded at a wedding.
Iran’s health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 wounded in the US strikes across Iran on the night of Sept 1.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society said four people were killed and 67 wounded at a wedding ceremony near the coast of the Strait of Hormuz.
The return of combat operations has alarmed countries throughout the region, as Iran launched missile and drone attacks against what it said were US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq.
Kuwait’s army reported further missile and drone attacks early on Sept 3, saying they were intercepted by air defence systems.
The guns had largely gone silent since the previous exchange in July, although peace talks failed to advance in the interim.
US President Donald Trump threatened to unleash yet more military force, even though the war is unpopular at home and has driven up the cost of petrol.
Top aides to Trump are pushing to keep the war from escalating before November’s midterm elections to staunch Republican electoral losses, and White House officials will consider ramping up military action after the vote on Nov 3, four people familiar with the discussions said.
Iran, for its part, has remained defiant, despite suffering heavy military and economic losses.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran”, and called for an immediate cessation of military action, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
“The Secretary-General condemns all attacks against civilians. He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution,” Dujarric said.
The deaths would be in addition to the 3,636 people documented as killed in Iran as at April 7, including 1,701 civilians, according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), an independent Iranian rights group.
The US has reported 18 military personnel killed and more than 750 wounded.
“We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The US military never targets civilians, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for the US military’s Central Command, said in an e-mail.
The Iranian Red Crescent Society released a video showing debris strewn on the ground next to a building with a large hole in the roof, accompanied by still images showing people, some in Red Crescent vests, at a damaged building and a utility tower lying on the ground.
Reuters was able to verify the location using satellite imagery, which showed the fallen tower was 136m from the damaged building.
The wedding incident recalled the blast at a school in Minab that killed 160 people at a girls’ school on the first day of the war.
The Pentagon has yet to issue an official finding on the Minab strike, which would be the US military’s largest civilian casualty incident in decades.
It may have been the result of US use of outdated targeting data, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Democratic members of the US Congress have called on the administration to release findings of its investigation of the incident, but the report has not been sent to lawmakers.
US defenders of the Iran war also point to civilian deaths that resulted from Iranian attempts to put down street protests that embroiled the country in December and January, before the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28.
HRANA has put that death toll at more than 7,000, while Iranian exile groups claim the number is much higher.
Trump has cited an incentive for Iranians to overthrow their government as one reason for the war, in addition to seeking to halt Iran’s nuclear programme and ending its support for militant groups abroad such as Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis.
Iran has also responded to the US attacks by threatening any oil tankers that transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian authorisation, severely curtailing traffic in a waterway that before the war carried 20 per cent of the world’s oil supply. REUTERS

The far-right leader pushing Germans to forget the Nazi past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:01:00 UTC
11:01:00 KST

The man leading the charge to make Germany proud again won’t say he wants his fellow Germans to “forget” the Nazi past, but that is where his ideas invariably lead.
Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a 48-year-old lawmaker for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, was until recently little known beyond his largely rural constituency. But he may soon be in a position to help realize one of the greatest ambitions of the party’s most extreme faction: remaking his country’s postwar identity and steering Germans toward leaving behind the Nazi past.
That history “remains present in a peculiar way — yes, like a zombie,” Tillschneider told POLITICO in July on the sidelines of an AfD conference in the eastern city of Magdeburg. “It’s an undead entity. And that is not normal. That is not good.”
Advertisement
Germany’s much-vaunted Erinnerungskultur, or culture of remembrance, is central to its self-conception — and long served as an existential imperative. Though halting, West Germany’s reckoning with Nazi crimes and the Holocaust in the decades after the end of World War II served to help restore the country’s standing among democratic nations, making possible its membership in Western alliances. The country’s constitution was shaped in repudiation of Nazism, with safeguards intended to prevent its resurgence.
But for the AfD’s most extreme leaders — many now concentrated in rural areas of the former East Germany — the culture of remembrance has merely perpetuated what some, including Tillschneider, call a “guilt cult” designed to instill self-loathing in the German Volk, a term for “people” which is imbued with near-mystical significance on the far right. Without openly denying Nazi crimes, they argue the cultural and political reckoning with them has damaged the Volk’s identity, leaving Germans weak, atomized, and vulnerable to “globalist” forces such as the EU and the U.S., long viewed by the far-right as a corrosive force due to the homogenizing influence of its individualist, consumerist culture — at least until U.S. President Donald Trump’s arrival.
Tillschneider’s ideas aren’t new. The backlash against Germany’s culture of remembrance is as old as the effort to reckon with the past itself. But as the intellectual architect of the party’s blueprint for governing in Saxony-Anhalt ahead of a Sept. 6 election in the state — where the AfD is so far ahead in the polls it’s within striking distance of an outright majority in parliament — he could soon wield more tangible power than any other far-right figure in Germany’s postwar history to turn those ideas into reality. Tillschneider, currently the AfD’s spokesperson for culture and education policy in the state parliament, is a leading candidate to become the head of a future ministry that would oversee school curricula and cultural funding in the state.
“We want to spread the joy of being German,” Tillschneider said at a pre-election AfD “family fest” on an overcast August afternoon in Querfurt, a small medieval fortress city in his Saxony-Anhalt constituency. “It’s a celebration. Celebrate the fact that you’re German.”
This did not mean, he added, that the AfD would eliminate school lessons on Nazi crimes. Rather, it would “shift the emphasis,” he said, so the Nazi past loses its contemporary urgency.
“Of course, I’d also like to see history classes on the Third Reich,” he said, “But good history classes. Good history classes convey a sense of the otherness of the past.”
‘More Bismarck, less Hitler’
In some ways, Tillschneider, a bearded, bespectacled former university lecturer, seems an unlikely figure to advance the revolution in German identity the far-right has long sought.
Born in Romania during the Cold War, Tillschneider grew up in a German-speaking minority community whose roots in the region stretched back to Habsburg rule. His family moved to West Germany when he was still a child. At university, he became interested in Islamic studies, drawn — as he now explains it — to the subject because it was foreign and unfamiliar. He later studied in Syria before earning a doctorate and publishing a book on “the origins of legal hermeneutics in early Islam.”
Advertisement
After moving to eastern Germany in subsequent years, Tillschneider came to depict Islam as fundamentally incompatible with German society and became a prominent figure in the so-called “New Right,” a network of radical intellectuals known for recasting old, extremist ideas in more culturally palatable terms. He also became associated with an extreme faction within the AfD called Der Flügel (“the Wing”) alongside Thuringian politician Björn Höcke, who drew widespread condemnation in 2017 for calling Berlin’s prominent Holocaust memorial, located near the Brandenburg Gate, a “monument of shame” and demanding a “180-degree turn” in Germany’s memory politics. Der Flügel was dissolved in 2020, but its members, including Tillschneider, have only grown more influential in the party since then.
Tillschneider was the main author of the AfD’s program for how it will wield power in Saxony-Anhalt. At the root are myriad measures aimed at “stabilizing” German identity by redirecting cultural funding and revising school curricula, over which states have primary authority. Tillschneider has announced plans for changing history lessons so that they are oriented toward “more Bismarck, less Hitler,” — controversial phrasing that has recently been removed from the governing manifesto. The party’s program also proposes cutting funding for “anti-German art” and developing a “patriotic tourism” strategy for the state.
Party leaders say they don’t intend to eradicate memorials to Nazi crimes but will fund and restore those that “honor the sacrifices of soldiers” in both world wars. “This support should benefit all monuments equally, without petty political judgments,” the program reads. “Fallen soldiers gave their lives to defend their country. Recognizing and honoring this great sacrifice is a first sign of a patriotic turnaround.”
It’s perhaps no coincidence that such a revolution in German identity would take root in the former East Germany, where the AfD is ascendant. While West Germany was attempting to undertake a confrontation with the past, imperfect as it was, the state narrative in the former East Germany was that its people had vanquished fascism, which in any case was a product of the West. Many of the AfD’s supporters in the East believe a West German narrative about the Nazi past was imposed on them after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
But for Tillschneider, there’s another reason the revolution will begin in the East — because eastern Germans already know what it means to see a political regime collapse.
“As a result of the peaceful revolution, people have witnessed a change in systems and, as a result, have gained some distance, are more reflective,” he said at the AfD family festival, speaking in a breathless torrent. By contrast, he added, western Germans “have been stewing in the same soup for 80 years.”
‘Love for the homeland is not a crime’
As attendees queued for beer and free bratwurst at the AfD family festival — held on an arid field on the outskirts of Querfurt, beside an agricultural-machinery plant — Tillschneider took the stage before an “Our Country First” placard and declared that they had ample reason to celebrate: the establishment parties, he said, were nearing their demise.
“We’re celebrating the fact that the policies that are directed against us — which take away our freedom, which strip us of our autonomy, which impoverish us — will come to an end,” he yelled, his booming voice saturating the speakers. “On Sept. 6, for the first time, we have a realistic chance — and this isn’t just campaign rhetoric — a realistic chance to end this nightmare, to put an end to this horror!”
Advertisement
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt and its potential future premier, then took to the stage to a rock-star reception. Charismatic and very popular online, his quick smile belies the radical politics of the state branch of his party, which domestic intelligence authorities have classified as an extremist organization seeking “to abolish parliamentary democracy in its current form.” AfD politicians in the state, including Siegmund and Tillschneider, deny being extremists, portraying the label as state repression that undermines the democratic will of their supporters.
If Siegmund is the face of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt, Tillschneider supplies much of the brains. Siegmund alluded to this during his speech, thanking Tillschneider for spending “hundreds of hours” on the party’s governing manifesto.
“I’ll need him over the next five years because we’re making history together,” Siegmund said of Tillschneider. “The sun rises in the east, but it will shine over all of Germany!”
As people waited in line for hours to get Siegmund’s autograph, Tillschneider darted frantically from tent to tent, making sure things were running smoothly. “Don’t sell them for less than €10!” he shouted to a group of volunteers as he handed them a box of tote bags emblazoned with Siegmund’s face.
One of those volunteers, Gesine Sauer, a 48-year-old social worker from the area, said she agreed with Tillschneider’s ideas about making Germans proud of their history.
“People always focus on just a very small part of German history — and that has nothing to do with anyone trying to deny it, or trying to dismiss it — but German history is so much more than that,” she said. “And time and again, from all sides, we’re being forced to grapple with this question of guilt. That’s wrong, and it’s not a positive development. Instead, we should reflect on what we were once capable of achieving,” she added, going on to list German historical accomplishments in medicine and industry.
Others put it more simply. “I’d say that was all 90 years ago, and at some point we should just let the past be the past,” said one woman in her 60s wearing a bracelet in the colors of the German flag.
Advertisement
“With us, if you say you love your homeland, you’re stamped as a Nazi,” said one man, a 51-year-old railroad track worker, as he waited in the long line for beer wearing a shirt that read “Love for the homeland is not a crime.”
Most attendees, however, cited other reasons for voting for the AfD: economic and industrial decline; refugees receiving state support while Germans struggled to pay their bills; the government’s refusal to accept cheap Russian natural gas while sending billions in federal aid to Ukraine.
For Tillschneider and his fellow far-right ideologues, these more tangible issues are all connected to the crisis of German identity: the country’s reluctance to pursue its own interests, they argue, stems from an “anti-German” strain of thinking within the country.
“That’s why we have policies that are self-destructive in every area — because we have a cracked identity,” Tillschneider said from underneath a tent at the festival.
He rattled off ideas for repairing the German soul: a “pride month” celebrating German cultural heritage and a festival of German music — not “Baroque music or European music,” he clarified, but “German music.”
He denied the goal was to make Germans forget the Nazi past. Yet he went on to describe a process that seemed to amount to just that.
The goal, he said, was for this history to “no longer be so urgent, no longer so intrusive, no longer so present.”
He added: “Just because something is no longer present doesn’t mean it will be forgotten.”
Nette Nöstlinger contributed reporting.

Hong Kong’s first high-end expo with yachts and supercars to launch in November
SCMP learns inaugural Festival of Connoisseurs to receive some of HK$100 million set aside for MICE sector under 2026-27 budget
Hong Kong will roll out its first cross-industry exhibition for high-end products ranging from haute jewellery to supercars, yachts and private jets in November, as part of efforts to attract big spenders and cement the city as a global conference and event capital.
The South China Morning Post learned on Wednesday that the inaugural Festival of Connoisseurs will receive some of the HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) set aside in Hong Kong’s 2026-27 budget to attract large-scale international exhibitions to the city.
Event organiser Informa Markets will use AsiaWorld-Expo, located near Hong Kong International Airport, as its primary venue for the event running from November 4 to 6.
Other elements of the exhibition will be held in various locations across Hong Kong in an unprecedented “city-as-your-showroom” format.
A source said the exhibition was the first of many such projects to involve the meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector.
“The government is in discussions over other projects, which will elevate Hong Kong’s offerings and experiences on MICE events and, of course, will in turn boost high-end tourism,” the insider said.
“The festival will be spread across several days, cater to different appetites of high-net-worth individuals and maximise interactions with them in iconic venues.”

Pedro Sánchez’s Ceuta crisis just got a lot worse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

A new report alleging Moroccan involvement in the migrant surge threatens to upend the Spanish PM’s narrative and further erode his standing with voters.
A large group of migrants crowd outside the entrance of the Loma del Colmenar reception center, waiting for admission, in Ceuta on September 1, 2026. | Antonio Sempere / AFP via Getty Images
When Pedro Sánchez agreed to appear in the Spanish parliament’s hearings on the Ceuta migration crisis, he knew he would face a hostile audience.
But Thursday’s session promises to be a political reckoning for the Spanish leader, with an emboldened opposition and increasingly distrustful coalition partners seizing on a police report claiming that Morocco played a direct role in last month’s sudden arrival of 72,000 migrants in the autonomous city in North Africa.
The report has dramatically raised the stakes for Sánchez. With the prime minister’s credibility eroding, lawmakers are demanding to know how Spain’s security services failed to detect a hostile operation by a supposedly close ally — and whether the government knew more about Morocco’s role than it previously admitted.
Advertisement
“This wasn’t a spontaneous migration movement, but rather an operation that originated in Morocco and was spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco,” center-right People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said at a rally in Ceuta on Wednesday.
“The government knew and covered it up,” he added, calling for snap elections. “They lied to our faces.”
In the immediate aftermath of the surge, Sánchez described it as an “attack on the territorial integrity of Spain,” but insisted Rabat had nothing to do with it.
He doubled down on that position on Monday, assuring the public he had “no information from Spanish security forces or our intelligence services that would cast any doubt on Moroccan authorities,” and instead accusing Russia, Israel and “an international far-right group” of orchestrating the operation.
But according to the police report, first revealed by Spanish newspaper El Español, Moroccan agents helped orchestrate the mass entry of migrants into the exclave. El País later published a page from the document with images that appeared to show uniformed Moroccan security officers guiding groups of people toward the beach from which they could cross into Ceuta.
The document was commissioned by a judge investigating the surge and drawn up by the National Center for Immigration and Borders, a specialized intelligence unit within Spain’s National Police.
Advertisement
In a letter to National Police Director Francisco Pardo, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska on Wednesday denied knowing of the report’s existence and expressed irritation that its contents had not been shared with the top officials convened to manage the crisis.
Justice and Presidency Minister Félix Bolaños said the government had only learned of the document through the press and declined to comment on it until it had been properly examined.
The report complicates the government’s efforts to avoid a direct clash with Rabat, whose assistance is needed both to deport unauthorized migrants and to prevent future surges. Sánchez on Monday insisted the crisis could “only be resolved with cooperation,” and that “showing a lack of confidence in Morocco will only aggravate this situation.”
Political reckoning
The report has turned Thursday’s hearing into a much more consequential political test for Sánchez.
Far-right Vox party MEP Jorge Buxadé on Wednesday urged Spain’s parliament to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution, which provides for criminal proceedings against members of the government in certain circumstances.
“This was an invasion of our territory, an act of hybrid war orchestrated by Morocco,” he said. “And this report shows the government knew about it beforehand and did nothing to stop it.”
Advertisement
Demands for accountability are also now coming from Sánchez’s own coalition government.
The junior partner in the executive, Sumar, has long questioned Rabat’s role in the crisis, and on Wednesday one of its member parties demanded Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska — who has always attributed the surge to human smuggling mafias — to step down if the information in the police report is proven to be true.
“Not a leaf stirs in Morocco without the government knowing about it, and between 70,000 and 80,000 people don’t move en masse to the Ceuta border in trucks or on foot without being detected,” said Antonio Maíllo, coordinator of the United Left party, which is part of Sumar. “The Moroccan government’s involvement in the crisis is obvious.”
The government’s parliamentary allies — among them the Republican Left of Catalonia and the Basque Nationalist Party — are expected to grill Sánchez on who knew what when, potentially exposing just how little room the prime minister has left in an increasingly uneasy coalition.
That political isolation was also on display on Spain’s streets on Wednesday evening, with tens of thousands of protestors in participating in nationwide demonstrations condemning the situation in Ceuta. Protests were held in more than 260 cities, with dozens of Socialist mayors defying orders from the party leadership and taking part in rallies in support of the exclave.
Their revolt underscores Sánchez’s difficulty enforcing party discipline among local politicians who increasingly see him as a political liability. With municipal and regional elections next May, the protests are a stark sign of the prime minister’s fragile standing heading into a crucial political year.

Nigel Farage’s Reform show gets a reboot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The Reform UK leader will use his conference to strike a ‘very serious tone’ after spending the summer fighting a by-election challenge from Count Binface.
LONDON — Nigel Farage had a silly summer squaring off against Count Binface. Now he wants to get serious.
The Reform UK leader will use his annual party conference, kicking off in Birmingham Thursday, to attempt to move on from a by-election dominated by novelty candidates and questions over his finances. He will try to signal how he would govern if he wins power at the next U.K. general election.
The leader and his four top lieutenants will use their speeches in Britain’s second-largest city to unveil what one senior party official described as “key pledges” for the first 100 days of a Farage premiership.
Advertisement
“It will be a very serious tone this conference,” the official — granted anonymity to discuss internal planning — said.
That’s the hope anyway, because public infighting, questions over undeclared donations, and splits on the right of British politics have dogged Farage’s summer — and could still overshadow proceedings.
Bardella and Farage show
Reform says the conference will be the party’s biggest yet — up by 2,000 attendees on last year, according to internal figures.
They’re boasting big business attendance and a diplomatic presence, too. Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right French party National Rally, will provide a set-piece attraction. Farage and Bardella have bonded over tackling small boat crossings in the Channel — the major public grievance that has fueled Reform’s success.
But Farage knows this event must offer more than a shift in tone. Not only has his party’s polling slumped as Labour rebounds after the ousting of Keir Starmer, but Farage is suffering a severe dent to his personal figures too.
A YouGov survey released this week suggests his net favorability rating has fallen from its peak of -27 last summer to -44. Just 19 percent of Brits now see him as a prime minister-in-waiting — down seven points since June, before he called his “people versus the establishment” by-election in Clacton.
Advertisement
The party knows looking credible is key. That’s why Farage will be leading the pledge-making to the public, culminating in a policy-laced but unscripted speech on Friday. Robert Jenrick, Zia Yusuf and Richard Tice — his spokespeople for the Treasury, home affairs and business briefs, respectively — will be making them too.
“It will be very serious about the problems the country faces and how we intend to fix them in the first 100 days,” the official cited above said.
Some in Reform had hoped the conference would mark the moment Farage announced an expanded front bench. Key posts like health and defense remain unfilled, despite Farage trying to demonstrate the party is no one-man band. But the party will hold off until after the Birmingham jamboree is over, instead announcing “a couple of new people” later this month and in October, according to the official.
Summer of scrutiny
Farage’s return to the limelight, which he has uncharacteristically dodged ever since his re-election in Clacton, began on Wednesday, with an interview with the BBC’s political editor.
The Reform leader has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.
Farage continued to insist Wednesday that he has “done nothing wrong” in not declaring the support in the run-up to the 2024 general election. He argued that the intense scrutiny of Reform’s funding is down to an “establishment” stitch-up, and railed against living in a “complainants’ society.” He compared his situation to the investigations faced by fellow “outsider” Donald Trump.
Advertisement
But Farage’s victory in Clacton last month served to restart the parliamentary standards commissioner’s investigation into the Harborne funding. Farage himself suggested that an interview with the investigator is on the horizon — and a sanction could well trigger another by-election for the Reform leader. He is keen to press the need to fund personal security for politicians in a dangerous world.
Reform’s conference opens Thursday with a day of trying to charm businesses, while the main event gets underway Friday.
Underlining the threat that Farage argues politicians now face, the conference will start with a tribute to Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old Reform spokesperson killed in her own home in July.
Restore a ‘shiny object’
Reform top brass seems keen to avoid talking about one elephant in the room: Restore Britain.
The right-wing splinter group, formed by sacked Reform MP Rupert Lowe, has been sucking small but significant support from Farage’s right flank in recent months.
Restore is talked of derisively as a “statistical anomaly” inside Reform, but tackling the threat is likely to be a topic of conversation in the conference center. “New shiny objects often attract support. That’s the way human beings are,” Farage dismissively told the BBC Wednesday, in an indication he believes support for Lowe’s outfit could tail off.
Advertisement
For Restore’s part, a disruptive intervention this week seems unlikely. “Let’s let them fight among themselves,” said one well-connected figure in Restore circles.
Indeed, the plea for unity that Farage wrapped last year’s conference with will be put to the test again in Birmingham. The party goes into this conference with open disagreement in its ranks.
Farage this summer publicly reprimanded his home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, for calling a Conservative former defense secretary a “traitor” in a series of angry online arguments. Reform then suspended political commentator Tim Montgomerie for criticizing senior party figures — including Yusuf.
Trade unions meanwhile look unlikely to leap at Farage’s call to ditch their historic ties with Labour and attend Reform’s conference. “I don’t think any unions are seriously going to take up his invitation to attend Reform conference,” predicted one union leader.
But for all the sniggering at Farage’s fight with Binface this summer, there are more optimistic takes inside the party about the resilience of its base.
Farage not only saw increased support in Clacton — but Reform’s polling is not collapsing in the face of its most intense scrutiny to date.
Advertisement
“Despite a summer that you might say hasn’t been brilliant,” said a second Reform official, “what we’ve learned is that our polling base is around 20-21, which is a step up in two years.”
It’s this core that will be drinking up the Farage show in Birmingham. But it’s the rest of Britain he’ll need to aim at this week.

How Merkel and Merz lost eastern Germany to the AfD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, took to the stage in the central marketplace of the town of Naumburg and declared there was a new “awakening” in eastern Germany.
Ahead of a vital election in the region of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — in which Siegmund is within striking distance of becoming the first far-right leader to govern a German state since 1945 — that appeal to an eastern identity struck a chord.
A young man beside me was hollering “Ostdeutschland!” although he was too young to have lived in the communist German Democratic Republic. “It was purer there,” he explained. “More German. Not America-Germany like the West.”
Advertisement
Elements of Siegmund’s new awakening sounded reminiscent of the old East, and his speech would certainly have played well in the Kremlin. He condemned the foolishness of supporting “corrupt” Ukraine and addressed the need to return to oil and gas supplies from Russia.
East Germany formally dissolved in 1990, but it did not disappear. Its struggles for identity within the sprawling German federal system, with power concentrated in Berlin, have fueled the ascent of the far right.
If the AfD does secure an outright victory this weekend, it will raise profound questions about how chancellors such as Helmut Kohl, Angela Merkel and Friedrich Merz failed to manage the post-unification transition and prevent large parts of the east from veering off on a political trajectory toward the far right.
Sausages and strongarms
In a generally upbeat line for sausages and beer in Naumburg, there were also some less cheery sorts in neo-Nazi T-shirts and regalia. One of the crowd told me the government in Berlin “sends our tax money to the Jews in Israel and [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy instead of spending it here.”
It is important to stress that the eastern political identity is not monochrome nostalgia for the GDR. Indeed, the AfD is repurposing the slogan of the 1989 demonstrations against communism — “Wir sind das Volk” – “We are the people” — for its own ends.
Advertisement
That taps into memories of marching for freedom in the last days of the socialist state.
“And now we will show the world again,” said Dirk Huzenlaub, a metalworker in his blue overalls, whom I spoke to on another campaign pit stop in the nearby town of Lützen
He has done well as a self- employed worker, supplying many local companies. But he adds that the “people at the top don’t want us to do well — they keep us down on purpose.” A welter of internet conspiracy theories followed, including the notion that Merz and his predecessor Merkel “betrayed us — we risk our country collapsing the way the old East Germany collapsed.”
Beyond the conviviality of the sausage line, the mood can sour fast — as I discovered when I sought to speak with Siegmund in Lützen, only to be told “mainstream” press were not welcome. I was roughly jostled aside, my arm twisted by a musclebound heavy flanking Siegmund, who sported an earpiece and a lavishly tattooed neck.
“Move or I will take you to the police,” he barked. We had a short, unproductive debate about the constitutionally guaranteed right to report freely in public places.
Another hard arm twist and shove ensued, ending with me stumbling over a curb and being dragged to a police car. No one seemed much bothered by this.
Advertisement
“This woman is being un-co-operative,” the minder snarled. At the next stop in Naumburg, another attentive policeman enjoined me to stay away from “Security Zone 1” — anywhere near the stage.
Then came the more chilling warning.
“It’s for your own safety,” he added. “Best remember, in that zone, the AfD are the masters.”
Merkel and the migration backlash
The last two chancellors — Merz and Merkel — have provoked a strong backlash in eastern Germany.
For Merkel, the outcome could have been more positive. She hailed from the East herself and was an active participant in the Wende, or “turn”, away from communism. She inherited Kohl’s pledge to produce “flourishing landscapes” in the “new federal states.” Forlorn towns and cities were restored, the air pollution from brown-coal energy supplies ended, and potholed roads are now smooth enough to roar along in Mercedes and BMWs.
But the East responded far more negatively to Merkel’s decision to allow a mass influx of asylum seekers from Syria and North Africa in 2015 and 2016. She signaled her empathy for that in a conversation with me in 2018, saying she understood the heartache of easterners seeing their communities empty out demographically and traditional jobs disappear.
“Of course, these disturbing personal experiences affect people and leave a deep mark — we need to understand this,” she said.
Advertisement
But Merkel’s responses did not go far enough for people worried about the speed of social change. And from 2015, the AfD began to soar.
The Covid era deepened divisions too: a social media campaign demanded the introduction of the Russian Sputnik V vaccine ahead of better options. That demonstrated a complex blend of attitudes which feature strongly in AfD lore to this day: Distrust of Western capitalism and an acceptance of Russia.
The veteran sociologist Detlef Pollack diagnoses a “victim mythology” western politicians find hard to combat without sounding aloof. Fully three-quarters of voters who lean towards the AfD think the unified Germany has robbed them of their just deserts, in comparison with two-fifths of the public in the old GDR.
Frustration came to mark the dealings of Merkel and her successor Merz in talking about the mood in the old east.
“There is no point trying to convince you [about the justification for accepting over 1 million refugees],” she said at a rally I attended in her final election campaign in 2017 in the industrial town of Bitterfeld as a hostile mob booed and blew horns to stop her being heard. Backstage she shook her head, clearly furious.
The more she was lionized as a Gloriana of international liberal democracy for her robust dealings with U.S. President Donald Trump, the more alienated she became from socially conservative easterners. The AfD also learned from the MAGA movement how to unite multiple strands of thought into campaign messages, interwoven with slugs of fake or exaggerated stories.
Advertisement
The arrival of Merz, a western politician not armed with a vast array of communication skills, together with struggles of the wider German economy — like the symbolic hit of massive projected job losses at the VW plant in Wolfsburg close to the old border — have taken a further shine off the lure of the Federal Republic’s prosperity model.
Falling behind
An assessment from the Halle Institute for Economic Research noted that, after the 1990s, the “initial catch-up momentum came to a halt. Since then, the East German economy has mostly grown even more slowly than the West German one.”
It blamed the “lack of productivity of East German companies,” as well as a protracted brain drain and a low rate of business formation. A German defense official, granted permission to speak confidentially to POLITICO, added: “Overwhelmingly, the new defense industries which will drive prosperity and security are based in the old Federal Republic. That gives the east less interest in arming against Russia — it’s a double hit we need to address.”
Merkel has demanded more “courage” to “fight for democracy,” channeling her own brand of 1989 nostalgia. These messages embolden the AfD’s opponents, including churchgoers now rallying as they did against the regime in 1989. Problematically, though, her appeals can also come across as “Bevormundung,” with eastern Germans feeling like they are being treated with haughty condescension.
Merz warns that a far-right government in Saxony-Anhalt would mean “foreign investors steering clear of the state in future” and that the state “will face considerable problems.”
Whether that scare tactic proves persuasive remains to be seen.
(For his part, Siegmund has shed the miserabilist mantras of other AfD luminaries. “My God, the women are great-looking in this town,” I hear him announce to giggling selfie-seekers in Lützen. “Better not tell my wife.”)
Merz also does not exude much personal interest in the East, other than seeing it as a problem to be kept at bay. Very few of his Cabinet hail from that part of Germany — though the party cites the rise of a new generation of eastern Germans to the next tier of ministerial posts. That may need to accelerate soon to combat the rising mood of alienation.
Advertisement
Arriving on a whistlestop visit on Monday to support Sven Schulze as his party’s candidate for minister-president, the chancellor condemned “people who trade on anger.” He did venture out among voters — something many leading politicians avoid.
Saxony-Anhalt is a small state in population — with just over 2 million inhabitants. But it is also the cradle of the Lutheran tradition of challenging the mighty — a theme that the more historically minded rally-goers raised with me.
As Siegmund puts it: “Even if we don’t get there [to an overall majority], we are not going away.” That too was a stubborn cry from the streets in late 1989. And in 2026, it spurred huge roars of approval through the marketplace in Naumburg, drowning out the counter-protests.
On Sunday, the AfD will be put to the test.
So too will a German political establishment that won unification, only to lose much of its grip on people power.
Anne McElvoy is a former correspondent in East Germany and author of The Saddled Cow, East Germany’s Life and Legacy.

Current cricket schedule could hurt women's game, says Perry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:58:58 UTC
10:58:58 KST

Ellyse Perry says the fact that Australia's women will not play international or WBBL cricket during the school holidays could hurt the growth of the game.
Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer through to the end of 2029 are white-ball games against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.
Perry says it is important to "carve out" a period during the peak of the Australian summer for women's matches.
Ellyse Perry has called for Australia's women to be given regular cricket in the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule could stunt the game.
Australia will play nine white-ball matches at home this summer against Bangladesh and New Zealand, with all confined to October and March.
The Australian team has not played a game at home during the summer school holidays since January 2025, while the WBBL also now falls entirely during the school term.
Part of the issue for officials has been India's WPL moving to the January window, with a common fear it will eventually extend into most of February.
Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer under the current program, which runs until the end of 2029, are white-ball ones against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.
Australian players have long pushed for a regular spot in the summer, much like the Boxing Day Test in Melbourne and New Year's Test in Sydney are part of the national calendar.
"It's the best time of year to play across that school-holiday window," Perry said.
"People are at home, everyone's head is in cricket too. There is a lot on the schedule in both the men's and women's game. It's a nice time to go out and watch.
"But also for them to be inspired to play themselves and be involved in cricket, it's really important.
"I don't know what the perfect window is, but I think somewhere in the peak of the Australian summer is important to carve out.
"Where and how you do that is more of a strategic planning opportunity that will take some time to find. But we should be prioritising that for the Australian team."
There is the view that being pushed to the outskirts of summer also has the potential to stunt any momentum around the team after its dominant T20 World Cup.
The timing of the WPL means the only real window during the school holidays would be in the second half of December, perhaps in the lead-up to Christmas.
"It's not just for Australia and all the southern-hemisphere countries … to make sure we're encouraging people to come along to matches," Perry said.
"It's a really tricky one; the scheduling and planning is a matrix I would never want to look at.
"But it would be really nice for us to preserve a window there where people know the Australian women's team is playing so they have the means and opportunity to come watch.
"That's really important in terms of continuing to grow the game for young boys and girls. But also we want to play in front of a home crowd with good opposition each year."

Germany hails Israeli LORA missile after secret naval test, eyes Russia deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:51:38 UTC
10:51:38 KST

German newspaper Bild reported Wednesday that the German Navy had completed what it described as a “secret test” of the Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile in the North Atlantic.
According to the report, the German military expects to advance plans to purchase the missiles, which have a range of more than 500 kilometers. “The range exceeds anything we have known until now,” German Navy chief Vice Adm. Jan Christian Kaack said of the Israeli missiles.
In an article praising the capabilities of the Israel Aerospace Industries-made missile, Bild also highlighted the country Germany increasingly views as its primary security threat: Russia.
Germany accused Russia only days earlier of being behind an explosive drone found last month near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport. The aircraft was carrying military ammunition, and German officials said an explosion could have caused devastating damage.
Bild wrote that acquiring the system would form part of Germany’s rearmament plans launched after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, aimed at deterring Moscow. Concern among Germany’s allies is growing over possible aggression by Russian President Vladimir Putin, the newspaper wrote.
Its headline read: “Secret mission! German Navy tests Israeli missile,” accompanied by Kaack’s comments about the weapon’s range. The LORA ballistic missile is now expected to be offered to Germany in a deal potentially worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Germany has already purchased Israel Aerospace Industries’ Arrow 3 missile defense system in major deals. The Bild report described the latest test as a significant step toward a possible acquisition. Two LORA missiles were launched from a German Navy warship, and according to reports on the test, both struck their designated targets at sea.
If Germany decides to buy the missiles, it would join a small group of countries known to possess the Israeli system, including Azerbaijan and India.
The test also marks a milestone for the German Navy because Germany currently does not possess ballistic missiles. According to German reports, the missiles were launched from the frigate Sachsen-Anhalt, one of four F125-class frigates operated by the German Navy. Two frigates were sent to an area between Ireland and Iceland for the test.
Germany already has a similar long-range strike capability through its Taurus cruise missiles, of which the German military holds about 600. Their official range also exceeds 500 kilometers.
Unlike LORA, however, the Taurus is launched from fighter jets and flies toward its target at low altitude. The Israeli missile can also be launched from ships, climbs to altitude and travels toward its target on a ballistic trajectory at much higher speed. Germany is also developing an upgraded version of the Taurus, known as Taurus NEO, with production expected to begin in 2029.
Bild said Israel Aerospace Industries describes LORA as a precision “tactical missile” that Israeli security forces have used in Lebanon and, in an aircraft-adapted version, in Iran.
Israel Aerospace Industries unveiled the air-launched version, known as AIR LORA, at the ILA aerospace exhibition in Berlin last year. The missile is designed to be launched from fighter aircraft while they remain far from the target and outside the range of enemy air-defense systems.
Calcalist on Wednesday quoted senior Israeli defense officials as saying that the emerging German deal would focus, at least initially, on the naval version of the ballistic missile.
They added that follow-on deals could also be possible in the coming years. According to the officials, the prospects for a deal are very high because LORA has proven operational experience, including in fighting between Azerbaijan and Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh in recent years.
The LORA is part of a broader German effort to expand its long-range strike capabilities in response to the Russian threat.
According to Bild, Berlin is also planning to purchase Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States, with a range of up to 2,500 kilometers, while working with allies on the development of European-made long-range missile systems.
Germany regards its shortage of long-range precision weapons as one of the capability gaps it is now seeking to close.
Germany is also among the relatively small number of European countries that maintained comparatively stable relations with Israel while Jerusalem faced sharp criticism over its conduct in Gaza following the October 7 massacre.
Unlike many other European countries, Germany took a relatively restrained approach, although it restricted sales of offensive weapons to Israel for several months before later lifting those limitations.

Trump threatens more strikes as death toll in Iran rises to 18
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:45:32 UTC
10:45:32 KST

Trump threatens more strikes as death toll in Iran rises to 18
Trump says US can hit Iran ‘anytime we want’ as Tehran says deadly strikes, including on wedding party, a war crime.
Trump says US sees ‘everything’ Iran does, threatens further attacks
United States President Donald Trump has threatened more attacks on Iran, warning that Washington could hit Iran “anytime we want”, as the death toll from the latest US strikes climbed to 18, with at least 108 others wounded.
Trump’s threat on Wednesday came after the US and Iran exchanged their biggest barrage since July. The US military struck cities and areas along Iran’s southern coast, near the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, including a wedding party in the city of Kuhestak.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Republican senator calls on Trump to fire Secretary of Defence Hegseth
- list 2 of 4Israeli PM says Israel is working to overthrow Iran’s government
- list 3 of 4The long-term implications of Pete Hegseth’s US military purges
- list 4 of 4Trump suggests renaming Strait of Hormuz as Trump Strait amid Iran war
Iran retaliated with attacks on US bases across the Middle East, including Bahrain, Iraq and Jordan.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said, “We hit them very hard last night” and that the strikes “took out all of the new equipment that they tried to build along the Strait of Hormuz”.
“It was a very heavy attack last night. And we’re prepared to do another one. And anytime we want,” he said.
Iranian officials said at least 18 people were killed in the US strikes.
The victims included two children, according to Mohammad-Reza Zafarghandi, Iran’s health minister. One of them was a four-year-old who was killed in the strike on the wedding party in Kuhestak in Sirik county.
At least four people were killed in that strike.
Esmaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, described the Kuhestak attack as a “war crime” and hit back at US claims that it does not target civilians.
“The reality is so horrifying that even American propaganda has never dared make the claim [the US military] is making today. Sirik is not a story. The civilians are real. The victims are real”, Baghaei wrote on X.
Iranian media said the funeral for the four Kuhestak victims will be held on Thursday.
‘Uncomfortable strategic position’
The six-month war has led to a spike in oil prices, roiled the global economy and posed increasing political problems for Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections in the US.
Only 31 percent of Americans approve of the war, while some 63 percent disapprove, according to a poll by the Reuters news agency and the Ipsos polling firm in August. Voters are particularly unhappy about high gas prices. Since the fighting resumed this weekend, the price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, has climbed to about $95, up more than 30 percent from the start of the war.
Trump’s approval rating has also fallen from 40 percent to 33 percent since the conflict began, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
On Wednesday, Trump said he did not think the renewed military campaign would last long. He also reiterated his position that the upcoming elections were not a factor in his Iran strategy.
“Number one, I’m not running. My party is running, and I’m going to help my party,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “But I think my party respects the fact that we’re not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Iran has denied seeking a nuclear weapon.
Tariq Khan, a retired Pakistani lieutenant-general and former commander of the Pakistan Army’s Frontier Corps, said the US “now finds itself in an increasingly uncomfortable strategic position in the Iran war”.
“The US has not succeeded in restoring the maritime environment that existed before the war, and is now expending military resources to deal with a problem the war itself helped create,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The strait was a free-flowing international waterway carrying roughly one-fifth of the world’s traded oil before the war. Tehran shut the waterway in response to the US and Israeli strikes on February 18 that began the war. Despite repeated US claims that the strait remains open, only a handful of vessels now pass through each day, and Iran continues to target ships attempting the crossing.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two oil tankers had struck mines and were disabled while attempting an unauthorised transit. Separately, Saudi shipping firm Bahri reported that two Filipino sailors were killed in an attack on their vessel earlier in the week.
Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), which Tehran set up to police the Strait of Hormuz, added 11 more ships to its blacklist for alleged “noncompliance” this week, on top of the 45 blacklisted last week. The PGSA said the vessels will face fines, seizures or confiscation unless they submit required documentation to Iran before attempting to cross the strait.
Strait of Hormuz
At the same time, the US has intensified an economic isolation campaign against Iran, threatening to slap countries that trade with Tehran with massive sanctions, while also maintaining its own blockade in the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump on Wednesday continued to insist that Washington was in control of the strait, saying US forces were helping bring “lots of boats out every day with millions of barrels of oil”.
“We are, for the most part, doing it without trouble. Every once in a while they shoot a drone, and we knock it down. We have control, very strong control,” he said.
On Tuesday, he had claimed the US Navy was helping escort some 30 ships out of the strait every day. Before the war, some 130 ships transited the waterway daily.
Khan, the former Pakistani general, said Iran understands it cannot defeat the US conventionally and is seeking to make the war costly for Trump.
“If Trump escalates, Iran can portray America as being drawn deeper into another Middle Eastern war; if he restrains himself, Tehran can claim that American military superiority cannot compel Iran to surrender,” he said.
“Iran does not need a battlefield victory; it needs to remain standing, keep the economic disruption alive, and make the war politically costly for the US. Tehran has to make American victory increasingly unaffordable – militarily, economically and electorally.”

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia will never chase after Europe and plead for sanctions to be lifted, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said during a lecture organized by the Znanie (Knowledge) Society on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
He said that Russia has never constructed walls or isolated itself from Europe, and it was the European Union’s choice to do this.

Hong Kong’s culture chief has paid tribute to veteran actor and dancer Lau Siu-ming following his death on Wednesday at the age of 94, praising his outstanding artistic achievements and contributions to the cultural sector.
Lau, affectionately known as Ming Sir, died at about 6pm on Wednesday, according to media reports citing voice actor Ding Yue.

Born in 1931, Lau was among the first Hong Kong dancers to pursue formal training in Europe. He was known for incorporating his experiences and Chinese heritage into his work.
He was later invited to perform with the Brussels Ballet du XXe Siècle. Rebirth of the Phoenix was among his best-known works and was performed in France during the 1960s, according to the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts.

For many clients, however, the motivation for hiring a companion is convenience rather than loneliness.

AFRL Seeks Payload-Agnostic, Affordable Hypersonic Cruise Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:36:44 UTC
10:36:44 KST

The Air Force Research Laboratory has signaled to industry it wants to develop a low-cost hypersonic cruise missile to deliver a wide range of payloads at a range up to 500 nautical miles.
In a brief one-page notice released Sept. 1, posted on Sam.gov, AFRL gave the broad outlines of its new project, which falls under the broader Pioneering Aerospace Capabilities, Engineering & Research program.
“Offerors are encouraged to consider modular open systems architectures, together with aggressive application of digital engineering advanced manufacturing techniques,” according to the note.
That note signals an openness to using 3D printing as a way to make a more affordable hypersonic missile than the Air Force has pursued in other programs, such as its two other hypersonic weapons, the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile and the Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon.
HACM is an ongoing Air Force effort with RTX to build a scramjet-powered, air-breathing hypersonic missile to reach and maintain speeds of Mach 5 or greater, capable of being carried on tactical fighters and bombers; Northrop Grumman developed the engine.
ARRW is a Lockheed Martin-built, boost-glide, air-launched hypersonic weapon designed primarily to be carried by bombers.
Payload
The new AFRL project has “no specific payload requirement,” according to the notice.
That agnostic payload approach differs from HACM, which from the outset was based around a kinetic warhead to strike heavily defended targets. The new project’s lack of specific warhead requirements means it could carry kinetic strike options, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance payloads, or electronic warfare gear.
But the strike option remains.
“It could provide new ‘middle ground’ options for precision strikes against time-sensitive targets,” retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, director of future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “Depending on its seekers and warhead variants, a 500-nautical mile hypersonic weapon could be used against ground fixed and relocatable targets, moving maritime targets, and possibly even high-value airborne targets like [Airborne Early Warning & Control] aircraft.”
More Options
Such a weapon would given Air Force planners a wider range of options, especially in far-flung regions of the Pacific, where an adversary such as the Chinese military uses complex anti-access, area-denial systems, Gunzinger said.
The hypersonic focus is also crucial for overcoming much of the Chinese military’s capabilities, he said.
“The capability and capacity to conduct prompt maritime strikes against moving targets such as the [People’s Liberation Army Navy] Type 055 Renhai class cruisers and Type 52D Luyang-III class destroyers will be critical to defeating an assault on Taiwan or other scenario,” Gunzinger said. “I would also stress the value of using hypersonic class weapons to counter high-value airborne aircraft like KJ-500/600 AEW&C aircraft, which will be key to countering the PLA Air Force’s long-range kill chains.”
And, if right-sized, that kind of missile could be used across a variety of platforms, such as the F-15EX, as well as the B-21, B-2, F-47 and even the F-35, he said.
“Frankly, sixth-generation stealth aircraft will not need 500 [nautical mile] standoff, but it would increase their ability to avoid the highest risk threat areas and expand areas it can attack in a single sortie,” the retired colonel and former B-52 pilot said.
While the Air Force is still working to field HACM, Gunzinger sees the potential of a low-cost cruise missile as an added, not replacement, capability. Especially, he said, if the future weapon could carry EW payloads, which are critical for suppression of enemy air defenses.
Scaling Hypersonics and Cost
The 3D-printing option might give the Air Force a way to scale the weapons in a way that Gunzinger and Mitchell have long advocated.
“Affordability can be a barrier to fielding hypersonic weapons at scale—the Army’s ‘Dark Eagle’ ground-launched boost-glide weapon that costs $40 million or more for a single warhead is a good example of this,” Gunzinger said. “So, an air-launched weapon that costs low single-digit millions of dollars each would increase the potential to acquire them at scale.”
The Air Force is seeking $1.96 billion in hypersonic funding for HACM and ARRW in its fiscal 2027 budget request, currently winding its way through Congress.
Most of that, about $1.2 billion, is for HACM: $404 million to buy the first operational lot of missiles and $806 million for continued dollars for research, development, test, and evaluation.
The service is also seeking around $748 million for ARRW—$452 million for procurement and $296 million for an Increment 2 version of the weapon work to be adapted for long-range counter-maritime missions.
But even beyond hypersonics, the Air Force is keenly interested in developing cheaper munitions. It is pursuing many of them through its Family of Affordable Mass Munitions program, which seeks to field 28,000 low-cost cruise missiles over the next five years. The Pentagon announced in July it was awarding multiyear contracts with companies Anduril, CoAspire and Zone 5 Technologies to produce those non-hypersonic weapons at a quick clip, starting in 2027.
The Project
The affordable hypersonic missile project will consist of two rounds. The first will have AFRL accept white paper submissions from industry, followed by a second round in which industry will submit full technical and cost proposals.
The lab first posted a notice for a potential “focused call” or technology demonstration competition in January, titled “Rapid Maturation and Demonstration of Hypersonic Weapon Concepts.” Then on March 16, it released a call for “Hypersonic Affordable Mass Weapon Concepts,” Molly Lachance, an AFRL spokesperson, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“Following internal reviews and refined program requirements for the Hypersonic Affordable Mass Weapon Concepts (HAMWC) effort, we updated key project parameters to better align with mission priorities. Because these adjustments represented a material change to the original scope, a resolicitation was required,” Lachance wrote.
For the Sept. 1 notice, AFRL expects to post amendments within 30 days, according to the notice.

Meta Pushes Its New AI Agent on Employees—but Eases Off on Tokenmaxxing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:32:02 UTC
10:32:02 KST

Meta is formally ending what amounted to a tokenmaxxing incentive program for employees. In an internal announcement this week, the social media giant told workers that their performance evaluations would no longer be dependent upon how much they used AI tools, three employees who received the message tell WIRED. But as Meta workers simultaneously begin testing a new agentic AI tool known as Hatch, they say their token consumption continues to surge.
Almost a year ago, Meta had said workers would be graded on their "AI-driven impact,” which in practice meant evaluating the extent to which they used chatbots and agents to improve their day-to-day work, Business Insider reported at the time. Usage correlated with employees receiving labels such as “AI Native,” “AI First,” or “AI Enabled,” according to a lawsuit filed in July by about two dozen employees arguing that Meta violated US antidiscrimination laws when laying them off in May. (Workers on health and family leaves say they couldn’t accumulate usage and were unfairly penalized as a result; Meta has denied the allegations in the ongoing case.)
New guidance for performance reviews unveiled this week replaces references to evaluating employees based on criteria like “usage of AI” and their “AI Native” designation, with looser wording, which caveats that “these outcomes can be supported by AI or other means.” It restores Meta’s focus to grading employees on their impact, with less regard to how it is achieved. Some Meta employees tell WIRED the changes are subtle but welcome, freeing them from feeling pressured to use AI in situations in which it doesn’t make sense.
Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton tells WIRED that the updates this week aim to emphasize what has always been the case—Meta evaluates employees based on their contributions. He adds that labels such as “AI Native” were never used for performance evaluation. Engineers across the company were told this week that the company “will not use AI adoption dashboards or token counts to evaluate impact,” The Information reported on Wednesday.
For months, some Meta employees say, their colleagues prompted AI tools repeatedly—or what they viewed as frivolously—to maximize internal usage measurements, like the amount of tokens, or AI units, they consumed. The tokenmaxxing era reached a high point when one Meta worker created an internal leaderboard for tracking how much employees used AI, labeling them as, for example, a “Token Legend.” After details of the dashboard leaked, the employee took it down in April. A couple of months later, Meta moved to ration employees’ AI usage.
More recently, Meta has been encouraging—but not requiring—employees to use its most advanced AI experiment, an agentic tool that can autonomously carry out actions on a computer. Known as Hatch and similar to the viral sensation OpenClaw, it can browse the web and operate other applications. Employees have been able to test Hatch for the past several weeks on their corporate devices ahead of an expected public release.
Some employees have been hesitant to connect Hatch to their personal email, calendar, and other nonwork digital accounts because of privacy worries, as well the possibility that the AI could mess up something important, two current Meta employees familiar with the concerns tell WIRED. Meta previously ran a project that tracked employees’ keystrokes and other activity on their work devices to collect data for training AI systems. The project, which Meta has since paused, eroded many employees’ trust in the company’s AI tools, the sources say.
However, no longer having to fear being dinged on performance reviews for sitting out AI testing could help boost morale and, ultimately, rebuild trust among Meta’s workforce. Already, some employees say they have embraced Hatch for booking personal appointments and organizing their life outside of work. They describe the tool as effective, though some worry about the environmental and economic trade-offs of using large amounts of tokens and other computing resources to automate tasks.
Meta declined to comment on Hatch testing.
Though employees may no longer be intending to maximize their token usage, Hatch is still consuming more than standard chatbots and software coding assistants of yesteryear, workers say. And employees believe management still is interested in seeing them prove they can effectively wield AI tools.
If Hatch ends up boosting productivity as intended, some employees fear Meta could carry out additional job cuts. Last week, Reuters reported that Meta was gearing up for another round of major layoffs on top of the 8,000 jobs cut in May, but it called off the plans amid an increase in software bugs linked to reliance on AI and slower-than-anticipated progress on agent development. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said further mass layoffs are not expected this year.
Additional reporting by Zoë Schiffer.

Remains of 17 Polish Army soldiers and seven German troops exhumed in Lviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:31:00 UTC
10:31:00 KST

Remains of 17 Polish Army soldiers and seven German troops exhumed in Lviv
Lubomyr Horbach, Head of the Pamiat (Memory) Society for Searching for War Victims, told Ukrinform.
“The burials are arranged in three rows, each 45–50 meters long. In the first row, which we have partially examined, we found about 20 burial pits. We exhumed the remains of six Polish Army servicemen from them. There are items confirming this: uniform buttons bearing the Polish coat of arms, various fasteners, hooks and rings characteristic of Polish soldiers’ equipment. We did not find any military identification devices, also known as dog tags, in these burials,” the head of the society said.
Search teams also exhumed from the first row the remains of seven soldiers from German armed formations, specifically the 1st Mountain Division of the German Wehrmacht, which was partly made up of Austrian citizens. Three of them had identification tags.
“We notified the German War Graves Commission in Ukraine about this. They immediately found in their archival records a list of German servicemen who died in Holoskiv, which gives dates of death ranging from September 14 to 20, 1939. We also know that Polish soldiers died during the same period. The German servicemen were buried among the Polish soldiers. They had no military equipment or weapons with them. All these indications suggest that local residents buried the dead after the fighting had ended, as the military units did not take the bodies with them,” Horbach said.
Search teams have also fully examined the second row of graves, where they found approximately 40–50 individual burial pits.
“Here we exhumed the remains of 11 people. One of them had an identification tag clearly indicating that he was a Catholic, so he was most likely Polish by nationality. It is difficult to identify the nationality of the other exhumed Polish Army servicemen because there are no items in the graves that could help establish their identity. This unit included Poles, Ukrainians and representatives of other nationalities who served in or were mobilized into the Polish Army,” the head of the Pamiat Society for Searching for War Victims added.
Ukrainian and Polish specialists are continuing the exhumation work at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv. The work is preliminarily expected to continue until October 2.
As reported by Ukrinform, on August 25, about 30 specialists from Ukraine and Poland began search and exhumation operations at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which will continue until October 2. The exhumation research is being conducted in implementation of agreements reached through the work of the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on National Memory.
On the Ukrainian side, the search and exhumation work is being carried out by a team from the Pamiat Society for Searching for War Victims; on the Polish side, by staff of the Institute of National Remembrance of the Republic of Poland and Wroclaw Medical University.
According to search operations conducted in 2010 and 2019, 110–120 individual graves of Polish Army soldiers were identified at the cemetery. The soldiers were killed in battles against units of German military formations that surrounded Lviv from the west and south in September 1939.
Photos provided by Lubomyr Horbach

How Hongkong Post can ensure it’s not boxed out of the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:30:06 UTC
10:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
How Hongkong Post can ensure it’s not boxed out of the future
Regardless of which direction is chosen for the postal service, any reductions in staffing must be done with sensitivity and transparency
3-MIN READ3-MIN
5
 Listen
Mike Rowse is an independent commentator. 
The great debate about what to do with Hongkong Post has begun. There will be many twists and turns before we know the final outcome, but one thing is clear: it is vital to keep the staff on board at every step. We ultimately want to have an organisation of committed professionals running a world-class outfit. Early indications are that there could be problems.
We are here because of a sharp deterioration in the post office’s financial position starting in 2017-18. A loss of more than HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) that year was followed by losses of over HK$200 million in 2018-19 and more than HK$300 million in 2019-20. Total losses in the past eight years amount to HK$2.9 billion, and the Legislative Council recently approved a HK$4.6 billion capital injection to cover the expense of maintaining the postal service’s operations for the next three years while a review considers options for the long term.
This is a far cry from the heady days of 1995, when the post office was turned into a trading fund. That means it enjoyed more flexibility in business matters but had more responsibility for its overall financial situation. The sudden swerve to substantial losses does not mean the original decision on trading fund status was wrong, but it is a reflection of the enormous changes in the operating environment in recent years.
Mail volumes everywhere have collapsed as people switch to email and other forms of electronic communication. Why bother with a long letter from home to a child studying overseas when you can make a free call on your mobile phone and see each other in the process?
The situation is still changing. In the past, the post office could count on substantial revenue from philatelic sales to offset shortfalls in other areas. In the era of screens and electronic games, though, do children still collect stamps with the same fervour of previous eras? Will this funding stream also fade in time?
Options being floated for the future include wholesale privatisation, corporatisation or reversion to normal government department status.

US forces struck nearly 60 Iranian military targets around the waterway during the operation, two US officials familiar with the operations told CNN.
The operation targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications installations. US forces also destroyed several anti-ship cruise missiles during the escort.
Before the war began more than six months ago, roughly 20 million barrels of oil transited the strait daily. On Monday, more than 17 million barrels passed through, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC.
US military officials anticipate additional strikes near the strait in the coming days, said one of the officials, as he claimed Iranian forces have demonstrated the ability to rebuild their capabilities quickly, requiring sustained offensive pressure.
The US and Iran remain locked in a bitter dispute about control of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global oil shipments. Fighting has repeatedly flared around the waterway since the war began in late February.
US President Donald Trump declared American dominance over the strait. "We now control the Strait of Hormuz. We control it...They get nothing, and we took out ships," Trump said Wednesday.
In a post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump floated renaming the waterway. "Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to Trump Strait???," he wrote.
Tehran has rejected Washington's assertions of control. Iranian officials have repeatedly stated the strait will remain closed or heavily restricted until the US meets conditions tied to an interim deal reached in June.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has dismissed US claims that the strait is "open," accusing Washington of manipulating oil markets and concealing military failures.
The US has conducted mine-clearance operations and pre-emptive strikes on Iranian systems it alleges were preparing to deploy mines, describing the actions as efforts to restore safe passage.

US export curbs have reshaped China’s tech scene around ‘chokepoints’: report

US export curbs have reshaped China’s tech scene around ‘chokepoints’: report
China’s tech start-ups now focus far more on key ‘chokepoint’ technologies, especially in the chip supply chain, Morgan Stanley report finds
Chinese technology companies seeking public listings are increasingly concentrated in areas where Beijing is trying to break its reliance on foreign technology, as years of US export controls reshape the country’s pipeline of stock market hopefuls.
About 20 per cent of companies that have launched initial public offerings on Shanghai’s Star Market so far this year are engaged in tackling key technological “chokepoints” facing China, compared with just 8.1 per cent in 2022, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis of 229 IPOs between 2022 and mid-July 2026.
About 60 per cent of firms in 2026 contributed to China’s push for supply chain self-sufficiency, up from 41 per cent four years ago, said the report published on Friday.
China’s critical tech bottlenecks have also narrowed since 2022, from a broad mix of strategic goods to a focus on the semiconductor supply chain, according to the investment bank. Driven by expanding foreign trade curbs, the pressure points have moved upstream to raw materials, complex machinery, specialised parts and core manufacturing tools.
Of the 21 companies Morgan Stanley identified as addressing chokepoints this year, 19 are in the semiconductor supply chain. There is a particular focus on chokepoints in electronics, with 15 of the firms coming from that sector.
“As the chokepoints expanded in the past three to four years, more domestic companies became dedicated in those areas and by 2026 some of them had grown to a stage ready to tap into the capital market to further scale up,” the bank’s analysts wrote.
