When a passport becomes a prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:28 UTC
01:37:28 KST

Taiwan is home to thousands of foreign residents who build careers, families and lives here. However, what happens when one of those residents loses the ability to prove his identity — not because he has broken Taiwan’s laws, but because his own government refuses to renew his passport?
That is the situation my husband, Matteo (not his real name), a Nicaraguan national, has found himself in.
After about three years of attempts to renew his passport, our future in Taiwan remains uncertain.
It all comes back to Taiwan’s giant geopolitical issue: the multitude of countries cutting diplomatic ties with Taiwan in favor of the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Following Nicaragua’s decision to sever diplomatic relations with Taiwan in 2021 and recognize the PRC, Matteo’s circumstances changed dramatically. The Nicaraguan embassy in Taipei closed, leaving him to pursue passport renewal through Nicaragua’s diplomatic representatives in Japan and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Despite repeated efforts, his application remains indefinitely “on hold,” without a clear explanation or timeline.
This is particularly concerning given growing reports of the Nicaraguan government denying passports, restricting citizens’ abilities to return or leave the country, and stripping people of their nationality.
Matteo’s story is not unique; thousands of other Nicas abroad find themselves de facto stateless due to Nicaragua’s deliberate tools of transnational oppression. We have genuine fears that returning Matteo to Nicaragua could put him at risk of retaliation and potentially leave him unable to ever leave. Those concerns have also made us extremely cautious about speaking publicly, as we fear retaliation against his family members still in Nicaragua.
The consequences here in Taiwan have been profound. His legal stay has been maintained through one-month extensions from the National Immigration Agency (NIA), leaving us uncertain about what would happen from one month to the next. Without a valid passport and current alien resident certificate, Matteo has lost access to his bank account and the National Health Insurance system. He cannot renew his driver’s license, maintain his mobile phone service, pursue further education or work normally.
We have not passively waited for a solution. We have contacted Taiwanese authorities, human rights organizations, international human rights groups, as well as local and international lawyers. None of those options have resolved our situation. In January, Matteo was interviewed by the United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua, who informed him that his circumstances constitute de facto statelessness — a situation in which a person cannot obtain protection or documentation from his country of nationality.
In February, Matteo applied for Spanish citizenship through the Carta de Naturaleza process as a possible long-term solution. However, we have learned that Spain is inundated with applications by thousands of other people who find themselves in the same situation, and Matteo’s application would expire after one year, thus leaving us in limbo while we wait for another country to determine whether he can obtain a new nationality.
In June, we traveled to Taipei for a meeting with representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the NIA and the National Human Rights Commission. We presented documentation regarding Matteo’s situation, international human-rights information and our concerns about the potential consequences of returning him to Nicaragua. However, since that meeting we have received no substantive response to our inquiries and no apparent progress toward a resolution.
We are grateful that Taiwan continues to grant Matteo temporary extensions, but they are not a sustainable solution. Life as a stateless person in a country with no asylum laws or protections has taken its toll on us mentally, physically and financially. I have been hospitalized due to stress-induced illness, and Matteo battles newfound anxiety and depression, never knowing if he would see his family again or if we would be able to move forward with our lives.
Our case also raises a broader question about Taiwan’s place in the international community. Taiwan has long faced diplomatic isolation and pressure from Beijing. However, when diplomatic relations disappear, the consequences can extend beyond governments and treaties to ordinary people who suddenly find themselves caught between political realities.
For our family, this is not an abstract geopolitical issue. It is our life. For Taiwan, it is an opportunity to demonstrate that when extraordinary circumstances fall outside ordinary immigration procedures, compassion, human rights and practical solutions can coexist with the rule of law.
How Taiwan responds could matter not only to us, but to others who might one day find themselves in the same position.
Nicole Roberts, a pseudonym, is a permanent resident of Taiwan, and a certified teacher from the US with more than 16 years of experience in international education.

The company is working with the Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Kaohsiung City Government on the plan, which is expected to improve validation efficiency by 25 to 50 percent, TSMC vice president of advanced packaging technology and service Jun He (何軍) said at a 3D IC global summit held ahead of the Semicon Taiwan trade show, which opened in Taipei yesterday.
TSMC would also conduct process research and development at the park with the aim of building a world-class training base for advanced packaging talent and connecting local suppliers with global supply chains, He said.
Photo: CNA
The company is planning to develop a 3-hectare site in the Baipu Industrial Park that would include two buildings featuring modular facilities that can be reconfigured as technology evolves, he said.
The site would include small clean rooms and laboratories for testing and joint development involving advanced packaging technologies, equipment and materials, he said.
The move comes as demand for advanced packaging has surged amid the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, he said.
photo: CNA
Given that demand, TSMC expects its chip-on-wafer-on-substrate advanced packaging capacity to grow at a compound annual growth rate of more than 80 percent through next year, with growth expected to remain robust through 2029, He said.

“It’s not going to be a straight line,” he said. “We’re going to have to learn how to deal with and navigate through the new opportunities and new headwinds.”

Taiwan faces twin demographic milestones in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:23 UTC
01:37:23 KST

Taiwan’s population faces two key milestones in 2027: the number of 18-year-olds will fall below 200,000 and the 85-and-older group will surpass 500,000 for the first time, according to the latest government projections.
Taiwan’s 18-year-olds, the typical age for entering college, will fall below 200,000 for the first time in the 2027 academic year to 195,309, down from 200,406 in 2026. The figure is projected to decline further to less than 150,000 by 2040, according to the National Development Council (NDC).
The 15-year-old high-school-bound population is projected to fall from 189,168 in the 2026 academic year to 122,566 by 2040 -- a drop of 66,602, or 35 percent, the report showed.
Photo: CNA
During the same period, populations in younger age groups will fall even more sharply, by more than half.
The number of junior high school entrants (age 12) is projected to fall from 207,790 in the 2026 academic year to 88,519 (down 57.3 percent) by 2040. Primary school entrants (age 6) will drop from 169,420 to 75,311 (down 55.6 percent), according to the NDC.
The demographic decline across all educational tiers will force school closures, mergers, and class reductions, weakening the nation’s labor supply and capacity for talent development, the NDC stated in a news release.
At the other end of the age spectrum, the 85-and-older group is projected to rise from 484,168 (9.97 percent of all seniors) in 2026 to 503,723 (9.99 percent) in 2027, surpassing the half-million mark for the first time, the projections by the National Development Council (NDC) released on Friday showed.
That figure is expected to top 1 million by 2039, the NDC said.
For the senior population as a whole, the NDC projected that the share of adults aged 65 and older will reach 30 percent of the population (6.52 million) by 2037, after crossing the 20 percent threshold in 2025, which at that time made Taiwan officially a super-aged society.
According to NDC projections, Taiwan’s population is set to drop from the current figure of 23.19 million to under 20 million by 2045. Meanwhile, the median age will climb from 46.4 to 57.2.
Projections show that seniors aged 65 and older will make up 41 percent of Taiwan’s total population by 2050, marking a historical peak.
By 2051, the working-age population (aged 15 to 64) will drop below 10 million, shrinking to 53.4 percent of the total population, according to NDC projections.
Meanwhile, the population aged 65 and older is projected to reach its peak around 2050 at roughly 7.7 million, before exceeding half of the total population (50.4 percent) by 2065.

Everything you need to know about the 2026 Venice Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:21 UTC
01:37:21 KST

Some of Hollywood’s biggest stars are heading to Venice, Italy, for the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival, which kicked off yesterday.
Here’s a rundown of everything you need to know about the festival, the Oscar buzz and who’s going.
STAR POWER
Photo: AFP
It’s one of the most prestigious film festivals in the world, second only to Cannes, and technically the oldest. Venice is also a reliably starry affair, gathering some of the best films in international cinema, and it often factors into the Oscars race.
The film festival was established in 1932, then a non-competitive event, by the La Biennale di Venezia, hosting films like Grand Hotel and It Happened One Night. By 1935, it decided to make it an annual event. Suspicions that the festival was succumbing to fascist influences actually led to the establishment of the Cannes Film Festival as an alternative after the 1938 edition.
The Golden Lion award as we know it today wouldn’t be introduced until 1949. Rashomon won in 1951, and other winners throughout history include Belle de jour in 1967, Au revoir les enfants in 1987, Brokeback Mountain in 2005, Somewhere in 2010, Poor Things in 2023 and, last year, Father Mother Sister Brother.
FILM FEST SEASON
The festival runs through Sept. 12, when the awards will be announced. The opening night film is Danny Boyle’s Ink, an adaptation of the acclaimed stage play about the early years of Rupert Murdoch — played by Guy Pearce — and his acquisition of the daily newspaper The Sun. Jack O’Connell and Claire Foy also star.
George Clooney is back to being a near-annual fixture. This time he’ll be at the festival to pick up a lifetime achievement award. He’s also a producer on Furies. Other stars expected include Noel and Liam Gallagher of Oasis, Rooney and Kate Mara, Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Pamela Anderson, Sam Rockwell, John Malkovich, Louis Garrel, Cho Yeo-jeong and Ellen Burstyn, who is also getting a lifetime achievement award.
As far as awards are concerned, perhaps the most anticipated is Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy Wild Horse Nine, starring Rockwell and Malkovich as a pair of CIA agents before the 1973 Chilean coup. McDonagh’s previous films The Banshees of Inisherin and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri premiered at Venice and went on to receive best picture nominations. There is also excitement about Pattinson playing To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen in Primetime, Cruz and Bardem co-starring in Florian Zeller’s psychological drama Bunker, the Mara sisters playing twins in Werner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard and Lee Chang-dong’s first film in eight years, Possible Love.
In the documentary category, Alex Gibney is bringing Musk, his nearly four-hour investigation into the world’s richest man, and Julia Loktev continues her sprawling portrait of independent Russian journalists in My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exilev. Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger also follows the Gallagher brothers during their reunion tour last year.
CONTROVERSIES ARE BREWING
Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s film DAU, inspired by the lives of the Soviet physicists working on the atomic bomb, has been at the center of some heated discourse. Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Culture and the Embassy of Ukraine in Italy questioned its inclusion in the festival, where it’s playing in competition, calling it a “project linked to the Russian state and its networks of influence.”
Festival director Alberto Barbera defended its selection, writing in a statement that it “is not a Russian film. It is not pro-Putin propaganda. It is a film that denounces totalitarian regimes and their intrusion into citizens’ lives to restrict their freedom.”
Khrzhanovsky also wrote a lengthy rebuttal on Facebook, writing that the movie “should not be prematurely judged on the basis of false associations, distorted chronology, or assumptions that contradict the documented history of the project. I have been and remain opposed to Russia’s war against Ukraine and to the political system that made this war possible.”
The filmmaker renounced his Russian citizenship and is currently a citizen of Germany, UK and Israel.
Earlier this year, geopolitical tensions spilled over into the Venice Biennale contemporary art exhibition after the jury quit in protest over the participation of Russia and Israel.
The group Venice4Palestine, which last year hosted a large scale protest during the festival, asked that it “suspend all agreements with entities and institutions linked to the Israeli government,” although it did not specify any films. It also asked that the Palestinian flag be flown “throughout the festival.” There are two Palestinian films in the official selection: Al Mowaten Osama by Ahmed Hassouna and Hiwar ma’ albahr by Muayad Alayan.
Among the narrative films, To Catch a Predator host Hansen may be concerned about his portrayal in Primetime, which is based on the 2007 Esquire article, Tonight on Dateline, This Man Will Die. He was not involved in the making of the film, which was written by Ajon Singh and directed by Lance Oppenheim.
Also, out of 21 films in competition for the Golden Lion, only one was directed by a woman, May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown. The last time the competition had only one woman, in 2018, the festival committed to have at least half of the films in competition be directed by women by 2020. It has yet to happen.
FESTIVAL LOCATION
When people think of Venice, they usually think of landmarks like the Ponte di Rialto and the Piazza San Marco. The festival takes place elsewhere, on a nearly 11-kilometer barrier island called the Lido, which is about a 20-minute ferry, or vaporetto, ride away.
A military outpost in the 12th century, it transformed into a seaside resort, a favorite of European aristocrats, by the end of the 19th. The Venice Lido was the primary setting for Thomas Mann’s novella ###OSCAR RACE
Barbera thinks Venice’s place in the Oscar race was solidified in 2013 when they hosted the premiere of Gravity, which went on to win seven Oscars the following March, establishing Venice as a place to launch a campaign. It’s only intensified as the membership of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has gotten more international. Since 2014, the festival has hosted four best picture winners — Birdman, Spotlight, The Shape of Water and Nomadland.
Last year, it hosted two best picture nominees in Frankenstein and Bugonia.
The flooding in Kaohsiung after the recent torrential rains has become an issue for mayoral candidates of both major parties. Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) brought in hydraulic-engineering professor Lee Hong-yuan (李鴻源), who called for comprehensive flood control measures on the Dianbao Creek (典寶溪), according to local media. Ko attacked the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) for being behind on flood control measures, but as the city administration observed, there are many weaknesses in how the government can mitigate extreme rainfall. Nor is the river entirely under the management of the city. The low-lying Dianbao River

Taiwan to launch NT$400m AI-assisted fishing project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:20 UTC
01:37:20 KST

Taiwan is to launch a four-year, NT$400 million (US$12.61 million) project that would use artificial intelligence (AI) to help trawlers fish in the Pacific Ocean, Minister of Agriculture Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said.
The program, which is to begin next year, would use AI to integrate satellite imagery and oceanographic data to find fish, Chen said at an event celebrating National Fishers’ Day in Taipei on Tuesday.
The Ministry of Agriculture and the National Science and Technology Council’s joint program would enhance fishers’ ability to find tuna and mackerel in the high seas and predict yields ahead of time, he said.
Photo: CNA
Fishers need to make greater use of technology amid the challenges posed by climate change on global fisheries, he added.
Taiwan’s fishing trawlers last year reported a gross income of NT$96.5 billion, a worrisome sign of decline, Chen said.
Historically, fishing trawlers had an annual income of between NT$95 billion and NT$110 billion, while the fisheries industry typically generated NT$350 billion annually, he said.
The program would also monitor fisheries in Taiwan’s near seas, he said, adding that data about inland fisheries and fish farms would gradually be incorporated into the database.
Chen did not give a timeline for when the system would be available for fisheries, saying that it is still in early development.
Taiwan leads in data on Central and Western Pacific fisheries, Fisheries Agency Director-General Wang Mao-chen (王茂城) said.
Foreign partners in the program would likely include Australia and island nations in the Southern Pacific, although Taiwanese fishers would have priority access, he said.
The agency does not rule out commercializing access to the predictive data, should the technology prove successful, he added.
A Fisheries Agency spokesperson said the ministry is working on an AI-driven ecological monitoring and digital governance system that encompasses aquaculture, high seas fisheries management and harbor administration.
The event also awarded 12 exemplary fishery workers, including Wu Tien-nan (吳天南), a 95-year-old man from Tainan who became a fisher when he was 13.
Wu’s career as an aquafarmer, which focuses on prawns, sea bass, milkfish and groupers, is a microcosm of the sector’s history in Taiwan, agency officials said.
Wu received special commendation for his role in preserving the craft of bamboo raft making, old fishers’ rhymes for counting fries during trading and promoting educational programs that allow children to experience fishing village life, they said.
Wu said he still inspects his grow-out ponds daily.
Two of the fishery workers who received commendations were women.
Yu Chin-feng (于錦鳳), who designed a cutting-edge fish farm in Kaohsiung that utilizes smart technologies, liquefied natural gas-cooled water and cocktails of beneficial microbes, was awarded for introducing innovation in the industry.
Lei Xi-ying (雷細英), a naturalized Taiwanese national from China, was commended for holding classes on cooking fish at home to popularize seafood and charitable works in Yulin County.
Additional reporting by CNA

Sindarov focused on prep ahead of Gukesh match
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:19 UTC
01:37:19 KST

Javokhir Sindarov said he is preparing for the strongest version of world champion Gukesh Dommaraju rather than reading into results as the Uzbek prodigy gears up for the youngest World Chess Championship match in history.
The 20-year-old secured a shot at the crown by winning this year’s Candidates Tournament, adding to the World Cup title he captured earlier in the season and cementing his place among a new generation reshaping elite chess.
Sindarov is to face defending champion Gukesh, also 20, in Geneva, with the title to be decided over 14 classical games from Nov. 24 to Dec. 12.
Photo: EPA
Speaking ahead of the fourth season of the Global Chess League, where he would represent the FYERS American Gambits as the team’s icon player, Sindarov said he expected an engrossing battle.
“Gukesh is very strong. I played with him a few times and I really feel he is a very strong chess player,” Sindarov said in a video call. “I cannot say a lot of things before the match. I just want to play my good chess and enjoy it.”
While much of the pre-match discussion has centered on Gukesh’s uneven results since lifting the world title in Singapore in 2024, Sindarov said recent form offered little indication of how the championship would unfold.
“I didn’t take what he played in the last tournaments seriously because during a match he can be completely different. I’m trying to prepare for his best chess form,” Sindarov said.
While several leading players, including Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamura and Fabiano Caruana, have weighed in on the contest, Sindarov said outside opinions would not shape his preparation.
The challenger pointed to Gukesh’s victory over Ding Liren in 2024 in Singapore as a reminder that expectations and rankings can quickly become irrelevant once a world championship begins.
“People said Ding would lose very easily, but during the match we saw how well he played and how close it was,” Sindarov said.
Sindarov will enter the match after arguably the strongest season of his career. He won the Candidates with a round to spare, stringing together four consecutive victories against elite opposition in one of the most dominant performances in recent memory.
His preparations for Geneva are being overseen by coach Roman Vidonyak, with Sindarov determined not to overhaul a formula that has already delivered major success.
“We will not change a lot of things because what we did worked in our last tournaments,” he said. “We will just improve what we did before the Candidates and the World Cup.”
The Uzbek has not been immune to setbacks.
At the Sinquefield Cup last month, he suffered a defeat by another Indian grandmaster, R. Praggnanandhaa, one of only two losses he has recorded this year.
Sindarov acknowledged that Praggnanandhaa has often posed unique challenges throughout their careers but stopped short of reading anything into suggestions that the Indian could help Gukesh prepare for the title match.
“I think Gukesh doesn’t need his advice because both of us understand where we have weaknesses and where we are not strong,” he said.

MOFA scorns paper’s allegations of influence-buying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:17 UTC
01:37:17 KST

Taiwan yesterday rebuffed a Solomon Islands media report saying that Taipei engaged in “checkbook diplomacy” in the South Pacific, saying that the report “deviated from the truth” and was “driven by malicious intent.”
The report published on Tuesday by the Solomon Star, a newspaper in Taiwan’s former diplomatic ally, said that “Taiwan’s foreign ministry reportedly allocated nearly $281,000 in direct cash gifts for Palauan political figures” to secure support at the Pacific Islands Forum.
That included $30,000 for the former president, $5,000 each for senior executive and legislative leaders and $2,000 for individual lawmakers, the Solomon Star said, without specifying the currency.
Photo: CNA
“Taiwan [also] increased its annual aid to Palau from $18 million last year to $25 million this year,” the media outlet wrote, citing only “reports” without any attribution.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Taiwan’s cooperative projects with Palau and other diplomatic allies are tailored to local needs and implemented in line with the administrative procedures of both governments.
“Taiwan’s approach to the implementation of cooperation projects follows the same principles followed by other like-minded countries in carrying out similar projects across the Pacific region,” the ministry said.
The ministry said that some Solomon Islands media outlets are on the payroll of China, citing foreign media reports, and that the latest report targeting Taiwan without any evidence or attribution was an example of China’s use for them.
A 2023 report by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) said the Solomon Star received nearly US$140,000 in funding from the Chinese government and, in return, pledged to “promote the truth about China’s generosity and its true intentions to help develop” the Pacific island nation.
The OCCRP is a US-based nonprofit investigative journalism organization.
The Solomon Star story showed overweening concern for Taiwanese taxpayers, saying that “such spending deserves far greater public scrutiny. These are not private funds belonging to Taiwan’s political leaders.”
“More importantly, this approach risks turning diplomacy into a form of transactional politics,” it added.
It did not report that when China established relations with the Solomon Islands in 2019, Beijing promised US$500 million in financial aid, according to Australian news outlet ABC News, citing Chinese and Taiwanese media.
Palau is one of Taiwan’s three diplomatic allies in the Pacific. The other two are the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu.

Nicaragua approves banning opposition from elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:16 UTC
01:37:16 KST

Nicaragua’s lawmakers approved a constitutional reform restricting opposition participation in elections, Nicaraguan National Assembly leader Gustavo Porras said on Tuesday.
The new amendment extends presidential terms to seven years from six and bans any member of the opposition involved in planning or carrying out a coup d’etat from running for office.
Porras said the general vote was “approved unanimously” in a special session held in front of Leon Cathedral, 90km northwest of the capital, Managua.
Photo: AFP / EL 19 DIGITAL
The change is a win for Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, 80, who has been in power since 2006 and rules along with his wife, co-president Rosario Murillo.
The constitutional reform is the pair’s latest attempt at tighter control of the Central American nation.
In 2018, the suppression of anti-government protests left more than 300 dead, UN data showed.
Following the protests, thousands of Nicaraguans were exiled, among them opposition leaders and rights advocates, journalists, intellectuals and priests.
Political opposition in the country has been greatly diminished since then.
Ortega and Murillo have described the protests as “an attempted coup” financed by the US.
Leaders-in-exile warn that the new amendment is designed to ensure succession of power within the Ortega-Murillo family if the president succumbs to his lupus and kidney problems.
With these changes, “people will only be able to choose among the dictatorship’s options,” exiled opposition lawyer Juan Diego Barbarena told reporters.
The US, the EU and the UN have condemned the initiative.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously said on X that the US “will not stand by as the Murillo-Ortega dictatorship deepens repression at home and manufactures instability that threatens US national security.”
The EU condemned “the systemic repression by Nicaraguan authorities” and urged them to hold free elections.
The Organization of American States — a Washington-based body that works to promote development and cooperation in the Americas — has approved an emergency foreign ministers’ meeting to discuss sanctions against Nicaragua.
The date of the meeting is not confirmed.
After Tuesday’s approval, the reform is expected to be ratified in a second legislative session set to begin early next year.
Ortega first became president of Nicaragua after the Sandinista revolution toppled the regime of former Nicaraguan president Anastasio Somoza in 1979.
Ortega served one term, from 1985 to 1990, before running for election again in 2006. He has been re-elected three times since.
Almost 1 million Nicaraguans have sought exile in Costa Rica, the US or Spain over the past eight years.

Groups call for release of HK democracy advocate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:12 UTC
01:37:12 KST

Taiwanese civic groups and Taiwan-based Hong Kongers in Taipei yesterday voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong (黃之鋒), calling on the Hong Kong government to drop the charges against him and immediately and unconditionally release Wong and other Hong Kong political prisoners.
Wong, the former secretary-general of pro-democracy group Demosisto, is imprisoned in Hong Kong’s Stanley Prison for his conviction for “subversion of state power.”
While serving his sentence, he was charged again by Hong Kong police. Prosecutors alleged that between July and November 2020, Wong conspired with former lawmaker Nathan Law (羅冠聰) and others to call on foreign governments and organizations to impose sanctions, a blockade or other hostile actions against Hong Kong and China.
Photo: AP
This is the second time Wong has been prosecuted under the Hong Kong National Security Law. Under the law, the offense generally carries a prison sentence of three to 10 years. If the offense is deemed “serious,” the sentence can be increased to 10 years or more, up to life imprisonment.
Wong yesterday pleaded guilty to foreign collusion in a second national security trial against him that could see him jailed for life.
At the Taipei rally in front of the Legislative Yuan, Hong Kong Outlanders secretary-general Sky Fung (馮紹天) said that Hong Kong’s national security laws were being used to suppress dissidents and restrict Hong Kongers’ freedoms.
The groups put forward four demands.
The first is for all charges against Wong to be dropped and for him to be released immediately and unconditionally.
The second is for the Hong Kong government to stop using the Hong Kong National Security Law and the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance to suppress peaceful advocacy, freedom of expression, freedom of association and international human rights efforts.
Third is the immediate release of all Hong Kong political prisoners jailed for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly.
Fourth, they called on the Taiwanese government to publicly voice its support and work with the international community to monitor Wong’s case, his treatment in prison and the plight of Hong Kong political prisoners.
Hong Kong Human Rights Front founder Henry Tong (湯偉雄) said that many Hong Kongers have been imprisoned for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly since the anti-extradition protests.
Shih Yi-hsiang (施逸翔), a senior researcher at the Taiwan Association for Human Rights, said the Hong Kong government had signed the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), yet has deprived Wong of his liberty for more than 2,100 days.
In its 2022 concluding observations, the UN Human Rights Committee directly criticized the Hong Kong government for applying the National Security Law in an overly broad and arbitrary manner, criminalizing legitimate cross-border advocacy and using it to suppress freedom of expression and the right to participate in public affairs, Shih said.
New School for Democracy Association secretary-general Kung Chin-lung (龔欽龍) said the National Security Law had helped silence criticism in Hong Kong and abroad by creating fear of imprisonment.
Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che (李明哲) said that regardless of the outcome of Wong’s trial, the case would go down as one of the most shameful episodes in human history, adding that it reflected the corruption of the Chinese government.
“Taiwan should learn from Hong Kong’s experience and reject the Chinese government’s attempts to exert influence over Taiwan,” he said. “Taiwan must refuse to become the next Hong Kong.”

Hit by deadly floods, Nepal renews push for Chinese data and early warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:09 UTC
01:37:09 KST

Three months before a wall of water, mud and rock killed hundreds when it hurtled down a Himalayan valley bordering Nepal and China, experts and officials from both countries met in Kathmandu to discuss the risk of such disasters.
At the May 27 meeting in Nepal’s capital, 10 officials from Nepal and about a dozen from China, including the Tibet region where the disaster struck, discussed bolstering cooperation to monitor and respond to floods, weather and glacier-related hazards, an agenda prepared by the Nepalese side showed.
The participants called for joint risk-reduction measures, including inventories of glacial lakes and hazard mapping.
Illustration: Yusha Illustration: Mountain People
However, two Nepalese officials said they did not receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels after the meeting, and they feared insufficient data sharing could hamper their ability to anticipate and prepare for major disasters.
“What we actually wanted from them, and still want, is if there are early movements of glaciers and early movements around that area, we would want to know a bit early,” said Nepalese Flood Forecasting Division hydrologist Sauhardra Joshi, who was in the May meeting.
No officials or experts have blamed either side for the natural disaster, which is estimated to cost one-10th of Nepal’s annual economic output to recover from. Nepalese officials say the priority is to deepen cooperation with China.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the two sides have maintained “sound cooperation in the fields of meteorology, water resources and disaster prevention and mitigation.”
“China will continue to strongly support Nepal’s disaster relief efforts, strengthen cooperation in disaster prevention and mitigation, and safeguard the common interests of the two peoples,” the ministry said in a statement.
Last week, the sudden collapse of a glacier on Nepal’s Langtang mountain range into a valley that divides Tibet and Nepal set off a catastrophic flood that killed more than 1,000 people and about 5,000 are still missing on both sides of the border.
It is unclear what data — if any — China had before the disaster of the conditions of the glaciers in the area, especially those lying outside its borders.
“Detecting such failures before they occur is extremely difficult,” Fan Xuan-mei (范宣梅), director of the State Key Laboratory of Geohazard Prevention and Geoenvironment Protection at Chengdu University of Technology, told Chinese state-run China Daily.
Potential source areas are often above 5,000m, where conventional field monitoring is difficult. Satellite observations can be limited by snow and ice cover and steep terrain, while monitoring equipment has to operate in extreme cold and high-altitude conditions.
At the meeting in Kathmandu, the Chinese officials said they did not have the mandate to sign an agreement to meet Nepal’s requests, asking for further discussions, Nepalese government hydrologist Binod Parajuli said.
Details of the meeting and Nepal’s demands for broader cooperation in monitoring the glaciers that threaten communities on both sides of the border have not previously been reported.
The Chinese embassy in Nepal said in a statement on social media on Saturday that Beijing and Kathmandu had kept in close contact on the issue and had made “substantial progress” at the meeting in May on promoting cross-border disaster information sharing.
Nepal raised similar concerns last year, officials said, although experts and officials cautioned that what they describe as slow progress was not a significant factor in the latest disaster.
Rejecting criticism from some Nepalese social media users that China had failed to provide adequate warning, the Chinese embassy said Chinese and international experts faced significant challenges monitoring hazards in the remote Himalayan region.
Chinese teams had shared important information with Nepal “in a timely manner,” it said.
At last year’s meeting, Nepal raised concerns about a flood in the same area, triggered by the sudden release of water from a glacial lake in Tibet that killed at least nine in Nepal and left more than a dozen missing.
“When the Chinese side sees a heavy precipitation forecast in the Tibet area, then they provide us that forecast and those observations,” but “not for avalanche and water level, landslides, extreme events,” Parajuli said.
China began sharing forecasts of heavy rain in Tibet over China’s WeChat messaging app and e-mail a month ago, Parajuli said.
Twelve days before the disaster, China’s World Meteorological Center told Nepalese officials in an e-mail that a monsoon depression was forecast for the area from Aug. 14 to 19.
“Enhanced rainfall is likely across much of Nepal, and we wish to draw your attention to the potential for secondary and cascading hazards, including but not limited to landslides and flash floods,” China said.
The Chinese embassy said Beijing has been sharing information including monitoring data on a lake formed by debris from last week’s calamity.
The discussions over data-sharing underline the complexity of monitoring, forecasting and providing early warning in a region where regional geopolitical rivals — including China and India — control remote mountainous areas holding vast quantities of ice and snow that loom over densely populated South Asian plains.
Last week’s catastrophe was sparked by the collapse of the glacier in a relatively unmonitored area, and a lack of bilateral cooperation was not a significant factor in Nepal’s response, said environmental anthropologist Austin Lord, senior fellow at the Washington-based Stimson Center think tank.
“That’s not to forgive the fact that there isn’t really a well-articulated system, and there is very limited exchange between Nepal and China,” said Lord, who is part of a team supporting the Nepalese government on disaster and climate risk management.
“Chinese scientists have a much greater capacity, have much greater resources for monitoring than those on the Nepal side overall,” he said.
The time that the torrent took to reach Nepal shows the value of early-warning systems, Parajuli said.
At about 8:32am Nepal time on Wednesday last week, the deluge blasted through a border crossing in Tibet as people attempted to flee, according to surveillance footage that has become a defining image of the disaster.
Twenty-six minutes later, Parajuli got a call from the chief of the Nepali National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, alerting him to a flood on the Trishuli River. Parajuli’s team found that a border monitoring station had not transmitted any data since 8:40am.
“We also then tried to contact downstream stations, but downstream stations also couldn’t post the data,” leaving the team to suspect those devices had been washed away, he said.
After contacting local Nepalese authorities to confirm the flooding, Parajuli said, his team sent a public alert to mobile phone users at 9:13.
At least four monitoring stations were destroyed by the flood that rampaged 168km downstream from the Nepal-China border, carrying about 57.4 million cubic meters of water, more than half again as much as normal, according to a Nepalese government assessment.
Surging floodwaters, which dislodged giant boulders and pulled large buildings into the overflow, damaged 19 bridges and about 40km of highway, and knocked out more than 10 percent of Nepal’s power-generation capacity, the Stimson Center said.
“It wasn’t water. It was a huge gush of mud coming straight at us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral of Tupche village, about 25km downstream of the border. “I tried to grab my wife’s hand, but she was swept away by the mud.”
When part of the glacier broke away, crashing to the valley floor hundreds of meters below, it unleashed high-speed flash floods, according to preliminary assessments by Nepalese authorities.
The Hindu Kush Himalayas, home to hundreds of millions of people from Afghanistan to Myanmar, contain the world’s largest volume of ice outside the poles, with more than 63,700 glaciers covering about 56,000km2, almost the size of Croatia, and storing up to 5,700km3 of ice.
By comparison, the glacier chunk that caused the latest disaster carried an estimated 5 million cubic meters of ice and rock, said Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Center for Disaster Studies in Nepal’s Tribhuvan University.
Driven by climate change, glacier melt is accelerating as snow cover declines and snowfall becomes more erratic, a 2023 study by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development showed.
These changes would increase the likelihood of floods and landslides, as mountain communities also deal with such hazards as sedimentation and erosion, the center projects.
Several of Nepal’s major river systems originate in Tibet, then flow through one of the world’s most seismically active and flood-prone regions.
Nepalese authorities would seek to work with China to conduct research and build systems to monitor avalanches and the release of water from glacial lakes — major risks for mountain communities, Parajuli said.
He said his department would propose a data-sharing agreement with China, along the lines of an arrangement that Nepal has with neighboring India, for more frequent information on precipitation and river levels, not just high-precipitation forecasts.
Nepal would seek data every 10 minutes so that “we can warn our people, save our people,” he said. “Our main target is we shouldn’t miss any future disaster.”

Russia’s and Iran’s war efforts are being materially supported by Chinese supplies of drone components and missile fuels. Taiwan virtual asset rules could take effect in Q1 2027: FSC head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:07 UTC
01:37:07 KST

Taiwan could roll out regulations governing virtual assets and stablecoins as early as the first quarter of next year, Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) Chairman Peng Jin-lung (彭金隆) said yesterday.
In his opening remarks on the first day of the Asia FinTech Alliance (AFA) Summit in Taipei, Peng said global discussion surrounding virtual assets and stablecoins have shifted from “whether they should be developed to how they can develop soundly.”
Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value, typically by being pegged to a fiat currency such as the US dollar.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan’s first legal framework governing stablecoin issuance was established earlier this year, when the Legislative Yuan passed the Virtual Asset Services Act (虛擬資產服務法) on June 30.
Nine sets of supplementary regulations under the act are “being actively drafted,” including rules on stablecoins, Peng said.
Those regulations could be “formally announced and implemented as early as the first quarter of next year,” Peng said, adding that once the new law takes effect, Taiwan’s virtual asset and stablecoin market would “take on a completely new look.”
Taiwan’s stablecoin market consists of foreign-issued stablecoins such as USDT and USDC being traded and used in Taiwan.
What Taiwan has lacked is a fully implemented domestic regulatory framework for locally issued stablecoins that began with the new act and would be supported by supplementary regulations.
These actions are needed, Peng said, because the integration of artificial intelligence and finance had entered a stage of “full practical application.”
The FSC would continue to promote the use of technology in fraud prevention and financial digital transitions while managing related risks, he said.
Meanwhile, Taiwan FinTech Association (臺灣金融科技協會) chairwoman Jennifer Wang (王儷玲) said that stablecoins could help money move more efficiently alongside goods and information in global supply chains.
For multinational companies, stablecoins could improve liquidity management, while exporters and importers could benefit from shorter settlement cycles, she said.
“The importance of the stablecoin actually is not about the coin, it’s about being stable,” Wang said, adding that stability depended on trust in reserves, redemption, technology and regulation.
“Cross-border innovation requires cross-border governance,” she added.
Though Wang cited a possible use for stablecoins and the need for cross-border regulation, critics of digital assets abound, questioning their function and the lack of transparency regarding companies that issue the digital asset.
Ben McKenzie, co-author of the book Easy Money, testified before a US Senate committee in late July on how digital assets such as Tether have been abused by criminals.
“Much has been written about how Tether is used by organized crime all over the world,” he said. “In a UN report from 2024, it notes that Tether is the ‘preferred choice’ for crypto money launderers in Southeast Asia.”
Tethers have been used for international drug cartels and terrorist organizations and also used for sanctions and tax evasion, he added.
None of the speakers yesterday morning directly addressed those issues, though Peng did say detailed regulations would be forthcoming.

Students spending too much time online, survey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:06 UTC
01:37:06 KST

Students spend more than 60 hours a week online on computers or mobile devices, but less than 10 hours a week exercising, a Cyber Angel’s Pick survey found.
The survey, titled “FOMO Generation: Digital Resilience and Internet Use Trends Among Taiwan’s Children and Youth,” polled students from third-grade through fourth-year university across 22 administrative regions.
Thirty-one elementary schools, 27 junior-high schools, 24 senior-high schools and 19 universities were invited to participate. Of the 10,000 questionnaires distributed, 8,465 valid responses were collected.
Photo: Spencer Platt, Getty Images via AFP
Results of the survey were unveiled in a news conference in Taipei yesterday, jointly held by the non-profit association and Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chiu Chih-wei (邱志偉).
National Chengchi University Department of Radio and Television professor Vivian Huang (黃葳威) said the survey showed there was a serious imbalance between the digital and physical activities of respondents.
About 86 percent of the respondents reported that they have their own mobile phones, Huang said.
Photo: CNA
They spend an average of 31.22 hours online on computers per week and 30.71 hours using mobile phones, but only spend 9.79 hours exercising over the same period, she said.
On weekends, respondents reported that they spend nearly 6 hours per day online with their mobile phones and spend only 1.67 hours exercising per day, she said.
YouTube was the most-accessed Web site, with 26 percent of the respondents saying that it was what they used most frequently, the survey found.
It was closely followed by Google (22.1 percent) and Instagram (22 percent), it found.
Compared with the previous years, the percentage of students who reported using search engines fell significantly this year, and close to 60 percent said they frequently access social media.
Meanwhile, 45.7 percent reported that they often go online without adult supervision, while only 5.1 percent said they access the Internet with their parents, she said.
Without adult oversight, students risk being exposed to fraud, money laundering schemes and sexual exploitation, Huang said.
The survey also gauged the resilience of students, Huang said.
While they know they should not give personal data to random strangers, their scores were lower in terms of managing time spent on the Internet and distinguishing the real identities of the strangers they come across online, she said.
Chiu said the problems highlighted by the survey are alarming and urged the government to fund the protection of children and adolescents’ physical and mental health.
He cited as an example Meta Platform’s US$18 billion settlement, in which it agreed to change the design of Facebook and Instagram over allegations that they were addictive and had misled consumers about platform safety.
Chiu also called for the adoption of Huang’s POINT system: parenting, online social and emotional learning, innovation to counter addictive algorithms, neighborhood-based community support and teaching children to distinguish humans from artificial intelligence.
Those aim to tackle the most pressing challenge of today: the erosion of people’s psychological autonomy by “algorithmic black boxes,” he said.
Protecting the next generation’s mental and physical well-being cannot be left to parents to tackle alone, Chiu said.
Government agencies, including the Ministry of Digital Affairs, Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Health and Welfare, should allocate sufficient funding to build a comprehensive safety net, he said.
Making addiction indicators and risk assessment reports more transparent would help bolster digital safety and give children room to grow, free from being manipulated by algorithms, he added.
Additional reporting by Lin Che-yuan

Air force planning major base maintenance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:05 UTC
01:37:05 KST

The air force plans to spend NT$3.57 billion (US$112.52 million) from next year to 2031 to upgrade the physical infrastructure of Chiashan Air Force Base in Hualien County, Taiwan’s largest underground aircraft shelter.
The “Chiashan Base System Performance Enhancement Project” was included in the general budget for next year submitted to the legislature on Monday.
Dug into the mountains near Hualien, Chiashan’s aircraft shelters and ammunition storage facilities are protected by the Central Mountain Range and designed to withstand bombardment and strong earthquakes.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
The base, which was completed in the early 1990s, can reportedly accommodate about 250 fighter jets underground and is considered as an important facility for preserving the air force’s combat capabilities in the event of an enemy first strike, particularly a missile attack.
Under the proposal, the air force has earmarked NT$3.57 billion over five years to upgrade 10 major systems at the facility, including instrumentation and control, ventilation and air-conditioning, emergency power supplies, elevators, security doors, fire protection, auxiliary facilities, electricity, water supply and drainage.
The upgrades would harden the facility’s defenses against chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats, as well as electromagnetic pulses.
The air force said the project is intended to implement Taiwan’s military strategy of “resolute defense and multilayered deterrence.”
Under the strategy, the air force’s fighter squadrons would be dispersed to Chiashan in Hualien and Shizishan in Taitung County during wartime to preserve combat capabilities as ordered.
However, systems at Chiashan have been in operation for more than 30 years, and are facing the end of their service lives and diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages
Such shortages can occur when original manufacturers discontinue production, suppliers leave the market or components become unavailable, making equipment maintenance and replenishment increasingly difficult.
The air force said most of the systems inside the underground facility are specialized electromechanical integrated systems, and that maintenance of some equipment is complicated by regulations, overseas procurement requirements, patents and exclusive agency rights.
Upgrading the systems would help ensure that the facility can continue to fulfill its mission of preserving combat capabilities, the air force said.
The air force has also earmarked about NT$6.88 billion from next year to 2031 to build 22 hardened aircraft shelters at Chiashan and four at Shizishan.
The air force said the project is intended to improve the blast-protection capabilities and effectiveness of existing aircraft shelters in relation to the number of fighter jets they are intended to accommodate, to ensure the survivability of Taiwan’s air combat capabilities.

Eaton’s core businesses span electrical power distribution and management, backup power and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, and circuit protection.
Photo courtesy of Eaton Corp
The company plans to add four to six production lines for UPS products at its plant in New Taipei City’s Sijhih District (汐止), Lin said.
The company plans to expand the plant’s power capacity from 1.5 megawatts (MW) to 2.5MW to support the production and testing of larger UPS systems and other high-power equipment, he said.
The plant also produces cable insulation sleeves and other products for Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電), he added.
Eaton operates another plant in Tainan’s Guanmiao District (關廟) to produce industrial products, and has manufacturing sites in China, the US and the Philippines, Lin said.
The company’s main customers in Taiwan are in the semiconductor and data center sectors, as well as the enterprise market, he said.
Traditional data centers typically route medium-voltage AC from the grid through medium-voltage switchgear, step-down transformers and low-voltage switchgear, followed by multiple AC/DC and DC/DC conversions, Lin said.
Eaton’s MV SST shortens this process by accepting 10kilovolts (kV) to 34.5kV medium-voltage input and converting it directly into power suited to 800-volt DC architecture, with conversion efficiency of up to 98.5 percent.
The system could eliminate at least four conventional conversion stages and significantly simplifies the data center’s power architecture, he said.
Mass production of the product is slated for the first quarter of next year, he said.

Unknown Publisher

Taipei prosecutors yesterday indicted 57 people over alleged involvement in a romance scam ring, seeking a 25-year sentence for one.
A man surnamed Huang (黃) and his wife, surnamed Hsu (許), allegedly set up a romance scam ring that utilized artificial intelligence (AI) tools, the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said in a statement.
Members of a “list team” used photographs of women to create accounts on dating apps and when a person made contact via the fake account, members of a “new customer team” would take over, claiming they were short of their sales target and persuading them to purchase products such as fish oil, Antrodia cinnamomea (a species of medicinal mushroom) or power banks costing about NT$1,000 to NT$2,000 (US$31.52 to US$63.04), the prosecutors’ office said.
Photo: Wu Sheng-ju, Taipei Times
After people made a purchase, the new customer team would send their personal information and chat records to a group chat, where members would decide whether to pass the account on to a “cultivation team” or a “returning customer team,” it said.
Members of the “cultivation team” would use photos of women as they chatted and built relationships with targets, it said.
They would asked for gifts such as smartphones, air purifiers and hair dryers, while also soliciting money, it said.
The group employed a software engineer who developed an AI voice-changing program capable of mimicking and learning the voiceprints of women, with the program taking over some of the conversations with targets, the office said.
The software engineer also created an employee performance management system, it said, adding that members of the group would be subjected to “inhumane physical and sexual punishments” if they failed to meet performance targets.
The prosecutors’ office concluded its investigation yesterday and indicted 57 people, including Huang, over alleged contraventions of the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act (詐欺犯罪危害防制條例), the Money Laundering Control Act (洗錢防制法) and the Criminal Code, including fraud, money laundering and jointly committing fraud over the Internet as a group of three or more people.
Huang and Hsu targeted men who were genuinely seeking romantic relationships, exploiting their trust and ultimately causing them to lose their savings, prosecutors said.
The scheme inflicted severe financial losses, and undermined trust and stability in society, with some of the people targeted taking on debt to cover their losses, prosecutors said.
The group’s illicit proceeds totaled at least NT$900 million and more than 20,000 people were targeted, prosecutors said, adding that they have asked the court to impose a sentence of at least 25 years in prison for Huang and at least 18 years for Hsu.

FDA issues red alert for US heart pump system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:02 UTC
01:37:02 KST

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) yesterday issued its highest-level consumer safety alert after US regulators warned that a defect in a temporary heart pump system has been linked to three deaths and 37 serious injuries overseas.
The warning came after the US Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday last week announced that Abiomed Inc, a subsidiary of Johnson & Johnson, was recalling its Automated Impella Controllers due to a cartridge recognition malfunction.
The defect could prevent the controller from confirming whether the cartridge was installed properly, potentially affecting the device’s operation, the US agency said.
Photo: Taipei Times
As of Aug. 17, Abiomed had reported 37 serious injuries and three deaths related to the issue, it said.
The Impella ventricular support system, described as the world’s smallest heart pump, provides temporary circulatory support for people with severe heart conditions, including cardiogenic shock, as well as those undergoing high-risk procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass graft surgery, FDA Medical Devices and Cosmetics Division Director Chien Chia-hung (錢嘉宏) said.
Taiwan has one approved product license for the device, which is used by 19 medical institutions, Chien said.
The affected products in Taiwan include 102 purge cassettes, 26 controllers and 97 introducers, the director said.
No injuries or adverse events related to the defect have been reported in Taiwan, Chien said, adding that the devices are used under close supervision by medical professionals.
The FDA has instructed the local license holder, Johnson & Johnson MedTech, to notify healthcare providers of the alert and implement the manufacturer’s corrective measures, including replacing affected components, updating software and bolstering monitoring procedures.
The agency said it has been monitoring safety information on the product throughout the year and issued several notices on its Web site, but none had involved a recall.
The agency’s consumer safety alert system has three tiers: red, yellow and green.
A red alert, the highest level, is issued when products that are available in Taiwan report incidents overseas that involve serious injuries or deaths, or when defects could cause severe harm and require risk-control measures.

THSRC hardens security after spoofing incident
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:37:02 UTC
01:37:02 KST

Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) yesterday said it is hardening its radio communications security, including enhancing the monitoring and inspection of handheld radio devices, and incorporating stronger identity authentication and encryption mechanisms.
The measures were introduced after a Providence University student allegedly learned the frequencies of the company’s terrestrial trunked radio (TETRA) radio system and programmed them into a radio device, allowing him to impersonate an authorized terminal and listen to internal communications. He later allegedly transmitted a general alarm signal, which the railway’s control center treated as a genuine emergency.
The center ordered three trains to make emergency stops and normal operations resumed after the entire rail line was inspected.
Photo: Hou Cheng-hsu, Taipei Times
The incident was reported to the Railway Police Bureau and the Criminal Investigation Bureau’s Electronic Surveillance Brigade for investigation.
The railway bureau said it conducted an inspection on May 8 and proposed that the company address problems involving its TETRA handsets and TETRA ID parameters.
To better monitor the use of TETRA radio handsets, the company was asked to add a detection function to identify short-interval registrations of the same TETRA ID from different locations, the bureau said.
The company must update the TETRA ID codes on all its radio handsets, the bureau said, adding that its procedures for the custody and management of handheld radios must be revised and strictly followed by employees.
The bureau recommended that the operator adopt advanced authentication and encryption technologies to prevent external interference.
The operator said it has enhanced the monitoring of handheld radio devices and updated their ID codes, adding that the bureau has confirmed that the two issues have been addressed.
It is developing an identity authentication and encryption system, which would be launched as soon as development is completed, the THSRC said.

====================================================================================================

Book review: Inside Taiwan’s anti-LGBTQ movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:36:59 UTC
01:36:59 KST

The legalization of same-sex marriage in 2019 generated a lot of positive publicity for Taiwan, and a detailed account of how the country got there could make for a successful work of popular history. Kao Ying-chao’s (高穎超) Fear of Queer Taiwan: Anti-LGBTQ Movements Between Taiwan and the US Religious Right isn’t that book — but if a volume with mainstream appeal is ever written, it’s hard to imagine there’ll be many sources more important than his study.
This is a highly academic work, and some readers might not want to persist when confronted with jargon like “rigidly linear temporality of developmentalism.” For those who, like this reviewer, have neither a social sciences background nor much knowledge of LGBTQ issues, a strong interest in Taiwanese society and/or politics should be enough to see them through to the end.
In his introduction, Kao explains that he was intrigued by two “empirical and theoretical puzzles.” The first was the leading role of Taiwanese Christians in organizing opposition to marriage equality, despite their being a small religious minority. The second revolves around “two polarized ideologies” — namely that Taiwan is perceived by some in the US as a beacon of progress, while also being “portrayed as a center of cultural conservatism where heteropatriarchal sexism remains influential.”
In his search for answers, the author — an associate professor of sociology at Virginia Commonwealth University — joined anti-LGBTQ groups’ political rallies and church services, and attended training camps for religious youth and abstinence-only sex education instructors. Along the way, he gathered insights on their organizational strategies and internal dynamics.
As Kao points out, until fairly recently, “anti-LGBTQ conservatives had no need to organize social movements because Taiwan’s state apparatus itself served as a powerful anti-LGBTQ oppressor,” depriving gay people of equal rights and spreading homophobic prejudice. What he terms “heteronormative exclusion” was so ingrained that not until 1994 did the Ministry of Justice explicitly define marriage as a union of one man and one woman. Like a state-run corporation that’s been privatized — my analogy, not the author’s — anti-LGBTQ conservatism now has to survive in the marketplace.
Reminding us that Christians in Taiwan (as in every other country) aren’t a monolithic block, Kao explains that, during the Martial Law period, Mandarin-speaking churches “enjoyed a kind of privilege and protection” that wasn’t extended to the Hoklo-speaking (better known as Taiwanese) Presbyterian Church of Taiwan. By the 2010s, however, “demonizing same-sex marriage seemingly united the Christian churches.”
The pro-KMT alignment of Mandarin-speaking churches forced Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) to walk a tightrope during his 1998-2006 stint as Taipei mayor and his 2008-2016 presidency.
“Ma’s ambivalence regarding conservative, traditional voters and international impression management for liberal openness produced complex relationships between anti-LGBTQ conservatism and conservative-leaning parties in Taiwan,” Kao writes.
During one pro-LGBTQ event, Ma was unexpectedly absent from the official press conference while mayor, to avoid offending a core constituency: “But, after seeing overwhelming media coverage and event crowds, Ma attended the second day of the international conference and gave a speech.”
The overlap between Taiwanese Christian conservatism and its American counterpart is only partial, Kao argues. Both stress Christian morality and “heteropatriarchal privilege,” but the former “further includes Confucian filial piety and Han Chinese or Taiwanese nationalism” while lacking “the hierarchies of white supremacism and Christian nationalism that American conservatives are safeguarding.”
Joining an anti-LGBTQ protest or signing a petition doesn’t necessarily mean an individual holds strong anti-LGBTQ views. Some Taiwanese Christians interviewed by Kao “needed and relied on some of the functions that churches provided for their material and spiritual lives… and found themselves under huge peer pressure.”
The coalition opposing same-sex marriage included non-Christian religious representatives. Rather than invoke precepts of their faiths, however, they tended to rely on secular beliefs, such as traditional ethics, patriarchal family values, the necessity of procreation, and even pro-China nationalist ideology. They were countered by Buddhists, Catholics, and Protestants who stressed the tenets of “tolerance, justice, and freedom” to support reform.
When Kao asks how Christian-led anti-LGBTQ movements could mobilize votes “at a scale that was strong enough to potentially win a presidential election with a landslide victory,” he’s talking about five referendums held in late 2018. To the dismay of LGBTQ citizens and their allies, the anti-LGBTQ side won all five by clear margins.
Kao attributes this setback to there being insufficient time “to educate people in the background knowledge necessary for the voters to make a rational choice regarding LGBTQ-related policies” and the confusing nature of the ballot questions themselves.
The first argument comes perilously close to claiming that anyone who disagreed with him simply lacked understanding. As for the second, he doesn’t cite a source when he asserts that “Many voters had no idea what the complex and convoluted propositions meant” — but a Nov. 25, 2018 News Lens International report documents voters who later realized they’d inadvertently voted contrary to their sympathies.
Kao wasn’t impressed by the behavior of queer radicals during the campaign for marriage equality. Some spent their time opposing “not homophobic and transphobic conservatives, but rather the pragmatic pro-LGBTQ liberals, state feminists and gender-mainstreaming movements.”
By advocating for the abolition of capitalism and marriage, local radicals inadvertently provided conservative critics with ammunition, the latter leveraging these positions “to defame and demonize pro-LGBTQ moderate liberals’ policy changes as extreme and destructive.”
Their focus on abstract ideological debates, rather than the practical needs of same-sex couples and their families, pushes Kao to characterize what the radicals did to moderate liberals as “stabbing them in the back.”
From a scholar who comes across as painstakingly evenhanded, it’s a scorching indictment.
The flooding in Kaohsiung after the recent torrential rains has become an issue for mayoral candidates of both major parties. Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) brought in hydraulic-engineering professor Lee Hong-yuan (李鴻源), who called for comprehensive flood control measures on the Dianbao Creek (典寶溪), according to local media. AI is reviving Chinese Marxist economics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
16:36:56 UTC
01:36:56 KST

As China embraced capitalism, its leading universities adopted mainstream Western textbooks to mold their students’ thinking about the economy.
“Most of my colleagues pay only lip service to Marxism,” an economics professor in one of China’s top economics departments confessed to me. “Only a tiny minority take Marx seriously.”
That was two years ago. Today, the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution is giving Chinese Marxist economics a mighty boost.
Chinese Marxists have long feared that the country’s capitalist turn would lead it into the “rent trap” familiar from the North Atlantic economies: a period of asset-price inflation, a rapid slowdown, stagnation, deindustrialization and social discord. When competition in the productive sectors drives profit rates down, rent-yielding property becomes more attractive to investors seeking the greatest risk-weighted return.
The more wealth chases rents, the higher asset prices rise, and the faster wealth moves from industry to the rentier sector. Rent traps hollow out industry and turn once-proud industrial powerhouses, such as England’s North and the US Midwest, into wastelands.
China already came close to a rent trap with the collapse of real-estate developer Evergrande — the tip of a speculative iceberg that nearly sank the Chinese economic miracle. Chinese loyalist academics dismiss such fears, confident that the Chinese state, unlike its Western counterparts, knows how to direct investment to evade the rent trap. They point to success stories such as critical minerals, green energy, electric vehicles, ultra-fast railways, microchips and, more recently, AI.
The minority of Chinese economists who remained loyal to Marxism secretly worried that the Chinese state, however competent, might not be enough for China to sidestep its rent trap. Early last year, several of them suggested to me that they saw the country’s enormous trade surplus as the result of a vicious class war against the Chinese and the Western working classes in which the only victors are Chinese and Western capitalists.
If the emergent Chinese capitalist class channels the approximately 170 trillion yuan (US$25.29 trillion) of accumulated savings from the surplus into asset purchases, China would not avoid its rent trap. If, alternatively, the savings are invested abroad, for example in the BRICS+ countries or in Africa, China would become, like the West before it, a rentier extracting surpluses from developing countries — not exactly a Marxist goal. Moreover, by sending their savings overseas, Chinese savers would one day find themselves bound, like German savers before them, to the whims of foreign borrowers — another unappealing prospect.
A similar sense of unease used to engulf China’s Marxist economists when facing the standard policy recommendation, mainly by Anglo-Saxon economists, that China must increase domestic expenditure — private and public — to avoid a rent trap. China’s Marxists doubt that consumerism could steer the country clear of capitalism’s rent trap sustainably.
“I have read [John Kenneth] Galbraith’s The Affluent Society, and thus I know that running faster on the consumerist treadmill is a special kind of hell,” one of them told me.
To understand how China’s AI-driven robots helped its Marxist economists to return from the sidelines, we must recall a fundamental tenet of Marxist economics: Economic value is created only by human labor. A widget’s value reflects the minimum labor time required to produce widgets, given the current state of technology and expertise. Capitalists can never extract surplus value from a machine — only from human beings. Industrial machines might be immensely useful, but they merely transfer the value infused in them by the humans who built them.
Since the invention of the steam engine, as machines progressively replaced human labor, the value of commodities dropped, profit margins shrank and the rent trap deepened. Soon, to restore value creation, capitalism needed a war to shrink the labor supply or a major crisis to cheapen labor. This is the standard Marxist critique of capitalism.
Chinese Marxists believe that this is happening with renewed vigor in the US, courtesy of “big tech.” Silicon Valley pays little attention to material production, but is obsessed with building AI agents to rent out to people and companies as service providers. While the US’ service sector sheds human labor and loses its capacity to generate surplus value, US tech lords siphon off more surplus value from the material production that AI leaves relatively unaffected. The US’ rent trap grows, as does inequality, populism and social strife.
In contrast, Chinese AI firms have been focusing on material production, deploying their industrial robotics to the production of things, including vegetables. Entire supply chains are being automated, including the design of the production process itself.
Moreover, all these AI capabilities are open source, available to the smallest Chinese manufacturer for a pittance. This is not merely a technology that grants a competitive advantage to a Henry Ford or a Steve Jobs. In China’s emergent AI-driven industrial model, Chinese Marxists detect the material basis for the abolition of value itself.
When necessary labor time shrinks to nothing across all industries at once, goods become so abundant that their exchange-value plummets. What is left is massive use-value, utility and usefulness. Suddenly, wealth no longer props up asset prices, the rent trap disappears, and it becomes possible to fathom a future China that no longer needs to export to maintain its internal equilibrium.
The deeper point that Chinese Marxists are making is that capitalism cannot survive the AI great leap forward. Sooner or later, it must spit out crises and wars to survive. However, China is not constrained by the same logic of capitalist wealth accumulation. Because it operates within a state-capitalist framework that privileges long-term objectives over short-term gains, it can push automation to its logical conclusion without fear of falling profits. It can absorb the shock, redistribute the gains in the form of dirt-cheap, high-quality goods and services, and create the material preconditions for a realm of free association where we produce according to ability and distribute according to need, and where the state, having helped deliver the communist utopia, withers away.
Even if China’s renascent Marxists are right, hard questions remain: When this productivity singularity arrives, would the Chinese state ensure that the goodies and free time enabled by AI-driven robots are used to enable genuine human flourishing? Would it wither away eagerly? Or would it give rise to a parasitic elite using AI, as “big tech” does, to enrich itself?
Yanis Varoufakis, a former finance minister of Greece, is leader of the MeRA25 party, professor of economics at the University of Athens, and a senior research fellow at Fudan University.
