French-Saudi ‘Dragon Ball’ theme park puzzles Japanese manga fans
Plans to build a manga-themed park outside Paris have sparked excitement in France, one of the first Western countries to fall in love with Akira Toriyama’s iconic “Dragon Ball” franchise. Saudi bankrolling of the project, however, and the lack of response from Japanese licence holders, have raised eyebrows among experts and fans alike.
Fans of Dragon Ball, the iconic Japanese manga series, are accustomed to characters merging in the heat of battle to magnify their skills and strength. Few would have anticipated France teaming up with Saudi Arabia to write a new chapter in one of the most successful media franchises of all time.
As the gaming website Polygon put it, “this is one pairing we didn’t see coming”.
The French presidency has announced plans to build three theme parks near Paris under a €6 billion ($7 billion) deal agreed with Saudi Arabia. The “colossal” development is expected to include a manga-themed park, which President Emmanuel Macron’s entourage said would be inspired by the Dragon Ball franchise.
Read moreSaudi Arabia to invest €6 billion in theme parks near Paris, Macron says
“You know my interest for manga,” Macron – who owns an original Dragon Ball drawing among other gifts related to the manga – wrote in a post on X last week, hailing an investment not seen “since Disneyland Paris”.
The announcement capped a two-day state visit to France by Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, which saw the two leaders attend the Esports World Cup final. An aide to Macron said the project stemmed from a previous discussion between the two leaders about their “shared passion” for Japanese comics, “in particular Dragon Ball”.
“No, you’re not dreaming: Dragon Ball is coming to Ile-de-France,” declared a beaming Valérie Pécresse, the head of the Paris region, in a video message posted shortly after Macron’s message. “Son Goku will have his own theme park, just a stone’s throw from Paris,” she said, citing the fictional character created by the late Akira Toriyama.
As manga experts were quick to point out, there was no mention of Toriyama’s home country Japan, nor of the various Japanese companies that own licensing rights for the myriad comics, animes, video games and merchandising spawned by the hugely successful saga.
A manga park – without Japan?
French media have suggested the new parks could be built on the site of the former Mirapolis theme park in Cergy-Pontoise, northwest of Paris, which closed in 1991 just four years after its opening. The new project will be led by Qiddiya Investment Company (QIC), owned by Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, which in 2024 announced plans to build a Dragon Ball theme park near the country’s capital, Riyadh.
That plan, however, was unveiled as part of a “strategic partnership” with Japan’s Toei Animation, the powerful studio behind the Dragon Ball cartoon and films, notes Julien Bouvard, a manga expert and senior lecturer in Japanese language and civilisation at Jean-Moulin Lyon-III University.
“When the Saudi park was presented, Toei confirmed its involvement through social media posts. Whereas this time, they’ve said nothing,” said Bouvard. “Their silence suggests that the Paris theme park is still only a proposal, and that the astronomical investment figures put forward are far from definitive.”
Negotiating licences is a tricky business in Japan, where copyright law offers strong protection and where companies can impose draconian conditions on the use of a character or license. In Dragon Ball’s case, licensing rights are split between multiple companies, including Toei, the publisher Shueisha (best known for the manga hit-machine “Weekly Shonen Jump”), video game giant Bandai Namco, and Toriyama’s own company Bird Studio.
“It’s very difficult these days to launch a new project based on Dragon Ball, as you need the consent of each of the rights holders,” said Bouvard, stressing that Japanese companies are also very particular about the use of their characters abroad.
“Manga publishers in France are forced to go back and forth constantly, sending their French versions to Japan for verification. Sometimes the colour balance changes slightly during printing, and the Japanese publishers don’t like that,” he added. “Qiddiya will also have to go back and forth to build its parks. This is a project not just for three, four or five years, but probably a lifetime’s work to convince everyone.”
According to promotional videos, the park near Riyadh will include a 70-metre-tall statue of the magical dragon Shenron, who grants a wish when the seven “dragon balls” are gathered, among other attractions covering a million square metres. No official opening date has been announced and little information has emerged regarding the site’s development. Critics already question whether the project will ever be completed, noted the International Business Times, “pointing to Saudi Arabia's record of announcing large‑scale developments, including the Neom ‘Line’ project, that are later scaled back or abandoned”.
The Paris project is yet to get its own design, on top of licensing rights and other likely hurdles, including the transport woes that hampered the short-lived Mirapolis park, which was also spearheaded by a Saudi investor, millionaire Ghaith Pharaon.
A cherished culture
News of the French and Saudi plans has raised eyebrows in Japan, including in Toriyama’s hometown Kiyosu, near Nagoya, where local officials expressed surprise at the lack of Japanese involvement and warned that the theme park would struggle to win over license owners.
In an interview with France Info, the mayor of Kiyosu, Sumio Nagata, recalled that even Toriyama had faced “huge restrictions” when drawing a logo for the town. Others, like local councillor Tetsuo Takahashi, lamented the failure to build an amusement park on home soil.
“Toriyama’s works are global, and so is he, but his roots are here,” Takahashi told the French broadcaster. “We must take care of our cultural heritage.”
The councillor also warned against projects motivated solely by financial gain, echoing past criticism of the Saudi theme park voiced by Kazuhiko Torishima, the influential manga editor who helped discover Toriyama and create the Dragon Ball franchise.
At last year’s Japan Expo in Paris, an annual fair dedicated to Japanese popular culture, Torishima warned that “expanding the license just for the goal of making money” would fatally undermine the country’s treasured manga culture. He doubled down in a recent interview with Japanese business website Diamond Online, stating that he would never have approved the Saudi park if he had still been in charge.
“To act purely for short-term profit is to lose sight of manga’s true essence,” he said, highlighting the bond between Japanese comics and their loyal – and youthful – readership back home. “Nowhere else in the world do children spend their own money to buy a magazine,” he added. “That’s why I believe we must not ignore the culture that Japanese children have built.”
France’s ‘Gagaballiens’
Bouvard said Japanese reactions to the French-Saudi venture, and the apparent lack of Japanese involvement, feed into an underlying narrative about the country’s relative decline – a narrative he also associated with the French.
Another trait France shares with Japan is a passion for manga, in which Dragon Ball holds a special place, making it a legitimate host for a theme park in the eyes of many observers.
“France is the world’s second-largest manga market after Japan. And with Japan Expo, Paris is home to the most popular manga event, which attracts over 200,000 people a year,” said Bouvard. “It wouldn’t be surprising to have a manga-themed park as well.”
He pointed to the early success of new attractions at the Spirou amusement park in southern France, based on the popular manga series “Naruto”.
Bouvard said France was fortunate to have early French-language adaptions of the Dragon Ball manga, the cartoon and subsequent video games, generating a powerful media mix that turned Goku and his companions into household names in the 1990s. Dragon Ball-mania even spawned the term ‘Gagaballiens’ to refer to fans who were gaga about the series and “only loved manga through Dragon Ball”.

Saudi ‘parkwashing’
Saudi Arabia’s interest in the world created by Toriyama has shallower roots, driven in large part by the crown prince’s personal taste for manga and gaming.
The country that once issued a fatwa against Pokemon has since performed a U-turn on such media franchises, investing heavily in Japan’s animation and gaming industries, and playing a leading role in global esports events (competitions involving video games). The planned Dragon Ball park near Riyadh is part of the broader Vision 2030 platform to grow its own entertainment and tourism industries.
Critics have labelled the project an example of “parkwashing”, arguing that high‑profile entertainment investments are a way to soften Saudi Arabia’s image and distract from its record on human rights, including curtailing women’s rights and the criminalisation of homosexuality, which can carry the death penalty.
Macron was one of the first Western leaders to meet Bin Salman in the wake of the 2018 killing of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, which US intelligence says was ordered by the Saudi crown prince. When asked about entrusting an amusement park to Riyadh despite scrutiny of its human rights record, Macron’s office replied: “At no point, when we attract a project, do we seek to lecture others.”
Some Dragon Ball fans, however, have expressed reservations about the Saudi link on social media, saying it ran counter to the spirit of the manga series.
“Toriyama's stories are frequently built around characters standing up to tyranny and oppression, which makes the funding source feel uncomfortable to a segment of the fandom. None of this means the park won’t happen, but it does explain why the reaction hasn’t been pure excitement,” wrote manga enthusiast Sora Tanka.
Such qualms may well disappear over time if the planned parks end up being a success, Bouvard cautioned.
“Everyone would have preferred it to have been a deal between France and Japan, without Saudi Arabia. But that’s where the money comes from,” he added. “A lot of people are sceptical – and a little sad, too – but if they end up building the parks, and doing a good job, I expect many fans will be thrilled to go there.”

Back or elbow pain? You might be gaming too much on your phone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:41:47 UTC
22:41:47 KST

A new study has found a strong association between mobile gaming addiction and musculoskeletal pain, with addicted students more than three times as likely to report neck pain and more than four times as likely to report elbow pain.
Mobile gaming may be taking a physical toll on young people, according to new research that links problematic gaming behaviour with significantly higher rates of pain in the neck, upper back, elbows and wrists.
As gaming becomes an increasingly routine part of young people’s digital lives, a few more breaks — and perhaps a little less time hunched over a phone — could matter for physical health as well as digital wellbeing, researchers say.
The study surveyed 364 medical students at universities in Jordan and examined whether mobile gaming addiction was associated with musculoskeletal problems.
About 9% of the students — 34 people — met the study’s criteria for mobile gaming addiction.
The differences in reported pain were particularly striking in parts of the upper body commonly involved in prolonged handheld-device use.
Among students classified as addicted, 85.3% reported neck pain, compared with 65% of those who were not classified as addicted. Upper-back pain was reported by 64.7% of addicted students, compared with 55% of their peers. The gap was even wider for elbow pain: 41.2% of addicted students reported it, compared with 12.5% of those who were not addicted. Addicted students also reported more wrist and hand pain — 41.2% compared to 34%.
The study found that students with gaming addiction were also more likely to report that musculoskeletal problems interfered with everyday activities, including studying and hobbies. Some were more likely to have sought medical attention for pain affecting their wrists and hands, hips and knees.
Prolonged mobile gaming can also create an ergonomic problem: holding a phone for extended periods can involve sustained gripping, fixed arm and neck positions and repetitive movements.
The authors argue that gaming should therefore not be viewed solely as a question of screen time or psychological wellbeing.
The researchers call for greater awareness of digital health, ergonomic education, posture training and behavioural changes among students. Universities could incorporate guidance on breaks, device positioning and healthy gaming habits into student health programmes, particularly for groups spending long periods studying or working on screens.

As schools re-open, Congo drops remote learning plan in Ebola red zone
BENI, Democratic Republic of Congo, Sept 2 - Schools reopened this week in areas of Democratic Republic of Congo hardest hit by Ebola, after authorities decided the risk of transmission was outweighed by the risk of pupils struggling with remote learning, an official told Reuters on Wednesday.
The death toll from the outbreak - the worst in Congo's long history with the disease - has exceeded 3,000, according to government data published on Wednesday, with cases spread across six provinces and a mortality rate of 48.6%.
More than 1,000 schools in Ituri are classified as being in the "red zone", meaning a high-risk zone or zone of active transmission, according to an education ministry document seen this week by Reuters.
Ministry regulations published on August 19 stipulated that schools in the red zone would temporarily replace in-person classes with "distance learning" involving worksheets distributed every two weeks and programmes broadcast on the radio and television.
But schools opened as usual this week in Ituri, an education ministry official said.
"The government reviewed its initial decision at the request of provincial authorities who wanted to ensure that students living even in red zones would not fall behind in the school curriculum compared to others," said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
"At the first sign of a case, we will close and implement distance learning, but for now, that's not the case."
Schools also reopened in areas of North Kivu and South Kivu provinces controlled by the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 rebels, who staged a lightning offensive in the region last year, according to a rebel official. Authorities are requiring hand-washing and social distancing in classrooms, the official said.
PARENTS ON HIGH ALERT
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo species, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
Anxiety about Ebola was evident this week well beyond the epicentre.
La Reine Vahwere stocked her three young children's backpacks with bottles of disinfectant before sending them off to school in the city of Beni, in North Kivu province, which accounts for 868 of Congo's 6,186 confirmed cases.
"I told them to avoid touching each other, physically touching their classmates," she said.
"Also, as I am accompanying them to school, I am going to ask the authorities to apply the protective measure of distancing within the classrooms. Because it would really be sad to see a child affected at school when at home the child is respecting the protective measures."
As students entered the school compound, a staff member instructed them to wash their hands with hand sanitiser and explained to them where to find wash basins and toilet paper.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.
The education ministry official said hygiene kits had been installed in red zone schools. REUTERS

Mongolia’s President at the SCO Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:41:00 UTC
22:41:00 KST

Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa is attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of State in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan as the organization recognizes its 25th anniversary. While the SCO spent much of its existence focused on security and regional cooperation, the Bishkek Declaration demonstrates a much larger global agenda. Mongolia, in the new partner state status, is seeking deeper ties with SCO member states in emerging sectors via robust bilateral links.
For example, Khurelsukh and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, the summit’s host, held bilateral talks to accelerate political, economic, and trade relations under the Comprehensive Partnership Agreement that was signed during Khurelsukh’s state visit to Bishkek in 2025.
Mongolia and Kyrgyzstan are aiming to boost regional trade turnover to $100 million. During Khurelsukh’s remarks, he noted the trade volume between the two countries had grown from $2.6 million in 2023 to $19 million as of 2025. The Mongolian side expressed interest in further Kyrgyz investments and joint projects in developing industries, minerals exploration, transport and logistics, and direct flights.
Mongolia’s interim free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) creates additional trade opportunities for the two countries. Kyrgyzstan will be chairing the EAEU in 2027.
But there were more leaders in Bishkek than just Japarov. For Mongolia, the SCO Summit was a valuable opportunity for face-to-face diplomacy as the world faces major geopolitical and economic challenges.
On August 31, Khurelsukh held bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. During their meeting, Xi reiterated Beijing’s long-term support for Mongolia as close neighbors and promised to support “win-win cooperation.”
Mongolia and China discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in emerging sectors such as green minerals, AI, digital economy, and supporting Mongolia’s efforts in combating desertification and climate issues. According to the Mongolian presidential office, Khurelsukh and Xi discussed several projects that are underway, including China’s support for the operation of the Erdeneburen Hydropower Plant, a long-stalled mega-project that received new life in 2022.
Xi and Khurelsukh also discussed the need to make progress on constructing the Shiveekhuren-Sekhee, Bichigt-Zuunkhatavch, Khangi-Mandal railways which are crucial to the countries’ bilateral economic activities.
Moreover, one of the most important discussion points was China’s willingness to continue exporting petroleum product supplies to Mongolia amid fuel shortages triggered by supply disruptions from Russia. The two sides are currently aiming for Mongolia to import 71,000 tons of petroleum product per month from China.
More broadly, Xi promised to support Mongolia’s fuel industry, and cooperate in the exploration of oil and gas, a key priority for Mongolia as it seeks to address its energy dependencies.
While China is a leading investor in Mongolia’s mining sector, it has yet to allocate investments into the renewable energy sector. Considering Mongolia’s push to transition to renewable energy and diversify its energy sources, Beijing’s contribution will be crucial in the coming years.
Khurelsukh also met with Russian President Vladimir Putin while in Bishkek. During the meeting, Putin reiterated the historic links between Mongolia and Russia. He expressed hope that Ulaanbaatar’s interim free trade agreement with the EAEU will provide “preferential treatment for Mongolian traditional exports across the customs territory of our association.”
Moreover, Putin highlighted that Mongolia – previously an observer in the SCO – now will receive “partner state” status. Last year, the SCO streamlined its various levels of participation to just two: full members and partner states. Mongolia thus became a partner state along with other states previously recognized as observer states. The debate on whether Mongolia should join the SCO as a full member has been a hot topic among scholars and policymakers in the last decade.
The Khurelsukh-Putin summit was also attended by the Russian energy minister and president of Rosatom, Russia’s nuclear power corporation. Rosatom’s leader reportedly met with Mongolian partners to discuss small modular nuclear reactors as a way to diversify Mongolia’s energy mix.
According to Russia’s Pivot to Asia official website, “Mongolia is reviewing a proposal from the Russian state nuclear corporation to build a small modular nuclear reactor in the country, which may be built near New Kharkhorum, a planned new capital city located about 230 kilometers west of Ulaanbaatar.”
Following Khurelsukh’s high-level meetings with both Xi and Putin, separately, Xi and Putin resumed high-stakes negotiations on the construction of Power of Siberia 2, a long-discussed gas pipeline that would bring LNG from Russia’s Yamal gas fields to China via Mongolia.
According to Pipeline Technology Journal, “Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov confirmed Friday that the flagship energy project will feature prominently during talks in Bishkek.” Ushakov added that discussions will continue at the Eastern Economic Forum currently underway in Vladivostok, where Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang will meet with Russian officials.
Russia is keen to export more gas to China, and Mongolia has welcomed the construction of the pipeline. However, China has been driving a hard bargain on pricing, especially as it moves away from fossil fuels toward renewable energy.
There was no China-Mongolia-Russia trilateral meeting scheduled in Bishkek. However, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor is in Vladivostok through September 4, so trilateral talks might be resumed there.
The three heads of state gathered last year in Beijing shortly after the 2025 SCO summit in nearby Tianjin. At that meeting, Mongolia emphasized the importance of trilateral cooperation and reaffirmed its commitment to jointly implementing the projects and programs outlined in the Economic Corridor Construction Program.
As evidenced by the Bishkek Declaration, the SCO is setting itself up as a much larger player in global political, economic, and security arenas. As SCO member states encompass approximately 42 percent of the global population, SCO-linked global governance, multipolarity, and economic and trade are set to expand in the organization’s next 25 years.
While Mongolia’s participation in this year’s SCO in Bishkek has been primarily economically motivated, Ulaanbaatar is aware of the shifts in global geopolitics. Mongolia engagement in the SCO is underpinned by its bilateral relationships: comprehensive strategic partnerships with Russia, China, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan, coupled with strategic partnership frameworks with other SCO members such as India and Kazakhstan. In all of these relationship, Mongolia envisions greater cooperation in emerging critical sectors and seeks to strengthen the country’s political, economic, and cultural capital. Ulaanbaatar can achieve that through robust bilateral links without having to a commit to the SCO as an organization.

Chevron to expand Venezuela oil operations with US$7 billion plan
The US energy giant aims to double production, even as analysts warn that the nation’s decrepit infrastructure would take years to fix
Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it would expand operations in Venezuela after US President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits.
Chevron, the only US oil company with a major presence in Venezuela, said on Wednesday that it had been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where it has active operations.
The company plans to invest more than US$7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day.
“Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement.
Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven reserves, totalling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to Opec’s 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels.
Yet because Venezuela’s energy infrastructure is severely degraded and the nation is operating under international sanctions, its daily production is just over 1 million barrels, compared with the 10 million to 11 million barrels that Saudi Arabia produces each day. The US produces almost 14 million barrels per day.

The book of poetry I wrote for the home I lost in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:38:27 UTC
22:38:27 KST

Share & more
Almost three years after the beginning of the Gaza genocide, I am publishing a book of poetry about a house that no longer exists, in a language my mother cannot read, in a country where my family cannot follow.
The first two poems I wrote in my life were called Lemon Tree and Hope. I wrote them two or three months after the genocide began in a purple notebook that my sister gave me as a gift, in my now destroyed childhood home, about a tree I will not see again.
The book is named for that house, and it will be published in French on 9 September. When the collection comes out, I will be asked to sign copies of it in a city where nothing that belonged to me has ever been demolished.
The book is called This is My House – in French, Ceci est ma maison. The title has a double meaning. It refers to the house in the north of Gaza where my brothers were married, where my older sisters gave birth, and where their children learned to walk on a rooftop that I could describe to you tile by tile. It also refers to Gaza, my home and the home of more than two million other people. Both have been reduced to rubble.
I want to tell you how I learned that my childhood home had been destroyed because the shape of that experience is the shape of exile: It was at the end of September or early October last year when our neighbours saw the destruction. They told my family, and my family told me. That was the order. The people standing in the street knew before its owners, and I – writing a book about it – was the last to be told.
Distance is not a feeling. It is a delay measurable in hours, and I have been at the far end of that delay since I crossed the border and left Gaza in July 2025. Perhaps I will be at the far end of it for the rest of my life.
I was the last to find out about the destruction of my own house, where I lived since I was five. I was in my room studying when I found out, the French daylight filtering through the window in a country where the electricity does not go off, from a voice on a phone that had already said it out loud to someone else first.
◇◇◇
Everything that was in the house was lost. The oil paintings I had made and never showed to anyone – some of them finished, some still works in progress. My books in three languages, Arabic, English, and French. The room I wrote in. The walls that held space for weddings and births. The rooftop. The particular way the afternoon light came into the kitchen.
A house is not just a structure. It is a set of instructions for where the light falls in space, and those instructions have been deleted from the world. There is no copy. Except one. It is not a good copy, but it is what remains, consisting of over 50 poems in a language I was not born into.
The poems are not gentle memories. I have not been able to write about anything except this: the house; the yearning for what no longer exists; what has been done to the people who called it home; the children killed in numbers that stopped being numbers; massacres that have names in Arabic and no names at all in the papers here; a boy who is now alone in the world because everyone who knew his name was killed on the same afternoon and who is expected to keep waking up.
I did not choose these subjects. There was nothing else in the room.
I wrote the poems for myself and for my family. That was the readership I imagined. I did not intend to create a manuscript. The poems were phrases in notebooks I already owned and that I was already using for something else. There are French verb tables in those notebooks and lecture notes.
I was not making a book. I was catching sentences before they disappeared like everything else.
When I started writing the poems I was a student of English and French literature. My university’s campus was destroyed, like virtually all the university campuses in Gaza. The university continued teaching online throughout the genocide, and I continued attending – which sounds absurd. So was scrawling half a line of a poem about a dead child at the top of a page about the subjunctive. I was not making a book. I was catching sentences before they disappeared like everything else.
I wrote the poems in English even though Arabic is my first language. I’ve never been able to fully account for that. Maybe writing in a foreign language allows for more emotional distance. The words land with less force. The pictures they summon are dimmer.
English was not a literary choice. It was a pane of glass. In Arabic, everything would have been too close and loud.
Dimmer is what I needed. English was not a literary choice. It was a pane of glass. In Arabic, everything would have been too close and loud. In English, I could stand on the other side and look in.
Every poem in this book was written through that pane of glass by a woman who could not have written a word of it without that separation. But that pane of glass also disappears, even in a second language, when I write about my mother or my younger sister. I can write in English about a child I never met, but I cannot say my own address out loud.
◇◇◇
The poems left me before any publisher was interested. I started reciting them on Instagram while I was still in Gaza. People responded, and I liked that they responded.
Some of the notebooks I wrote the poems in were destroyed with the house. Some stayed behind with my sister. What is being published is what escaped from a fire and across the borders. My first book is the surviving portion of something that was never assembled.
There is a moment in every one of these conversations where the interviewer asks a perfectly reasonable question and I cannot answer.
Then it was translated, and the translation is extraordinary. Lisa Ducasse did what I would have told you could not be done. Writers I know and trust, Karim Kattan among them, have said so too, and they are right. I want to state my admiration without a single qualifier attached to it. And still, reading it, I meet a stranger who knows everything about me.
Now, I sit down for interviews to talk about the book. There is a moment in every one of these conversations where the interviewer asks a perfectly reasonable question and I cannot answer. I stop. The kind person across from me waits. The waiting becomes its own weather in the room because now I have made them uncomfortable, and I find myself apologising to someone for the destruction of my own street.
At the launch event in Paris, there will be a table with volumes of the book piled high. My name will be said into a microphone. People will be genuinely moved, and then they will go home, which is the correct thing for them to do and I hold it against nobody. There will be a picture of me smiling, and the smile will be real because this is the thing every writer is supposed to want, and there was a girl in that house who wanted it more than she wanted almost anything else.
At the same time, my mother will not be in the room, nor will my younger sister. Neither can read the language the book is printed in.
Both of these things are true at once, and neither cancels out the other: This is my dream, and it has been handed to me in exchange for everything I had. Nobody consulted me on the rate.
◇◇◇
There is one more thing – the worst of all – which I am going to set down rather than continue to carry: The book matters because Gaza is still happening. Its relevance is my family’s ongoing danger. I wrote the poems because I wanted people to look and see what was happening. That was always the whole of it. I didn’t want people to look away.
In Paris, when they look at me they might see a woman who evacuated from Gaza to continue her studies at one of the best universities in Europe. But it turns out that being looked at and being read are not the same thing. When people read, they might understand the pain and agony of what we have gone through.
The book matters because Gaza is still happening.
If you pick up the book, know that these poems were written by a student who still had French homework, in notebooks that mostly no longer exist, for an audience of her mother, her sister, and herself. And notice the tense of the title – This is My House. The house is gone, but the sentence is in the present tense.
A demolition takes an afternoon, but a house can be kept somewhere else, in a borrowed language, between two covers, as long as someone is still reading the words.
Edited by Eric Reidy.

EU or Eurasia: Why Putin sparred with Armenia’s PM
Relations between Russia and Armenia have reached historic lows as Yerevan pivots towards the West.
Russia President Vladimir Putin has warned Armenia’s Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan that Yerevan’s bid to join the European Union could disrupt trade with Moscow.
Relations between the two countries have reached historic lows as Yerevan pivots towards the West, prompting sharp economic and political retaliation from Moscow.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Is Trump wooing Russia again – and why?
- list 2 of 3Iran and Russia vow to stand against US ‘unilateralism’
- list 3 of 3Germany says Russia preparing ‘hybrid’ attacks over Ukraine support
In a tense meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital on Tuesday, Putin said that Moscow needs clarity on whether Yerevan wants to join the EU so it can decide on the future of bilateral trade with Armenia.
Putin also said that Armenia joining the EU would be tantamount to declaring a break from the Eurasian Economic Union (EEU) – a Russia-led grouping of several post-Soviet states.
Last April, Yerevan decided to adopt a law to launch the process of EU accession – a sticking point for Russia, which views its neighbouring post-Soviet countries as a vital security shield between its borders and the European Union.
In Bishkek, Armenia’s Pashinyan stressed that Yerevan has not violated any of its obligations towards Russia through its EU accession process and did not want to leave the EEU.
What happened at the meeting? Here’s what we know:
What did Putin tell Pashinyan?
At their meeting on Tuesday, according to the Kremlin, Putin told Pashinyan that while Russia is a key economic and trade partner to Armenia, Yerevan’s EU aspirations could create complications for its EEU membership.
“Armenia’s aspiration to join the EU is the natural and legitimate right of the country and its people. Armenia is a sovereign state, and it is for the Armenian people to determine the trajectory of their own development,” Putin said.
“Nevertheless, this unquestionably creates complications for Armenia’s continued membership in the Eurasian Economic Union, and threatens to erode the advantages the Republic enjoys on the EEU market and to sever established trade links,” he added.
Pashinyan, however, said Armenia’s decision last year to adopt a law launching the process of EU accession did not violate its obligations to Russia or the EEU and that it was only an alternative his government had given to the people of Armenia.
What are Armenia and Russia’s relations like?
After the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, Armenia became Russia’s closest ally in the South Caucasus, with the two nations developing their trade, economic and political ties. Armenia has also long been Russia’s closest regional ally, a Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO) member, host to a Russian military base and is dependent on Russian gas.
Currently, Russia is Armenia’s key trade and economic partner, accounting for roughly 30 percent of its trade, and an investor in Armenia’s economy. In the first half of this year, bilateral trade also reached $2.5bn.
But despite economic ties, relations between the two countries have been tense since 2023, after the historical conflict in the Nagorno-Karabakh region of Azerbaijan erupted again.
Russia, which is fighting its own war in Ukraine, did not intervene militarily when Azerbaijan launched a major military offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh, which had a large Armenian population and had been de facto independent since the 1990s.
Laurentiu Plesca, a political analyst and researcher focusing on EU enlargement and European security at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Al Jazeera that Moscow decision not to support Yerevan during the Karabakh war in 2023 led to Armenia’s pivot towards the West.
He said that this, in turn, upset Moscow, further souring relations.
“Russia started blocking imports of Armenian goods and is threatening to suspend the duty-free supply of gas, oil products, and diamonds to Armenia,” he said.
“The EU, in turn, has pledged economic support to offset that pressure,” he added.
In early July, the European Commission’s President Ursula von der Leyen also told Yerevan that it could count on the EU amid any economic pressure from Russia and pledged an additional 18 million euros (about $20m) as part of a broader 52 million euros (about $60m) economic support package.
What are Armenia’s EU plans?
Last April, Armenia’s president signed into law a bill that set the legal foundation for the country to move towards joining the EU.
Pashinyan, who took power in 2018 and was part of launching the EU bid, has repeatedly stressed that the bill did not represent an application to join the EU, but the start of a broader process of integration.
However, in July this year, Pashinyan told lawmakers in the country that Armenia would decide its future EU membership by holding a referendum “in the near future”.
Yerevan has significantly deepened its European ties, hosting its first official EU summit last month alongside a wider European gathering attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Armenia also hosted French President Emmanuel Macron for a high-profile state visit, which provoked sharp criticism from the Kremlin after a video emerged of Macron singing while Pashinyan played the drums.
What is the EEU?
Putin has previously warned Armenia that it views membership in the EU as incompatible with the EEU, and Armenia would have to leave if it joins the EU.
The EEU is a group of former Soviet Union countries that coordinate economic and trade policies. Its members are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. The group’s treaty was established in May 2014, and it began its operations in January 2015.
According to a 2022 Chatham House report, the EEU is in effect a Russian-led effort to create a Eurasian counterpart to the EU.
So why is Armenia’s EU bid a point of tension for Russia and the EEU?
According to the Chatham House report, the EEU serves an important geopolitical purpose for Russia.
“Putin sees it as part of his drive to re-establish the Russian sphere of influence lost by the dissolution of the Soviet Union,” the report’s writers emphasised.
That’s why Armenia seeking closer ties with the EU represents an attempt to break from Russia’s dominance of its neighbourhood, in the eyes of the Kremlin.
In June, Pashinyan rejected a call from Moscow to hold an immediate referendum on leaving the EEU to join the European Union.
Tensions had boiled over at the EEU summit in Kazakhstan on May 29, as Putin and fellow bloc members Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement urging Armenia to hold the referendum “as soon as possible”.
Putin also appeared to make a barely veiled threat at the EEU summit, warning Armenia against pursuing its Western ambitions, and referring to Russia’s war in Ukraine, said that the “Ukrainian scenario” had also begun with Kyiv’s EU aspirations.
In a video address broadcast on social media, Pashinyan had responded to Putin and stated that his government would continue working within the EEU until a choice between the two blocs “becomes unavoidable”, noting that any referendum before Armenia formally applies for EU candidate status remains purely theoretical.
“Putting a theoretical choice to a referendum is, of course, neither very sensible nor justified,” Pashinyan had said.
At the SCO summit, however, he reiterated that Yerevan had no plans to leave the EEU and said that Moscow has always supported the development of friendly and mutually beneficial relations with Yerevan.
Plesca, the political analyst, said that at its core, there is a tug-of-war over Armenia’s strategic alignment, playing out on two fronts.
“But the pro-EU stance is already clear, and Moscow wants to reverse it. Having failed to do so at the ballot box in the recent parliamentary elections in June, it is now compensating with economic blackmail,” he said. During Armenia’s parliamentary elections in June, Moscow was accused of seeking to tip the scales by exerting economic and diplomatic pressure on Pashinyan’s government.
He noted that while Armenia does have the legal right to join the EU, doing so while still inside the EEU customs union would be legally ambiguous.
“There’s no mechanism to expel a member, and Armenia hasn’t triggered the six-month exit notice, so an EU bid doesn’t automatically breach” its obligations towards the EEU, Plesca said. “That’s exactly the trap Yerevan is navigating, keeping a foot in both camps for now, while Moscow insists that’s not possible.”
He added that for Russia, Armenia’s EU bid is also more about losing a foothold in the South Caucasus region.

Liao added that rotation between sectors and individual stocks is likely to remain a key feature of trading. He recommended watching the optical communications sector and focusing on companies with stable fundamentals, clear revenue growth, and the ability to hold up relatively well when the broader market comes under pressure.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taipei City Fire Department said Tuesday that it has won an award for its 3-second inflatable rescue mat designed for quick evacuations in tight spaces.
A press release said firefighters perform long rescue operations in tough environments while wearing up to 25 kilograms of gear. Its solution is a compact, lightweight rescue mat that can be quickly deployed to carry the injured to safety.
The 2.8 kg inflatable safety mat can be rolled onto a firefighter’s carrying frame and secured with straps. The device takes 3 seconds to extend and is made of a fire-retardant rip-stop fabric with 5-centimeter-thick padding to reduce friction, allowing rescuers to transport with ease.
The department said the mat reduces user muscle strain, lowering the chances of physical injury. It also plans to extend use to hospitals and retirement homes for moving patients and seniors.
The operators who designed the device won the city's innovation award for excellence. The department noted that the less stress on firefighters, the greater the chances of survival.

Alzheimer’s may leave a mark on the brain long before plaques appear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:33:57 UTC
22:33:57 KST

Alzheimer’s may leave a mark on the brain long before plaques appear
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oslo
- Summary:
- Brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s may begin at least seven years before amyloid plaques become detectable with current PET scans. Researchers uncovered the signal by tracking healthy older adults with repeated brain imaging over nearly 20 years. The discovery could help scientists identify Alzheimer’s earlier and suggests that important disease processes may start before visible plaque buildup.
- Share:
A new study suggests that brain imaging could reveal changes linked to Alzheimer's disease more than seven years earlier than researchers previously believed. The work was led by scientists in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oslo and was published in Nature Neuroscience.
The study suggests that the current gold standard for Alzheimer's imaging (amyloid-PET) may not be sensitive enough to capture some of the earliest brain changes associated with the disease. These include processes related to the buildup of amyloid plaques. The researchers identified structural changes in the brain at least seven years before plaques became visible on scans.
"We found that structural changes in the brain occur many years before high levels of plaque are seen on PET scans, which is the brain scan currently used to identify the earliest signs of Alzheimer's disease," says James Michael Roe.
At the time the research was carried out, Roe was a postdoctoral researcher at the Center for Lifespan Changes in Brain and Cognition (LCBC) at the Department of Psychology, University of Oslo. He now works as International Scientific Lead at Cercare Medical. Roe was the study's main researcher while working at LCBC.
Earlier Brain Changes Could Improve Detection
According to Roe, the results suggest that disease-related processes may already be developing in the brain long before they can be seen with today's most sensitive imaging methods.
"We found the earliest signal detected on brain scans to date, which could be useful for tracking the disease before symptoms emerge and may help with earlier detection," he says.
To uncover these early changes, the researchers followed healthy individuals who underwent regular brain scans (MRI) for nearly 20 years. The long span of imaging data allowed the team to determine when plaques first became detectable and which participants eventually developed them.
The researchers then looked back at MRI scans collected during the previous decade. They compared changes in brain structure among people who later showed plaques with changes seen in people who did not.
"The most groundbreaking aspect of this study is that we found structural changes in the brain many years before the first signs of plaque buildup, which is considered to be the earliest sign of Alzheimer's disease," says Anders Martin Fjell, Professor at the Department of Psychology, and head of LCBC.
"These are cognitively well-functioning older individuals. What is unique here is that we have examined changes in brain structure in the years before the first scan revealed plaques," says Fjell.
Rethinking the Earliest Stages of Alzheimer's
Fjell notes that Alzheimer's disease remains extremely difficult to treat. One reason is that it is closely connected with aging and is probably influenced by several different biological factors.
"These findings suggest that there are brain changes that precede the first detectable signs of plaque accumulation, which is considered the earliest phase of the disease and occurs many years before cognitive symptoms start showing," he says.
Fjell says there are two possible explanations for what the researchers observed:
1. Harmful processes that either contribute to plaque accumulation or result from it may already be active in the brain even though the plaques themselves cannot yet be detected by scanning,
or
2. Other biological processes may be causing changes in the brain even before amyloid plaques begin to accumulate.
Potential Implications for Alzheimer's Treatments
The second possibility could be particularly important for the development of future Alzheimer's therapies. If brain changes begin through mechanisms that are separate from amyloid plaque accumulation, researchers may need to continue investigating treatments that target other biological processes.
"If the latter is true, it suggests it is important to continue developing drugs that target processes other than amyloid plaque accumulation. But we need more research on this," says Anders Martin Fjell.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oslo. Original written by Gro Lien Garbo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- James M. Roe, William J. Jagust, Susan M. Landau, Theresa M. Harrison, Håkon Grydeland, Maksim Slivka, José-Luis Alatorre-Warren, Pablo F. Garrido, Øystein Sørensen, Edvard O. S. Grødem, Tyler J. Ward, Esten H. Leonardsen, Alice Murphy, JiaQie Lee, Tormod Fladby, Atle Bjørnerud, Kristine B. Walhovd, Anders M. Fjell, Didac Vidal-Piñeiro, Yunpeng Wang. Cortical thickness changes precede high levels of amyloid by at least 7 years. Nature Neuroscience, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02363-4

Where is the best bar in Europe? It’s in Budapest according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:31:27 UTC
22:31:27 KST

From Budapest’s famous ruins to centuries-old Belgian boozers and wonderfully eccentric drinking dens, these are the European bars where atmosphere, character and local culture matter more than polish, according to a new ranking.
You can learn a lot about a city by ticking off its top landmarks, museums and monuments, but if you really want to get under its skin, there’s arguably no better place to start than at the bar.
From centuries-old pubs to gloriously chaotic drinking dens, Europe’s best watering holes offer a glimpse into local life that you won’t find in your usual guidebook.
Now, the European Bar Guide, an independent website which publishes reviews of the best pubs and bars across the continent, has revealed its annual ranking of Europe’s 100 best bars.
On its website, the guide says it rates venues “simply on how well they do what they’re trying to do”, with a focus on “spectacle, atmosphere, social scene, intriguing customs, local culture and yes, the quality and choice of drinks”. It also adds that “sometimes a bar’s deficiencies can be handsomely compensated for in other ways”.
That means that, unlike other rankings, glitz and glamour are not the most important thing, so it’s little surprise that Szimpla Kert, Budapest’s original ruin bar, topped the list.
These are the top 10 best bars in Europe, according to the ranking.
The 10 best bars in Europe
Szimpla Kert, Budapest, Hungary
The Hungarian capital is well-known for its ruin bars – spots that are housed inside abandoned or “ruined’ buildings, and Szimpla Kert was the first, launching in 2002.
Located inside an abandoned factory, the bar guide calls a visit here “like entering a portal to another dimension”.
It’s a maze of graffiti-covered rooms, mismatched furniture, fairy lights and wonderfully random objects, all arranged around a leafy courtyard.
Throughout the week, you can drink pálinka, a traditional fruit spirit, or smoke shisha while sitting in a converted car or a bathtub chopped in half.
On Sundays, though, the chaos takes a more wholesome turn as local producers fill the space with cheese, bread, honey and Hungarian treats, often accompanied by live films and music.
Retsins Lucifernum, Bruges, Belgium
Famous for its vast array of beers, Belgium appears five times in the top 10 and Retsins Lucifernum is in second place, with the guide calling this spot in Bruges “a departure into another world entirely” and “simply unmissable”.
This quirky bar is actually the home of a local celebrity named Don "Willy" Retsin, who introduces himself at the door as the "butler" and claims to be a vampire.
The space is packed full of antiques, gothic art and ephemera which leads to a downstairs bar and courtyard garden.
The bar seats just 20 guests, so advance planning is a must if you want to sample unusual cocktails and speak to others experiencing the madness too.
La Fleur en Papier Doré, Brussels, Belgium
La Fleur en Papier Doré is a wonderfully atmospheric Brussels brown café - a traditional, cosy neighborhood pub named for its dark wood interiors and warm lighting – with frosted windows, stained glass, wood, old tiled floors and walls crowded with medieval-style artwork and floral curiosities.
Once a favourite meeting place for Magritte and Brussels’ surrealist crowd, it now draws a cosmopolitan mix of locals and curious travellers.
The Belgian beer list is reasonably priced, while music and local events add to the cosy, lived-in atmosphere.
Goupil Le Fol, Brussels, Belgium
Goupil Le Fol is a candle-lit rabbit hole of low ceilings, vinyl records, old books, portraits and 1950s jazz memorabilia, hidden just off Brussels’ tourist trail.
Follow the narrow passage past the original Wurlitzer jukebox and into its cosy upholstered rooms, where records hang from the ceiling and books cover the walls.
The Belgian beer selection is solid, but fruity wines laced with Cassis and Cognac are the real draw.
Zlatna Ribica, Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina
According to the guide, many bars in Bosnia and Herzegovina are a little too western-influenced, but this must-visit place in the capital Sarajevo is a true tribute to what makes the country special.
Zlatna Ribica, which translates as gold fish, is described as wonderfully eccentric and like a mad professor’s study, crammed with antiques, ornate lampshades, waxed sideboards and books, with the clutter spilling out onto the street.
Every surface seems to hide another oddity, from crenellated furniture to a tiny black-and-white TV in the bathroom showing lions mating in the Savannah.
Recline among the chaos with a cocktail or local beer and enjoy one of Europe’s most quirky drinking spots.
Papa Joe’s Jazz Lokal, Cologne, Germany
The ranking’s authors say Papa Joe’s is “one of the ultimate jazz bars on the globe”, and it’s actually one of Germany’s oldest jazz bars.
This wonderfully unpretentious watering hole is all about fun, with stage-like seating facing daily live concerts, a scoreboard announcing the evening’s line-up and mechanical puppets seemingly playing instruments behind the bar.
There’s even a cocktail machine and Roman ruins tucked beneath the entrance.
Friendly, loud and very unrefined, it’s the kind of place that sweeps you up in the action.
t’Brugse Beertje, Bruges, Belgium
Despite not being the first pub in Bruges in this list, the ranking hails t’Brugs Beertje as “the best pub” in the city.
A cosy, wood-panelled brown café, it boasts an enormous Belgian beer menu which comes in an almanac-style book that takes time to work through, while shelves of gleaming glasses hang above the bar.
Pair a Flemish red or Oud Bruin with Gouda, meat platters or other simple snacks, then settle into the snug, communal atmosphere. It’s hugely popular, but the wait is worth it.
Bar Marsella, Barcelona
Bar Marsella has welcomed plenty of famous names over the past two centuries, with the likes of Ernest Hemingway, Pablo Picasso and Salvador Dalí all said to have drunk here.
Today, you can order the same famous absinthe and imagine the artists and writers who once soaked up the bar’s wonderfully bohemian atmosphere.
Barcelona’s Bar Marsella looks as though it has barely changed in two centuries – and that’s exactly the appeal.
Behind its faded façade are cracked plaster walls, dark wood panelling, dusty bottles and a wonderfully decaying old-world atmosphere. Order the famous absinthe, settle in and soak up one of the city’s most atmospheric drinking institutions.
U Hrocha, Prague, Czechia
Described as “the epitome of a traditional Czech boozer” in the ranking, U Hrocha – or ‘the hippo’ – is a wonderfully old-fashioned Czech pivnice in the Malá Strana district, with five communal tables, leaning posts, a tiny bar and plenty of atmosphere.
Though opened as a pub in 1994, it feels far older.
Try well-priced Czech beer as the room fills with locals and visitors. Intimate, traditional and unpolished, it’s Czech pub culture at its best.
Le Pot au Lait, Liège, Belgium
Le Pot au Lait is one of those bars where the décor is almost as much of a draw as the drinks.
Hidden behind a narrow courtyard in the heart of Liège, this 19th-century former house is filled with bizarre artwork, cartoon gorillas, carnival scenes, macabre taxidermy, graffiti and huge plants, creating a wonderfully surreal, slightly spooky atmosphere.
It began life as a student meeting place in the 1970s and has since become a much-loved local institution, with communal tables, a terrace and plenty of strange little corners to settle into.
Expect Belgian beers, a lively crowd and the feeling that you’ve stumbled into a bar, art gallery and funfair all at once.

Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks stall
Unknown

13:31:11 UTC
22:31:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli strikes kill one in south Lebanon as Rome talks remain stalled
Israeli strikes killed one person and wounded another in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh on Wednesday, according to Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency, after the Israeli military said it had struck the area in response to an alleged Hezbollah drone attack on its forces.
The NNA said the casualties resulted from an Israeli drone strike on the al-Ruwaiss and al-Maasouma Garden neighbourhoods of Nabatieh. Further Israeli strikes later hit the Nabatieh area, with local media reporting heavy explosions around Kfar Tebnit and circulating footage of a large column of smoke.
The Israeli military claimed that Hezbollah had launched two explosive drones overnight towards soldiers operating near the Ali al-Taher Ridge, close to Nabatieh. It said troops fired at and intercepted one of the drones and that no Israeli personnel were injured. Israel said it subsequently targeted what it alleged to be "Hezbollah infrastructure" used to plan attacks on its troops and civilians.
Hezbollah had not publicly commented on the Israeli allegation by Wednesday afternoon. The group has not claimed responsibility for attacks on Israeli targets in recent weeks.
Air raid sirens sounded briefly on Tuesday night in Tuval and Ma’ayan Baruch in northern Israel, near the Lebanese border, amid the alleged drone incident. Lebanese media later reported additional Israeli attacks across the south, including in Mansouri, Houla and Qantara.
The Ali al-Taher Ridge, a high point near Nabatieh overlooking areas of south Lebanon and northern Israel, has become a particular focus of Israeli operations. Israel has alleged that Hezbollah maintains underground military infrastructure in the area, while the elevation gives forces operating there a wide view of the surrounding border region.
Rome talks remain deadlocked
The attacks came a day after US Ambassador to Lebanon Michel Issa and US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. Israeli National Security Adviser Shmuel Ben Ezra also attended the meeting, according to images issued by Netanyahu’s office, which did not disclose the substance of the discussion.
The meeting took place before an anticipated eighth round of US-mediated Lebanese-Israeli talks in Rome. No official date has been announced, though Lebanese broadcaster MTV reported that the next session could be held on 15-16 September. In a statement on X, Huckabee claimed Hezbollah was the only obstacle to progress in the negotiations.
The talks are based on a US-brokered framework agreed on 26 June, under which Israeli forces would withdraw in phases from southern Lebanon while the Lebanese army deploys to designated areas and non-state armed infrastructure is dismantled. The arrangement has been slowed by disagreements over the sequencing of any Israeli withdrawal, the scope and pace of the Lebanese army’s deployment, and how compliance would be independently verified.
Israel has demanded assurances that areas transferred to Lebanese state control are clear of Hezbollah weapons and military positions. Lebanon, meanwhile, has sought a further Israeli withdrawal and resisted proposals that could amount to a permanent "security belt" or buffer zone inside its territory. Hezbollah has rejected arrangements affecting its weapons, leaving the army’s role in any eventual implementation politically sensitive.
Separately, the Lebanese Armed Forces said it was responding to what it described as "fabricated claims" by Israeli media concerning the army’s positions and operational role in southern Lebanon. In a statement issued on Wednesday, it said the reports sought to undermine internal cohesion and public confidence in the institution and its leadership.
The statement did not identify a specific report or outlets. But it appears to be intended to counter claims often by Israeli media outlets to cast doubt on the Lebanon army’s performance, loyalties or ability to carry out its southern missions at a moment when it is expected to be central to any eventual Israeli withdrawal and security arrangement. The army said its personnel remained committed to the command’s directives and to defending Lebanese sovereignty, security and stability.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities erupted in October 2023.

Kaushik Kappagantulu’s Greenhouse in a Box Is Aiding India’s Farmers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:37 UTC
22:30:37 KST

Kaushik Kappagantulu’s grandmother raised eight kids and 20 grandkids, including him, mostly by herself in the bustling Indian city of Hyderabad. An educated woman, she taught Kappagantulu that if you work hard, you will succeed. But after graduating from engineering college and doing a volunteer program teaching homeless kids, Kappagantulu realized this was not the case for everyone. “In rural India, most of the people work really hard, but because of a lack of access to different things, their hard work does not convert into success,” he tells TIME.
This revelation prompted Kappagantulu to dedicate himself to uplifting others. For six years he worked with school dropouts, helping them access jobs through vocational training. “Every single one of those kids was from a farming family and they were coming to us because farming was failing,” he says.
Sensing a systemic problem that needed addressing, Kappagantulu pivoted to agriculture. In 2015, he launched an agri-tech enterprise called Kheyti, which means farming in Hindi. The goal was to help the more than 100 million smallholder farmers who produce the bulk of India’s staple foods like rice, wheat, and pulses. And one of the biggest challenges facing farmers today is the changing climate.
In India, the combination of extreme heat, unseasonable rain, and depleting groundwater is making it difficult for farmers to grow during the summer season from March to June. During a heatwave this April, sensors installed by Kheyti recorded ground temperatures on multiple farms hitting 125 degrees Fahrenheit. “Climate change is wiping out their hard work,” says Kappagantulu, adding that the average Indian farmer earns about $1,000 a year. “It is not even enough for them to make ends meet,” he says.
Kheyti’s solution was a low-cost modular “greenhouse-in-a-box.” These net houses are designed to be smaller than conventional greenhouses, suitable for the one-acre farmer. They have shade cloth on top, which reduces internal temperatures by about 9 degrees Fahrenheit, and drip irrigation. Each greenhouse is also paired with an AI-powered tool that offers farmers advice on things like choosing the best crops and managing pests. This model works: Farmers reduce their crop losses by 58% while using 67% less water and 70% less fertilizer. Farmers using Kheyti’s structures also increased their net income, earning three times what non-Kheti farmers did on the same amount of land. And thanks to Kheyti’s partnerships with local governments, subsidies and low-cost loans mean the greenhouses are relatively affordable, each costing between $200 to $300. “We have to be the bridge that makes high tech agriculture accessible to the poorest farmer,” Kappagantulu says.
The greenhouse-in-a-box concept won the Earthshot Prize in 2022. It’s been growing ever since, with Kheyti now working with roughly 7,000 farmers across eight Indian states. Kappagantulu aims to double this over the next 12 months with the support of the Indian government, which has recommended states partner with the company.
Kappagantulu hopes to take the greenhouses global in the next three years and has a pipeline of other products, including flexible solar panels that can be installed on top of the greenhouses. His aim is to help one million farmers build secure, climate-smart livelihoods by 2033. But he knows he can’t do it alone. “Long-term change in the climate sector for agriculture doesn’t happen through one solution or one organization,” he says, “but through forming coalitions.”

Introducing TIME Trailblazers: Designing and Making the Future

2026-09-02

22:30:37 KST

In 2005, following Hurricane Katrina’s devastating August landfall, Resilience Force founder and executive director Saket Soni moved to Louisiana to help the workers facilitating the state’s recovery. Confronted by the realities of the storm’s aftermath, Soni had a clarifying conversation with his mentor, historian Vincent Harding, who, he said, told him that the country they lived in was a work in progress: "This is a place that's still being built, and you're part of building it.”
To this day, it’s this ethos that underpins Soni’s advocacy, in which he supports and protects the crews who rebuild after disaster. It also provides a powerful shorthand for the apparent mission of every innovator featured on our inaugural TIME Trailblazers list, which recognizes those leaders who, across the world, are designing and making the future.

This is a world full of potential, promise, and problems to solve. This is a world that is still being built. These 14 Trailblazers are standout examples of the many committed to building it.

Why Erika Woolsey Sees Virtual Reality Tech as an Ocean Conservation Tool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

Marine biologist Dr. Erika Woolsey once led a 450-person dive on the kaleidoscopic coral reefs of Palau, a tropical archipelago nation east of the Philippines. How was a group expedition of such scale possible? Each participant was in fact seated in a Washington, D.C., National Geographic auditorium with an Oculus Go virtual reality (VR) headset strapped to their face.
Woolsey is chief scientist and CEO of the nonprofit The Hydrous, which creates augmented and virtual reality experiences that connect people with the marine environment. She has guided many such virtual dives over the years. In fact, some 2.75 million “virtual divers” have experienced The Hydrous’ immersive ocean experiences. Usually a backup screen provides two-dimensional visuals for anyone who gets cybersick. In one experiment, some young students got the full treatment—Woolsey narrating as they interacted with the 360-degree underwater footage—while others just watched the 2D screen. Kids without the VR asked her the typical questions: “What's your favorite fish?” “How much money do you make?” But for those who experienced the VR, there was a distinct shift. "The students asked questions about what they saw," Woolsey says. "This young girl said, 'I could see inside the manta ray's mouth, and it looked hollow. Where are its organs?'" As Woolsey puts it, instead of just seeing a scientist on stage, these students became scientists themselves.
TIME Trailblazers: Erika Woolsey
Woolsey’s goal is to make the ocean more accessible to the masses so that they might strive to protect it. After all, it’s “our life-support system on Earth,” she says. Indeed, humans rely on the ocean for food security, economic stability, marine-derived medicine, and climate regulation. Yet "our ocean is overexploited, underprotected, and pretty much out of mind,” she adds, recalling the unprecedented global mass-bleaching event that inspired her to join The Hydrous as a cofounder in 2016: "It was really shocking to see how an ecosystem or a site that I had studied for years could be essentially destroyed in a really short period of time, and yet the public response was not proportional to what was really happening."
For the past few years, Woolsey has been touring North America with National Geographic Live to help more people experience virtual dives. Now The Hydrous is teaming up with Silverback Film –the natural history production company behind Netflix’s “Our Planet” and “The Dinosaurs”–and immersive production studio Submersa Studios to bring innovative and interactive ocean experiences to new audiences in museums, aquariums, and other venues.
An affiliate at Stanford's Virtual Human Interaction Lab, Woolsey has also been conducting research that suggests immersive tech bolsters not just education but empathy. "We're seeing significant increases across both ocean literacy [...] as well as emotional connection," she says.
The research supports something Woolsey has observed first-hand in her work with The Hydrous. "When people come out of the VR headset, it reminds me of people taking off a dive mask, when you're floating with your buddy on the surface of the water, and they just want to tell you what they saw," she says. "Sometimes, people have tears in their eyes when they come out of the VR.”

Zoox’s Aicha Evans Is Reimagining Urban Mobility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

Aicha Evans recalls the first time she saw the Zoox robotaxi, a driverless vehicle with no steering wheel, no pedals, and no front or back. “I fell in love,” she says.
She went home and told her husband she was taking the job as CEO of the startup. Amazon acquired Zoox the following year for $1.3 billion, keeping her in the top slot. That was in 2020. This August, six years later, Zoox began charging for rides in Las Vegas, and has since announced plans to expand into Los Angeles, Atlanta, Miami, and Austin. Later this year, Zoox taxis will also become available in the Uber app.
All that might seem like a blip compared to the success of Zoox’s main competitor, Waymo, which now provides roughly 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 U.S. cities. But while Waymo adapts existing cars to be driverless, Zoox builds its driverless vehicles entirely from scratch, and in doing so is reimagining urban mobility.
"We are in the people-moving space, and we happen to use self-driving technology to realize the vision," Evans says. She believes the experience of driving should be a bit more like that of flying: You don’t spend a plane journey monitoring the pilot. You’re simply along for the ride, and can use that travel time however you wish. "We want you to be you and do you," Evans says.
Without a steering column or driver's seat to design around, Zoox's engineers built what Evans calls a horseshoe airbag, one that envelops a passenger rather than deploying at them from a dashboard. It's the kind of safety innovation possible only because the vehicle wasn't inherited from a century of cars built for a driver. In fact, the entire vehicle is built around the rider rather than a driver. The bench seats face each other, so friends ride face to face.
Evans sees the Zoox robotaxi’s sliding doors as an entry into a journey that goes beyond merely getting from point A to B. "I'm not opening doors," she says. "I'm being welcomed into this space that's going to be mine while I'm being transported." She envisions Zoox riders looking up at skyscrapers, trees, and stars from an angle they can’t access from behind a wheel. "You can dream," she says.
Evans herself has been dreaming big since childhood. Born in Senegal and raised in Paris, she recalls feeling like a bit of an outsider in school. “Most of the time nobody looked like me,” she says. She took inspiration from Marie Curie, the Polish-born French physicist who became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize for her research on radioactivity. Curie has been a lasting companion for Evans, not just as a scientist but as “a wife, as an immigrant,” someone who crossed languages and cultures as Evans has. She often returns to one of Curie’s mottos: “Nothing needs to be feared. Everything needs to be understood.”
Correction, Sept. 2 
The original version of this story misstated Zoox taxis' availability on Uber. The taxis will become available on the app later this year; they are not available yet.

How Eloy van Hal’s ‘Dementia Village’ Is Transforming Patient Care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

At Hogeweyk, a nursing home in the Netherlands, residents live in small groups in separate homes where they cook together and share meals, go grocery shopping with aides, and even enjoy concerts or nights out at restaurants. None of that sounds particularly out of the ordinary, except that all of the people living in Hogeweyk have dementia.
The facility, just outside of Amsterdam, is breaking the mold for dementia care, thanks to the passion of its co-founder, Eloy van Hal. For years, he was the facilities manager for traditional nursing homes, where residents were generally confined to their rooms and offered only a limited variety of strictly supervised activities throughout the day. But he became convinced that those with memory and cognitive issues needed–and deserved–something better. “Why do we think that’s a good place for people who already have cognitive impairment or even worse, dementia or severe dementia—to be in places they don’t understand, and where they aren’t happy?” he says.
When van Hal arrived at the “very ugly institutional building” practicing this model of care that preceded Hogeweyk, he helped launch a pilot program focused on giving the residents back some of their autonomy. “We immediately saw improvement in how people reacted and responded,” van Hal says. “They became more active, less stressed and less agitated.”
That became the seed for Hogeweyk. When the nursing home eventually needed to be upgraded, its owner agreed to rebuild with patient autonomy in mind. Instead of a high rise institutional facility, they built homes to accommodate six or seven people with similar backgrounds and interests, and created a neighborhood to better resemble the real world. The key was to think of the people living in Hogeweyk as residents, not patients. “With the word ‘patient,’ the focus is on the disease instead of the human being in front of you,” van Hal says. “If you look outside, it’s difficult to see the difference between a visitor, a resident, a volunteer or a staff member. You just see people meeting, smiling and walking around.”
Studies show the residents at Hogeweyk are on average happier and use less medication than those in traditional nursing homes, and care providers around the world have taken inspiration from van Hal’s approach. One such facility is Agrace in Wisconsin, which is building the first Hogeweyk-style facility for dementia residents in the US, scheduled to open in 2027. Lynne Sexten, Agrace’s president and CEO, says that during her visits to Hogeweyk, she was struck by how few residents were bed-bound, or needed oxygen, and how their days were less regimented and repetitive compared with those of memory care residents in the US. “It’s monumentally different from what we see in memory care in the US.” Van Hal is hoping more facilities like Agrace take Hogeweyk’s lead to reframe how society thinks about and treats people with dementia. He now advises people interested in mirroring Hogeweyk’s model through his own consulting company. “It’s about changing our perspective on people with dementia from thinking of them as patients with dementia to thinking of them as persons living with dementia,” he says. “That’s my mission now.”

Bjarke Ingels Is Designing Better Spaces for People and the Planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

If you want to know what moves Bjarke Ingels, consider where he lives: In 2016, the renowned Danish architect purchased a retired ferryboat and transformed it into a chic floating home. What previously was an open driveway for cars is now a spacious living room with sliding window walls and an outdoor terrace. Where once stood chimney stacks and a navigation bridge is now a glass-enclosed primary bedroom. And below deck, the hull is now a whimsical playroom for his son, Darwin.
“I’ve taken a piece of decommissioned port infrastructure and converted it into infrastructure for my family life,” boasts Ingels, whose home in Copenhagen’s historic harbor embodies the climate-resilient designs he champions as founder and creative director of Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), his eponymous architecture firm.
The “SS Ingels” overlooks yet another prime example: CopenHill, a BIG-designed skiing slope-cum-hiking trail that occupies the pitched roof of a low-pollutant waste-to-energy power plant. At once fun and functional, it exemplifies Ingels’s self-described “hedonistic sustainability” point of view. “Hedonism is about hot showers while sustainability is about cold showers,” he says. “But somehow, when you integrate the two, you have a building or city that’s more environmentally friendly and therefore more enjoyable to live in.”
“Utopian pragmatism” is another term Ingels uses to describe his work. “A utopia is a place so perfect that it can only exist in your imagination while pragmatism deals with the reality of the everyday,” he says. “Every time architects get called upon to imagine a space or place, we try to make that little corner of the world exactly like our dream world.”
In his dream world, the environment is protected and the people living in it are happy, says Ingels, who sees sustainability not as a political or social issue, but rather as a design challenge. “As designers and architects, it’s our job to make the sustainable alternative more desirable,” he says, citing CopenHill as an example. “Normally, if you propose building a waste management facility and power plant in their backyard, people protest. But when you build a power plant with a ski slope on it, what might have been a problem suddenly becomes an asset.”
Ingels seeks the same outcome from The Dryline in New York, which he conceived after Superstorm Sandy in 2012. America’s largest urban climate adaptation project, it’s a 10-mile, U-shaped flood barrier that reimagines environmental infrastructure as social spaces like parks and bicycle paths. The first of several planned segments—the East Side Coastal Resiliency Project, spanning 2.5 miles from Montgomery Street to East 25th Street along the East River—began welcoming visitors last year.
“It’s designed like an archipelago of green islands where each island has been tailored to the requests and requirements of the people living close to it,” Ingels says. “Not only is it going to make the waterfront more enjoyable and accessible … but it also will stop the next Sandy from flooding the East Side.”
