How Mike Schultz’s Prosthetics Are Powering Paralympians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

Paralympian Mike Schultz craves adrenaline. The rush he gets when he’s kicking dirt on a motocross bike, shredding moguls on a snowmobile, or catching air on a snowboard is thrilling. But that’s not why he competes. What he really seeks from extreme sports is self-improvement.
“I’ve had a long career in competitive sports, and what keeps me motivated is the process of progression,” Schultz says. “Every time I’m on a bike, a snowmobile, a snowboard, I’m trying to learn something so I can be better.”
That pursuit nearly broke him in 2008: Schultz was competing in snocross when he was thrown from his snowmobile and fractured his left knee. Despite multiple surgeries, doctors had to amputate his leg above the injury.
When he began using a prosthetic leg soon thereafter, its limitations were obvious. “The first one I got was a basic free-swing hinge,” Schultz recalls. “It would swing when I walked, but if I got it wrong, it would just collapse and I’d fall over.”
Schultz didn’t just want to walk. He wanted to compete again. But existing prosthetics didn’t support the squatting positions his favorite action sports demand. So, he decided to make his own prosthetic.
“I went full ‘mad scientist’ in my garage,” continues Schultz, who used his experiments to establish the company BioDapt in 2010. His first product—a prosthetic knee called the Moto Knee—uses a high-pressure mountain bike shock absorber to mimic quadricep muscles by stabilizing an athlete’s stance and absorbing heavy impacts. It provides the range of motion athletes need to stand up and sit down on a bike or snowmobile. His next product, a foot-ankle contraption called the Versa Foot, provides the same shock absorption for sports that demand toe pressure and ankle tension, like snowboarding.
Using his own creations, Schultz has won four Paralympic and seven World Championship medals, not to mention 10 X Games gold medals across three different sports. Meanwhile, over 90% of lower‑limb athletes competing in Para snowboarding competitions use BioDapt’s products, and more than two dozen used them to compete this year at the Paralympic Winter Games in Italy.
Schultz says his proudest moments are when athletes try his prosthetics for the first time. “Once they understand how to move in it and what it allows them to do, it opens a huge door for them and puts a big ole smile on their face, just like I had when I tested it for the first time.”
To date, BioDapt has sold nearly 2,000 units, according to Schultz, who retired from the U.S. Paralympic snowboard team this year to focus on his business. In partnership with technology company Autodesk, he’s currently working on new equipment to help athletes train for the 2028 Summer Paralympic Games in Los Angeles.
“Para athletes today are doing things nobody thought would be possible 10 years ago,” Schultz says. “It’s been awesome to be part of that.”

Saket Soni Wants to Protect the Workers Rebuilding Communities After Disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:36 UTC
22:30:36 KST

When Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans in 2005, hundreds of thousands of residents fled, many never to return. Saket Soni did the opposite: He relocated to the waterlogged city—a seemingly confounding choice to anyone who doesn’t know him. As a young community organizer, Soni had been working with renters in Chicago, many of whom were Black and from the South. “I watched Katrina unfold in their living rooms through their eyes," he says. He moved to Louisiana to support the cleanup crews. There he found a mentor in Vincent Harding, a historian and activist who'd counseled Martin Luther King Jr. "He always told me that America is a country that is still being born," says Soni. "This is a place that's still being built, and you're part of building it." Soni took it literally.
In 2017, the New Delhi emigrant cofounded Resilience Force, a nonprofit that protects the rights of workers who make a living cleaning up after natural disasters. There's a long, quiet history of disenfranchised people climbing slick ladders and crawling under wrecked, mildewing homes to make things right after devastating storms—"America’s white blood cells," as Resilience Force puts it. As extreme weather events become more severe and more frequent, this itinerant cleanup crew, often comprised of undocumented workers and likely numbering in the hundreds of thousands, is a growing sector of the economy.
TIME Trailblazers: Saket Soni
"Go to any fire- or hurricane- or flood-hit town in America, and you'll see the labor shortage," says Soni. "Even if the money comes, if the workers aren't there to repair, then people won't be coming home." Soni hopes to continue developing this much-needed workforce over the next decade.
As well as providing legal advocacy for resilience workers, Resilience Force collaborates with third-party contractors to ensure laborers get better pay and safety standards. The nonprofit also offers a structured certification program that gives workers the technical and safety skills to perform roof repairs and other hands-on, AI-proof jobs. Then it puts people on the job directly, too, a blueprint with which they've seen success in states as politically and environmentally diverse as Louisiana and Colorado. While its in-house activities are paid for by philanthropy, Resilience Force provides free assistance to uninsured homeowners when it can.
As budget and staffing cuts at the Federal Emergency Management Agency further complicate recovery for communities affected by disasters, the Resilience Force model aims to directly confront three intersecting crises: climate change, the housing shortage, and a difficult job market. Inherently, Resilience Force also addresses a fourth crisis: anti-immigration sentiment.
Soni recalls a time he arranged help for a conservative Florida family whose home had been damaged by Hurricane Michael. "There was darkness all around,” he says. “They lost their electricity. Their roof was blown. They put up a sign that said, 'Strangers will be shot.'" Nevertheless, Soni rolled up with a squad of Resilience Force workers, many of whom were immigrants, and rebuilt the house. In short order, the family took the sign down. "Everybody's focused on how polarized the country is," Soni says. "I see the opposite."

Tadeu Carneiro Is Trying to Make Steel Sustainable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:35 UTC
22:30:35 KST

In more ways than one, Tadeu Carneiro loves heavy metal. As a young music fan, he adored Led Zeppelin and other classic metal bands. At the same time, while studying metallurgical engineering at the University of São Paulo, he cultivated a passion for the Periodic Table of Elements. Music and metals have more in common than one might expect.
“Music is math, and math helps you organize things,” explains Carneiro, who spent nearly 30 years organizing ions at Brazilian metals company CBMM, the world’s leading producer of niobium metal and alloys for use in automotive manufacturing, aerospace engineering, medical technology, and more. In 2017, Carneiro accepted an offer to lead Woburn, Mass.-based Boston Metal, which began at MIT in 2013 with the goal of commercializing a cheaper, easier, and cleaner method of producing steel and other metals.
“A technology that will revolutionize the way metals are manufactured is something you cannot say no to after working your whole career with metals,” he says.
That technology is Boston Metal’s Molten Oxide Electrolysis, or MOE. Whereas traditional steelmaking involves mixing iron ore with coking coal, then melting them together in a giant blast furnace that emits massive amounts of carbon dioxide, Boston Metal’s patented MOE technology uses scads of electricity to melt iron ore and separate its contents, dividing pure liquid iron from impurities like magnesium, silica, and calcium. Instead of carbon dioxide, the only byproduct is oxygen. This is potentially revolutionary, because steelmaking by some estimates generates nearly 10% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.
“We’re not transforming the way steel is manufactured for the ego of it. It’s necessary,” Carneiro says. “A process is needed that will eliminate 10% of the CO2 in the world, and this is the only process that can scale to do that.”
To be clear, there are other viable options for decarbonizing steel. But Boston Metal argues that MOE is superior because it’s more forgiving: The leading alternative, hydrogen direct reduced iron, extracts pure iron from iron ore using hot hydrogen gas instead of coal or coke. Although it’s clean, it requires high-quality inputs with few impurities, whereas MOE works with all grades of iron ore.
There’s just one catch. “The electricity needs to be clean,” Carneiro says. “Otherwise, it defeats the purpose.”
Despite the persistence of petroleum, he has faith in renewable energy’s future. “There are places in the world today where you already have clean electricity at affordable prices,” Carneiro says, citing examples like Canada, Scandinavia, and his native Brazil, where Boston Metal is opening its first industrial facility later this year.
Because steelmaking is extremely capital-intensive and cost-sensitive, that facility won’t make steel. Neither will two more planned facilities in Pennsylvania and Texas, both of which are expected to come online in 2029. Instead, all three will use MOE to recover from existing mining and metallurgical waste streams low-volume, high-value metals like niobium, tantalum, and nickel that are used in industries like electrification, AI, and defense. Given the low supply of these metals globally, Boston Metal is betting its technology can satisfy demand in a way that’s faster, more cost-effective, and more sustainable than establishing new mines.
Investors seem to agree: In May 2026, the company announced $75 million in new venture capital, bringing its total raised to over $500 million. That money and the metal-recovery operations it funds will generate the income, interest, and evidence Boston Metal needs to tackle steelmaking. “Once we mature the technology and scale it with planned efficiencies, we can be competitive with the way steel is manufactured today,” Carneiro says.

====================================================================================================

Salum Mshamu Showed How Smarter Home Design Can Prevent Deadly Diseases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:35 UTC
22:30:35 KST

More than half a million people die annually from malaria, many of them children. When Salum Mshamu was studying abroad, he got a call from his parents, who were caring for his two-year-old daughter. “She was having convulsions,” the Tanzanian public health researcher recalls. He urged them to rush her to the hospital, where they confirmed what he suspected: She had severe malaria, a dangerous complication of the mosquito-borne disease. For Mshamu, who was born in a rural village and grew up in the city of Dar es Salaam, it recalled a moment in his childhood when his own sister had similar symptoms. “If you haven't seen a child with severe malaria, you will not understand,” he says. But for Mshamu, breaking the cycle of devastating childhood diseases is personal.
Mshamu first trained as a nurse, but felt he could make a bigger difference in public health. After he got his master’s at Lund University in Sweden, he teamed up with architect Jakob Brandtberg Knudsen, and Lorenz von Seidlein, professor at the Mahidol Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit in Bangkok, Thailand. Soon, with Mshamu as a doctoral student at the University of Oxford, the three were collaborating on an exciting new project in Tanzania called Star Homes, focusing on trialing homes designed to reduce the spread of malaria, as well as diarrheal infections, which kill nearly 2 million children in middle- and low-income countries annually, and respiratory infections, which account for about 350,000 childhood deaths annually in sub-Saharan Africa.
At first glance, the homes, of which 110 were built across more than 50 villages, seem an odd fit. Their concrete floors and metal roofs look nothing like the region’s traditional rammed earth houses. But earthen houses are often too hot at night for their inhabitants to use protective mosquito netting, and problems with sanitation and ventilation increase disease risk. Mshamu and his colleagues were interested in trying another way.
The Star Homes team put an air-permeable mesh around the entire home to reduce internal temperatures while still allowing good airflow. This lowers indoor carbon dioxide, which attracts malaria mosquitos. They also raised the sleeping areas high enough to deter the insects, which prefer to stay close to the ground. The houses have their own water filtration systems, latrines, and solar-powered lights, plus a ventilated kitchen space with a lockable storage area to keep pests out of food.
In April 2026, the Star Homes project published the striking results of a randomized controlled trial involving more than 600 families. Compared to children living in a traditional home, those living in a Star Home saw a 44% drop in malaria risk, 30% fewer diarrheal infections, and 18% fewer acute respiratory infections. In a part of the world where climate change promises even greater challenges going forward, Mshamu hopes others across the continent will draw inspiration from these innovative structures.
“We have to engage the policy makers and see how to scale this up—maybe a mortgage program that can be helpful for the people in the villages,” he says. “We are just exploring different options, but we really would like to see the scaling up of this project, to see that people are actually using the design.”

These California Architects Found a Faster Way to Rebuild After Fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:35 UTC
22:30:35 KST

When the Eaton Fire tore through Los Angeles on January 7, 2025, husband and wife Alex Athenson and Cynthia Sigler fled their Pasadena home, certain it would not survive the blaze. By a stroke of luck and some shifting winds, their block was saved, but some 6,000 nearby homes were destroyed. As architects, Athenson and Sigler understood immediately that recovery would be a challenge.
"Building and construction is incredibly difficult, incredibly time-consuming, incredibly expensive, especially in Los Angeles," Athenson tells TIME.
One week later, while the couple was still sleeping on an air mattress at a friends' home, they launched the Foothill Catalog Foundation to help their community rebuild. The idea was to offer pre-approved housing plans, which would streamline the otherwise arduous rebuilding process and save homeowners time and money.
They took inspiration from an early 20th-century Sears program that let buyers pick from an array of home designs. The retailer then shipped some 30,000 pre-cut pieces for homeowners to assemble onsite. While Athenson and Sigler weren't interested in mail-order kits, they liked the idea of a catalog of pre-approved homes from which buyers could choose and bypass lengthy review processes.
Los Angeles County didn't have a mechanism for pre-approving plans for primary residences, so the couple worked with officials to get one in place. By mid-June, just five months after the fires, the county had pre-approved the Foothill Catalog Foundation‘s first plan: a 1,200-square-foot bungalow called "The Lewis.” Today, the nonprofit offers more than 70 pre-approved housing plans. More than 100 homeowners have chosen designs, with more than 40 structures under construction in Altadena.
The plans cost $5 per square foot. For a 1,200-square-foot home, this is just $6,000, compared to custom architectural work, which can run upwards of $100,000. All the plans are designed to comply with California's Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone requirements, which mandate things like non-combustible exterior materials, vents fitted with ember-resistant wire mesh, and roofs made with Class A fire-rated materials.
Athenson and Sigler worked closely with designers to ensure each model preserves the unique character of Altadena, a neighborhood with more than a century of history rich in diversity of race and class.
"What we are really trying to advocate for is to honor the regional specificity of the place where we're working and listen to the people and study the architecture [so we know] what and why people love the place that they call home," Sigler says.
The group is also using this “place-based design” approach for the Palisades, which Athenson and Sigler say has a very different aesthetic from Altadena, despite being just 30 miles away. “In housing today, there's a flatlining in a lot of what we see built,” Athenson says. “And as natural disasters accelerate and the housing shortage grows, you see an exacerbation of that flatlining [and a loss] of the really unique regional character that defined a lot of these communities."
The Foothill Catalog Foundation’s model has the potential to be replicated across the country. "There's a lot of lessons to be learned that can serve other communities in times of disaster," Athenson says. "But we really are just trying to find more efficient ways to make quality housing more attainable."

Jason Ballard Is Using 3D Printing to Take on America’s Housing Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:35 UTC
22:30:35 KST

Jason Ballard understands first-hand the fear of losing a home to disaster. Growing up on the Gulf Coast, he watched hurricanes level his town again and again. “My family has spent Christmas in FEMA trailers,” he tells TIME. “The global housing crisis isn’t a statistic to me. It’s something I've experienced in my own life and in the lives of my neighbors and the people I love.”
Today, nearly 750,000 people are experiencing homelessness in the U.S. This crisis is compounded by worker shortages and supply chain volatility in the construction industry. After working at a homeless shelter in Boulder, Colo., Ballard became convinced that the way America builds homes needed a fundamental rethink.
In 2017, he co-founded ICON, a construction company that uses large-scale 3D printers to erect buildings by layering a proprietary concrete-like material. As of this year, the Austin-based company has 3D-printed 260 houses and other structures. It says its construction system can print a 2,500-square-foot home in under seven days, while cutting construction waste, lowering building costs, and producing walls that can withstand fires, hurricanes, and other natural disasters.
“Construction has always been about showing up with saws and nail guns and tape measures,” Ballard says. “In the future, builders will show up with tablets and advanced materials and robots.”
Ballard has been waiting for lenders to catch on, but there were concerns that 3D-printed homes would not appreciate in value as quickly as traditional houses. Then, in May, Wells Fargo announced that it would write mortgages on ICON's 3D-printed houses and give buyers a credit for choosing one. The lender believes the technology has the potential to bring down construction costs and building time.
ICON recently started taking reservations for its Titan printer—which, unlike earlier models, can print multistory buildings—at about $899,000, with deliveries expected in 2027. For the first time ever, the company had more orders than it could fulfill this year. “For eight years we fought so hard for every project, so it felt strange to have to pass on some,” he says. “But the demand convinces me this approach is going to become part of humanity’s toolkit.”
Ballard is starry-eyed for sure, with big visions for the future. He can barely contain his excitement when describing ICON’s work with NASA to develop concepts using 3D printing to build structures on the Moon from lunar materials. “The story of exploration is you have to learn to live off the land,” he says. “I don’t think the Moon is going to be the exception.”
He’s also deeply down-to-earth. Speaking with a slight Southern drawl and the fervor of a preacher, he explains how his grandfather, "Papaw," a poor, uneducated refinery worker, taught him the romance and dignity of working with your hands. “I ride horses and build robots,” Ballard says. “I don’t think of myself as a cowboy or a tech guy, but as someone who follows his heart.”

Tammy Eagle Bull Is Weaving Indigenous Design Into Modern Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:34 UTC
22:30:34 KST

As extreme weather intensifies and America’s housing crisis deepens, it’s becoming clear that the conventional ways in which we build new structures are no longer working. In response, some architects are starting to place greater weight on weaving resiliency, cultural literacy, and a deep understanding of the natural environment into their work.
Tammy Eagle Bull has been advocating for these practices for decades. As the first Indigenous woman licensed to practice architecture in the United States, she has spent her career incorporating the historical and cultural knowledge of Indigenous tribes into her work. For many years that has meant designing for tribal communities, like the Porcupine School on South Dakota's Pine Ridge Reservation, which was the state's first LEED Silver-certified school, or the Oglala Lakota Artspace, which was designed around the Lakota belief that stars are connected to "sacred histories, stories, and knowledge." Still, she knew these approaches weren’t only relevant to tribal projects. "There's an [Indigenous] philosophy and methodology and pedagogy that is very applicable to everything that architects and designers do," Eagle Bull tells TIME.
Where conventional architectural practices are often guided by technical factors like zoning, Eagle Bull takes a different approach. "I like to go further back into the deep temporality of the site,” she says. “What was it originally? Who lived here? How did they live?"
She says this is especially important when thinking about extreme heat in a place like Phoenix, which had a record 113 consecutive days of 100-plus degree temperatures in 2024. "People are like, 'This is so inhospitable. It's too hot. People can't thrive here,'" she says. "[But] people did. They had thriving cities, they had agriculture, and they were able to sustain life. And so, if we look back, we can see that living in modern day Phoenix shouldn't be such a struggle. There were strategies that were employed to manage water and to manage heat."
These design principles are at the root of many modern models, says Eagle Bull, such as the “Passive House” concept, in which the built environment is crafted to work with things like weather systems and wind flows, and “life-centered design,” which takes local ecology and circularity into consideration. "The heart of all that is really what Indigenous design has been practicing for millennia," she says.
As a professor of practice at Arizona State University’s Design School, Eagle Bull is helping educate the next generation of architects in these design principles. For example, some of her students recently imagined solutions for unhoused Indigenous populations in Phoenix, focusing on how shelters might be deployed quickly and safely while still centering Native culture and practices. One idea floated was co-housing, which isn't typically embraced in shelters, where men and women tend to be separated. But Eagle Bull argues these kinds of approaches have their place. "There are a lot of times where it's an extended family, maybe the son's taking care of the mother or the grandmother," she explains. "So the idea is being flexible, employing different strategies and ideas in a balance that can work best for whatever situation."
In 2025, Eagle Bull became the director of a new Master's program at ASU. The M.S. in Indigenous Placekeeping and Design was founded by Wanda Dalla Costa, the first First Nations woman to be a licensed architect in Canada and a leading figure in Indigenous design in North America. It is one of only a handful of degree programs in the U.S. that focuses on both the history and practical application of Indigenous design. "There are a lot of things that we can learn from [Indigenous] cultural practices," Eagle Bull says. "They can help us not only manage the ecology and environment, but also how people exist with each other and thrive and create places that support who they are and support their community."

Free Solo’s Alex Honnold Is an Unexpected Solar Power Champion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:34 UTC
22:30:34 KST

Most people probably know Alex Honnold from the 2018 documentary Free Solo, which captured his historic climb on Yosemite's El Capitan without a rope or protective harness. Over his nearly two-decade rock climbing career, he has free-summited landmarks around the world, most recently a 101-story skyscraper in Taiwan. 
But fewer people likely know about Honnold’s other great passion: solar power. He started the Honnold Foundation in 2012 with the goal of giving away one-third of his income to community solar projects. In the years since, HF has grown into a 501(c)(3) with an executive director, full-time staff, and over $11 million committed to 75 solar projects in 2026 alone. Today, Honnold funds the operational costs, so outside donations can largely go to projects in need.
The idea sprouted from Honnold’s desire to offset his own travel emissions. But he knew that in order to gain traction and funding, his sustainability efforts would need wider impact. “Nobody cares about the environment unless their basic needs are met," he says. "So if you're trying to protect the environment in a broad sense without protecting or improving the lives of human populations, you're facing an uphill battle."
Today, at least 600 million people live without access to electricity. Solar power could hugely improve their lives, with the added benefit of reducing the global reliance on fossil fuels. HF focuses on solar projects that sit at the intersection of climate, equity, and human impact, with grant recipients typically receiving between $50,000 and $150,000. More than 1,200 organizations applied in 2026—a far cry from Honnold's early days of researching and funding projects on his own. Recent recipients include the Cambodian Center for Human Rights, which will install solar lighting and power to protect against illegal fishing and mangrove destruction; Integrated Health Outreach in Antigua and Barbuda, which will power a female-led beekeeping and honey-processing facility; and the Hopi Utilities Corporation in Arizona, which will install solar panels and battery storage on tribal land to power groundwater pumps.
One oft-cited recipient of an HF grant is Kara Solar, which provides solar-powered boats to the Achuar people in Ecuador and Peru. The partnership, which began in 2020, has helped facilitate commerce, health care, and education in the region, while also reducing reliance on gasoline. Kara Solar recently received a large grant from a global foundation, which built on earlier success: In 2024, thanks in part to HF’s support, it created a for-profit manufacturing company to produce electric motors for its boats.
"That's the ultimate success for a project if it takes off beyond the philanthropic money," Honnold says. "And then the real success will be in 20 years if everyone's riding an electric boat."
Honnold believes the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable. And while the foundation doesn't fund policy work, he says some projects have exposed the need for solar incentives in states with policies that limited rooftop solar. "I personally like funding projects in states that are really regressive, anti-solar states," he says. "Because it's like a big middle finger to the man. I think there's a little of the anti-authority, rock climbing streak.”

Ebola kills over 3,000 in DR Congo as UN warns response lagging

KINSHASA, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 3,000, as the United Nations (UN) warned that the virus is spreading faster than response efforts.
As of Aug. 31, the DRC had recorded 6,186 confirmed cases and 3,007 deaths, according to an official situation report. A total of 1,409 patients have recovered, while 830 others remain in isolation or Ebola treatment centers.
The outbreak has affected 60 health zones across the six provinces of Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uele. Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 81.9 percent of all confirmed cases nationwide.
During Tuesday's online briefing, Tom Fletcher, UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, warned that the virus was still outpacing the scaled-up response.
"Unless we scale up urgently, more lives will be lost and the threat will grow," he said.
According to Fletcher, nearly 11 million people in the DRC already need humanitarian assistance, while conflict-driven displacement, acute food insecurity and malnutrition are compounding the health emergency.
An incremental response is no longer sufficient for an exponentially growing epidemic, Fletcher said, urging a sustained, large-scale operation involving expanded treatment capacity, more safe and dignified burial teams, and better access for humanitarian personnel and supplies.
The UN official also revealed that over 40 health workers have died from Ebola while responding to the outbreak, while treatment centers and ambulances have also come under attack.
Following the DRC's launch of a vaccination campaign with the Ervebo vaccine, the World Health Organization (WHO) recently issued updated emergency guidance on the use of Ervebo, currently the only licensed Ebola vaccine available.
Ervebo was prequalified by the WHO in 2019 for the prevention of the disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus.
The two viruses cause clinically similar Ebola disease, but are genetically and antigenically distinct, and the extent to which immunity induced by Ervebo can provide clinically meaningful protection against Bundibugyo virus remains unknown, the WHO said.
Current evidence does not support the programmatic use of Ervebo to prevent Bundibugyo virus disease, the WHO noted, suggesting that it be used against the virus only within a research protocol.
The health organization also stressed that vaccination must not replace established outbreak-control measures, including surveillance, rapid diagnosis, isolation and clinical management, infection prevention and control, comprehensive contact tracing, and safe and dignified burials.
The International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision has approved an immediate initial release of 70,000 doses of Ervebo following a request from the DRC government. Of the allocation, 20,000 doses will be used in a Phase 3 clinical trial to assess the vaccine's impact against the Bundibugyo virus, while 50,000 doses are intended for frontline and health workers.
The current outbreak, declared in May, has since become the country's largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic on record and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

In Yemen, dates provide lifeline for farmers with few economic options
Hindered by poor infrastructure and climate challenges, farmers in Yemen cling to traditional methods to harvest dates.
Hajr, Yemen – Under the scorching sun of eastern Yemen’s Hadramout region, locals – young and old – immerse themselves in the annual date harvest, working among dark mounds of freshly harvested fruit spread across stones.
Farmers here in Hajr, about two hours west of Hadramout’s provincial capital of Mukalla, picked the dates about a week ago from vast palm groves nearby. They then brought them to this open ground so the dates can be dried, cleaned, and eventually sold, following traditional techniques that have endured for centuries.

Nabeel Ahmed and his family arrive before sunrise and head directly to their spot on the rocky ground, where their dates are spread out.
“My wife, my brothers and I come here before sunrise and stay until the sun gets hot,” Nabeel tells Al Jazeera, as he runs his hands through a pile of dates and holds up a handful.
Farmers and their families return every day to turn and sort the dates, removing rotten or damaged fruit before preparing the harvest for sale. Their aim is to make the dates as attractive as possible to buyers.
“These rocky grounds are used to spread out the dates, clean them, and sell them to customers,” Nabeel says.
As the farmers work, buyers move between the piles, inspecting the fruit in search of good-quality dates at the lowest possible prices. Nabeel is fortunate: someone eventually agrees to buy some of his harvest.
“I harvest the dates and sell some of them, while keeping some for my family to eat. I put some into small bags for Ramadan and other days. We usually eat dates with coffee every day. This is my sole source of income,” he says, pointing to small bags filled with dates.
Beyond providing an annual source of income, dates also offer a basic food safety net for some of Hajr’s poorest families. “If a farmer cannot provide food for his children, he gives them dates and coffee, because some families cannot even afford fish and rice,” Nabeel says.
A struggling district
Hajr consists of scattered communities along a long valley filled with palm trees and traversed by a river. The main road connecting the district with other parts of Hadramout has deteriorated after years of poor maintenance, while roads linking its communities are largely unpaved and dusty. The district has no electricity, and mobile phone services are poor.
It has also experienced repeated outbreaks of cholera, which locals and health officials attribute mainly to inadequate sanitation and a lack of access to clean water.
Hajr might be far from Yemen’s front lines, but it is still suffering from the effects of more than a decade of war in the country, and the lack of a stable government that can alleviate poverty.
It’s why Hajr’s vast date palm groves are a lifeline here, providing income and opportunities. There are no official figures on the number of palm trees or the district’s annual date production, but local officials told Al Jazeera that there are at least 2 million palm trees in the district.
The palm trees are effectively the centre of Hajr’s economy.
At the open-air drying ground, which turns into a temporary market during the harvest season, Rashed Mohammed, a father of four, has turned down offers from several buyers at prices he considered too low.
But he worries that if he cannot sell his harvest during the few remaining days of the season, he will be unable to repay his debt to a local grocery shop.
“I owe 1 million Yemeni riyals [$640] to the grocery, and I will not be able to pay it back if I don’t sell the dates,” Rashed says.
Like many farmers in the district whose main source of income is selling dates, Rashed buys essential food for his family on credit throughout the year, promising to repay the shopkeeper after the harvest. Other farmers put off weddings, building houses or buying essential goods until they have harvested and sold their dates.
At the end of the day, if no buyers arrive, family members return home while Rashed and other farmers stay behind, sleeping in makeshift shelters built from palm fronds. They remain partly to protect their harvest from thieves and stray dogs, but also to be available around the clock in case a buyer turns up.“The customer can come at any time, so I sleep here,” Rashed says.
Abject poverty
Farmers say one reason they continue to market their dates at the open-air market is that they cannot afford to transport their harvest to larger markets elsewhere in Yemen. Poverty is so severe, they say, that some farmers do not have enough cash to pay drivers to transport their dates and instead compensate them with plastic crates filled with dates.
Awadh Mubarak, a farmer and the head of a local farmers’ committee in Hajr’s Jawl region, says many farmers have abandoned agriculture for other jobs, including joining the security and military services, as palm trees die and date production dwindles.
Farmers say floods a few months ago destroyed a small dam that diverted water from the river to their farms, significantly reducing the amount of water reaching their palm groves and contributing to the death of trees.
The damage is visible along the road through Hajr, where numerous palms stand bare or nearly leafless, their dried fronds hanging from dead and dying trunks.
Awadh says rebuilding the dam is the farmers’ most pressing demand.
“Our primary demand is the reconstruction of the dam. The situation is extremely difficult. Many farmers have abandoned their palm groves and gone to other jobs, or emigrated,” Awadh says, showing Al Jazeera water flowing away from farmland instead of being diverted towards the groves.
Farmers have also called on investors and the government to build a date-processing and packaging factory, saying it would save them time and help them market their produce.
“We need a date-packaging factory to handle the large quantities of dates produced in the district,” Awadh says. “Instead of my family and me going out every day to clean the dates, for example, we could take them to the factory, where they could be processed in a day, saving us time and effort.”
For buyers such as Omer Mohammed, who travelled from a mountainous village in Hadramout, the reputation of Hajr’s dates and their perceived health benefits make the long journey to the district worthwhile.
“Hajr dates are the best in Hadramout because they are low in sugar,” says Omer, as he rests inside a makeshift shelter while workers pack the dates he has bought into bags.
“Back in my school days, when doctors needed blood, they would take it from residents of Hajr because they ate dates,” he says, recalling a local belief about their health benefits.
“I buy enough dates for myself and my relatives to last the entire year. If I have dates in my house, I feel food secure, even if I don’t eat them.”

VENICE, Italy, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Dozens of visitors lined up at the China pavilion of the Venice Biennale, waiting for their turn to see something unusual: a robot slowly moved its mechanical arm, guiding a traditional Chinese calligraphy brush across a sheet of paper.
Stroke by stroke, the brush wrote two Chinese characters which mean "Dream" and "Stream" respectively.
The scene was unfolding recently at the China pavilion of the 61st International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia in Venice, Italy. "Dream Stream," inspired by Dream Stream Essays, an encyclopedia written by Shen Kuo in China's Song Dynasty, is the theme of this year's China pavilion exhibition.
As the 83rd Venice International Film Festival opens on Wednesday, Venice is welcoming visitors from around the world, with the Biennale also seeing a surge in visitors. At the China pavilion, the blend of traditional Chinese culture, contemporary art and modern technology has drawn many curious visitors.
"It is the first time I have seen a robot writing," Andrea, a visitor from Austria, told Xinhua. "What makes it even more special is that it is writing Chinese calligraphy with a traditional brush," she said.
Visiting the pavilion with her daughter, Andrea said they both enjoyed experiencing the combination of traditional Chinese culture and modern technology. "We were really surprised by what we saw here," she said.
Another attraction for visitors is a playable section featuring scenes from the globally acclaimed Chinese video game "Black Myth: Wukong".
A giant widescreen unfolds before visitors, creating an immersive experience that brings them into a world inspired by traditional Chinese mythology. Beside the screen stands a sculpture of "the Destined One", the game's iconic protagonist.
After playing for several minutes, Thomas, a visitor from Germany, said he was impressed by the game's beautiful visuals and smooth controls.
He asked how to download the game, saying he hoped to experience the full version and learn more about the traditional Chinese mythology behind it.
According to the organizers, the exhibition combines calligraphy, video, digital art, multimedia installations and robot display to present Chinese tradition in new forms.
Works such as "Liangzhu Highlight" and "Kinetic Droplet Instrument" transform diverse Chinese cultural elements into experiences that can be seen, felt and interacted with, creating a space for dialogues between the ancient and the contemporary, while highlighting cultural exchanges and mutual learning between China and other parts of the world, according to the organizers.
At the opening ceremony of the China pavilion in May, Curator Yu Xuhong, also president of the China Academy of Art, said the theme "Dream Stream" draws on the Eastern wisdom embodied in Dream Stream Essays, particularly its spirit of exploring the principles of things and seeking harmony between humanity and nature.
Through the integration of tradition and innovation, as well as art and science and technology, the exhibition seeks to create an immersive and perceptible Eastern visual system and a distinctive way of understanding the world, said Yu.
For visitors, that vision comes to life through the artworks and interactive experiences on display. Eszter Nagy and Adam Lendvai, visitors from Hungary, told Xinhua that the exhibition offered a glimpse into the intersection of Chinese culture and digital technology.
"What we saw here was just a small part of each. We believe there is still so much more to explore," they said, adding that they would be interested in seeing more and perhaps visiting China one day to experience its culture firsthand.
This year's China pavilion exhibition will run through Nov. 22. ■

China Focus: China's manufacturing powerhouse blends research, industry to fuel innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:29:38 CST
22:29:38 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Holding up a small vial of fine white powder, Su Hongjiu said it took his company only 14 months to turn a laboratory sample of the ultrapure nanosilica abrasive, a key chip-polishing consumable, into China's first mass-produced version.
"Overseas companies once held more than 90 percent of the market. Now we can make this type of abrasive ourselves," said Su, founder of Ningbo GSi Electronic Materials Co., Ltd.
Incubated by Yongjiang Laboratory (Y-LAB), a government-approved materials research institution in Ningbo city, GSi is among a crop of startups emerging in Zhejiang, a province that was home to 2,167 national 'little giant' enterprises by the end of 2025 -- about 12 percent of the country's total.
The title is a government designation for top-tier small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that excel in niche markets with strong innovation capabilities and core technologies.
Thanks to established mechanisms connecting researchers and manufacturers, and bridging lab-factory gaps, Zhejiang has grown from a manufacturing powerhouse to a fertile ground for innovative enterprises.
CO-BUILDERS, NOT TAKERS
Y-LAB has established joint innovation centers with local tech companies, with a clear division of labor: the lab provides technology and talent, while the companies offer application scenarios and market access.
Some enterprises want even closer ties, giving rise to the role of "part-time technology vice president" -- a title for university or research institution researchers who take part-time executive posts at companies.
They help identify technical problems, coordinate joint research and strengthen in-house innovation. By July, 2,017 such appointments had been made across the province.
Zhang Ruihua, a professor at Lishui University, was paired with Zhejiang Lishui Jiexiang Technology, a leading domestic maker of rolling functional components.
Zhang brought students onto the shop floor, mapped production bottlenecks, and focused on the automated assembly of guideway blocks, a hurdle for domestic high-end machine tools.
The resulting equipment works six to eight times faster than manual labor, and 11 enterprises now use multiple sets of the intelligent equipment developed by the team.
The company-university partnership has since expanded into a joint provincial engineering research center and a master's program, with 15 graduate students whose research topics all come from factory production.
Other companies team up with researchers even earlier. Ningbo Yongxin Optics Co. hired a Zhejiang University professor as its technology vice president, to steer pilot projects.
The partnership resulted in the firm's four-color laser confocal microscope which broke a decades-long foreign monopoly.
"You can't wait until a paper is published or a prototype is built -- by then the technical route is set," said Cui Zhiying, a company technician in the joint team.
"We want to be co-builders of original innovation, not takers of hand-me-down technology," Cui said.
FROM MARKET FRONTIER TO UNIVERSITY CLASSROOMS
Wang Xingxing, founder of the world's leading robot maker Unitree Robotics headquartered in Hangzhou, capital of Zhejiang province, also serves as an "industry professor" at his alma mater, Zhejiang Sci-Tech University, with the standard academic requirements waived.
"We have long cooperated with Unitree, but the company and the school were still disconnected. With Wang Xingxing as our industry professor, we can go all out in both student training and research," said Chen Gang, a professor at the university.
To bridge the gap between fast-moving industry and university education, and to make up for students' lack of firsthand, real-world experience, senior technical professionals were introduced into Zhejiang's universities for such part-time positions.
So far, Zhejiang has appointed 973 of them.
In Ningbo, Jing Ge, chief engineer of a local new-energy subsidiary of CRRC, the world's top supplier of rail transit equipment, wears a second hat as an industry professor at Zhejiang Wanli University, where he helps set up the discipline, from which courses to offer to what they should cover.
Jing was also a key contributor to a project on ultra-high-power supercapacitors that won the 2025 national sci-tech award.
Citywide, more than 70 percent of Ningbo's industry professors have helped design academic programs, co-written 74 textbooks, developed 178 courses, and mentored more than 660 students.
FROM SCIENTISTS TO CEOs
When Zhejiang University professor Li Jingbo set out to build a company around his team's new silicon carbide chip, investors pushed back. A production line could cost hundreds of millions of yuan, and they were not ready to bet on a lab-born technology.
The hurdle Li faced is common. Researchers-turned-founders need more than scientific expertise -- they must pick a market, assemble a team and raise capital for technologies that can take years to mature.
Li found a partner in the Hangzhou Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, or SIOM-H, founded in 2019. It is among China's first "excellent-level" technology business incubators, built to help researchers clear exactly those barriers.
Qi Hongji, head of SIOM-H, calls the institute an "entrepreneurial partner." Its professional team fills gaps scientists often face in product development, marketing, team building and financing.
SIOM-H stepped into Li's project with 15 million yuan (about 2.2 million U.S. dollars) in angel investment, followed by other investors.
"It enabled us to make a start," said Li, chairman of startup Zhejiang XinKe Semiconductor.
Within months, SIOM-H helped attract nearly 50 million yuan from market investors, enough for second-hand equipment. In 2023, it helped secure hundreds of millions more, allowing Li to upgrade the production line.
Li's story is not an exception. As of July, SIOM-H had incubated more than 70 companies and attracted over 5 billion yuan in external capital, with the incubated firms' combined valuation exceeding 50 billion yuan.
"With stamina, passion and a team, we can take a company to the global forefront," Qi said. ■

CANBERRA, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A simple, low-cost bedside ultrasound scan of the thigh could help predict which heart surgery patients are most at risk of serious lung complications, new Australian research shows.
The study, led by Australia's Calvary Adelaide Hospital (CAH) in partnership with Adelaide University, is exploring whether a quick, non-invasive ultrasound of the thigh can flag early signs of post-operative decline in cardiac patients, according to a university statement released Wednesday.
Researchers will assess whether measuring the rectus femoris muscle, a major thigh muscle, can predict complications following major heart surgery. If successful, it could provide the first objectively verified bedside method to identify cardiac patients at higher risk of pulmonary complications, the statement said.
Around 10-25 percent of post-operative cardiac patients develop pulmonary complications, which can lead to rapid deconditioning, delayed mobilization and longer hospital stays, the researchers noted.
The project will be piloted over 12 months in South Australia, focusing on rural and remote populations where unique barriers affect access and continuity of care. ■

"We are working in close contact with the Ministry of Defence and the Russian National Guard. And I believe that we will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation,” he said.
Russia's civil aviation authority, Rosaviatsia said in a statement that Ukrainian approaches to international aviation bodies "have no legal force and violate the Convention on International Civil Aviation".
"Russia's air transport and its ground infrastructure continue to operate according to plan, handling arrivals and departures, including flights by foreign airlines," it said.
SOME FLIGHTS CANCELLED
Flightradar24 data showed disruptions on Wednesday at Moscow's main airport, while some airlines cancelled flights though they did not specify the reason for doing so.
"We continue to closely monitor the evolving situation in the region and adjust our flight schedules and routings as necessary," airline flydubai said in a statement.

RUSSIAN ATTACKS ON KYIV

From Partnership to Penalty: US Tariffs Shadow India Trade Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor recently claimed that the India-U.S. trade agreement is on the verge of finalization and that “almost everything” about the agreement was done “in principle.”
However, even as Gor was exuding confidence regarding the deal, two initiatives taken in Washington in just over a month have brought yet another round of the tariff war to India’s doorstep. These initiatives have the potential of increasing friction between the two countries, and could even torpedo the deal.
The most egregious of these developments is the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a bipartisan bill proposed in the U.S. Senate, which has the backing of the U.S. President Donald Trump.
The second development is Trump’s proposal to impose 100 percent tariffs on generic medicines from 2028, unless the firms exporting these medicines do not reshore their operations to the U.S. This proposal could significantly affect India’s pharmaceutical industry since the U.S. is its largest export market.
The bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named after the late Republican senator, who was the bill’s strongest proponent, was overwhelmingly voted by the Senate (86-11) in early August. The House of Representatives will take up the bill for consideration after it reconvenes in early September, and could push for its early adoption.
The primary objective of the bill is to tighten the economic sanctions on Russia for its continued war on Ukraine. The bill proposes 500 percent tariffs on all goods imported into the U.S. from Russia. It also proposes 100 percent tariffs on all goods imported into the U.S. from the five largest importers of crude oil or natural gas, by total volume, originating in the Russian Federation. As one of the largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil, India also faces penal tariffs for facilitating Russia’s sanctions evasion.
Market analysts put India as the second-largest buyer of Russian crude oil in July 2026, valued at over $7.3 billion, or about 37 percent of Russia’s global exports.
According to Indian government data, India’s dependence on Russian crude oil increased from 30 percent to nearly 43 percent of its total imports between January and June 2026. In February 2026, after the U.S. and India reached a framework for an interim agreement as a step toward finalizing the trade deal, Trump announced that the 25 percent tariffs imposed on India in August 2025 for importing Russian crude oil was withdrawn.
India, according to Trump, had “committed to stop directly or indirectly importing Russian Federation oil, has represented that it will purchase United States energy products from the United States.”
However, after the conflict in West Asia, India’s dependence on Russian crude increased to record levels, and simultaneously, its imports from the U.S. dropped from 13 percent in April 2025 to three percent in June 2026. Trump would surely have viewed this development as a trigger for action against India.
India’s generic pharmaceutical industry faces uncertain times following Trump’s post on Truth Social announcing his decision to impose a 100 percent tariff on all generic medicines from 2028, and increased to 200 percent a year by 2029. The objective of this proposed increase in tariffs is to “Reshore Generic Pharmaceutical Production into America, with a penalty to those Companies that decide not to build Plant and Equipment within the stated period of time given to them.”
This announcement followed an earlier decision by Trump to impose a 100 percent tariff on patented pharmaceuticals and associated pharmaceutical ingredients from July 31, 2026, if the companies exporting them do not declare plans to start producing in the US. Thus, Trump has put in place an expansive plan to control the global pharmaceutical industry.
Pharmaceuticals are the second largest products in India’s export basket to the U.S., accounting for about 13 percent of total exports in 2025-26. More importantly, the U.S. is the largest export market for all major Indian pharmaceutical companies.
The U.S. accounted for about a third of the total sales of most companies, but two Indian pharma companies — Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories and Zydus Life Sciences — are considerably more dependent on the US market: their shares of sales to the US were close to 50 percent in 2023-24.
Besides, all the top Indian companies have invested in production capacities in the U.S. through their subsidiaries, with the largest company, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries having 21 subsidiaries in 2025-26.
Trump’s insistence that the generic pharmaceutical companies must invest in the US to escape 100 percent tariff in 2028 has had its desired effect as Indian companies, including pharmaceutical companies have already announced their plans to invest over $19.1 billion to increase their production capacities in the US.
Only time will tell whether these investments will result in diversion of India’s domestic pharmaceutical production to the U.S., and the implication this could have on the availability of medicines in India.

A coffee-table-size scorpion roamed Earth before forests existed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:23:16 UTC
22:23:16 KST

A coffee-table-size scorpion roamed Earth before forests existed
- Date:
- September 2, 2026
- Source:
- University of Manchester
- Summary:
- A meter-long scorpion with massive pincers stalked ancient Britain 415 million years ago, long before forests and the better-known age of giant insects. Its surprising size and possible semi-aquatic lifestyle could reshape ideas about how early arthropods became giants.
- Share:
A newly analyzed fossil predator from what is now England and Wales has been identified as the largest scorpion known to science. Researchers from The University of Manchester and the Natural History Museum reached the conclusion after revisiting fossils that had remained in museum collections for more than 150 years.
The animal, Praearcturus gigas, reached roughly one meter in length and carried pincers more than 16 centimeters long. Around 415 million years ago, it would have been an imposing predator in the floodplain environments of the Early Devonian.
A study published in Palaeontology used modern analytical methods and comparisons with more recently described fossil species to determine that Praearcturus was a scorpion and represented a distinct species.
A Giant From Before the Age of Trees
Dr. Richard J. Howard, Curator of Fossil Arthropods at the Natural History Museum, London, and lead author of the study, said: "When we think of giant arthropods, people often picture Carboniferous rainforests with giant millipedes or dragonfly-like insects from later in Earth's history. But Praearcturus lived at least 50 million years earlier, well before the evolution of trees, when life on land was only just getting started.
"Confirming that this animal is a scorpion fundamentally changes our understanding of how and when these creatures evolved to such extraordinary sizes."
The discovery pushes the story of giant arthropods much further back in time than the period usually associated with enormous insects and other invertebrates.
Dr. Russell Garwood, Paleontologist at The University of Manchester, added: "Praearcturus has puzzled us paleontologists for more than a century. By bringing together material from several collections and using cutting-edge imaging techniques, we've been able to build a clearer picture of the animal than was previously possible, which is really exciting.
"What makes Praearcturus so interesting is that it became enormous at a time when life on land was otherwise very small. But it was a world that could somehow support a giant predator. To try and better understand this ancient world, we compared the size of fossil scorpions with other animals alive at the time. To reach such extraordinary sizes, and conclude that perhaps it lived in water, where life was bigger."
Why Did This Scorpion Grow So Large?
Praearcturus gigas lived during the Early Devonian, when terrestrial ecosystems were still in their infancy. Small plants and fungi had only recently begun spreading across the landscape, while forests and other complex land ecosystems had not yet developed.
That timing is important because Praearcturus lived before the high atmospheric oxygen levels associated with the later rise of forests. Those oxygen-rich conditions have often been linked to the enormous size of some later arthropods.
Instead, the researchers suggest that ecological opportunity may help explain the animal's extraordinary size. With few other large predators competing for resources, Praearcturus may have been able to dominate its environment in a way that became much harder once terrestrial ecosystems grew more crowded and complex.
A Scorpion That May Have Lived in Water
The fossils also provide clues that Praearcturus may have spent part of its life in aquatic environments. Some specimens preserve flap-like structures on the abdomen resembling features seen in modern crustaceans such as lobsters, raising the possibility that the giant scorpion could move between water and land.
An analysis of the broader arachnid fossil record, led by Dr. Garwood and the team, also found that scorpions are unusually common in rocks from this period compared with other arachnids. That pattern supports the possibility that some early scorpions occupied freshwater environments, where their remains would have had a greater chance of being preserved as fossils.
This places Praearcturus at an especially important stage in Earth's history, when animals were beginning to explore habitats beyond the oceans.
This places Praearcturus at a pivotal moment in Earth's history when animals were first experimenting with life outside the oceans.
Dr. Greg Edgecombe, Merit Researcher at the Natural History Museum, London, and co-author of the study, said: "The boundary between land and sea was much less defined at this time. Praearcturus gives us a fascinating glimpse into how early animals adapted to these changing environments.
"It may even represent a lineage that returned to the water after earlier ancestors had already begun living on land."
A 150 Year Fossil Mystery
Scientists first described Praearcturus gigas in 1871, but at the time it was interpreted as a giant crustacean resembling a woodlouse. The fossils were incomplete and lacked important anatomical features, including a tail, which made confident identification difficult for more than a century.
The new interpretation became possible after researchers compared the historic specimens with better preserved fossils discovered more recently. Those newer remains revealed anatomical traits found specifically in scorpions, giving scientists the evidence needed to reassess Praearcturus.
The finding also demonstrates how older museum specimens can continue to produce major discoveries long after they were first collected.
Dr. Howard added: "Specimens collected over a century ago can still hold entirely new insights. By revisiting them with modern techniques, we can uncover discoveries that reshape our understanding of life on Earth."
Rethinking Prehistoric Arthropod Gigantism
Finding such an enormous scorpion so early in the history of terrestrial life challenges traditional ideas about why prehistoric arthropods sometimes evolved to gigantic sizes.
The results suggest that high oxygen levels and other environmental conditions may not have been the only factors involved. Ecological opportunity, particularly the absence of competing large predators, may also have allowed animals such as Praearcturus to reach remarkable sizes.

Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:22:57 UTC
22:22:57 KST

OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting.
The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’s ChatGPT chatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children.
“These were people who really endured just total hell that day,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “Young kids who watched their teachers die, watched friends die and thought they were going to get shot and killed.”
These new lawsuits, filed in federal court for the northern district of California, come after Edelson filed seven initial suits in April – bringing the total number of cases against OpenAI for the Tumbler Ridge shooting to 37. All of the suits allege that the violent intentions of the shooter, identified as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, were well-known to the senior leadership of OpenAI, which failed to report her to the authorities.
Employees on the company’s safety team had flagged the shooter’s account to executives eight months before the attack, describing her in internal messages as “a credible and specific threat of gun violence against real people”, according to court filings. OpenAI banned her account, but she was able to quickly create a new one, the suits claim.
The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, of negligence, aiding and abetting a mass shooting and product liability.
Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement that he thinks about what happened at Tumbler Ridge every day and that the company works hard to create standards for reporting cases to law enforcement.
“The professionals working on these teams choose to do this incredibly difficult work because they care so deeply about keeping people safe,” Kwon said. “They come to work every day knowing that they may have to make a decision that they’ll think about for the rest of their lives.”
A groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University.
The shooting in Tumbler Ridge took place in a secondary school, shortly after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old brother in their family home. The new tranche of lawsuits includes cases from the family of one girl who was shot, along with the principal, teachers and students.
The attack was one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. In the aftermath, questions swirled in the small British Columbia town about how it could have happened.
Edelson singled out Chris Lehane, who is OpenAI’s head of global affairs and a former member of Bill Clinton’s administration who specialized in opposition research. He said Lehane was one of the people who received warnings from the company’s safety team but overruled repeated appeals to alert the authorities. That decision was also sanctioned by Altman, the lawsuits allege.
“What’s clear is that OpenAI over and over has made decisions to hide how dangerous their platform is because they’re worried about regulation and public pushback,” Edelson said.
In response, OpenAI’s Kwon said: “It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision … It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”
When the first seven lawsuits were filed against OpenAI in April, the company published a blogpost about its “commitment to safety”. Altman also sent a letter to the Tumbler Ridge community apologizing for not notifying Canadian police about what OpenAI knew regarding the shooter’s potential threat.
“While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote.
David Eby, the British Columbia premier, posted the letter to social media with the comment: “The apology is necessary, and yet grossly insufficient for the devastation done to the families of Tumbler Ridge.”

Britain’s new finance minister sets date for first big speech on growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:22:11 UTC
22:22:11 KST

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on a visit to Kiln Park Holiday Centre to highlight the Great British Summer Savings campaign on August 27, 2026 in Tenby. | Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain’s new top finance minister plans to give his first major speech in the role next week, which is expected to focus on boosting Britain’s ailing economic growth.
Chancellor John Healey intends to give the address on Sept. 7, said four people with knowledge of the date who were granted anonymity to discuss internal planning, following weeks of preparation since Prime Minister Andy Burnham gave him the role in July. Officials are looking at staging it at a manufacturing plant outside London.
The Treasury declined to comment.
Advertisement
Burnham revealed in mid-August that Healey was working on a speech on the government’s economic agenda. The date of next Monday was first reported by Politics at Sam and Anne’s, the morning briefing podcast by POLITICO and Sky News.
The speech will focus heavily on growth, said two of the people quoted above — weeks after Burnham moved responsibility for local economic growth strategy from the Treasury to his new prime ministerial office in Manchester, No. 10 North.
One of the four people cited at the start of this story said the speech is likely to focus less on individual spending policies ahead of the Oct. 28 budget and more on a broader vision and initiatives, including Burnham’s promises to hand more economic levers to regional leaders.
“This isn’t a rushed job — it’s a serious bit of thinking,” they added. Another of the four people said: “It’s the government’s version of their theory of growth.”
A government official, who is not one of the four individuals cited above, said the speech has involved work by multiple government departments contributing potential ideas. “It’s crossed a lot of people’s radar,” they added.
Some in Westminster may see the speech as Healey seeking to emphasize his own role.
Advertisement
A Treasury official, also not one of the cited individuals, said growth would be a dual mission for both the prime minister’s and chancellor’s offices. They added the Treasury would drive growth policy across Whitehall, that every department would have a focus on growth and Burnham’s pledge of “good growth in every postcode” would take the whole government working as one to achieve.
Burnham told MPs on Tuesday that he believed growth had to be “driven with the full authority of the very center of government, in close partnership with the Treasury.” Louise Haigh, his first secretary who has previously described the Treasury as “imperial,” joked about the change of responsibilities Wednesday: “It's a little bit of a chip on its empire.”
Britain’s GDP grew by 0.4 percent in the three months to June, while rising bond yields have left Healey with the highest cost of servicing government debt for decades. Both squeeze his ability to intervene in key industries. Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the budget.
One banking lobbyist briefed separately on the event said Healey’s speech could be “shaped by market movements” seen this week, with the finance minister likely using it to calm bond traders with a pro-growth but policy-lite approach.
The speech is also likely to touch on Burnham’s promises to “reindustrialize” Britain, given the continuing focus on the defense industry. Healey is under pressure to pledge that Britain’s military spending will reach 3 percent of GDP by 2030, as he demanded when he resigned as the U.K.’s defense minister earlier this year. He has said he will not name a date for hitting 3 percent until next year.

Manipur assembly passes third resolution seeking NRC update before census
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:21:17 UTC
22:21:17 KST

File photo: People raise slogans to press for the implementation of National Register of Citizens (NRC) updation before conducting the census in Manipur
NEW DELHI: The Manipur Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution urging the Centre to update the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in the state before conducting the census exercise.This is the third such resolution adopted by the assembly since 2022.“The House once again reaffirms its previous resolution passed on August 5, 2022, and March 1, 2024, to urge the government of India to update the National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Manipur before conducting the census in the interests of the state in particular and the nation in general,” speaker Th Satyabrata Singh said.
The resolution comes after the Centre deferred the census exercise in Manipur on Monday, a day before the house-listing exercise was scheduled to begin in the state.According to a statement issued by the chief minister's secretariat, the decision was taken after Union home minister Amit Shah chaired a high-level meeting in New Delhi to review the situation in Manipur.“The meeting agreed to defer the proposed Census exercise in the state considering the feelings and aspirations of the people of Manipur,” the statement said.
The demand for implementing and updating the NRC has stemmed from apprehensions among sections of the Meitei and Naga communities that a census without the exercise could result in “demographic changes” in the state due to the alleged entry of illegal immigrants from neighbouring Myanmar, who have ethnic ties with the Kuki people.
Shutdowns over demand for clear NRC roadmap
The Centre's decision to defer the census did not end protests over the demand for a clear roadmap on updating the NRC.Manipur's five valley districts witnessed a near-complete shutdown on Tuesday during a 24-hour general strike called by the Campaign for Just and Fair Delimitation.The organisation said the deferral of the census did not meet its main demand for a clear assurance that the NRC would be updated before any population enumeration.Meanwhile, a Kuki-Zo organisation questioned the Centre's decision to defer the census exercise, alleging that the matter had been decided while ignoring the voice of the community.
