Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on September 2, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:19:27 CST
22:19:27 KST

People’s Daily: This year marks the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. Yesterday, President Xi Jinping attended in Bishkek the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO and the SCO Plus Meeting. Could you please provide more information on this?
Guo Jiakun: On September 1, President Xi Jinping attended the 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and delivered important remarks titled “Toward Higher Quality Development of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.”
President Xi pointed out that over the past 25 years, the SCO has traveled an extraordinary journey. Its biggest achievement is that it has steadily grown into a new type of regional cooperation organization with the largest land area and population and enormous development potential. Its most valuable spiritual asset is that it pioneered, and has since followed invariably, the Shanghai Spirit of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development. Its most important experience for cooperation is that it has found the right way of coexistence featuring non-alliance, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, enabling regional countries to build a common home together.
President Xi put forward four points for the SCO’s future development, namely, staying committed to putting development first and opening up the prospects for shared prosperity, staying committed to taking security as a key goal and fostering an environment of common security, staying committed to a people-centered approach and cementing the foundation for everlasting friendship, and staying committed to dialogue and consultation and striving for more equitable and orderly governance. President Xi stressed that China will work with all parties to continue to hold high the banner of the Shanghai Spirit, implement the development strategy of the SCO for the next decade, and pursue development with higher quality, so as to make greater contributions to a community with a shared future for humanity.
On the same day, President Xi attended the SCO Plus Meeting and delivered an important statement titled “Jointly Advocating an Equal and Orderly Multipolar World and Making Global Governance More Just and Equitable.” In his remarks, President Xi provided a profound analysis on questions such as what kind of multipolarity the world needs and how countries and the SCO are going to take part in and promote an equal and orderly multipolar world. He proposed three points on better leveraging the role of the SCO, namely, advancing common prosperity in the vast continent straddling Asia and Europe with the SCO Strength, promoting the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom, and guiding the reform and improvement of global governance through the SCO Action. President Xi stressed that a more united and vibrant SCO is fully capable of making greater contributions to a multipolar world.
All parties expressed appreciation for China’s important contribution to the organization’s development as a founding member, and agreed to actively implement the strategic vision set out at the 2025 Tianjin Summit, continue to uphold the Shanghai Spirit, promote institution-building, enhance political mutual trust, deepen cooperation in various areas, strengthen people-to-people bonds, and jointly respond to new types of security challenges, with a view to writing a new chapter of lasting peace and common development.
Pheonix TV: We have learned that the Second Meeting of G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors held from August 31 to September 1 failed to issue a communiqué due to China’s differing view on global imbalances. Would you like to comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: As an important member of the G20, China places high emphasis on the organization’s role as the premier forum for international economic cooperation. Since the United States assumed the 2026 presidency of the G20, the Chinese side has participated in relevant discussions including along the Finance Track in an active and constructive manner and contributed to practical outcomes under various mechanisms.
We have noted that parties hold diverging views on certain issues at the recent Meeting of G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors. We regret that the meeting failed to issue a communiqué. The G20, as the premier platform for global economic cooperation, should play its coordinating role on key issues concerning the global economy in an objective, impartial and balanced manner based on the principle of consensus through consultation and equal participation. We hope the United States in its presidency and other members will abide by this principle, give full respect to all parties’ legitimate concerns, and strive for a fruitful Miami Summit. China stands ready to work with the United States to act on the important common understandings reached between the two presidents and join hands with fellow members to enable the G20 to play a positive role in deepening macroeconomic policy coordination, improving global economic governance, and boosting world economic growth.
The Paper: It was reported that the second batch of relief supplies provided by China has been delivered to the Nepalese side yesterday. Can you share more details? Can you also update us on what China has done on sharing information about foreign nationals who remain unaccounted for?
Guo Jiakun: The second batch of emergency relief supplies provided by China to Nepal arrived in Kathmandu yesterday afternoon. Five DNA forensic experts were also on the plane to assist Nepal in their operations. The Nepalese side thanked China for urgently sending more supplies and providing technical support. China is preparing the third batch of emergency relief supplies based on the request of Nepal. These supplies will include Bailey bridges, mortuary refrigerators, epidemic prevention supplies and emergency communication equipment. China will also send a second group of DNA experts.
In the wake of the disaster, China has kept close communication with relevant countries’ embassies in China to jointly identify missing personnel and properly handle follow-up matters. As we speak, residents of the border areas and pilgrims who were previously stranded in the disaster-hit areas are leaving China via land or air transportation in an orderly manner. Yesterday, the foreign ministry briefed relevant foreign embassies in China on the missing foreign nationals. China will continue to keep the channel of communication with relevant embassies unimpeded by various means.
China attaches great importance to the safety of Chinese nationals and institutions in Nepal. We are working with Nepal to make all-out effort to search for and rescue missing Chinese nationals, and assisting the relocation of many Chinese nationals to safety. The Chinese embassy in Nepal will continue to do all we can to assist Chinese nationals in need.
AFP: Can the Chinese foreign ministry please provide an updated toll of those who are still missing from the mudslide disaster? Are there new figures since Sunday? And specifically, how many foreigners are missing on the Chinese side? What is the breakdown of their nationalities? How many Chinese citizens are among the dead in Nepal and how many Chinese citizens remain missing in Nepal?
Guo Jiakun: The authorities of the Xizang Autonomous Region shared detailed information at the recent press briefing. Yesterday the foreign ministry also informed relevant countries’ embassies in China. According to the latest information, a total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are among those missing. We will continue communicating and coordinating with relevant parties to jointly identify missing persons and properly handle follow-up matters.
Nearly 100 Chinese nationals remain unaccounted for in Nepal. We thank the Nepali side for rescuing and transferring Chinese nationals in Nepal and hope these efforts will continue.
Ukrinform News Agency: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine will intensify deep strikes on military facilities within the Russian territory, which is why the airspace of Russia became dangerous. He has instructed the Ukrainian foreign ministry to inform other countries about the danger of flying in Russian airspace. Chinese airlines companies continue to use Russian skies for passenger and other flights. I’d like to ask whether the foreign ministry has already received a warning from the Ukrainian side and will China respond to the increasing danger？
Guo Jiakun: Dialogue and negotiation is the only viable way out of the Ukraine crisis. We urge the parties concerned to remain calm and exercise restraint, jointly work toward early deescalation and accumulate conditions for the political settlement of the crisis.
Asahi Shimbun: Iranian media reported that the Chinese and Iranian leaders had a brief conversation during the SCO Bishkek summit. Can you confirm that? What topics did they discuss?
Guo Jiakun: We have released information on President Xi Jinping’s participation in the SCO Bishkek summit, during which he had cordial exchanges with leaders of various countries.
Bloomberg: The Russian president and the Chinese leader reportedly discussed holding a trilateral meeting with the U.S. president. That would be when China hosts the APEC summit later this year. Would the foreign ministry like to comment on that?
Guo Jiakun: On this question, I have no information to share at the moment.
As the host for this year’s APEC, China stands ready to work with all parties for the full success of the APEC China Year and make new contribution to the economic growth of the Asia Pacific and beyond.
Beijing Daily: Recently, Mr. Ronald Sakolsky returned to China for the first time in 27 years and was reunited with Ms. Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker and renowned figure in China’s fight against desertification. Their moving story has attracted widespread attention. What is your comment?
Guo Jiakun: Recently, our American friend Mr. Ronald Sakolsky, affectionately known in China as “Saikaosi” for supporting China’s fight against desertification, visited China upon invitation after 27 years. During his visit, Mr. Sakolsky traveled to Inner Mongolia, where he joined Ms. Yin Yuzhen, a national model worker, and revisited the forest he helped fund years ago, and together planted a tree of friendship. He also returned to the school in Luoyang, Henan Province, where he once taught, to meet with teachers and students. He visited Beijing as well.
Throughout his visit, Mr. Sakolsky witnessed firsthand the remarkable changes that have taken place in China and once again experienced the warmth and hospitality of the Chinese people. He was deeply moved and shed tears on several occasions. I noted that in an interview with the media, Mr. Sakolsky said that Ms. Yin and he have shown that they can bridge cultures and break down boundaries. He said that the American and Chinese people both want to live in peace. China and the United States are like two roads, they may take different routes, but they can still lead to the same destination. His sincere words have touched many people. They reflect a shared aspiration of the people of both countries.
The hope of the China-U.S. relationship lies in the people, and its foundation lies in grassroots connections. The many inspiring stories written together by the Chinese and American people are a vivid testament to our people-to-people friendship. They also once again demonstrate that China and the United States, as two major countries, can achieve mutual success, and contribute to the well-being of the world. China will, as always, support more visits and exchanges between the two peoples, so that we can continue to write new chapters in our people-to-people friendship and make greater contributions to the development of China-U.S. relations.
Global Times: Eighty one years ago today, Japan officially signed the Instrument of Surrender, marking the ultimate triumph of the global fight against fascism. We notice that MFA spokesperson has shared China’s views on the “Enemy State Clauses.” But some believe that there’s no longer an “enemy state” in the world anymore. The “Enemy State Clauses” have expired and are no longer relevant. What’s your take on that? Can you give us more information on China’s position?
Guo Jiakun: On September 2, 1945, the Japanese government officially signed the Instrument of Surrender, and accepted all the terms of the Potsdam Proclamation, establishing the undeniable historical conclusion that the war waged by Japan’s militarists was for aggression. It is also a part of the postwar international order that shall not be challenged. The “Enemy State Clauses” are still in the UN Charter and consist of Article 53, 77 and 107. It is a special set of rules for defeated states, aiming to prevent them from threatening international peace and security once again, and has provided important institutional safeguards for defending postwar international order. Japan joined the UN after recognizing its militarist crimes and accepting the UN Charter in its entirety.
Today, however, those running the Japanese government keep sidestepping the issue of historical crimes, and even go to great lengths to distort and whitewash its crimes of aggression and move faster to remilitarize Japan. They continue to pay tribute to Class-A war criminals in WWII and attempt to revise the pacifist Constitution. What’s worse, Japan’s ties with nearly all its neighbors have witnessed increased tension. Japan blatantly interferes in the internal affairs of other countries, and even threatens to use force. The “gray rhino” of Japan’s neo-militarism is charging towards us, and posing a threat to peace and stability in the Asia Pacific once again. Against such backdrop, it is extremely necessary to reaffirm the commitment to the UN Charter, in particular, the “Enemy State Clauses.”
We urge the Japanese government to earnestly abide by its international obligations stipulated by the Instrument of Surrender, face up to and learn lessons from history, make a clean break with militarism, and earn the trust of its Asian neighbors and the rest of the world with concrete actions.
PTI: Reports say that the high-altitude Himalayan region is warming significantly, faster than the global average. Studies have shown since 1981, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau have lost roughly 20 percent of its glaciers attributed to the climate change crisis. In the light of the August 26 glacier collapse, how does China view the glacier retreat crisis impacting the Himalayan region and the calls for formation of a coordination mechanism by China with neighbouring countries, to strengthen cooperation to deal with such disasters affecting the fragile region?
Guo Jiakun: China has responded to similar questions. According to the assessment of Chinese and Nepali experts, long-term effects of global warming have made glaciers unstable, and this disaster was triggered by the collapse of a glacier in Nepal, resulting in a rapid crash of ice and rocks which took away a chunk of the mountain. The Xizang Autonomous Region shared relevant information at its press conference.
China and Nepal have maintained sound cooperation in meteorology, water conservancy and disaster prevention and reduction. In the wake of the disaster, China has shared with Nepal important information such as images, satellite, and hydrological data of the disaster-affected areas, including early-warning information on an upstream barrier lake. We will continue to give strong support to Nepal in its relief efforts and strengthen cooperation on disaster prevention and reduction.
Climate change is a common challenge facing all humanity. No country can stay immune from such risks. China will continue to work with the international community to strengthen exchanges and cooperation and effectively prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change. As for your specific question, I’d refer you to competent authorities.
AFP: I wonder if China has been told if any Chinese citizens were among the dead in Nepal from the disaster last week? And also are you able to provide a specific figure on the number of Chinese nationals missing in China?
Guo Jiakun: I just shared the information we have. As we speak, intensive rescue and relief operations are still underway. For the specific information you asked for, there will be continued updates.

X's new payments app X Money hit by mass hacking attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:17:46 UTC
22:17:46 KST

Unsolicited password reset emails have hit X users after the launch of X Money, with the platform warning that hackers could be behind a wider phishing attempt.
X has revealed that hackers could be trying to attack users after the launch of X Money.
This follows several X users receiving surprise password reset emails. Although the social media giant has been looking into the issue, there is no evidence so far that these attack attempts were successful.
It is believed that attackers could be mass-triggering the form for password resets using public usernames
X Money, the platform's payments service, launched on an invite-only basis in July before expanding to all Premium and Premium+ subscribers on 31 August.
It allows users to hold money, make and receive payments, as well as carry out peer-to-peer transfers, all on the X platform.
As such, any access that attackers may get to these users' accounts could have significant financial implications.
The company's general counsel, James Burnham, highlighted that "the legal and security teams @X will stop at nothing to identify, locate, and hold criminally accountable any person anywhere on or off earth who attempts to victimize our platform's users."
This has led to a flood of users taking to the platform to both spread awareness that this is happening and also remind others to use two-factor authentication, if they aren't already, for an added layer of protection.
The social media platform's Grok chatbot has also chimed in, replying to some posts with practical measures users can take to do so.
Could this be hiding a more dangerous phishing attack?
Although receiving an email for a supposed password change request doesn't automatically mean your account has been breached, especially if you have multi-factor authentication, some users are concerned that this latest incident could be hiding a wider phishing attempt.
Several users have also claimed that follow-up phishing emails have been sent out, along with these password reset confirmation emails. These have been framed as legitimate emails coming from X, which has added to the confusion and fear.
These emails have been urging users to change their passwords, which is an expected follow-up after a security breach. However, they include a fake X link for users to do so, which can trick them into providing their login credentials to attackers.
As such, this is more likely to be an elaborate multi-step hacking and phishing attempt than previously expected.
X Money has already faced scrutiny for its reliance on partner banks like Cross River Bank, due to past regulatory enforcement actions against the bank, as well as the underlying reasoning behind the promotional 6% yield on deposits, compared to federal benchmarks.

Hope, Dopamine and whatever 'Perfecth' means: Euronews Culture’s Fall music preview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:16:46 UTC
22:16:46 KST

Hope, Dopamine and whatever 'Perfecth' means: Euronews Culture’s Fall music preview
Euronews Culture looks ahead to the last four months of 2026 and picks the hotly anticipated albums you won’t want to miss.
It’s been a very solid year so far in terms of new album releases, with neo-soul goodnessfrom Jill Scott, intoxicating hip-hopfrom Irish trio Kneecap, Olivia Rodrigo’sbed-bouncing pop, and Phoebe Bridgers delivering the best album of her career so far – to name but a few.
And 2026 isn't over yet...
Now that we’ve given you our massive Fall movie preview, highlighting the films that should get you rushing to the cinema, it’s time to look ahead to the crowded release schedule when it comes to music.
We've handpicked 15 hotly anticipated records you won’t want to miss before the year ends.
Ezra Collective – Here Because Of Hope
Release date: 18 September
The MOBO and Mercury Prize-winning British jazz-afrobeat-soul quintet follow up their excellent 2024 album 'Dance, No One’s Watching' with their much anticipated fourth LP. Having become the first jazz band to win Group of the Year at the Brit Awards last year, Ezra Collective are hoping to impress their fans once again with their “most ambitious and personal record of their career”. According to a press statement, 'Here Because Of Hope' is split into “three spiritual and geographical movements” as the album aims to trace the movement of Black people across continents and decades - “from the music of Africa to the rhythms of the Caribbean, and home to the streets of London”. We can’t wait.
Beck – Ride Lonesome
Release date: 18 September
Following his 2015 Grammy Album of the Year ‘Morning Phase’, Beck’s output has been a smidge disappointing. 2017’s 'Colors' was an underwhelming 80s-indebted effort, while 2019’s 'Hyperspace' worked as a synth-pop collaboration experiment but lacked the complexity of his past efforts. Here’s hoping this year fares better... We’ve already had his Valentine’s Day-themed compilation album ‘Everybody’s Gotta Learn Sometime’ - which was delightful – and his 15th studio album ‘Ride Lonesome’ is about to drop. Already released singles – the country-coded ‘Ride Lonesome’ and the gentle ‘Disappearing Act’ - have a ‘Sea Change’ / ‘Morning Phase’ melancholia to them. Add the fact that Nigel Godrich is back on mixing duties, and this could be a return to form.
Tove Lo – Estrus
Release date: 18 September
Swedish pop star Tove Lo has explained that the title of her sixth album refers to an animal in heat. “It’s primal, contradicting emotional chaos. It’s my mind and my body wanting different things, wanting everything,” the ‘Talking Body’ singer said, adding: “There’s no good advice on this album... just a lot of feelings, no solutions.” That last part happens to be the title of the opening track of ‘Estrus’, which is followed by lead single ‘I’m Your Girl Right?’ - a propulsive dance track that will hopefully be playing on heavy rotation in clubs around the world. We’re looking forward to the rest, as Tove Lo’s capacity to deliver euphoric sultry banger after euphoric sultry banger continues to impress. And be bafflingly underrated.
Agnes Obel - The Meaning Of Flowers
Release date: 18 September
A lot of albums coming out on the 18th... But one that has us giddy with excitement is Agnes Obel’s fifth album ‘The Meaning Of Flowers’ - her first since 2020. We’ve been fans of the Danish singer-songwriter here at Euronews Culture for a while now - even including her 2016 album ‘Citizen Of Glass’ in our list of the Best European Albums of the 21st Century. Her immersive chamber-pop never fails to captivate, and judging by her textured new single ‘Laymelli’, we’re in for an atmospheric treat with her latest – one reportedly inspired by themes of maternity and metamorphosis, as well as the ideas of philosophers Hannah Arendt and Emanuele Coccia. Listen to ‘Laymelli’ and try telling us you’re not already entranced.
M83 – I Wrote You A Letter
Release date: 25 September
Is this the year French outfit M83 remind the electro scene they’ve still got it? Here’s hoping... Anthony Gonzalez’s 10th studio album follows a string of disappointing releases, including the aptly named 'Junk' (2016), the very average 'DSVII' (2019), and slightly course-correcting but hardly exhilarating ‘Fantasy’ (2023). In fact, it’s no stretch to say that M83 haven’t had a fully energising release since 2011’s ‘Hurry Up, We’re Dreaming’, and many fans still miss the glory days of the early 2000s with the back-to-back triumphs of ‘Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts’ and ‘Before The Dawn Heals Us’. Fingers crossed that the titular letter brings good news.
Soft Cell – Danceteria
Release date: 25 September
Legendary British synth-pop duo Soft Cell are about to release their swansong, following the death of co-founder Dave Ball last year. The band’s sixth and final studio album, ‘Danceteria’, was completed before Ball’s death and will hopefully serve as a fitting tribute. “There can be no more recordings of Soft Cell without Dave, it would not be possible,” said singer Marc Almond. “The sad reality is that Dave Ball was half of Soft Cell, and live work aside, I can't write Soft Cell songs without him." Considering the title and the already released singles, it’s fair to say that this album will channel the spirit of the 80s New York club scene – much like Madonna’s latest record.
The Avalanches – No Bad Memories
Release date: 16 October
Fans of plunderphonic geniuses The Avalanches had to wait 16 long years after the seminal ‘Since I Left You’ for a decent follow-up album. 'Wildflower' (2016) was a playful and welcome return, but didn’t strike the same winning chord; and you’d be forgiven for not knowing a third album followed, as 2020’s slightly underrated ‘We Will Always Love You’ didn’t make too much of a splash. Billed as “an ambivalent ode to the nostalgic pull of commercial jingles, proprietary start-up sounds, and long-forgotten audio logos,” the Australian band’s fourth album will hopefully right that wrong. It features the likes of Karen O, Jamie xx, Jessy Lanza and Nikki Nair, and spans a whopping 31 tracks. So they’re not messing about.
Eels – Cookie Happened
Release date: 16 October
For more than a decade, like clockwork, we get a new Eels album every two years. And like some of previously mentioned artists on this list, Mark Oliver “E” Everett needs a proper comeback this year, as he hasn’t had the greatest of runs of late. ‘The Deconstruction’ (2018) fell short compared to previous discography standouts; ‘Earth To Dora’ (2020) was too far familiar for comfort; ‘Extreme Witchcraft’ (2022) was a dreary affair; and ‘Eels Time!’ (2024) barely registered. We’re rooting for E, as he’s given us some of the greatest storytelling gems over the years, and ‘Cookie Happened’ could very well be a return to past form. Already on the plus side: the Sesame Street character Cookie Monster is an influence on the album. That, and the cover’s all kinds of fun.
Rachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too Soon
Release date: 16 October
English singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri follows her critically acclaimed alt-indie pop debut album ‘What A Devastating Turn Of Events’ (2024) with ‘I Think I Spoke Too Soon’. Her sophomore effort features collaborators like Mary Weitz and Lucy Dacus, and the first cut ‘One Song Away From Crying’ suggests she’s moving away from the guitars and embracing synths a bit more. The song explores that all-too-familiar moment on the dancefloor when you’ve “never looked better” but “never felt worse”. It sounds fantastic so far, and it’s worth noting that Chinouriri is currently touring Europe, with September dates in Dublin, London, Brussels, Paris and Berlin. If you can get your hands on a ticket, consider yourself very lucky indeed.
Fontaines D.C. – Dopamine Chamber
Release date: 16 October
Talk about a busy day in October for new releases... and this one is hands down our most anticipated of the lot. Every single Fontaines D.C. album release has marked leaps and bounds in terms of songwriting and sound evolution. They’ve been going from strength to strength ever since their 2019 debut ‘Dogrel’ and 2024’s ‘Romance’ felt like a consecration. There’s no suggestion that the Irish indie heroes won’t continue their winning streak with fifth LP, ‘Dopamine Chamber’, which should once again cement their status as the most consistently exciting band around. They’ve already premiered new tracks ‘Marianne’ and ‘Six Shot Morning’ live. Spoiler: they’re both brilliant, sounding Depeche Mode-ish and very synth noir. Let’s hope the rest of the album tracklist will stimulate the reward system in the same way.
Editors – Surface, Echo & Sound
Release date: 30 October
Sounding similar to Foo Fighters’ ‘Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace’, the title of Editors’ eighth studio album could signal a return to a rawer and rockier sound. Following the disappointing new wave / indietronica ‘EBM’ in 2022, the band apparently wanted to come back to a more natural approach with regards to songwriting and recording, harking back to their early days. Music to our ears, and fans will doubtlessly be delighted if ‘Surface, Echo & Sound’ recalls the sound of their pretty much flawless original album run, with ‘The Back Room’, ‘An End Has A Start’ and ‘In This Light And On This Evening’ having made them one of the rare British bands to escape the dreaded Indie Landfill era of the 2000s.
Queens of the Stone Age – Perfecth
Release date: 30 October
"Nothing in this world is perfect, but everything seems to be 'perfecth'," according to Queens of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme. "And that title is funny when you're in a group, but it ain't so funny when you're alone." Prefaced by the songs ‘Easy Street’ and ‘Insignificant Other’, QOTSA’s ninth studio album promises to be a nine-track rock opus dealing with “family, friends, and others both significant and insignificant”. So far, it sounds like a departure from the band’s heavier sound, with the acoustic ballad ‘Easy Street’ still maintaining some of their trademark humour but showcasing a much gentler side, while ‘Insignificant Other’ features a sleazy groove but couldn’t be more different from the sledgehammer blows of past glories found on ‘Songs For The Deaf’ and ‘...Like Clockwork’.
La Roux - Old Flames
Release date: 6 November
We haven’t had a new release from the British synth-pop act formed by singer Elly Jackson since 2020. That third album, ‘Supervision’, was a frustrating follow-up to her charting debut ‘La Roux’ (2009) and ‘Trouble In Paradise’ (2014). The ‘In For The Kill’ and ‘Bulletproof’ singer will hopefully wow fans once again, with a new album in which she addresses the collapse of a relationship and tackles themes of forbidden love and the loneliness that comes from addiction. The first album teaser, the R&B-tinged earworm ‘Cabin Fever’, is excellent and there’s every chance La Roux’s upcoming LP will be the late-year pop surprise we’ve been waiting for.
Los Bitchos – Los Bitchos & Friends Vol. 1
Release date: 13 November
Pan-continental instrumental group Los Bitchos have already given us two stellar albums (‘Let The Festivities Begin’ and ‘Talkie Talkie’), which have led them to open for various acts like Belle & Sebastian, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, Parquet Courts and Wet Leg. Now, the trio consisting of guitarist Serra Petale, bassist Josefine Jonsson, and drummer Nic Crawshaw, will continue their rave-reviewed blend of Cumbia, rock-pop and Latin American rhythms in their third long-form project. But there's news: they're welcoming vocal collaborators. Gasp! (Although the title was a bit of a giveaway.) For a band who’ve never seen vocals as a necessity, this new direction could add a new dimension to their work, with King Gizzard’s Ambrose Kenny-Smith, Black Pumas’ Adrian Quesada and Kit Sebastian all lending their voices. November seems like a long way away considering how promising this sounds...
Labi Siffre – Unfinished Business
Release date: TBD
As we noted in our selection of the Most Underrated Albums, there’s been renewed interest in Labi Siffre’s music, chiefly due to some of his songs appearing in films like The Holdovers and Sentimental Value. With the British poet and folk musician’s 1972 album ‘Crying Laughing Loving Lying’ gradually becoming recognised as the masterpiece it is, 2026 brought some surprising news: the 80-year-old artist is returning with a new album appropriately titled ‘Unfinished Business’. It will be his first LP in 28 years and we’ve already had a taster with the gorgeous piano ballad ‘Far Away’. This is one comeback you won’t want to miss, and we’re waiting (somewhat impatiently) for a release date. In the meantime, we’ll be listening to ‘Crying Laughing Loving Lying’ all over again, as well as his last record to date, the 1998 spoken-word poetry collection ‘Monument’, which is also well worth your time.
There we have it. Which albums are you most looking forward to? For up-to-date music news and reviews, head to Euronews Culture's Music section, and be sure to check out our picks for the Best Albums of 2026... So Far.

Germany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

22:15:48 KST

Germany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy
Two incidents that disrupted power distribution systems in Germany are being investigated for sabotage, authorities said Wednesday, while one of them was also being examined for possible terrorism links. Meanwhile Russia said it was summoning Germany's charge d'affaires after Berlin blamed Moscow for last month's attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.
German authorities on Wednesday were investigating two attacks on electricity substations in different parts of the country, the latest suspected sabotage targeting critical infrastructure.
Police launched a terrorism probe over the first incident, which saw improvised explosives fired early Tuesday at a site in eastern Brandenburg state, damaging power cables.
In the second sabotage attack, unknown perpetrators allegedly caused a deliberate short-circuit by targeting overhead power lines at a substation in Bergheim in North Rhine-Westphalia state.
North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said officials were probing whether the attack was directed by a "foreign state" or left-wing extremism.
Neither attack caused widespread power outages, although operations at nearby coal-fired power stations were affected.
Germany has faced repeated attacks on electricity infrastructure, with far-left militants claiming responsibility in some cases.
Berlin, a key supporter of Ukraine in its fight against Russia, is also on alert for Moscow-backed sabotage plots.
"More sabotage, more hybrid attacks – interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference.
"And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country."
The attacks came the same day that Germany formally blamed Russia for an attempted "hybrid attack" involving an explosive-laden drone at a strategic airport in Leipzig last month and announced diplomatic counter-measures.
Read moreGermany blames Russia for Leipzig airport drone attack, orders Russian consulate closed
Russia summons German envoy over 'anti-Russian actions'
Russia on Wednesday said it was summoning Germany's charge d'affaires to protest what it called "anti-Russian actions", after Berlin announced sanctions on Moscow over an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport.
Germany announced counter-measures on Tuesday, saying it would shut Russia's consolate in the western German city of Bonn and cancel a contract for a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
Russia has described Germany's allegations as unsubstantiated and "absurd".
"On September 2, Germany's charge d'affaires in Moscow... was summoned to the Russian foreign ministry amid yesterday's anti-Russian actions and statements by the German authorities," said Russia's foreign ministry.
Meanwhile German authorities have identified two suspects in connection with an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport but will unlikely be able to detain them, German daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Wednesday.
The newspaper, which collaborated on the report with broadcasters Norddeutscher Rundfunk (NDR) and Westdeutscher Rundfunk Köln (WDR), said that investigations into the two men, one a Russian-born Latvian national and the other a Russian national from Belarus, underpinned allegations by the German government that Russia was behind the incident.
Latest infrastructure attack
In the Bergheim incident, police were called to the substation late Tuesday. Perpetrators are suspected of causing a short-circuit in overhead power lines by placing "conductive material" on them, according to officials.
Energy company RWE said five power-generating units at two of its coal-fired plants in the region were knocked out by the disruption at the substation, although there was no widespread disruption for customers.
Three of the units were expected to go back online later Wednesday while the two others should be restarted at the weekend.
The earlier attack in Brandenburg saw improvised explosives – which resembled large fireworks – fired at a substation in Preilack, causing damage to power cables and a brief supply disruption.
The substation distributes power from the nearby Jaenschwalde plant.
Police announced Wednesday they had launched a terror probe into that incident. They are also investigating the attack on suspicion of disrupting public services and destroying essential equipment, according to a statement.
Reul said authorities were trying to figure out if there was a link between the two attacks, adding: "We are in close contact with our colleagues in Brandenburg."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

Can the US deport you for what you say? A federal judge says no
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

A federal judge in California has ruled that immigration provisions used by the US administration to target non-citizens over political speech are unconstitutional, delivering one of the strongest legal challenges yet to its use of immigration law against pro-Palestinian activists.
US District Judge Noel Wise ruled on August 28 that the government's application of the provisions to revoke visas and pursue deportations over protected speech violated the First and Fifth Amendments.
The case emerged from a fear already taking hold on university campuses: that an international student's words could put their legal status at risk.
The Stanford Daily, Stanford University's student newspaper, and an anonymous F-1 visa holder identified as Jane Doe challenged the policy, arguing that it pushed international students to delete posts, avoid political activity, and think twice before reporting on Gaza.
Wise's 90-page decision sided with the plaintiffs on six of eight claims. It also challenged the breadth of the government's claimed authority, finding that its application of the provisions to constitutionally protected speech amounted to viewpoint- and content-based restrictions.
Too many brave and principled pro-Palestinian voices have become collateral damage due to Washington’s attempts to suppress criticism of the genocidal Israeli state, according to human rights lawyer and writer Maria Kari.
"I cannot think of anything more profoundly un-American than silencing students and activists for voicing opposition to the US government funding genocide, war crimes and the murder of thousands of babies and for that reason Judge Wise's ruling is a very welcome and significant victory," Kari tells TRT World.
Kari has represented several people targeted by the administration's immigration crackdown, including Momodou Taal, Yaakub Ira Vijandre and Mahmoud Khalil.
“...Constitutional rights are inalienable and belong to the people and that the free speech rights of noncitizens are not any less than citizens," she adds.
An undefined line
At the centre of the dispute are the provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, which US administration invoked to revoke visas and pursue the removal of non-citizens whose presence and activities were deemed to have potentially serious foreign policy consequences for the United States.
Under the administration's interpretation, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had broad discretion to determine when a non-citizen's presence threatened a compelling US foreign policy interest.
The judge rejected that logic. The government cannot punish protected speech simply because it objects to the viewpoint behind it, she wrote.
Rubio's own arguments showed just how far the provision could reach.
He suggested that protests over something as mundane as paper straws could theoretically fall under the same authority, even as his department was using it against people whose speech concerned Gaza.
"If you're complaining about paper straws, then we're obviously not going to yank a visa over that," he said.
The ruling, which cites the founding fathers of the US, Benjamin Franklin and James Madison at length, therefore goes beyond the fate of the students named in the lawsuit, putting a constitutional limit on a strategy Washington has increasingly used against non-citizens whose political speech it considers objectionable.
However, when it comes to the practical, beneficial impact this ruling can have, Kari believes the answer is, unfortunately, not much.
"This ruling is declaratory and not injunctive which means it does not stop the Secretary of State from future visa revocations nor does it free those in ICE prison currently facing detention and deportation.”
From Columbia to Stanford
By the time the Stanford Daily case reached the courts, the policy's consequences were already evident on university campuses.
In March 2025, Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia University graduate and legal permanent resident, was detained by ICE for his role in pro-Palestinian campus organising.
Weeks later, federal agents detained Rumeysa Ozturk, a doctoral student at Tufts University, after she co-wrote an op-ed criticising her university's response to the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Their cases were followed by those of Cornell University student Momodou Taal and Columbia student Mohsen Mahdawi, turning a series of individual immigration actions into a wider fight over whether political activism could become grounds for removal.
In a January 2025 executive order, the US administration directed federal agencies to identify and remove non-citizen students and faculty whose political activity was deemed contrary to US foreign policy.
Now, with Wise's ruling on the books, the administration faces a choice. According to Kari, the US government will most certainly appeal, and has sixty days to do so.
"When something is on appeal it means that other judges in other jurisdictions are more likely to say, 'that case is on appeal, I don't have to rely on it'.”
But these plaintiffs have an advantage on appeal, because the court that will hear it, the Ninth Circuit, has already ruled that free speech protections apply to noncitizens too, she adds.
Colliding with constitutional limits
The Stanford Daily's lawsuit took that policy beyond individual activists and into the newsroom itself.
The newspaper argued that international students were deleting pro-Palestinian posts, avoiding political activity and steering away from stories critical of Israel because they feared what speaking out could mean for their immigration status.
The result was a form of censorship that did not require the government to silence every student directly, as the possibility of deportation was enough to make some students think twice.
"I think Judge Wise's decision does a brilliant job of laying out the pattern we've seen unfold since March 2025 when the foreign policy grounds provision was invoked after three decades of non-use with Mahmoud Khalil's request," Kari says.
"Since then… campuses are quiet, protests for Palestine have died down and people - citizens and noncitizens alike - are scared.”
Wise's decision follows a similar ruling last year in Massachusetts in AAUP v. Rubio. In September 2025, US District Judge William Young found that the US administration's policy of arresting, detaining and seeking to deport non-citizen students and faculty for pro-Palestinian advocacy violated the First Amendment. A remedial order followed in January 2026.
Together, the cases reinforce a principle the Supreme Court recognised decades ago: constitutional free-speech protections do not disappear at the border or depend on US citizenship.
The ruling does not undo what Mahmoud Khalil, Rumeysa Ozturk, Momodou Taal, Mohsen Mahdawi and others went through, and the administration is expected to appeal.
Kari says what is most alarming now is how the provision is being weaponised against people targeted purely for their family ties, regardless of anything they've said or done.
"All the cases discussed in the Stanford Daily case involved people who were targeted by the government for their political speech."
"Now, ICE is going after people not because of something they said or did but who they're related to. This is the new and terrifying frontier that's opened up," Kari says.
"I predict the legality of using the foreign policy grounds provision in this way will be tested in the courts next," she adds.

Directorate of Defence Safety and Support (DDSS)
Our vision for safety in Defence is to establish a world-leading safety culture, eliminate fatalities, and enhance our capability through learning and safe practices.
Documents
Details
Please note the Defence Safety Function was formally referred to as ‘Health, Safety and Environmental Protection (HS&EP)’. Some documents may still refer to HS&EP as they are being updated.
The Ministry of Defence is acutely aware of the duty of care it owes to its people, the public and the environment and therefore takes its safety obligations extremely seriously.
The Safety Function Owner is the Director General People, who has delegated authority to lead the Function to the Director Defence Safety and Support.

President of French far-right party Rassemblement National Jordan Bardella reacts as he speaks to the press during a visit to the agricultural fair in Châlons-en-Champagne on August 29, 2026. | Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — French far-right leader Jordan Bardella is taking on more international responsibilities for his party, the National Rally, as part of a push to reassure international markets worried about the cost of Marine Le Pen’s populist platform.
An aide to Bardella told reporters that the National Rally president’s Friday speech at the Reform UK party congress in Birmingham and visit to the Ambrosetti Forum in Italy on Saturday are the beginning of a concerted campaign to strategically deploy the 30-year-old.
Bardella is also slated to give 10 interviews to international media outlets in the coming days.
Advertisement
“Bardella has always been attached to the international credibility of the National Rally,” said the aide, who was granted anonymity to share details of Bardella’s plans. “He will give great attention to the international press during the campaign.”
Since shooting up the National Rally’s ranks in his twenties, Bardella has brought a polished professionalism to a party that long struggled to run a tight ship. He led the party to impressive victories in the 2019 and 2024 European elections and is now the head of the Patriots group in the European Parliament. The party is now more popular than ever, and Le Pen is the front-runner to win next year’s presidential election.
But when it looked like an embezzlement conviction would doom Le Pen’s chances at running for the presidency, Bardella, as the National Rally’s presumptive candidate, tried to woo more fiscally conservative voters — including France’s business elite — by flirting with a more market-friendly platform than his mentor.
But Bardella has been adjusting to a secondary role since an appeals court cleared a path for Le Pen to run as the party’s presidential nominee — and she has made clear that fiscal discipline won’t come at the expense of the promises she has made to her core voters. That includes her pledge to lower the retirement age for most workers to 62 at a cost of €9 billion per year.
Bardella is now eyeing a role similar to the one Giorgia Meloni held before she became Italian prime minister in 2022.
Bardella “watched with great interest the campaign of Giorgia Meloni, who flooded the international press to reassure institutions and the financial markets,” the aide said.
Advertisement
The carving up of roles between Bardella and Le Pen also makes sense given Le Pen’s spotty track record of international trips — notably her reported failed attempt to meet U.S. President Donald Trump — and the difficulties in shedding the toxic baggage linked to her name. Her father, party founder Jean-Marie, was notorious for downplaying the Holocaust and was convicted of hate speech multiple times.

Angola takes delivery of six Swiss-made HT-100 drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:05:18 UTC
22:05:18 KST

- ANAVIA completed customer acceptance of six HT-100 Naval unmanned helicopters for the Angolan Navy, to be deployed two per ship across three new BR71 MK II corvettes.
- The HT-100 Naval features an autonomous radar-guided deck landing system and a six-hour flight endurance, part of a roughly $1.1 billion Angolan naval modernization program.
Swiss manufacturer ANAVIA completed on-site customer acceptance of six HT-100 Naval unmanned helicopters purchased by the Angolan Navy, the company said, following individual flight tests and sign-offs for each aircraft delivered.
The acceptance was conducted jointly with ADSB, a partner involved in the delivery. ANAVIA said each of the six aircraft underwent its own flight test and verification process rather than a single blanket acceptance for the batch, with the customer verifying each system firsthand.
“This milestone shows our ability to deliver a complete system, closely aligned with our customer’s operational requirements,” said Ishan Sahgal, founder and co-CEO of ANAVIA.
The delivered package includes electro-optical and infrared sensors, maritime control stations, and the helicopters themselves, all tested together on site as an integrated system rather than as separate components. The six aircraft will be split two per ship across three new BR71 MK II-class corvettes the Angolan Navy is bringing into service, extending each vessel’s reconnaissance reach.
The HT-100 Naval is a maritime variant of ANAVIA’s HT-100 unmanned helicopter, built around a Flettner intermeshing rotor system, two counter-rotating main rotors that eliminate the need for a tail rotor. ANAVIA says that design sends roughly 30 percent more of the aircraft’s power into useful lift rather than countering torque, resulting in longer endurance and higher payload capacity compared with a conventional single-rotor design. The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 120 kilograms (265 pounds), a payload capacity of 60 kilograms (132 pounds), and a flight endurance of six hours, powered by a 15-kilowatt turbine engine that burns roughly 9 liters (2.4 gallons) of Jet A-1 fuel per hour. The HT-100 has a maximum mission range of 600 kilometers (373 miles).
For shipboard use, the Naval variant adds a fully autonomous, radar-guided deck landing system that measures the aircraft’s position, velocity and attitude relative to the moving vessel independent of GPS, allowing it to land without a human operator steering the approach, even in conditions up to Sea State 3. The airframe uses a corrosion-resistant carbon composite structure with sealed electronics rated for continuous saltwater exposure, along with emergency equipment including a harpoon deck-securing system, flotation gear and an emergency locator transmitter.
The three BR71 MK II-class corvettes form part of a roughly €1 billion ($1.16 billion) naval modernization program for Angola. The first of the three vessels, the NRA Ekuikui II, was launched in Cherbourg, France, on March 4, 2026. ANAVIA is a Swiss company headquartered in Bilten, with additional operations in nearby Näfels; the UAE-based EDGE Group acquired a 52 percent majority stake in the company in late 2023.

Fact check: How inaccurate and conflicting claims may have affected Iceland's EU referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:02:52 UTC
22:02:52 KST

The Icelandic EU referendum raised a number of important issues for voters, but also a series of unclear claims.
Uncertainty over fishing quotas may have made many Icelandic voters reluctant to embark on an EU membership pathway.
The country voted no on 29 August on resuming negotiations with Brussels by 52.8%, with the talks between the two on hold since 2013.
The campaign was fierce and, as with many crucial public votes in recent years, was also marked by inaccurate claims circulating online and among media channels.
One of them involved the referendum's main sticking point: fisheries.
A few media outlets reported on talks between Iceland's foreign affairs minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten about a special exemption from the EU's Common Fisheries Policy.
They said that Gunnarsdóttir claimed that such exemptions were discussed and that the Dutch government strongly denied her version of events.
However, Gunnarsdóttir later rejected those claims, prompting the press to admit the story had been largely misreported.
Yet it touched a sensitive nerve: control over fishing grounds is fiercely guarded in Iceland, so much so that it led to a series of confrontations between Iceland and the UK in the 1950s and the 1970s — known as the Cod Wars.
Joining the EU would likely mean giving up part of its quota, under the Common Fisheries Policy, although there is no consensus on how much exactly Iceland would have to give up.
Some experts argue the quota would be minimal, mainly involving pelagic fish species (i.e. herrings, sardines, mackerel) that migrate across the sea and so are not stationed permanently in Icelandic waters.
However, failing to address this sensitive issue early on may have dulled voters' enthusiasm for EU membership, according to international relations expert Arno Minasian.
"Iceland didn't get to negotiate fisheries and agriculture in 2009, either," he told Euronews' fact-checking team, The Cube. "The EU and Iceland never actually got to those chapters, which is concerning, because those are the really big, important chapters for Iceland."
Some 4% of Iceland's workforce is employed in fisheries, and the sector accounts for around 8% of its GDP. "So fisheries have a lot of economic and political weight," Minasian added.
"If Iceland and the EU cannot negotiate this in the first place, it's quite unrealistic that Icelanders would agree on imposing these quotas through the Common Fisheries Policy," he said.
All of the obligations, none of the benefits?
Another misleading claim was about Iceland's EU-related rights as a non-EU member.
Some, such as former Prime Minister Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson, said that, since Iceland is already part of the European Economic Area, it already enjoys all the benefits of EU membership.
Gunnlaugsson, who is now leader of the Centre Party, added that joining the EU would mean taking on just downsides and obligations, rather than any extra benefits.
While it is true that, as a member of the European Economic Area, Reykjavík is already playing by much of the EU's economic playbook, by not being a member of the EU itself, it has no seat at the table when the rules are defined.
Iceland does not have votes in the European Parliament, nor a role in the European Commission. It also misses out on certain EU subsidies and funds, to name just a few.
When it comes to the cost of accessing the EU, the opposing camps cited drastically different numbers.
The "No" front set the figure as high as €1 billion a year, while prominent pro-EU figures said it would be just over €50 million.
The latter seems much closer to the truth, according to a study by the independent think tank Evropustraumar, which claimed Iceland's net EU membership cost would be around €60 million a year.

Thousands protest in Ceuta as Spain rallies over enclave’s migrant crisis
- Thousands protested in Ceuta against Spain's handling of the July migrant surge, demanding better border defence and government accountability.
- Over 10,000 migrants remain stranded in Ceuta, causing tension and near-daily protests calling for their return or redistribution.
- Political deadlock persists between Spain's government and opposition, with increased but insufficient resources to manage the crisis effectively.
AI generated
CEUTA, Spain – Residents of Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta took to the streets on Sept 2 to protest the handling by Madrid of a migration crisis caused by a deadly border surge in July when at least 72,000 people crossed from Morocco.
Thousands of people marched through the streets of the city of about 80,000 residents in a protest that coincided with the annual Ceuta Day. Waving Spanish flags and blowing whistles, they chanted: “Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended.”
One placard read, “SOS. Europe, save us from our traitor government”, while some demanded that the authorities should “expel the invaders”. Others called for Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to resign as demonstrations also took place in other cities across Spain, including Madrid, Barcelona and Bilbao.
Nearly five weeks after the surge, over 10,000 migrants, including unaccompanied minors, remain stranded in makeshift camps or scattered across streets and beaches in the enclave, according to Ceuta’s authorities.
Their presence has triggered near-daily protests by locals against the Spanish government’s management of the crisis, with demonstrators calling for the migrants to be sent back to their countries of origin or redistributed across Spain.
“The response has been inadequate, late and, to top it all, has involved a complete dereliction of duty on the part of the government. We cannot be second-class citizens, and our border must not be sidelined,” said David Hernandez, a 45-year-old teacher.
Recent protests featured sporadic attacks against a makeshift migrant camp at El Trampolin beach and arrests of Moroccan citizens who lobbed stones and bottles at army patrols.
Political deadlock hampers solution
The Sept 2 Spain-wide protests were called by the FEMP federation of municipalities, dominated by the main opposition conservative People’s Party (PP).
Spain’s leftist government distanced itself from the initiative, accusing the right of exploiting the crisis for political benefit.
“This is not about defending Ceuta and the Ceutans, it is about attacking the government,” Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres told radio station RNE.
A manifesto by citizens’ initiative “Por Ceuta” (For Ceuta), which calls for respect for residents’ and migrants’ human rights, the orderly return of those without the right to remain and more security reinforcements, has garnered nearly 65,000 signatures. The initiative says it has no political affiliation.
Left-wing collectives and unions organised counter-gatherings in several cities, including Madrid, to condemn “racist and Islamophobic persecutions and attacks” against migrants in Ceuta since the rush.
Negotiations between local and central government on how to handle the crisis are deadlocked, with the PP, which governs most regions, some in coalition with the far-right Vox, calling for all those remaining, including minors, to be deported.
The government has increased capacity at temporary accommodation centres to more than 3,400 places from about 500, and deployed over 1,600 police.
But local groups and political leaders say this still falls far short of what is needed to keep citizens and migrants safe.
“The central government needs to provide funds and the local government needs to provide space... that’s the battle we’re in,” said Juan Miguel Morales, director of Sur Acoge charity. “The response has lacked agility: that much is clear.” REUTERS

Heavy ChatGPT use linked to intellectual laziness and social isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

Artificial intelligence has woven its way into everyday life, prompting questions about how reliance on generative tools affects the human mind. A recent small study published in Applied Cognitive Psychology suggests that leaning heavily on ChatGPT can reduce critical thinking, diminish memory, and lead to social isolation. However, users who engage with the software intentionally can also harness it to boost their creativity and reasoning skills.
Over the last few years, tools that generate human-like text have become wildly popular. ChatGPT reached one million users within a week of its launch and currently boasts over 180 million active users. People use the program for everything from writing emails to solving programming problems.
As these programs become a regular part of daily workflows, researchers are trying to understand the psychological and cognitive costs. Zeineb Farhat, a researcher at ISC Paris, initiated the research to investigate what happens when habitual use turns into dependence. Much of the early research on generative software has focused on its benefits in education and the workplace.
Farhat wanted to document the potential downsides of outsourcing mental effort and emotional needs to a machine. The research draws on established ideas in psychology regarding how people manage mental effort and motivation. One concept is cognitive offloading, which happens when individuals use external tools, like calculators or search engines, to reduce the amount of information they need to process or remember.
Another core idea involves the psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and social connection. When people feel capable and in control of their actions, they are generally more motivated. Farhat set out to see how constant access to an intelligent digital assistant might alter these processes.
The researcher wanted to know if offloading cognitive tasks to an algorithm would compromise a user’s ability to think independently. To explore these dynamics, Farhat conducted a small study involving 45 young adults in France. The participants, aged 18 to 25, were all regular users who interacted with ChatGPT daily.
The researcher conducted semi-structured interviews with each participant, either face-to-face or via video call. These interviews lasted between 45 and 60 minutes. The conversations covered how the participants used the software, how it affected their study or work habits, and how it made them feel.
Farhat then analyzed the interview transcripts to identify recurring themes in the users’ experiences. The analysis revealed that heavy reliance on the software often discouraged independent thought. Participants reported that having instant answers at their fingertips made them less likely to analyze problems deeply or evaluate sources.
Some described experiencing intellectual laziness, noting that their attention spans felt shorter. Users also reported trouble retaining information. They were externalizing their memory by relying on the chatbot to retrieve facts rather than practicing active recall.
“I used to take notes and actively review materials, but now I just ask ChatGPT whenever I need something,” one student noted in the study. “The problem is, I don’t retain much. I feel like my memory has become weaker because I rely on ChatGPT instead of trying to recall things on my own.”
Psychologically, the interviews indicated that heavy use eroded the participants’ sense of autonomy and self-trust. Many users started second-guessing their own judgment. They began seeking the software’s validation for simple decisions, like choosing the right words for a basic email.
The ease of getting quick answers also lowered their intrinsic motivation to learn new things. Without the struggle normally required to master a topic, the learning process felt less rewarding. Some participants even reported anxiety and a sense of paralysis when the software was offline for maintenance.
One participant recalled a time when the system went down, bringing their workflow to a complete halt. “I needed it for a work project, and I felt completely paralyzed without it,” the user shared. “It’s like my safety net is gone.”
The study also uncovered shifts in social behavior. Participants frequently chose to interact with the software instead of discussing ideas with peers or teachers. This preference sometimes led to feelings of social isolation, as users lost the habit of engaging in deep conversations with other people.
A few participants began to treat the text generator as a companion, projecting human traits onto it. “ChatGPT has become my friend; it knows everything about me,” one participant stated. “It’s always there, always ready to listen, and it feels like it understands me better than most people do.”
While this offered temporary comfort, it substituted genuine human connection with a machine response. Relying on an algorithm for emotional support risks blurring the line between technological mediation and true social interaction. Over time, this dynamic can weaken interpersonal skills and empathy.
Despite these negative reports, the study identified a pattern of constructive use. Some users treated the software as a collaborative tool rather than a replacement for their own brains. By allowing the program to handle tedious tasks like structuring data or summarizing dense text, these individuals freed up mental energy for complex reasoning.
They used the tool to brainstorm or overcome writer’s block. Instead of copying what the program generated, they used the output as a starting point to think differently. When used reflectively, the software actually increased users’ confidence and reduced their anxiety about challenging tasks.
Because the research relies on qualitative interviews with a small group of young adults in France, the findings reflect a specific demographic and cannot be broadly generalized. People from older generations or different cultural backgrounds might interact with the software differently. The study also captures user experiences at a single point in time.
It remains unknown whether these cognitive and social habits change over years of use. Future research will need to track larger and more diverse groups over longer periods to see if these patterns persist. Additional studies could also explore how to best train people to use these tools adaptively rather than dependently.
The study, “When AI Thinks for Us: Unveiling the Cognitive and Social Toll of ChatGPT Over-Reliance,” was authored by Zeineb Farhat.

How horse milk ‘kymyz’ became a drink still in demand thousands of years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

Fermented horse milk, known as kymyz, is a traditional Central Asian drink with thousands of years of history. In Kazakhstan, it remains an important part of nomadic heritage, cuisine and hospitality.
Kymyz is a traditional drink made from mare's milk and drunk in many countries across Central Asia. Peoples ranging from northern Han Chinese to Kazakhs, Bashkirs, Kalmyks, Kyrgyz, Mongols and Yakuts say their ancestors have been drinking kymyz since time immemorial.
The earliest Western text that mentions it is by Herodotus, who, in his 5th-century BC Histories, describes the Scythians’ processing of mare's milk.
Kazakhstan holds a special place in kymyz production. In the Copper Age necropolis of the Botai culture, located in modern-day Kazakhstan, archaeologists found evidence of the world’s earliest horse domestication. They also found traces of horse milk on pottery.
Kymyz also provided energy to nomadic warriors during wartime. Rich in vitamins and nutrients, kymyz is attracting scientific interest as researchers explore its potential benefits.
Gaukhar Konuspayeva, a professor of food biotechnology, has spent the past 26 years studying camel and horse milk. She says there is still much more to learn about the potential of kymyz.
“According to our research, mare’s milk is very rich in vitamins A, B1, B2, B5 and B6. But what makes kymyz unique is its fatty acid composition and the presence of prebiotic bacteria,” she added.
Kymyz was not forgotten during the Soviet era, when many of the peoples with a tradition of drinking it lived within the Soviet Union. Soviet state farms in the region kept hundreds of thousands of mares for their milk and dairy products, including kymyz.
Inside the tradition of kymyz making
There are different types of kymyz. Its taste depends not only on the region where the horse grazes and the grass it eats, but also on how the drink is prepared.
Every farmer has their own recipe, but the freshest mare’s milk, known as saumal, is considered the most valuable. You won’t find it in supermarkets, as it stays fresh for only a few hours. To try it, you usually have to go to the countryside.
In the village of Zhanaarka in the Ulytau Region, Aiman Kutzhanova showed us how she milks her mares. She works as a deputy principal at a local school and also raises horses with her husband.
There is a traditional way of milking a mare. First, the foal is allowed to feed, and only then is the milk collected.
Unlike cows, mares need to be milked every one to two hours, and they can produce only about a litre of milk a day.
“Horses are sacred animals. They choose the person who milks them. For example, my mares won’t let anyone else milk them. Even if I come wearing different clothes, they won’t let me milk them,” says Aiman Kutzhanova.
After milking, the milk should either be drunk fresh (saumal) or used to make kymyz. To prepare it, the milk is stirred in deep wooden vessels called ‘kubi’. The inside of the vessel is traditionally coated with butter before the milk is added.
In the past, leather sacks filled with mare’s milk were hung from the top of the yurt or attached to a saddle, allowing the milk to be shaken throughout the day.
Today, there are also many different varieties of kymyz, including versions made with honey, smoked flavours, herbs and even horse meat.
The celebration of mare milking
For centuries, Kazakhs lived as nomads, moving between winter and summer pastures with their herds. The start of the mare-milking season coincided with the move to the summer pastures, where families would set up their yurts(portable homes used by nomadic families).
The first milking of the season marked the beginning of a new season and was celebrated as a big event. The tradition is known as ‘Kymyz Muryndyk’, which refers to the first kymyz of the season.
This tradition is still alive today. Festivals dedicated to Kymyz Muryndyk are held in two regions of Kazakhstan: Ulytau and Almaty, often far from the cities and close to the steppe.
The celebrations bring together local families, farmers and visitors.
The BaiKymyz festival
Every year, Astana also hosts the BaiKymyz Festival, where producers compete to find the best kymyz. The festival brings together farmers and kymyz producers from across the country.
The festival was created by Zhumazhan Kaltayev, who drew inspiration from Germany’s Oktoberfest and adapted the idea to Kazakhstan, putting kymyz and nomadic culture at the heart of the event.
“I went to Oktoberfest in Munich in 2020. I saw that it was a family celebration, and I also saw how much it could contribute to the local economy. We didn’t have anything like that in Kazakhstan,” Zhumazhan Kaltayev said.
“People really liked our festival because it is not just about the drink. It represents our national identity, our culture, our spirit and our history.”
The competition is not only about taste. This year, producers also competed for the title of kymyz with the best nutritional composition, with experts examining the quality and characteristics of the drink.
“The total prize fund this year is 45 million tenge. The main prize, the Grand Prix, is a car,” Kaltayev added.
The new life of kymyz
In Kazakhstan, the drink has become part of everyday life. You can now find bottled kymyz in supermarkets and order it in cafes and restaurants.
For a drink with centuries of history, kymyz is finding surprisingly modern ways to reach a new generation.
One of the latest trends is the rise of kymyz houses (kymyz-khana). Here, visitors can try different types of kymyz, including traditional varieties as well as versions made with honey, herbs and other ingredients.
Kymyz is also reaching international markets. Dried mare’s milk and other kymyz products are exported to countries such as China, Russia and Germany.

In Bishkek, US envoys shadow the SCO summit in challenge on Beijing and Moscow’s turf

In Bishkek, US envoys shadow the SCO summit in challenge on Beijing and Moscow’s turf
Central Asian countries in focus as Washington pursues outreach serving to blunt Chinese influence in strategically valuable region
As China and Russia rallied dozens of countries in Bishkek to shape a multipolar world order, Washington’s envoys were splitting the spotlight by meeting several Central Asian presidents in the Kyrgyz capital this week.
The manoeuvring showed that the US was likely to continue its outreach to the region and seek to blunt Beijing’s influence, but it would be “unrealistic” for Washington to force Central Asian countries to choose sides, according to a leading Chinese analyst.
US Senator Steve Daines and Sergio Gor, America’s special envoy for South and Central Asia, met Kyrgyzstan’s Sadyr Japarov, Tajikistan’s Emomali Rahmon and Uzbekistan’s Shavkat Mirziyoyev separately in Bishkek on Monday.
The summit brought together the three Central Asian presidents alongside other notable leaders, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Swedish minister defends strict post-Brexit removals of Britons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
12:59:23 UTC
21:59:23 KST

The Swedish government has doubled down on its position on removing and deporting British citizens on the grounds they were late to apply for permission to stay after Brexit.
The migration minister, Johan Forssell, issued a robust defence of the Swedish migration agency’s implementation of the Brexit withdrawal agreement on Wednesday in response to a question from an MP about the case of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old British widow who has been ordered to leave the country after 21 years.
Forssell said the European Commission, which is legally mandated to ensure EU member states implement the withdrawal agreement correctly, was onboard with Sweden’s approach.
“The migration board has followed up on the application of the withdrawal agreement and the assessment is that Sweden has fulfilled its commitments. This assessment is shared by the commission,” he said.
There has been growing controversy over removal orders issued to British citizens who did not know that Sweden was one of 13 countries in the EU that required formal applications to stay in the country post-Brexit.
In another case, a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, has been deported despite having lived in Sweden since he was 10.
Thomas’s local MP, Häkan Svenneling, of the Left party, told the Guardian: “It seems to me that the Swedish government thinks everything is fine even though British citizens are being deported from Sweden right now. Not acting is also an action in this situation. What Sweden needs is a new government and a new migration minister who stops deporting people with strong connections to Sweden.”
In his written answer to Svenneling, Forssell offered British citizens facing deportation a sliver of hope. He said: “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future.”
Thomas has been told she must remove herself from Sweden by Tuesday 8 September or face deportation and a potential ban from the Schengen area.
She is one of several British citizens who have been faced with removal orders after the migration agency rejected their late applications to stay.
The UK Foreign Office has raised Sweden’s approach to late applications for post-Brexit residency a number of times in the specialised committee on citizens’ rights, a structure set up to ensure the withdrawal agreement is implemented properly.
David Milstead, who runs the grassroots organisation Brits in Sweden, said the Swedish response was not a surprise. “The government was hardly going to disown the decisions of [the migration agency] or the Swedish courts. The real question is whether Sweden’s approach is consistent with EU law and the [withdrawal agreement],” he said.
He pointed out that under the agreement, the UK was obliged to set up a statutory body, the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), to independently ensure the Home Office implemented the Brexit deal correctly, while the European Commission performed the correspondent role for EU member states.
“The IMA has taken a much more robust approach. It is hard to imagine it not challenging the UK had it operated a policy like Sweden’s, which would have put the rights of around a quarter of a million successful late applicants [in the UK] at risk,” Milstead said.
“Sweden’s approach now needs either to be tested before the European court of justice or addressed through measures that remedy the problem. The government’s response leaves open the possibility of change, and that must include fixing unjust deportation decisions.”
The European Commission has been approached for comment.
According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025 a total of 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. Analysis by the Foreign Office found this was 32.9% of the 7,565 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU member states over this period. Although it is not possible to determine exactly how many were in Sweden prior to the end of the UK-EU transition period, it is likely that the majority will have been.
Thomas has been in Sweden for 21 years and says her late husband inquired about the impact of Brexit and was told by the authorities there was nothing they needed to do to remain in the country legally.
The couple moved to the country to be close to their son and grandchildren, and Thomas said she had been left feeling sick with worry after receiving the removal order.

Drone incident in Germany has ‘hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism’, EU's Kallas says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
