"Passing ball to new Duma convocation" and Far East’s development: Putin’s speech at EEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:43:36 UTC
20:43:36 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) that he wants to "pass the ball to the new convocation of the State Duma," adding that he expects deputies to play an active role in improving the country’s business climate.
The Russian leader also announced the move to the next stage of the development of the Far East, a renewed strategy for the coming decade.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the head of state.
Far East’s development
Russia’s strategic policy is to turn the Far East into an area for cooperation and dynamic change: "Russia is an active participant in investment and trade cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region. We interact on an equal footing with our partners and the region’s leading integration associations. Our strategic policy is to make the Far East an area for cooperation and dynamic change in the economy and infrastructure, technological development, workforce training and, of course, the social area."
Around 25 trillion rubles ($287 bln) in capital investments have been invested in the Russian Far East over the past 11 years, while the region's gross product has more than tripled: "I would like to point out that about 25 trillion rubles in capital investments have been attracted to Russia's Far Eastern regions over 11 years. The rates of investment activity, industrial growth, and construction here consistently surpass the national average. As a result, the gross regional product of the Far East has more than tripled over 11 years, which is a very rapid pace."
Unemployment in the Far East has recently fallen fourfold to 2.2%, reaching the national average: "Unemployment in the Far East has decreased fourfold. This year it has been at 2.2%, which is the level of the national average. This unemployment figure is a record low for the region."
The Russian Far East is currently experiencing growth, with high economic activity recorded in nearly all of its constituent entities: "High economic activity is recorded across practically all Far Eastern regions of the [Russian] Federation. This is particularly noticeable in small and medium-sized businesses, which employ approximately one-third of the working population. This is a strong indicator. What does it show? It shows that the Russian Far East is on the rise. Businesses and entrepreneurs see clear prospects for developing and expanding their enterprises. Whereas citizens understand that their in-demand knowledge and competencies can yield tangible results, both for the region and for the country as a whole, and for people individually."
Russia is moving into the next stage of the Far East’s development, an updated development strategy for the next 10 years: "We are moving to the next stage - implementing an updated development strategy for the Far East, the Far Eastern Federal District, designed for the next 10 years, through 2036. The key task is to maintain the strong pace of development achieved so far and launch new investment cycles in the region."
Quantum communication networks must be expanded to all regional capitals in the Far East by 2030: "As of today, the length of the main quantum network in Russia already exceeds 7,800 kilometers. It connects 27 constituent entities of the Russian Federation, including 13 cities with populations of over one million. I would like to draw the attention of the government and my colleagues at Russian Railways to the fact that quantum communication networks must be extended to the Far East by 2030, reaching all its regional capitals, thereby integrating them into a high-speed information and data exchange network."
Infrastructure loans repaid by Far East regions may be reinvested into the implementation of master plans in those constituent entities.
Unified preferential treatment
Unified preferential treatment for the Far East and the Arctic will take effect on January 1, 2027: "We are launching a business support system that is unprecedented in scale and scope. A unified preferential regime will begin operating across the entire Far East and Arctic starting as early as January 1 of next year."
The concept behind preferential treatment is to ensure that support tools are not tied to a specific special zone or priority development area, but are instead carefully and effectively tailored to specific types of activities across the entire region: "In other words, an investment project anywhere in the Far East or the Arctic will have access to its own specific menu of incentives."
The full range of available mechanisms will include reduced insurance contributions, tax and customs incentives, and assistance with infrastructure connections and constructing production facilities, among other things.
Existing benefits for residents of existing priority development areas in the Far East will remain even after the introduction of the unified preferential regime: "At the same time, existing benefits for current residents of priority development areas and the Free Port of Vladivostok will be preserved in full, of course."
The system of preferential regimes has already been successfully implemented in the Far East and the Arctic zone: "They include priority development areas, the Free Port of Vladivostok, the special administrative region on Russky Island, and special tax treatment on the Kuril Islands."
These tools have already made it possible to attract trillions of rubles in investment and generate 200,000 new jobs.
"Passing ball to new Duma convocation"
Putin would like to "pass the ball to the new convocation of the State Duma," counting on deputies to play an active role in improving the business climate: "I want to pass the ball, so to speak, to the new convocation of the Russian State Duma, which will be elected soon, in September. I am expecting deputies to take an active stance and engage in fruitful legislative work to improve the business climate."
It is important to continue establishing favorable and predictable conditions for investors, relying on requests from entrepreneurs and needs of regions, being guided by Russia’s national interests.
Need to remove barriers for business
It is necessary to remove bureaucratic barriers for business and avoid excessive control and "tightening the screws": "We need <...> to consistently lift bureaucratic barriers for entrepreneurs and reduce the administrative burden. It even makes no sense to introduce tax incentives while simultaneously, so to speak, tightening the screws through additional inspections and excessive control and oversight. I am saying excessive in particular. <...> I believe colleagues from relevant ministries and agencies will hear the message."
It is important to eliminate the risk of double taxation for businesses in the Far East: "I’m asking to adjust the legal framework accordingly. It is important to continue creating favorable, predictable conditions for investors, relying on the requests of entrepreneurs and the needs of the regions, being guided by Russia’s national interests."
Extraction of resources
Russia will continue to expand mineral extraction in the east and north of the country, including oil, gas, and gold: "For industrial growth and the development of high-tech industries of the future, we need to strengthen our foundation, our resource base. <…> We will continue developing mineral extraction in the east and north of the country, including oil, gas, coal, gold, and rare earth metals. Of course, [we will do so] using clean technologies, as is already being done at a number of our enterprises."
Natural resources extracted in the Far East and the Arctic should increasingly be processed locally: "This refers to metallurgical, gas, and petrochemical facilities, fertilizer production, etc. ensuring that value chains are established, jobs are created, and regional and municipal budget revenues grow right here, in the Far Eastern and Arctic constituent entities of the Federation."
Special legal regime
A special legal regime designed to rapidly test advanced technologies, including UAVs for use in the civilian economy, is set to launch in the Russian Far East starting January 1, 2027: "Its essence lies in the rapid, unhindered testing of cutting-edge technologies, such as agricultural drones, industrial robots, telemedicine, or artificial intelligence for medical diagnostics."
Eased public procurement system
A streamlined public procurement system, including through marketplaces, will launch in Russia on October 1 as a pilot project: "A new federal law enabling more active use of platform-based solutions for procurement at regional and local levels, initially on a trial basis, comes into force on October 1. This applies not only to the Far East and the Arctic but to all constituent entities of the Russian Federation. Their educational institutions, such as kindergartens, schools, and colleges, will be able to purchase goods directly, so to speak, from the shelf of domestic marketplaces."
Transportation
Russia plans to make navigation along the Northern Sea Route year-round.
Authorities expect the volume of freight traffic along the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor to reach at least 70 mln tons per year: "This means it will at least double from the current level."
It is planned to link the Arctic marine terminals with rail and inland waterway networks to ensure cargo flows from Central Russia, the Urals, and Siberia: "We also plan to connect Arctic marine terminals with rail and inland waterway networks so that cargo flows from Central Russia, the Urals, and Siberia could gradually be tied to this route, and to facilitate the delivery of imported goods, of course."
Transportation of civilian cargo using low-altitude drones needs to be tested in the regions of the Far East and the Arctic: "As unmanned aviation develops, low-altitude airspace is becoming a transport artery as busy as railways and waterways. It is essential to establish standards for autonomous transportation of civilian cargo using drones already now."
Vostok Oil
The first oil from Vostok Oil will be shipped shortly: "I would like to note a milestone event that will take place soon. At Vostok Oil, one of our largest Arctic projects located in the Krasnoyarsk Region, a trunk oil pipeline to the new Bukhta Sever terminal will be put into operation. The first oil will also be loaded and delivered to buyers via our Arctic sea routes."
Creation of modern financial center on basis of Eastern Exchange
The government and the Central Bank must carefully consider the creation of a modern financial center based on the Eastern Exchange: "To expand the participation of international capital in our Far Eastern and Arctic projects, we need to leverage the potential of the Eastern Exchange. As I said earlier, we plan to establish a modern financial center on its basis. I’m asking the government and the Bank of Russia to thoroughly address all these issues."

11:41:00 UTC
20:41:00 KST

Estonia might have to return European Peace Facility sums over ammo procurement mess
It is not yet clear whether Estonia will have to repay the money it received from the European Peace Facility to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine, European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said.
It emerged Wednesday that Estonia had sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to an Indian supplier that had never previously sold a single shell. Part of the money came from the European Peace Facility.
European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said it is not yet clear whether Estonia will have to repay the money. He said the European Peace Facility is an important instrument for providing military assistance to Ukraine and enabling the delivery of equipment.
The European Commission is in contact with Estonian authorities to examine the matter more closely. Wigand confirmed that measures are in place to ensure that European Union funds are used properly.
Speaking at the government press conference on Thursday, Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur, who announced his resignation Wednesday, said Russia had wanted the same shells as Ukraine. "The countries where they were available weren't nice, friendly countries where you could just go and make an elegant purchase. This involved risk," Pevkur said.
Minister: There should ne no risks for Estonian taxpayers
He continued that, under all the contracts signed, equipment and ammunition worth hundreds of millions of euros has reached Ukraine.
"The general rule is that if due diligence has been carried out and the funds have been managed prudently, there should be no risk to the Estonian taxpayer," Pevkur said. He added that if any company deliberately defrauded the Ukrainian people and failed to deliver the ammunition, criminal proceedings should be launched against it.
In August 2024, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) signed its first purchase contract with Italy-registered company Datasel S.R.L. and transferred the first €15 million. The money did not come from Estonia's state budget, but from the European Peace Facility.
RKIK signed a second contract with Datasel in October 2024, again transferring an advance payment of more than €10 million. Two more contracts were signed at the end of 2024 and advance payments were made, bringing the total to around €70 million.
While the company delivered some components to an intermediary warehouse in a European country, RKIK found the shipment to be incomplete and not of sufficient quality, terminated its contracts with Datasel last fall and requested the company return advance payments.

After conquering screens across the globe, Turkish dramas eye China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:40:36 UTC
20:40:36 KST

- China should be next major target for Turkish television industry as producers seek to expand global footprint, Catay tells Anadolu
- Turkish dramas act as an ‘open invitation’ to Türkiye, boosting interest in country’s culture and tourism, says producer Birol Guven
Sprawling Bosphorus mansions, elaborate family breakfasts and endless glasses of Turkish tea have become familiar sights far beyond Türkiye, carried into homes around the world by the country's hugely popular television dramas.
Over nearly two decades, Turkish stories of love, betrayal, family and power have traveled to the Middle East, Latin America, Europe and Asia, turning the country's television industry into a global cultural export worth more than $1 billion.
Now, producers are looking for their next big audience – China.
Kerem Catay, CEO of production company Ay Yapim, told Anadolu that Turkish productions now reach well over 100 countries, with successful projects potentially reaching audiences of around 1 billion people.
The industry's two biggest overseas markets remain the Middle East and Latin America, where Turkish dramas have become deeply embedded in popular culture.
Turkish dramas have helped familiarize foreign audiences with the country's food, clothing, language and everyday customs, while their popularity has also been linked to increased interest in Türkiye as a tourist destination.
For Birol Guven, a producer and director general of cinema at Türkiye's Culture and Tourism Ministry, that cultural influence is one of the industry's most significant achievements.
“Turkish dramas are also an invitation,” he said. “When people watch a Turkish drama, they want to travel to Türkiye.”
From regional hit to global phenomenon
Turkish dramas began developing a major international presence in the late 2000s.
Catay pointed to Yaprak Dokumu (The Fall of Leaves) as one of the productions from the early years of that expansion, followed by major successes including Ezel, Ask-i Memnu (The Forbidden Love) and Kara Sevda (Endless Love).
“We had great success starting from 2007, 2008,” he said on the sidelines of the Turkish Series Symposium in Istanbul.
The Middle East provided the industry's first major international audience before the phenomenon spread dramatically across Latin America.
Since then, Turkish productions have become hits in European countries like Spain, Italy and many Eastern European nations, as well as Asian markets.
Other landmark productions, including Kurtlar Vadisi (Valley of the Wolves), Muhtesem Yuzyil (Magnificent Century), Dirilis: Ertugrul (Resurrection: Ertugrul) and Cukur (The Pit), further expanded the industry's international reach and attracted devoted audiences around the world.
“We even have Vietnam. I mean, we have been selling content to Vietnam for years,” Catay said. “We have Asia, all around the world.”
And the industry has become large enough internationally that Guven argues “Turkish drama” is now effectively a global brand of its own.
“Türkiye is the only country whose content is referred to by a name such as ‘Turkish drama,’” he said. “You do not hear terms such as ‘English drama’ or ‘American drama.’ We are the only country that refers to its television series as ‘Turkish drama.’ This is very important.”
Guven pointed out that Türkiye has long been a country that punches beyond its weight in terms of cinema.
“We have a long history, and our history of cinema goes back to the invention of cinema,” Guven told Anadolu. “Over the last 20 years, we have built a very large television industry on top of this heritage.”
Could China be next?
Yet one enormous television market remains largely beyond the industry's reach.
Despite Turkish dramas' success elsewhere in Asia, Catay said establishing a meaningful presence in China is now one of the industry's major ambitions.
“The next region should be China for us,” he said.
Turkish producers traveled to China last year with Türkiye's Culture and Tourism Ministry to explore opportunities for bringing their productions into the market, according to Catay.
Breaking into China could offer Turkish producers another massive audience with an appetite for serialized television dramas. Domestic Chinese dramas currently dominate the market, but Korean dramas have also had a major following.
Meanwhile, the industry requires continued effort to maintain the momentum of Turkish series in markets where they have already broken through.
“The main issue is that all the Turkish production companies have to keep on having this success around the world,” Catay said.
At the same time, measuring the industry's global audience has become more difficult as streaming platforms play a larger role in international distribution.
Catay said traditional television ratings provide audience data in some markets, while global digital platforms generally do not disclose detailed viewing figures to producers. Instead, companies often gauge a production's performance through indicators such as whether it enters a platform's top 10 rankings in individual countries.
“If it’s a digital one, if it’s a platform one, we don’t know the ratings because they’re not giving out the ratings,” he said.
Catay estimated that a successful Turkish production could potentially reach around 1 billion people through the industry's presence in roughly 140 countries.
More than a television export
The industry's influence is increasingly measured in more than dollars and viewers.
Guven compared Turkish dramas with American television, which for decades exported images of US lifestyles and consumer culture alongside its entertainment.
“When American television series enter a country, they bring elements of American daily life with them, such as hamburgers and coffee,” he said.
Turkish dramas are doing something similar, he argued, exposing viewers to Türkiye's landscapes, traditions and everyday life.
Research has found evidence of that cultural spillover. Studies of audiences abroad have linked Turkish series with greater interest in Turkish culture and language, as well as increased interest in traveling to the country.
The effect is particularly visible in Istanbul, where locations used in internationally popular series have themselves become attractions for foreign fans.
For Guven, that makes television part of something much larger than the entertainment business.
“The effects and side effects of Turkish dramas are significant,” he said. “Generally speaking, Turkish dramas serve as an open invitation to people all over the world.”
“This is a new form of heritage today,” he added.

Jam season is here - bottle that sunshine now to brighten up the winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:35:34 UTC
20:35:34 KST

The ideal time to make lemonade, when lemons are juicy and plentiful and cheap, is in the dead of winter, when the last thing you want is a cooling glass of lemonade. Similarly, jam-making is best done on a grey November afternoon, when the windows are steamed up and the kitchen is the warmest place in the house. Winter is exactly when you want to be standing over a great pot of bubbling fruit and boiling sugar, but much less so in summer, which is when all the good fruit is in season. From May until mid-October, our fruit supplier bills spike exponentially as boxes and boxes of seasonal fruit in its absolute prime make their way to our kitchen for a jam session, and the practice of turning them into a sweet spread is part profession, part obsession. Jam is very much our jam.
Early in the season, we can just about cope. The soft fruits start to come in when the weather is still behaving itself, and we love giving them a little seasonal accent – elderflower comes with the last rhubarb, as well as with the first strawberries and apricots, and it pairs wonderfully with all of them (if you are starting there, Felicity Cloake has a very thorough guide to the perfect strawberry jam). Cherries, meanwhile, go with just about anything, while young bay leaves often find themselves heading into the blackcurrant pot. Fennel fronds and peaches are another favourite, and we make some whenever we can get those two at the same moment. It is an amazing combination: sweet, perfumed and just a little bit green.
For us, the real preserving frenzy begins round about now, at the deep, sticky end of summer. In fact, September may well be the best jam month of all. The days are not too hot and the produce – figs, plums, grapes – are the ultimate jammers. Plums offer near endless possibilities and, depending on the variety, can take a surprising amount of spice: cassia bark, star anise, perhaps a clove or two. Nigel Slater’s collection of late-summer jams and pickles is exactly the sort of thing to read when the fruit bowl begins to look threatening.
Grapes, meanwhile, are a bit of a challenge, not least because most of the varieties grown commercially are chosen for their sweetness, whereas you want something else for jam: there needs to be some acidity, some funk, some flavour in there. Fragola grapes, with their musky, intoxicating, wild strawberry flavour, are a rare treat – we usually get only one delivery of them each year, which makes them all the more special, and all the more worthy of preserving for the rest of the year.
Figs, especially those beautiful, black bursa ones, make the best jam of all, and the one that we and our customers crave the most. The fruit hardly needs any help, either, although its honeyed sweetness loves nothing more then a few pods of cooling cardamom for balance (that said, we are more than a little intrigued by Lillie O’Brien’s earl grey combo).
Our annual September challenge, then, is simple: make enough fig jam to last until Christmas. Every year, we make what looks like an absurd quantity. And every year it disappears far too quickly, which is exactly the point – spend a bit of the summer sweating over the pots so that in winter, when we aren’t sweating at all, there’s a little bit of jarred sunshine ready for us when it is most desperately needed.
Our month in food
The sweet spot | Jams aside, our pastry kitchen currently smells heavily of honey and spice as we get busy baking loaves and loaves of honey cake in readiness for the Jewish new year next week, which this year is coming round earlier than usual. It is traditional to start the year with something sweet, be that an apple dipped in honey, dates, sweet challah bread and, of course, honey cake. You don’t need to be Jewish to enjoy this delicious tradition: on the 11th, wish your Jewish friends a happy new year, and have something sweet for yourself.
Local attraction | Our love for Jackson Boxer’s cooking knows no bounds, and even though his Brunswick House is so close to our home in south London that we are there more often that is OK to admit, whenever he opens a new place, we go. Vesper is on Exmouth Market in the centre of London, and it made us question our loyalty not only to Brunswick House, but also to our own home and our beloved neighbourhood, because the fried potato pizzette is something we need to live closer to.
Book marks | We got a sneak preview of two new books that are already making our autumn look much more delicious, and both of which are published today. Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghi is full of mouthwatering recipes that look and taste as good as they are easy to make, and promises to add a touch of glamour to our midweek meals. The second is the new one by Fuchsia Dunlop, a perennial favourite of ours, and Five Tastes: The Magic of Flavour in a Chinese Kitchen is a deep and delicious dive into the flavours that are the cornerstones of Chinese cooking. We are into all of them.

Iran threatens U.S. with forceful response if Israel attacks south Lebanon ridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:35:12 UTC
20:35:12 KST

Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah fighters, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
A foreign official with direct knowledge of the message said it was delivered around mid-August and that Israel had put off storming the area as a result of U.S. pressure.
According to Lebanese security sources, Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon. The ridge has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
Hezbollah said in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.
The Israeli military has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the U.S. had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.
Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.
Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message but said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.
"Iran considers any Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.
Iran fired missiles towards Israel in early June in retaliation for attacks on Hezbollah on the Lebanese capital's outskirts.
Despite a ceasefire announced in June, the Israeli military has said Hezbollah is still operating around the ridge and twice over the last week launched explosive drones towards Israeli troops near the ridge.
In July, it said it had launched an air strike on a Hezbollah fighter near an access shaft to the underground site at Ali al-Taher and vowed not to allow Hezbollah to operate in the area or pose a threat to Israeli soldiers.
An Israeli military official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters in June that Hezbollah fighters were stuck underground without food or water. Israeli newspaper Maariv, citing a military source, said on Thursday that the Israeli military assessed there were no IRGC forces in Ali al-Taher and that some Hezbollah fighters had died without food and water.
The third official said Israel's military was trying to smoke out Hezbollah and IRGC personnel by besieging them, shooting down attempted drone deliveries of food and water to the ridge.
"What we have seen over the past month is Israeli pressure to besiege Ali al-Taher in order to impose a reality within this facility that renders it uninhabitable. This approach, and the absence of a large-scale attack, means that it is possible a message was conveyed through several countries -- this is a natural conclusion," Hezbollah's media office told Reuters.
A Lebanese source briefed by Hezbollah said the group's fighters can still access their positions through the ridge's northern side.
Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher, which Israel's military has included in a self-declared security zone occupied by its troops and off-limits to Lebanese.
Despite Iran's warning, the Lebanese source and a senior Lebanese security official said an Israeli military operation to capture the ridge was still possible in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah said any large-scale attack on Ali al-Taher would mean a return to full-blown war, and could see missiles landing on northern Israeli communities.

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. The value of shipments under the parallel import mechanism may reach $20.5 billion in 2026, Russian Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov told reporters on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"In 2026, the projected value of parallel imports is estimated at around $20.5 billion," he said.
Parallel imports for the first seven months of this year amounted to approximately $12.2 billion, and the figure could reach $13.8 billion for the January-August period," the minister specified.
"As we have repeatedly stated, the decline in parallel import volumes is a natural trend, driven, among other things, by the development of domestic production and the substitution of goods from unfriendly countries with alternatives from friendly nations," Alikhanov noted.
The total volume of parallel imports into Russia exceeded $23.1 billion by the end of 2025, with the monthly average reaching about $1.9 billion, Roman Chekushov, State Secretary and Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade, reported earlier.
The parallel import mechanism has been in effect since March 2022. The government allowed the import of popular original foreign-made goods into the country without the consent of the copyright holders. Since then, the list of goods permitted for import has been updated several times.
The Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) is being held on September 1-4 in Vladivostok on the campus of the Far Eastern Federal University. The event is organized by the Roscongress Foundation with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation. TASS is the general media partner.

Geneva Airport generates over CHF3 billion for regional economy: report

Geneva Airport generates over CHF3 billion for regional economy: report
Geneva Airport, the operator of the international airfield at Cointrin, generates CHF3.3 billion ($4.08 billion) in added value and provides nearly 22,000 jobs, a new study shows. The airport's chief executive intends to continue strengthening air connectivity, which is particularly important for businesses.
Of the CHF3.3 billion, nearly CHF2 billion went to the canton of Geneva, more than CHF550 million were generated in the neighbouring French region, and around CHF770 million in the rest of Switzerland, according to a study conducted by the Zurich-based consultancy firm Infras and published on Thursday.
“The direct, indirect and induced effects of the hub play a major role in the regional economy,” said Geneva Airport CEO Jean-François de Saussure on the airport terrace. The airport services around 147 routes operated by 57 airlines.
Altogether the direct impact of the 270 companies operating out of the airport amounts to around CHF1.66 billion and 11,500 full-time-equivalent (FTE) jobs. This activity accounts for 2.6% of the canton of Geneva’s gross domestic product (GDP), with the canton having a total of 353,000 jobs (FTE).
+ Flying in Switzerland set to become even more expensive
The economic benefits extend in particular to suppliers, shops, hotels, restaurants and service providers operating in the Swiss-French cross-border region. The indirect effects are linked to purchases made by companies at the airport and the effects generated by employees’ spending.
The contribution of general and business aviation and air freight activities, taking all effects into account, amounts to CHF330 million and CHF350 million, respectively. In terms of freight, some 96,000 tonnes passed through Geneva Airport.
Direct routes to Singapore and São Paulo under consideration
Air connectivity is presented as a key factor for the regional economy, businesses and International Geneva. It facilitates businesses’ access to international markets, the arrival of talent and visitors, and enhances Geneva’s standing as a diplomatic, scientific and financial centre.
More
Swiss budget cuts increase pressure on International Geneva
“During the G7 summit [in nearby Evian, France, last June], all the leaders passed through Geneva, even though the city was not necessarily their final destination,” said de Saussure. Furthermore, “international organisations represent a significant source of activity, with around 4,600 official delegations and 6,000 conferences per year. When their budgets are cut, we see a drop in passenger numbers”.
In 2025, the airport handled 17.8 million passengers, “in an airport designed for 5 million”, said the CEO. “We need to establish new long-haul routes to improve our positioning.” Two direct routes to Singapore and São Paulo are currently under consideration. Furthermore, services to China have increased from five to seven flights a week.
“We now have more passengers travelling to China than to the United States,” de Saussure said.

Russia remained India’s top oil supplier in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:33:08 UTC
20:33:08 KST

Russia remained India’s top oil supplier in August
Russia remained India’s largest supplier of crude oil in August, selling around 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd), or 45% of the country’s total imports, data from maritime intelligence firm Kpler shows.
Russian shipments were down from a record 2.8 million bpd in July, when they accounted for more than half of India’s crude purchases. However, India’s overall imports also declined to around 4.6 million bpd in August, nearly 8% below the more than 5 million bpd bought the previous month.
Indian refiners ramped up purchases in May, June, and July to guard against potential supply shortages amid the conflict in the Middle East. The August decline reflected some normalization after months of heavy buying, scheduled maintenance at Indian refineries, and lower availability of Russian crude, according to Kpler.
“August was less a story of India voluntarily stepping away from Russian oil than of Russia having fewer barrels to offer,” Abu Dhabi-based commodity analyst Natalia Katona told the Financial Express. Lower Russian seaborne exports and stronger competition from Chinese refiners for available cargoes also weighed on supplies to India, she said. 
The United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela were among India’s other leading oil suppliers during the month. Venezuelan shipments rose sharply, reaching their highest level since 2020, according to Kpler data. 
Russian oil has remained an important part of India’s energy mix as it seeks to secure supplies amid disruptions affecting shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. India imports around 90% of the crude oil it consumes.
The purchases have continued despite the prospect of new US tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which cleared the US Senate last month, would allow tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil. The bill has US President Donald Trump’s backing but still has to pass the House. 
India maintains that its oil purchases are guided by affordability, availability, and national energy security rather than geopolitical considerations.

A Sverdlovsk region judge has reportedly ordered the nationalization of Ventprom, Russia’s largest manufacturer of industrial ventilation equipment for mines, tunnels and metros.
Yekaterinburg’s Leninsky District Court on Aug. 17 ruled to transfer a 100% stake in the Artyomovsky Machine Engineering Plant Ventprom to the state, according to the Interfax news agency.
“Nothing has changed for us except the shareholder,” a Ventprom spokesperson told Interfax on Thursday.
The government seized the strategic factory after branding its former owners and associates an “extremist organization,” the regional news outlet Vecherniye Vedomosti reported earlier.
The Sverdlovsk region’s deputy prosecutor filed a lawsuit against eight individuals and two foreign companies in connection with the “extremist” designation. They include former Ventprom executives Oleg, Igor and Olga Gorshkov, as well as companies registered in Britain and Germany.
Court records published by Vecherniye Vedomosti show Google and Russia’s communications watchdog Roskomnadzor as being among third parties listed in the court case.
Defense lawyers declined to discuss specifics of the case with the news outlet due to client confidentiality. Unverified reports claimed the “extremist” designation stemmed from a bank transfer that was made to a Ukrainian citizen, as well as to the fact that Gorshkov has lived outside of Russia since 2023.
Vecherniye Vedomosti said Google was likely drawn into litigation since one of the Ukrainians listed in the case, Viktor Litovchenko, is a popular blogger on YouTube, which the tech giant owns. Neither Litovchenko nor the second Ukrainian, Natalia Prushinskaya, reportedly held shares in Ventprom.
Ventprom, which supplies ventilation systems to the Moscow, St. Petersburg, Novosibirsk and Minsk metro networks, as well as to Lukoil, Alrosa and Rusal, reported more than 3 billion rubles (almost $35 million) in revenue last year.

Maduro, wife want US drug charges dismissed on immunity grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:24:00 UTC
20:24:00 KST

Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife asked a U.S. judge Wednesday to dismiss drug trafficking charges against them, arguing they are immune from prosecution as the former leader and first lady of a foreign country.
In papers filed in Manhattan federal court, lawyers for Maduro said a judge was required by law to reject the indictment because it cannot be brought against a foreign leader.
"No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought," the lawyers wrote.
"That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own," they added.
Maduro and his wife are scheduled to go on trial on drug trafficking charges next June 1. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein has set oral arguments for Nov. 17 on motions to dismiss the indictment.
Maduro, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, 69, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York.
In separate papers filed Wednesday, lawyers for Flores said she too has immunity from U.S. prosecution on sovereign immunity grounds.
"It is an attribute of Venezuela’s sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it,” her lawyers wrote.
Maduro's lawyers said that even if Maduro were not entitled to sovereign immunity as the head of state, the case against him must be dismissed because he is also entitled to conduct-based sovereign immunity.
Meanwhile, the lawyers argued, Maduro "vehemently denies the allegations against him."
"If this case were to proceed to trial, it would be apparent that he has been falsely accused," they said.
Both have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against numerous alleged co-conspirators.
They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
Federal prosecutors are scheduled to file a response to the arguments later this month.
President Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
U.S. prosecutors claim Maduro carried out a conspiracy to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the U.S. by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins.

Iran tests Trump with Gulf strikes as US touts Hormuz oil surge and battered carrier raises alarms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:23:40 UTC
20:23:40 KST

Iran launched a new round of missile and drone attacks against bases used by U.S. forces in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, testing President Donald Trump’s threat of retaliation even as Washington touted a sharp rise in oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and fresh images highlighted the strain on its naval forces.
Sirens sounded in Kuwait early Thursday, and several hours later the Iranian military said it had targeted Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base, which is used by U.S. forces. Tehran said another attack struck concentrations of American troops and radar systems at Al Minhad Air Base in the UAE. The United States did not announce fresh strikes on Iran overnight, despite Trump warning earlier this week that Washington would respond forcefully to further attacks.
The current escalation began Sunday when the United States struck launchers on Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, saying they were preparing to deploy naval mines against passing vessels. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks on Gulf states, prompting a broader U.S. strike Tuesday against around 60 targets in southern Iran and the Hormuz area. Asked Wednesday about another response, Trump said he was “ready,” but added that the confrontation “will not last long.”
A U.S. official told CNN on Thursday that American forces expect operations around Hormuz to continue because Iran still retains the ability to threaten shipping. The official described the expected strikes as “mowing the grass,” aimed at steadily degrading Iranian capabilities. Recent U.S. attacks have targeted radar systems used to track ships, mine-laying capabilities and communications infrastructure.
US touts oil surge through Hormuz
At the same time, the Trump administration is portraying its naval operation in the strait as an increasingly successful effort to restore the flow of oil from the Persian Gulf. Two U.S. officials told CNN that American warships escorted 40 commercial vessels through Hormuz on Tuesday carrying a combined 18 million barrels of oil.
If accurate, that would be close to the roughly 20 million barrels that passed through the strait on an average day before the war. U.S. warships also shot down Iranian drones and intercepted anti-ship cruise missiles during the operation, according to the officials.
Washington says the figures show that Iran is losing leverage over one of the world’s most important energy routes. But maritime experts and industry figures remain skeptical. Shipping trackers still show relatively low traffic, while U.S. officials argue that many vessels are switching off their transponders to make them harder for Iranian forces to target.
A source connected to the maritime industry told CNN that he knew of no one who believed daily traffic had genuinely returned to the levels claimed by Washington.
Trump has meanwhile emphasized economic pressure as his preferred tool against Tehran. The United States continues to restrict Iranian oil exports and has threatened sanctions against countries that maintain economic ties with the regime.
Battered carrier shows toll of deployment
The campaign is also putting pressure on U.S. military resources. The USS Abraham Lincoln arrived this week at Laem Chabang in Thailand after completing 268 days at sea during its Middle East deployment, where it supported operations against Iran before being replaced by the USS George Washington.
Its roughly 5,000 crew members are now receiving a week of rest, but photographs taken after the carrier arrived showed extensive rust across large sections of its exterior.
Former U.S. Navy Capt. Carl Schuster told CNN that rust itself is common on warships, but said the unusually long deployment made regular maintenance difficult and allowed corrosion to spread. Based on the images, he estimated that removing it could require about 30 days of preservation work.
“Rust is like a contagious disease. It spreads,” Schuster said, warning that untreated corrosion can eventually weaken steel structures such as decks, passageways and railings.
The Lincoln’s condition adds to broader concerns over prolonged deployments, ammunition stocks and the strain on U.S. forces as Washington tries to keep shipping moving through Hormuz while maintaining pressure on Iran.
For Trump, the latest Iranian attacks sharpen that tension: Tehran is still testing Washington militarily even as the administration argues that its economic and naval strategy is beginning to work.

Interview: SCO offers unique model for global governance, says SCO secretary-general
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
19:22:22 CST
20:22:22 KST

BISHKEK, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) can serve as an example for modern global governance, SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbayev has said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, he said that within the organization, decisions are made by consensus, countries have equal rights, and the interests of each participant are taken into account.
In the 25 years since its founding, the SCO has been advocating for strengthening multilateralism, abiding by international law, equal dialogue, and the development of a fair system of international relations, he said.
"The SCO has every opportunity to become a 'laboratory' for global multilateral cooperation -- a space where ideas of peace, security, development and dialogue take concrete forms," Yermekbayev noted.
In his opinion, one of the SCO's main achievements is the formation of a unique space of trust and cooperation among countries with their own historical, political and civilizational traditions.
"Over the years, member states have developed a sustainable culture of multilateral interaction based on equality, mutual respect, consideration of each other's interests, and the search for consensus," he noted.
He said the organization has established sustainable mechanisms to combat terrorism, separatism, extremism, transnational organized crime, drug trafficking and other modern threats, while offering substantial opportunities for cooperation in such fields as trade and investment, transport connectivity, energy, the digital economy, agriculture, environmental protection, education, science, culture, healthcare and tourism.
The secretary-general said the "Shanghai Spirit" of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations, and pursuit of common development is the important philosophical foundation for the SCO's development, allowing SCO countries to cooperate successfully.
"States from various regions see the SCO not as an instrument of geopolitical rivalry, but as a platform for equal dialogue, mutually beneficial cooperation, and the joint search for answers to common challenges," he said.
Yermekbayev emphasized China's significant role in the SCO's formation and development.
"Over the past 25 years, China has consistently supported the development of the organization and made a significant contribution to strengthening its institutional capacity," he said.
In this regard, it is of great significance that Chinese President Xi Jinping has put forward important concepts, such as building an even closer SCO community with a shared future, as well as building a common home featuring solidarity and mutual trust, peace and tranquility, prosperity and development, good-neighborliness and friendship, as well as fairness and justice, the SCO secretary-general noted.
"These concepts largely reflect the philosophy of the Shanghai Spirit, giving it new meaning applicable to modern conditions," he said.
Yermekbayev noted that the four global initiatives put forward by Xi -- the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative, and the Global Governance Initiative -- have been widely praised. "This is a complementary system of ideas and practical approaches aimed at addressing pressing contemporary challenges and building a just, peaceful, and sustainable world order," he said.
As the 2025 SCO Tianjin Summit marked the commencement of a new stage in the organization's development, Yermekbayev said, the decisions adopted at the meeting defined strategic guidelines for the organization until 2035.
"The SCO faces great opportunities," he said, expressing hope that the just-concluded Bishkek summit will inject new impetus into the SCO's development.
He also voiced hope that participants of the summit will work together, maintain strategic mutual trust, and safeguard peace and development interests, and that the SCO will make even more significant contribution to building a secure, just, and prosperous Eurasian region and the entire world. ■

Government to discuss new defense minister candidates next week
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has ruled out Reform Party Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga as Estonia's next defense minister, saying the party will begin discussing candidates to replace Hanno Pevkur next week.
Although Reform Party Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga has been mentioned in the media as a possible candidate for defense minister, Prime Minister Kristen Michal ruled out the possibility, saying the two roles are incompatible.
Michal said Vaga would continue as Reform Party secretary general and suggested he take the speculation as a compliment.
Vaga also said he was not in line to become defense minister. He thanked journalists, businesspeople and friends who had asked about the possibility, calling the speculation "a great honor and a vote of confidence."
Vaga said he would remain focused on his work as Reform Party secretary general until the elections while helping the party find a strong new defense minister. He said the next minister should continue strengthening Estonia's defense capabilities, ensure transparency over defense spending of more than 5 percent of GDP and maintain Estonia's unwavering support for Ukraine.
According to Michal, Reform Party members will begin discussing potential candidates next week. The new minister will be able to take the oath of office when parliament reconvenes the following week.
Michal also praised outgoing Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur for taking political responsibility, while stressing that this did not mean Pevkur was personally responsible for any wrongdoing.
"If, in the course of helping Ukraine, someone in his area of government took risks that should not have been taken and for which he is assuming political responsibility, that does not mean he bears personal responsibility," Michal said.
Pevkur announced Wednesday on ETV news show "Aktuaalne kaamera" that he was resigning as defense minister. He had held the post since 2022.
Prosecutors opened criminal proceedings Tuesday to investigate circumstances within the Ministry of Defense's area of government that were addressed in National Audit Office audits this year and last year. No one has been named as a suspect.
It emerged Wednesday that Estonia had sought to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and paid €70 million in advance to Indian businesspeople who had reportedly never previously sold artillery shells.

Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:12:03 UTC
20:12:03 KST

Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
The industry has increasingly focused on the risks of what was previously a booming private credit industry
Hong Kong’s market regulator has reclassified some of the city’s authorised funds with exposure to private market assets above a certain amount as complex products, raising the threshold for selling these products to retail investors.
Funds with exposures to direct or indirect private market assets amounting to 50 per cent or more of their net asset value would be recategorised.
The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said that it observed some funds gaining indirect exposure to private market assets through layered structures and complex instruments, which might lack transparency.
This structure made it difficult for retail investors to fully understand the underlying risks, the SFC said in a circular released on Thursday.
Due to low liquidity, valuation challenges and higher credit risks, funds with exposure to private credit and private equity would need to enhance their transparency regarding underlying investments and associated risks, according to the SFC.
Funds classified as complex products are subject to the SFC’s selling requirements, which include ensuring product suitability, the regulator added.

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:09:58 UTC
20:09:58 KST

China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
Indrajeet Rai / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Sep 03, 2026, 17:06 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
India-China ties have thawed since the border skirmish in 2020.
Former foreign secretary Vijay Gokhale argues that China waits for a strategic opening, acts pre-emptively and then builds a narrative of self-defence.His new book, “China’s Wars: The Politics and Diplomacy Behind its Military Coercion”, examines past conflicts and China’s recent grey-zone tactics.In an interview with Indrajeet Rai, Gokhale explains why the India-China relationship has entered an era of “armed coexistence”, why a full-scale war is not the most likely outcome but cannot be ruled out, and how political uncertainty after Xi Jinping could produce global economic shocks or military adventurism. Edited excerpts:You describe China as an opportunistic power. What does that mean, and when does Beijing decide to act pre-emptively?By opportunistic power, I did not intend to suggest that China is very different from other major powers. In the case studies in my book, China waited for the international situation to turn favourable, or for some advantage to accrue from its relations with other major powers, before carrying out conflict with a neighbour or another country. It used opportunity strategically to achieve its goals.The Chinese idea of preventive deterrence or preventive conflict differs from the Western concept. In the West, deterrence is a counteraction intended to stop the adversary from escalating. In the Chinese context, it is pre-emptive: China acts even before the adversary has had the chance to act first. The aim is to deliver a political and psychological shock so the adversary desists or fears retaliation.The 1962 conflict is one example. There was no indication that India intended to launch a military assault. But China used the words of then PM Jawaharlal Nehru and an international situation dominated by the Cuban missile crisis to act pre-emptively against India.
China often depicts its own aggressive action as defensive and blames the other side. How central is this narrative warfare to its strategy?The Chinese Communist Party utilised China’s difficult circumstances after the collapse of the empire and projected itself as the only organisation capable of pulling the country out of its problems. It placed the blame for China’s declining economy and global influence on external circumstances. It played the victim’s card: China was perennially the victim, and the party was the instrument that would restore it as a major power.
China’s grey-zone strategy seeks to steadily pressure and exhaust rivals while avoiding the escalation of tensions into full-scale war.
The blame, therefore, was always placed on somebody else: The colonial powers, the United States in the Korean War, India in the 1962 war and the Soviet Union in the 1969 conflict. There was never an acknowledgement that some responsibility also fell on China.This is not limited to foreign policy. The party does not take responsibility for major domestic failures either: The Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen incident. Blame falls on an external force or a few bad elements, never the party itself.You argue that China is pursuing sustained grey-zone coercion. How does this work against India?Since 1979, China has not fought a real conflict. The leadership made economic development the priority, and successive leaders after Mao Zedong focused on reform and opening up.But China was not willing to give up the use of force; it changed the manner in which force was used. Instead of hot wars or major conflict, it engaged and continues to engage in very low-intensity military conflict, popularly known as grey-zone warfare.Grey-zone warfare uses threats or actual force while staying below the threshold that might tempt the rival to launch a counteroffensive. It punishes or deters, but stops short of making the rival feel compelled to push back with force. We see it along the Line of Actual Control, in the South China Sea and in the East China Sea.I have characterised the situation on the LAC after 2020 as the end of peaceful coexistence and the beginning of armed coexistence. Armed coexistence does not mean conflict. It means China will continue to take grey-zone military action around the LAC to keep us tied down and to exhaust us not only financially - because keeping forces and equipment at those heights costs a lot - but also in terms of men and material.This fulfils a key Chinese objective: Keeping India confined to South Asia.
Apart from the United States, there are few potential rivals in this century, and India is one. If you look at India, it's geographical location, its population size, its territorial size, its talent, it's economic potential. All of it lends a credence to the belief that India can become a major power in this century. And clearly, China would like to delay that possibility.Does that mean a large-scale India-China war is unlikely in the foreseeable future?Nobody can predict this definitively. China and its decision-making processes are opaque, and there are no alternative channels of information such as free media or civil society.China is a mature state focused on becoming the strongest economy and power in the world. On a rational cost-benefit analysis, the price of a major war with India could exceed the benefits. Logically, China would be reluctant to engage in such a conflict.At the end of the day, however, it is impossible to predict. We have to be prepared for the worst, while logically understanding that a hot conflict with India may not be in China’s interest in the foreseeable future.China’s capabilities against Taiwan have grown, while the US is distracted by several conflicts. Could Xi Jinping move on Taiwan to secure his legacy?An American commander of the Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Philip Davidson, suggested that by 2027 China would have the military capability to launch an assault on Taiwan. Some interpreted that to mean China would attack by 2027, but he did not actually say this.China’s capabilities for an assault on an island have substantially increased: Landing craft, area-denial capabilities, communication systems and anti-ship missiles.It is one thing for a major power to bomb another country and destroy its infrastructure, and quite another to occupy or conquer it. That requires a very large commitment of forces and material, with no assured guarantee of victory.China’s demographic decline is already causing anxiety. An assault would mean mass casualties because boots on the ground would be required. After Galwan, India acknowledged within days that 20 soldiers had been martyred; China took much longer to admit fatalities. With Taiwan potentially producing casualties in the hundreds or thousands, Beijing will worry about the domestic impact.This is where democracy, for all its weaknesses, becomes a strength. A democratic government has electoral and constitutional legitimacy to act, including in war. In China, the party claims it has popular support but has never tested that proposition. The reaction to large-scale war casualties is unpredictable.Xi has removed the age and term limits that helped institutionalise succession. What happens after him and why should India worry?Deng Xiaoping introduced two reforms that stabilised succession: Those above 68 could not continue in top party positions, and the president was limited to two five-year terms. This helped ensure smooth transitions from Jiang Zemin to Hu Jintao and then to Xi Jinping.Xi has abolished the age and term limits. In an authoritarian system, no leader will voluntarily give up power because enemies may find it easier to target him, and he cannot be certain a successor will not misuse authority against him.China could enter a period of political uncertainty and potentially turmoil as Xi ages and factions emerge in a contest for power. It is unclear whether this happens before or after his death, or whether he intends to stand for a fourth term.Because China is the world’s second-largest economy, domestic turmoil would affect its economy, military and diplomacy and create huge ripple effects abroad. Beleaguered regimes also sometimes use an external threat to divert attention. India must consider whether turmoil could produce military adventurism and how to preserve its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.China has few formal allies and did little visibly to support Iran. Does it lack the partnerships needed to become a global leader?China lacks the United States’ large network of treaty allies. But we should not underestimate the goodwill it enjoys. The Belt and Road Initiative has been welcomed as an alternative route to development. Western assistance often came with harsh conditions; China offers fewer and less onerous strings. Nobody gives aid for free, but China has built substantial diplomatic influence.There was little need for China to do more in the Iran war. It could neither persuade the United States to stop nor force peace. It protected its oil interests and relations with Iran and the Gulf countries without entering the mediation game.
When the conflict ends, Iran will rebuild using its oil and gas wealth. It is unlikely to trust the West, while China can build infrastructure at a scale few others can match. China needs energy; Iran needs infrastructure and money. That creates an enormous downstream economic opportunity and a win-win situation. Why would China get significantly involved now when there seems to be no clear way out of the conflict?As US-China rivalry intensifies, which side of the emerging world order should India prefer?India should not look at the world order through an either-or lens. The United States and China will both remain major powers. The question is how, in a triangular or quadrangular relationship, including the European Union if it acts as a union, we create an international framework relevant to this century.
India has objective advantages: Its location, demographics and consumer base; tested political stability; an independent military capability and growing defence industry; and talent.I do not see how India can fail to become a major power in this century. The international order is disintegrating and all states are hedging their bets; India is doing so too. The task is not to choose a US-led or China-led order. It is to help build an order in which India is one of the leaders.
Indrajeet Rai is the editor for TOI Online. He holds a PhD in International Politics from JNU. He has experience in both research and the social sector. He enjoys the fast-paced world of “breaking news”—as well as the equally important work of breaking down news for readers.

Feminist Activist and Icon Gloria Steinem Dies at 92
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:09:46 UTC
20:09:46 KST

Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist who inspired a generation of women and fought for gender equality, has died at age 92.
Her foundation announced the news in a social media post Thursday morning, sharing that Steinem had "passed away peacefully" at her home in New York City the day before, surrounded by her loved ones.
"Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor," the statement read.
"Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle."
Steinem was a celebrated writer and magazine editor, who became the face of the women’s movement.
In the 1970s, Steinem co-founded a number of trailblazing initiatives, including the Women's Action Alliance, a feminist organization dedicated to fighting sexism, Ms. magazine, a publication focusing on women’s issues, and the National Women’s Political Caucus, a multi-partisan grassroots organization aimed at increasing women’s participation in the political process.
Steinem avidly campaigned for women's reproductive rights and later supported the legalization of same-sex marriage. Much of her work centered on pushing for equal rights and pay for women.
"Feminism has never been about getting a job for one woman. It’s about making life more fair for women everywhere. It’s not about a piece of the existing pie; there are too many of us for that. It’s about baking a new pie," she wrote in a 2008 op-ed for the Los Angeles Times.
Steinem’s early years
Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio, on March 25, 1934. The family moved a lot, somewhat due to her father’s profession as a traveling antiques dealer, and Steinem didn’t attend school full-time until she was around 12 years old. After her parents separated, Steinem lived with, and helped care for, her mother, who suffered from depression.
In her 2015 memoir, My Life On The Road, Steinem credited her mother for influencing her journey to activism.
“Depression is anger turned inward; thus women are twice as likely to be depressed,” she wrote. “My mother paid a high price for caring so much, yet being able to do so little about it. In this way, she led me toward an activist place where she herself could never go.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

Construction of British deep space radar to begin in 2027
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:25 BST
20:00:25 KST

Construction of the British site for the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability will begin in April 2027 under a contract the United States Space Force signed with Northrop Grumman in August 2024, with planning permission sought in March this year and initial authority to operate already issued, according to a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what progress had been made on establishing the capability, referring to paragraph 81 of the Defence Investment Plan.
Mr Pollard said: “The Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability (DARC) is a ground-based radar system that will provide 24/7, all-weather capabilities to detect, track, identify and characterise objects up to Geostationary Earth Orbit. DARC will require three permanent radar sites and a radar operations centre to provide 360-degree coverage: in Australia, the UK and the US. Construction of sites in Australia (Exmouth) and the US (IROC, Eglin) have been completed.”
He said: “The USSF signed a contract with Northrop Grumman on 23 August 2024 for construction of the UK site starting April 2027.”
On the regulatory position, he said the department has completed an environmental impact assessment including a landscape and visual impact assessment, to ensure the project has minimal impact on the local skyline, and that this formed part of a town planning application submitted to the local planning authority in March 2026.
He added: “The Defence Electromagnetic Authority, working with the Office of Communications, has issued an initial Authority to Operate. MOD and the Civil Aviation Authority is completing the necessary safety of flight procedures for local airspace.”
What DARC does
Most existing radars are optimised for low Earth orbit, where the majority of satellites and debris sit a few hundred kilometres up, and objects in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres have been tracked largely by optical telescopes, which depend on clear skies and darkness. A radar capable of reaching that altitude works regardless of weather or time of day, which is what the reference to 24/7 all-weather capability in the answer describes. The three sites, spread across Australia, Britain and the United States, provide continuous coverage of the geostationary belt as the Earth turns.
Geostationary orbit holds communications satellites, missile warning satellites and a substantial share of the space infrastructure military operations depend on, and both Russia and China have demonstrated satellites capable of manoeuvring close to others, which is a behaviour that cannot be characterised without being able to see it happening.
The United Kingdom site is at Cawdor Barracks in Pembrokeshire, west Wales, an existing defence site the Army had been due to vacate. The answer’s references to the local skyline and to safety of flight procedures for local airspace reflect the physical scale of the installation, which involves large parabolic dish antennas across a substantial footprint.
The programme is a trilateral effort under the AUKUS partnership, jointly funded by the three nations, with the American site at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and the Australian site at Exmouth in Western Australia, which the answer confirms are both complete.
Britain’s wider space programme sits under UK Space Command, established at RAF High Wycombe in 2021, which brings together military space operations alongside the existing space domain awareness assets including the Fylingdales radar in North Yorkshire, itself part of the American ballistic missile early warning system.

India targets weapons self-reliance with fully local assault rifle

India targets weapons self-reliance with fully local assault rifle
India has been slowly trying to reduce its reliance on Russian-made weapons as Moscow prioritises its own needs for its ongoing war with Ukraine
The Sher, or Tiger, will replace the older, heavily criticised Indian National Small Arms System (INSAS) service rifles used by the Indian Army.
Complaints about the INSAS emerged just a year after it was adopted by the army. Indian soldiers fighting the high-altitude Kargil war in 1999 against Pakistan-backed forces in Ladakh, then a part of Kashmir, said the firearm tended to jam or its magazine would crack in the freezing temperatures.
After the Sher was successfully test-fired on August 23 at an ordnance factory in the northern town of Amethi, experts celebrated having cracked the Kalashnikov code without having to import any parts.
This is a significant victory as most of India’s military weapon systems – from Su-30MKI fighter jets to several warships and submarines – come from Russia.
India has been slowly trying to reduce its reliance on Russian-made weapons, as Moscow prioritises its own needs for its ongoing war with Ukraine, by buying equipment from France, Israel and the United States as well as boosting domestic manufacturing.
