Germany's far-right AfD aims for breakthrough in state election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:56:22 UTC
18:56:22 KST

Germany's far-right AfD aims for breakthrough in state election
BERLIN, Sept 3 - Voters in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt go to the polls on Sunday in an election where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is hoping to win power for the first time and mark a historic shift in German politics.
State Premier Sven Schulze from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) says the election in Saxony-Anhalt is "a decision that will set the course for Germany."
Opinion polls in the state have put support for the AfD, which wants to restrict immigration, restore ties with Russia and quit the euro, at more than 40%, 15 to 20 points ahead of the CDU, which rules in a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and pro-free-market Free Democrats (FDP).
Most other parties running have refused to cooperate with the AfD, designated by the local office of Germany's domestic intelligence service as extremist right-wing, meaning that a CDU-led coalition may keep it from power in Saxony-Anhalt.
But the size of its support, fuelled by disillusion with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's unpopular government in Berlin, has laid bare how far German politics has moved in the decade or so since the party's formation in 2013.
'MY BEAUTIFUL, OLD, SAFE GERMANY'
Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old hoping to become the first AfD state premier, has campaigned for months, drawing crowds to packed rallies in village halls and town squares across the state.
"I want my beautiful, old, safe Germany back," he tells supporters at his rallies.
Formed in western Germany at the height of the euro zone debt crisis, the AfD has increasingly drawn its support from the formerly communist states in the east, where surveys show a lingering sense of dissatisfaction with the results of reunification in 1990.
Siegmund, who rejects the far-right label, says he speaks "the language of the people" with a smiling approach that avoids the rhetoric of party colleagues like Bjoern Hoecke from the neighbouring state of Thuringia, who has been twice convicted for using Nazi slogans.
He has shrugged off criticism that his policies would deepen the problems of a state with a declining population, which economists say will depend on immigration to fill a shortage of workers in sectors from healthcare to tourism and the state's large chemicals industry.
The region has suffered along with the rest of Germany during the recent downturn, with unemployment running at around 8%. But economists say Saxony-Anhalt, a heavily rural state, has done relatively well in recent years, with the establishment of new industrial sectors, including logistics and renewable energy.
"Taking a broad view over the past 10 to 15 years, economic development in Saxony-Anhalt has been more than satisfactory. I would even say it has been quite good," said Thomas Brockmeier, head of the Halle-Dessau Chamber of Industry and Commerce.
Instead, Siegmund has focused on issues ranging from "culturally alien" immigrants and asylum seekers to leftist teachers, gender ideology or the cost to German industry of losing access to cheap Russian oil and gas through support for Ukraine.
Germany's most influential news magazine, "Der Spiegel", dubbed Siegmund "Germany's most dangerous man" in a cover story last month. Siegmund himself, a practised social media user, saw the headline as "good advertising" and posted footage of himself signing the cover on his Instagram account.
DECISIVE ELECTION
Across Europe, anti-establishment parties have made gains and Sunday's vote will be a test of whether the far-right can form a government in the continent's largest economy.
The AfD sees Saxony-Anhalt, which will be followed by two other state elections in the northeastern region of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and in Berlin this month, as a stepping stone to victory in national elections due in 2029.
Although its support is strongest in the east, the party scored around 20% in elections in the western states of Baden-Wuerttemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate earlier this year, underlining its growing nationwide appeal.
State governments in Germany make up the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, and have wide powers over education, culture and domestic security and an AfD state government would complicate everyday politics for Merz.
This week, the SPD interior minister of Thuringia warned that an AfD state interior minister would be a "flagrant security risk for the Federal Republic" because of the possibility of security information leaking to extremist groups.
"The consensus-driven model we have been used to within Germany over the last decades is now threatened," said Janos Richter, an analyst with the Verfassungsblog, a public law forum for constitutional and public law.
Siegmund has promised to recruit politically sympathetic officials from other states to help an AfD government to push through changes to schools, law enforcement and asylum centres, pointing to probable clashes with the federal government and other states. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

1 in 5 children in 21 countries face sexual abuse linked to online contact: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:56:11 UTC
18:56:11 KST

An estimated 20 million children aged 12 to 17, or nearly 1 in 5, experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse in a single year across 21 countries, UNICEF said on Thursday.
The findings are included in a new report titled Through Children’s Eyes: How Digital Technologies Enable Child Sexual Abuse, which combines survey data with testimonies from children who experienced abuse.
“The report reveals a painful reality. More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play, and connect with friends,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said.
“Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away,” she added.
The report estimates that more than 15 million children were exposed to unwanted sexual content, while nine million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will.
Around four million had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.
Most cases occurred on social media platforms
Nearly 60 percent of cases occurred on social media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and WhatsApp, while 14 percent took place in online games, according to the report.
The report found that 57 percent of cases involved someone the child already knew, including peers, romantic partners, friends and family members. At the same time, 38 percent of children first encountered the perpetrator online, with abuse facilitated through tools such as fake accounts and private messaging.
The experiences had a significant impact on children’s emotional well-being, sense of safety and trust in others, with research participants describing feelings of fear, shame, confusion and isolation, according to the report.
Children who experienced technology-facilitated exploitation were four times more likely to report suicidal thoughts or behaviours and self-harm, and also reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, the analysis found.
In Mexico and North Macedonia, the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviours was more than eight times higher among children who experienced abuse, while in Pakistan the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher, according to the report.
Children suffer in silence
More than 40 percent of cases were never shared with anyone, while fewer than one percent were reported to authorities including police, social workers or helplines.
The most common reason children remained silent across the countries surveyed was not knowing where to go or whom to tell, UNICEF said.
The report calls on governments, technology companies and other stakeholders to strengthen protections for children online, including stronger privacy safeguards, restrictions on unsolicited contact from adults, safer recommender systems and improved detection and reporting of abuse.
It also calls for stronger laws and enforcement measures, improved reporting and support systems, and greater support for families, schools and communities.
“All of us, including governments and technology companies, must do more to protect children online,” Russell said.
The report draws on nationally representative surveys of approximately 21,000 internet-using children aged 12 to 17 across 21 countries, alongside in-depth interviews with 100 young people who experienced abuse in childhood.
UNICEF said the survey findings are representative of internet-using children rather than all children, particularly in countries with lower internet connectivity.

Greater Taipei buses free for World Car-Free Day

2026-09-03
09:56:03 UTC
18:56:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Greater Taipei's transport departments announced Thursday that bus rides will be free on Sept. 22 for World Car Free Day to encourage use of public transport.
CNA reported the free rides will cover 719 city bus routes served by 5,842 buses across Taipei and New Taipei. Officials said the program is aimed at people who usually drive or ride scooters, encouraging them to use public transport instead.
Taipei Deputy Mayor Chang Wen-te (張溫德) said the city has taken part in International Car-Free Day for 25 years. He said this year's campaign is intended to encourage people to consider alternatives to their usual way of getting around.
Bus operators will deploy as many vehicles as possible to meet higher demand, the Taipei City Bus Joint Management Committee said. Staff will also be assigned to major stops and transfer stations to help passengers, per Rti.
Taipei Transport Commissioner Hsieh Ming-hung (謝銘鴻) said that about 3,500 bus drivers work across the two cities. Operators will increase service while complying with working-hour rules, and officials hope daily bus ridership will rise 5% to 10% from the current 2 million passenger trips a day.
New Taipei Transport Commissioner Chung Ming-shih (鍾鳴時) said the two cities estimated the program would cost about NT$50 million (US$1.64 million) in subsidies. New Taipei is expected to provide about NT$20 million, while Taipei will provide about NT$30 million.
Participating buses will display signs showing that rides are free, Chung said. Card readers and fare boxes will also be covered to prevent passengers from paying by mistake.
CTEE reported that intercity and highway buses are not included in the program. Passengers using those services will still have to pay the normal fare.
World Car Free Day is held each year on Sept. 22 to promote alternatives to driving. It grew from European car-free campaigns in the 1990s and later spread worldwide.

6 Taipei must-see galleries in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:55:25 UTC
18:55:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — From open-call showcases spotlighting emerging local talent to intimate botanical portraits, Taipei's art spaces are brimming with creative vitality.
Setting the tone, Whitestone Gallery’s contemporary art exhibition dedicated to the virtual pop icon Hatsune Miku drew massive crowds and long queues on opening day, underscoring the powerful convergence of youth culture and fine art.
Here are six gallery exhibitions to explore in Taipei this month.
"Song of Youth: Brushing the Sun"
After previously spotlighting European and US masters as well as young creators from China, Bluerider Art turns its focus back to local soil.
Selected from nearly 2,000 submissions by 500 applicants nationwide, this open-call exhibition presents nearly 60 works by 21 emerging Taiwanese artists born after 1985. The show highlights the dynamic interplay between heritage and experimentation in contemporary Taiwanese art.
The exhibition title draws from ancient poetry and Qu Yuan’s (屈原) classic Li Sao, blended with poet Rainer Maria Rilke’s mandate to “live the questions.”
Among the highlights are Wu Shang-wei (吳上瑋) and Lin Po-yang (林博揚). Li Hsiao-sheng (李曉昇) and Tsai Ming-tsan (蔡名璨) break traditional ink conventions. Chen Kuan-ray (陳寬睿) uses chemical pigments to generate natural rust on canvas.
Location: Bluerider Art Taipei Dunhua
Date: Aug. 1 – Oct. 4
"Objects of Desire: Where Micro and Macro Open in All Directions" and "Shelter Island"
Double Square Gallery is staging a compelling dual solo exhibition. Spanish artist Ana de Alvear, winner of the Edge Artist Award at Taipei Dangdai 2025, presents "Objects of Desire: Where Micro and Macro Open in All Directions."
Drawing inspiration from Susan Stewart’s cultural analysis “On Longing,” Alvear uses hyperrealistic colored-pencil trompe-l'œil techniques in series like “Moss and Void Labyrinth” to challenge spatial perception.
Sharing the gallery space, Taiwanese artist Chang Shan-hsueh (張善學) presents "Shelter Island," an inquiry into natural ecosystems and Taiwan’s historical role as a glacial refugium. Elevating flora from background motif to primary subject, Chang delivers vertical botanical portraits alongside his Datun Volcano Group landscape triptych.
At the center of the gallery sits a live installation of ferns cultivated on the artist's apartment balcony, transforming the concrete urban residence into a living sanctuary.
Location: Double Square Gallery
Date: Aug. 15 – Sept. 26
"A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks"
A favorite in fashion and street-culture circles, Taiwanese artist Sangna Take (桑拿大可) makes his return to Eslite Gallery with his second solo show, "A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks."
Named after fundamental daily garments, the exhibition reflects the unvarnished vulnerability and relaxed state of returning home and shedding societal roles. Featuring 34 new paintings and six ceramic sculptures, the exhibition reveals heavy stylistic influences from Nara Yoshitomo and Jean-Michel Basquiat.
Sangna Take departs from traditional centered compositions, intertwining his signature slacker boy figures with new characters such as fairies and anthropomorphic plants.
The exhibition also debuts Sangna Take's first official self portrait.
Location: Eslite Gallery
Date: Aug. 15 – Oct. 10
"Professional Amatures"
Curated by TKG+ Projects exhibition planner Huang Chung-li (黃仲笠), "Professional Amatures" emerges from an insider's critique of institutional art structures. The exhibition brings together five artists to examine how art market mechanisms define concepts of professionalism and value.
Lin Guan-ming (林冠名) uses photography to document stylized public visuals and labor. Hsu Chia-chen (許家禎) reinterprets Taiwanese sculpture history through public monuments and traditional molding.
Cheng Po-tsung (鄭帛囱) crafts intimate micro-paintings using everyday stationery, while Yang Hui-ching (楊惠青) showcases "blind drawings" cultivated from her background in art education and theater. Curator Huang Chung-li (黃仲笠) reclaims his identity as a painter with works that question formal canvas orthodoxy.
Location: TKG+ Projects
Date: Aug. 22 – Oct. 31
"Art of Miku"
Making its overseas debut at Whitestone Gallery, the "Art of Miku" contemporary art exhibition has entered its second stage, introducing a refreshed roster of artworks and international artists.
The showcase gathers more than 20 creators across diverse cultural contexts, including Auto Moai, Clasutta, Fabien Verschaere, and more. Through painting, sculpture, and multidisciplinary visual formats, the participating artists deconstruct and reframe the virtual idol Hatsune Miku, exploring the possibilities of virtual existence within contemporary art.
Online ticket reservations are required, with exclusive Taipei-edition merchandise available on-site.
Location: Whitestone Gallery
Date:Aug. 29 – Sept. 20
"The Binding Strand of" and "While Everything Falls Away"
Mind Set Art Center presents two concurrent solo exhibitions investigating materiality and sensory awareness.
Portuguese artist Rui Miguel Leitao Ferreira presents "The Binding Strand of," displaying 14 abstract paintings executed since 2020 that layer acrylics, repurposed canvases, and found objects.
Ferreira builds on geometric grid frameworks before allowing fluid paint application and exposed canvas seams to subvert the traditional flatness of modernist painting.
In dialogue with Ferreira's work, Taiwanese artist Huang Kuan-chun (黃冠鈞) presents "While Everything Falls Away."
Drawing on his background in sculpture and fiber arts, Huang stacks acrylic paint layers on glass before peeling them off to create freestanding "paint bodies." Inspired by Marcel Duchamp’s concept of subtle nuance, works like “Sky” are applied directly onto gallery windowpanes, allowing natural sunlight to filter through translucent paint films and dynamically evolve throughout the day.
Location: Mind Set Art Center
Date: Aug. 29 – Oct. 8

Putin says the war isn’t driving Russia’s falling birth rate
The war in Ukraine is affecting Russia’s birth rate, but it isn’t the main cause of the country’s demographic crisis, Vladimir Putin said at a plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum.
”SVO, of course, has some effect, but the SVO isn’t the reason. After all, Japan doesn’t have any SVO, and neither does South Korea, yet their birth rate is lower than ours. Yes, of course, we need to pay attention to all the factors. But that’s probably still not the main one,” Putin said.
Putin said there is no simple explanation for the falling birth rate: “We both know that in post-industrial societies the birth rate is low, while in countries with relatively poor populations it is high,” he said.
Putin said raising the birth rate will require new incentives for families and young women, along with a shift in “public consciousness.” He noted that Russia reversed the negative demographic trend and achieved a noticeable increase in the birth rate in the mid-2000s. “We have the experience, and we will definitely repeat it,” he said.
Rosstat stopped publishing monthly regional data on births and deaths in 2025, then completely removed the demographic section from its monthly report on Russia’s socioeconomic situation.
The move came amid a historic decline in Russia’s birth rate: an average of 3,012 children were born per day in March 2025, the lowest figure in nearly 200 years of record-keeping. Putin, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum, called demographics a matter of national security.

You go to bed Kuwaiti, you wake up stateless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:45:03 UTC
18:45:03 KST

Breadcrumb
You go to bed Kuwaiti, you wake up stateless
Since the decrees withdrawing Kuwaiti nationality began to pour down, Sunday, the day on which the official gazette Kuwait al-Youm appears, has become a day of anxiety. Kuwaitis feverishly await its appearance, snap it up immediately to see if their name is in it, or if they are to remain Kuwaiti for another week.
Since 2024, with the accession of Sheikh Meshaal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah to the ruler’s throne, the campaign of re-examining and withdrawing nationality has acquired new dimensions. Indeed, the new Emir announced that he meant to put an end to the cases of fraudulent nationality acquisition - the use of forged documents, false declarations, etc. – and to track down cases of dual nationality, forbidden by the law of the land.
The net turned out to be cast wide, since several categories of citizens naturalised quite legitimately were caught in it: people whose residence In Kuwait since 1965 or before had been one of the criteria for naturalisation on the basis of the 1965 census; people who had been granted citizenship in recognition for “eminent services” rendered to the nation”; women having acquired it through marriage to a Kuwaiti; as well as certain children of a Kuwaiti mother and foreign father who did not acquire citizenship automatically through their mother but could be naturalised. These citizens had started families. Their children and grandchildren were born and had grown up under these perfectly legal regulations.
Now those who cannot point to a “nationality of origin” risk becoming stateless, and swelling the ranks of the hundreds of thousands of biduns, the “withouts”, the approximately 10% of the population who are stateless. Mostly from the bedouin tribes, these residents did not acquire Kuwaiti nationality when the country became independent in 1961. They are now deprived of most of the rights of citizens, mainly the right to vote, and to access various other privileges such as property ownership and state support.
This radical change in the notion of citizenship has far-reaching consequences since it affects by extension the children and grandchildren of the excluded, who may became excluded themselves. It is still too recent for its effects to be to fully measured (some will be specified by decree) and to understand its deeper reasons. However, the consequent stiffening of nationality policy appears to be the fulfilment of the promise “to give Kuwait back to its original inhabitants, cleansed and rid of its impurities” made by the new sovereign when he ascended the throne.
A broad aim
Kuwait’s nationality law makes a sharp distinction between citizens “of origin” and citizens “by naturalisation”. That distinction is reaffirmed by the 2026 reform: Kuwaitis of origin are defined in particular on the basis of their establishment in the country before its creation in 1920 and the resulting affiliation, along with continuity of residence, while people having acquired the nationality through naturalisation – as well as their descendants in certain cases – remain legally bound by this status. The rules for withdrawal or revocation are not identical in these different categories and in certain cases specified by law, may have consequences for the descendants. According to the new dispositions, naturalised citizens no longer have voting rights, and are no longer able to stand in elections or be appointed to any representative body.
Among those affected by the withdrawal of nationality are prominent figures in Kuwaiti public life: doctors, professors, historians, athletes and former diplomats. Some have represented Kuwait or contributed for decades to its institutions and cultural and scientific life. Such is the case with Bader al-Awadhi, former Kuwaiti ambassador to the United Kingdom, deprived of his Kuwaiti citizenship by filiation in January, a repercussion of the posthumous withdrawal of his father’s nationality. Since May, this high-ranking civil servant has been a citizen of neighbouring Bahrain.
These revocations have also hit people known for their political stances.
How to live?
An official decision can take just a few lines. Its consequences may begin the very next day. Losing Kuwaiti nationality isn’t just a matter of losing one’s passport. Citizenship is linked to a vast array of rights, services and accesses: voting, education and scholarships, certain public sector and military offices, housing, health care, pensions, subsidised welfare benefits, certain banking services, inland travel, stability of one’s judicial status. The question which the excluded person asks is not “What have I lost?” but “How can I live?”
After their citizenship has been withdrawn, the person concerned can only travel for a short time on their Kuwaiti passport. When that has expired, someone who hasn’t been able to get a passport corresponding to their original nationality or some other travel document, may find themselves unable to leave the country.
According to several witnesses, the regularisation procedure involves great pressure to hand over their nationality documents, to have their fingerprints taken and sign documents connected with their change of status. They explain that the non-fulfilment of these procedures can have consequences for their family’s access to certain benefits, especially in the areas of education and health. So for many families what is involved is not merely an administrative formality but an unavoidable step if they want to leave their children’s daily lives undisturbed.
The latter are in some cases the first collateral victims if one of their parents should lose their Kuwaiti nationality: it’s called “revocation by dependence”. Their number is unknown but some estimates put the total at 200,000.
Consequences for employment, housing, property
The change of status also directly affects work. Public service jobs reserved for Kuwaiti citizens are no longer open to these people. In the military and security sectors, where only citizens can be engaged, certain employees may be transferred to civilian functions, in the best of cases. Access to certain management or supervisory positions may also be restricted. When the person concerned is also the family’s main breadwinner, these modifications have a direct effect on the economy of the whole family.
The change of status may also entail major financial burdens, in particular for people who have benefitted from a public real estate loan. Several people questioned about this explain that they were informed by the Kuwait Credit Bank that they could be obliged to pay back all the remaining capital due in a relatively short time, which might amount to more than $100,000.
Housing is also a major source of worry according to many witnesses. Several people deprived of citizenship explain that they no longer benefit from the same property rights or public facilities as a Kuwaiti citizen. In the event that the accommodation had been obtained via some state agency, some families say they have had to look for a trustworthy Kuwaiti citizen in whose name to register their property.
The wall of regularisations and appeals
For many, regularising their situation does not simply mean filling out some administrative forms: it means having to reconstruct, in just a few months, a judicial status and daily security which up till then had been taken for granted.
In practical terms, the “deprived” have to establish a “nationality of origin”, then regularise their legal situation within a limited amount of time. But how do you find a “nationality of origin” when you were born in Kuwait, when your father and grandfather were also born there and when your family lived there under the British protectorate? How can you demonstrate your connection with another state in which no one in your family has ever lived and from which your family may not possess a single document?
Today several thousand people, including those with nationality revoked by dependence, are simply unable to claim a “nationality of origin”. Their official status is that of “non-Kuwaiti”. This does not yet mean that they are legally stateless, but this status shows that no other nationality has been established.
In Kuwait, nationality issues count as “acts of sovereignty”
The shock of the announcement is compounded for many by not knowing the reasons. In many cases, no precise or personalised justification is provided, which in itself makes any attempt to lodge an appeal useless. An online portal for complaints was opened by the authorities in May 2025, but it has been deactivated since the beginning of 2026. So in practice anyone who has been deprived of their nationality in 2026 has no access to that means of recourse, any more than those who lodged an earlier appeal.
In Kuwait, nationality issues are treated as “acts of sovereignty”, which drastically limits the criteria for submissions to the courts in the event of an appeal. The possibilities for review are slight indeed, despite appeals from human rights organisations and UN experts in favour of legal oversight and more effective channels for appeal.
Becoming an “illegal resident”
The fear of statelessness is very real in a country which officialised this status shortly after independence, considering as “irregular residents” the tens of thousands of (mostly) bedouins who were not registered with the nationality committees set up under the Nationality Act of 1959, shortly before independence in 1961.
People stripped of their nationality without recourse talk of “civil death”, witnessing as they do the disappearance of the rights that structured their place in society, while remaining physically present there. “What am I after losing my nationality?” What seemed to constitute one’s life in the city has suddenly taken the form of a stack of files to be updated: ID papers, education, employment, travel, accommodation, income, as well as the children’s rights.
I am still attached to my country, though the way I’m defined has been changed on paper. I look at the country where I was born and grew up and for the very first time, I ask myself a question I would have thought impossible: If I am no longer Kuwaiti, what am I?

Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:42:18 UTC
18:42:18 KST

Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
More students in the Netherlands are staying in their parents’ home or giving up the search for a place of their own, as the shortage of student housing remains high despite thousands of new rooms being built each year.
The country is short of more than 20,200 student rooms, barely down from 21,000 a year earlier, according to the annual student housing monitor from knowledge centre Kences, published this week.
Social housing providers have built nearly 5,000 units a year since 2022, meeting the targets they were set.
Kences had expected the shortage to climb, because private landlords have been selling up in response to new rent rules and higher taxes. Some 32,300 fewer students have rented from private landlords since 2024.
That did not translate into a sharp rise, largely because student numbers have also dropped, including among international students. The share of students living away from home has fallen from 50% to 43% over eight years.
Fewer rooms, riskier ads
 The rooms still on the private market are increasingly hard to rent safely. Many are advertised above the legal limit.
Scammers, meanwhile, have flooded TikTok with fake listings that pocket deposits for rooms that do not exist.
Internationals are especially exposed to housing fraud, as they rarely have a family home to fall back on and often do not know their rights.
Kences wants the profit tax paid by housing associations scrapped, which it says would fund 15,000 to 25,000 more student homes over ten years. “Every euro we hand to the tax office, we would rather put into housing,” director Reijnder Jan Spits told broadcaster NOS.
Even if every current building plan goes ahead, the centre warned, the shortage could still stand at between 10,000 and 35,000 rooms in eight years.

Putin's autocratic regime not enough to freeze assets of Russia-linked companies, EU's court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:41:42 UTC
18:41:42 KST

Autocratic rule alone is not enough to freeze the assets of Russia-linked firms, the EU's top court has said in an influential ruling on Thursday. National authorities need solid, objective proof of actual control.
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) ruled on Thursday that Russia's autocratic regime is not, on its own, enough to justify freezing the assets of a company indirectly linked to someone under EU sanctions, as any such measure must be backed by objective and solid evidence.
Brussels has currently blacklisted around 3,000 entities and individuals considered to be part of the Russian industrial-military complex that is participating in the invasion of Ukraine, pending extension on 15 September.
The judgment sets clear limits on how far national authorities can go when freezing the assets of entities not directly listed under EU sanctions, but alleged to be linked to a sanctioned individual.
The case concerns Inter Rao Lietuva, a Lithuanian electricity company that Lithuanian authorities placed on the national asset-freeze list despite it not being directly targeted by EU sanctions against Russia.
Lithuanian authorities argued that the company's ownership structure made it sufficiently connected to sanctioned individuals to justify the freeze: 51% of its shares are owned by Rao Nordic, a Finland-registered company wholly owned by PJSC Inter RAO, a major Russian state-controlled energy firm.
Since the company was ultimately controlled by the Russian state, the authorities concluded it was under the indirect control of President Vladimir Putin, who is himself subject to EU sanctions.
The CJEU rejected that reasoning, ruling that restrictive measures must rest on proven control over the entity concerned, supported by objective and sufficiently solid evidence.
As a result, the judgment concludes that the mere fact that Russia's political system is autocratic and oligarchic — giving Putin virtually unlimited power — does not by itself amount to sufficient evidence of his control over the company.
At the same time, the national authorities might take into account all relevant information to assess the effectiveness of the control, even of an informal nature, by another person or entity subject to EU sanctions.

Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:41:30 BST
18:41:30 KST

Italian Grand Prix declared heat-hazard race
- Published
The Italian Grand Prix has been declared a heat-hazard race as high temperatures continue in the country following the summer heatwave.
A heat hazard is an official designation for an event where it is forecasted that temperatures will be more than 31C at some point during the race on Sunday.
The ambient temperatures around Monza, north-east of Milan, are expected to be in the mid-30C region all weekend.
They peaked at 36C on Wednesday afternoon near Milan's Linate airport.
The ruling means drivers can use a system that flows cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls.
The cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure they do not have a competitive advantage.
- How to follow Italian Grand Prix on the BBC 
  - Published2 hours ago
Italy is the second race this year to be declared a heat hazard. The first was Austria early in the summer heatwave.
Some drivers prefer not to use the cooling kit because of discomfort, and because there have been issues with the coolant running out before a grand prix is finished.
In that case, the liquid ends up at car temperature, which is considerably higher than ambient.
Temperatures in the cockpit of an F1 car can be more than 40C, and drivers are wearing several layers of fireproof clothing in addition to a balaclava and helmet, so overheating is a serious concern.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:33:12 UTC
18:33:12 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Norway's seizure of the Russian research vessel Professor Molchanov is real piracy, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in an interview with TASS on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
"Seized is a better word than detained. Detained is about something legal. Now we see the big picture of what's happening. Earlier, perhaps even 10-15 years ago, one could have harbored illusions that this was some kind of legal procedure, that there were some legitimate claims that could somehow be fought off in court or arbitration. You see what's happening now. The West has legalized, or rather, I would say, simply lifted the veil on piracy, uncovering a seemingly relic, not even of the Cold War – there was nothing like this during the Cold War – a relic of the period <...> from the Middle Ages to the Great Geographical Discoveries, literally making Jack Sparrow its own symbol of modernity," Zakharova said, answering a related question.
"This is precisely one element of this new interpretation of maritime affairs, or the maritime agenda, in the West. Previously, in recent decades, the post-war period, and even the pre-war period, maritime affairs were dominated by maritime law. It was developed, it was elaborated at the national level, at the regional level, at the international level. It was precisely this law that was relied upon in dealing with civil matters. The militaries and navies of various countries had their own laws, both for their conduct in peacetime and for the conduct of military operations. Today, everything is jumbled, everything is thrown off, everything is mixed up. They have simply resorted to real piracy. This is monstrous, this is degradation, this is throwing them and the entire world back. But this is also reality," Zakharova stated. "What you are talking about, is one of the manifestations."
Earlier, the official website of the Governor of Svalbard published a statement that Norwegian authorities had seized the Russian research vessel Professor Molchanov following a complaint from the Ukrainian company Naftogaz.

Families in flood-hit areas of Nepal are holding symbolic funerals for missing loved ones as the death toll from last week's flash floods rose to 1,252, with more than 4,200 people missing, official data showed on Thursday.
In neighbouring China, 21 people were killed and 541 remained missing, including 261 foreigners, according to local authorities.
The combined death toll from both countries stood at 1,273, while 4,757 people remained missing, including 844 foreign nationals.
In Rasuwa, one of Nepal's hardest-hit districts, families created funeral effigies using kaas-kush, or sacred grass, and performed final rites to "liberate the souls" of missing relatives after losing hope of finding their bodies, the Kathmandu Post reported.
On Wednesday, dozens of such effigies were cremated in a mass funeral at Pashupati Aryaghat temple in Kathmandu on the banks of the Bagmati River.
In Chitwan, another badly affected district, authorities buried unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples because the number of remains made individual identification and storage difficult.
Many flood victims have been left without places to observe mourning rituals after floodwaters swept away both family members and homes in several districts.
Those who lost everything and travelled to Kathmandu seeking shelter have also been unable to find space at public facilities for the rituals.
Military personnel, police and others continued search and rescue operations in flood-hit areas on Thursday.
Rescuers, however, faced difficulties as roads, power supplies and communications remained disrupted across wide areas.
They were also working to deliver relief supplies and maintain hygiene in shelters to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 metres, triggering an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley, while also burying the Gyirong border crossing in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.

Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
Nigeria has confirmed that around 200 US troops deployed to support its fight against armed groups will begin leaving the West African country, with most expected to withdraw by late September.
A smaller advisory and intelligence team will remain, while cooperation in training and information sharing will continue, Nigerian military spokesperson Major General Samaila Uba said on Tuesday. “The deployment of United States personnel was tied to specific operational and counterterrorism objectives,” Uba said, according to AP.
The troops arrived in February to provide intelligence, targeting, and training support. Washington subsequently deployed MQ-9 Reaper surveillance drones to Bauchi Airfield in northeastern Nigeria. The mission came after US President Donald Trump accused the Nigerian authorities of failing to protect Christians and threatened military action.
Nigeria rejected claims that Christians were being systematically targeted, saying jihadist violence, banditry, and communal conflicts affect citizens of different faiths.
The two countries conducted coordinated airstrikes against alleged Islamic State fighters in Sokoto State in December 2025. In May, Nigeria’s Defense Headquarters and US Africa Command said a joint operation in the Lake Chad Basin killed senior Islamic State figure Abu-Bilal al-Minuki. Trump described him as the group’s second-highest-ranking leader globally.
US Africa Command chief General Dagvin Anderson announced in July that most of the American troops had been withdrawn, saying the campaign had successfully degraded Islamic State’s leadership and disrupted its wider network. Samuel Memeh, chairman of Nigeria’s Democratic Leadership Alliance, disputed that assessment. Memeh told RT that the deployment had produced no significant improvement in security and argued that foreign forces alone could not defeat the country’s armed groups.
Nigeria continues to face overlapping threats from Boko Haram and its Islamic State-affiliated offshoot in the northeast, armed bandits operating across the northwest and central regions, and intercommunal violence. More than 40,000 people have been killed since the insurgency began in 2009, UN News reported in January.
Major attacks continued during the US deployment. On August 21, gunmen attacked several communities in Niger State, reportedly killing 30 people and abducting hundreds of worshippers from a mosque. Residents put the number of captives as high as 600, although the authorities said the figure had not been verified. At least 2,000 people reportedly fled into neighboring Benin.

China lambasts France’s ‘discriminatory’ fast-fashion law

The law, which targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein and Temu, aims to curb the industry's environmental and local economic impacts.
China urged France on Thursday to abandon its recently implemented law on ultra-fast fashion, lambasting the new measure targeting major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein and Temu as "clearly discriminatory".

Read moreFrance targets Shein and Temu with new fast fashion levy
"China urges France to immediately halt the implementation of the anti-ultra-fast fashion law," commerce ministry spokeswoman Huang Ling said when asked about the law at a news conference.

Under the French legislation, ultra-fast fashion is determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.
Shein, known for its ultra-low prices and rapidly produced clothes, made a tepid Hong Kong Stock Exchange debut on Tuesday, after previous plans for initial public offerings in New York and London were derailed.
The online retailer moved its headquarters to Singapore between 2021 and 2022, which analysts say was intended to avoid increasing global scrutiny of Chinese firms.

At the end of last year, two men fled Iran. Aso and Baran* were strangers at the time. The way their stories would cross, then diverge, reveals the cruel arbitrariness of the UK asylum system in general, and the government’s controversial one in, one out scheme in particular.
Before he left Iran, Aso, 28, had converted from Islam to Christianity, putting his life in imminent danger. “I had to keep my conversion to Christianity a secret,” he says. “I knew if I was caught, I risked being executed by the Iranian regime … one of my relatives, who I trusted, paid smugglers to get me out last November.”
A few weeks later, at the end of December, Baran fled too. The 33-year-old had been politically active against the Iranian government, he says, and “feared being punished by the ministry of intelligence. I had previously been targeted by the Iranian authorities, shot at with rubber bullets and hit on the back of my head. My house was raided by intelligence officers one day when I wasn’t at home. They confiscated my ID. Relatives contacted me and warned me not to return home. They took me to another village and, from there – with the help of these relatives, who paid smugglers – I was taken out of Iran and crossed the border to Turkey.” A rubber bullet remains lodged in his genitals.
The men made their way separately to northern France. There, their paths converged – but they were still yet to meet.
In January this year, Aso and Baran boarded the same small boat, bound for the UK. Aso says the crossing was “terrifying”. His legs had been hit with a pipe by the smugglers the night before, and he spent eight excruciating hours in the dinghy on his knees. “There was no room to sit, and the waves were crashing into us. It is the most frightening thing in the world.”
On arrival, they were taken to a detention centre, where they finally met. Aso says he could immediately see that Baran “was a good and kind person, despite the difficult conditions in the detention centre – being locked in our cells for up to 12 hours a day, not knowing what was going to happen to us and feeling terrified of being returned to France. Despite all the stress, Baran was very calm and I always felt comfortable with him.”
Their fears about being sent back to France were well founded. The UK government’s one in, one out scheme was announced last July by then prime minister Sir Keir Starmer and France’s president, Emmanuel Macron. It is being piloted until 1 October, and aims to deter people like Aso and Baran from crossing the Channel in small boats to seek sanctuary in the UK. Since it began, more than a thousand asylum seekers have been selected by the Home Office, apparently at random, to be returned to France.
The idea is that one person who arrives here in a small boat is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another who is brought legally to the UK from France. Those who are brought to the UK are distinguished by the fact they have not previously tried to cross the Channel in a small boat. The aim of the scheme is to make the UK so unappealing that refugees choose somewhere else – anywhere else – to seek safety. In effect, people like Aso and Baran, who want to settle in the UK, are used as reluctant human shields to protect our border from others in the same predicament as them.
Today, Baran is living on the outskirts of Lille, sleeping under a tree in the park. I meet him in the centre of the city, and he appears to have no belongings beyond the frayed jeans, battered trainers and ancient fleece he is wearing, and a package wrapped in black plastic, holding his Home Office documents. His curly hair is prematurely streaked with grey, and the smell of wood smoke hangs around him, from his time spent huddled over an open fire.
In January, when Baran first realised he was at risk of being returned to France, he begged the Home Office not to deport him. His Home Office detention notes, shared with the Guardian, refer to his “food and fluid refusal” – a hunger strike – and it is recorded that he told officials: “I would rather die than return to France.”
They ignored him. He was returned to Paris in the middle of February.
“When I was returned to France, I was in so much pain from the bullet lodged in my genitals that I travelled to the local hospital to see if they could treat me,” he says. The smugglers knew the location of the shelter where he was being housed and found him there. “Because I was sent back to France, rather than staying in the UK, my family did not pay the smugglers, so they came after me to catch me and punish me, because they didn’t get their money.
“After they caught me, they took me to the Jungle in Dunkirk [an informal refugee encampment, known for its poor conditions], beat me with sticks and with their hands, and threatened me with guns. I was a slave for the smugglers. They forced me to wash dishes and clothes for eight to 10 hours every day, without breaks … even to go to the toilet. When I did not follow their instructions, they hit me in the mouth and used a log to hit me in the leg.”
Many of those who have been returned to France, after failing to access immigration lawyers who could successfully fight their case, have boarded the flight from Stansted to Paris’s Charles de Gaulle airport in a quietly hopeless state. But there have also been protests against these forced removals inside detention centres, and multiple suicide attempts.
In March, a month after Baran was sent back to France, Aso was sent back there too.
He says he was accompanied by Home Office guards on the flight out of the UK, which he found frightening. “It really is a terrible feeling. Two officers hold you and sit right next to you on the plane, treating you as if you’ve committed a major crime, as if you had killed someone or you are a dangerous person. My mental health was completely shattered.”
On arrival, Aso was placed in an immigration camp in Paris, “that was incredibly cold, with inhumane conditions and inadequate food”.
He sent me a message: “Please help me. I don’t know what to do here. We cannot have a shower because the water is ice cold. We are completely lost and confused. I am so scared. Please let me be safe. I don’t want to die. I want to live. I am deeply heartbroken. It has been four months since I last had any news of my mother and my country is now torn by war. If I am sent back to Iran, I will be executed, because I converted to Christianity.”
He was later evicted from the shelter – returnees are generally only accommodated there for a few days – and left homeless. “I found no support in Paris, and went back to the Jungle in Dunkirk, living in the forest there with a couple of other people I knew.” On 28 March, Aso sent me a WhatsApp message from the Jungle: “l am terrified here. These smugglers are heartless. They will hurt me wherever they find me.”
While Aso was searching for a safe place to stay in France, Baran was already back in the UK. At the beginning of March, he travelled back to Britain. A lorry brought him to Dover, and he was found hiding in it before being arrested and returned to a UK detention centre for the second time.
Baran is far from the only refugee who has been deported under the one in, one out scheme, then risked their life to return.
The Guardian has tracked more than 30 people who have been forcibly returned to France after arriving in the UK on a small boat. All say they have received minimal support in France and, at times, outright hostility. Some have crossed borders to Italy, Germany, Sweden, Spain and the Netherlands. While critics and Home Office officials call this “asylum shopping”, the asylum seekers see it very differently. They say all they are looking for is a place they can live safely without being thrown out, detained or forcibly returned either to their home country or another country they passed through on their journey.
Many, like Baran, have returned to the UK after being deported, finding conditions in France too difficult, particularly due to threats from the people smugglers who transported them across the Channel the first time.
Asylum seekers themselves estimate that approximately 200 of those who have been deported have returned to the UK – some, like Baran, by lorry, a route that smugglers have been using increasingly since the start of the scheme.
Previously, all asylum seekers crossing the Channel declared themselves to the Home Office on arrival in the UK, hopeful that they might be granted asylum and the chance to build a new and legal life. But now some are living under the radar, a development that critics claim actually reduces control of UK borders. The Home Office accepts that about 50 returnees have been detained a second time after returning to the UK. The Guardian has been given names, ages and nationalities of more than 30 returnees from 10 different countries, including Somalia, Georgia, Afghanistan and Syria, some of whom are living under the radar.
Every time I called Baran at the detention centre he was anxiously awaiting news about his case. “Many other asylum seekers have been released into the UK community or sent to France by plane,” he said. “But I am being locked up for many months here with no update about my case. Do you know what will happen to me?”
Aso was still struggling in France. On 3 May, I received another message from him. “Even though I am only 28, I feel like a 60-year-old man because of all the stress, grief and depression I’ve experienced. I am constantly living in fear of falling back into the hands of the smugglers or being deported to Iran by France.
“Unfortunately, the Home Office didn’t listen to us when we said France wasn’t safe. I’m aware that many asylum seekers in France burn off their fingerprints to avoid being sent back to countries like Bulgaria. A question: if you burn your fingerprints, will your fingerprints disappear?”
By 16 May, he was even more frantic. “I don’t want to hide it from you,” he wrote. “I can’t stay in France any more. Either I will return to Iran and let them execute me or I will go back to the UK. I have no choice. My life is ruined here. I have no money, no clothes and there is absolutely no one to help me. Living here is like dying every single day. It has been 50 days since I returned. I’m losing my mind. Of course I am under threat in the Jungle. I am so stressed, I don’t know what to do. I’m dying here every single day.”
In the middle of June, Aso returned to the UK in a lorry, just as his friend Baran had three months before. He was immediately detained too. “If France were safe and my life were not in danger, I would never have risked returning to the UK,” he told me. “I do not feel safe anywhere else. The United Kingdom is the only place where I am protected from the Iranian regime and criminal smuggler networks.”
Baran ended up being detained for more than four months on his return to the UK, longer than the usual timeframe for people detained under the one in, one out scheme. While in detention, he was told he needed surgery to remove the rubber bullet from his genitals. The Home Office declined to arrange it and said the surgery could be performed in France.
In July, France finally accepted the readmission request that had initially been made for him in March. Although Baran’s ability to speak and write English is very limited, he drafted a note to the Home Office in clear script just before his second removal to France, stating: “I can’t go back to France because over there is not safe for me. Don’t let them to send me back.” Since being returned there, he has been unable to access any health, housing or welfare services.
Aso’s life took a different path. While in detention in the UK, not knowing whether he would be returned to France for a second time, he became increasingly distressed. But a friend in Swansea offered to support and accommodate him, and he was overjoyed to be granted bail. For the first time since I got to know him, his messages became more positive.
“I feel like I’m getting better. I’m feeling safe,” he said in a message on 12 August. “It’s very hot here. I’ve decided to hit the beach for a dip to cool off.”
But Aso is desperately concerned about his friend. “I really don’t know why they sent Baran back to France for the second time but have allowed me to stay in the UK. It is honestly such a sad situation for Baran.” The two men have been in contact on WhatsApp, but Baran sometimes struggles to charge his phone, so many of Aso’s calls go unanswered.
The images of people in orange lifejackets arriving in the UK on overcrowded dinghies have been used by Reform UK and other right-wing political parties and commentators to claim the country is being overrun. In fact, the UK takes only a tenth or less of asylum seekers arriving in Europe and ranks 15th in Europe per head of population for asylum claims.
One in, one out was supposed to act as a deterrent, but it is not clear whether it has succeeded. The number of asylum seekers who have crossed the Channel so far in 2026 is down 40% on the same period last year, but that is in the context of asylum seeker arrivals to Europe being down significantly overall. Windy weather has also made crossings more difficult, and some people are travelling to the UK from France in lorries, uncounted in the immigration statistics. The Home Office has been reticent about what, if anything, will replace one in, one out when the pilot scheme finishes.
In Lille, Baran remains downcast. I offer to take him to the supermarket so he can choose a few essentials. He is too dejected to even look at the shelves. His chin sinks towards his chest and he says food no longer interests him. Under pressure from me to choose something, he puts a single apple, two bananas, a packet of nuts and a box of Ritz crackers in the shopping basket.
“I don’t have any friends in France or any plan,” he says. “A few guys who live near the park I’m sleeping in help me with food and sometimes let me have a shower at their place. The smugglers caught me before and I am frightened all the time that they will catch me again. My only hope is to find a way to return to the UK. But I don’t know how.”
Baran last made contact with the Guardian just before midnight on 24 August. His current whereabouts and condition are unknown.

Center Party eyes no-confidence motion against prime minister
The opposition Center Party is approaching other parties on a potential no‑confidence motion against Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform).
The party's Riigikogu faction leader Lauri Laats said Michal lacks the trust of the people and the minority government he heads cannot count on getting a majority in upcoming votes.
"Estonia needs a government capable of governing the country and taking responsibility. The Center Party is to begin consultations on a no‑confidence motion against the prime minister," he said.
Wednesday's resignation of Hanno Pevkur (Reform) as defense minister following a munitions procurement scandal is not enough to atone for the situation, Laats said, adding the head of government must also take political responsibility.
The issues according to Laats no longer relate to a single minister or a single area. "The prime minister cannot hide behind his ministers indefinitely. When problems affect one area after another, it is a problem with the management of the government as a whole. The defense minister's resignation does not absolve the prime minister of responsibility."
The management of national security is in dire straits, he went on, and should be more accountable if paying for defense procurement is in part accomplished through higher taxes. "For years, we have heard that Estonian people and businesses must contribute ever more to ensure the security of our country and its people. We have now learned that there are also serious problems in the management of national defense that have remained unresolved for years. If people are being asked to contribute ever more money in the name of security, the state must be able to take responsibility for how every euro is spent," Laats said.
"The Reform Party has led the government for years. During that time, the country's debt burden has grown, problems have piled up in healthcare, and we are now seeing serious problems in an area the government calls its highest priority – national defense," the MP added.
Pevkur announced on ETV's "Aktuaalne kaamera" on Wednesday evening he would resign from his post, after questions over a procurement of shells for Ukraine from an Indian firm.
A motion of no confidence needs at least 21 signatures from MPs to be heard. Center currently has seven seats.
Center, together with Isamaa and EKRE, recently called for snap elections ahead of the scheduled March 2027 Riigikogu election.
One of the most significant upcoming votes at the Riigikogu will be on the 2027 state budget.

RKIK head assumes responsibility: Agency failed to make sure contract reached audit office

Unknown Publisher

RKIK head assumes responsibility: Agency failed to make sure contract reached audit office
Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Elmar Vaher took responsibility for the fact that the National Audit Office did not receive the contract for a €70 million artillery shell deal despite repeatedly requesting it.
The National Audit Office has previously criticized the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK), which is responsible for procurement, for failing to provide it with the contract for a €70 million artillery shell deal despite repeated requests. RKIK maintained that the contract had been sent on June 5. The National Audit Office maintained that it had not received the contract.
Anastassia Kovalenko-Kõlvart (Center), chair of the Riigikogu Anti-Corruption Select Committee, asked for an explanation of the situation at Thursday's meeting.
RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher said he was responsible for the error. He explained that at 3:26 p.m. on June 5, RKIK's head of audit sent four contracts to the National Audit Office. "We were convinced that the contract had been sent, but it turned out it hadn't been," Vaher said.
He added that he had also spoken with National Audit Office Director Janar Holm, who asked why RKIK had not sent the contracts. "I asked my staff and they said we had sent them and that was where the matter ended," Vaher said.
In his view, RKIK was at fault for failing to make sure the email had reached the National Audit Office. "We didn't put them in the cloud," Vaher said. He noted that the files consisted of four PDF documents that should have gone through by email. "I don't understand why they didn't," he said.
Kovalenko-Kõlvart then asked whether, given that the contracts were confidential, RKIK should have obtained confirmation from the National Audit Office that the email had arrived. "I wouldn't be inclined to regulate everything," Vaher replied. He added, however, that RKIK could do a better job of sending documents in the future.
The Anti-Corruption Select Committee held an extraordinary public meeting Thursday to discuss problems with the use of funds and corruption risks in the defense sector in light of a National Audit Office audit.
Estonia made €70 million in advance payments to a company for shells for Ukraine, but the firm had no record of producing the required ammunition and failed to deliver. The dispute is now in court.

Aamir Latif
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
A record six million Afghan refugees have returned to their country in less than three years, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said Thursday.
"Recent history hasn’t seen a return movement on this scale," the UNHCR said in a post on the US social media company X.
"It is critical that all returns everywhere are voluntary, safe and dignified," it added
The UNHCR did not provide further details on refugees' return; however, a bulk of them is believed to have been repatriated from neighboring Pakistan and Iran.

Pakistan had been hosting millions of Afghan refugees who fled their country following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 and the years of conflict and instability that followed.
According to the latest UN figures, over 777,000 documented Afghan refugees are still residing in Pakistan, whereas the number of illegal refugees is believed to be over 1 million.

Green party leader Zack Polanski seeks to stand in byelection for Keir Starmer seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:08:45 UTC
18:08:45 KST

Zack Polanski will seek to stand as a candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, he has announced.
The leader of the Green party in England and Wales told the Camden New Journal on Thursday he would “stand up for people struggling to pay their bills” if he was elected as the representative for the area, which became vacant when Keir Starmer announced he was standing down as an MP.
In an effort to stave off accusations he was parachuting himself into the seat, Polanski said he had lived and worked in “this community” over many years. “I know it well and I love it. It represents so many of the things that make London so special. I am so excited by the prospect of representing this place in parliament,” he said.
Local Green party members will have the final say on the selected candidate, but the Guardian understands that they are supportive of Polanski running, and that there is no clear local activist with significant support expected to oppose him.
The Green leader, who has led the party to record election results in Camden – the local authority that covers the constituency – and across the country, already represents the area as a city-wide member of the London Assembly. “Holborn and St Pancras has everything that’s the best of our country and so much potential – but for too long now it’s been held back by governments who have failed to make the changes to improve people’s lives.”
Polanski said he was confident that the Greens could win the seat. Holborn and St Pancras has traditionally been viewed as a Labour stronghold, but the Greens have gained ground there over the last year.
“We know that the Greens can win here, and by electing me, voters will have someone who will always fight their corner – never scared of big donors or the party whip,” said Polanski. “Too often Labour has stood up for corporations and big money. I will stand up for people struggling to pay their bills.”
Adding that the byelection was a chance for the community to “make history” by electing London’s first Green MP, Polanski emphasised that the contest would be a two-dog fight between Labour and the Greens.
“We know that people are struggling – that the things we used to afford are increasingly out of reach – and this is a chance to send a very clear message that we won’t sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top,” he said.
The Greens are likely to pose the greatest threat in the byelection to Labour, which has held the central London constituency continuously since the seat was created in 1983, winning at least 40% of the vote at every election.
Only two Labour MPs have ever represented Holborn and St Pancras: the former health secretary Frank Dobson, from 1983 to 2015, then Starmer.
At the most recent general election in 2024, Starmer held the seat with 48.9% of the vote, ahead of the independent candidate Andrew Feinstein in second place on 18.9% and the Greens in third on 10.4%.
The Conservatives came fourth on 7.2%, Reform finished fifth on 6.1% and the Liberal Democrats were sixth on 5.8%.
The popularity of the independent and Green candidates at the 2024 contest, finishing second and third respectively, may have been partly owing to former Labour voters protesting against Starmer’s refusal to take a stronger position on Israel’s actions in Gaza in its war with Hamas.

Desperate to save Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Ukrainian forces counterattack and reinforce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:08:34 UTC
18:08:34 KST

- The pace of the Russian advance across Ukraine slightly increased in August
- The Russians' main objective is unchanged: to get forces in place for a siege of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk no later than next year
- Ukrainian counterattacks and reinforcements could slow the Russian plan
In August, Russian gains ticked upward in key sectors along the 1,200-km front line of Russia's 55-month wider war on Ukraine.
The coming winter could slow Russian advances as the trees lose their leaves and infantry infiltrators have nothing to conceal them from overhead drones. But for the next month or two, the trees will still have their leaves, and the infiltrators will still have their cover.
And that means, as fall wears into winter, Ukraine may lose yet more ground in the north and especially in Donbas region in the east, where Russia enjoys a substantial manpower and firepower advantage. "Russian forces still hold the operational initiative and are slowly capturing ... Donetsk Oblast as well as border zones in Sumy and Kharkiv Oblasts," mapper Thorkill warned.
The Russian gains belie a greater truth, however. In the middle of the fifth year of wider war, the situation on the ground only changes along the margins even as thousands die.
According to Thorkill's tally, the Russians occupied just under 220 square km of Ukrainian soil in August. That's 25% more territory than they captured in July. "The situation has deteriorated sharply in the Donbas in August," mapper Clément Molin explained.
To be fair, the Russians are advancing much more slowly than they did a year ago. "Compared to August 2025, Russian gains are down by nearly half," Molin noted. That's cold comfort to Ukrainian civilians and defenders in the areas where the Russians are still gaining ground, however. And the sheer proximity of the most aggressive Russian formations to the most vulnerable Ukrainian settlements means it might not take much more effort on the part of the Russians to turn these settlements into battlegrounds.
The Russians' main effort is still directed at the last big free cities in Donetsk. Inching forward at great cost from several directions, Russian forces are slowly closing a pincer around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk and the tens of thousands of civilians who still live in the adjacent cities.
Thorkill's map places the forwardmost Russian forces in Mykolaivka, just 4 km east of Sloviansk. This is the middle joint of the Russian pincer. The pincer's southern claw is a zone of disputed control stretching along the road between the ruins of the city of Kostiantynivka and the battleground town of Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka.
If the Russians can march through Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka, they can lay siege to the town of Druzhkivka, a few kilometers to the northwest. If they can capture Druzhkivka, they can turn north and assault Kramatorsk, a mere 6 km away.
Ukrainian counterattacks
The most fragile part of the claw is to the north. Bucking the overall trend of Russian gains in August, Ukrainian forces counterattacked in several sectors the same month. Most dramatically, a clutch of Ukrainian mechanized and air assault brigades extended a slow advance through the town of Nove, mostly cutting across a 100-square-km salient of Russian forces around 25 km northeast of Sloviansk.
The Nove counterattacks offer some hope that targeted Ukrainian action may slow the Russian march on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk from the north. Meanwhile, a reshuffling of Ukrainian units south of Kramatorsk could improve Ukrainian defenses against an assault on the twin cities from the south.
As new Ukrainian commander-in-chief Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi gradually addresses some of the imbalances in the Ukrainian ground forces, certain key units are getting help. Most notably, the 425th Assault Regiment is now subordinate to the 1st Azov Corps, which is responsible for the defense of Kramatorsk.
Trending Now
Keenly aware that the Russians intend to slowly infiltrate front-line settlements with small teams of infantry rather than rushing them with masses of easily-droned armored vehicles, the 1st Azov Corps has assigned the aggressive 425th Assault Regiment "to clear enemy infiltrators from the brigades’ areas of defense," the corps stated.
Infiltrators aren't the only problem, however. The Russians' favorite tactic combines small teams of infantry with massive aerial firepower in the form of precision-guided KAB glide bombs flung by supersonic Sukhoi Su-34 fighter bombers.
"Glide bombs hurt," Ukraine's 4th National Guard Brigade reported. "It's about 200 kg of explosives flying your way. And you can't really shoot them down like you can shoot down drones. They can collapse fortified buildings, bunkers, and entire urban blocks much more effectively than artillery."
After the dust settles from the glide bomb impacts, Russian infantry "infiltrate through the damaged areas, using the ruins for cover and concealment," the national guard brigade explained.
The same lack of long-range air defenses that exposes Ukrainian cities to relentless Russian bombardment also deprives front-line forces of protection from the Su-34s and their glide bombs. And so the Russians can keep bombing and keep infiltrating as long as the trees offer some concealment for the infantry.
The clock is ticking. The Russians will aim to position their forces for more direct assaults on Kramatorsk and Sloviansk no later than next year. The Ukrainians will aim to slow down the Russians, trading a little space for more time. Time Drapatyi may use to institute further reforms in the Ukrainian ground forces.
Zooming out and taking the long view, no one should expect major changes on the map of Russia's wider war as the fifth year of fighting grinds toward the sixth. Yes, the last two big free cities in the Donbas are in trouble. But "the overall situation remains unchanged since October 2023," Thorkill wrote.
The Russians slowly advance. The Ukrainians slowly fall back. And losses deepen on both sides.

Maduro, wife seek dismissal of drug trafficking indictment on immunity grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:08:00 UTC

Maduro, wife seek dismissal of drug trafficking indictment on immunity grounds
New York — Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife asked a judge on Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
In papers filed in Manhattan federal court, lawyers for Maduro said a judge was required by law to reject the indictment because it cannot be brought against a foreign leader.
"No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought," the lawyers wrote. "That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own."
Maduro and his wife are scheduled to go on trial on drug trafficking charges next June 1. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein has set oral arguments for Nov. 17 on motions to dismiss the indictment.
Maduro, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, 69, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York.
In separate papers filed Wednesday, lawyers for Flores said she too has immunity from U.S. prosecution on sovereign immunity grounds.
"It is an attribute of Venezuela's sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it," her lawyers wrote.
Maduro's lawyers said that even if Maduro were not entitled to sovereign immunity as the head of state, the case against him must be dismissed because he is also entitled to conduct-based sovereign immunity.
Meanwhile, the lawyers argued, Maduro "vehemently denies the allegations against him."
"If this case were to proceed to trial, it would be apparent that he has been falsely accused," they said.
Both have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against numerous alleged co-conspirators. They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
Federal prosecutors are scheduled to file a response to the arguments later this month.
President Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
U.S. prosecutors say Maduro carried out a conspiracy to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the U.S. by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins.
Maduro has remained defiant. On Sunday, he posted pictures of himself from prison on social media, saying he was "standing firm."
"I send these photos as a small gift to all my grandsons and granddaughters, to the boys and girls, and to all the noble people who love us," he wrote.
"I want you to know that we stand firm, with our hearts full of your love, that love that reaches us transformed into prayer, into constant action, into solidarity and true support. Infinite thanks for every word, for every gesture, for every blessing," he went on to say.
On the Telegram messaging service, he added, "We will remain strong, calm and confident: God is with us. God will provide. Venezuela will rise again," French news agency AFP reported.

The confirmed case involved a plant operated by Polish defense contractor WB Electronics in Skarżysko-Kamienna, a city in south-central Poland.
“In the case of Skarżysko-Kamienna, there is no doubt that it was deliberate arson, an act of sabotage,” Tusk said.
The fire broke out early on Monday at the WB Electronics facility. Prosecutors said warehouse facilities were destroyed, causing damage estimated at no less than 15 million zlotys ($4 million).
Polish prosecutors opened an investigation into suspected activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service and a terrorism-related offense. Investigators said the fire had been started using a device containing flammable materials, Euronews reported.

Second fire in Lublin
Tusk said investigators had not found evidence that a separate fire at a production and storage facility in Lublin was deliberately started. He added that arson could not be ruled out because of the nature of the company’s work.

The Lublin facility is operated by JFG Composites, which produces components used in aircraft construction.

Why is Tusk pushing cryptocurrency regulation?
Tusk linked the sabotage threat to a parliamentary vote scheduled for Friday, Sept. 4, on legislation regulating Poland’s cryptocurrency market. He argued that tighter oversight would make it harder to finance terrorism, sabotage, and arson in the country.
Tusk said Russia uses cryptocurrency as a primary mechanism for paying and recruiting people to carry out such operations. He also claimed that the “overwhelming majority” of terrorist operations identified by Polish authorities rely on cryptocurrency.
Poland’s intelligence services were consulted during the drafting of the bill and concluded that the legislation was needed to restrict the financing of terrorist and other criminal activities, Tusk said.
The prime minister urged opposition lawmakers to override President Karol Nawrocki’s veto of the legislation. Under Polish parliamentary procedure, a successful vote would pass the bill again and require the president to sign it.
Nawrocki vetoed legislation regulating the cryptocurrency market for a third time in June, arguing that the proposed rules would overregulate the sector and failed to address concerns raised by his office.
