Face Recognition Is Becoming the Norm for Dating Apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

In 2025, AI deepfakes flooded Tinder. According to the company, 98 percent of the content-moderation actions on the app were focused on combating fake accounts, scamming, and spam, pushing the company to expand its moderation efforts for its 60 million global users.
The problem is not unique to Tinder. The spread of AI-generated fake accounts has become a rising concern for dating apps, as things like chatfishing and voice cloning have gotten more widespread across the industry.
Among current online daters in the US, nearly half have been targeted by a dating scam, with US romance scams surpassing $4 billion between 2015 and 2025, according to the FBI.
The issue has forced just about every dating platform to adopt stricter authentication tools to ward off scammers. More and more, apps are asking that you surrender your most unique attribute in order to ensure that you’re a real person: your face.
More than a dozen major dating apps and sites use face recognition to verify users, often relying on liveness checks, 3D authentication, video selfies, or biometric ID to demonstrate humanness.
To combat the issue, Tinder launched the mandatory face-screening tool Face Check for new members in October 2025. “It’s not a feature. It’s a statement about what human connection online should require,” Yoel Roth, head of trust and safety for Match Group, which owns Tinder, said to WIRED in an email. Match Group tells WIRED that it is also starting to require Face Check for existing users in several of Tinder’s core markets, including the US and UK.
As face verification slowly transforms into a prerequisite for participation across the industry, the collective drive to combat bad actors has created a necessary and equally concerning new standard where “proof of human” profiles may soon be the norm.
Underpinning the shift, however, is a grim irony: In attempting to solve the problem of knowing whether someone is real, Big Dating is potentially creating more opportunities for privacy and security risks by forcing users to give up biometric data, while also legitimizing a culture of surveillance.
One company pushing for the use of ID-verification tech in dating apps is Tools for Humanity. The AI company created World ID, an iris-scanning biometric verification system, and partnered with Tinder in April, though it’s still optional for users. The most distinct feature about World ID is that confirmed users receive a “verified human” badge on the app after undergoing the process, which requires them to scan the colored part of their eye using the company’s orb device. They are given an identification number as their official World ID.
“In the near future, any dating app, like most online platforms in general, will need some sort of proof-of-human system like this,” says Tiago Sada, chief product officer at Tools for Humanity, adding that the way the majority of dating platforms handle verification is “super creepy, because you have to give your personal data to every single app that you want to use.” As stipulated by World’s policy, the orb does not share or retain any data; it is able to verify users without ever sending their data to a server. Once your image is confirmed, the orb sends the coded image to your phone before permanently deleting it, the company claims. Likewise, Face Check collects and stores an encrypted map of information about the shape of the user’s face, not the actual picture, Match said.
But even as dating apps claim that your biometric data is safe, security continues to be a significant concern.
Dating apps are subject to occasional data breaches, and while the inherent premise in these ID systems is that verification equals trust, cybersecurity researcher Katie Moussouris says that they are mostly a smoke screen. “Normalizing the idea that a face scan provides any assurance of identity or age is security theater.”
A liveness check requiring face scanning and live video only indicates a person was present at sign-up and does not guarantee that the person was not using AI to alter their appearance in real time. Likewise, an ID scan indicates an ID was presented, not that it belongs to the person who presented it. “Neither should be confused with trust,” Moussouris says. “A verified profile can still belong to a romance scammer who took over an account or created one using AI tools.”
And while passwords and usernames are interchangeable, faces are not, which makes them unique targets for attacks. More than that, biometric verification sets a risky precedent, says Woodrow Hartzog, a technology law professor at Boston University who previously served on the Massachusetts special commission on facial recognition.
“When we get accustomed to having our face scanned for everything we do online, it is really dangerous, not only potentially for the privacy risks but also to acclimate an entire population into thinking that that is normal behavior,” he says. “Facial recognition is the most dangerous surveillance tool ever created.”
Existing privacy laws are not equipped to deal with biometric verification on dating apps, according to Hartzog. He believes policies should ensure that less invasive options are used when they're available. In the case of biometrics, for example, your face, which can be monitored everywhere you go, is much more dangerous to collect than your thumbprint.
Utah’s State-Endorsed Digital Identity law, which went into effect in May, was one of the first major attempts at that. It limits the kinds of data that can be requested to only what is absolutely necessary while establishing a “duty of loyalty,” meaning platforms and providers cannot engage in practices that “conflict with the best interests of an individual” or “result in a disproportionate risk” to them. The law attempts to mitigate situations where people might have to present ID every time they log online, and also includes significant rules on the entity that’s collecting the data. The American Civil Liberties Union called it “the nation’s strongest digital identity bill.”
“Look at how easy it is to channel people's choices into agreeing to have their faces scanned as a condition of a good or service,” Hartzog says. “The more we can lean into policy frameworks that require strong protections from the company—rather than putting the onus on the person whose face is being scanned or who has to reveal their identity—then the better off I think we’ll be.”

Threats to civilian ships and aircraft constitute ‘state terrorism’ – Putin
The seizing and targeting of Russian civilian vessels constitute acts of “state terrorism,” President Vladimir Putin has said, warning that these actions are making peace talks with Ukraine more difficult.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Thursday, the Russian president denounced the recent captures of Russian civilian vessels and pointed to Kiev’s threats against passenger aircraft.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky previously stated that the “safe days” in Russian skies are over, addressing foreign airlines, insurers, and governments whose aircraft continue to use Russian airspace.
“This, of course, is a manifestation of state terrorism,” Putin said, adding that these actions “undoubtedly complicate the possibility of bilateral peace negotiations.”
He also warned that “those who remain silent and do not pay attention to this become accomplices in international terrorism,” referring to Kiev’s Western backers.
Putin’s remarks came a day after the Norwegian authorities seized the Russian research vessel the Professor Molchanov in Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s state-owned Naftogaz. The ship was detained while docked in the Russian settlement of Barentsburg.
The Professor Molchanov is a Russian state-owned research vessel that operates regular passenger and cargo services between Murmansk and Svalbard, carrying scientists, workers, their families, tourists, and supplies to Russian settlements on the archipelago. Moscow has said the seizure will be challenged in court.
The detention follows a series of Western seizures of Russian-linked vessels accused of belonging to a so-called “shadow fleet,” although the Professor Molchanov itself was seized in connection with a legal claim by Ukraine’s Naftogaz against Russia. Moscow has rejected the “shadow fleet” label as having no basis in international law and accused Western states of using sanctions as a pretext to interfere with civilian maritime trade.
Putin warned last month that attempts to seize Russian ships and sell their cargo amounted to “piracy and robbery,” saying Moscow is prepared to respond in kind in any part of the world.
Kiev has also stepped up attacks on civilian shipping. Putin said earlier this week that around 100 Russian merchant vessels had been damaged over a 40-day period, with sailors killed in the attacks, including Russian and foreign nationals.

Ig Nobel Prizes land in Switzerland amid stricter US border policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:46:59 UTC
17:46:59 KST

Ig Nobel Prizes land in Switzerland amid stricter US border policy
For the first time in their history, the Ig Nobel Prizes are being awarded outside the United States. On Thursday evening, Zurich’s Kongresshaus will be the venue for one of the world’s most unusual scientific events.
The awards recognise research that sounds so bizarre that one can’t help but laugh at first. That is precisely the principle behind the Ig Nobel Prizes: “It makes people laugh, then think.”
The prizes have been awarded for 35 years. Until now, they have always been handed out in the US: the first ceremony took place in 1991 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT); later, they were presented at Harvard University, and most recently at MIT again.
The fact that this long-standing event is leaving the US is down to changes in American immigration policy.
“The laureates travel from all over the world. With the current policy in the US, it has become more difficult to ensure that everyone can actually enter the country,” Mirko Bischofberger, one of the organisers of the Zurich Ig Nobel Prize ceremony, told the Keystone-SDA news agency. That is why they looked for a venue that would be easily accessible to the international scientific community.
More
ICE operations divide Swiss Abroad in United States
Switzerland has a number of key advantages in this regard, said Bischofberger: “We are a country that prize-winners can enter easily; we are at the heart of Europe; there are many direct flights; and we enjoy long-term stability.”
Will Swiss humour be a good fit?
It now remains to be seen whether the infrastructure and Swiss sense of humour are a good fit. The Ig Nobel Prize thrives on a particular brand of humour. The award ceremony itself does not take itself too seriously: traditionally, the audience throws paper aeroplanes onto the stage. Acceptance speeches may last no longer than 60 seconds. And anyone who goes over time must expect some unusual consequences. At a previous ceremony, a child would take to the stage and repeat tirelessly into the microphone: “Please stop, I’m bored!”
More
A Swiss Ig Nobel laureate talks about side effects and placebo effects
Even the prize money is part of the joke: award-winning researchers receive a genuine, albeit completely worthless, 10-trillion-dollar note from Zimbabwe.
Irony aside, the Ig Nobel Prizes are not intended as a mockery of science. Rather, they aim to show that even unusual or, at first glance, absurd questions can lead to research. It is therefore well-respected researchers who are honoured.
There is even an Ig Nobel laureate who went on to win the Nobel Prize: André Geim. And real Nobel laureates are always present at the award ceremonies. Those expected in Zurich are Tim Hunt, Esther Duflo, Abhijit Banerjee and Michel Mayor.
Switzerland is also a laureate
Bischofberger promises that things may well get a bit wild at the awards ceremony in Zurich. “Humour in Switzerland may not be quite the same as the geeky humour found in the world of science,” he said. However, he believes that the Zurich audience will be just as enthusiastic about it.
A look back at history shows that Switzerland is by no means lacking in Ig Nobel potential, according to Bischofberger. In 2008, the Ig Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the Swiss National Ethics Commission and the entire Swiss population. The reason: Switzerland had enshrined in law the principle that plants, too, possess dignity.

Apartment associations seek greater power over rentals and tenants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:46:00 UTC
17:46:00 KST

Apartment associations seek greater power over rentals and tenants
Apartment associations should have more authority in regulating rental relationships, says the Estonian Union of Cooperative Housing Associations, pointing to New York as an example, where a co‑op board can even decide whether a specific long‑term tenant is acceptable.
Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo said the associations' concerns are understandable, but any restrictions must be approached cautiously because private property is inviolable.
The union proposed this week that apartment associations be given the right, through a general meeting of owners, to prohibit renting out apartments. The decision would require more than half of the votes and more than half of the co‑ownership shares — a qualified majority.
"Rental relationships play a major role in the daily life of an apartment association. More and more associations have turned to us because they are unhappy with what is happening in rental apartments that are offered short‑term through various platforms," said Urmas Mardi, board member and head of the union's legal department.
He said constantly changing strangers treat shared property carelessly, make noise, ignore waste‑handling rules, smoke wherever they want and park their cars however they please.
"There have also been cases where co‑owned property has been damaged — for example, a late‑night guest arriving at a rental unit smashed the front door glass with a brick after failing to find the key. Other residents do not want to pay for damage caused by a short‑term rental operator," Mardi said.
The union presented its position to the Ministry of Economic Affairs, which earlier this summer completed a draft plan to amend the Tourism Act, aimed at organizing the short‑term rental market. The current law does not separately regulate short‑term rentals, even though the market share of guest apartments is steadily growing.
According to Mardi, associations in attractive tourist destinations are in the most difficult situation. In some buildings, only a few apartment owners live on site, while the rest are investment units. In such cases, permanent residents find it almost impossible to improve their building, because other owners simply are not interested.
"The value of the homes of resident owners also decreases when the building becomes a kind of passageway full of strangers instead of a home. This can create a trend where permanent residents give up, move away and the entire residential area changes," Mardi noted.
The union believes rental regulations must be carefully analyzed, because entrepreneurial freedom is a fundamental right and restrictions must be proportionate. At the same time, people also have a fundamental right to feel safe in their homes and to rest.
The union also pointed to practices in other countries. For example, in Spain, since last year, an owners' association may approve or restrict short‑term tourist rentals with at least a 3/5 majority. In France, tourist accommodation can be prohibited under certain conditions with a two‑thirds majority.
Workable solutions must be found
Minister of Economic Affairs Erkki Keldo said he understands the concerns of apartment owners and associations.
"If short‑term rentals bring noise, constant guest turnover or other disturbances, people must be able to protect their peace at home. No one should suffer because the use of a neighboring apartment clearly disrupts daily living conditions," Keldo said.
He said workable solutions must be found, and associations should be given better tools to deal with specific disturbances when necessary.
At the same time, restrictions must be approached very carefully. Keldo said most apartment owners use their property responsibly, and isolated problematic cases should not lead to limiting everyone's rights.
"A person must have the right to decide whether they live in their apartment, rent it out long‑term or use it in some other lawful way. It is not the state's role to decide how an owner must use their property if it does not violate others' rights," the minister said.
Keldo added that the inviolability of private property and the right to use one's property are cornerstones of a free society.
"If the state begins to restrict that right, there must be a very clear and weighty reason. Restrictions must be the last, not the first solution. Private property is sacred and must be protected," Keldo said.
Income goes to the owner, but the impact affects all residents
Short‑term rentals are also a concern in Pärnu. Deputy mayor Sander Kilk believes apartment associations need expanded decision‑making power over the provision of accommodation services and the distribution of related costs.
"In an apartment building, the impact is borne by permanent residents, the income goes to the unit owner, and the association currently has no effective lever," Kilk said.
Pärnu's distinct feature is strong seasonality: in summer, apartments are heavily used for short‑term accommodation, but outside the season they often remain empty. According to Kilk, this may not support the city's overall development, as community cohesion may weaken, local services may decline and problems may arise with heating and maintaining unused apartments.
He referred to a recent applied study showing that growth in short‑term rentals reduces the supply of long‑term rentals and increases housing prices.
"The impact is greatest in areas attractive to tourists. Therefore, in Pärnu this is not an abstract future risk but a question of the local living environment and housing market, and the state's own commissioned study has already identified it," Kilk said.
He stressed that Pärnu does not seek to ban short‑term rentals, but wants to find a balance between tourism, entrepreneurship and year‑round living conditions — and for that, legal and economic tools are needed. Where seasonal accommodation concentration begins to harm residents' interests, there must be a way to regulate the situation.
Thus, Kilk said owners' motivation to rent out apartments long‑term should be increased, and suitable incentives created.
The deputy mayor proposed defining in law that renting an apartment for up to 60 nights per year counts as sharing economy, but renting it out more than that constitutes economic and professional activity.
Kilk also wants single‑bed accommodation providers to be required to submit statistics, because most operators in Estonia are small‑scale. Under the current threshold, he said, the part of the market most important for housing policy, tourism planning and security considerations is left out.
He emphasized that Pärnu does not seek to restrict short‑term rentals or impose new requirements on any market participant, but wants the same rules to apply to the same service, while people who occasionally rent out their home should remain exempt.
Interior Ministry wants access to guest data
The Interior Ministry considers it important that the obligation to register accommodation users apply to all providers, and that providers share this data with security agencies upon request.
Ott Aarma, adviser at the ministry's law‑enforcement and criminal procedure department, said this is necessary for threat prevention: it is important to know who is staying at an accommodation facility, regardless of the form or platform through which the service is offered.
"If someone is a wanted person — usually dangerous to themselves or others — we must be able to locate them within the same 24‑hour period. To know where they are, such an obligation is necessary. And given how much of the market new accommodation providers now make up, this is a significant part," Aarma said. "Otherwise, people who do not want to be found will simply use only those services."
Currently, hotels mostly use paper cards where guests write down their information. Aarma said a more efficient solution would be a central portal where service providers enter guest data and where authorities could check information automatically.
"Then we can compare it with our list of wanted persons — both those wanted by police and others. And if we get a response that yes, this person is at accommodation X, we can act. That is the reason," Aarma said.
According to the draft plan, the Ministry of Economic Affairs wants to organize the short‑term rental market so that regulation is simpler, clearer and easier to implement, without creating disproportionate administrative burdens for the state, municipalities or businesses.
The ministry hopes to send the draft for approval in the last quarter of this year, with the expected entry into force next year or the year after.

Moldova records rise in attempts to recruit its citizens for sabotage abroad
Moldova's intelligence service has recorded a rise in attempts to recruit Moldovan citizens for sabotage activities abroad, mostly actions targeting Ukraine.
Source: Newsmaker, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Alexandru Musteață, Head of Moldova's Intelligence and Security Service, said there had been an increase in the number of recorded attempts to recruit the country's citizens for sabotage activities abroad, as well as in the number of people who agreed to take part.
"There is such a phenomenon as 'low-level agents'. People are found on Telegram and offered €20, €50, €100 or more, depending on the task. Often, it can be 'go there and take a photo', 'go to another place and take a photo', or 'see what is there'. If they see that a person is performing well, both the amount of money and the complexity of the tasks increase," he explained.
"It can then get to the point of 'go there, take a bag and put it under a car', or something similar. We are currently working on this issue together with our Ukrainian counterparts, because many of these operations are specifically aimed there," Musteață added.
He said that Moldovan police have already carried out several successful counter-operations together with Ukrainian law-enforcement agencies, while several others were conducted separately in Moldova and helped thwart malicious plans.
Musteață noted that no similar orders for operations on Moldovan territory have been observed so far. "But that means we have to prepare – and we are already in the process of intensive preparations," the official added.

Australian researchers create floating titanium metamaterial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:42:40 UTC
17:42:40 KST

- RMIT-led researchers built a 3D-printed titanium lattice that floats and stays buoyant even after significant structural damage.
- The material was 70% stronger than stainless steel or high-density plastic used in marine infrastructure at the same density.
Australian researchers have built a 3D-printed titanium structure that floats in water and keeps floating even after significant damage, according to a study led by RMIT University.
The material is a lattice made of hollow, interconnected titanium struts filled with polyurethane foam. Researchers said it withstands seawater exposure and is stronger than the stainless steel or high-density plastic currently used in jetties, buoys and floating sensors.
“Although metallic lattices can be incredibly light, with densities less than one-tenth the density of water, their open, interconnected spaces allow water to enter, causing them to sink,” said Dr. Jordan Noronha, lead researcher at RMIT’s Centre for Additive Manufacturing. “This has made these strong, lightweight structures unsuitable for marine infrastructure, until now.”
“By filling only the hollow titanium struts with polyurethane foam, we created a structure that allows water to flow through it while remaining buoyant even after significant cracking and damage,” Noronha said.
The researchers said the work is the first reported demonstration of a floating metal-hybrid lattice metamaterial. Samples floated in freshwater for more than two months during testing, according to the study.
To design the structure, the team introduced a measurement they call skeletal density. Conventional density calculations count all the open space inside a lattice, including space that water can fill and that therefore does not help the structure float. Skeletal density instead counts only the titanium walls and the sealed, foam-filled channels, the parts of the structure water cannot enter.
“This gives engineers a simple design rule: if the skeletal density is lower than that of the surrounding liquid, the structure will float, even when water flows through all its external openings,” Noronha said.
In compression testing, the titanium structure was 70% stronger than stainless steel or high-density polyethylene at the same overall density, the researchers said. In a two-week corrosion test using seawater from Melbourne’s Port Phillip Bay, the lattice lost 0.15% of its mass and less than 1% of its strength.
The structure also kept floating after damage that included cracking, failure at connection points and the fracture of an entire lattice layer, according to the study. It sank only after being severely crushed and compacted.
“Tiny, sealed cells in the foam trap gas and prevent water from flooding the hollow struts,” Noronha said. “In this way the foam acts as a distributed barrier that helps the structure remain afloat after damage, unlike conventional hollow marine structures, which can rapidly fill with water after cracking.”
The team built a 3D-printed marine buoy to test the concept and placed it in a turbulent seawater tank, rotating it up to 45 degrees. The researchers said the buoy remained stable without a sealed casing, protective coating or added flotation.
Project leader Distinguished Professor Ma Qian said the next steps include scaling up the demonstration parts and testing long-term performance under realistic marine and deep-sea conditions. Qian said the structure’s properties can be tailored by changing the material inside the titanium framework, opening potential uses beyond marine infrastructure in areas such as energy absorption, thermal management and vibration control.
RMIT’s Centre for Additive Manufacturing led the project with the Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers in France. The Australian Research Council and RMIT’s School of Engineering supported the research.
The study, “Breaking the surface: buoyant metal-polymer open-cell hybrid lattice metamaterials,” was published in the journal Advanced Materials.

Kommersant: Russian oil companies failed to fulfill about 60% of gasoline exchange contracts — due to Ukrainian attacks on refineries

Unknown Publisher

17:40:37 KST

Kommersant: Russian oil companies failed to fulfill about 60% of gasoline exchange contracts — due to Ukrainian attacks on refineries
Russian oil companies failed to fulfill about 60% of gasoline supply contracts on the St. Petersburg exchange between May and September, according to estimates from industry sources who spoke to the Russian business daily Kommersant.
About 20% of the deals fell through entirely, ending in default or cancellation, while another 39% remain unfulfilled. Of those, 24% have exceeded the standard 30-day shipment window.
Lukoil and Rosneft accounted for the bulk of the unfulfilled contracts, at 46% and 28%, respectively. A source told Kommersant that Ukrainian drone attacks hit their refineries hardest.
The source said oil companies prioritized state tasks first, such as supplying defense and industrial enterprises, leaving gas stations “on one of the last lines” of that list.
Independent gas stations are the exchange’s main buyers of fuel. Russian law requires vertically integrated oil companies to send a portion of their output there.
Russia’s second fuel crisis wave began in August, driven by Ukrainian drone strikes on oil refineries. Gasoline prices rose and lines reappeared at gas stations, just as they had in June.

Estonia’s Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur announced on Wednesday that he would step down from his political post after it emerged that the government had used European Union funding to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine from companies with no previous track record of producing the weapons.
Estonian public broadcaster ERR reported on Wednesday that the government struck a deal in 2024 to acquire artillery shells for Ukraine, paying €70 million upfront from the EU’s European Peace Facility to fund the purchase.
The companies involved, however, had never previously sold a single artillery shell. Estonia is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg.
Pevkur, who has served as defence minister since 2022, addressed the scandal while announcing his resignation on public broadcaster ETV. He said that, as minister, he must accept responsibility for the entire area under his authority.
“Although the minister does not count socks and ammunition or conduct contract negotiations, the National Audit Office’s criticisms, primarily concerning the activities of the Defence Forces and the Centre for Defence Investments, raise the question of political responsibility,” Pevkur said.
Estonia’s National Audit Office criticised the Baltic country’s defence spending last month, including investments made by its armed forces. It also raised concerns about the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments, the country’s military procurement agency.
Addressing the artillery contracts, Pevkur stressed that he had not read them, saying the defence minister is not traditionally involved in the details of individual procurement deals.
“The defence minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defence minister does not count socks and ammunition,” Pevkur said, adding: “The defence minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine.”
The European Peace Facility is an EU funding instrument established before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It aims to strengthen the bloc’s ability to prevent conflicts, build and preserve peace, and reinforce international security and stability. It has increasingly been used to support Ukraine through military assistance and procurement.
European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said Brussels was in contact with the Estonian authorities to investigate whether Estonia must pay back the €70 million of European Peace Facility funds.
“There are, of course, safeguards and there are recovery processes in place to make sure that taxpayers' money is well spent," he said, adding that he could not clarify when the talks would take place.
Pevkur’s resignation follows the high-profile departure of Latvia’s Defence Minister Andris Sprūds in May.

Hanwha unveils drone-guided K9 howitzer concept in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:35:31 UTC
17:35:31 KST

- Hanwha unveiled a K9 howitzer concept using fire-guidance drones for target acquisition and battle damage assessment at Estonia's K9 User Club.
- The presentation follows Hanwha's $100.3 million US Army contract to build wheeled K9-based howitzer prototypes for the Mobile Tactical Cannon program.
Hanwha Aerospace showed off a new K9 howitzer operating concept built around fire-guidance drones this week, unveiling the plans at the fifth K9 User Club gathering in Estonia.
The three-day forum, hosted by the Estonian Defence Forces at the Estonian National Museum in Tartu from September 2 to 4, drew more than 200 military and industry representatives from seven K9 operator nations: South Korea, Estonia, Poland, Norway, Finland, Romania and Australia. Spain and Sweden sent observer delegations.
“The K9 has established itself as an outstanding and highly capable artillery system. Its performance, reliability, and operational capabilities have earned the trust of a growing number of NATO allies and partner nations,” said Major General Viktor Kalnitski, Deputy Commander of the Estonian Defence Forces.
“The K9 User Club brings together commanders, artillery officers, operators, technical specialists, and representatives of industry. It provides an opportunity to exchange practical experience and to discuss the challenges that each of us faces.”
The centerpiece of Hanwha’s presentation was an operating concept that pairs the K9 with a vertical take-off and landing drone for target acquisition and battle damage assessment. Hanwha said the drone detects and tracks targets, generates coordinates and transmits them to the K9’s fire-direction system, then stays over the target area to observe impacts and assess results after the engagement. The company said the approach is meant to shorten the time between spotting a target and firing on it, while reducing the need for forward observers in exposed positions.
Hanwha also presented wheeled artillery concepts that apply technology from the tracked K9A2, including its automated turret, to wheeled platforms. The company said the wheeled concepts are meant to offer greater mobility and deployment flexibility than the tracked K9 while drawing on the same underlying technology base.
The presentations follow a contract Hanwha Defense USA won from the US Army last month. On August 18, the Army awarded the company an Other Transaction Agreement worth $100.3 million initially, with a cumulative value of up to $262.9 million if all options are exercised, to build prototypes for the Army’s Mobile Tactical Cannon program. The deal covers six prototype wheeled self-propelled howitzers based on the K9 design, with an Army option for 12 more, and marks Hanwha Defense USA’s first major US Army contract. If the Army moves forward with fielding, the Mobile Tactical Cannon is intended to replace M777 towed howitzers in some formations.
Hanwha also used the Estonia forum to promote its TOMMS sustainment platform, a digital system for spare-parts procurement and logistics. The company said TOMMS combines requests for quotation, purchase orders and delivery tracking in one system and includes a catalog covering 700 to 800 frequently requested spare parts. Hanwha said it plans to link TOMMS to a spare-parts warehouse in Poland to support European K9 operators, and eventually use maintenance data to forecast parts demand before shortages occur.
“The K9 User Club has become much more than an annual gathering. It is a collaborative platform where users, operators and industry work together to transform operational experience into future capability development,” said Peter JK Bae, Senior Executive Vice President and Head of the MRO Business Division at Hanwha Aerospace. “Every lesson learned in the field helps shape the next generation of K9 capabilities, from new operating concepts and mobility solutions to smarter sustainment.”
More than 2,400 K9 family systems have been ordered by more than 10 countries across Europe, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region, according to Hanwha. The company’s roadmap for the platform includes the digitalized K9A1, the K9A2 with its automated turret, a future K9A3 designed for autonomous and uncrewed operation, and the wheeled artillery concepts shown this week.
Australia will host the next K9 User Club in 2027.

designboom guide to Paris Design Week 2026
Paris Design Week returns from September 10th to 19th, 2026, bringing exhibitions, installations, showrooms, galleries, and events to venues across the French capital. Taking place alongside Maison&Objet Pulse, the 2026 edition once again spreads across four districts, with designers and brands presenting new work in museums, historic buildings, galleries, boutiques, and public spaces.
With hundreds of events spread across the city, knowing where to begin can be a challenge. designboom’s guide to Paris Design Week 2026 highlights the exhibitions, installations, launches, and unexpected encounters worth seeking out, while designboom itself joins the program with paris.designboom, its temporary home at 72 rue des Archives, hosting podcast sessions, workshops, and the paris.designboom apéro, bringing together the wider design community for drinks and conversation.

MAISON&OBJET pulse 2026
Maison&Objet’s September edition returns as Maison&Objet Pulse, running from September 10th to 14th, 2026, at Paris Nord Villepinte. The new identity marks a shift for the fair, which positions its September edition around design in motion, emerging talent, craftsmanship, and new approaches to interior architecture, retail, and hospitality.
The theme for this edition, Pulse in Motion, focuses on movement, collective energy, and the role of design in bringing people together. Across seven sectors, the fair presents immersive spaces, new products, craftsmanship, materials, and emerging designers, alongside programs including Design District, Future On Stage, the Rising Talent Awards South Africa, and (im)Pulse.
For 2026, Valencia-based studio Masquespacio serves as ambassador for both Maison&Objet Pulse and Paris Design Week. The duo has developed installations for the fair and the city, as well as the visual identity for the September edition, bringing their colorful and expressive approach to the theme of movement.

For its 2026 edition, Paris Design Week Factory brings together a new generation of designers across four venues in the Marais. Curated by Jean-Baptiste Durand and Simon Geringer, the program takes an intentionally open approach to emerging design, bringing together practices across design, art, and craftsmanship.
At Espace Commines, around 40 proposals are presented within a scenography conceived like a photographic studio, with each work isolated and framed to give it a sculptural presence. The exhibition continues at 116 rue de Turenne, where the works are arranged as a more experimental environment, allowing different objects and practices to overlap and enter into dialogue.
The Factory also expands beyond emerging French design. At 10 rue de Turenne, the China Creative Pavilion presents BON GOÛT! GOODTASTE!, bringing together designers, artists, and creators working across design, materials, and gastronomy. At 16 rue des Minimes, established designers and publishers present work spanning contemporary design, materials, and craftsmanship.

Joseph Walsh – Arcanum Formae
Irish designer Joseph Walsh presents Arcanum Formae at the Hôtel de Sully. The site-specific installation brings two monumental outdoor sculptures to the historic 17th-century hôtel particulier, placing Walsh’s work between the Orangerie and its surrounding grounds. The exhibition remains on view through Paris Fashion Week and Art Basel Paris, allowing the sculptures to be experienced in relation to the architecture, gardens, changing light, and history of the site.

Hanjimania – Hôtel de la Marine
At the Hôtel de la Marine, Hanjimania brings French and Korean designers together around hanji, the traditional Korean paper made through a centuries-old craft tradition. Curated by Catherine Lurault and An KangEun, the exhibition pairs six French designers, Studio KO, Pierre Yovanovitch, Constance Guisset, Aline Asmar d’Amman, Harry Nuriev, and Jérémy Pradier-Jeauneau, with Korean artists and master artisans working with hanji.
A second parcours through the intendants’ apartments brings works by Korean artists into the monument, while perfumer Domitille Michalon has created a fragrance inspired by hanji to extend the material exploration beyond the visual. The exhibition is co-organized with the Province of Gyeongbuk as part of the 140th anniversary of diplomatic relations between France and Korea in 2026.
where: Hôtel de la Marine, 2 Place de la Concorde, 75008 Paris, France

Maison Lacmé — Astre Mobile
Maison Lacmé presents Astre Mobile at the Hôtel de la Marine, a transparent car reimagined as a mobile cabinet of curiosities. Artistically directed by Antoine Tauvel, ten French craftspeople collaborate for this project, reinterpreting familiar automotive components through materials including onyx, porcelain, wood, leather, lacquer, feathers, and shells.
Astre Mobile approaches the car as a collection of individual objects. A speedometer becomes a feather marquetry piece, the gearshift is made of porcelain, the steering wheel uses driftwood, and white onyx hubcaps can be detached and used as lamps. Other details, including the car’s logo, are transformed into jewelry, turning the automobile into a display of craftsmanship as much as a functional object.
where: Hôtel de la Marine, Cour de l’Intendant, 2 Place de la Concorde, 75008 Paris, France
when: September 9th – 27th, 2026
Frederik Molenschot — Legenda
Carpenters Workshop Gallery’s Legenda is an exhibition of three new sculptures by Dutch artist Frederik Molenschot. The works, CL Sable, CL Mer, and CL Paradis, are part of his City Light series and draw on the dune landscapes and beaches of the Dutch coast, where Molenschot lives and regularly walks.
Form, volume, and balance are central to the artist’s process, with color introduced afterward and drawn from the landscape. In this series, the palette acts as a kind of key to the coastal environments that inform each sculpture, translating the changing character of sand, sea, and terrain into abstract form.
where: Carpenters Workshop Gallery, 54 rue de la Verrerie, 75004 Paris, France
when: September 17th – December 19th, 2026
image courtesy of Carpenters Workshop Gallery
WU BIN (W.DESIGN) — THE PAVILION OF TIME
Chinese designer and interior architect Wu Bin of W.DESIGN presents The Pavilion of Time in the Palais-Royal Garden for Paris Design Week. The installation uses mirror-polished stainless steel and a translucent membrane inspired by the texture of traditional Xuan paper to explore the relationship between architecture, light, reflection, and the passing of time.
The pavilion’s reflective surfaces capture the surrounding trees, sky, and visitors, allowing the structure to visually shift with its environment. Its circular plan is divided into three 120-degree sectors, creating a route through the installation rather than a single fixed viewpoint. As sunlight passes through the translucent membrane, changing conditions of light alter the interior throughout the day. The pavilion therefore uses the movement of the sun as part of its spatial experience, turning light and reflection into elements that continuously reshape the architecture.
where: Palais-Royal Garden, Paris, France
when: September 9th – 20th, 2026
image courtesy of W.DESIGN
de gournay x antoine billore
For Paris Design Week, de Gournay invites antiques dealer and scenographer Antoine Billore to take over its Rue des Saints-Pères premises. The presentation brings together de Gournay’s hand-painted wallpapers and porcelain with pieces designed by Billore, alongside newly installed wallpapers and fabrics.
Known for his eclectic selection of historic and unsigned objects, Billore approaches interiors through combinations of pieces with distinct characters and histories. His contribution introduces this sensibility to de Gournay’s artisanal environment, creating a setting where the company’s painted surfaces and porcelain meet antique and upcycled furniture.
where: de Gournay, 15 rue des Saint-Pères, 75006 Paris, France
when: September 10th – 13th, 2026

Pli Office — Tout est Chaos
Following Pour que tu m’aimes encore at the Pavillon de l’Arsenal in 2024 and Design Disco Club at Lafayette Anticipations in 2025, Pli Office returns to Paris Design Week with Tout est Chaos, an exhibition at La Gaîté Lyrique. Curated by Christopher Dessus and staged by PAF atelier, the exhibition brings together 10 designers around the theme of wonder.
The project looks at a world increasingly filled with objects that are designed to solve problems, questioning what happens when function, efficiency, and mass production leave little room for surprise. The invited designers are asked to create installations, objects, or specific situations that make space for gesture, storytelling, experience, and doubt.
Alongside the main exhibition, Pli Office is launching an open call for designers with less than five years of experience, inviting a younger generation to present work that finds its capacity to surprise through materials, form, use, history, or production methods.
where: La Gaîté Lyrique, Paris, France
when: September 10th – 14th, 2026
ROCHER FATALE | image courtesy of Pli Office
Yves de la Tour d’Auvergne — Plier la matière
Pulp Galerie presents Plier la matière, a retrospective of French designer and sculptor Yves de la Tour d’Auvergne (1927–2023), bringing together works from the 1980s and 1990s and focusing on the artist’s exploration of folding, a gesture he translated from paper into furniture and sculpture.
Initially trained as a painter, de la Tour d’Auvergne began experimenting with paper sculptures through an interest in light, using folding, tearing, and cutting to shape the material. He later developed a process combining resin and marble powder, allowing him to reproduce the whiteness and texture of paper while giving the works greater structural and sculptural qualities.
The exhibition includes the Alpha armchair (1982), Demi-Lune stool-table (1984), Olta chairs (1984), Albatros lamps (1988), Marmora chairs (1989), and Ellipse Pise table (1994). Across these pieces, the fold functions less as decoration than as a way of constructing form, organizing space, and catching light.
where: Pulp Galerie, 30 rue de Seine, 75006 Paris, France
when: September 10th – October 31st, 2026

UK mortgage borrowers brace for rate jump amid global bond sell-off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:25:18 UTC
17:25:18 KST

Homeowners in the UK are braced for a jump in mortgage rates, driven by higher inflation and interest rate increase expectations amid turmoil in the global bond markets.
UK swap rates, which lenders use to price mortgages, have risen to a three-year high, as this week’s global bond market sell-off ripples through the economy.
The five-year swaps rate rose above 4.52% on Wednesday, the highest level since October 2023. This is expected to result in higher interest rates on fixed-term mortgages.
A jump in oil prices, as the US and Iran have exchanged fire this week for the first time in a month, has led to fears of higher inflation, leading investors to sell bonds, which pushes up their yield, or interest rate. The moves in gilts, as UK government bonds are known as, have been bigger than those in other countries.
Although the turmoil in the bond markets eased on Thursday, the consequences of the jump in bond yields could be serious for borrowers.
That is because UK swap rates – the interest rates that banks charge when they borrow from each other – have been pushed up by the rise in gilt yields.
Russ Mould, the investment director at the trading platform AJ Bell, said: “Credit card, mortgage and auto loan interest rates will rise if bond yields rise, as the lenders seek to preserve loan book margins and manage their risk.”
If the cost of government borrowing continues to remain high, it could undermine Andy Burnham’s efforts to ease cost of living pressures.
The new prime minister attempted to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday, using his first appearance at prime minister’s questions to promise decisions for the autumn budget would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.
He spoke as the yield on UK 10-year government debt hit its highest level since 2008 for a second day, before retreating thanks to a drop in the oil price. On Thursday, Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dipped 0.6% to $95 a barrel.
Oil has been one of the key factors driving the bond market sell-off, as inflationary pressures from high prices could force central banks to raise interest rates, along with worries over high government spending. Government bonds are also competing with a flurry of corporate debt issuance by technology companies keen to fund their spending on AI infrastructure.
Tom Simpson, the managing director of homes at Yorkshire Building Society, said swap rates were now 0.7% above where they were a year ago, but there was “much more volatility” in March, at the start of the Iran war.
“All things being equal, you would expect a modest increase in mortgage rates based on what we’ve seen so far,” he told the BBC, advising people who were worried about this to speak to an independent mortgage adviser.
“When there is a movement in the market, that can pull forward demand. People will try to lock those rates in.” However, he added that the 0.1 percentage point increase over the past week was below the 0.5 percentage point increase in the 10 days after the US and Israel first launched airstrikes on Tehran.
Fixed-year mortgage rates were unchanged on Thursday, according to the latest figures from Moneyfacts. The average two-year fix is 5.59%, while a typical five-year fixed deal costs 5.63%.

US Senate pushes UBS for new details on Nazi-linked accounts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:24:53 UTC
17:24:53 KST

US Senate pushes UBS for new details on Nazi-linked accounts
UBS is coming under renewed United States pressure over Credit Suisse’s handling of Nazi-linked accounts.
The Senate Judiciary Committee is demanding new responses from the Swiss lender’s management to dozens of questions as part of its investigation.
UBS’s previous responses “did not fully address this Committee’s questions,” Senator Charles Grassley said in a July 17 letter to the bank. UBS declined to comment on Senator Grassley’s letter, which hasn’t previously been disclosed. The bank is currently working on a response, according to a person familiar with its planning.
+Read more about the Holocaust assets controversy
The back-and-forth is the latest flashpoint in a tense year between the bank and the committee, which has called on UBS to ensure a complete and transparent investigation of the handling of Nazi-linked accounts by Credit Suisse. UBS bought its troubled rival out of near collapse in 2023, acquiring all its legal liabilities in the process.
Senators criticised UBS at a hearing in February, but the bank has pushed to end a six-year-old probe at the end of this year and limit its scope, criticising the independent ombudsman overseeing it as biased.
The bank has argued that a settlement reached with Jewish groups in the 1990s under which it paid $1.25 billion to Holocaust victims covers all potential exposure from its ties to its handling of Nazi-related accounts, saying the current probe is purely aimed at completing the historical record.
More
US court rules UBS cannot limit liability over Nazi-linked accounts
But those groups, backed by the Senate panel, have argued that the investigation is revealing new information potentially not covered by the 1990s settlement. The latest probe began after records emerged showing Credit Suisse serviced accounts for Nazis and related entities, including the so-called Rat Lines through which they escaped to Argentina after World War II.
Grassley who chairs the committee, remains committed to ensuring a thorough investigation of Nazi-linked accounts at Credit Suisse and continues to call on UBS to fully cooperate and produce the records requested by the ombudsman, according to a committee official.
The Republican senator from Iowa plans to hold another hearing on the issues, although he hasn’t set a date, and wants to create a historical repository of Credit Suisse records linked to the Nazi accounts. He included a list of 62 questions for the bank to answer in his July letter.
In May, Neil Barofsky, the ombudsman overseeing the investigation, wrote to the committee, accusing UBS of making “false and misleading statements” related to “previously unreported examples of Credit Suisse executing forced transfers of Jewish clients’ assets into the accounts of Nazi-affiliated banks” and withholding records from the probe.
UBS fired back with a public statement saying it rejects Barofsky’s narrative as lacking objectivity. The bank turned down his appeal for more time, saying he should complete his report by the end of the year.
More
Historian claims Swiss banks may hold further Second World War secrets
The Senate Committee and Barofsky last month gained an ally in Helen Junz, an economist and respected former member of the Volcker and Bergier Commissions, which led the the original 1990s-era investigation into the Swiss banks’ Nazi past.
In a five-page letter to the committee chairmen on August 6, she criticised UBS’s response for taking an overly broad view of the terms of that 1998 settlement, which the bank argues covers any potential future exposure.
The suggestion that any actively concealed Nazi-linked assets would be covered in the settlement is “inconsistent with, and violative of, the principles of good-faith that are the bargained-for core” of that settlement, she wrote.
“The bank’s response — in fact non-response — is part and parcel of a long-established pattern of Credit Suisse’s stonewalling any and all investigations into these matters.”
“This pattern appears now to have been embraced by UBS after the merger with Credit Suisse with regard to the legitimate demands for access to records that reveal the Swiss banks’ links to Nazi entities,” she wrote.
UBS says it has spent more than $100 million financing Barofsky’s team of investigators and shared more than 19 million documents with them. The bank is willing to cooperate with inquiries it views as legitimate, but will not continue to let the investigation drag on indefinitely.

UK seeks vehicle-mounted laser defence against drone swarms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:23:35 BST
17:23:35 KST

The Ministry of Defence has opened a competition for new counter-drone technologies intended to protect deployed troops from mass and low-cost aerial threats, with particular interest in laser directed-energy weapons and a requirement for an eventual system capable of autonomous operation from an Army vehicle, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The tender notice published on 2 September begins an iterative procurement process through the Commercial X Dynamic Market. The wider procurement carries an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, or £150 million including VAT, although the MOD makes clear that this funding has not yet been approved and later stages will depend on future funding decisions.
Setting out the operational requirement, the MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
On existing counter-UAS approaches, the notice states: “Current approaches are constrained by limited magazine depth, high cost-per-engagement, limited manoeuvrability, workforce intensity and the difficulty of adapting capabilities at pace as UAS threats evolve.” The MOD added: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The first phase will focus on technologies which already exist and could be accelerated towards a deployable system rather than procuring a finished counter-UAS capability immediately. The MOD stated: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
For later phases, the department said: “Over later Phases, the Authority’s intent, aligned with their Integrated Procurement Model, is to identify and rapidly mature promising technologies as demonstrable Minimum Viable Products (MVPs). The Authority may then, at its discretion (and the criteria detailed below) select projects to be iteratively developed, integrated and proven as Minimum Deployable Capabilities (MDCs) for an initial operational user group.”
The notice continues: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record. Suppliers will be notified of the criteria, selection processes, and competition format as these Phases arise.”
The intended configuration is also set out in the requirement. The MOD stated: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
On the attacks the system is expected to counter, the department said: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus is on representative Class 1 uncrewed aerial systems and related small aerial threats, covering single attacks as well as repeated, sequential and simultaneous profiles. The notice states that this includes threats intended to disrupt operations, conduct surveillance, target fixed or mobile assets, overwhelm local defences or force the disproportionate use of high-cost munitions.
The MOD also plans for the system to move beyond a crewed Army vehicle. It stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
Stage 1 will assess whether industry proposals can meet the problem statements, with suppliers required to submit an evidence-based high-level programme plan supported by demonstrations, modelling, analysis and testing where appropriate. The MOD states: “No contract shall be awarded at this stage, but success is required to continue to Stage 2. All suppliers who demonstrate achievement of the threshold criteria shall be invited to Stage 2.”
Stage 2 will require successful suppliers to develop their initial proposals into fully costed and contractable projects running for around six months. Contracts at this point will be awarded according to evaluation scores and available funding within a £5 million limit, with technical factors expected to account for between 60% and 80% of the assessment and commercial factors between 20% and 40%.
Stage 3 could involve either a further competition or negotiation of a single direct award depending on how many suppliers remain. The MOD says contracts at that stage will cover scaling and production alongside testing, assurance, safety and security, with break points where aspects of the system cannot be demonstrated within the required timescales.
The department states: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.” It adds: “The intention is to begin Stage 1 with immediate effect, but future stages will not proceed until funding has been allocated and approved.”
The MOD also warns suppliers that later funding is not guaranteed, stating: “There is no guarantee that future funding will be allocated or approved and the Authority may cancel the procurement process at any time. Bidders proceed knowing and accepting this risk that no effort shall be compensated.”

Risk appetite in global markets rise as geopolitical tensions somewhat ease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

17:23:15 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Recent developments in the Middle East boosted risk appetite in global markets as US President Donald Trump said attacks against Iran may not last very long, driving November delivery Brent crude oil down 0.5% to $95.1 a barrel.
The US 10-Year Treasury yield dropped two basis points to 4.78% at the same time, supporting global equity markets on Thursday.
New York Fed President John Williams said US inflation continues to slow due to the weakening impact of tariffs and that high energy prices have yet to spill over into other service sectors, helping ease risk aversion, but the ongoing conflict in the Middle East keeps concerns alive.
Meanwhile, US ADP private-sector employment rose by 38,000 in August, below estimates, signaling that the labor market may have stabilized somewhat and that inflationary pressures could slightly ease.
The likelihood of the Fed hiking rates this month fell from 70% to 62% in money market estimates, encouraging investors to turn to riskier assets. The Fed’s Beige Book report showed that economic activity saw a modest increase in recent weeks, while uncertainty over high prices, current policies and international conflicts increased.
At the same time, the Bank of Canada maintained its policy rate at 2.25%.
The US dollar declined 0.2% to 99.4 due to the strengthening of the yen, while gold traded up 1.1% at $4,436 per ounce on Thursday.
Falling US dollar demand and the slowing pace of the rise in oil prices drove up gold prices.
The ounce price of gold is attempting to hold above $4,400 on the back of weak US employment after dipping below $4,300 following the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium.
Silver also climbed 1.3% to $66.2 per ounce at the same time.
The New York Stock Exchange saw a positive trend on Wednesday, with US oil giant Chevron’s shares rising 0.4% after it said it plans to invest $7 billion in Venezuela.
Chipmaker Nvidia’s shares rose 3.2% due to optimism that corporate artificial intelligence demand is on the rise.
The US manufacturing sector’s new order value increased 0.9% on a monthly basis in July.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.56%, the S&P 500 rose 0.46%, and the Nasdaq was up 0.45% on Wednesday. US indexes opened Thursday on a positive trend.
Meanwhile, European stock markets traded lower on Wednesday due to geopolitical risks in the Middle East.
Joachim Nagel, president of Germany’s Bundesbank, said the country’s economy is on a path to higher growth based on data from the first two quarters, expecting a growth rate of around 1% in 2026.
German automaker Volkswagen’s shares dropped 3.8% after it was removed from the STOXX 50.
France’s CAC 40 dropped 0.26%, Italy’s FTSE MIB contracted 0.24%, Germany’s DAX 40 lost 0.5%, and the UK’s FTSE 100 fell 0.3% on Wednesday. European indexes began Thursday on a mixed trend.
At the same time, Asian equity markets traded higher near Thursday’s close as the positive trend in the US carried over.
China’s Ratingdog services Purchasing Managers’ Index rose from 50.4 to 51.4 in August, while Japan’s services PMI rose from 52.3 to 52.5 at the same time, indicating a recovery trend in domestic demand in the region.
The US dollar/Japanese yen exchange rate fell 0.6% to 157.7 after Bank of Japan policy board member Hajime Takata said the bank must hike rates to counter inflationary pressures.
While Japanese authorities have yet to confirm currency interventions, investors are looking out for potential actions to strengthen the yen further.
Near Thursday’s close, South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.7%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 increased 0.2%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng climbed 0.02%, and China’s Shanghai Composite was up 0.4%.

1 in 5 children in 21 countries face tech-facilitated sexual abuse, UNICEF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:23:12 UTC
17:23:12 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
An estimated 20 million children aged 12 to 17, or nearly 1 in 5, experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse in a single year across 21 countries, UNICEF said.
The findings are included in a new report titled Through Children’s Eyes: How Digital Technologies Enable Child Sexual Abuse, which combines survey data with testimonies from children who experienced abuse.
“The report reveals a painful reality. More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play, and connect with friends,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said.
“Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away,” she added.
The report estimates that more than 15 million children were exposed to unwanted sexual content, while 9 million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will.
Around 4 million had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.
Most cases occurred on social media platforms
Nearly 60% of cases occurred on social media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and WhatsApp, while 14% took place in online games, according to the report.
The report found that 57% of cases involved someone the child already knew, including peers, romantic partners, friends and family members. At the same time, 38% of children first encountered the perpetrator online, with abuse facilitated through tools such as fake accounts and private messaging.
The experiences had a significant impact on children’s emotional well-being, sense of safety and trust in others, with research participants describing feelings of fear, shame, confusion and isolation, according to the report.
Children who experienced technology-facilitated exploitation were four times more likely to report suicidal thoughts or behaviors and self-harm, and also reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, the analysis found.
In Mexico and North Macedonia, the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviors was more than eight times higher among children who experienced abuse, while in Pakistan the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher, according to the report.
Children suffer in silence
More than 40% of cases were never shared with anyone, while fewer than 1% were reported to authorities, including police, social workers or helplines.
The most common reason children remained silent across the countries surveyed was not knowing where to go or whom to tell, UNICEF said.
The report calls on governments, technology companies and other stakeholders to strengthen protections for children online, including stronger privacy safeguards, restrictions on unsolicited contact from adults, safer recommender systems and improved detection and reporting of abuse.
It also calls for stronger laws and enforcement measures, improved reporting and support systems, and greater support for families, schools and communities.
“All of us, including governments and technology companies, must do more to protect children online,” Russell said.
The report draws on nationally representative surveys of approximately 21,000 internet-using children aged 12 to 17 across 21 countries, alongside in-depth interviews with 100 young people who experienced abuse in childhood.
UNICEF said the survey findings are representative of internet-using children rather than all children, particularly in countries with lower internet connectivity.

Spain's PM Sanchez says no evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta border surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:21:15 UTC
17:21:15 KST

Spain's PM Sanchez says no evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta border surge
MADRID, Sept 3 - Spain has found no evidence to conclude that July's deadly border rush from Morocco into its enclave of Ceuta was orchestrated by Moroccan authorities, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Thursday, countering allegations in a Spanish police report.
Speaking in parliament, Sanchez responded to claims in the report that emerged this week suggesting the entry of over 70,000 people into Ceuta was not a spontaneous migration but a planned effort to overwhelm border controls.
"I can assure you that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever," Sanchez said.
However, Moroccan police did allow crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on July 30, when migrant arrivals peaked, he said. Spanish authorities had yet to determine whether this was due to inaction or inability to contain the influx, Sanchez added.
Sanchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat's cooperation in returning the majority of the migrants in the days following the surge.
But on Thursday he said Spain summoned Morocco's ambassador on August 21 because of "unacceptable statements" made by two Moroccan ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, Spain's other North African enclave. Morocco's Justice Minister Abdellatif Ouahbi last month publicly reiterated Rabat's sovereignty claims over the cities.
FEWER MOROCCAN POLICE THAN USUAL AT BORDER
The police report, commissioned by a High Court judge last month and seen by Reuters, alleged that Moroccan security forces were initially deployed in smaller numbers than usual near the border breakwater and did not make a serious attempt to disperse the crowds.
Some uniformed Moroccan officers gave directions towards the crossing point, while other unidentified people appeared to guide or monitor the flow of people, the report said. It did not identify individual officers or provide independently verified evidence of orders from Moroccan authorities.
It cited some migrants as saying in interviews they had received guidance from Moroccan security forces to make the crossing.
"The police response in Morocco to the mobilisation and mass influx of migrants into Ceuta has been, to say the least, one of total permissiveness, with no serious attempt recorded to reduce, disperse or remove the crowd from the border perimeter," the report said.
Moroccan authorities did not respond to a Reuters request for comment but previously denied any permissiveness, blaming the crossing on traffickers, the misinterpretation of a Spanish court ruling that appeared to open a legal loophole for arrivals by sea and the use of social media to disseminate information about a mass crossing.
Justice Minister Ouahbi told Al Arabiya TV on August 22 that Moroccan authorities did not attempt to stop people marching toward Ceuta in order to avoid bloodshed, but they handled the crisis "wisely and with sang-froid".
The police report said trafficking groups in Morocco could mobilise a maximum of about 300 migrants a day, lacking the capacity to orchestrate an event of those dimensions. REUTERS

‘Military production cannot be the answer’: Critics slam Volkswagen’s defense plan with Israel’s Rafael
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:21:11 UTC
17:21:11 KST

- 'We reject the false claim that the only alternatives are unemployment or arms production,' Left Party's Thorben Peters says
- ‘Production for an Israeli arms company amounts to de facto support for the wars Israel is waging against the Palestinians, Lebanon, Iran,’ peace activist Marie Dominique Guyard says
Volkswagen's revived plan to produce military equipment at its Osnabruck factory with Israel's Rafael has drawn fresh opposition after reports that the state of Lower Saxony could step in to help overcome objections that had stalled the project.
The proposal comes as Volkswagen undergoes a sweeping restructuring amid falling profits, weaker demand in China and growing competition from lower-priced Chinese brands in Europe, with vehicle production at the Osnabruck plant set to end after 2027.
Thorben Peters, co-chair of the Left Party in Lower Saxony, said thousands of jobs at the factory, along with its industrial expertise and know-how, must be preserved without a shift to arms production.
"Replacing civilian production with military production cannot be the answer to the automotive industry's current crisis," Peters told Anadolu.
"The state of Lower Saxony, in particular, should not use public funds to participate in an arms-related joint venture. We reject the false claim that the only alternatives are unemployment or arms production."
Volkswagen confirmed in March that it was in talks with several defense contractors about the Osnabruck plant.
A blocked plan and a new workaround
The proposal has faced opposition from peace groups, labor movements and opposition parties for months, particularly over potential cooperation with Israel's state-owned defense firm Rafael.
In July, Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, Volkswagen's third-largest shareholder, blocked the plan.
Now, management has revived the idea with a structure that could overcome that obstacle.
According to recent German media reports, Volkswagen would transfer parts of the Osnabruck site to the state of Lower Saxony, which could then form a joint venture with Rafael to manufacture military equipment. 
The project could manufacture key components for Israel's Iron Dome air defense system, including launchers, transport vehicles and power generators.
The Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung reported that Lower Saxony could invest at least €200 million ($232 million) in the project.
The Left Party argues that if the state is prepared to spend public money to preserve production and jobs at the site, it should instead invest in civilian alternatives.
Peters said those could include special-purpose and environmentally friendly vehicles for public transport.
Volkswagen's supervisory board is due to meet on Sept. 4.
Peters said his party opposes converting civilian industrial capacity to military production as a matter of principle, regardless of the nationality of the company involved.
In the case of Israeli defense company Rafael, however, he said the war in Gaza raises additional concerns.
"Given the massive human rights violations and serious allegations regarding breaches of international law in connection with the war in Gaza, there must be particularly rigorous scrutiny,” he said.
"The guiding principle for public investment must be that human rights and international law are non-negotiable."
'City of Peace' pushes back
The debate has particular resonance in Osnabruck, a city that has long promoted itself as a "City of Peace" because of its role in the negotiations that led to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War.
The prospect of military production at the Volkswagen plant has sparked repeated protests in recent months, bringing peace activists, anti-war groups and local initiatives onto the streets.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative argues that Lower Saxony should use any public money earmarked for the plant to support a socially responsible and environmentally sustainable transition rather than subsidize weapons production.
"Production for an Israeli arms company amounts to de facto support for the wars the state of Israel is waging against the Palestinians, Lebanon and Iran," Marie Dominique Guyard, spokesperson for the initiative, told Anadolu.
"Defense equipment for the Iron Dome plays a role in Israel's aggressive, offensive military activities, as it provides the protective shield enabling Israel to act aggressively toward its neighbors."
Speaking on behalf of the Osnabruck Peace Initiative, Guyard said the group's position is also informed by international legal proceedings concerning Israel's conduct.
She pointed to a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory unlawful and said states must not provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by that presence.
She cited International Criminal Court arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant on war crimes and findings by a UN commission of inquiry and Amnesty International accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
But she also pointed to Osnabruck's own history to explain the depth of local opposition.
The city was repeatedly bombed during World War II, when it was home to arms-related industry. About 65% of Osnabruck was destroyed, including 95% of its historic old town.
For Guyard, the prospect of military production returning to the city some eight decades later makes the debate about more than the future of one Volkswagen factory.
"When arms factories are once again established in the city some 80 years after the last war, one can only despair at the decision-makers' disregard for history," she said.
“We do not wish to support such a disastrous development and will continue to build opposition to ensure that work in the city serves peace rather than war.”

Norway has seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.2 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets following the 2014 annexation of Crimea, officials said late on Wednesday.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a 24-hour standoff with the Norwegian Coast Guard, according to Covington, the U.S. law firm representing Naftogaz.
Russian state news agency TASS quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesperson as saying the seizure of the ship amounts to an act of "piracy."
Naftogaz has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea.
A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.2 billion plus interest and legal costs.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said.
Covington, the law firm, said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a Russian-owned vessel that is used for commercial cruises, for months.
Anticipating the ship's arrival in Svalbard en route to Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement, Naftogaz's lawyers applied to a Norwegian court for the vessel to be arrested there and subject to a compulsory sale.
The application was approved by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court on Monday. In its ruling, it required the governor of Svalbard to enforce the order, supervise the vessel and ensure that it is not moved.
The governor's office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held on Svalbard.
Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement measures across multiple jurisdictions, including the United States, France, the United Kingdom and Finland, where Russian assets have been frozen. Russia is appealing the process, saying no notice was given.
"We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid," the Ukrainian company said.
