Police raided several locations in Yavne’el on Thursday morning and detained 16 suspects for questioning — minors and adults — on suspicion that they had recently married or had begun making concrete preparations for an illegal wedding ceremony involving underage brides.
Among the suspects is a prominent activist in the fight against child marriage in the town, who is suspected of having organized a wedding for her daughter when she was 16
“The Northern District Police is conducting an ongoing campaign against the phenomenon of child marriages allegedly taking place illegally within a small and closed community whose main activity is centered in the town of Yavne’el in the Lower Galilee. After more than 20 suspects were detained for questioning several weeks ago on suspicion of involvement in child marriages in the community, dozens of Northern District officers again raided several locations in Yavne’el this morning and have so far detained 16 minors and adults for questioning,” the Israel Police said in a statement.
This is the second wave of detentions, after more than 20 suspects were questioned in June over alleged involvement in child marriages in the community.
According to police, the weddings are usually held in the morning with only a small number of people present, and the location is not disclosed until the ceremony begins. They are held without photographs or cellphones, out of concern that the wedding will be documented.
“After the religious ceremony, in many cases another event is held for the wider public under the guise of an ‘engagement party,’ to which all relatives of the bride and groom are invited,” police said.
In light of these efforts to conceal the ceremonies, police are unsure whether the activist campaigning against the phenomenon ultimately married off her daughter, or whether the wedding did not go ahead. However, police say they have evidence that allegedly points to preparations for such a wedding.
In recent months, the child marriage affair in the town has drawn public attention, in part following ynet reports about underage girls from the local Hasidic community who arrived to give birth at nearby hospitals.
Police explained that enforcement is complicated because the wedding ceremonies are generally held in secret. Even when police discover a festive gathering, participants do not issue invitations using the word “wedding,” do not sign a ketubah, or Jewish marriage contract, and do not hold a chuppah ceremony in front of guests, so that there will be no evidence that a wedding took place.
“Kudos to the Northern District fraud unit, which is conducting this complicated investigation. We will not relent until all the offenders who abuse underage girls and boys are behind bars, ”Knesset lawmaker Meirav Cohen of Beyachad-Yesh Atid, chair of the Knesset Committee on the Status of Women and Gender Equality, said.
Cohen visited the community Wednesday after, according to her, a school principal married off her daughter while she was still a minor to a young man from the community. During the visit, Cohen entered a local council meeting, where her personal aide said he was shoved and nearly assaulted by one of the employees there.

Swiss inflation rate jumps to highest level in two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:11:12 UTC
17:11:12 KST

Swiss inflation rate jumps to highest level in two years
Swiss inflation accelerated far more than analysts anticipated to the fastest pace since September 2024, suggesting a weaker franc is feeding through to the economy.
Consumer prices rose 0.8% in August from a year earlier, up from 0.4% in July, the Federal Statistical Office said on Thursday. The result was higher than every single forecast of 16 economists in a Bloomberg survey.
The reading is the last that Swiss National Bank (SNB) officials will see before their interest-rate decision later this month. While the result notably exceeded expectations, it remains consistent with the average for the current quarter predicted by the central bank.
More
How the war in Iran is affecting Swiss consumers
The pick-up in inflation will be welcomed by policymakers in a country where consumer price growth has often been feeble and even turned briefly negative last year. The outcome still underscores how benign the Middle East energy shock has been for Switzerland at a time when its neighbors are seeing costs surge.
In the euro area that surrounds the country, consumer prices rose 3.3% in August, the highest in almost three years. Following the harmonised European methodology, that compares to a Swiss rate of 0.9%.
Clothing prices down
SNB has predicted a mild, temporary acceleration of consumer-price growth that may now be assisted by the weaker franc, which this week reached a one-year low against the euro.
+ Rising rents are heavy burden on many Swiss households
The franc extended gains after the data to rise 0.4% to CHF0.9385 per euro, after Wednesday’s CHF0.9435 low.
With rates at zero, the central bank expects the quarterly average to peak at 0.8% by early next year, comfortably within its targeted range of 0-2%.
Last month, higher costs for petroleum products were partly offset by lower ones for clothing and footwear, the statistics office said. So-called core inflation, which excludes volatile elements such as energy, picked up to 0.4% from 0.3% – that’s the first acceleration this year.
More
Switzerland faces a steep energy bill due to the Middle East conflict
The reading coincides with a potential upswing of the Swiss economy. Output adjusted for major sports events expanded by 1.5% in the second quarter, five times more than had been expected.
That growth was driven by exports, particularly in pharma and chemicals, according to a detailed breakdown of drivers published Thursday.
Manufacturing contributed more than services, which is unusual for Switzerland. Government spending continued to outpace private consumption for a third quarter.
Rate hike possible
While economists question if that the reading might be an outlier rather than a sustainable acceleration, a key leading indicator of growth has reached the highest level in almost five years. Also, wages appear to keep rising, outpacing inflation, and manufacturing in August exceeded expectations.
Helping the outlook for export-focused Switzerland is a trade deal with China that will remove almost all tariffs on goods bound for Asia’s biggest economy. The agreement, which has yet to be ratified, envisions Swiss signature goods including watches, pharmaceuticals and precision instruments being imported fully duty-free.
While the Iran war prompted a surge in the franc earlier this year that alarmed the SNB enough to spark interventions to stem the gains, the currency has dropped against the euro since then. Officials have still kept up the threat of cutting borrowing costs below zero if necessary.
In July, Bloomberg reporting indicated that inside the SNB the rate is expected to stay at zero through next year before it then probably rises. That view is still in line with what most economists predict.
“Price risks have shifted to the upside in Switzerland as well,” Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank in Vaduz, said in reaction to the inflation data. “A rate hike in December cannot be completely ruled out.”

German startup TYTAN debuts new rocket-boosted interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:11:10 UTC
17:11:10 KST

- TYTAN Technologies said it showed German Cabinet officials a new rocket-boosted interceptor drone during the government's August retreat in Brandenburg.
- The company has not disclosed the new system's speed, range, or a timeline for testing or production.
Munich-based counter-drone company TYTAN Technologies said it demonstrated a new rocket-boosted interceptor drone to the German Federal Cabinet last month, presenting what the company described as a new category of system built for greater range and speed against aerial threats.
TYTAN said the demonstration took place during the Cabinet’s annual retreat at Schloss Neuhardenberg in Brandenburg. The two-day retreat, held August 25 and 26, brought together Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and other Cabinet members to discuss economic growth, competitiveness and technology policy, according to the German government. TYTAN said Merz, Klingbeil and Pistorius were the first officials to see the new interceptor.
The company said the system uses rocket boosters to extend its range and speed compared with TYTAN’s existing interceptor line, and that it was developed in response to changing drone threats observed in Ukraine. TYTAN has not disclosed the new interceptor’s speed, range, altitude ceiling, or a timeline for testing or delivery.
TYTAN’s existing product line includes the EOS, a short-range multicopter interceptor built for NATO Class I drones weighing up to 150 kg (330 pounds), and the METIS, a long-range fixed-wing interceptor for Class II drones between 150 and 600 kg (330 and 1,320 pounds). The company has said METIS can reach speeds of 350 km/h (217 mph), fly out to 25 km (15.5 miles) and operate at altitudes up to 5,000 meters (16,400 feet). TYTAN’s smaller interceptor drones use computer vision to track and ram hostile drones rather than carrying an explosive warhead, with a reported top speed above 250 km/h (155 mph), a range beyond 15 km (9.3 miles) and a weight around 5 kg (11 pounds).
TYTAN raised €30 million ($34.8 million) in a Series A round in February 2026, co-led by Armira and the NATO Innovation Fund. In January, the company signed a cooperation agreement with German sensor maker HENSOLDT to integrate TYTAN’s interceptors with HENSOLDT’s Elysion Mission Core command-and-control software.
The company said it was founded by two international engineering students two and a half years ago and has grown to around 200 employees. TYTAN opened a serial production line in Bavaria this year with capacity for 3,000 interceptor drones per month, with production activity scheduled to begin in August, CEO Balázs Nagy told Defense News in June.
TYTAN said its interceptors are already deployed in Ukraine, along with Germany and Baltic states listed among its customers. The company said frontline feedback from Ukrainian operators is incorporated into its systems through software updates rather than hardware redesigns, which it said lets it shorten the gap between identifying a capability gap and fielding a fix.
Nagy has said the company’s pricing model is built around cost, telling Defense News in June that TYTAN aims to protect the same airspace “200 times cheaper than with legacy systems.”

UK Green leader to seek parliament seat vacated by Starmer
LONDON, Sept 3 - The leader of Britain's left-wing Green Party intends to stand in an election for a seat in parliament vacated by former Labour prime minister Keir Starmer, a local newspaper reported on Thursday.
Zack Polanski told the Camden New Journal he would be the Green candidate for Holborn and St Pancras, a left-leaning constituency which Starmer held comfortably in 2024 though with a much-reduced vote share.
"Labour stands up for corporations and big money," Polanski posted on X. "I'll stand up for people and our communities."
In an election two years ago, an independent candidate who campaigned primarily on opposition to Israel's war in Gaza took nearly 19% of the vote while the Green candidate received over 10%, giving the party hope of taking the seat this time.
Since Polanski became Green leader a year ago the party has had success in taking support from Labour's left, winning a surprise by-election victory in Greater Manchester – where current Prime Minister Andy Burnham was a long-serving mayor – and nationally polling as high as 20%.
But Polanski's personal popularity took a hit after he criticised police officers for the way they arrested a man who allegedly stabbed two Jewish people in north London in April, according to pollsters YouGov.
A national YouGov poll on Wednesday put Labour tied with the right-wing populist Reform UK party of anti-Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage on 23% with the opposition Conservatives on 20% and the Greens on 13%. REUTERS

Taylor's claim teachers push 'political agenda' prompts backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:55:06 UTC
16:55:06 KST

Teachers hit back at Nationals claim about 'anti-boy' ideology in schools
In short:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says teachers are pushing political agendas to students, while his counterpart rallied against anti-boy ideology in the classroom.
A teachers' union has labelled the remarks "ignorant".
What's next?
It remains unclear how the government intends to give Australians more control over their content amid pressure to back an algorithm opt-in model.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says teachers are pushing agendas in the classroom, while his Nationals counterpart believes the school curriculum is teaching "anti-boy" ideology.
The comments have sparked a backlash from teachers, who labelled the views "fundamentally incorrect".
Nationals leader Matt Canavan rallied against the "lecturing" of young men in schools, alleging that a state-funded Respectful Relationships curriculum could be turning them to harmful online content.
He said the program provided opportunity for "young boys to reflect on their male privilege and power", and while well-intentioned, could be having an adverse effect.
"I think this anti-boy ideology has no place in our schools," he told reporters on Thursday.
"They have counter-productive results and then drive young boys to toxic voices online because they're looking for someone to provide them with respect and support."
The Respectful Relationships national framework, established to teach both primary and secondary students about respectful relationships, gender equality and consent, does not mention male privilege.
Its inclusivity outcome instructs teachers to help students, without specifying gender, "to consider how their identities and experiences — including those related to power and inequality — affect their relationships and lives, in ways that suit their age and development".
It also sets out to help "boys and young men to explore concepts of masculinity in healthy ways".
The debate was initially stirred up on Wednesday, when Senator Canavan blamed the "feminisation" of the curriculum for driving young men towards "manosphere" content online.
He said programs like Respectful Relationships were "essentially a recruitment ground for Andrew Tate", a self-proclaimed misogynist with a large online following.
Teacher fury over 'agenda push' remarks
Asked about Senator Canavan's comments on Thursday, Liberal leader Angus Taylor pushed back against the "politicisation" of the curriculum by teachers.
"The idea that we have a balanced curriculum being run at the moment, that there are not agendas being run by some teachers, I think is wrong," he told the ABC.
"We do see those agendas being run."
Mr Taylor insisted teaching consent was important, while calling for a "degree of balance".
The Australian Education Union has fired back at the criticisms, labelling them a "fundamentally incorrect portrayal" of the education system.
"These comments are either a malevolent mischaracterisation of Australia's education system for political gain, or a display of complete ignorance of how the teaching profession operates," the union said in a statement.
The teachers' union said the remarks by Senator Canavan, Mr Taylor and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who claims schools are "brainwashing students", further fueled the "aggression and disrespect" towards teachers, which was already on the rise.
Last week, a national survey of 2,600 teachers, conducted by Monash University, found that 78 per cent had observed or experienced sexism or misogyny in school.
One in three teachers said that the presence of gendered violence made them "occasionally" consider leaving the profession.
The report's author, Stephanie Wescott, said for many teachers, schools had become "unbearably hostile places to work, with levels of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment that have made their jobs untenable".
A separate government-funded study into misogyny and youth radicalisation found one in three teenage boys express "misogynistic attitudes, mistrust of women and a belief in traditional gender roles".
Almost a quarter of generation Z males believed feminism "should be resisted with violence if necessary".
Call for more male teachers
While Senator Canavan did not offer any alternatives for respectful relationship and consent education on Thursday, he doubled down on a call for more male teachers.
"Maybe we should look at getting more male teachers in. That used to be an agenda, I don't know what's happened to that. But maybe we should have more male role models in schools," he told Nine.
"I just know young boys often feel that they don't get any kind of instruction, leadership. They're not cherished there."
Currently, only one in four teachers are male.
While Education Minister Jason Clare agreed that students would benefit from more male teachers, he said ultimately, it was a discussion about respect.
"Teaching boys to respect girls isn't woke, it's common decency," he told reporters.
Mr Clare said the focus should not be on teachers, who he labelled "heroes".
“The bad guys here are the big tech companies, they're the ones poisoning our kids with algorithms that are shovelling shit into their heads."
On Wednesday, sexual consent advocate Chanel Contos called on the government to mandate an opt-in model for social media algorithms, to allow teenagers to avoid harmful messaging including manosphere content.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has flagged support for giving Australians more control over their online content but has stopped short of backing the algorithm opt-in model proposed by Ms Contos.

Font size
A small change can set much bigger changes in motion — this idea lies at the heart of the new national campaign “Hits with a 1% Change” by the One Percent Change organization. The charity campaign brings together some of Bulgaria’s most beloved contemporary artists to give iconic songs from the 1990s and the early 2000s a fresh interpretation.
At the heart of the project is a deeply symbolic musical transformation: popular songs originally written in a minor key will be performed in a major key. With just one small change, they will take on a new emotional quality, conveying hope, light and the sense that every difficult story can have a different ending. This musical change is also a metaphor for the mission of One Percent Change to make regular charitable giving a natural habit for more Bulgarians.
PHOTO YouTube /MOLEC
The campaign kicks off with one of the best-loved songs in Bulgarian pop music, “Byagstvo” (Escape) by Duet Avenue, which was given a fresh interpretation by Molec.
PHOTO YouTube /MOLEC
“When we heard the idea behind the project, we liked the fact that the change is not only musical. It carries a message. If a song can make someone stop and think, and then inspire them to do something good, then music has done its most important job”, the members of Molec say.
The “Hits with a 1% Change” campaign will continue with two more musical surprises, which will be unveiled in the coming weeks.
Because sometimes all it takes is a 1% change to set something much bigger in motion.

LeVanta Tech shows off its unusual HALIA drone at sea test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:53:51 UTC
16:53:51 KST

- LeVanta Tech demonstrated its unusually shaped HALIA float-and-fly drone with partner STR at ANTX Coastal Trident.
- HALIA can land on the open ocean, float for weeks, then relaunch at speeds LeVanta Tech has reported above 100 knots.
LeVanta Tech said it demonstrated its HALIA unmanned system at ANTX Coastal Trident last month, showing how the platform can link air, surface, subsea and seabed assets over long distances.
Photos of HALIA show an unusual design. The drone sits low in the water with a dark, angular hull riding hull-down, mostly submerged. Two cylindrical engine pods sit side by side on top of the fuselage, feeding what appear to be ducted fans, while swept white wings and twin tail fins jut out near the back, just clear of the waterline. A small sensor mast pokes up from one wing root. Little about the shape resembles a conventional aircraft or boat.
HALIA is a “float-and-fly” drone: it flies to a location, lands directly on the open ocean, and can sit there for weeks in a low-power floating mode before relaunching to reposition or leave the area, according to LeVanta Tech, which profiled the company in September 2025. The company said HALIA does not require a dedicated ship or fixed infrastructure to operate, since it can move between the air and water on its own.
At Coastal Trident, LeVanta Tech worked with STR, a defense technology firm with undersea systems and sensor work based near Boston, to demonstrate a communications architecture connecting air, surface, subsea and seabed systems. STR provided what the companies called a “rapidly repositionable” command-and-control air-water gateway, using what the companies described as high technology readiness level components to deliver over-the-horizon, real-time command-and-control links to subsea and seabed systems.
ANTX Coastal Trident is an annual exercise run by the Naval Surface Warfare Center Port Hueneme Division at the Port of Hueneme, California, bringing together Navy, other government agencies, academia and industry to test maritime and port security technology in an operational setting.
LeVanta Tech, founded in 2023, started out building real-time maritime monitoring tools for the offshore wind industry before shifting to a defense-first focus. The company’s leadership includes CEO Kelly Echols, an engineer and patent attorney by background; Chief Aviation Officer Jon Smith, a former P-3C Orion instructor pilot and Navy unmanned aircraft test project manager; and CTO Johnny Doo, who has more than 40 years in aircraft and hovercraft development, according to Defense Tech Signals.
The company was one of six finalists selected from 260 applicants for the 2024 Gulf Blue Navigator accelerator. A demonstration that year drew interest from the Air Force, which led to a $1.8 million Direct-to-Phase II Small Business Innovation Research award. The Air Force Research Laboratory followed with a Phase II SBIR contract worth $1.76 million running through December 2026, covering a project titled “Floating and Loitering Ocean Advanced Technology Sensing,” according to federal contract records cited by Defense Tech Signals. LeVanta Tech has also raised more than $1.1 million in early funding, including an $800,000 credit investment from Leonid Capital Partners in April 2025.
LeVanta Tech is developing HALIA in two configurations: a battery-electric version for tactical missions and a hybrid-electric version built for longer range. Both are designed to scale into larger platforms, the company has said. HALIA uses variable buoyancy combined with a hovercraft-assisted launch and recovery system, intended to let it take off and land in rough seas. Its top speed has been reported at more than 100 knots (185 km/h), with loiter times of weeks in its powered-down floating mode.
The platform carries a modular payload bay that LeVanta Tech says can support intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sensors, electronic warfare packages, kinetic payloads and communications equipment, feeding into wider command-and-control networks. The distinctive hull shape and twin engine pods are part of what LeVanta Tech describes as a design built specifically for surviving repeated transitions between air and water, rather than adapted from an existing aircraft or boat.

Germany Identifies Russian-Backed Suspects in Leipzig Drone Sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:52:11 UTC
16:52:11 KST

- Category
- World
Germany Identifies Russian-Backed Suspects in Leipzig Drone Sabotage
German law enforcement agencies have identified two suspects involved in an attempted FPV drone sabotage operation at Leipzig Airport, according to Bild.
The incident took place on August 5, when explosive-laden drones were discovered near four Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators determined that the planned attack was carried out by a native of Russia holding a Latvian passport and a Belarusian citizen who also holds Russian citizenship. Authorities are currently searching for at least four individuals whose movements and phone numbers were tracked using cell tower location data.
German Federal Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt stated that Russia directly organized the attack, with the perpetrators acting on instructions from Russian intelligence services.
The Federal Criminal Police Office suspects that more unmanned aerial vehicles may have been deployed than initially thought, as remnants of three devices have been recovered so far.
The first suspect, a Russian native, acted as a logistical coordinator and instructor while maintaining direct ties to Russian intelligence. He arrived in Germany at the end of July via Berlin Brandenburg Airport, traveled toward Leipzig in a rental vehicle, and departed the country by plane two days before the attack was executed. The second suspect, a citizen of Belarus, was identified through DNA evidence left at the scene.
Traces of his genetic material were recovered directly from one of the drones, from the inner side of a tin can containing explosives, and from a signal amplifier antenna mounted on a tree near the airfield. Matching these genetic traces against European databases revealed prior records in Lithuania and Finland, where the individual had previously been prosecuted for other offenses.
He entered the Schengen zone using an Italian tourist visa issued in Minsk in late April. The sabotage attempt unfolded on the night of August 5, when a shuttle bus driver spotted the first explosive drone at 00:42 near four Ukrainian An-124 heavy transport aircraft.
Following the discovery of a second device, air traffic over the airport was completely suspended. During the airspace closure at 01:03, a inbound DHL cargo plane was forced to abort its landing approach and collided with another flying object, likely a second drone, at an altitude of 400 meters. A third drone was discovered on August 14 in a field in the municipality of Kabelsketal, bordering the western side of the airport.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the drone incident at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport as an attack carried out by Russian intelligence operatives using military-grade materials on European Union territory.
Speaking in Brussels ahead of a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, von der Leyen stated that the EU would not tolerate such actions and expressed full solidarity with Germany. She noted that if Russia had intended the incident to make European countries reconsider their support for Ukraine, it had instead strengthened their determination to continue backing Kyiv.
Von der Leyen characterized the sabotage operation as a new escalation on EU territory directly linked to Moscow, forming part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous hybrid activities. Consequently, she pledged that the EU would maintain and intensify pressure on Russia until it ended its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, emphasizing that the bloc remained prepared to introduce additional sanctions and close existing loopholes.

Germany Ends Russian House Agreement and Orders Expulsion of Employees

Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechaev stated that while the intergovernmental agreement governing the center's activities expires in the summer of 2027, staff members representing the facility and Rossotrudnichestvo must depart within a week, according to The Moscow Times.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In addition to the expulsions, Germany is shutting down the Russian Consulate General in Bonn starting September 18, with diplomatic staff and their families required to leave quickly.
German investigators discovered a drone carrying explosives near the military transport plane and later located a second drone along with about 50 grams of explosives on August 4.
Following the investigation, Germany officially accused Russia of organizing the sabotage attempt. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul stated that Berlin will continue to support Kyiv and take steps to disrupt similar Russian operations across Germany and Europe.
To bolster defense capabilities, Berlin plans to deliver additional Iris-T air defense missiles and several thousand strike drones to Ukraine, with shipments potentially beginning as early as September.
Germany also intends to deepen intelligence sharing with Kyiv while pushing for stricter sanctions against Moscow, stronger entry controls on Russian citizens, and increased restrictions on Russia’s shadow fleet. European officials also pledged to increase support for Ukraine and tighten sanctions against Russia.
Previously, Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev threatened direct military strikes against German infrastructure.
“They deserve a direct strike on all German military equipment production facilities for the Bandera clique. And quite possibly on several other locations in Berlin as well,” Medvedev wrote on Telegram social media, claiming without evidence that Berlin had fabricated the Leipzig incident.

Lithuanian agriculture minister says regulating food prices is impossible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:44:00 UTC
16:44:00 KST

Regulating food prices is an impossible task, Lithuanian Agriculture Minister Kęstutis Mažeika said Thursday, arguing that the experience of a government-appointed food council showed the difficulty of achieving such a goal.
“The goal of regulating food prices is probably impossible, as we can see from reality,” Mažeika told the Žinių Radijas radio station.
Mažeika recently abolished the Food Council, established by the government of then-Prime Minister Gintautas Paluckas in 2025 with the task of monitoring food prices. He said the council had failed to produce any results and that some of its own members had become frustrated with its work.
“Several dozen people would meet and discuss things for several hours, but no decisions were made,” Mažeika said. “From the statements of some council members, it was clear that they were disappointed.”
The Food Council was abolished in late August. It was replaced, along with the Agriculture Science Council, by a new ministry body known as the College.
According to Mažeika, the College will analyse trends in agricultural supply chains and food and raw material prices and will bring together experts to provide advice, discuss possible measures and seek solutions.
“The restructuring is probably emotionally important for the other council members who will continue their work,” Mažeika said. “It’s not that completely different people will participate in the College. Experts will be brought together for consultations, discussions and the search for solutions.”
The Food Council began work in February 2025. At the time, then-Agriculture Minister Ignas Hofmanas said its initial task would be to analyse the food supply chain and develop proposals for reducing food prices.
By February this year, the council had yet to identify measures to lower prices. Then-Prime Minister Inga Ruginienė said it should meet more frequently and work more actively.
The 27-member council included representatives of government ministries, farmers, food processors and retailers, as well as universities and the State Consumer Rights Protection Authority.

The strike, which took place at 9:30pm local time (18:00 GMT) on Tuesday, killed at least four people and wounded 67, the group said, warning that the number of deaths may increase “given the critical condition of some of the injured”.

‘Horrifying’ attack

Neither the US nor Iran are party to the ICC’s Rome Statute, meaning the court does not have automatic jurisdiction over either nation.
But Dawn, a human rights group, has previously said Iran could still accept the court’s ad hoc jurisdiction over crimes committed on its territory from a specific date. “By filing such a declaration, set to the beginning of the war, Iran would grant the ICC jurisdiction over every strike on Iranian soil,” the group said.

Iranian authorities say at least 3,468 people were killed in the initial phase of the US and Israel’s war, which began on February 28 and ended with a ceasefire on April 8. A second round of hostilities, from July 27 to August 24, killed a further 59 people and wounded 666.
The deadliest single attack of the war, in terms of civilian casualties, destroyed an elementary school in Minab on the war’s first day. At least 156 people, including 120 children, were killed. A separate strike that day hit a sports hall in Lamerd, killing 21 people, including four children.
Over more than six months of war, the US and Israel have also struck oil and gas facilities, fuel depots, steel and petrochemical factories, airports, ports, bridges, power installations, medical centres and water facilities across Iran.

San Diego USV maker says Quickfish has entered production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:41:01 UTC
16:41:01 KST

- Seasats said its Quickfish interceptor USV has entered production, offering 40-plus knot speeds and weeks-long endurance at sea.
- The company deployed Quickfish and four other USVs during the Navy's Silent Swarm 2026 electromagnetic warfare exercise in Alpena, Michigan.
San Diego-based unmanned surface vessel maker Seasats said its Quickfish interceptor-class USV has entered production and is now available at scale.
The company said Quickfish is built on Seasats’ existing technology stack and can sprint at more than 40 knots (74 km/h) while remaining at sea for weeks at a time. It has a large modular payload bay designed to carry a range of mission systems, including unmanned aircraft, according to Seasats. The company said the hull is self-righting and built to survive Sea State 10 conditions, the roughest classification on the World Meteorological Organization’s sea state scale.
Seasats took part in Silent Swarm 2026, a two-week Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations experimentation event run by the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division. The exercise took place July 13 to 24 at the Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center in Michigan, part of the National All-Domain Warfighting Center, and drew participants including the Michigan National Guard, NOAA, the Army’s C5ISR Center and the Air Force Test Center.
Seasats said it deployed a fleet of five autonomous surface vessels during the exercise, including its Lightfish and Quickfish platforms, to demonstrate coordinated multi-platform operations with a small number of operators. The company said the event also involved integrating maritime sensing and electromagnetic spectrum equipment across the fleet.
A production-run Quickfish completed the full two-week exercise while carrying multiple payloads, Seasats said. The company described Quickfish as built on the Lightfish hull and electronics stack, adding high sea state performance, long range and a payload bay sized for aerial vehicles. Seasats also said the boat includes an on-station patrol mode that allows it to stay deployed for weeks without refueling.
Seasats credited the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division for the opportunity to test the technology.
The company said Quickfish’s payload bay is watertight and can hold several unmanned aircraft of different types and sizes. That allows a single vessel to be reconfigured for different missions, such as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications relay or strike, without modifying the boat itself, according to Seasats. Because the aircraft ride inside the enclosed bay, the company said a Quickfish on patrol gives no outward sign of what it is carrying.
Seasats linked that capability to the Defense Innovation Unit’s Suitable Warfighting Adaptive Payloads program, known as SWAP-USV, which is seeking mature, affordable unmanned surface vessels that can integrate with unmanned aircraft to counter asymmetric threats at sea. The company said Quickfish is in production now and can be delivered on DIU’s timeline.

Report: Iran warns US of major retaliation if Israel storms Hezbollah-held ridge in Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:39:27 UTC
16:39:27 KST

Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on the mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon known as the Ali al-Taher ridge, where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah fighters, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.
Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources, and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
Hezbollah has said in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.
The Israeli military has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the U.S. had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the U.S. Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.
IRGC forces holed up there, officials say
Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.
The third source, a foreign official with direct knowledge of the message, said it was delivered around mid-August and that as a result of U.S. pressure Israel had put off storming Ali al-Taher.
Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message but said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.
"Iran considers any Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.
Iran fired missiles towards Israel in early June in retaliation for attacks on Hezbollah on the Lebanese capital's outskirts.
Israel seeks to besiege Hezbollah fighters
Despite a ceasefire announced in June, the Israeli military has said Hezbollah is still operating around the ridge and twice over the last week launched explosive drones towards Israeli troops near the ridge.
In July, it said it had launched an air strike on a Hezbollah fighter near an access shaft to the underground site at Ali al-Taher and vowed not to allow Hezbollah to operate in the area or pose a threat to Israeli soldiers.
An Israeli military official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters in June that Hezbollah fighters were stuck underground without food or water. Israeli newspaper Maariv, citing a military source, said on Thursday that the Israeli military assessed there were no IRGC forces in Ali al-Taher and that some Hezbollah fighters had died without food and water.
The third official said Israel's military was trying to smoke out Hezbollah and IRGC personnel by besieging them, shooting down attempted drone deliveries of food and water to the ridge.
"What we have seen over the past month is Israeli pressure to besiege Ali al-Taher in order to impose a reality within this facility that renders it uninhabitable. This approach, and the absence of a large-scale attack, means that it is possible a message was conveyed through several countries -- this is a natural conclusion," Hezbollah's media office told Reuters.
Hezbollah threatens retaliation
A Lebanese source briefed by Hezbollah said the group's fighters can still access their positions through the ridge's northern side.
Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher, which Israel's military has included in a self-declared security zone occupied by its troops and off-limits to Lebanese.
Despite Iran's warning, the Lebanese source and a senior Lebanese security official said an Israeli military operation to capture the ridge was still possible in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah said any large-scale attack on Ali al-Taher would mean a return to full-blown war, and could see missiles landing on northern Israeli communities.

Diesel prices in Estonia top €2 per liter amid global oil surge

By midday Wednesday, diesel prices in Estonia had risen above €2 per liter at a number of filling stations nationwide. The Circle K station (pictured) adjacent to the Methodist Church in central Tallinn posted a diesel price of €2.029.
Diesel prices last exceeded €2 a liter on March 20, when fuel prices were at their highest level since spring 2022 in the immediate aftermath of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Gasoline prices at the pump have risen too – the same filling station was quoting a price of €1.999 for a liter of 95‑octane. In late April, the price had fallen to below €1.600 a liter.
Market participants' biggest concern has become the threat to the strategically critical Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil consumption passes. U.S.‑Iran tensions and recent strikes have disrupted Persian Gulf supplies, with crude oil prices rising sharply — Brent crude futures rose 1.1 percent to over US$95 a barrel on Wednesday, following a four‑dollar jump on Tuesday, as hopes of a quick easing of Middle East tensions faded.
Trump remained confident this was only a temporary state of affairs, back in April. "The gas will go down as soon as the war is over. It will drop like a rock. There's so much of it. It's all over the place, sitting all over the oceans of the world, and it'll go down," he said at the time.

"It is such a concrete identification and preparation that we find it necessary to go out with the message that it is a threat that must be taken seriously," he said.
The Confederation of Danish Industry said it was taking PET's assessment seriously and was in close contact with relevant authorities.
"The changed threat picture calls for increased attention from companies, but also for calm and proportionality," said Rasmus Anderskouv, head of security and preparedness at the organization.
Anderskouv said companies should assess their specific exposure and ensure their security and emergency preparedness measures were functioning properly.
Flemming Splidsboel, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, described PET's announcement as serious and said the threat was "new," "concrete" and "advanced."
Former Defense Intelligence Service chief analyst Jakob Kaarsbo said PET's decision to speak publicly could be intended to signal to Russia that Danish authorities were aware of its activities.

Russia preparing new AK-12+ rifle for serial production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:25:20 UTC
16:25:20 KST

- Kalashnikov unveiled a mock-up of its new 5.45mm AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, saying serial production is being prepared.
- The rifle, built for special forces, has a thicker barrel, modified sights and removed sling, bayonet and grenade launcher fittings compared to the standard AK-12.
Kalashnikov Concern unveiled a mock-up of its new AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, presenting a 5.45mm weapon built for improved shooting precision.
The rifle is on display in the Voin Center pavilion at the Far East Street exhibition, part of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, running September 1-4 on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University.
Kalashnikov, part of the state defense conglomerate Rostec, said the weapon is now being prepared for serial production. The company described the AK-12+ as a high-precision small-arms system built on the existing AK-12 platform, intended primarily for special forces units.
The system was developed under the supervision of Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Presidential Plenipotentiary Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev, the company said.
The AK-12+ carries a thicker barrel than the standard AK-12, with a threaded muzzle designed to accept a flash suppressor or a muzzle brake. Kalashnikov modified the rifle’s mechanical sights and widened the contour of the gas cylinder to match the new barrel profile. Fittings previously used to attach a sling swivel, an underbarrel grenade launcher and a bayonet have been removed. The mock-up shown in Vladivostok featured an extended stock.
The rifle will also carry electro-optical sights. Kalashnikov said the sights are meant to improve accuracy at medium range in both daytime and nighttime conditions.
At the forum, Kalashnikov and the Voin Center signed a cooperation agreement. Under the deal, the two organizations will jointly develop engineering skills among the center’s cadets and expand the material and technical resources at its regional branches.
The Voin Center, formally the Center for Military-Sports Training and Patriotic Education of Youth, was created on presidential order in 2023. It trains teenagers aged 14 to 18 and reservists aged 18 to 35, and now operates branches in more than 20 Russian regions.
Kalashnikov already produces several variants of the AK-12 platform. The baseline AK-12 is chambered in 5.45x39mm, weighs about 3.6 kg (7.9 pounds) unloaded, has a 415 mm (16.3 inch) barrel and fires at a cyclic rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. The family also includes the AK-15, chambered in 7.62x39mm, and the export-oriented AK-19, chambered in 5.56x45mm NATO.

The former vice mayor said she held no regrets about her long political career.

Chalmers can't avoid questions on house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:22:15 UTC
16:22:15 KST

analysis
Chalmers questioned about house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Jim Chalmers sits alone in a darkened press conference room, selfie camera on, chatting to his social media followers about the latest economic data.
But of course he wasn't asked any questions in his pre-filmed video. It was more an avenue for him to declare the economy was "robust" despite challenges from the Middle East war, point out more people are switching to EVs and that housing construction is up before he had to face reporters half an hour later.
He fronted up to the press conference for a tense back and forth where almost every single question was house prices.
When the government made the U-turn on its promise not to wind back negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, it did so armed with Treasury forecasts. Growth, the budget papers said, would slow by 2 per cent over a number of years.
Property data firm Cotality this week flagged drops in every capital city in August, and predictions from the Commonwealth Bank that prices could drop as much as 13 per cent have some mortgage holders understandably worried.
Chalmers has largely brushed off movements in price as not unusual and backed in his department's forecast. "Buying a house is a long-term proposition," he said.
The major factor at play here is recent interest rate rises, he argued, not the government's tax changes.
That argument wasn't made easier for him either, after fellow frontbencher Matt Thistlethwaite declared on News24 (formerly Sky News Australia) there was "no doubt" the tax changes contributed to house prices falling.
"I think that's one of a number of reasons," Chalmers told ABC's Sally Sara when asked again this morning.
Opting out of algorithms?
Thistlethwaite may have made the sell a little bit harder for Chalmers, but the treasurer named the "disturbing rubbish" pushed by social media algorithms as the thing making his job more difficult.
"Our society, our social cohesion, the way that we come at big problems including in my part of the shop in the economy is hampered, not helped, by the way algorithms are dominating people's day," Chalmers said.
It's a similar argument that's been put before by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who has said algorithms are fuelling polarisation. Albanese is supportive of the idea that Australians should have more control over what they are shown online.
But that doesn't go as far as what consent advocate Chanel Contos has put forward: an opt-in algorithm for social media accounts. If adopted, it would be a world where we'd return to chronological feeds where our friends' content is shown instead of strangers. It's an idea backed by some of the crossbench and the Greens amid concerns social media is exposing young people to misogynistic content.
There seems to be no disagreement among the leaders of the major political parties that some of the content fed to people is toxic. But for some it's a bit of a chicken and egg argument.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan, for example, this week argued it is the "feminisation" of the school curriculum and a lack of male teachers that pushes boys towards such content. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor also accused teachers of running agendas in the classroom.
Contos argued the algorithm is the missing piece here — young boys are being shown this content whether they seek it out or not.
Coalition focuses on tobacco
Meanwhile, the Coalition finally released its plan to slash the tobacco excise. The plan also included a proposal to legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches.
An estimated 80 per cent of the cigarettes and other nicotine products consumed in Australia last year were illegal, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Last month, One Nation revealed its own plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent. The opposition went one further, revealing a proposal to cut the excise by 80 per cent. It argues it would be enough to tip the scales and redirect customers towards legal tobacco.
The Parliamentary Budget Office costed the policy but the Coalition has not released the costings or the assumptions underpinning them.
It says its plan, paired with a further $200 million spend on law enforcement to support more raids, arrests and closure of illegal tobacco shops, would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over the first four years — double the current forecasts.
That hinges on the idea that cutting the price would encourage Australians to ditch the black market and that illegal distributers wouldn't also drop prices to compete — something Taylor disagrees with.
Back in the Pacific
While this was all going down at home, Albanese returned to palm tree-lined beaches and crystal clear blue water of Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF).
It's not the first time the prime minister has visited — he made the trip to the small Pacific nation last year for a pre-wedding holiday with now wife Jodie Haydon.
The early stages of the meeting were overshadowed by tensions between China and Taiwan about Taipei's increased presence at the gathering (Palau has diplomatic ties with Taiwan) and the number of leaders who decided to skip the annual forum.
Albanese said he wasn't distracted by all that as he pressed on with discussions about climate change and tackling the issue of drug trafficking in the Pacific, where Australia and New Zealand's appetite for illegal drugs has caused real issues.
Leaders were also due to discuss the matter of China's test-fire of a nuclear-capable missile carrying a dummy warhead in the Pacific — with host nation Palau indicating it would like to issue a united statement about the test.
Despite escaping PIF without another T-shirt faux pas, it wasn't all smooth sailing for Albanese, who had a tense press conference of his own at the forum about United Nations climate event being held in Fiji and Tuvalu next month.
The pre-COP events are organised by Australia and are part of the compromise Australia struck with Türkiye last year after we bowed out of hosting the climate conference in Adelaide.
But so far just five leaders from outside of the Pacific have confirmed they're making the trip, which was designed to highlight the impact of climate change on Pacific nations. It's not typical that leaders usually attend a pre-COP event.
Asked about this, Albanese said the focus on the non-Pacific leaders was "disrespectful".
Loading
Treaty yourself
And finally, have you been looking for the perfect gift for the Kiwi in your family? Or perhaps you have a long-distance American pen pal you need a stocking stuffer for?
Don't worry, Defence Minister Richard Marles has you covered for inspiration. He presented a framed copy of the full text of the ANZUS Treaty on vellum, and signed by Albanese, to a member of the Trump administration.
Vellum is a thin, translucent material made of calfskin and commonly used by artists.
Why are we presenting Albanese autographed military treaties to our allies? To mark the 75th anniversary. You can't get that at the shops.

Kyiv • UNN
Meghan Markle allegedly held talks about a role in the third season of "The Gentlemen." The series' actors and producer commented on the rumors.
Meghan Markle, the wife of Britain's Prince Harry, reportedly held talks about appearing in Guy Ritchie's series "The Gentlemen." Show star Theo James said he was "intrigued" by the speculation, UNN writes, citing Reuters.
Where the rumors came from
At the end of August, reports emerged that Markle could play a role in the third season of the crime drama, shortly after she and Prince Harry announced plans to return to the United Kingdom. However, subsequent media reports suggested that the offer had been withdrawn amid a "negative reaction" to the rumors.
What the actors and series producer say
While "Breaking Bad" star Giancarlo Esposito said that someone with such popularity could be "both a huge plus and a huge minus," Hugh Bonneville dismissed the reports as a "brilliant marketing ploy."
"I suggested Keir Starmer for the role, but apparently no one showed any interest," joked the "Downton Abbey" actor.
Series co-writer and executive producer Matthew Read noted that Ritchie has "a wonderful tradition of inviting people from unexpected places," adding that the level of interest in potential cast members demonstrates how strongly viewers are interested in the series.
What season two of "The Gentlemen" is about
After the success of its debut season in 2024, the second season of "The Gentlemen" returns with Eddie Horniman, played by James, seeking to expand his criminal empire a year after inheriting his family's vast estate and title.
James, who rose to fame through his role in "Divergent," told Reuters that the new season explores what "generations of land ownership" and enormous inherited wealth can do to a person.
"(Horniman) starts to understand that violence creates a feeling of power, and he is willing to resort to violence to get what he wants," he said.
In the new season, filmed in locations such as Italy's Lake Maggiore, Horniman joins forces with drug empire heiress Susie Glass and her father Bobby, played by Ray Winstone, seeing him as the perfect candidate for the criminal world.
Crime-film veteran Winstone said the series resonates with viewers because it blurs the line between organized crime and the establishment.
"Who are gangsters? Is it really the guy from the street, or is it the hierarchy, the aristocracy? Because how did they get there in the first place?" he said. "It's like turning everything upside down a little."
The second season features several new actors, including "365 Days" star Michele Morrone, "The Leopard" actress Benedetta Porcaroli, and British television presenter Maya Jama.
James joked that the newcomers needed to be "briefed" on Ritchie's unconventional directing style before filming began. "We always say... imagine you have a script, and then burn it, because you will never say any of those lines," he said.
Bonneville, another newcomer to the series, said that Ritchie's "unorthodox and crazy" approach to filmmaking creates a lively atmosphere on set, while Esposito noted that it is connected to a feeling of "danger." "Well, it's show business, and that's a wonderful thing," he added.
The second season of "The Gentlemen" will be released on Netflix on Thursday.

MOD targets two-year contract deadline for major platforms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:05:36 BST
16:05:36 KST

The Ministry of Defence has set a target of reducing the average time to first contract for major platforms such as tanks, frigates and aircraft from six years to two, alongside faster targets for upgrades and uncrewed systems, according to a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Stuart Anderson, the Conservative MP for South Shropshire, who had asked about the planned reforms set out at paragraph 27 on page 64 of the Defence Investment Plan.
Mr Pollard said the National Armaments Director Group launched a segmented approach to procurement on 1 April 2026, tailoring acquisition routes to the type of capability, the supplier and the level of risk.
Three segments have been established, the Minister says. Major platforms, covering tanks, frigates and aircraft, carry the target of moving from six years to two. Pace-setting modular upgrades, covering communications, sensors and weapons improvements, are to come down from three years to one. Rapid commercial exploitation, which the answer illustrates with uncrewed systems, carries a target of three-month acquisition cycles.
On the commercial machinery behind that, Mr Pollard said: “These reforms are supported by the Accelerating Commercial Pathways (ACP) programme, which aims to improve the Ministry of Defence’s ability to harness flexibilities in the commercial process and ensure that commercial approaches are tailored to the needs of individual procurements, including through the use of flexibilities provided by the Procurement Act 2023. The programme has launched six Commercial Pathways and, since March 2025, over 300 procurements have self-selected one or more pathways.”
What the targets mean
Time to first contract measures the period between a requirement being identified and a supplier being placed under contract to deliver it, which is the stage before any metal is cut and where a great deal of British procurement time has historically been consumed.
The three-month target for uncrewed systems is the one that departs furthest from existing practice, and it reflects a problem the war in Ukraine has made unavoidable, where the useful life of a small drone design is measured in months before countermeasures catch up.
The segmented approach is the same framework that appeared in a market engagement notice published on 18 August, which set out a £1.9 billion requirement running from 2028 to 2037 and described the department as considering multi-supplier frameworks alongside individual contracts, with details of the competition promised no later than the first quarter of 2027.
The National Armaments Director Group was established on 1 April 2025 as one of the four groups now making up the Ministry of Defence, bringing together Defence Equipment and Support, the Defence Infrastructure Organisation, the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, Defence Digital and the commercial, international collaboration and exports functions.
Rupert Pearce took over as National Armaments Director on a five-year fixed-term contract from October 2025.
The Procurement Act 2023 introduced the notice structure and the competitive flexible procedure now used across British public contracting, replacing the previous set of public contracts regulations, and the flexibilities Mr Pollard refers to include the ability to design a procedure around a particular requirement rather than following a fixed process.

Nearly 9,000 Ukrainian Drones Targeted Moscow in August, Mayor Says
Nearly 9,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Moscow and the surrounding region throughout August, according to a statement by Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 2.
He stated that between 8:30 a.m. on August 1 and 8:30 a.m. on September 1, a total of 8,670 drones flew toward the Moscow region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He claimed that air defense forces intercepted the vast majority of the unmanned aerial vehicles before they reached the outer areas of the Russian capital, with 795 drones destroyed as they approached the city itself.
Sobyanin did not state how many drones managed to penetrate air defense layers around Moscow, nor did he provide information regarding casualties or damage caused by falling debris.

====================================================================================================

China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry Elliott
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:00:47 UTC
16:00:47 KST

Almost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. The collapse of the property market. Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.
Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing while China would be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.
This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.
Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.
The market in solar panels was captured. It became the world leader in batteries and electric vehicles. It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.
Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides for failing to boost domestic demand for its products.
Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.
In July, a Chinese startup called Moonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 model and it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.
As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shock might not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power,” says Campanella.
Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington to antagonise its traditional allies by whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.
The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.
Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI could prick the stock market bubble.
Finally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.
There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.
The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.
- 
  Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

UN officials call for investment, connectivity to advance Sustainable Development Goals
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:49:35 CST
15:49:35 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- United Nations (UN) officials on Thursday called for investment in resilient infrastructure, cross-sector partnerships and greater regional connectivity in transport, energy, trade and digital technologies to advance the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which are "far off course" from being achieved.
Only 36 percent of SDG targets are on track or making moderate progress, while 15 percent are in decline, said Sanda Ojiambo, assistant secretary-general and CEO of the UN Global Compact, in an address to the Second Global Business Summit on Belt and Road Infrastructure Investment to Accelerate the SDGs held in Singapore.
Companies worldwide are navigating infrastructure challenges intensified by climate change, technological disruption, shifting supply chains, resource constraints and growing scrutiny from investors and consumers, Ojiambo said.
The majority of the SDG targets rely on infrastructure investment, she said.
Ojiambo urged companies to view development challenges as investment opportunities. Creating demand for green energy, for example, can secure long-term off-take for clean power and provide predictable financial returns, while investment in resilient infrastructure can accelerate innovation and growth, strengthen competitive advantage and reduce billions of dollars in repair and recovery costs, she said.
She also called for stronger partnerships across sectors and industries.
"It is particularly encouraging to see growing cooperation among companies and partners from China, Singapore, Indonesia and across the Asia-Pacific region. These connections are not only building smarter infrastructure, but also trust, knowledge and shared prosperity," she said.
Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, executive secretary of the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, called for greater regional connectivity to advance the SDGs, including through smart transport systems, clean energy sources, more efficient trade and information and communications technology connectivity.
On transport, she said the challenges of sustainable transport development cut across sectors, dimensions and national boundaries, a dynamic that is particularly evident in Asia and the Pacific, which accounts for the largest share of global freight and passenger transport flows.
On energy, she said cross-border power-grid connectivity is a key strategy for increasing the share of renewable energy across Asia-Pacific, given the region's complementary renewable energy resources and differing demand profiles. Both exporting and importing countries can benefit, she said.
The summit was organized by the UN Global Compact Action Platform on Sustainable Infrastructure for the Belt and Road Initiative to Accelerate the SDGs, and the UN Global Compact China Office. ■

China’s support for Iran shows its limits as US ramps up pressure on Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
06:48:46 UTC
15:48:46 KST

China’s support for Iran shows its limits as US ramps up pressure on Tehran
Beijing’s support for Tehran is balanced against other relationships in the region, analysts say.
China has long been a rare partner to Iran, with the economic heft to blunt the United States’ efforts to strangle the Iranian economy.
Yet even as China opposes US President Donald Trump’s latest pressure campaign, few observers expect it to go much further than the modest economic links it has thus far forged with Iran to shield it.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US urges G20 to cut trade imbalances, focus on China
- list 2 of 4US House passes funding bill to avert government shutdown ahead of midterms
- list 3 of 4Cisco accused of fostering a hostile workplace for Muslim and Arab employees
- list 4 of 4Fernandez transfers to Man City from Chelsea in joint British record fee
While China opposes the Trump administration’s military attacks and sanctions against Iran, Beijing’s relationship with Tehran is just one consideration in a foreign policy that seeks to balance relations with numerous countries, including the US and the Gulf states, limiting its appetite to prop up the Iranian leadership at any cost, analysts say.
“China, with broader global interests, can only actively promote de-escalation of the US-Iran conflict, and cannot and will not engage in fierce confrontation with the US for Iran’s sake,” said Hongda Fan, director of the China-Middle East Center at Shaoxing University in China.
“Ultimately, the US-Iran conflict must be resolved by the two countries themselves,” Fan said.
China and Iran share substantial trade links, particularly in energy, and a mutual suspicion of US dominance, but their relationship is heavily lopsided, with Tehran depending on Beijing far more than vice versa.
That asymmetry in ties was on full display this week at the annual gathering of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a 10-member bloc widely seen as a counterbalance to US hegemony, where Chinese President Xi Jinping joined more than a dozen non-Western leaders, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
While Iranian state media reported that Pezeshkian held a “brief meeting” with Xi on the sidelines of the summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Chinese outlets made no mention of the encounter.
Xi immediately followed his attendance at the summit with his first visit to Egypt in a decade on Tuesday, using the visit to call on countries in the Middle East to oppose “external interference” and reiterate his calls for a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war.
As Iran’s top trade partner, China has taken up to 90 percent of Iranian oil exports since the US and Israel launched their war in late February.
Iranian crude, however, accounts for only about 2 percent of China’s overall energy mix.
While China’s oil purchases have been an economic lifeline for Tehran, Chinese importers have not been immune to fears of exposure to US sanctions.
China’s major state-owned refiners such as Sinopec and PetroChina have shunned Iranian oil for years, leaving the trade to independent “teapot” refiners with minimal links to the dollar-based global financial system.
Though the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on these “teapot” refiners and a limited number of China- and Hong Kong-based firms and individuals, it has yet to target major Chinese banks accused of facilitating Iranian oil purchases.
The Trump administration has hinted at targeting China’s financial system as part of its ramped-up sanctions campaign, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast”, though analysts are sceptical that Washington will risk provoking Beijing’s ire as the sides seek to lower the temperature in their trade war before a scheduled summit between Xi and Trump on September 24.
“The legitimate question is why third countries should be expected to adopt Washington’s unilateral economic policy towards another sovereign state,” said Zichen Wang, deputy secretary-general of the Center for China and Globalization (CCG) think tank in Beijing.
“That does not, however, mean that Beijing will provide Tehran with a blank cheque,” Wang said.
“China is likely to continue opposing US secondary sanctions politically and to defend what it considers legitimate Chinese commercial interests. But past behaviour also shows that major Chinese banks and state-owned companies are highly conscious of sanctions exposure.”
Rhetoric versus reality
Even as Beijing and Tehran have forged closer ties, their relations have for years been marked by a substantial gap between rhetoric and reality.
While China pledged to invest up to $400bn in Iran over 25 years as part of a “comprehensive strategic partnership agreement” signed in 2021, few projects have materialised amid what analysts say is Chinese firms’ reluctance to navigate sanctions and the opaque Iranian bureaucracy.
In 2023, Iran’s then deputy economy minister, Ali Fekri, complained that he was “not satisfied” with China’s level of investment since the agreement, saying it had only amounted to about $185m.
“Iranian experts often blame their government for not doing enough to attract Chinese investors or not pushing Chinese companies to share more technology,” said Andrea Ghiselli, head of research at the ChinaMed Project.
“However, the reality is that there is no point for Chinese companies to give up their ties with the international financial system to expand their business in Iran,” Ghiselli said.
“It is much easier and more profitable to trade and invest elsewhere. Iran’s own domestic physical and bank infrastructure is also an obstacle.”
Meanwhile, the most tangible measure of China’s economic support, purchases of Iranian oil, has been dwindling amid the US blockade of Iranian ports.
Iranian crude exports via the Strait of Hormuz, mostly bound for China, fell from an estimated 1.85 million barrels per day (bpd) in March-April to just 240,000bpd in August, according to data from ship-tracking platform Kpler, though millions more barrels shipped before the blockade are still at sea.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said “only” about 30 million barrels of Iranian oil remained on the water and Chinese remittances to Iran were “going to run out”.
Kpler last month estimated that about 80 million barrels were in on-water shortage, enough to provide revenues to Tehran for up to six months.
“For China, Iran is valuable – but replaceable across many dimensions. Iranian oil matters, but China can obtain energy from Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, the UAE, and numerous other suppliers,” said Mordechai Chaziza, an expert on China’s Middle East policy who lectures at Ashkelon Academic College in Israel.
“Iran offers geopolitical access, but China possesses relationships throughout the region. Iran supports China’s multipolar agenda, but so do many other states.”
China’s support for Iran is also not risk-free for Beijing, given its important relationships with Iranian rivals such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, Chaziza said.
“Saudi Arabia and the UAE are major energy and commercial partners.
“Gulf stability is vital because China obtains roughly half of its crude imports from the Middle East,” he added.
The “ideal outcome” for Beijing, Chaziza said, would be “a stable, sovereign, economically connected, and internationally non-Western” Iran, but not one “whose confrontation with Washington, Israel, or the Gulf monarchies forces China to choose sides”.
Wang, at the CCG, said that while Beijing appears determined to defend Chinese commercial interests, it is unlikely to sacrifice its broader interests in the region or elsewhere.
Beijing’s warning that it is ready to take countermeasures against unilateral sanctions is “not the same thing as promising to underwrite the Iranian economy”, Wang added.
For China, Iran is seen more as a customer than an ally, said Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior official at the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control.
“I don’t think this is the alliance some people think it is, even though there’s real support. I think of a more like a customer relationship that Iran can’t walk away from,” Bitsoff said.
“And it was good for China – they got cheap oil, they got a US tied up in the Middle East, but I think that only lasts up until the point where it threatens China’s other interests,” she added.
