As Animalia turns 40, its author reflects on its extraordinary success
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
03:06:20 UTC
12:06:20 KST

As Animalia turns 40, Graeme Base reflects on the story behind the classic picture book
In 1986, Graeme Base was a 28-year-old illustrator who had published one picture book, My Grandma Lived in Gooligulch, and was about to publish another.
His sophomore effort was an alliterative alphabet book lavishly illustrated in his baroque style, titled Animalia.
Whether the world needed another A-B-C book was debatable, but his publisher, Bob Sessions, was willing to take a punt.
The first hint of the phenomenal success the book would garner — coming in at number five on the New York Times list of the bestselling books of 1987 — was the response to an exhibition of the artwork held in the lead up to the book's publication.
Every piece — bar the two Base held onto (his favourites, Lazy Lions and Horribly Hairy Hogs) — sold before opening night.
It was a life-changing moment for Base and his wife, Robyn.
"Suddenly we had this little pot of money," Base says.
"We didn't invest it or put a deposit on a house — we bought two round-the-world air tickets and shot through for a year."
They were backpacking through India and Nepal when Animalia came out, and received updates on the road.
"We were getting telegrams — that shows how long ago this was — from Bob saying 'we've reprinted again'," Base says.
The initial standard print run of 5,000 was doubled to 10,000, making the book a success from the outset.
"Three weeks later, they did another 10,000, then another 10,000, then another 10,000," Base says.
"Then they stopped mucking about and did 25,000. And then while we were away, we got news that they had just reprinted 50,000."
Animalia has enjoyed unflagging popularity since it was first published four decades ago, with anniversary editions reprinted in 1996 and 2012.
It has sold more than 5 million copies worldwide and, earlier in 2026, was voted fifth in Guardian Australia's poll of Australia's best children's picture books.
In 2026, the book is being celebrated again, with the release of the Animalia: 40th Anniversary Edition and an Animalia Colouring Book.
A lucky break
Born in the UK, Base came to Australia when he was eight.
In England, Base had been a cocky and confident kid — "one of the lads", he says.
"When I got to Australia, I was anything but … I was this new kid in a tough Australian primary school with a very strong English accent who didn't know any of the schoolyard games.
"Any kid who finds himself in that position probably starts trying to figure out if they're good at something, start doing it to carve your niche in the playground and to make friends."
For Base, that was drawing.
After graduating from graphic design at university, Base followed his classmates into advertising, which he soon realised was not the industry for him.
"I lasted maybe 18 months, went through three jobs, got fired from the third one," he says.
All the while, art remained his passion. He used his last pay cheque to print of some of his best illustrations, which he showed to publishers in the hope of finding work creating book jackets.
The work trickled in and after illustrating a couple of picture books, Base decided he could try his hand at writing one himself.
The result was My Grandma Lived in Gooligulch, published in 1981.
When Base showed Sessions the first completed pages — Crafty Crimson Cats and the Horrible Hairy Hogs — of his next book, the publisher was enthusiastic.
Sessions took the finished pages to the high-profile Bologna Book Fair, where they caught the attention of publisher and editor Paul Gottlieb, who agreed to publish it in the US.
Base says it took him three years to finish the book, because he "was trying to be a rock star at the same time".
Still in his 20s, Base was leading a "double life", working on his children's book by day and playing in a rock band — named Rikitikitavi in a nod to Rudyard Kipling — at night.
The real drawcard, however, was the lead singer, Robyn, who Base, of course, ended up marrying.
The pair recently celebrated their 45th wedding anniversary — "a happy story," Base says.
From the US to China
What sent Animalia into the stratosphere was its unprecedented success in America.
Upon its US publication, the Bases, still on their round-the-world adventure, detoured to New York to do publicity for the book.
Base's first interview was a big one, with Charlie Gibson on Good Morning America — one of the country's most popular TV anchors on one of the highest rating shows.
When the cameras started rolling, Base responded to Gibson's warm welcome with a laconic "g'day".
The TV host was immediately charmed. "We just started riffing," Base says.
In his inexperience, Base forgot all about mentioning his new book — the reason he was there — which was sitting untouched on the coffee table.
Fortunately, Gibson was more on the ball.
"With 30 seconds to go … he picked up the book off the coffee table and he held it to camera and did a hard sell that I couldn't have done to save my life — one of those, 'If you buy one book for your kids this Christmas, it's this one'."
The effect was dramatic.
"The book just flew off the shelves. Bookstores were caught unawares," Base says.
"The publishers went back to press and managed to catch the wave, and that year Animalia was the fifth biggest-selling book on the New York Times bestseller list."
For Base, it was a vindication of his youthful impetuosity.
"If we hadn't been stupid and bought around-the-world tickets we wouldn't have got ourselves to New York … [and] I wouldn't have done that interview," he says.
"[It's one of] those amazing things that do happen in life."
The success of Animalia kicked off a successful 30-year publishing career in the US, a rare feat for an Australian author.
While he says his "star has largely set in America", he has since found a growing market in China, after a trip to the Beijing Book Fair in 2017 led to a publisher picking up The Waterhole, a counting book full of elephants, giraffes and zebras.
The book "caught fire" and was added to a government-issued recommended reading list for schools.
"Every primary school in China finished up with multiple copies of The Waterhole, and it set off an interest in my work there," Base says.
Today, more than 20 of Base's books have been published in China, including Moonfish, a 2019 picture book inspired by a trip he took to Wuhan.
The Eleventh Hour
After the success of Animalia, Base faced a fresh challenge: how to write another book just as popular.
"The well-known term 'one-hit wonder' had a terrifying sort of resonance for me," he says.
An alphabet book offered limited scope for a sequel, so Base was compelled to come up with a new idea.
He'd read a few Agatha Christie novels during his travels and wondered if he could write a whodunnit for kids, where the clues were in the artwork rather than the text.
"I started working on that concept and almost immediately, the title, The Eleventh Hour, fell out of the air — I thought that's a great title for a mystery story," he says.
"I knew my story had to be centred around the number 11: 11 guests, an 11th birthday party, and at 11 o'clock something happens."
It took some time to work out just what that something was. Initially, Base envisaged the victim as a dog, depicted slumped dead in a chair, killed by poison.
After Sessions gently pointed out that a picture book was not the place for a dead dog, Base went back to the drawing board.
He toyed with the idea of a jewellery heist but settled on a more kid-friendly crime: the theft of the party food.
The Eleventh Hour was published in 1989 and became another global bestseller.
It was the joint winner (with Allan Baillie and Jane Tanner for Drac and the Gremlin) of CBCA's Picture Book of the Year.
Base believes his books are so popular with kids because he treats them "like grown-ups".
"I don't talk down to any perceived audience," he says.
"If there's a word in Animalia that they don't know or understand, well, you can look it up. That's what a dictionary's for.
"I'm not being arrogant about that. I think that's part of the fun of learning and discovery."
The sophisticated language of Animalia's V page — Victor V Vulture, the vaudeville ventriloquist, versatile virtuoso of vociferous verbosity, vexatiously vocalising at the Valhalla Variety Venue — did elicit a raised eyebrow from Sessions.
"Bob did say when I came to him with that one, 'Gee, that's pretty tough, isn't it?'" Base recalls.
"I said, 'Yeah, it is, but that's OK — I didn't know what vociferous meant until I looked it up. Surely kids can do the same."
Sessions was persuaded and the text stayed as it was — a decision Base believes would never be made today.
"I don't think there is a snowflake in hell's chance that that would have got through a committee without being simplified in this day and age," he says.
"These days, it's a lot more complicated. There are all sorts of reviews and anonymous readers and sales and marketing and cover committees … who will all put in their 20 cents worth, and you finish up with this thing which is trying to please too many masters."
He says he's never had any complaints from kids that his books are too hard.
"You're so much better off with kids not to put your hands on your knees and talk down to them, but to aim over their heads and challenge them to rise to the occasion," he says.
"And they will."
Animalia: 40th Anniversary Edition and an Animalia Colouring Book are published by Penguin Random House Australia.

Israel's election mudslinging hits a new low with toxic October 7 treason theories - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
03:06:15 UTC
12:06:15 KST

We’re still almost two months away from the fateful October 27 election, but the level of personal mudslinging has already reached a dismal nadir.
The worst are this week’s claims by Sara Netanyahu, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s wife, that Yair Golan, leader of The Democrats party, had prior knowledge of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack in which over 1,200 Israelis were slaughtered and that launched the war that continues to this day.
Golan is a former deputy IDF chief of staff, and as the events of October 7 unfolded, he donned his IDF uniform and drove to the Supernova music festival in the South to help.
Golan is no saint, however. By May 2025, he had soured on the war efforts and proclaimed that Israel was killing babies in Gaza “as a hobby.” As a result, Defense Minister Israel Katz was permanently barred from reserve duty and called his remarks a “blood libel.”
His political views are one thing, but thinly veiled claims of treason are another. Sara Netanyahu, in an interview with the right-wing Channel 14 on Monday, said he must have had advanced warning of the Hamas attack.
Claims Netanyahu intentionally not informed of October 7 attack
“A military man of such high rank, claiming that you fought on October 7, that already early in the morning you were there, already dressed and ready at a very, very early hour when others didn’t know, such as the prime minister...” she said.
In an Instagram post, the prime minister did not go as far as his wife, but he did say that IDF officers deliberately did not wake him for over an hour because they knew he would prevent the massacre.
According to Yaakov Katz, co-author of While Israel Slept and a former The Jerusalem Post chief editor - who wrote about Netanyahu’s comments and the failure to prevent October 7 - the prime minister would likely not have done anything differently after receiving flawed assessments from the military and intelligence echelon that Hamas was probably not preparing for a major attack.
But in election season, apparently, anything goes.
According to N12’s Dafna Liel, the media statements by both Netanyahus weren’t random but part of a deliberate Likud campaign ahead of the election to spread conspiracy theories and distance the premier from the massacre.
The October 7 conspiracy theory is nothing new and is bandied about by those on the Right whenever it comes in handy.
In a Knesset session only three weeks after the October 7 attack, Likud MK Tali Gotliev referred to a social media post by Golan in September 2023 that said, “October is approaching; the hour of decision is coming.”
Golan’s post was referring to the opening of the Knesset’s winter session and the judicial reform issue, but Gotliev’s comments unleashed a floodgate of unfounded claims that have gained steam over the ensuing three years.
Threat of lawsuit against Sara Netanyahu, conspiracy theories likely to expand
It’s time to put them to rest.
Whether Golan’s demand for an apology and threat of a hefty lawsuit against Sara Netanyahu will deter future outrageous statements about a conspiracy is questionable.
As Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, wrote on Tuesday on X/Twitter: “The outrageous conspiracy theory of treason... is intended solely to fan hatred and perpetuate the Netanyahu government, whose only way of ruling is to divide.
“Netanyahu is running from responsibility for the worst failure in Israel’s history, to which he led us blindly - through negligence and by ignoring every warning sign. Some people claim that they ‘weren’t woken up,’ while others got up and rushed into action -without asking questions.”
The surest way to get to the bottom would be to hold an official state inquiry.
However, those opposed to the inquiry and those who have prevented it are the same ones perpetuating the conspiracy theories. Interesting.
The most infuriating aspect of the attention this issue has received is that it takes up the bandwidth that should be provided to the real, critical issues facing the country as it heads to Election Day.
Here’s some advice for all of the candidates: Instead of blaming others for what they did or didn’t do, focus the campaign on what you intend to do to help the country.

Preview: New-look China faces stern test at Women's Basketball World Cup
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:34:34 CST
11:34:34 KST

by sportswriters Su Bin and Zhao Jiantong
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Returning to the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup after a record-tying runner-up finish, China faces a critical generational transition and needs to address its squad cohesion, offensive coordination and outside shooting to stay competitive.
The 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup will be held in Berlin from September 4 to 13, featuring 16 teams. China has been drawn in Group D with defending champion the United States, Czechia and Italy.
With the return of WNBA-based center Han Xu, China finalised its World Cup roster. The squad began training in mid-April and spent more than four months in preparation, yet full-team practices were rare. Yang Shuyu and Chen Mingling, who competed in Australia's second-tier National Basketball League 1 South league, rejoined the national team in late July. Guards Wang Siyu and Li Yuan headed to Australia to play for clubs there, while several players had to balance training with academic study.
Han's late return presents tactical challenges: how quickly she can merge the team's offensive and defensive systems remains uncertain, and the absence of fellow WNBA centre Li Yueru reduces China's interior strength.
China needs smart off-ball movement to open up court space, which calls for both positioning from centers and well-timed passing from their teammates.
Also, that strength will create open looks for outside shooters, and the team's ability to convert those opportunities will weigh heavily on match results. In some recent warmup games, China's three-point shooting success rate dipped below 20 percent.
Compared with the silver-medal winning squad four years ago, the current group is younger and lacks major competition experience. China has to keep its composure against defensive pressure, reduce mistakes and limit opponents' fast breaks.
Coach Gong Luming, who took charge last year, said the young roster is gradually taking shape. "Ever since we assembled this squad, we have worked on physical conditioning, technical skills, tactics and accumulating big-game experience. Now we can see tangible progress," he said.
China will open its campaign against the United States in a rematch of the 2022 World Cup final. Seeking its fifth straight title, the U.S. roster is stacked with elite talents, including six WNBA No. 1 draft picks and multiple players who averaged over 20 points per game in the league. Even with stars A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum sidelined by injury, the U.S. remains the title favorite.
With the U.S. seemingly difficult to beat, Czechia and Italy will be China's main targets in the group stage. China beat Czechia 84-74 in the World Cup qualifiers after a hard-fought battle in March. However, Czechia center Emma Cechova, who scored 23 points and grabbed 13 rebounds in that game, will be sidelined due to injury, dealing a blow to their overall strength.
Italy's main scoring threat comes from WNBA-based forward Cecilia Zandalasini, who averaged 13.8 points in the qualifiers. China lost both warmups against Italy in August and needs to figure out ways to break Italy's pressure defense.
16 teams are divided into four groups. Group winners directly qualify for the quarterfinals, while second- and third-placed sides will compete in a qualification to quarterfinals round to decide the remaining four berths.
Over the past month, China has played a series of warmup games to face varied styles. China played three matches against Nigeria at home to simulate the U.S. game, followed by six games in Europe against five opponents to adapt to European team play and physical contact.
Gong said the team will progress step by step to build major tournament experience. "Our ultimate goal is the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. We will give our all in every game and strive for the best possible results," he said. ■

11th–13th-century Polovtsian stone sculpture disappears from beach in Kharkiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:28:00 UTC
11:28:00 KST

11th–13th-century Polovtsian stone sculpture disappears from beach in Kharkiv
Alina Kharlamova, an archaeologist and researcher from Kharkiv, drew attention to this and spoke to Ukrinform about it.
“There used to be a stone Polovtsian sculpture on the beach. I study these sculptures and can confirm that it is authentic and dates back to the 11th–13th centuries. When I recently visited the beach, I saw that the statue was gone,” says Kharlamova.
According to her, it is not known exactly when the sculpture first appeared at the resort, but even before the full-scale Russian invasion, the archaeologist had approached the beach’s leaseholders—representatives of “Aquazhur”—with a request to transfer the artifact to the appropriate institutions.
“They simply ignored me. When I told the representative of what was then a paid beach that this sculpture should be handed over to a museum, she made a face as if I were joking. Perhaps people really didn’t view the statue as something valuable, but considered it a prop,” Kharlamova speculates.
The sculpture may have been brought from the Azov region, the researcher believes.
Currently, the municipal enterprise “Kharkivzelenbud” is responsible for the beach in question. The enterprise’s press office told the agency’s correspondent that the sculpture was not present when the territory was taken over, adding that before the municipal workers began landscaping the area, the former tenants had the opportunity to remove their property.
“It is very unfortunate that while our defenders are evacuating such monuments from areas under fire, they are disappearing right here in our city. I urge anyone who may have taken the sculpture or knows where it is to contact me personally or the Museum of Archaeology at V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University at 067-397-97-59,” Kharlamova said.
The beach in Zhuravlivka has been leased since January 17, 2008. The term of the agreement, signed between the Kharkiv City Council and “Kontakt Plus” LLC, was 49 years—until April 1, 2056. In 2018, the city council attempted to terminate this agreement through the courts, but its request was denied.
In May 2026, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in an interview with Ukrinform that Zhuravlivka Island had been returned to the ownership of the local community.
“I fought very hard, and I can say that we won this battle—and it really was a battle, as you can imagine! After all, land like this is very attractive. Not only that, but they (the tenants—ed.) weren’t paying under this contract, yet they were charging people money (for admission and access—ed.). I can tell you what a struggle I went through and how many enemies I made,” the mayor said at the time.
According to the NGO “Kharkiv Anti-Corruption Center,” “Contact Plus” LLC is linked to the business structures of former People’s Deputy Dmytro Shentsev of the now-banned “Party of Regions” and former Kharkiv Regional Council deputy Davyd Chikhladze (who served twice for the “Party of Regions” and once for “Vidrodzhennia”).
As previously reported, in February, soldiers from the Sicheslav Brigade, together with museum staff, volunteers, and philanthropists, evacuated 11th–13th-century Polovtsian stone statues—unique stone monuments from the Steppe era—from Vasylkivka in the Synelnykivsky District of Dnipropetrovsk region.

Pedro Sánchez’s Ceuta crisis just got a lot worse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

A new report alleging Moroccan involvement in the migrant surge threatens to upend the Spanish PM’s narrative and further erode his standing with voters.
A large group of migrants crowd outside the entrance of the Loma del Colmenar reception center, waiting for admission, in Ceuta on September 1, 2026. | Antonio Sempere / AFP via Getty Images
When Pedro Sánchez agreed to appear in the Spanish parliament’s hearings on the Ceuta migration crisis, he knew he would face a hostile audience.
But Thursday’s session promises to be a political reckoning for the Spanish leader, with an emboldened opposition and increasingly distrustful coalition partners seizing on a police report claiming that Morocco played a direct role in last month’s sudden arrival of 72,000 migrants in the autonomous city in North Africa.
The report has dramatically raised the stakes for Sánchez. With the prime minister’s credibility eroding, lawmakers are demanding to know how Spain’s security services failed to detect a hostile operation by a supposedly close ally — and whether the government knew more about Morocco’s role than it previously admitted.
Advertisement
“This wasn’t a spontaneous migration movement, but rather an operation that originated in Morocco and was spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco,” center-right People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo said at a rally in Ceuta on Wednesday.
“The government knew and covered it up,” he added, calling for snap elections. “They lied to our faces.”
In the immediate aftermath of the surge, Sánchez described it as an “attack on the territorial integrity of Spain,” but insisted Rabat had nothing to do with it.
He doubled down on that position on Monday, assuring the public he had “no information from Spanish security forces or our intelligence services that would cast any doubt on Moroccan authorities,” and instead accusing Russia, Israel and “an international far-right group” of orchestrating the operation.
But according to the police report, first revealed by Spanish newspaper El Español, Moroccan agents helped orchestrate the mass entry of migrants into the exclave. El País later published a page from the document with images that appeared to show uniformed Moroccan security officers guiding groups of people toward the beach from which they could cross into Ceuta.
The document was commissioned by a judge investigating the surge and drawn up by the National Center for Immigration and Borders, a specialized intelligence unit within Spain’s National Police.
Advertisement
In a letter to National Police Director Francisco Pardo, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska on Wednesday denied knowing of the report’s existence and expressed irritation that its contents had not been shared with the top officials convened to manage the crisis.
Justice and Presidency Minister Félix Bolaños said the government had only learned of the document through the press and declined to comment on it until it had been properly examined.
The report complicates the government’s efforts to avoid a direct clash with Rabat, whose assistance is needed both to deport unauthorized migrants and to prevent future surges. Sánchez on Monday insisted the crisis could “only be resolved with cooperation,” and that “showing a lack of confidence in Morocco will only aggravate this situation.”
Political reckoning
The report has turned Thursday’s hearing into a much more consequential political test for Sánchez.
Far-right Vox party MEP Jorge Buxadé on Wednesday urged Spain’s parliament to invoke Article 102 of the Constitution, which provides for criminal proceedings against members of the government in certain circumstances.
“This was an invasion of our territory, an act of hybrid war orchestrated by Morocco,” he said. “And this report shows the government knew about it beforehand and did nothing to stop it.”
Advertisement
Demands for accountability are also now coming from Sánchez’s own coalition government.
The junior partner in the executive, Sumar, has long questioned Rabat’s role in the crisis, and on Wednesday one of its member parties demanded Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska — who has always attributed the surge to human smuggling mafias — to step down if the information in the police report is proven to be true.
“Not a leaf stirs in Morocco without the government knowing about it, and between 70,000 and 80,000 people don’t move en masse to the Ceuta border in trucks or on foot without being detected,” said Antonio Maíllo, coordinator of the United Left party, which is part of Sumar. “The Moroccan government’s involvement in the crisis is obvious.”
The government’s parliamentary allies — among them the Republican Left of Catalonia and the Basque Nationalist Party — are expected to grill Sánchez on who knew what when, potentially exposing just how little room the prime minister has left in an increasingly uneasy coalition.
That political isolation was also on display on Spain’s streets on Wednesday evening, with tens of thousands of protestors in participating in nationwide demonstrations condemning the situation in Ceuta. Protests were held in more than 260 cities, with dozens of Socialist mayors defying orders from the party leadership and taking part in rallies in support of the exclave.
Their revolt underscores Sánchez’s difficulty enforcing party discipline among local politicians who increasingly see him as a political liability. With municipal and regional elections next May, the protests are a stark sign of the prime minister’s fragile standing heading into a crucial political year.

Nigel Farage’s Reform show gets a reboot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The Reform UK leader will use his conference to strike a ‘very serious tone’ after spending the summer fighting a by-election challenge from Count Binface.
LONDON — Nigel Farage had a silly summer squaring off against Count Binface. Now he wants to get serious.
The Reform UK leader will use his annual party conference, kicking off in Birmingham Thursday, to attempt to move on from a by-election dominated by novelty candidates and questions over his finances. He will try to signal how he would govern if he wins power at the next U.K. general election.
The leader and his four top lieutenants will use their speeches in Britain’s second-largest city to unveil what one senior party official described as “key pledges” for the first 100 days of a Farage premiership.
Advertisement
“It will be a very serious tone this conference,” the official — granted anonymity to discuss internal planning — said.
That’s the hope anyway, because public infighting, questions over undeclared donations, and splits on the right of British politics have dogged Farage’s summer — and could still overshadow proceedings.
Bardella and Farage show
Reform says the conference will be the party’s biggest yet — up by 2,000 attendees on last year, according to internal figures.
They’re boasting big business attendance and a diplomatic presence, too. Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right French party National Rally, will provide a set-piece attraction. Farage and Bardella have bonded over tackling small boat crossings in the Channel — the major public grievance that has fueled Reform’s success.
But Farage knows this event must offer more than a shift in tone. Not only has his party’s polling slumped as Labour rebounds after the ousting of Keir Starmer, but Farage is suffering a severe dent to his personal figures too.
A YouGov survey released this week suggests his net favorability rating has fallen from its peak of -27 last summer to -44. Just 19 percent of Brits now see him as a prime minister-in-waiting — down seven points since June, before he called his “people versus the establishment” by-election in Clacton.
Advertisement
The party knows looking credible is key. That’s why Farage will be leading the pledge-making to the public, culminating in a policy-laced but unscripted speech on Friday. Robert Jenrick, Zia Yusuf and Richard Tice — his spokespeople for the Treasury, home affairs and business briefs, respectively — will be making them too.
“It will be very serious about the problems the country faces and how we intend to fix them in the first 100 days,” the official cited above said.
Some in Reform had hoped the conference would mark the moment Farage announced an expanded front bench. Key posts like health and defense remain unfilled, despite Farage trying to demonstrate the party is no one-man band. But the party will hold off until after the Birmingham jamboree is over, instead announcing “a couple of new people” later this month and in October, according to the official.
Summer of scrutiny
Farage’s return to the limelight, which he has uncharacteristically dodged ever since his re-election in Clacton, began on Wednesday, with an interview with the BBC’s political editor.
The Reform leader has faced repeated questions over a £5 million donation from crypto-entrepreneur Christopher Harborne, as well as support from convicted fraudster George Cottrell.
Farage continued to insist Wednesday that he has “done nothing wrong” in not declaring the support in the run-up to the 2024 general election. He argued that the intense scrutiny of Reform’s funding is down to an “establishment” stitch-up, and railed against living in a “complainants’ society.” He compared his situation to the investigations faced by fellow “outsider” Donald Trump.
Advertisement
But Farage’s victory in Clacton last month served to restart the parliamentary standards commissioner’s investigation into the Harborne funding. Farage himself suggested that an interview with the investigator is on the horizon — and a sanction could well trigger another by-election for the Reform leader. He is keen to press the need to fund personal security for politicians in a dangerous world.
Reform’s conference opens Thursday with a day of trying to charm businesses, while the main event gets underway Friday.
Underlining the threat that Farage argues politicians now face, the conference will start with a tribute to Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old Reform spokesperson killed in her own home in July.
Restore a ‘shiny object’
Reform top brass seems keen to avoid talking about one elephant in the room: Restore Britain.
The right-wing splinter group, formed by sacked Reform MP Rupert Lowe, has been sucking small but significant support from Farage’s right flank in recent months.
Restore is talked of derisively as a “statistical anomaly” inside Reform, but tackling the threat is likely to be a topic of conversation in the conference center. “New shiny objects often attract support. That’s the way human beings are,” Farage dismissively told the BBC Wednesday, in an indication he believes support for Lowe’s outfit could tail off.
Advertisement
For Restore’s part, a disruptive intervention this week seems unlikely. “Let’s let them fight among themselves,” said one well-connected figure in Restore circles.
Indeed, the plea for unity that Farage wrapped last year’s conference with will be put to the test again in Birmingham. The party goes into this conference with open disagreement in its ranks.
Farage this summer publicly reprimanded his home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, for calling a Conservative former defense secretary a “traitor” in a series of angry online arguments. Reform then suspended political commentator Tim Montgomerie for criticizing senior party figures — including Yusuf.
Trade unions meanwhile look unlikely to leap at Farage’s call to ditch their historic ties with Labour and attend Reform’s conference. “I don’t think any unions are seriously going to take up his invitation to attend Reform conference,” predicted one union leader.
But for all the sniggering at Farage’s fight with Binface this summer, there are more optimistic takes inside the party about the resilience of its base.
Farage not only saw increased support in Clacton — but Reform’s polling is not collapsing in the face of its most intense scrutiny to date.
Advertisement
“Despite a summer that you might say hasn’t been brilliant,” said a second Reform official, “what we’ve learned is that our polling base is around 20-21, which is a step up in two years.”
It’s this core that will be drinking up the Farage show in Birmingham. But it’s the rest of Britain he’ll need to aim at this week.

====================================================================================================

How Merkel and Merz lost eastern Germany to the AfD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, took to the stage in the central marketplace of the town of Naumburg and declared there was a new “awakening” in eastern Germany.
Ahead of a vital election in the region of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — in which Siegmund is within striking distance of becoming the first far-right leader to govern a German state since 1945 — that appeal to an eastern identity struck a chord.
A young man beside me was hollering “Ostdeutschland!” although he was too young to have lived in the communist German Democratic Republic. “It was purer there,” he explained. “More German. Not America-Germany like the West.”
Advertisement
Elements of Siegmund’s new awakening sounded reminiscent of the old East, and his speech would certainly have played well in the Kremlin. He condemned the foolishness of supporting “corrupt” Ukraine and addressed the need to return to oil and gas supplies from Russia.
East Germany formally dissolved in 1990, but it did not disappear. Its struggles for identity within the sprawling German federal system, with power concentrated in Berlin, have fueled the ascent of the far right.
If the AfD does secure an outright victory this weekend, it will raise profound questions about how chancellors such as Helmut Kohl, Angela Merkel and Friedrich Merz failed to manage the post-unification transition and prevent large parts of the east from veering off on a political trajectory toward the far right.
Sausages and strongarms
In a generally upbeat line for sausages and beer in Naumburg, there were also some less cheery sorts in neo-Nazi T-shirts and regalia. One of the crowd told me the government in Berlin “sends our tax money to the Jews in Israel and [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy instead of spending it here.”
It is important to stress that the eastern political identity is not monochrome nostalgia for the GDR. Indeed, the AfD is repurposing the slogan of the 1989 demonstrations against communism — “Wir sind das Volk” – “We are the people” — for its own ends.
Advertisement
That taps into memories of marching for freedom in the last days of the socialist state.
“And now we will show the world again,” said Dirk Huzenlaub, a metalworker in his blue overalls, whom I spoke to on another campaign pit stop in the nearby town of Lützen
He has done well as a self- employed worker, supplying many local companies. But he adds that the “people at the top don’t want us to do well — they keep us down on purpose.” A welter of internet conspiracy theories followed, including the notion that Merz and his predecessor Merkel “betrayed us — we risk our country collapsing the way the old East Germany collapsed.”
Beyond the conviviality of the sausage line, the mood can sour fast — as I discovered when I sought to speak with Siegmund in Lützen, only to be told “mainstream” press were not welcome. I was roughly jostled aside, my arm twisted by a musclebound heavy flanking Siegmund, who sported an earpiece and a lavishly tattooed neck.
“Move or I will take you to the police,” he barked. We had a short, unproductive debate about the constitutionally guaranteed right to report freely in public places.
Another hard arm twist and shove ensued, ending with me stumbling over a curb and being dragged to a police car. No one seemed much bothered by this.
Advertisement
“This woman is being un-co-operative,” the minder snarled. At the next stop in Naumburg, another attentive policeman enjoined me to stay away from “Security Zone 1” — anywhere near the stage.
Then came the more chilling warning.
“It’s for your own safety,” he added. “Best remember, in that zone, the AfD are the masters.”
Merkel and the migration backlash
The last two chancellors — Merz and Merkel — have provoked a strong backlash in eastern Germany.
For Merkel, the outcome could have been more positive. She hailed from the East herself and was an active participant in the Wende, or “turn”, away from communism. She inherited Kohl’s pledge to produce “flourishing landscapes” in the “new federal states.” Forlorn towns and cities were restored, the air pollution from brown-coal energy supplies ended, and potholed roads are now smooth enough to roar along in Mercedes and BMWs.
But the East responded far more negatively to Merkel’s decision to allow a mass influx of asylum seekers from Syria and North Africa in 2015 and 2016. She signaled her empathy for that in a conversation with me in 2018, saying she understood the heartache of easterners seeing their communities empty out demographically and traditional jobs disappear.
“Of course, these disturbing personal experiences affect people and leave a deep mark — we need to understand this,” she said.
Advertisement
But Merkel’s responses did not go far enough for people worried about the speed of social change. And from 2015, the AfD began to soar.
The Covid era deepened divisions too: a social media campaign demanded the introduction of the Russian Sputnik V vaccine ahead of better options. That demonstrated a complex blend of attitudes which feature strongly in AfD lore to this day: Distrust of Western capitalism and an acceptance of Russia.
The veteran sociologist Detlef Pollack diagnoses a “victim mythology” western politicians find hard to combat without sounding aloof. Fully three-quarters of voters who lean towards the AfD think the unified Germany has robbed them of their just deserts, in comparison with two-fifths of the public in the old GDR.
Frustration came to mark the dealings of Merkel and her successor Merz in talking about the mood in the old east.
“There is no point trying to convince you [about the justification for accepting over 1 million refugees],” she said at a rally I attended in her final election campaign in 2017 in the industrial town of Bitterfeld as a hostile mob booed and blew horns to stop her being heard. Backstage she shook her head, clearly furious.
The more she was lionized as a Gloriana of international liberal democracy for her robust dealings with U.S. President Donald Trump, the more alienated she became from socially conservative easterners. The AfD also learned from the MAGA movement how to unite multiple strands of thought into campaign messages, interwoven with slugs of fake or exaggerated stories.
Advertisement
The arrival of Merz, a western politician not armed with a vast array of communication skills, together with struggles of the wider German economy — like the symbolic hit of massive projected job losses at the VW plant in Wolfsburg close to the old border — have taken a further shine off the lure of the Federal Republic’s prosperity model.
Falling behind
An assessment from the Halle Institute for Economic Research noted that, after the 1990s, the “initial catch-up momentum came to a halt. Since then, the East German economy has mostly grown even more slowly than the West German one.”
It blamed the “lack of productivity of East German companies,” as well as a protracted brain drain and a low rate of business formation. A German defense official, granted permission to speak confidentially to POLITICO, added: “Overwhelmingly, the new defense industries which will drive prosperity and security are based in the old Federal Republic. That gives the east less interest in arming against Russia — it’s a double hit we need to address.”
Merkel has demanded more “courage” to “fight for democracy,” channeling her own brand of 1989 nostalgia. These messages embolden the AfD’s opponents, including churchgoers now rallying as they did against the regime in 1989. Problematically, though, her appeals can also come across as “Bevormundung,” with eastern Germans feeling like they are being treated with haughty condescension.
Merz warns that a far-right government in Saxony-Anhalt would mean “foreign investors steering clear of the state in future” and that the state “will face considerable problems.”
Whether that scare tactic proves persuasive remains to be seen.
(For his part, Siegmund has shed the miserabilist mantras of other AfD luminaries. “My God, the women are great-looking in this town,” I hear him announce to giggling selfie-seekers in Lützen. “Better not tell my wife.”)
Merz also does not exude much personal interest in the East, other than seeing it as a problem to be kept at bay. Very few of his Cabinet hail from that part of Germany — though the party cites the rise of a new generation of eastern Germans to the next tier of ministerial posts. That may need to accelerate soon to combat the rising mood of alienation.
Advertisement
Arriving on a whistlestop visit on Monday to support Sven Schulze as his party’s candidate for minister-president, the chancellor condemned “people who trade on anger.” He did venture out among voters — something many leading politicians avoid.
Saxony-Anhalt is a small state in population — with just over 2 million inhabitants. But it is also the cradle of the Lutheran tradition of challenging the mighty — a theme that the more historically minded rally-goers raised with me.
As Siegmund puts it: “Even if we don’t get there [to an overall majority], we are not going away.” That too was a stubborn cry from the streets in late 1989. And in 2026, it spurred huge roars of approval through the marketplace in Naumburg, drowning out the counter-protests.
On Sunday, the AfD will be put to the test.
So too will a German political establishment that won unification, only to lose much of its grip on people power.
Anne McElvoy is a former correspondent in East Germany and author of The Saddled Cow, East Germany’s Life and Legacy.

Current cricket schedule could hurt women's game, says Perry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:58:58 UTC
10:58:58 KST

Ellyse Perry says the fact that Australia's women will not play international or WBBL cricket during the school holidays could hurt the growth of the game.
Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer through to the end of 2029 are white-ball games against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.
Perry says it is important to "carve out" a period during the peak of the Australian summer for women's matches.
Ellyse Perry has called for Australia's women to be given regular cricket in the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule could stunt the game.
Australia will play nine white-ball matches at home this summer against Bangladesh and New Zealand, with all confined to October and March.
The Australian team has not played a game at home during the summer school holidays since January 2025, while the WBBL also now falls entirely during the school term.
Part of the issue for officials has been India's WPL moving to the January window, with a common fear it will eventually extend into most of February.
Australia's only home matches in the middle of summer under the current program, which runs until the end of 2029, are white-ball ones against Ireland in the first half of December 2028.
Australian players have long pushed for a regular spot in the summer, much like the Boxing Day Test in Melbourne and New Year's Test in Sydney are part of the national calendar.
"It's the best time of year to play across that school-holiday window," Perry said.
"People are at home, everyone's head is in cricket too. There is a lot on the schedule in both the men's and women's game. It's a nice time to go out and watch.
"But also for them to be inspired to play themselves and be involved in cricket, it's really important.
"I don't know what the perfect window is, but I think somewhere in the peak of the Australian summer is important to carve out.
"Where and how you do that is more of a strategic planning opportunity that will take some time to find. But we should be prioritising that for the Australian team."
There is the view that being pushed to the outskirts of summer also has the potential to stunt any momentum around the team after its dominant T20 World Cup.
The timing of the WPL means the only real window during the school holidays would be in the second half of December, perhaps in the lead-up to Christmas.
"It's not just for Australia and all the southern-hemisphere countries … to make sure we're encouraging people to come along to matches," Perry said.
"It's a really tricky one; the scheduling and planning is a matrix I would never want to look at.
"But it would be really nice for us to preserve a window there where people know the Australian women's team is playing so they have the means and opportunity to come watch.
"That's really important in terms of continuing to grow the game for young boys and girls. But also we want to play in front of a home crowd with good opposition each year."

Germany hails Israeli LORA missile after secret naval test, eyes Russia deterrence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:51:38 UTC
10:51:38 KST

German newspaper Bild reported Wednesday that the German Navy had completed what it described as a “secret test” of the Israeli-made LORA ballistic missile in the North Atlantic.
According to the report, the German military expects to advance plans to purchase the missiles, which have a range of more than 500 kilometers. “The range exceeds anything we have known until now,” German Navy chief Vice Adm. Jan Christian Kaack said of the Israeli missiles.
In an article praising the capabilities of the Israel Aerospace Industries-made missile, Bild also highlighted the country Germany increasingly views as its primary security threat: Russia.
Germany accused Russia only days earlier of being behind an explosive drone found last month near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport. The aircraft was carrying military ammunition, and German officials said an explosion could have caused devastating damage.
Bild wrote that acquiring the system would form part of Germany’s rearmament plans launched after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, aimed at deterring Moscow. Concern among Germany’s allies is growing over possible aggression by Russian President Vladimir Putin, the newspaper wrote.
Its headline read: “Secret mission! German Navy tests Israeli missile,” accompanied by Kaack’s comments about the weapon’s range. The LORA ballistic missile is now expected to be offered to Germany in a deal potentially worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Germany has already purchased Israel Aerospace Industries’ Arrow 3 missile defense system in major deals. The Bild report described the latest test as a significant step toward a possible acquisition. Two LORA missiles were launched from a German Navy warship, and according to reports on the test, both struck their designated targets at sea.
If Germany decides to buy the missiles, it would join a small group of countries known to possess the Israeli system, including Azerbaijan and India.
The test also marks a milestone for the German Navy because Germany currently does not possess ballistic missiles. According to German reports, the missiles were launched from the frigate Sachsen-Anhalt, one of four F125-class frigates operated by the German Navy. Two frigates were sent to an area between Ireland and Iceland for the test.
Germany already has a similar long-range strike capability through its Taurus cruise missiles, of which the German military holds about 600. Their official range also exceeds 500 kilometers.
Unlike LORA, however, the Taurus is launched from fighter jets and flies toward its target at low altitude. The Israeli missile can also be launched from ships, climbs to altitude and travels toward its target on a ballistic trajectory at much higher speed. Germany is also developing an upgraded version of the Taurus, known as Taurus NEO, with production expected to begin in 2029.
Bild said Israel Aerospace Industries describes LORA as a precision “tactical missile” that Israeli security forces have used in Lebanon and, in an aircraft-adapted version, in Iran.
Israel Aerospace Industries unveiled the air-launched version, known as AIR LORA, at the ILA aerospace exhibition in Berlin last year. The missile is designed to be launched from fighter aircraft while they remain far from the target and outside the range of enemy air-defense systems.
Calcalist on Wednesday quoted senior Israeli defense officials as saying that the emerging German deal would focus, at least initially, on the naval version of the ballistic missile.
They added that follow-on deals could also be possible in the coming years. According to the officials, the prospects for a deal are very high because LORA has proven operational experience, including in fighting between Azerbaijan and Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh in recent years.
The LORA is part of a broader German effort to expand its long-range strike capabilities in response to the Russian threat.
According to Bild, Berlin is also planning to purchase Tomahawk cruise missiles from the United States, with a range of up to 2,500 kilometers, while working with allies on the development of European-made long-range missile systems.
Germany regards its shortage of long-range precision weapons as one of the capability gaps it is now seeking to close.
Germany is also among the relatively small number of European countries that maintained comparatively stable relations with Israel while Jerusalem faced sharp criticism over its conduct in Gaza following the October 7 massacre.
Unlike many other European countries, Germany took a relatively restrained approach, although it restricted sales of offensive weapons to Israel for several months before later lifting those limitations.

NEW YORK, September 3. /TASS/. The defense team of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro has requested a New York judge to dismiss all charges against him citing the doctrine of sovereign immunity for heads of state from prosecution abroad, according to the legal motion obtained by TASS.
"Mr. Maduro is entitled to sovereign immunity. The Indictment itself concedes that he exercised the powers of several official positions including Venezuela’s Presidency and remained, at minimum, the country’s de facto head of state, notwithstanding the Executive Branch’s subsequent political non-recognition of his de jure status," the document reads.
"Common law sovereign immunity deprives the Court of jurisdiction to adjudicate charges against Mr. Maduro as both a sovereign head of state and a foreign official prosecuted for acts attributable to the sovereign," the defense team continued. "The Court lacks jurisdiction over the prosecution of Mr. Maduro and must dismiss the Indictment against him, with prejudice."
In line with the international law, heads of state and high-ranking officials are granted personal immunity from criminal prosecution.

G20 ministers concluded a two-day Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on Wednesday, reaching a consensus on the governance and deployment of emerging technologies.
“Achieving consensus in the G20 is no small feat, but the topic of innovation as a driver of growth brought us together for a historic moment of unity,” said US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He asserted that the agreement provides entrepreneurs with the confidence to invest while ensuring that intellectual property frameworks foster and protect innovation.
The consensus statement, known as the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, outlines shared objectives in six critical pillars. They include pro-innovation policy frameworks, technology for opportunity and prosperity, and skilled technical workforce development. The principles specifically urge member nations to invest in foundational research and strengthen commercialization pathways.
The framework also prioritizes intellectual property policies for Artificial Intelligence (AI) alongside the creation of standards for AI systems and industrial innovation through investment in supply chains.
The meeting also launched the AI Prosperity Objectives and the AI Prosperity Compact to further “technical workforce development across G20 nations and expand opportunities for private sector partnership.”
Michael Kratsios, director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), which advises the US executive branch on tech issues, noted the vision relies on flexible policy frameworks to drive global growth.
The summit, hosted by the US Commerce Department and OSTP, featured high-level fireside chats with prominent tech leaders including Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, Jensen Huang of NVIDIA, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta.
The meeting included representatives from 20 nations and unions, including Türkiye, China, the European Union, Russia and the UK.

Chevron CEO says patience pays off in giant Venezuela oil deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:15:00 UTC
10:15:00 KST

Chevron CEO says patience pays off in giant Venezuela oil deal
HOUSTON – Big Oil has often employed the “hang around” playbook: secure legal rights to a giant resource – and then, eventually, figure out how to produce it profitably. But few companies have taken it to the extremes of Chevron.
For two decades, Chevron stayed in Venezuela while all its major peers quit after former President Hugo Chavez nationalised foreign assets atop the world’s largest oil reserves in the mid-2000s.
The Houston-based company endured US sanctions, accounting write-offs, arrests of its employees and accusations of collusion with a regime rife with corruption and human rights abuses.
The payoff came on Sept 2: a landmark deal that will provide Chevron with billions of barrels of reserves, enough to last into the 2040s – and perhaps beyond.
It still remains to be seen how easy it will be to boost output in a country where there are still significant political and legal questions.
It is unclear whether whoever succeeds US President Donald Trump in the White House will stick to his strategy in Venezuela. And in Caracas, there is no guarantee that whatever leader comes after acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodriguez will remain as cooperative with the US.
But for now, at least, Chevron is encouraged by its long game.
“You have to have some patience and look at this out over time and not become discouraged. Not pick up and leave when things are difficult,” Chevron chief executive officer Mike Wirth said in an interview.
“You have to hang in there until all the conditions come together: the technology, the economics, the markets, the politics.”
The strategy had its costs.
Employees worked through hyperinflation, power cuts and frequent breakdowns in law and order, while executives spent countless hours and political goodwill in Caracas and Washington to keep the operations in good working order.
Cash flow was minimal. Executives, including Wirth, typically met questions from analysts and reporters with terse, legally-worded answers.
Rivals including ExxonMobil Holdings and ConocoPhillips instead chose to pursue compensation claims from the Chavez nationalisation through international arbitration and court orders.
Chevron plans to invest US$7 billion over the next five years through its joint venture partnerships in Venezuela.
The deal is part of a US government-led push to revive the Latin American country’s oil industry.
Executives from Chevron, GE Vernova and Eni SpA on Sept 2 joined US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Rodriguez to unveil a wave of energy deals aimed at boosting the nation’s crude production. Wright said the deals represented “tens of billions” worth of investments.
Within five years, Chevron estimates it will be producing 600,000 barrels of Venezuelan crude per day at a cost of less than US$20 a barrel. Brent crude closed near US$95 a barrel on Sept 2.
At current prices, Chevron’s Venezuelan oil would be among the most profitable barrels on the planet.
Things changed for Chevron on Jan 3 when US special forces captured Venezuela’s former leader Nicolas Maduro.
Though the strongman leader was arrested on narco-terrorism charges, US President Donald Trump was clear the raid was also about reclaiming what he called “our oil.”
As the only US oil major operating in Venezuela, Chevron immediately moved into pole position to ramp up production and lay claim to the country’s best oil fields.
“Chevron was pragmatic,” said Miguel Tinker Salas, Venezuelan historian and emeritus professor at Pomona College in California.
“They understood they were sitting on the largest deposit of oil in the world and that the government needed them, especially with ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips leaving.”
To be sure, Eni of Italy and Spain’s Repsol SA also stayed in Venezuela during the years of hostility with the US and operated under similar restrictions as Chevron.
Eni on Sept 2 signed a 25-year contract for the Junin 5 field, which has about 35 billion barrels of oil in place, as part of the broader unveiling of deals.
The US is meanwhile coming under increased scrutiny for its foray into Venezuela, particularly after Trump announced a plan late last week to take majority control over a huge amount of the nation’s oil wealth in an unprecedented maneuver.
The venture comes months after Trump laid out his vision for what he called the Donroe Doctrine – a 21st century version of the Monroe Doctrine that warned European powers against interfering in the Western Hemisphere.
The developments are spurring analysts and academics to look back to an earlier era of neocolonialism, when the US exerted out-sized power over Latin America and its natural resources.
For Chevron, it is not the first time the company has employed the “hang around” strategy to considerable effect.
When Chevron merged with Texaco in 2001, it inherited vast swathes of drilling rights in the Permian Basin at a time when there was little knowledge of how to extract crude profitably from shale.
Rather than selling, as some of its rivals did, Chevron stayed put.
About 15 years later, when smaller companies perfected horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing techniques, Chevron was sitting on an area the size of Yellowstone National Park in the heart of what became America’s most prolific oil field.
In 1993, Chevron signed what some called the “deal of the century” to develop the giant Tengiz field in Kazakhstan soon after the fall of the Soviet Union.
Cost overruns, technical difficulties and political complexity meant the production ramp-up was slower than expected.
It was only in 2025 – more than 30 years later – that Tengiz reached its full potential of 1 million barrels of oil equivalent a day.
“It’s important to be in good, high-quality resource positions,” Wirth said. “They’re also sometimes not the easiest resource to produce.”
The big test for Chevron now is to prove that this time, in Venezuela, it will be different. A change of government in Caracas or Washington could just as quickly upend the deals signed today.
But Chevron is in a strong position to weather whatever storm may be coming, according to Schreiner Parker, partner and head of emerging markets at Rystad Energy.
“Chevron made its Venezuela bed a long time ago, and now it is finally in a position to sleep in it,” he said. “That patience has given Chevron decades of relationships, infrastructure and operational knowledge that its rivals cannot easily replicate.” BLOOMBERG

- In response, Rosaviatsia posted a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM), stating that all documents posted by Ukraine concerning Russian airspace had no legal force and violated the Convention on International Civil Aviation.

US Congress rejects constitutional amendment to restrict Supreme Court size
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
01:06:24 UTC
10:06:24 KST

US Congress rejects constitutional amendment to restrict Supreme Court size
Republican Mike Johnson slams Democrats for voting against ‘defending the integrity’ of the court.
A proposed amendment to the United States Constitution has fallen short, after Republicans attempted to cap the number of seats on the nation’s Supreme Court.
On Wednesday, the House of Representatives failed to advance a joint resolution championed by Republicans that would have permanently limited the court to its current number of justices: nine.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US Supreme Court allows Trump’s ballroom project to continue for now
- list 2 of 3US Supreme Court sides with Trump administration on mail voting
- list 3 of 3White House construction on $400m ballroom can go on, says US Supreme Court
The amendment’s final vote, which was mostly along party lines, was 212 in favour and 206 opposed.
A simple majority is needed to pass most legislation in the House, but constitutional amendments require two-thirds support.
Representative Don Davis of North Carolina was the only Democrat to vote in support of the amendment, while independent Representative Kevin Kiley of California, who caucuses with Republicans, voted against it.
The vote comes a day after the House voted 220 to 192 in favour of adopting a resolution condemning socialism. Eight Democrats joined with Republicans to advance the measure.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson on Wednesday took to social media to chide Democrats who voted against the two bills.
“For members of Congress who swore an oath to support and defend the Constitution, condemning socialism and defending the integrity of the Supreme Court shouldn’t be a controversial vote,” Johnson wrote on X. “Sadly, for today’s Democrats, they are.”
Both efforts effectively amount to messaging exercises by Republicans, who are attempting to put their Democratic counterparts on the record as not denouncing socialism and any Supreme Court expansion.
The manoeuvres come less than two months before November’s pivotal midterm elections, which will decide which party controls the chambers of Congress.
Some Democrats have called to add justices to the nation’s highest court to counter its conservative supermajority. The process, known among its opponents as “court packing”, is controversial.
But support for the idea gained momentum after US President Donald Trump appointed three justices to the bench in his first term. That conservative-led court has since handed him a string of legal victories.
In April 2021, four Democrats in the US Congress introduced a bill that would have created a Supreme Court with 13 justices.
They claimed it “would restore balance to the nation’s highest court after four years of norm-breaking actions by Republicans”.
The US Constitution establishes the Supreme Court but does not limit – or specify – its size, leaving the matter entirely to the nation’s lawmakers.
In 1789, the Judiciary Act established six justices: a chief justice and five associates. The court changed in size several times over the next century. The current number of seats was set in 1869 and has been subject to debate since.
The most famous attempt to change the court’s composition was under former President Franklin D Roosevelt.
After winning the 1936 election, Roosevelt proposed expanding the court, which would have added one justice for each justice over the age of 70, with a maximum of six additional justices.
Since then, advocacy groups, including the Brennan Center for Justice, have proposed structural changes to the court, such as term limits and ethics codes, while some Democratic lawmakers have unsuccessfully called for a Roosevelt-like expansion.
The issue has reemerged in the midterm election season. In an interview with NBC News last month, Democratic Senator Jim Clyburn of South Carolina embraced the idea.
“I think that we are in a position now that calls for some significant actions taken by the Congress, and we ought to expand,” Clyburn said.
“Thirteen is a pretty good number. A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court. I would hope that we would get people on the court who will follow the constitutional underpinnings of this great nation of ours.”
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee, also suggested that Democrats should have a “real conversation” about “expanding the court to 13 justices”.
But Republicans, including Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, have remained staunchly opposed.
“We must safeguard the independence of the federal judiciary to protect our constitutional freedoms and way of life for generations to come,” Grassley said in a statement in June, citing Harris’s statements.

10:06:00 KST

Mohan Malik is a veteran China-Asia analyst and military strategist who has advised senior brass on geopolitics at the U.S. Defense Department’s Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies and is a former director of Defence Studies at Deakin University in Australia.
Malik spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt, his former student, about how China, Asia, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are shaping up as U.S. President Donald Trump prepares for the mid-term elections and as the world marks 25 years since the 9/11 attacks that spawned the Global War on Terror.
Also known as the 9/11 Wars, the Global War on Terror ended with the withdrawal of U.S.-led forces from Afghanistan five years ago. Left behind was a vastly different geopolitical landscape, whose ramifications have continued to influence diplomacy in China, Asia, and ASEAN to this day.
ASEAN is divided between maritime and mainland countries but also by religion, mainly Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam, and Malik says they are still confronted by major problems. But some nations emerged from the 9/11 Wars stronger than others.
“Thailand, Indonesia, and India in South Asia, to some extent Sri Lanka to Bangladesh have done relatively better, they have been able to manage, contain the threat of domestic terrorism,” he said.
China also emerged in a stronger position and is now facing headwinds from the Trump administration and perhaps ASEAN, which wants to finalize its Code of Conduct in the South China Sea with Beijing by the end of this year.
“Even if Code of Conduct is concluded it’s not going to stop China’s creation of artificial islands and militarization of those artificial islands,” Malik said.
“It’s going to provide greater legitimacy to China’s efforts to subdue Southeast Asian countries and other rival claimants to the South China Sea.”

Premier League dominance, record fees define 2026 summer transfer window
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
00:36:31 UTC
09:36:31 KST

Record-breaking transfers, unprecedented spending and several dramatic deadline-day collapses defined the 2026 summer Premier League transfer window, which closed Tuesday in Europe’s major leagues.
Manchester City emerged as the biggest spender after committing £440.3 million ($594 million) to new players, while Premier League clubs collectively spent a record £3.48 billion.
The English top flight surpassed the previous summer’s record of £3.19 billion, underlining its growing financial advantage over the rest of Europe.
On deadline day, Enzo Fernandez completed the window’s most expensive transfer, moving from Chelsea to Manchester City for a reported £125 million.
The fee equaled the British transfer record and made the Argentina midfielder the first player to be transferred for more than £100 million twice, having joined Chelsea from Benfica for around £106.8 million in January 2023.
Fernandez signed a five-year contract with City as new head coach Enzo Maresca continued a major overhaul of the squad.
City had already paid Nottingham Forest £116 million for English midfielder Elliot Anderson, another of the window’s biggest moves.
Morgan Rogers joined Chelsea from Aston Villa for £117 million. becoming the most expensive English player in history.
Liverpool signed France forward Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain for an initial £107 million, with add-ons potentially taking the deal to £123 million.
Fernandez, Rogers, Anderson and Barcola were four of the 11 most expensive signings in Premier League history, illustrating the extraordinary scale of the spending.
The largest transfer outside England saw Real Madrid acquire Ivory Coast winger Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig for a reported £106.7 million.
Manchester City spent more than any club, with an outlay of £440.3, marking the beginning of a new era following Pep Guardiola’s departure after a decade in charge.
In addition to Fernandez and Anderson, City also signed Ayyoub Bouaddi for £85.7 million, Iliman Ndiaye for up to £65 million and Allan Elias for £32 million.
The investment was partly offset by outgoing transfers, including the sales of Savinho, Nico Gonzalez, Tijjani Reijnders, Rodri, James Trafford and Nathan Ake.
Chelsea ranked second among Premier League clubs with spending of £342.4 million.
Their headline acquisition was Rogers, while new head coach Xabi Alonso also brought in Maxence Lacroix for £52 million, Marco Palestra for £47 million and Geovany Quenda for £40 million.
Manchester United concentrated their investment on the midfield, signing Carlos Baleba for £70 million, Andrey Santos for £50 million and Youri Tielemans for £35 million.
PSG signed Mika Godts for up to €55 million, Ferran Torres and Maghnes Akliouche for about €50 million each and Lucas Digne for a reported €7 million.
Neither United nor PSG approached City’s overall expenditure, making the Manchester club the clear financial leaders of the window.
The Premier League’s control of the transfer market is not a recent development.
English clubs have been the biggest spenders during most of the past decade, but the gap between the Premier League and Europe’s other leading competitions has grown substantially.
Premier League clubs spent £3.48 billion in the summer of 2026, compared to £843.6 million in Serie A, £603.5 million in La Liga, £507.6 million in the Bundesliga and £490.6 million in Ligue 1, according to Sky Sports.
Much of the money also remained within the English top flight, with almost 40% of Premier League transfer spending going to other clubs in the division.
Even the promoted clubs demonstrated the league’s financial strength, with Ipswich Town, Coventry City and Hull City spending more than £400 million collectively as they prepared for the top flight.
The figures showed that the Premier League’s advantage extends beyond its traditional leading clubs, with newly promoted and mid-table teams increasingly able to outspend established sides elsewhere in Europe.
Several clubs ended the window without completing important moves, despite the record expenditure.
The most public dispute involved Barcelona’s pursuit of Atletico Madrid forward Julian Alvarez.
Barcelona President Joan Laporta confirmed the club’s interest, prompting Atletico to accuse the Catalan side of trying to unsettle the Argentina international.
Speaking to Spanish broadcaster Movistar Plus, Atletico CEO Miguel Angel Gil Marin accused Barcelona of dishonesty and a lack of ethics, transparency and professionalism, saying that if Alvarez left Atletico, “it will never, ever be Barcelona.”
Barcelona Vice President Rafa Yuste told the broadcaster that Gil Marin’s remarks showed a “lack of manners and respect” and had crossed a red line.
Although Alvarez reportedly favored Barcelona, Atletico’s board ruled out negotiations with the Catalan club and instead viewed Arsenal as its preferred alternative. The forward, however, decided against returning to the Premier League and remained at Atletico.
Chelsea’s proposed £47.1 million move for Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara also collapsed on deadline day after Monaco withdrew from a deal that had reportedly been close to completion.
Everton initially attempted to sign Manchester United forward Joshua Zirkzee on loan but had their approach rejected. They later agreed a deal worth around £40 million for Monaco’s Folarin Balogun, but the US international decided against completing the move after undergoing a medical.
The closure of the transfer window did not bring all recruitment activity to an end, as players without contracts can still join clubs as free agents.
Philippe Coutinho, Oleksandr Zinchenko, Jadon Sancho, Raheem Sterling, David Alaba, Dani Carvajal and Mauro Icardi were among the prominent players still listed as available after the deadline.
Their experience could attract clubs seeking reinforcements without paying transfer fees, although salary demands, injury histories and recent form may complicate potential agreements.
Dani Ceballos also spent much of the summer without a club after leaving Real Madrid, but the Spanish midfielder completed a return to Real Betis on a three-year contract.
Manchester City were among the window’s clear winners after giving Maresca a substantially rebuilt squad, although such unprecedented investment brings considerable pressure to deliver immediate results.
Chelsea added one of England’s most highly rated attackers in Rogers and raised significant income through sales, but the failure to replace Fernandez could leave the midfield unbalanced.
Liverpool secured Barcola in another nine-figure deal, while Real Madrid added one of Europe’s most exciting young wingers in Diomande.
Arsenal, Everton and Manchester United face some of the clearest risks.
Arsenal ended the window with Kai Havertz and Viktor Gyokeres as their main center-forward options after Gabriel Jesus joined Barcelona, while Everton were left with Thierno Barry as their only recognized senior striker following Beto’s move to Fiorentina.
United strengthened their midfield but did not recruit a specialist left-back despite targeting Newcastle United’s Lewis Hall and considering other options.
Luke Shaw remains United’s only recognized senior left-back, with right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui able to provide cover.
That lack of defensive depth could prove costly during a long season, and highlighted the central lesson of another frantic transfer window: spending heavily does not guarantee that every weakness has been addressed.

US judge blocks Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
00:33:06 UTC
09:33:06 KST

US judge blocks Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship
The ruling follows a 6-3 decision from the Supreme Court that found Trump’s effort to limit birthright citizenship was illegal.
A United States federal judge in Maryland has blocked President Donald Trump’s latest effort to roll back birthright citizenship, after the Supreme Court ruled that his last attempt violated the Constitution.
District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction on Wednesday against Trump’s new executive order, which was issued on August 6.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3What is birthright citizenship, and what does the Supreme Court ruling say?
- list 2 of 3Trump to ask US Supreme Court for new hearing on birthright citizenship
- list 3 of 3Trump faces lawsuit over push to limit birthright citizenship
The new order took aim at what Trump has called “birth tourism”, the practice of intentionally giving birth on foreign soil.
It sought to deny citizenship to children of foreign nationals in certain groups, including those accused of engaging in a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship or classified as an “alien enemy”.
Boardman, however, said the order was unconstitutional for the same reason Trump’s previous effort failed. She cited the Supreme Court’s June decision in the case Barbara v Trump.
The order “is almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class for the simple reason that the Supreme Court in Barbara already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth”, she wrote.
“This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them.”
In the Barbara case, the Supreme Court ruled six to three that birthright citizenship was protected under the Fourteenth Amendment of the Constitution.
Birthright citizenship confers automatic citizenship on anyone born in the US, outside of a handful of narrow exceptions, such as the children of diplomats or invading armies.
The constitutional basis for birthright citizenship has been upheld in several Supreme Court cases over the years, most notably in US v Wong Kim Ark, the case of an American man born to Chinese parents.
But Trump campaigned for a second term as president on the pledge to crack down on immigration into the country.
One of his promises was to reform the concept of birthright citizenship. Trump and his allies have argued that children of temporary or undocumented immigrants do not qualify for the right, as they are not under the “jurisdiction” of the US.
Since the Supreme Court defeat in June, Trump and his allies have continued to probe for ways to challenge the constitutional protections for birthright citizenship.
Wednesday’s legal challenge was brought by immigrant rights advocates and families, including groups like the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project.
They had previously won an injunction from Boardman last year, blocking the Trump administration from enforcing his initial executive order about birthright citizenship.
Last week, Boardman instructed the plaintiffs to revise their complaint to specifically address the second executive order, rather than relying on the same material used for the first.
But she signalled scepticism at the time about the constitutionality of Trump’s latest attempt, calling it “unprecedented”.
“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth’,” she wrote in Wednesday’s decision.
