US lawmakers demand explanation for ban on Army unit learning drone warfare from Ukrainian forces
A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is demanding that the US Army explain why a unit stationed in Europe was ordered to cease specialising in drone warfare, thereby depriving troops of the opportunity to learn from the Ukrainian Armed Forces' advanced battlefield experience.
Source: The Associated Press
Details: AP reported that the unit in question is the 600-strong Unmanned Assault Battalion of the 173rd Airborne Brigade. Its troops built their own drones and practised combat tactics pioneered on a large scale by Ukraine in the war against Russia.
The lawmakers sent a formal letter to acting US Army Chief of Staff General Christopher LaNeve and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, requesting an urgent briefing.
"We have deep concerns that eliminating this specialised drone unit will limit our ability to learn from allies, particularly the Ukrainian Armed Forces, and hinder our efforts to modernise drone warfare at the speed necessary to compete on the modern battlefield," the lawmakers wrote.
The letter was signed by Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen, Republican Senator Thom Tillis, independent Senator Angus King and Republican Representative Mike Turner.
The lawmakers stressed that the unit's creation had been a timely response to the challenges of modern warfare, as conventional units are unable to adapt quickly enough to emerging technologies.
Background:
- In April, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed Army Chief of Staff General Randy George, who had regularly stressed the need to accelerate the development of new unmanned systems and provide them not only to specialised units but also to ordinary soldiers. General Christopher LaNeve subsequently took over as acting Army chief of staff.
- In August, LaNeve ordered the experimental unmanned systems battalion to wind down its activities and return to its role as an airborne infantry unit. Shortly afterwards, US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who had also supported the rapid integration of innovations, resigned.

Thousands protest in Spain as Ceuta’s migration crisis festers a month on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:28:18 UTC
08:28:18 KST

Thousands protest in Spain as Ceuta’s migration crisis festers a month on
Spain faces unrest as residents protest, while migrants and asylum seekers search for shelter and resources in Ceuta.
Thousands of protesters have rallied across Spain against the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta, a small Spanish territory on the African coast.
Roughly 50,000 people gathered in Madrid alone on Wednesday. In Ceuta itself, residents draped Spanish and city flags over their shoulders.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Spanish police evict hundreds of migrants from Ceuta beach to shelters
- list 2 of 3Spain plans transfer of 500 migrant children from Ceuta to mainland
- list 3 of 3Migrant women face sexual assault in Ceuta
“Expel the invaders” and “Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended” were among the crowd’s chants.
The protests fell on Ceuta Day, a local holiday that marks the Portuguese takeover of the North African city in the 15th century.
They also come a little more than a month after more than 70,000 migrants and asylum seekers crossed en masse from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30 and 31. The deadly surge killed at least 80 people.
While many of the arrivals have returned to Africa, some remain. Estimates vary as to how many. The Spanish government places the figure at about 5,000 people, including 1,200 minors, but local statistics have a higher count.
Among those who remain stranded in the Spanish territory is Otman Ianaya, 40. He swam to Ceuta with his wife and two young daughters, searching for better prospects.
“There is no work in Morocco,” he told the news agency AFP. “I want to build a future in my life.”
Some migrants and asylum seekers sleep on Ceuta’s beaches. The Spanish government has worked to expand emergency housing and increase funds to social services, but critics have blasted the effort as inadequate to answer the needs of so many people.
The strain has sparked isolated instances of violence, including fights, the stoning of a military patrol and reports of sexual assault.
Residents in Ceuta have also clashed with police and burned items belonging to migrants and asylum seekers, in protest of the influx of people.
“The situation has been chaotic, so much so that you can’t go out onto the street,” said Gema Guillen, a protester.
The July incident has also underscored political schisms.
Ceuta’s regional leader, Juan Jesus Vivas, represents Spain’s conservative Popular Party and has called the crisis a “violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.
Meanwhile, Spain’s territorial policy minister, Angel Victor Torres, has accused the conservative and far-right opposition of exploiting the crisis “to attack the government of Spain” instead of helping the city.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has blamed the surge on a misread court ruling and online disinformation that he said encouraged people to cross the border.
He also said negative coverage of the crisis has since been amplified by Russian and Israeli-linked accounts, though he did not offer proof, instead citing findings from Spain’s intelligence community.
Madrid has pledged 309 million euros ($357m) in aid for Ceuta.
Amid the standoff, while some migrants are looking for economic opportunities, others are seeking asylum to escape alleged persecution back home.
“They are people in a vulnerable situation; we need to have a little bit of empathy,” said Halima Ahmed of Luna Blanca, a nongovernmental organisation that distributes food and aid to migrants and asylum seekers.
“People are tired, people are fed up… but that does not justify any type of violence,” she added.

US economy grows modestly, but inflation clouds outlook: Fed report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
23:24:34 UTC
08:24:34 KST

The US economy has continued to expand at a modest pace, with employment rising slightly and prices increasing moderately across most districts, according to a report by the Federal Reserve Board.
Ten of the 12 Federal Reserve districts reported slight to moderate economic growth since early July, while two reported no change, suggesting an economy still expanding but losing momentum.
Employment edged up overall, though labour markets remained largely flat in many regions. Wage growth stayed modest to moderate, with stronger increases concentrated in construction and manufacturing, where demand for skilled workers remains high.
American consumers kept spending, but growing price sensitivity contrasted sharply with continued demand for high-end goods.
Auto sales remained sluggish as weak consumer confidence, high fuel prices and rising financing costs kept buyers away.
Tourism, however, gained momentum, with airlines reporting strong demand despite higher fares.
Data centre drive
Manufacturing gained momentum across much of the country, driven by strong orders tied to defence and the rapid expansion of data centres.
Residential construction continued to decline, while nonresidential projects surged on the back of new data centre development.
US companies also reported mounting health care and insurance expenses, while expressing cautious optimism about the months ahead amid growing uncertainty over conflicts, policy changes and energy prices.
The report gives policymakers a real-time, on-the-ground view of US growth that will help shape the next interest-rate decision amid mixed labour, consumer, and geopolitical signals.

A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction Wednesday blocking the Trump administration from enforcing its most recent executive order to restrict birthright citizenship.
Authorities are "barred from taking any other action to interfere with, deny, or fail to recognize the citizenship of any member of the certified class,” the court for the District of Maryland wrote in its ruling.
The injunction applies to major federal bodies, including the State, Justice and Homeland Security departments. While the order is frozen, the court noted that the government may still issue public guidance related to certain sections of the policy.
The 2026 executive order sought to expand categories of those ineligible for automatic citizenship and targeted "birth tourism." Cyber Campaigning: Mid-Tier States Can Leverage Civilian Cyber Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Cyber Campaigning: Mid-Tier States Can Leverage Civilian Cyber Power
States lacking vast nuclear and conventional capabilities should team with the private sector via letters of marque and digital levée en masse.
States that lack nuclear arsenals and large conventional forces should make greater use of cyberspace as a strategic environment. Unlike the nuclear domain, cyberspace does not require enormous financial or technological investments to achieve strategic effects. It is accessible to states of different sizes and, importantly, to non-state actors and private companies. The war in Ukraine demonstrates this increasingly blurred boundary: not only states but cyber activists and technology companies such as Starlink, Amazon and Microsoft have impact on the conflict.
Cyberspace creates opportunities for mid-tier states. Rather than attempting to replicate the capabilities of major cyber powers they can exploit the distinctive logic of cyberspace and cooperation with civilian partners. Two mechanisms could operationalise this approach: Cyber letters of marque, whereby states authorise private technology companies to conduct specified cyber operations on their behalf; and a digital levée en masse, through which civilian cyber expertise is mobilised to strengthen national cyber resilience and, where appropriate, support operations during conflict.
Cyber Persistent Theory
For much of its development, academic thinking about cyber operations was framed through nuclear and conventional concepts, particularly deterrence and coercion. Cyber persistent theory offers a perspective away from the ‘deterrence default’: cyberspace should be understood as a distinct strategic environment with its own logic and dynamics. After all, empirical evidence indicates that cyber operations frequently remain below the threshold of armed conflict, are seldom coercive and involve a wide range of non-state actors.
A defining characteristic of this environment is interconnectedness. Constant interaction is a condition rather than a choice. Strategic success therefore depends on persistent engagement or cyber campaigning. Rather than waiting for conflict or seeking a single decisive battle, actors should maintain the initiative, shape the cyber environment to their advantage and accumulate smaller gains over time. This requires a degree of (tacit) understanding among competing actors about the boundaries of acceptable behaviour.
Private-sector activities authorised under a state strategy could therefore contribute to persistent engagement, provided that they remain coordinated and subject to clear legal constraints
Persistent campaigning is imperative in cyberspace if strategic gains are to be pursued. The question is how mid-tier states can develop sufficient capacity to create operation friction in cyberspace without building every capability themselves. In their RUSI comment, Kello and Harknett suggest that states with limited resources can concentrate their persistent campaigning on a relatively small number of targets that are critical to national interests. Complementing that, states can team up with civilian partners to achieve strategic effects.
Teaming up with civilian partners
Mid-tier states have three broad options. They can build national cyber commands, intelligence capabilities and supporting infrastructure from scratch to engage in cyber campaigning; cooperate with larger cyber powers’ campaigns, accepting a degree of dependency; or leverage domestic private-sector capabilities. In practice, a combination of these approaches may be appropriate.
This Commentary focuses on the third option of teaming up with private-sector companies as an extension of cyber campaigning. It is true that cooperation between governments and private companies in national security and defence raises significant legal and ethical questions. Yet, in the course of history, states often relied on civilian actors or privateers for military and security purposes, producing two aforementioned models that are particularly relevant to cyberspace: the letters of marque and the levée en masse.
Cyber Letters of Marque
Historically, letters of marque authorised private vessels to conduct operations against enemies on behalf of a sovereign. Even today, states still employ private actors in security and defence, including private military companies. The increasingly private ownership of digital infrastructure suggests a possible cyber equivalent: states could authorise (trusted) Information and Communications Technology (ICT) companies to conduct specified cyber operations in support of national objectives.
A US legislative proposal has already sought to create such a mechanism by allowing the President to issue ‘cyber letters of marque’. Under such a framework, a private entity could be authorised to conduct operations against designated targets, subject to government-imposed conditions. Potential activities could include intelligence collection, seizure of digital assets and disruption of malicious infrastructure.
The concept aligns with the central principles of cyber campaigning: initiative, cumulative gains, and agreed competition. States need to shape the digital environment continuously, and authorised cooperation with trusted ICT firms could allow states lacking substantial indigenous capabilities to remain proactive while retaining governmental control over inherently governmental functions.
Cyber operations can produce strategic effects through the accumulation of smaller actions (or gains) rather than a single decisive strike. Private-sector activities authorised under a state strategy could therefore contribute to persistent engagement, provided that they remain coordinated and subject to clear legal constraints.
Cyberspace is, finally, characterised by constant interaction among states and non-state actors via a system of tacitly agreed bargaining. Because the boundaries of acceptable behaviour are partly constructed through this interaction, uncontrolled or poorly understood activities can increase instability. Regulated cooperation between a mid-tier state and specific ICT firms could instead help reduce capability gaps and contribute to a more balanced cyber environment.
Digital Levée en Masse
A second model is digital Levée en Masse. In its strict legal sense, levée en masse refers to civilians spontaneously taking up arms against an invading force. The concept has historical roots in the French Revolution and was subsequently incorporated into the law of armed conflict. In a broader sense, however, it can describe the mobilisation of dormant civilian capabilities in response to a crisis, comparable to the stay-behind organisation that existed during the Cold War period. The Ukrainian IT Army similarly provides a contemporary cyber-related example.
For cyberspace, this concept could be adapted to mobilise the cyber expertise already present in critical sectors. Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) and their teams possess detailed knowledge of the vulnerabilities, systems and dependencies within their organisations and sector. Relying on a network of firms, for instance leveraging the NIS2 framework, these CISO-communities could cooperate with national cyber security centres and intelligence agencies during peacetime, while becoming more closely integrated with national cyber commands as tensions rise.
The principal value of such a network could be defensive. A national CISO-community could improve threat intelligence, monitoring and resilience across critical sectors, while providing government and ICT companies with sector-specific expertise. The knowledge these communities possess (on architecture and vulnerabilities in specific industries) can, however, also contribute to planning and conducting offensive cyber operations. Unlike cyber letters of marque, the CISO-community would not necessarily conduct operations itself. Rather, it would strengthen the wider ecosystem on which state cyber power depends.
It may sound counterintuitive, but for this notion to work the existence and role of the civilian cyber network should be sufficiently transparent to avoid surprising other states and to reduce the risk of miscalculation and unwanted escalation.
The Strategic Opportunity and Risks
Cyber Campaigning offers mid-tier states a way to pursue strategic advantage without possessing the nuclear or conventional capabilities of major powers. The key is not to reproduce the capabilities of larger states but to exploit the distinctive characteristics of cyberspace: persistent interaction, interconnectedness, civilian participation and the possibility of accumulating effects over time.
Cyber letters of marque and a digital levée en masse provide complementary mechanisms especially for mid-tier states. The former could allow trusted ICT companies to perform specified functions on behalf of the state; the latter could mobilise existing civilian expertise to strengthen national cyber defence and resilience. Used together, they could enable mid-tier states to remain persistently engaged in cyberspace despite limited resources.
There are, however, important risks. First, greater reliance on civilian cyber capabilities could deepen rather than reduce asymmetries between states, particularly because authoritarian governments may find it easier to mobilise (or enforce the alignment of) private actors than democratic governments. Second, involving civilians in cyber operations raises serious questions under international law, particularly when civilian actors participate directly in activities associated with armed conflict.
These concerns do not invalidate the concept, but they demonstrate the need for clear legal mandates, political oversight and carefully defined roles. If these conditions can be met, civilian cyber capacity could become an important force multiplier for mid-tier states. Rather than waiting and hoping to acquire the capabilities of major cyber powers, they can begin to shape the cyber environment with the resources already available to them.

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is urging President Donald Trump to replace Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth because of what he described as “inept management.”
The North Carolina lawmaker’s call to oust Hegseth comes after Dan Driscoll resigned from his role as Army Secretary on Monday, amid tension that had been reportedly broiling between Driscoll and Hegseth for months. In a social media post on Wednesday, Tillis thanked Driscoll “for his leadership to our Army and service to our country,” before going on to slam Hegseth.
“If we had a @SecWar who maintained the same priorities and forward-thinking, he would be fighting to retain talented leaders like Dan and the many flag officers he has forced into retirement,” Tillis said. “Instead, he is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks.”
Tillis, who previously served on the Senate Armed Services Committee, included in his post a link to a CBS News article that lists about 20 military and civilian leaders who have been ousted or stepped down since Hegseth was confirmed to lead the Department of Defense, including Driscoll. Also among them is Gen. Randy George, who was serving as the Army Chief of Staff until Hegseth requested that he retire, effective immediately, in the spring.
Tillis voted to confirm Hegseth as Defense Secretary last year, though he initially had reservations about him. Amid mounting controversy surrounding Hegseth’s nomination, three other Republicans broke from party ranks and voted against it, forcing Vice President J.D. Vance to be the tiebreaking vote. It was the smallest margin for the confirmation of a nominee to lead the Defense Department since the Secretary role was first formed in 1947, Senate records indicate.
Despite Tillis’ crucial vote in the confirmation, he has since publicly criticized the Defense Secretary. The Republican Senator told POLITICO in May that he thought that “Hegseth misinformed [the President] on the challenges” related to a war in Iran, adding that “I’m glad the president did what he did in Iran. I’m not glad that he has Hegseth advising him on the details.” He went on to tell the news outlet: “I’d love to see Pete Hegseth fired because he’s incompetent and doing a horrible job. That’s kind of on a Christmas wish list.”
And he renewed those calls on Wednesday.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis said in his post on X. He accused Hegseth of being “intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force.”
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” Tillis continued.
Tillis and Trump have clashed in the past, most notably when the North Carolina Senator joined two other Republicans in the upper chamber in voting against the President’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” last year. In the aftermath, the President lashed out at Tillis, threatening to back candidates who could challenge Tillis in a Republican primary race.
Soon after, Tillis announced that he would not seek reelection in the 2026 midterms, citing what he described as a shift away from bipartisanship in Washington in recent years.
“Too many elected officials are motivated by pure raw politics who really don’t give a damn about the people they promised to represent on the campaign trail,” Tillis said in a statement last June. He added that a choice “between spending another six years navigating the political theatre and partisan gridlock in Washington or spending that time with” his family is “not a hard choice.”
Trump has remained firm in his support for Hegseth. Amid speculation that Hegseth is considering launching a 2028 presidential bid, a reporter asked the President if he would back the Defense Secretary in such an event.
“I think he’s doing a fantastic job, but it’s very early to talk about that,” Trump said. “We have to get through the midterms first, and I think he’s a very good guy.”
“Right now, all [Hegseth] loves is, and all he cares about is, the military and taking care of the military,” he continued.
Hegseth has denied that he is considering running for President in 2028.

In a letter to International Civil Aviation Organisation Chairman Juan Carlos Salazar, a copy of which was exclusively shared with Reuters, Ukraine's Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk said Kyiv believed the risk of tragedies in the skies should be minimised.
Ukraine asked ICAO to encourage aviation authorities and airlines to safeguard civil aviation, "including by facilitating the full prohibition by ICAO member states of civil aircraft operations within the airspace of the Russian Federation".
While European and US carriers do not fly over Russia due to the war that erupted when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the airspace is used by airlines from countries such as China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf states.

ICAO cannot impose rules on its 193 member countries, but its decisions influence national policies. The Montreal-based UN agency uses consensus to set standards on everything from runways to seat belts.
While not mentioning any specific country, ICAO on Wednesday warned in a statement that the risk of weapons targeting commercial planes is growing and called for stronger commitments from countries to protect aircraft from conflict zone risks.
"ICAO is observing heightened risks of civil aircraft being targeted or caught in crossfire," the statement said. "While the aviation industry is able to reroute flights and maintain operations during conflicts, this operational flexibility does not address the fundamental security threat."
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an analysis that Ukraine's drone and missile attacks have already demonstrated their reach deep into Russia, leading to airport closures and flight cancellations.
"Zelensky is articulating publicly what Ukraine has been doing for months: systematically disrupting Russian airspace," Osprey said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Zelenskiy's comments amounted to "state terrorism". Moscow on Wednesday vowed to head off any disruption to civil aviation.
In 2024, 38 people were killed when an Azerbaijan Airlines plane heading to Russia's Grozny crash-landed in Kazakhstan after diverting from its course. Putin later said two Russian missiles detonated near the aircraft after Ukrainian drones entered the airspace.
Ukraine closed its airspace to civilian traffic when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, unleashing missile barrages without issuing warnings to civilian aircraft in Ukrainian airspace.
Airports have remained closed ever since, and SkyUp, Ukraine's only surviving airline, now operates from neighbouring Moldova.

US urges G-20 countries to allow AI training on creators’ work

US urges G-20 countries to allow AI training on creators’ work
- The US urged G-20 countries to allow AI companies to train their models using creators’ copyrighted work while protecting artists through fair use principles.
- Major US tech firms face lawsuits for using copyrighted material in AI training, with the US Justice Department supporting fair use in these cases.
- G-20 nations agreed to avoid new AI-specific regulations, focusing only on novel issues, with tech leaders calling for rules addressing real-world AI problems rather than theoretical harms.
AI generated
CHAPEL HILL, North Carolina – The US urged G-20 countries on Sept 2 to develop rules governing how AI companies use copyrighted material to train their systems, as major American technology firms face mounting lawsuits over the practice.
Companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta have been sued in the US by authors, publishers, media organisations and other creators who allege the firms misused their work to develop AI products.
Tech firms train their AI models to generate images and text by feeding them vast amounts of data, often including books, music and art. They have argued that using that work to build their AI tools is legal.
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told the G-20 officials at a tech-focused meeting in North Carolina that they should allow AI companies to train their models on creators’ work, while finding a way to “protect artists”.
He said the countries should embrace “fair use”, a principle that allows the unauthorised use of copyright-protected works under certain circumstances.
“We need frameworks that protect creators and inventors whose ingenuity drives our economies without creating the barriers that prevent the next generation of innovators,” Lutnick told the gathering of officials representing G-20 countries.
He did not offer specifics on how to accomplish that.
The US Justice Department separately on Sept 2 filed a brief supporting OpenAI in its dispute with The New York Times and several other newspapers over the company’s use of their work to train the large language models behind ChatGPT, saying AI training generally makes fair use of copyrighted material.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang appeared alongside Lutnick ahead of the commerce secretary’s speech on Sept 2.
Huang urged the G-20 officials to avoid writing AI regulations focused on “theoretical harms”, and instead develop rules addressing real-world problems tied to the technology. His message echoed those of the Trump administration and other American tech executives who addressed the gathering on Sept 1.
The G-20 nations will aim to avoid writing new regulations specifically for AI, according to a joint statement released on Sept 2 by the US. Any future rules should address only “novel considerations” posed by AI that are not already covered by existing laws, the statement said.
Government requirements could hurt the industry’s profits if they slow the release of new models or prompt the companies to change how their products perform to address security concerns.
China, which has already implemented a broad list of AI regulations, was among the signatories to the statement.
Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, Palantir’s Alex Karp and OpenAI’s Sam Altman also addressed the gathering on Sept 2. REUTERS

The incident is the latest deadly episode involving migrants attempting to reach the Canary Islands by sea from West Africa, one of the most dangerous migration routes toward Europe.

Cairo museum showcases Ottoman treasures from Egypt, Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:20:23 UTC
21:20:23 KST

Cairo museum showcases Ottoman treasures from Egypt, Türkiye
More than 100,000 Islamic artifacts include mashrabiya, carpets, ceramics and manuscripts reflecting Ottoman-era artistic ties between Cairo and Istanbul
Hussien Elkabany and Ikram Kouachi
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Archive
Cairo museum showcases Ottoman treasures from Egypt, Türkiye
CAIRO/ISTANBUL
In the heart of the Egyptian capital Cairo stands a unique cultural landmark housing treasures that span centuries of Islamic history.
The building’s significance extends beyond its striking architectural design, as it is home to what the museum describes as “the world’s largest specialized museum of Islamic art,” housing more than 100,000 rare artifacts that reflect the richness and diversity of Islamic civilization across different periods.
Its collections include a notable group of artifacts from the Ottoman era in Egypt and Türkiye, some of which reflect remarkable artistic exchanges between Istanbul and Cairo.
Anadolu visited the Museum of Islamic Art to view Ottoman-era works from Egypt and Türkiye, which showcase diverse aspects of Islamic art and craftsmanship.
The museum’s collections are notable both for their size and diversity, encompassing manuscripts and objects related to medicine, surgery, and herbal remedies, as well as astronomical instruments such as astrolabes, compasses, and celestial globes.
They also include applied arts associated with everyday life, including metal, glass, and ceramic vessels, as well as jewelry, weapons, woodwork, ivory, textiles, and carpets.
The collections feature many unique masterpieces that demonstrate the refined taste and exceptional craftsmanship achieved by Muslim artists.
Since its establishment, the museum has attracted kings and prominent figures from around the world, according to its official description.
Ottoman treasures
Among the most prominent artifacts is a turned-wood mashrabiya dating to the Ottoman era in Egypt in the 16th and 17th centuries.
According to the museum, wooden screens with openings used to cover windows appeared as early as the Ayyubid period and later developed into the form of the mashrabiya.
During the Ottoman period, mashrabiyas took the form of projecting balconies. Their functions included reducing the intensity of sunlight and humidity while preserving privacy in rooms overlooking courtyards or streets by preventing people outside from seeing into homes.
Another exhibit is a collection of Ottoman ceramic tiles dating to the 18th century. The tiles are painted in multiple colors beneath a transparent glaze and decorated with floral motifs centered around a mihrab from which a mosque lamp hangs.
The museum also displays a painted wooden fireplace decorated with ceramic tiles, dating to the Ottoman era in Egypt in the 17th century.
According to the museum, fireplaces became widespread in palaces and residential homes in Egypt and Türkiye during the Ottoman period.
Decorative designs featuring Ottoman floral motifs were often first produced in Türkiye and then transferred to Egypt, where local artists reproduced them. This contributed to similarities between many artistic works produced in the two countries during the period.
The collection also includes a ceramic panel depicting the Grand Mosque in Mecca, dating to the 17th-century Ottoman period in Egypt.
The museum also houses two stained-glass windows set in plaster, dating to the Ottoman era in Egypt in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Muslim artisans excelled at using the reflection of light to create aesthetic atmospheres inside buildings.
Among the museum’s Ottoman holdings is also a wool-and-cotton carpet dating to 16th-century Ottoman Egypt. The style is known as “palace carpets” or “court carpets,” an unconventional style in Ottoman carpet decoration.
The carpet’s field is decorated with intertwined floral motifs and surrounded by three borders, with the middle one being the largest. It has fringes at the top and bottom.
According to the museum, Islamic carpets served different purposes depending on their size and decoration.
This particular carpet was made to cover the floors of palaces and homes, while its motifs resemble those found on Ottoman ceramic tiles from the same period.
The collection also includes a wool-and-cotton prayer rug dating to the 18th century and attributed to the Turkish city of Kula.
The museum displays pages from “Al-Adwiya al-Mufrada” (The Simple Drugs) by al-Ghafiqi, dating to the 16th-century Ottoman period in Türkiye. Al-Ghafiqi was a physician who lived in Andalusia during the 12th century.
Among the exhibits are also two glass hourglasses dating to Ottoman Egypt in the 16th century.
The collection further includes an 18th-century Ottoman marble tombstone from Egypt. It consists of three sections, one side of which bears inscriptions in Thuluth script, including the Muslim declaration of faith.
Also on display are “khadda bowls” made of copper and bronze and engraved with talismans and inscriptions referring to their supposed therapeutic benefits. They date from the 12th through the 18th centuries and originate from Egypt, Iran, and Türkiye.
The gallery also displays two wool-and-cotton prayer rugs from 18th-century Ottoman Türkiye, attributed to the Turkish city of Gördes.
According to their display labels, Turkish cities were renowned for producing prayer rugs, with each city developing its own style for designing mihrabs. Türkiye also became known for another type called “saff carpets,” characterized by a series of adjoining mihrabs designed for use during congregational prayers.
Historic design
According to Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, the idea of collecting and displaying Islamic artifacts in a museum dates back to 1880. The building was officially opened in 1903 during the reign of Khedive Abbas Helmy II.
Its facade was designed in the Mamluk architectural style, and the museum is located next to the National Library and Archives.
The museum was damaged in the 2014 bombing of the Cairo Security Directorate before undergoing comprehensive restoration and renovation. It reopened in 2017.
Among its most prominent treasures are a key to the Kaaba from the Mamluk period and a textile fragment bearing the oldest known Kufic inscription in its collection.

US Treasury issues US$1 coin with Trump’s face on it
- The US Treasury issued US$1 coins featuring President Donald Trump's face to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence, despite legal restrictions against living presidents on currency.
- The coins are sold at a significant mark-up and are said to be "also in circulation", raising questions about their monetary status and legality.
- This move is part of Trump's broader effort to imprint his image on US institutions, including plans for a US$250 bill and his signature on paper money.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Treasury on Sept 2 issued US$1 coins featuring the face of President Donald Trump, the latest move in an unprecedented campaign by the Republican billionaire to put his personal stamp on national institutions.
The coins were minted to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States celebrated in 2026.
A roll of 25 US$1 coins was available for sale for US$61 (S$77.70) – a mark-up of 144 per cent – with a 100-coin bag available for US$154.50.
When the Treasury announced the plan, it was unclear if the coins would have monetary value or would be purely commemorative. But on Sept 2, the US Mint said the coins were “also in circulation”.
The move to put Trump’s countenance on a coin with monetary value runs counter to federal law that says no living president may appear on US currency.
Trump has aggressively defied precedent and legal challenges in his push to remake US institutions in his second term, putting his name on the Kennedy Center for the Arts and demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make room for a new ballroom, among other moves.
The new coin features Trump’s face on one side, with the words “Liberty” and “In God We Trust”. It also features the dates 1776-2026, marking 250 years of US independence.
The other side of the coin features a version of the US presidential seal, depicting an eagle clutching arrows and an olive branch while covered by a shield that says “250”.
This is just the latest in Trump’s campaign to put his face and name on US currency.
In May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department was pursuing a plan to issue a new US$250 bill with Trump’s face on it. He conceded that the move would require Congress to change the law barring living persons from appearing on currency.
The US Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether the new US$1 coin violates that law.
In March, the Treasury announced that US paper money would soon bear Trump’s signature – another first for a sitting US president. AFP

Palantir CEO Alex Karp says French restrictions on US software are ‘backfiring’
Palantir CEO Alex Karp said on Wednesday French restrictions limiting government use of US-made software were proving counterproductive. His comments followed France’s decision to replace Palantir with domestic provider ChapsVision at intelligence agency DGSI over data sovereignty concerns. Karp said Europe’s regulatory environment was hurting competitiveness.
Palantir chief executive Alex Karp said Wednesday that French regulatory restrictions, including limiting government use of US-made software, were proving counterproductive.
Karp's argument follows France's recent decision to drop Palantir at its domestic intelligence agency, the DGSI, in favor of French provider ChapsVision, over data sovereignty concerns.
"These things are backfiring," he said, adding that "the regulatory environment is obviously not helping Europe or France".
Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of a G20 gathering in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, Karp said the problem was that sovereignty decisions were being made by people without the expertise to judge them.
"You need to have regulation that actually helps. And to do that, you need to be a technical expert," he said.
The eccentric executive cast his criticism as friendly, invoking the French proverb "qui aime bien chatie bien" – spare the rod, spoil the child. "I care," he said.
Karp reserved his sharpest language for what he described as sovereignty in name only: contracting non-US firms to deploy American or Chinese closed models.
Read moreArtificial intelligence in Europe: Does advanced AI have a glass ceiling?
That, he said, was the technical equivalent of "un cinq a sept sans preservatif" – an afternoon tryst without protection.
France, he added, was "culturally the most important country in Europe, and economically the second most important".
Asked about European anxiety over dependence on US technology under President Donald Trump, Karp said the moment for hesitation had passed.
"It's game time," he said. "You've got to deal with the technical issues. There are legitimate concerns, but it's game time."
He drew a distinction between substantive objections and what he called alarmism.
"You cannot just pretend the technical concerns that are true are the same thing as the fearmongering," he said, adding that he was not arguing American companies should control everything.

ChapsVision, founded in 2019, reported €200 million ($232 million) in revenue last year, against Palantir's $4.5 billion.

A French security source told AFP the agency would keep using the software in the meantime, since it cannot afford operational disruptions while ChapsVision's tool completes development.
Deployment is expected to take several months or more.
Palantir has become somewhat of a lightning rod in Europe.
Rights groups have long objected to Palantir's role in mass surveillance, its facial recognition tools, and its work for the US government.
Co-founded by Trump ally Peter Thiel in the wake of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, the company has been accused of enabling Israeli targeting in Gaza.

Protests in Spain over government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
22:34:27 BST
06:34:27 KST

Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis
- Published
Thousands of people have protested in cities across Spain against the government's handling of the influx of migrants to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the north African coast.
Spanish opposition parties accuse Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of abandoning the residents of Ceuta, while the government says right-wing parties are exploiting the crisis.
On Wednesday a police report said Moroccan security forces showed "total permissiveness" during the unprecedented influx, days after Sánchez insisted Morocco was not responsible. Senior police officers have also stressed the report does not directly attribute what happened to the Moroccan government.
He has blamed trafficking gangs and online misinformation for encouraging people to cross the border. Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or scattered across the city's streets or on the beach - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Sánchez.
There have been near-daily protests by locals, with demonstrators calling for the migrants to be sent back to their countries of origin or redistributed across Spain.
Wednesday's rallies were called by city councils across Spain where opposition parties - the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party - govern or have significant popularity.
Demonstrators called on Sánchez to resign.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo was at the rally in Madrid, where more than 50,000 people gathered, according to government figures.
"A Spanish city has been invaded, occupied and, unfortunately, this happened with the knowledge of the Government of Spain," he said.
Vox leader Santiago Abascal meanwhile said Sánchez was "at the service, like a lackey, of the Moroccan regime".
There was also a major rally in Ceuta itself, with participants chanting: "Ceuta is not for sale, Ceuta must be defended."
"The response has been inadequate, late and, to top it all, has involved a complete dereliction of duty on the part of the government," 45-year-old teacher David Hernandez told Reuters.
"We cannot be second-class citizens, and our border must not be sidelined."
Pressure on Sánchez's government has intensified after Spanish media said the report submitted by the National Police's National Immigration and Borders Centre (CENIF) to the National Court pointed to the involvement of Moroccan gendarmes in the migrant crossings.
The police report claimed that the Moroccan police deployment around the border "was clearly smaller than usual" and cited migrants who spoke of a "passive attitude" as the crossings happened.
However the report did not categorically accuse Morocco of being behind the influx.
- Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say 
  - Published1 day ago
Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla, which have long been a flashpoint in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.
Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.

Faisal Mahmud
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has urged international support following deadly floods to be treated as climate compensation rather than charity, saying it is a “question of justice and fairness."
The death toll from the flash floods and mudslides that struck the Nepal-China border Aug. 26 has climbed to 1,225, while nearly 4,757 victims, including 541 in China, are missing.
Nepalese authorities have said 1,204 people were found dead, while China confirmed 21 fatalities by Wednesday.
Khanal said Nepal was suffering disproportionately from climate change despite accounting for a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"If you look at data, even our overall carbon footprint, greenhouse emission is less than a 10th of a percentage," Khanal told CNN’s Anderson Cooper 360°.
"The glaciers are melting. The permafrost are thawing, and there is a risk of glacier flood," he said, adding that the latest disaster involved a glacier collapse.
"What we are telling to the world is, look, our contribution in this changing climate is almost negligent," said Khanal.
He stressed that protecting the Himalayas should not be Nepal’s responsibility alone.
"Saving Himalayas has to be part of a global effort because today it’s impacting Nepal but it also impacted China," he said.
Khanal noted that Himalayan rivers eventually flow into India and, in some cases, Bangladesh, providing fresh water for agriculture and drinking to more than 2 billion people.
"Global communities have to come together and this cannot be seen merely as a charitable giving, but has to be part of a compensation process as well," he said.
"You don’t want foreign governments to look at this as giving aid to Nepal. You want this to be compensation," asked Cooper.
"Exactly, this should be seen from the perspective of justice and fairness," Khanal replied. "How fair is it for Nepali people and people of Himalayas to bear the burden of the climate change, where we have had very little contribution to it?"
Asked whether he regarded the disaster as a direct result of climate change, Khanal replied, "Absolutely, you know, there is no question that there is evidence."

Estonia's defence minister resigns amid scandal over ammunition purchases for Ukraine
Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his intention to resign amid criticism from the National Audit Office and a scandal over defence procurement, including ammunition intended for Ukraine.
Source: Pevkur in an interview on the ETV programme Aktuaalne kaamera, as reported by Estonia's public broadcaster ERR
Quote from Pevkur: "As defence minister, I of course have to recognise that I am responsible for the entire area under my ministry and if you are now waiting for that big answer, then, of course, a leader must have both the courage and the stature to take responsibility as a matter of political responsibility, even when there is no personal responsibility. I will take that responsibility and the prime minister will have to find a new defence minister."
Details: Pevkur said the findings of the state audit into the activities of the Estonian Defence Forces and the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK) were serious enough to raise the issue of political responsibility.
He said he will hand over the post to his successor at a time convenient for the prime minister, expressing his conviction that his actions had been the right ones to strengthen Estonia's security.
"I do so with the firm knowledge that we have made the right decisions to strengthen national defence. Estonia is better defended than ever before," he said.
Pevkur has headed the defence ministry since 2022.
The resignation announcement came after information emerged that Estonia had attempted to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine and had paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian companies that had not previously sold a single piece of ammunition.
Magnus-Valdemar Saar, the former head of RKIK, said that no important decisions had been made without the approval of the Defence Ministry's leadership. In addition to the minister, former permanent secretary Kusti Salm and current permanent secretary Kaimo Kuusk had been informed about the details of the contracts.
Pevkur said he had indeed not read the contracts, but confirmed that RKIK had provided him with the documents.
Quote from Pevkur: "Although the minister does not count socks and ammunition or conduct contract negotiations, the National Audit Office's criticisms, primarily concerning the activities of the Defence Forces and the Centre for Defence Investments, raise the question of political responsibility. I therefore believe it is right to take political responsibility today for the entire defence sector and hand over the defence minister's baton at a time suitable for the prime minister."
Background:
- Earlier, a special committee of the Estonian parliament (Riigikogu) held hearings following a summary report by the National Audit Office, which pointed to systemic problems and confusion in the defence sector's accounting.
- After the report was posted, Toomas Uibo, head of the Estonia 200 parliamentary faction, Lauri Läänemets, leader of the Social Democratic Party, and Urmas Reinsalu, leader of the Isamaa party, publicly called on Pevkur to resign.
- Prime Minister Kristen Michal convened a Cabinet meeting for the morning of 3 September to receive the Auditor General's report, noting that the absence of personal fault on the part of the minister did not rule out the need to assume political responsibility.

Nuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:30:35 UTC
06:30:35 KST

A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans.
Tobias Ellwood has said he unwittingly gave MPs incorrect information in 2018 when he told them he had been unable to locate information on veterans’ blood tests after being given incorrect information by officials at the Ministry of Defence (MoD).
Veterans have been fighting for years to see the records as many look to prove that years of serious illnesses such as cancer were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons. Ellwood’s admission will increase pressure on the MoD to explain whether its officials have helped prevent those veterans get justice.
In a piece for the Guardian, Ellwood says: “In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament.
“Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was ‘unable to locate any information’ suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests.
“I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them.”
He added: “This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “This government commissioned and completed an extensive records discovery exercise, examining tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme.
“The findings have now been published in full, following regular engagement between ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.”
Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout and many witnessed the first test wearing little more than short-sleeved shirts and shorts.
Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health.
Unlike other nuclear-armed countries such as France, the US and the Soviet Union, the UK has never compensated those involved in testing atomic bombs.
The case has been compared with the infected blood scandal, which saw more than 30,000 people contract HIV and Hepatitis C in the the 1970s and early 1990s after being given contaminated blood and blood products.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously said he was misled by officials when he claimed as health secretary in 2009 that there was no evidence that people were knowingly given contaminated blood. His claims echo those being made today by Ellwood.
Burnham has also been a vocal supporter of the nuclear test veterans in recent years.
As Greater Manchester mayor in 2022, Burnham said: “If the state was conducting medical tests upon servicemen and not informing them when they found serious irregularity, that is at least misconduct in public office, and more serious, perhaps gross negligence manslaughter, in respect of people who died as a result.
“Crimes have been committed.”
The prime minister is now coming under pressure to begin an inquiry and allocate government money for compensation to the victims.
One of the major problems with securing compensation so far has been the lack of medical evidence linking veterans’ health problems to their experiences helping with nuclear tests.
The government long maintained that it did not hold any such medical records – a claim that was proved incorrect in 2022 when the journalist Susie Boniface revealed the existence of a database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin.
That database had been put together in response to a 2007 lawsuit by 1,000 British test veterans and their families, but the information was classified.
Ellwood says he did not find out about the existence of this database until 2022, when details began to emerge in the press.
He writes in his piece: “If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?”

Andy Burnham will begin the process of courting European leaders when he welcomes Emmanuel Macron as the first foreign head of state to visit him in Downing Street.
The prime minister will meet the French president at No 10 on Thursday as he looks to make inroads on a number of foreign policy objectives, including curbing irregular migration and sealing a new deal with the EU.
The meeting marks one of Burnham’s first forays into foreign policy, having previously promised to remain mostly focused on domestic issues, and comes weeks before a crunch EU summit that could shape much of his future economic strategy.
Burnham said in a statement on Wednesday: “The progress we have seen this summer [in bringing down the number of small boat crossings] shows what can be achieved when the UK and France work together.
“But I am clear that we cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating the dangerous crossings.
“The small boats crisis is a shared European challenge, and no country can solve it alone. Working with France and our international partners, we will restore order and control to our borders and prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants.”
While Burnham has talked almost exclusively about domestic issues such as the cost of living since becoming prime minister, he is quickly finding himself having to deal with international crises as well.
Last month he met the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to help celebrate the country’s independence day, when he announced he would declassify sensitive military information to allow Ukraine to build more cruise missiles.
On Thursday he will discuss migration, EU relations, Ukraine and the war in Iran with Macron.
The two leaders will announce additional resources for French police to help stop small boats being launched from the country’s north coast and larger “mega-dinghies” departing from the west.
Downing Street said on Wednesday that the number of French officers dealing with small boat crossings in northern France would soon rise to nearly 1,050 officers – up by roughly a quarter in four months.
The teams will include a specialist 75-person team to seize equipment and arrest smugglers on land. A separate intelligence unit will be expanded from 18 to 30, while another 45 officers will be deployed to the west coast.
Irregular migration has fallen down the political agenda in recent weeks thanks to a drop in the number of small boat crossings.
This week, Burnham said the drop in numbers to a seven-year low was a result of efforts by his predecessor Keir Starmer to tackle smuggling gangs – though experts say external factors such as an improvement in Syria’s security situation have also played a role.
The prime minister will also use the meeting to press Macron to support his efforts to renegotiate Britain’s treaty with the EU.
Brussels postponed a planned summit from July to allow the new prime minister time to review tentative agreements made by Starmer, with a new one expected in early November.
European countries have been pushing hard for Britain to agree a new youth mobility scheme and to allow their students to pay home fees at British universities – both concessions that Starmer was ready to make, according to recent reports.
However, Burnham may take a tougher line on the number of young people he is willing to admit as part of the scheme, having promised to pass all government policies through a “Makerfield test” to measure them against the views of his constituents.
In return, Britain wants new agreements to ease trade in electricity and agricultural products, which officials hope will give a timely boost to the UK economy.
The prime minister told the Guardian last year he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, but has since said this would not be something he would actively pursue as prime minister.

Inside Kallas’ fightback against plans to tear up the EU’s diplomatic service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:13:30 UTC
06:13:30 KST

Inside Kallas’ fightback against plans to tear up the EU’s diplomatic service
Senior officials working for the foreign policy chief are sounding out capitals for ideas on how to reform the EEAS without drastic changes to its makeup.
European Commission High Representative and Vice President Kaja Kallas makes a point during a press conference with Ireland's Defence and Foreign Minister Helen McEntee in Wicklow, Ireland, on Sept. 1, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images
Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, is leading a fierce behind-the-scenes push against Franco-German plans to overhaul her diplomatic service — courting capitals and using a new secretary-general to develop alternative reform plans.
Kallas’ campaign involves convincing EU governments that the bloc’s foreign-policy problems stem from unanimous decision-making rules and poor implementation of its treaties — not from the current institutional setup, according to three EU officials informed of her plans. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive internal strategy.
The fight comes as the 15-year-old European External Action Service faces criticism that it is no longer fit for purpose at a moment when Russia’s war against Ukraine, Donald Trump’s demands on Europe, conflict in the Middle East and a more confrontational China are all testing the bloc’s ability to act abroad. The Commission is also expanding its role in foreign policy, while Berlin is pressing to cut EU operating costs amid negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget.
Advertisement
Kallas’ allies fear that an overhaul intended to make EU foreign policy more effective could instead give President Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission greater control over the work overseen by the high representative.
“If I have somebody above me who is actually deciding, then it doesn’t work,” Kallas told journalists Wednesday after a debate with EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland.
One diplomat, referring to the Franco-German plans, said: “She [Kallas] wants to delay the whole process because she doesn’t want to be subject to von der Leyen.” Another said “she wants this whole thing to go away.”
The pushback is taking shape through Kajsa Ollongren, the EEAS’ new secretary-general, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments.
Ollongren will brief staff on the findings from that tour at a town hall meeting with the EEAS this week, where Kallas will formally introduce her, according to the officials and an EU diplomat.
Ollongren is also expected to propose the creation of a “council of elders” task force to reflect on possible internal reforms, one of the officials said.
Advertisement
The group would include the EEAS’ former secretary-general, Belén Martínez Carbonell, who has delayed taking up a new role as head of the EU delegation in Mexico to advise Ollongren. Senior EEAS official Charles Fries is also set to contribute, according to the officials and the diplomat.
The push seeks to give the EEAS more control over a reform debate that could determine whether the service remains a distinct part of the EU’s foreign policy machinery or becomes more closely integrated into the Commission.
The Franco-German plans, set out in a paper seen by POLITICO, include moving much of the EEAS staff into the EU executive. Although they call for reinforcing Kallas’ formal role, her allies see them potentially allowing von der Leyen’s Commission to take greater control of foreign policy.
Kajsa Ollongren, who has been touring EU capitals to discuss reform proposals with national governments, making a statement during a meeting of NATO defense ministers in Brussels in June 2024. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
The EEAS currently straddles the Council and the Commission: Kallas works with national governments in the Council, where foreign policy decisions are made, while the service coordinates with the Commission on its external-facing work.
Kallas signaled her concern about the plans on Wednesday, saying a “majority” of EU foreign ministers had opposed the institutional change.
The letter opens the door to the selective use of qualified majority voting for foreign and security policy decisions. Currently, any decision on topics under those headings requires unanimous backing — leading to major bottlenecks under former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who opposed the bloc’s support for Ukraine.
While agreeing with the aim of making EU foreign policy faster-moving and better able to protect the bloc’s interests, Kallas argued Wednesday that the solution is to enforce EU treaties and legal texts that, in theory, give her oversight of the Commission’s external-facing policy units without requiring big reforms.
“The problem is not the treaties, the institutional setup,” she said. “The problem is the implementation.”
CORRECTION: A previous version of this article misstated the names of Kajsa Ollongren and Belén Martínez Carbonell.

Relatives of 2 loan scam accused may get Rs 3 crore after 35-year case
NEW DELHI: Relatives of two loan scam accused who died during the 35-year pendency of the criminal case may receive an unexpected windfall of Rs 3 crore, which may swell beyond this sum with compound interest for 15 years.Supreme Court, while acquitting the lone surviving accused in the 1991 loan scam case, discovered that the bank had auctioned the assets of two others for Rs 3.6 crore to satisfy a Rs 50 lakh loan liability but did not return the rest to their legal heirs.The lone survivor was a branch manager, accused of sanctioning loans of Rs 13.5 lakh and Rs 10 lakh but pocketing the amounts.After the registration of an FIR, the bank launched recovery proceedings in 2010. Auctioning the properties of one of the two accused fetched Rs 1.2 crore, from which Rs 16.4 lakh was adjusted towards satisfying the loan amount along with interest. In the recovery proceeding against a second person, the bank realised Rs 2.8 crore from the sale of his assets and adjusted Rs 40 lakh towards the loan liability.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran said, "The loan was availed in the year 1991-1992 and the property was auctioned in the year 2010.
Admittedly, the auction of properties was completed and the entire amounts due to the bank were received. More intriguing is the fact - as coming out from the testimony of the official witnesses - that the amounts received in auction in excess of the appropriation to the loan accounts are still remaining with the bank.
"While granting a clean chit to the lone surviving accused bank official and terming the case a fabricated one, the bench said, "We are surprised that no attempt was made to find the legal heirs and pass on the money."Supreme Court asked the manager of Indian Bank's Anna Nagar Branch to produce records relating to the utilisation of the money received from the auction, and the title deeds of the properties mortgaged against loans. The court said though the criminal case was disposed of, it was posting the matter for further hearing on Oct 5 to ensure that the excess money received from auction reached the legal heirs.

Magbegor in her prime-time era, leading Opals' World Cup charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
21:11:06 UTC
06:11:06 KST

Ezi Magbegor in her prime-time era, will carry Opals' hopes at Women's Basketball World Cup
In short:
The Opals begin their Women's Basketball World Cup campaign in Berlin this weekend, hoping for their first title since 2006.
Australia is ranked third in the world behind the USA and France.
What's next?
The Opals' first game is against Puerto Rico on Friday night AEST.
The Opals have produced a consistent pipeline of global superstars throughout their silverware-packed history, an impressive feat in one of the world's most competitive sports.
In the 2026 incarnation of the Opals, Ezi Magbegor, 27, carries that tag.
After bursting onto the international stage as a highly promising 18-year-old, she is now a defensive linchpin, a leader, and the type of player whose influence will likely dictate how far the Opals go at the Women's Basketball World Cup.
And she is in her prime-time era.
Throwing a fit
Magbegor entered this WNBA season as a hot commodity — becoming the equal highest paid Australian player in the league, and one of the richest female Australian athletes overall.
But an Achilles injury, then broken nose, wiped her out for most of the season, delivering a harsh reality check for the Seattle Storm forward-centre.
"I've been so blessed to not have many injuries at all in my first seven years of my W season," she told ABC Sport.
"You just realise injuries are a part of sport and it's about how you reset your mind and bounce back and prepare for the next thing.
"And so, yes, I was injured, but I just used it as a great opportunity to work on my body and put myself in the best position to be ready."
It also gave her a chance to spend some time on her 'tunnel fits', aka the casual outfits that players wear when arriving at arenas, which have become a core part of the WNBA.
"This year I really wanted to lean into my Nigerian culture and heritage, and my mum's been begging me to wear traditional clothing," she said.
"My favourite was definitely my traditional attire. My parents had bought the material from Nigeria and then one of our friends had sewn it together in Melbourne.
"I worry about being too dressed up sometimes, but my mum's like, yeah, it's not enough, nothing's too dressed up. So, it was really fun to be able to share that with her."
She traded high fashion for a protective face mask when she returned to the court for the Storm in late July, adding to her already intimidating aura as one of the league's best shot blockers.
And while her domestic season has been stunted, she is coming back to full fitness and form just in time for the World Cup, tipping-off in Berlin this weekend.
Opals going big
Magbegor was part of the team that won World Cup silver in 2018, bronze at home in Sydney in 2022, and bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics.
There has been substantial turnover since Paris with the emotional core of the team including Tess Madgen, Lauren Jackson, Cayla George, and Marianna Tolo, all missing.
And with captain and point guard Sami Whitcomb belatedly ruled out of this World Cup, the side's star power now largely shines around Magbegor and Alanna Smith.
"It's expected for me to pass on the cultural values and expectations onto the next group coming up," Magbegor said.
"But for me it's just about leading by example, touching base with my teammates, making sure that I'm being the best professional, best teammate, best person I can be come tournament play, and in the lead up as well.
"I've been in the Opals team and squad for a while now and I want to have an impact for the team in any way I can, whether that's on the floor, off the floor.
"But definitely looking to play my best basketball for the group and hopefully come away with the medal."
Smith, who was last year named WNBA defensive player of the year, had her own injury interrupted start to the season.
Coach Sandy Brondello is confident Magbegor and Smith are recovered and ready to lead Australia's charge in Berlin.
"They can hold themselves with any of the best post players in the world here. And that's what we're going to need from them without putting pressure," Brondello told ABC Sport.
"I've coached [Ezi] since she was 18. And this is her time, back healthy.
"The best is to come to her, but I'm just excited for her to get out, her athleticism, her rim protection. But now she's a three-level scorer, so that's a great asset.
"And Alanna was our best player in Paris, most consistent player over the whole tournament.
"And it's good to see her getting some rhythm now and getting that confidence back because we need them. We have to lean into them. They're our two best bigs."
Chasing the elusive gold
The Opals enter the World Cup ranked third. The Olympic bronze was followed by a breakthrough Asia Cup win last year, without any WNBA players, and they had a limited preparation for this tournament.
"The results that we've had, it shows that the continuity that we've developed over many years, not just one year, is showing because our chemistry is strong, our culture is strong," Brondello said.
"Everyone's accepting their roles and coming in and playing at a high level. And that's the beauty of Australian teams that we have."
Culture is always the constant with the Opals and what they attribute their sustained performance over decades to.
"It really just comes down our sisterhood and how gritty and tough we are and how we play together and we'll play whatever role to help us to have great success," Brondello said.
"These players, they've become family.
"Playing at the highest level just means everyone has to buy into the values for the success of the program. And there's no one player bigger than the program."
While the Opals are perennial podium finishers at major tournaments, gold has eluded them since their one and only world title in 2006.
"It's just something that comes with being an Opal, that legacy piece and recognising and acknowledging who put us in this position and who started that legacy," Magbegor said.
"Medals is quite synonymous with Opals, and we've won in the past and want to continue to win."
As had been the case for decades, the world number one USA is a seemingly immovable object from the top step of the podium, although was pushed all the way by France in the gold medal match at the Paris Olympics.
"[The USA are] the best of the best and they're great, but they've got the best talent," Brondello said.
"But we've got a talented group, we've built some more chemistry over the years, and that's what we have to lean into."
Growing the game
Half the Opals squad plays in the WNBA, the rest are in the local WNBL, and both leagues have experienced significant changes in the past year.
After drawn out, often bitter negotiations, the WNBA and players' association finally signed a new collective bargaining agreement which saw player salaries skyrocket.
Magbegor went from earning $US186,000 ($260,000) a year to $US1.25 million, a figure matched by Smith at the Dallas Wings, and significantly larger than the base salaries of other leading Australian female athletes in team sports, including the top Matildas and cricketers.
"I think that's just a testament to people that came before us and really pushing for the growth of women's basketball in particular, but just women's sports in general," Magbegor said.
"And I think now is a greater time than ever to push forward, invest in women's sports and just advocate for ourselves, but each other as well."
The WNBL has been making its own moves on a much smaller scale, including a new ownership group taking over last year.
And after starting her career there, Magbegor hopes it too can thrive.
"That's what is probably lacking right now, exposure, and knowing that it's going to pay off in the long run," she said.
"People need to see the product and see the game and realise that women's basketball, basketball is incredible.
"We have great athletes, especially coming up, and I think it's just a matter of investing, a matter of showing up and a matter of supporting."

KYIV -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for "accountability" and "personnel decisions" after a shoot-out in Kyiv involving the country's major security services.
In his daily evening video address, Zelenskyy said the incident took place between Ukraine's Security Service, known as the SBU, and the country's military intelligence agency, the HUR, calling it "absolutely disgraceful."
"The only people anyone should be shooting at are the Russian occupiers, in defense of Ukraine," he added. "No other exchange of gunfire will ever be treated by our state as something anyone is permitted to engage in."
Gunfire woke residents in Kyiv's Bereznyaky district early on September 2, with witnesses saying they saw wounded people and traces of blood at the scene of the incident.
Shortly after the stand-off had ended, conflicting reports of what had happened emerged.
The SBU issued two contradictory statements: first, saying it was working alongside the HUR to avert a Russian "terrorist attack," and then, saying it had resisted a "group of individuals" who had tried to block a search effort.
In a later comment to RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service, a commander of HUR's "Tymur" special forces unit said the SBU agents were "detaining HUR personnel and opening fire without warning" at them.
The Russian Volunteer Corps
The shoot-out appears to be connected to earlier reports concerning the arrest of Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, a Ukrainian-backed paramilitary group affiliated with the HUR.
Taras Borovskiy, Kaplunov's lawyer, told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service his client was "abducted" on August 23 and that his whereabouts remained unknown until September 1. He added the SBU had not responded to his requests for comment.
From here, the details of the story get even murkier.
According to Borovskiy, overnight on September 2, the SBU brought Kaplunov to his apartment to conduct a search. But HUR representatives and his friends were already present there.
The HUR commander said he reached an agreement with the SBU unit commander but "other SBU personnel" then opened fire.
Separately, Denis Nikitin, the commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps, told RFE/RL the SBU did not find anything compromising in Kaplunov's apartment.
Later, Zelenskyy said prosecutors would investigate the incident.
