Jason Ballard Is Using 3D Printing to Take on America’s Housing Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:35 UTC
22:30:35 KST

Jason Ballard understands first-hand the fear of losing a home to disaster. Growing up on the Gulf Coast, he watched hurricanes level his town again and again. “My family has spent Christmas in FEMA trailers,” he tells TIME. “The global housing crisis isn’t a statistic to me. It’s something I've experienced in my own life and in the lives of my neighbors and the people I love.”
Today, nearly 750,000 people are experiencing homelessness in the U.S. This crisis is compounded by worker shortages and supply chain volatility in the construction industry. After working at a homeless shelter in Boulder, Colo., Ballard became convinced that the way America builds homes needed a fundamental rethink.
In 2017, he co-founded ICON, a construction company that uses large-scale 3D printers to erect buildings by layering a proprietary concrete-like material. As of this year, the Austin-based company has 3D-printed 260 houses and other structures. It says its construction system can print a 2,500-square-foot home in under seven days, while cutting construction waste, lowering building costs, and producing walls that can withstand fires, hurricanes, and other natural disasters.
“Construction has always been about showing up with saws and nail guns and tape measures,” Ballard says. “In the future, builders will show up with tablets and advanced materials and robots.”
Ballard has been waiting for lenders to catch on, but there were concerns that 3D-printed homes would not appreciate in value as quickly as traditional houses. Then, in May, Wells Fargo announced that it would write mortgages on ICON's 3D-printed houses and give buyers a credit for choosing one. The lender believes the technology has the potential to bring down construction costs and building time.
ICON recently started taking reservations for its Titan printer—which, unlike earlier models, can print multistory buildings—at about $899,000, with deliveries expected in 2027. For the first time ever, the company had more orders than it could fulfill this year. “For eight years we fought so hard for every project, so it felt strange to have to pass on some,” he says. “But the demand convinces me this approach is going to become part of humanity’s toolkit.”
Ballard is starry-eyed for sure, with big visions for the future. He can barely contain his excitement when describing ICON’s work with NASA to develop concepts using 3D printing to build structures on the Moon from lunar materials. “The story of exploration is you have to learn to live off the land,” he says. “I don’t think the Moon is going to be the exception.”
He’s also deeply down-to-earth. Speaking with a slight Southern drawl and the fervor of a preacher, he explains how his grandfather, "Papaw," a poor, uneducated refinery worker, taught him the romance and dignity of working with your hands. “I ride horses and build robots,” Ballard says. “I don’t think of myself as a cowboy or a tech guy, but as someone who follows his heart.”

Tammy Eagle Bull Is Weaving Indigenous Design Into Modern Architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:34 UTC
22:30:34 KST

As extreme weather intensifies and America’s housing crisis deepens, it’s becoming clear that the conventional ways in which we build new structures are no longer working. In response, some architects are starting to place greater weight on weaving resiliency, cultural literacy, and a deep understanding of the natural environment into their work.
Tammy Eagle Bull has been advocating for these practices for decades. As the first Indigenous woman licensed to practice architecture in the United States, she has spent her career incorporating the historical and cultural knowledge of Indigenous tribes into her work. For many years that has meant designing for tribal communities, like the Porcupine School on South Dakota's Pine Ridge Reservation, which was the state's first LEED Silver-certified school, or the Oglala Lakota Artspace, which was designed around the Lakota belief that stars are connected to "sacred histories, stories, and knowledge." Still, she knew these approaches weren’t only relevant to tribal projects. "There's an [Indigenous] philosophy and methodology and pedagogy that is very applicable to everything that architects and designers do," Eagle Bull tells TIME.
Where conventional architectural practices are often guided by technical factors like zoning, Eagle Bull takes a different approach. "I like to go further back into the deep temporality of the site,” she says. “What was it originally? Who lived here? How did they live?"
She says this is especially important when thinking about extreme heat in a place like Phoenix, which had a record 113 consecutive days of 100-plus degree temperatures in 2024. "People are like, 'This is so inhospitable. It's too hot. People can't thrive here,'" she says. "[But] people did. They had thriving cities, they had agriculture, and they were able to sustain life. And so, if we look back, we can see that living in modern day Phoenix shouldn't be such a struggle. There were strategies that were employed to manage water and to manage heat."
These design principles are at the root of many modern models, says Eagle Bull, such as the “Passive House” concept, in which the built environment is crafted to work with things like weather systems and wind flows, and “life-centered design,” which takes local ecology and circularity into consideration. "The heart of all that is really what Indigenous design has been practicing for millennia," she says.
As a professor of practice at Arizona State University’s Design School, Eagle Bull is helping educate the next generation of architects in these design principles. For example, some of her students recently imagined solutions for unhoused Indigenous populations in Phoenix, focusing on how shelters might be deployed quickly and safely while still centering Native culture and practices. One idea floated was co-housing, which isn't typically embraced in shelters, where men and women tend to be separated. But Eagle Bull argues these kinds of approaches have their place. "There are a lot of times where it's an extended family, maybe the son's taking care of the mother or the grandmother," she explains. "So the idea is being flexible, employing different strategies and ideas in a balance that can work best for whatever situation."
In 2025, Eagle Bull became the director of a new Master's program at ASU. The M.S. in Indigenous Placekeeping and Design was founded by Wanda Dalla Costa, the first First Nations woman to be a licensed architect in Canada and a leading figure in Indigenous design in North America. It is one of only a handful of degree programs in the U.S. that focuses on both the history and practical application of Indigenous design. "There are a lot of things that we can learn from [Indigenous] cultural practices," Eagle Bull says. "They can help us not only manage the ecology and environment, but also how people exist with each other and thrive and create places that support who they are and support their community."

Free Solo’s Alex Honnold Is an Unexpected Solar Power Champion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:30:34 UTC
22:30:34 KST

Most people probably know Alex Honnold from the 2018 documentary Free Solo, which captured his historic climb on Yosemite's El Capitan without a rope or protective harness. Over his nearly two-decade rock climbing career, he has free-summited landmarks around the world, most recently a 101-story skyscraper in Taiwan. 
But fewer people likely know about Honnold’s other great passion: solar power. He started the Honnold Foundation in 2012 with the goal of giving away one-third of his income to community solar projects. In the years since, HF has grown into a 501(c)(3) with an executive director, full-time staff, and over $11 million committed to 75 solar projects in 2026 alone. Today, Honnold funds the operational costs, so outside donations can largely go to projects in need.
The idea sprouted from Honnold’s desire to offset his own travel emissions. But he knew that in order to gain traction and funding, his sustainability efforts would need wider impact. “Nobody cares about the environment unless their basic needs are met," he says. "So if you're trying to protect the environment in a broad sense without protecting or improving the lives of human populations, you're facing an uphill battle."
Today, at least 600 million people live without access to electricity. Solar power could hugely improve their lives, with the added benefit of reducing the global reliance on fossil fuels. HF focuses on solar projects that sit at the intersection of climate, equity, and human impact, with grant recipients typically receiving between $50,000 and $150,000. More than 1,200 organizations applied in 2026—a far cry from Honnold's early days of researching and funding projects on his own. Recent recipients include the Cambodian Center for Human Rights, which will install solar lighting and power to protect against illegal fishing and mangrove destruction; Integrated Health Outreach in Antigua and Barbuda, which will power a female-led beekeeping and honey-processing facility; and the Hopi Utilities Corporation in Arizona, which will install solar panels and battery storage on tribal land to power groundwater pumps.
One oft-cited recipient of an HF grant is Kara Solar, which provides solar-powered boats to the Achuar people in Ecuador and Peru. The partnership, which began in 2020, has helped facilitate commerce, health care, and education in the region, while also reducing reliance on gasoline. Kara Solar recently received a large grant from a global foundation, which built on earlier success: In 2024, thanks in part to HF’s support, it created a for-profit manufacturing company to produce electric motors for its boats.
"That's the ultimate success for a project if it takes off beyond the philanthropic money," Honnold says. "And then the real success will be in 20 years if everyone's riding an electric boat."
Honnold believes the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable. And while the foundation doesn't fund policy work, he says some projects have exposed the need for solar incentives in states with policies that limited rooftop solar. "I personally like funding projects in states that are really regressive, anti-solar states," he says. "Because it's like a big middle finger to the man. I think there's a little of the anti-authority, rock climbing streak.”

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on a visit to Kiln Park Holiday Centre to highlight the Great British Summer Savings campaign on August 27, 2026 in Tenby. | Matthew Horwood/Getty Images
LONDON — Britain’s new top finance minister plans to give his first major speech in the role next week, which is expected to focus on boosting Britain’s ailing economic growth.
Chancellor John Healey intends to give the address on Sept. 7, said four people with knowledge of the date who were granted anonymity to discuss internal planning, following weeks of preparation since Prime Minister Andy Burnham gave him the role in July. Officials are looking at staging it at a manufacturing plant outside London.
The Treasury declined to comment.
Advertisement
Burnham revealed in mid-August that Healey was working on a speech on the government’s economic agenda. The date of next Monday was first reported by Politics at Sam and Anne’s, the morning briefing podcast by POLITICO and Sky News.
The speech will focus heavily on growth, said two of the people quoted above — weeks after Burnham moved responsibility for local economic growth strategy from the Treasury to his new prime ministerial office in Manchester, No. 10 North.
One of the four people cited at the start of this story said the speech is likely to focus less on individual spending policies ahead of the Oct. 28 budget and more on a broader vision and initiatives, including Burnham’s promises to hand more economic levers to regional leaders.
“This isn’t a rushed job — it’s a serious bit of thinking,” they added. Another of the four people said: “It’s the government’s version of their theory of growth.”
A government official, who is not one of the four individuals cited above, said the speech has involved work by multiple government departments contributing potential ideas. “It’s crossed a lot of people’s radar,” they added.
Some in Westminster may see the speech as Healey seeking to emphasize his own role.
Advertisement
A Treasury official, also not one of the cited individuals, said growth would be a dual mission for both the prime minister’s and chancellor’s offices. They added the Treasury would drive growth policy across Whitehall, that every department would have a focus on growth and Burnham’s pledge of “good growth in every postcode” would take the whole government working as one to achieve.
Burnham told MPs on Tuesday that he believed growth had to be “driven with the full authority of the very center of government, in close partnership with the Treasury.” Louise Haigh, his first secretary who has previously described the Treasury as “imperial,” joked about the change of responsibilities Wednesday: “It's a little bit of a chip on its empire.”
Britain’s GDP grew by 0.4 percent in the three months to June, while rising bond yields have left Healey with the highest cost of servicing government debt for decades. Both squeeze his ability to intervene in key industries. Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the budget.
One banking lobbyist briefed separately on the event said Healey’s speech could be “shaped by market movements” seen this week, with the finance minister likely using it to calm bond traders with a pro-growth but policy-lite approach.
The speech is also likely to touch on Burnham’s promises to “reindustrialize” Britain, given the continuing focus on the defense industry. Healey is under pressure to pledge that Britain’s military spending will reach 3 percent of GDP by 2030, as he demanded when he resigned as the U.K.’s defense minister earlier this year. He has said he will not name a date for hitting 3 percent until next year.

In the light of the August 26 glacier collapse, how does China view the glacier retreat crisis impacting the Himalayan region and the calls for formation of a coordination mechanism by China with neighbouring countries, to strengthen cooperation to deal with such disasters affecting the fragile region?
Guo Jiakun: China has responded to similar questions. According to the assessment of Chinese and Nepali experts, long-term effects of global warming have made glaciers unstable, and this disaster was triggered by the collapse of a glacier in Nepal, resulting in a rapid crash of ice and rocks which took away a chunk of the mountain. The Xizang Autonomous Region shared relevant information at its press conference.
China and Nepal have maintained sound cooperation in meteorology, water conservancy and disaster prevention and reduction. In the wake of the disaster, China has shared with Nepal important information such as images, satellite, and hydrological data of the disaster-affected areas, including early-warning information on an upstream barrier lake. We will continue to give strong support to Nepal in its relief efforts and strengthen cooperation on disaster prevention and reduction.
Climate change is a common challenge facing all humanity. No country can stay immune from such risks. China will continue to work with the international community to strengthen exchanges and cooperation and effectively prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change. As for your specific question, I’d refer you to competent authorities.
AFP: I wonder if China has been told if any Chinese citizens were among the dead in Nepal from the disaster last week? And also are you able to provide a specific figure on the number of Chinese nationals missing in China?
Guo Jiakun: I just shared the information we have. As we speak, intensive rescue and relief operations are still underway. For the specific information you asked for, there will be continued updates.

Israel ready to 'remove Gaza population if US gives approval', boasts defence minister
Israel has plans ready to forcibly remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip but is waiting for the United States to figure out where to take them, the defence minister boasted on Wednesday.
Forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.
"There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration," Defence Minister Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
The Israeli government "is organised and prepared to get them out—by sea, by air, by every way possible", he said.
The US embassy referred requests for comment to the State Department in Washington.
US President Donald Trump, at the start of his second term, stunned much of the world by publicly calling for all two million Palestinians to leave the Gaza Strip.
Trump claimed of developing the Mediterranean territory, devastated by Israeli bombardment since the October 2023, into a luxury resort destination.
Trump walked back the idea following strong pushback including from Egypt, the only country other than Israel to neighbour Gaza.
The proposal was also condemned by Palestinians themselves, for whom any effort to force them off their land represents how the "Nakba", or catastrophe; their forced mass displacement by Zionist forces in 1948, is ongoing.
Announcing a supposed ceasefire in October, Trump laid out 20 points for the territory that included no forced displacement.
Katz, known for his xenophobic and horrific remarks, said that Trump had only "frozen" the idea as he looks for countries to take in Palestinians, as Egypt is not an option.
"The plan hasn't been cancelled; it is being discussed all the time, even now, and I think there is no other solution for everyone's good," he said.
"But for it to happen, we need the US. When will we get their approval? Whenever it becomes clear that Hamas is not meeting its obligations" under the ceasefire, he said.
Katz, without citing his source, said 80 percent of people in Gaza wanted to leave but that Hamas was preventing them.
The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Katz's predecessor Yoav Gallant over war crimes.
Israeli attacks have already internally displaced the vast majority of Gaza's people since October 2023.
Israel's genocidal war has since killing 73,470 in Gaza, with more than 1,400 since the alleged ceasefire.

X's new payments app X Money hit by mass hacking attempt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:17:46 UTC
22:17:46 KST

Unsolicited password reset emails have hit X users after the launch of X Money, with the platform warning that hackers could be behind a wider phishing attempt.
X has revealed that hackers could be trying to attack users after the launch of X Money.
This follows several X users receiving surprise password reset emails. Although the social media giant has been looking into the issue, there is no evidence so far that these attack attempts were successful.
It is believed that attackers could be mass-triggering the form for password resets using public usernames
X Money, the platform's payments service, launched on an invite-only basis in July before expanding to all Premium and Premium+ subscribers on 31 August.
It allows users to hold money, make and receive payments, as well as carry out peer-to-peer transfers, all on the X platform.
As such, any access that attackers may get to these users' accounts could have significant financial implications.
The company's general counsel, James Burnham, highlighted that "the legal and security teams @X will stop at nothing to identify, locate, and hold criminally accountable any person anywhere on or off earth who attempts to victimize our platform's users."
This has led to a flood of users taking to the platform to both spread awareness that this is happening and also remind others to use two-factor authentication, if they aren't already, for an added layer of protection.
The social media platform's Grok chatbot has also chimed in, replying to some posts with practical measures users can take to do so.
Could this be hiding a more dangerous phishing attack?
Although receiving an email for a supposed password change request doesn't automatically mean your account has been breached, especially if you have multi-factor authentication, some users are concerned that this latest incident could be hiding a wider phishing attempt.
Several users have also claimed that follow-up phishing emails have been sent out, along with these password reset confirmation emails. These have been framed as legitimate emails coming from X, which has added to the confusion and fear.
These emails have been urging users to change their passwords, which is an expected follow-up after a security breach. However, they include a fake X link for users to do so, which can trick them into providing their login credentials to attackers.
As such, this is more likely to be an elaborate multi-step hacking and phishing attempt than previously expected.
X Money has already faced scrutiny for its reliance on partner banks like Cross River Bank, due to past regulatory enforcement actions against the bank, as well as the underlying reasoning behind the promotional 6% yield on deposits, compared to federal benchmarks.

====================================================================================================

Hope, Dopamine and whatever 'Perfecth' means: Euronews Culture’s Fall music preview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:16:46 UTC
22:16:46 KST

Hope, Dopamine and whatever 'Perfecth' means: Euronews Culture’s Fall music preview
Euronews Culture looks ahead to the last four months of 2026 and picks the hotly anticipated albums you won’t want to miss.
It’s been a very solid year so far in terms of new album releases, with neo-soul goodnessfrom Jill Scott, intoxicating hip-hopfrom Irish trio Kneecap, Olivia Rodrigo’sbed-bouncing pop, and Phoebe Bridgers delivering the best album of her career so far – to name but a few.
And 2026 isn't over yet...
Now that we’ve given you our massive Fall movie preview, highlighting the films that should get you rushing to the cinema, it’s time to look ahead to the crowded release schedule when it comes to music.
We've handpicked 15 hotly anticipated records you won’t want to miss before the year ends.
Ezra Collective – Here Because Of Hope
Release date: 18 September
The MOBO and Mercury Prize-winning British jazz-afrobeat-soul quintet follow up their excellent 2024 album 'Dance, No One’s Watching' with their much anticipated fourth LP. Having become the first jazz band to win Group of the Year at the Brit Awards last year, Ezra Collective are hoping to impress their fans once again with their “most ambitious and personal record of their career”. According to a press statement, 'Here Because Of Hope' is split into “three spiritual and geographical movements” as the album aims to trace the movement of Black people across continents and decades - “from the music of Africa to the rhythms of the Caribbean, and home to the streets of London”. We can’t wait.
Beck – Ride Lonesome
Release date: 18 September
Following his 2015 Grammy Album of the Year ‘Morning Phase’, Beck’s output has been a smidge disappointing. 2017’s 'Colors' was an underwhelming 80s-indebted effort, while 2019’s 'Hyperspace' worked as a synth-pop collaboration experiment but lacked the complexity of his past efforts. Here’s hoping this year fares better... We’ve already had his Valentine’s Day-themed compilation album ‘Everybody’s Gotta Learn Sometime’ - which was delightful – and his 15th studio album ‘Ride Lonesome’ is about to drop. Already released singles – the country-coded ‘Ride Lonesome’ and the gentle ‘Disappearing Act’ - have a ‘Sea Change’ / ‘Morning Phase’ melancholia to them. Add the fact that Nigel Godrich is back on mixing duties, and this could be a return to form.
Tove Lo – Estrus
Release date: 18 September
Swedish pop star Tove Lo has explained that the title of her sixth album refers to an animal in heat. “It’s primal, contradicting emotional chaos. It’s my mind and my body wanting different things, wanting everything,” the ‘Talking Body’ singer said, adding: “There’s no good advice on this album... just a lot of feelings, no solutions.” That last part happens to be the title of the opening track of ‘Estrus’, which is followed by lead single ‘I’m Your Girl Right?’ - a propulsive dance track that will hopefully be playing on heavy rotation in clubs around the world. We’re looking forward to the rest, as Tove Lo’s capacity to deliver euphoric sultry banger after euphoric sultry banger continues to impress. And be bafflingly underrated.
Agnes Obel - The Meaning Of Flowers
Release date: 18 September
A lot of albums coming out on the 18th... But one that has us giddy with excitement is Agnes Obel’s fifth album ‘The Meaning Of Flowers’ - her first since 2020. We’ve been fans of the Danish singer-songwriter here at Euronews Culture for a while now - even including her 2016 album ‘Citizen Of Glass’ in our list of the Best European Albums of the 21st Century. Her immersive chamber-pop never fails to captivate, and judging by her textured new single ‘Laymelli’, we’re in for an atmospheric treat with her latest – one reportedly inspired by themes of maternity and metamorphosis, as well as the ideas of philosophers Hannah Arendt and Emanuele Coccia. Listen to ‘Laymelli’ and try telling us you’re not already entranced.
M83 – I Wrote You A Letter
Release date: 25 September
Is this the year French outfit M83 remind the electro scene they’ve still got it? Here’s hoping... Anthony Gonzalez’s 10th studio album follows a string of disappointing releases, including the aptly named 'Junk' (2016), the very average 'DSVII' (2019), and slightly course-correcting but hardly exhilarating ‘Fantasy’ (2023). In fact, it’s no stretch to say that M83 haven’t had a fully energising release since 2011’s ‘Hurry Up, We’re Dreaming’, and many fans still miss the glory days of the early 2000s with the back-to-back triumphs of ‘Dead Cities, Red Seas & Lost Ghosts’ and ‘Before The Dawn Heals Us’. Fingers crossed that the titular letter brings good news.
Soft Cell – Danceteria
Release date: 25 September
Legendary British synth-pop duo Soft Cell are about to release their swansong, following the death of co-founder Dave Ball last year. The band’s sixth and final studio album, ‘Danceteria’, was completed before Ball’s death and will hopefully serve as a fitting tribute. “There can be no more recordings of Soft Cell without Dave, it would not be possible,” said singer Marc Almond. “The sad reality is that Dave Ball was half of Soft Cell, and live work aside, I can't write Soft Cell songs without him." Considering the title and the already released singles, it’s fair to say that this album will channel the spirit of the 80s New York club scene – much like Madonna’s latest record.
The Avalanches – No Bad Memories
Release date: 16 October
Fans of plunderphonic geniuses The Avalanches had to wait 16 long years after the seminal ‘Since I Left You’ for a decent follow-up album. 'Wildflower' (2016) was a playful and welcome return, but didn’t strike the same winning chord; and you’d be forgiven for not knowing a third album followed, as 2020’s slightly underrated ‘We Will Always Love You’ didn’t make too much of a splash. Billed as “an ambivalent ode to the nostalgic pull of commercial jingles, proprietary start-up sounds, and long-forgotten audio logos,” the Australian band’s fourth album will hopefully right that wrong. It features the likes of Karen O, Jamie xx, Jessy Lanza and Nikki Nair, and spans a whopping 31 tracks. So they’re not messing about.
Eels – Cookie Happened
Release date: 16 October
For more than a decade, like clockwork, we get a new Eels album every two years. And like some of previously mentioned artists on this list, Mark Oliver “E” Everett needs a proper comeback this year, as he hasn’t had the greatest of runs of late. ‘The Deconstruction’ (2018) fell short compared to previous discography standouts; ‘Earth To Dora’ (2020) was too far familiar for comfort; ‘Extreme Witchcraft’ (2022) was a dreary affair; and ‘Eels Time!’ (2024) barely registered. We’re rooting for E, as he’s given us some of the greatest storytelling gems over the years, and ‘Cookie Happened’ could very well be a return to past form. Already on the plus side: the Sesame Street character Cookie Monster is an influence on the album. That, and the cover’s all kinds of fun.
Rachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too Soon
Release date: 16 October
English singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri follows her critically acclaimed alt-indie pop debut album ‘What A Devastating Turn Of Events’ (2024) with ‘I Think I Spoke Too Soon’. Her sophomore effort features collaborators like Mary Weitz and Lucy Dacus, and the first cut ‘One Song Away From Crying’ suggests she’s moving away from the guitars and embracing synths a bit more. The song explores that all-too-familiar moment on the dancefloor when you’ve “never looked better” but “never felt worse”. It sounds fantastic so far, and it’s worth noting that Chinouriri is currently touring Europe, with September dates in Dublin, London, Brussels, Paris and Berlin. If you can get your hands on a ticket, consider yourself very lucky indeed.
Fontaines D.C. – Dopamine Chamber
Release date: 16 October
Talk about a busy day in October for new releases... and this one is hands down our most anticipated of the lot. Every single Fontaines D.C. album release has marked leaps and bounds in terms of songwriting and sound evolution. They’ve been going from strength to strength ever since their 2019 debut ‘Dogrel’ and 2024’s ‘Romance’ felt like a consecration. There’s no suggestion that the Irish indie heroes won’t continue their winning streak with fifth LP, ‘Dopamine Chamber’, which should once again cement their status as the most consistently exciting band around. They’ve already premiered new tracks ‘Marianne’ and ‘Six Shot Morning’ live. Spoiler: they’re both brilliant, sounding Depeche Mode-ish and very synth noir. Let’s hope the rest of the album tracklist will stimulate the reward system in the same way.
Editors – Surface, Echo & Sound
Release date: 30 October
Sounding similar to Foo Fighters’ ‘Echoes, Silence, Patience & Grace’, the title of Editors’ eighth studio album could signal a return to a rawer and rockier sound. Following the disappointing new wave / indietronica ‘EBM’ in 2022, the band apparently wanted to come back to a more natural approach with regards to songwriting and recording, harking back to their early days. Music to our ears, and fans will doubtlessly be delighted if ‘Surface, Echo & Sound’ recalls the sound of their pretty much flawless original album run, with ‘The Back Room’, ‘An End Has A Start’ and ‘In This Light And On This Evening’ having made them one of the rare British bands to escape the dreaded Indie Landfill era of the 2000s.
Queens of the Stone Age – Perfecth
Release date: 30 October
"Nothing in this world is perfect, but everything seems to be 'perfecth'," according to Queens of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme. "And that title is funny when you're in a group, but it ain't so funny when you're alone." Prefaced by the songs ‘Easy Street’ and ‘Insignificant Other’, QOTSA’s ninth studio album promises to be a nine-track rock opus dealing with “family, friends, and others both significant and insignificant”. So far, it sounds like a departure from the band’s heavier sound, with the acoustic ballad ‘Easy Street’ still maintaining some of their trademark humour but showcasing a much gentler side, while ‘Insignificant Other’ features a sleazy groove but couldn’t be more different from the sledgehammer blows of past glories found on ‘Songs For The Deaf’ and ‘...Like Clockwork’.
La Roux - Old Flames
Release date: 6 November
We haven’t had a new release from the British synth-pop act formed by singer Elly Jackson since 2020. That third album, ‘Supervision’, was a frustrating follow-up to her charting debut ‘La Roux’ (2009) and ‘Trouble In Paradise’ (2014). The ‘In For The Kill’ and ‘Bulletproof’ singer will hopefully wow fans once again, with a new album in which she addresses the collapse of a relationship and tackles themes of forbidden love and the loneliness that comes from addiction. The first album teaser, the R&B-tinged earworm ‘Cabin Fever’, is excellent and there’s every chance La Roux’s upcoming LP will be the late-year pop surprise we’ve been waiting for.
Los Bitchos – Los Bitchos & Friends Vol. 1
Release date: 13 November
Pan-continental instrumental group Los Bitchos have already given us two stellar albums (‘Let The Festivities Begin’ and ‘Talkie Talkie’), which have led them to open for various acts like Belle & Sebastian, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, Parquet Courts and Wet Leg. Now, the trio consisting of guitarist Serra Petale, bassist Josefine Jonsson, and drummer Nic Crawshaw, will continue their rave-reviewed blend of Cumbia, rock-pop and Latin American rhythms in their third long-form project. But there's news: they're welcoming vocal collaborators. Gasp! (Although the title was a bit of a giveaway.) For a band who’ve never seen vocals as a necessity, this new direction could add a new dimension to their work, with King Gizzard’s Ambrose Kenny-Smith, Black Pumas’ Adrian Quesada and Kit Sebastian all lending their voices. November seems like a long way away considering how promising this sounds...
Labi Siffre – Unfinished Business
Release date: TBD
As we noted in our selection of the Most Underrated Albums, there’s been renewed interest in Labi Siffre’s music, chiefly due to some of his songs appearing in films like The Holdovers and Sentimental Value. With the British poet and folk musician’s 1972 album ‘Crying Laughing Loving Lying’ gradually becoming recognised as the masterpiece it is, 2026 brought some surprising news: the 80-year-old artist is returning with a new album appropriately titled ‘Unfinished Business’. It will be his first LP in 28 years and we’ve already had a taster with the gorgeous piano ballad ‘Far Away’. This is one comeback you won’t want to miss, and we’re waiting (somewhat impatiently) for a release date. In the meantime, we’ll be listening to ‘Crying Laughing Loving Lying’ all over again, as well as his last record to date, the 1998 spoken-word poetry collection ‘Monument’, which is also well worth your time.
There we have it. Which albums are you most looking forward to? For up-to-date music news and reviews, head to Euronews Culture's Music section, and be sure to check out our picks for the Best Albums of 2026... So Far.

Germany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
13:15:48 UTC
22:15:48 KST

Germany investigates suspected power substation sabotage, Russia summons German envoy
Two incidents that disrupted power distribution systems in Germany are being investigated for sabotage, authorities said Wednesday, while one of them was also being examined for possible terrorism links. Meanwhile Russia said it was summoning Germany's charge d'affaires after Berlin blamed Moscow for last month's attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.
German authorities on Wednesday were investigating two attacks on electricity substations in different parts of the country, the latest suspected sabotage targeting critical infrastructure.
Police launched a terrorism probe over the first incident, which saw improvised explosives fired early Tuesday at a site in eastern Brandenburg state, damaging power cables.
In the second sabotage attack, unknown perpetrators allegedly caused a deliberate short-circuit by targeting overhead power lines at a substation in Bergheim in North Rhine-Westphalia state.
North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said officials were probing whether the attack was directed by a "foreign state" or left-wing extremism.
Neither attack caused widespread power outages, although operations at nearby coal-fired power stations were affected.
Germany has faced repeated attacks on electricity infrastructure, with far-left militants claiming responsibility in some cases.
Berlin, a key supporter of Ukraine in its fight against Russia, is also on alert for Moscow-backed sabotage plots.
"More sabotage, more hybrid attacks – interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference.
"And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country."
The attacks came the same day that Germany formally blamed Russia for an attempted "hybrid attack" involving an explosive-laden drone at a strategic airport in Leipzig last month and announced diplomatic counter-measures.
Read moreGermany blames Russia for Leipzig airport drone attack, orders Russian consulate closed
Russia summons German envoy over 'anti-Russian actions'
Russia on Wednesday said it was summoning Germany's charge d'affaires to protest what it called "anti-Russian actions", after Berlin announced sanctions on Moscow over an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport.
Germany announced counter-measures on Tuesday, saying it would shut Russia's consolate in the western German city of Bonn and cancel a contract for a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.
Russia has described Germany's allegations as unsubstantiated and "absurd".
"On September 2, Germany's charge d'affaires in Moscow... was summoned to the Russian foreign ministry amid yesterday's anti-Russian actions and statements by the German authorities," said Russia's foreign ministry.
Meanwhile German authorities have identified two suspects in connection with an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport but will unlikely be able to detain them, German daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Wednesday.
The newspaper, which collaborated on the report with broadcasters Norddeutscher Rundfunk (NDR) and Westdeutscher Rundfunk Köln (WDR), said that investigations into the two men, one a Russian-born Latvian national and the other a Russian national from Belarus, underpinned allegations by the German government that Russia was behind the incident.
Latest infrastructure attack
In the Bergheim incident, police were called to the substation late Tuesday. Perpetrators are suspected of causing a short-circuit in overhead power lines by placing "conductive material" on them, according to officials.
Energy company RWE said five power-generating units at two of its coal-fired plants in the region were knocked out by the disruption at the substation, although there was no widespread disruption for customers.
Three of the units were expected to go back online later Wednesday while the two others should be restarted at the weekend.
The earlier attack in Brandenburg saw improvised explosives – which resembled large fireworks – fired at a substation in Preilack, causing damage to power cables and a brief supply disruption.
The substation distributes power from the nearby Jaenschwalde plant.
Police announced Wednesday they had launched a terror probe into that incident. They are also investigating the attack on suspicion of disrupting public services and destroying essential equipment, according to a statement.
Reul said authorities were trying to figure out if there was a link between the two attacks, adding: "We are in close contact with our colleagues in Brandenburg."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

MAPUTO, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese agricultural machinery manufacturer is seeking to expand its presence in Mozambique as companies from central China's Hunan Province explore business opportunities at the 61st Maputo International Trade Fair (FACIM) in the southern African country.
Zoomlion, a Hunan-based heavy equipment manufacturer, brought six machines to the trade fair, most of them targeting the agricultural sector, as the company seeks to make its technology more accessible to Mozambican farmers through local partnerships.
"We are one of the official representatives of Zoomlion in Mozambique, mainly for agricultural machinery," Jacinto Almeida, the company's Mozambican representative, told Xinhua at the exhibition venue. "The idea, in the end, is to bring technology to Mozambique at a competitive price, a price that small producers, communities and large producers can afford."
Almeida said the company's ambition extends beyond equipment sales to supporting broader agricultural mechanization in Mozambique.
"We are here representing Zoomlion, but with the final intention of bringing the business to Mozambique and bringing technology to agriculture in Mozambique," he said, adding that the company intends to work with local farmers and provide a broader package of agricultural solutions.
Zoomlion's participation is part of a broader Hunan business delegation organized by the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT) Hunan Sub-council, bringing about 13 companies to FACIM for the first time.
Amy Zheng, representing CCPIT Hunan, said the participating companies cover sectors including agriculture, medicine and construction, with many showing strong interest in the Mozambican market.
The participation, she added, provides an opportunity to deepen economic and trade ties between China and Mozambique. ■

19 killed in overnight U.S. attacks on Iran as Tehran retaliates across region
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
20:38:41 CST
21:38:41 KST

TEHRAN/KUWAIT CITY, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- At least 19 people, including military personnel and civilians, were killed in overnight U.S. strikes across several provinces in Iran, as the country's armed forces retaliated by attacking U.S. bases and assets in the region, Iranian media reported Wednesday.
The U.S. attacks on Iran's southwestern Khuzestan province killed seven people and wounded eight others, the semi-official Mehr news agency cited Valiollah Hayati, Khuzestan's deputy governor for security and law enforcement affairs, as saying.
The report said U.S. strikes on southern Lavan Island killed three members of the Basij volunteer force of Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), while four members of the IRGC's Aerospace division were killed in strikes on the western province of Kermanshah.
A commando, identified as Malek Mousavi-Tabar, was killed Wednesday morning during operations to counter the movements of an invading drone in Bahmai County in the western Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad province, it added.
It also cited provincial authorities as saying that four people were killed and 68 others wounded in a U.S. attack targeting a wedding ceremony in Sirik County in southern Hormozgan province. The victims included one four-year-old child, a teenager and two women.
In a post on social media platform X earlier in the day, U.S. Central Command said its forces had "successfully completed a wave of strikes against Iranian military targets," citing "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
In retaliation for the U.S. strikes, Iran's IRGC and army announced that they targeted U.S. bases and assets in Jordan, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In statements published on its official news outlet Sepah News, the IRGC said its forces shot down a "hostile" U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone and launched ballistic missiles toward Camp Titin in Jordan, reportedly killing "a large number of" U.S. troops and destroying several key facilities and combat helicopters.
The IRGC said its aerospace forces struck with ballistic missiles the hangars of U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-9 Reaper drones at the Prince Hassan Air Base in Jordan, destroying a number of the aircraft and setting the technical infrastructure facilities on fire.
It noted that its ground forces targeted with drones and missiles the headquarters and accommodation of the U.S. commander at the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, setting on fire a hangar of U.S. drones and a drone deployment ramp and destroying several unmanned aerial vehicles.
Its ground forces also launched a hybrid missile-drone strike on U.S. bases in Erbil, capital of Iraq's Kurdistan region, destroying a maintenance center, technical-equipment warehouses, and a system for guiding espionage balloons, all belonging to the U.S. Army, the IRGC added.
In statements published on its website, Iran's Army said its drone attacks targeted U.S. bases in Bahrain and the UAE.
It said it struck with kamikaze drones U.S. troops and radar facilities at the Shaikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain as well as the Al Minhad and Al Dhafra Air Bases in the UAE.
In a statement carried by Iranian media earlier in the day, Iran's main military command, Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, warned that continued U.S. "malicious" acts in the region would draw "heavier, more extensive and more devastating" responses.
Meanwhile, in a statement on its official X account, the Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the Iranian attacks, calling them a "blatant violation of its sovereignty" and reiterating its full right to take necessary measures to "protect its security and interests." ■

South Africa could see hottest year on record in 2027 amid strong El Nino: weather service
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
20:38:40 CST
21:38:40 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Africa could face its hottest year on record in 2027 amid an intensifying strong El Nino event, the South African Weather Service (SAWS) has said.
In a statement on Tuesday, SAWS said a strong El Nino had formed in the Pacific Ocean and was likely to intensify during the Southern Hemisphere spring.
"The latest predictions are indicative that the El Nino will likely intensify further to become the strongest event in living memory," it said.
The latest weekly averaged sea surface temperature anomalies in the eastern central tropical Pacific Ocean have already exceeded the threshold for a very strong El Nino, SAWS said.
A strong El Nino is defined as sea surface temperatures more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above normal, while a very strong event exceeds 2 degrees.
According to SAWS, current forecasts indicate that the anomaly could surpass 3 degrees Celsius.
"Most El Nino events bring conditions of below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures to the southern African region," SAWS said, while noting that not every El Nino event results in drought.
The weather service's October to December 2026 forecast indicates below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures over most of South Africa, with similar conditions expected from November 2026 to January 2027.
"It should be noted that the expected very strong El Nino of 2026/27, in combination with global warming, will likely result in 2027 being the warmest year ever recorded," it said.
SAWS said the 2015/16 El Nino brought unprecedented heatwaves to southern Africa and warned that, if the expected below-normal rainfall occurs, a high frequency of potentially severe heatwaves could accompany the current event.
The agency said uncertainty remained over the eventual strength and regional impacts of the El Nino and that it would closely monitor risks including heatwaves and water scarcity. ■

Deputy commander of Russian Volunteer Corps claims Ukraine's Security Service tried to discredit head of President's Office using his testimony
Stepan Kaplunov, Deputy Commander for Combat Operations of the Russian Volunteer Corps The Russian Volunteer Corps is a military and political organisation established in 2022 that consists of Russian volunteers who have been fighting for Ukraine since 2014 , has claimed that Ukraine's Security Service (SSU) has attempted to use him to discredit Timur Special Unit deputy commander Dmytro Ivanov and Head of President's Office Kyrylo Budanov.
Source: Kaplunov's video statement published on the Russian Volunteer Corps Telegram channel
Quote: "I, Stepan Kaplunov, was unlawfully abducted by SSU officers on 23 August. According to our information, for the first three days I was personally handled by [acting SSU Head] General [Oleksandr] Poklad. Through physical and psychological pressure, they tried to use me to discredit Dmytro Ivanov, the deputy commander of the Timur Special Unit, and Kyrylo Budanov in order to accuse them of cooperating with the FSB."
Details: He also added that, during his absence, SSU officers allegedly attempted to enter his home and "plant unknown items".
"They came in carrying large sports bags. We have video footage. Our side has contacted the State Bureau of Investigation to look into the situation," Kaplunov said.
Later, the Russian Volunteer Corps (RVC) posted CCTV footage on its Telegram channel showing a group of men wearing hoods and caps and carrying a large bag heading, according to the RVC, towards Kaplunov's apartment. The RVC said the incident took place on 24 August.
Background:
- On 1 September, the Russian Volunteer Corps said that its deputy commander for combat operations, Stepan Kaplunov, had been abducted by unknown individuals in the courtyard of a residential building.
- On the morning of 2 September, reports spread on social media about a shootout said to be between Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) and the Security Service of Ukraine in Kyiv's Dniprovskyi district, and that it was somehow connected to Kaplunov's disappearance.
- Meanwhile, the SSU said in the morning that, together with DIU, it had foiled a terrorist attack against a leader of a Russian opposition political national movement who had arrived in Ukraine.
- Later, Kaplunov's lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, said that the serviceman had been released, but his whereabouts were unknown.
- On the morning of 3 September, the SSU released a video in which Kaplunov admitted to having links to Russia's Federal Security Service and said an attempt had been made to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian military personnel and other individuals. However, his lawyer insists that the confession was made under duress.
- Kaplunov himself said on 3 September that he had been abducted by SSU officers and described how he had been made to confess under duress.
